11454-a-visit-to-the-united-states-in-18:
Joseph Sturge's Visit to the United States in 1841, published in Boston in 1842, records a Quaker abolitionist's American tour, framed by Cowper on liberty as life's flower. General observations lead to appendices on Friends' anti-slavery epistles, early Quaker efforts for Black Americans, the Amistad captives, William Jay on slavery. the opium war with China, Gerrit Smith's slaves, Friends and the Colonization Society, and a Boston memorial to the Admiralty. Sturge traces Friends' noiseless agitation that freed their own slaves before Clarkson's call.

The book links American slavery with wider reform causes, from opium to colonization. Its Quaker perspective is earnest and documentary. For transatlantic historians, it shows British abolitionists inspecting American slavery firsthand.
13639-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
The very first volume of Punch, for the week ending July 17, 1841, introduces the comic weekly to its readers with a statement of aims. The editors insist that their hero, merry Master Punch, is more than a clown for a thoughtless crowd. He is a teacher, and the paper will offer pleasant instruction as well as laughter.

Inside, jokes and sketches mock fashion, politics, and manners, from greasy velvet collars with showy seams to candidates canvassing under different phases, from flattery to scorn. The tone is already confident and satirical. This founding issue marks the start of a paper that would shape English humour for more than a century.
14920-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
A modest method of forming a new budget, so as to provide for the deficiency of revenue, fills Punch for the week ending 24 July 1841. Poor Mr. Dyer was dismissed from the commission of the peace. He had sought, humanely, the release of Medhurst from confinement. He thought two or three thousand pounds given to charity might persuade the Home Secretary to remit the rest of a sentence.

Punch whispers a secret to its reader. Had the Whig ministry not gone mad with election results, it would not have dismissed delectable Dyer. Instead it would have put him on the pension list, to a tune the reader can guess. The joke turns a budget shortfall into a satire on patronage, mercy and ministries that punish kindness while rewarding friends.
14921-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 31 July 1841, from its very first volume, shows the young magazine finding its voice. A letter on poetry on an improved principle begs Mr. Punch to publicise a new invention in the art of poetry, which its discoverer is willing to let others improve.

The writer laments that taste for poetry is on the decline. The public will no longer buy it as a luxury, yet modern poems do a vast deal of service for which they were never designed. Many have found their way into uses far from verse. The joke is early Punch in miniature: polite, mock-earnest and aimed at literary fashion.
14922-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Chapter two of The Wife-Catchers, a legend of my uncle's boots, fills Punch for the week ending 7 August 1841. Its hero is Timothy Thady Mulligin, who whenever he finished his tumbler of punch always wished it full again.

An uncle, eyes full and tumbler empty, mourns venerated family retainers, and his nephew diverts sorrow with the national proverb that a drink is better than a story. The old man's eyes glisten with pleasure as he grasps his nephew's hand, declaring him worthy of his name and unspoiled by school learning and college. The serial is Irish tall talk, told over punch in Punch's first year.
14923-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 14 August 1841 carries chapter three of The Wife Catchers, a legend of my uncle's boots, in four chapters. Its narrator, a boot, explains that haberdashers make the greatest show out of the smallest stock, whether of brains or ribbons, of any men in the world.

A stranger passing through Ballybreesthawn cannot miss a shop at the corner of Market Square and main street, its windows looking both ways for custom. Toys, stationery, perfumery, ribbons, laces, hardware, spectacles and Dutch dolls fill the glass, with patent medicines and Birmingham jewellery in a case on the counter. The serial is tall-tale comedy from Punch's first year.
14924-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Chapter four of The Wife-Catchers closes the legend of my uncle's boots in Punch for the week ending 21 August 1841. Conversation sinks to private and confidential whispers, from which the narrator learns Miss O'Brannigan has consented to quit her father's halls with Terence that very night.

Before the priest, she will become his true and lawful wife. Guests living at a distance are to sleep at the lodge that night, which favours the lovers' designs. Miss Biddy is to steal from her chamber at daybreak and fling gravel at her lover's window, while Terence's horse waits warranted for flight. The elopement is told with Irish comedy and a wink.
14925-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 28 August 1841 opens The Heir of Applebite, introducing the Applebite family and Agamemnon Collumpsion Applebite in particular. A guide to Parliament lists Isaac Applebite of Puddingbury, born in 1780, son of his line, and having issue.

A stone in Puddingbury church shows the first Mrs. Applebite, once a housemaid, scrubbing a large tea urn. A second figure, said to be the second Mrs. Applebite, points in blame at a fat cherub blowing himself into a fit. Stock virtues are blazoned forth on stone. The serial promises a comic saga of family pride, money and absurd respectability.
14926-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 5 September 1841 opens its tailor's manual, The Gentleman's Own Book. It asks what a well-dressed man is really built from: how his clothes are shaped, how they are finished, and how dress itself behaves.

Its central comparison treats shaping as the stamp on money. Just as a mint mark turns metal into accepted coin, a tailor's cutting turns fabric into a gentleman's standing, whatever the cloth costs. The article then sets tailoring beside sculpture. It argues that a cutter brings cloth to life much as an ancient sculptor brought marble figures to life. The piece is early Punch on fashion and manners: a gentleman made, not born, by how his coat is cut.
14927-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Chapter three of The Heir of Applebite, in Punch for the week ending 12 September 1841, follows the newly married couple on their trip to the seaside town of Brighton. The narrator pictures them travelling in a smart yellow carriage with pale grey-green upholstery, with a hamper of food packed for the road.

The bride sits in one corner, fair and blushing. Her mostly white bridal outfit is set off by darker pieces, in a blend the narrator compares to red and pale wines mixed together. Her bare hand shows a bright ring that stands for lasting hope. Beside her lounges her smiling husband, twenty-four years old, admiring his new wife. The honeymoon joke is gentle, visual and very Punch: marriage as a carriage ride with refreshments.
14928-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Chapter four of The Heir of Applebite, in Punch for the week ending 18 September 1841, has a great deal to say about someone else besides the hero. Kindness marks Agamemnon's disposition, so the month par excellence brings a succession of annoyances that, in the best regulated families, fall on the masculine progenitor.

Bachelors are warned in time. They should not let love link them to flowery traces and draw them into the temple of Hymen. Nor should they be deluded by Anacreon and Boccaccio, who were bachelors themselves. Nothing exhilarates in caudle, nor enchants in Kensington Gardens, when a man faces the duties of fatherhood. The comedy is domestic, rueful and very much of its age.
14929-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 25 September 1841 brings The Heir of Applebite to chapter five, showing that there is many a slip between other things beside the cup and the lip. The heir continues to squall and thrive, to his youthful mother's delight, and she determines to celebrate his first tooth with an evening party of great splendour.

Cards are issued requesting company to an evening party on Thursday, with quadrilles, and an answer will oblige. It is the first home-made party Collumpsion has ever given, for in bachelorhood the confectioner supplied his hospitality. The comedy lies in new parents, new money and a baby's tooth treated as a state occasion.
14930-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
The Tiptoes, a sketch in Punch for the week ending 2 October 1841, quotes Vanbrugh: the Wrongheads have been a considerable family ever since England was England. Morning and evening, from villages within three or four miles of London, a tide of young men wends to desks and counters in the city.

Preceded by errand boys and light porters, followed by plethoric elderly gentlemen in drab gaiters, these individuals call themselves gentlemen and are called persons by everybody else. They form the advanced guard of the Tiptoes, an army that invaded some thirty years before and has since advanced steadily. Punch's sketch satirises social climbing in the suburbs.
14931-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 9 October 1841 offers a manual of denouements, opening with a critic's line bidding swords and daggers fall in the king's name. A melodrama, the writer explains, is a theatrical dose in two or three acts, sized to the audience's constitution.

Its parts are a villain, a lover, a heroine, a comic character and an executioner, simmered and macerated through events, then strained together into the last scene. The effervescence that follows is the denouement, the soul of the drama. Natural, unnatural and supernatural kinds are distinguished, the natural being one where no probabilities are violated. It is a witty guide to stage endings.
14932-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
A trade report from Punch's own reporter fills the issue for the week ending 16 October 1841, with a market in a most extraordinary state all morning. Feathers grow very heavy, lead is brisker than usual, and in the fish market flounders are not so flat as they were, coming round rapidly to general surprise.

Deliveries of tallow are numerous and smooth the day's transactions, every species of fat is in high demand, but a glut of mutton checks general facility. The milk market is unsettled, late rains having caused unusual abundance, and a large order for skim follows. The report is a punning market bulletin, where every commodity's price is also a joke about its nature.
14933-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 23 October 1841 introduces Mr. Horatio Fitzharding Fitzfunk, a tall, thin, pale and decidedly knock-kneed young man. He belongs to the highly respectable firm of Tims and Swindle, attorneys and bill discounters of Thavies Inn, Holborn, who pay him one pound one shilling a week.

His work is peculiarly peripatetic, sending him out at all sorts of hours on errands for the firm. The Great Creature of the title is Fitzfunk himself, a clerk made comic by his name, his knees and his salary. Punch's early humour loves such figures: respectable on paper, absurd in person, and busy about a city that never quite notices him.
14934-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
The Great Creature returns in Punch for the week ending 30 October 1841, somewhat out at elbows, not in costume, for the plenitude of his wardrobe caused the effect. The word received cannot be found annexed to bills from Messrs. Moleskin and Corderoy, a slight on their penmanship that rouses their ire.

Through attorneys Gallowsworthy and Pickles of Furnival's Inn, the tailors forward a writ to the unfortunate Hannibal Fitzflummery Fitzflam, a new name for the great creature. Debt, dandyism and lawyers drive the joke. Punch's early serial loves a young man with more clothes than cash, and creditors who will not wait for fashion to pay.
14935-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 6 November 1841 opens A Day-Dream at My Uncle's. A serious talk between the author's parents ends in a resolution: it is high time for him to begin the world and do something for himself. The only problem left is how he had better commence.

Scheme after scheme is discussed and discarded, new plans breed new doubts, and impossibilities overwhelm every suggestion. At the critical moment when it seems clear either that he is fit for nothing or nothing is fit for him, an authoritative rat-tat sounds. The daydream that follows is Punch's joke on young men, parents and the difficulty of starting in life.
14936-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
The birth of the Prince of Wales fills Punch for the week ending 13 November 1841, by the Observer's own correspondent. Punch notes it was not premature in announcing the probability of a birth, and its positive tone shows the exclusive nature of its intelligence.

Now it can state that the Prince has already taken the title of Prince of Wales. He will enjoy it, if a child so young can be said to enjoy anything, until an event hoped to be postponed for a very long period. Should he survive his mother, he will ascend the throne. The piece satirises newspaper certainty about royal news.
14937-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 20 November 1841 tells of Myself, Punch, and the Keeleys. The narrator dines with his old schoolfellow Jack Withers, whom he met by chance on Cornhill the previous morning, after seventeen years apart, with a cry of recognition on both sides.

Withers, with a good mercantile connection, chose commerce and entered a counting house in Idol Lane in the same year the narrator, a raw youth, began his own path. A dinner, an old friendship and a theatre family, the Keeleys, give the piece its frame. It is early Punch as personal essay: London streets, old school ties and the pleasure of meeting a friend again.
14938-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
The physiology of the London medical student continues in Punch for the week ending 27 November 1841, with the sequel to the hall examination. Trembling, Mr. Muff trails the beadle out of the waiting room and into the council chamber, so rattled that he feels unsure whether he is upright or upside down, and suspects the latter.

He only regains his bearings once he takes his place at the head of a square table. Solemn examiners fill the other three sides, and the candles seem to wobble like street lamps he has watched on his way home from his singing club. A spread of books and specimens waits in front of him for the questioning to begin. Punch's medical student series turns student terror into comedy with precision.
14939-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 4 December 1841 prints what it calls the original draft of the official report of the fire at the Tower. Newspapers dressed it up for the public eye, but here it is given neat, in its precise language. Mr. Snooks, on watch on the night of Saturday 30 October, turned into his box and slept.

Amazed by shouts and rolling wheels, he looked out of an open upper door, struck his head violently against something hard, and found the lower door would not open. Thinking something wrong, he tried to make sense of a night gone wrong. Punch's joke is on official prose itself: a plain watchman's night turned into a report that explains everything except what happened.
14940-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
How Mr. Muff concludes his evening fills Punch for the week ending 11 December 1841, in the physiology of the London medical student. Essential as sulphuric acid is to lighting platinum in a hydropneumatic lamp, so is half-and-half to illuminating a medical student's faculties.

The Royal College of Surgeons may thunder and lecturers may threaten, all to no effect. Like slippers in an Eastern story, pots ordered away from the dissecting room always find their way back, time after time. All the world inclined toward beer knows a pot of half-and-half costs fivepence, and by that standard the student fixes expenses. The joke is on student drinking and discipline.
14941-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for the week ending 18 December 1841 closes its physiology of the London medical student with the college and the conclusion. Once again the hero must cram before he can sit his surgeons' examination in Lincoln's Inn Fields.

His anatomy needs a little brushing up first, so he turns to a private tutor. That tutor runs his college coaching just as the hall tutor runs his. Very often the two tutors are one person. He is a man who always claims room for another live-in pupil even when his house is already full. The series ends with a joke on cramming, examiners and students who learn just enough, just in time.
14942-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
How Mr. Chokepear keeps a merry Christmas fills Punch for the week ending 25 December 1841. Mr. Chokepear is respectable to the finger nails. The tax gatherer never calls twice for the same rate, he takes sacrament two or three times a year, and his cellar holds the oldest port in the parish.

He has subscribed to convert the Jews, and started a subscription to present Dr. Mannamouth with a superb silver teapot, cream jug and spoons, to show infidels that some men in the parish are true Christians. He respects Sir Peter Laurie since that worthy act. Punch's Christmas joke is on respectability itself: a merry Christmas kept by subscriptions, port and a teapot.
15918-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty-one, dated August 19, 1897. Five cents bought news, science, and stories in words young readers could follow. Four new subscribers earned a pocket Kodak, measuring two and a quarter by two and seven-eighths inches, making pictures one and a half by two. The paper mixed learning with prizes.

This number turns to the week's events abroad and at home, with nature notes and serial tales beside. Editors explain treaties and inventions in short, clear paragraphs. Picture items keep young eyes moving. Seen now, the issue captures late August 1897 for American children: summer ending, cameras in hand, and the world in a weekly paper.
4241-se-quo-yah-from-harper-s-new-monthl:
Harper's New Monthly Magazine published this piece in 1870. It tells the story of Se-Quo-Yah, the Cherokee man who gave his people a written language. The account opens on the Georgia frontier in 1768. Pack-horse traders, licensed agents, and Cherokee hunters fill that world. Their rough commerce shaped the world he grew up in.

From that frontier scene the account moves to Se-Quo-Yah himself. It covers his standing among the Cherokee and the alphabet he devised. With it, the language could be written and read. Readers get a sketch of frontier trade and an early popular account of an invention that changed Cherokee life.
54781-the-irish-penny-journal-vol-1-no-3:
The Irish Penny Journal for Saturday, 13 February 1841, is number 33 of the first volume of that paper. A picture of Cahir Castle in County Tipperary heads the issue. The lead piece takes up the town of Cahir itself. To a large part of our readers, the piece says, there is no need to state how strong a claim the town has to interest.

Cahir is held to be the most full of interest of its size in the province of Munster, and near in all Ireland. Part of that claim rests on the great beauty of its site and of the country round it. Part rests on a rarer trait in small towns: the beauty of its public buildings. A look of neatness and ease runs through the town. That look is tied to the care of the noble family to whom the town belongs.
5944-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
The road home fills chapters seventy-one and seventy-two of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter seventy-one tells what passed between Quixote and his squire Sancho on the way to their village. The vanquished and afflicted knight goes along downcast in one respect and happy in another. Sadness arises from defeat, satisfaction from the virtue shown in bearing it, and squire and master talk through both.

Chapter seventy-two tells how Quixote and Sancho reached their village, closing the journey that began in hope. Readers get a quiet, moving return, where defeat becomes dignity and friendship outlasts adventure. The part suits readers finishing volume two, since its road talk prepares the omens, sickness, and will that end the history.
a-visit-to-the-united-states-in-1841: Joseph Sturge visits the United States in 1841 in this volume published at Boston in 1842, under a Cowper epigraph on liberty as the flower of fleeting life. The appendices carry an anti-slavery epistle of Friends in Great Britain, early efforts in behalf of the Negro, and the Amistad captives. An essay by William Jay, the opium war with China, and Gerrit Smith's slaves complete the appendices. A Quaker traveller's record, it joins observation to the abolitionist cause.
al-masudi-meadows-of-gold-sprenger-1841:
Al-Masudi was a traveler from Baghdad. He saw India, Africa, and the Caspian lands in the tenth century, and he wrote the Muruj al-Dhahab, the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems. Aloys Sprenger gave the first part of it English form in 1841. Only this first volume of his version ever appeared.

The Meadows is a cabinet of the world. It holds the making of the earth, the kings of Persia and India, the seas, the wonders, and the tales told in ports. Al-Masudi asks questions everywhere he goes and writes down what he hears, gold and dross together. Sprenger's volume lets English readers taste the great Arab Herodotus. The full French version stands in the library beside it.
arxiv-2412-00841:
Yiyu Li and Liangang Peng add a coproduct to the semi-derived Ringel-Hall algebra, lifting it to a bialgebra. Their paper from twenty twenty-four starts from work by Lu and Peng. For a hereditary abelian category, that algebra has a natural basis. It matches the Drinfeld double Ringel-Hall algebra in structure. A coproduct that fits the product was the missing piece.

The authors write the coproduct in terms of the natural basis. They prove it meshes with the product rule. With both in place, the algebra gains a full bialgebra structure. That structure is then matched to the one on the Drinfeld double. The result rounds out the algebraic portrait of these Hall-type algebras. It serves representation theory, where such algebras encode how objects extend each other.
arxiv-2412-00941:
Ali Asadi, Krishnendu Chatterjee, Raimundo Saona, and Ali Shafiee settle a complexity question in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Their setting is decision making with partial information: an agent cannot see the full state of its world. The agent wants to reach a target with a chance as close to certain as desired. In full generality that question cannot be decided at all. Real agents, though, run on small memory.

The authors fix the memory size and ask how hard the problem becomes. They prove it is NP-complete, the classic class of hard search problems. That result tells algorithm designers not to expect a fast exact solver. Approximate or special-case methods are the practical path. The paper serves the formal methods and AI planning communities.
arxiv-2412-01241:
An Ning, Tai-Yue Li, and Nan-Yow Chen insert a quantum version of pointwise convolution into neural networks for image classification. Pointwise convolution mixes information across channels cheaply in classical networks. The quantum version maps data into a larger space with circuits, hoping to catch richer feature relationships. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team designs around today's noisy, small quantum hardware. Amplitude encoding packs more data into fewer qubits. A weight-sharing scheme reuses circuit parameters across pixels, avoiding retraining for each position.

On two standard image benchmarks, the hybrid model performed competitively against its classical counterpart, the authors report. The optimizations target deployability: the layer can drop into convolutional architectures broadly. Quantum machine learning here is an enhancement module, not a wholesale replacement.
arxiv-2412-01541:
Nikolaos Chandrinos and six co-authors compare two defenses against membership inference attacks in a two thousand twenty-four privacy paper. Such attacks reveal whether a certain person's data trained a model, a serious leak for private data sets.

L2 regularization is the standard cure for overfitting, and overfitting is exactly what makes membership inference succeed. Yet its protective value had never been measured across the board. The authors benchmark L2 regularization against differential privacy, the rule-based but often costly alternative. Their comparison asks how much privacy a cheap, familiar training knob in fact buys, telling practitioners who deploy machine learning as a service on sensitive data.
arxiv-2412-02141:
Yuci Liang and ten co-authors present, in a 2024 preprint, a language model that can discuss whole pathology slides, not just patches. A whole slide image is huge, and its diagnostic clues live in tissue shape. Patch-level models crop too narrowly and skip those clues. The team first builds WSI-Bench, a question-answer benchmark drawn from nearly ten thousand slides across thirty cancer types. Its one hundred eighty thousand pairs stress shape-aware understanding. Their model, WSI-LLaVA, trains in three stages: aligning slide and text, aligning feature spaces, then tuning on tasks.

Two new metrics score answers for precision and relevance in this setting. Across all measured skills, WSI-LLaVA beat other models. Its edge was largest on shape analysis, the skill pathologists prize. Scores there tracked diagnostic accuracy closely. The authors argue whole-slide understanding, not patch spotting, is the right target for pathology AI.
arxiv-2412-03841:
Yuan Xue, Qi Zhang, Chuanmin Jia, and Shiqi Wang build a frame to squeeze images for low-level machine tasks, not for human eyes. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Squeezing for machines most often serves high-level tasks, such as finding things. But real images are often of poor grade to start with. Low-level tools, such as image repair, can lift that grade, so their squeeze needs count too. The team's frame tunes squeeze and the low-level task as one. A large sight-language model guides the work. The frame is the first of its kind for this class of tasks.
arxiv-2412-05941:
Jian Chai and Shan Cheng add the gentle sideways wobble of quarks to the theory of pions and kaons, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Inside a fast-moving meson, partons stream along the direction of motion, but they also drift transversely, and standard factorization treatments of exclusive processes overlook that soft transverse motion.

The authors introduce intrinsic transverse momentum distribution functions, used alongside the familiar longitudinal distribution amplitudes. With both ingredients, they compute the pion and kaon electromagnetic form factors in perturbative QCD at next-to-leading order. Fitting data in the timelike region pins down a transverse size parameter for each meson. They also extract the pion's chiral mass from the analysis. The improvement extends trustworthy predictions toward lower momentum transfers. Meson form factors are basic fingerprints of quark binding, so sharper theory sharpens every comparison with experiment.
arxiv-2412-07241:
Fatma Yamac Sagirli, Xiaopeng Zhao, and Zhenbo Wang review human-computer interaction research for advanced air mobility, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Advanced air mobility means moving passengers and cargo through the air within and between cities. Urban growth and road congestion make the idea attractive for faster, cleaner travel.

The review surveys interface design for pilot training, air traffic management, and AI-assisted decision-making. It also covers immersive tools such as virtual, augmented, and mixed reality devices. Human-AI collaboration is a central theme throughout. The authors then analyze the challenges facing the field. Their synthesis maps where interface research must go before autonomous urban flight becomes routine.
arxiv-2412-07841:
Hugo Perrin, Sven Jandura, and Guido Pupillo wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies quantum error correction on neutral atom machines, where atoms can simply be lost mid-run.

The team adds loss detection units to the surface code. Two forms are tried: a plain unit and one built on teleportation. A fresh decoder uses the known loss spots, and cuts the logical error rate by near three orders of magnitude against a naive one. Circuit-level runs map the edge where errors stay in check. That edge slides in a straight line as loss and noise rates trade off. With no noise, the loss edge sits at about two point six percent.
arxiv-2412-08841:
Xiang Huang and six co-authors add structure awareness to probabilistic embeddings. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Probabilistic codes map each data point to a distribution, not a point. That spread captures uncertainty in the data. Most methods tune each latent variable on its own. Links between the variables go unused. The information bottleneck principle guides the usual trade-offs.

Their model, SEPC, adds a structural entropy term to the loss. Latent relations now shape the coding directly. A probabilistic encoding tree adapts the idea to regression tasks. Regression is recast as classification along the tree. Structure guides both compression and accuracy. Representation learning gains a way to respect its own wiring.
arxiv-2412-09741:
Serap Savari wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four on round-off errors and blur in superresolution and image registration. Superresolution rebuilds a sharp signal from blurred, noisy samples, and registration aligns sample sets of the same signal to fuse them. Digital images also carry quantization error from rounding pixel values.

Savari studies one-dimensional signals that are flat in steps, blurred by Gaussian or mixed-Gaussian kernels, and rounded. A signal-dependent measurement matrix captures both blur and rounding. Even without other noise, locating the step edges from two sample sets proves hard. With statistical noise added, data must be aligned and segmented first. Under stated conditions on blur, noise, and edge spacing, a dynamic programming method correctly aligns the sequences and finds the first sample after each edge.
arxiv-2412-11141: Zouhaïr Mouayn rederives a formula for the integrated density of states of the sub-Laplacian on Heisenberg groups. The note appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Heisenberg groups are the simplest stage where geometry twists away from the flat Euclidean kind. Their sub-Laplacian is a diffusion operator that moves only along allowed directions. The integrated density of states counts how many vibration modes sit below each energy. Mouayn reaches the known expression through the operator's resolvent kernel. The density of states feeds spectral counts across mathematical physics.
arxiv-2412-12841:
Ruikang Ni and colleagues build a benchmark to test whether large language models can do compositional relational reasoning, a hallmark of human intelligence. Whether transformer models can solve such tasks, and how, was unclear. Their synthetic benchmark, Generalized Associative Recall, unifies the essence of several mechanistic interpretability tasks into one framework.

Evaluation shows the benchmark is hard enough to expose a fundamental deficiency in current models' relational reasoning. It is also tractable enough for systematic interpretability study. Using attribution patching, the authors discover core circuits that one model reuses across different tasks, plus a set of vital attention heads. Interventions confirm those heads' correct functioning drives task performance. Most strikingly, two classes of heads encode the abstract notions of true and false for these tasks. They play a fundamental role across models and tasks. The dataset and code are public, inviting others to dissect how reasoning is implemented.
arxiv-2412-13241:
Sansrit Paudel and co-authors review assistive technologies for children with dyslexia from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-four, in work from twenty twenty-four. Dyslexia is a nerve based learning disorder that disrupts reading, writing, and spelling. It affects a large share of the world population, so good tools matter.

Digital tools lead the field, most of all mobile apps and augmented reality aids. Newer options include virtual reality, language processing tools, touch based tech, and hands on interfaces. Each tries to match the child's own needs and style. Non digital devices work less well on the whole. Still, they offer a useful fallback where tech access is thin. The review maps trends for builders and teachers.
arxiv-2501-02141:
Omar Nagib and Thad Walker wrote a physics methods paper in two thousand twenty-five about sensors based on Rydberg atoms. Heat makes the atoms move, and that motion blurs the signals the sensors read. The usual way to model the blur samples many speeds, which is slow and not exact.

The pair show that the blur can be found exactly by solving the motion just twice. They find a rule that turns the still-atom answer into the answer for any speed. Averaging that rule over the normal spread of speeds gives a direct formula. The method should save large amounts of time and memory.
arxiv-2501-02941:
Thomas Leyssens and four co-authors simulate flows where fluid and grains mix under a free surface, aimed at landslides, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. River sediments, reservoir soils, and silo contents all mix flowing water with granular matter. Their interfaces deform and reshape constantly, making the computation hard.

The team couples a particle method for the grains with a particle finite-element method for the fluid, exchanging forces both ways. A free-surface model handles the fluid-air boundary, and the fully Lagrangian description follows every interface's motion. Dam-break benchmarks validated the approach. A real landslide case then showed the method handling the coupled flow it was built for.
arxiv-2501-04341:
Zhu and five colleagues propose a prompting method to improve reasoning in language models in twenty twenty-five. Chain of thought prompting makes models show their steps before answering. It struggles when key facts are hidden or missing from the question. The steps then build on an incomplete picture.

Their method first extracts entities and their descriptions from the problem. It rates the reliability of each candidate fact pair. The two lowest rated pairs are merged into a new description, and the process repeats. At the end, one key fact pair remains and joins the question as input. Tests show a gain of about seven percent over existing methods. The approach can plug into varied reasoning frameworks.
arxiv-2501-04941:
Maxwell Sanderford and others release software that brings sparse machine learning to genome-scale evolution studies. Their method, evolutionary sparse learning, uses a penalized regression to connect a hypothesis, such as a trait or condition, to the genomic features that explain it. Sparsity is enforced within and between feature groups. Existing packages for grouped penalties strain at millions of sequence positions. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's tool ingests alignments and phylogenetic trees, converts them into features and responses. Runs a fast core written in C plus plus, with Python handling preparation and reporting.

Outputs come back as readable text and graphics summarizing the fitted model. A phylogenomics case study shows the pipeline on real genome-scale data, and the authors report the analyses performed as intended on empirical sets. The open-source package targets functional and evolutionary genomics groups with more data than their old tools could chew.
arxiv-2501-05241:
Guang Yang and a team of colleagues propose locating heart muscle scars without contrast dye, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. After a heart attack, scar tissue in the left ventricle guides treatment decisions. The standard scan, late gadolinium enhancement MRI, needs an injected agent with possible side effects and extra scan time.

Their framework instead uses ordinary cine MRI movies of the beating heart. It fuses cardiac motion with image texture to segment muscle and scar. Motion tracking is framed as registering the full cardiac cycle, solved by deep neural networks. Experiments showed accuracy comparable to the contrast-based standard. The authors present the method as a gentler alternative for scar detection.
arxiv-2501-06141:
Grant, Goodman, and McClelland ask whether neural networks secretly build symbol-like number variables in this 2025 paper. Classic programs use typed, changeable variables; networks use tangled neuron activity. The authors test how far the program lens can interpret network solutions to number tasks.

They trained recurrent networks and transformers on tasks where answers depend on hidden numeric values. Causal search methods aligned network activity with simple symbolic algorithms, working in subspaces rather than single neurons. Alignment was sometimes high, sometimes rough, sometimes absent, depending on design. They widened the search to linear alignment maps to cover the failures. The toolkit helps judge when a network really implements an interpretable algorithm.
arxiv-2501-06241:
Philip Adzanoukpe applies machine learning to Ghana's housing market in this two thousand twenty-five study. Renters and professionals in Ghana lack accurate, accessible information about what homes should cost to rent. Using a dataset of rental listings, the author trained and compared several models, including CatBoost, gradient boosting, and random forests. The goal was a predictor that captures the market's complex patterns.

CatBoost performed best, explaining about eighty-eight percent of the variation in rental prices. Feature importance analysis showed that location features matter most, followed by the number of bedrooms and bathrooms and whether a home is furnished. The findings offer practical guidance to real estate professionals, investors, and policymakers. The author suggests future work adding time trends and finer regional breakdowns to sharpen the predictions further.
arxiv-2501-08341:
Xiguang Yang, Krish Arora, and Michael Bachmann take apart the smallest useful neural network in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their network learns the XOR gate, a classic logic task that needs one hidden layer. Even this tiny system has a nine-dimensional space of weights and biases. The authors slice through that space to map where training loss is high or low. The shapes explain how backpropagation finds zero loss while weights still drift.

They borrow a tool from statistical physics, microcanonical entropy, to describe the network's states. Learning then looks like slow cooling, with jumps like phase changes in matter. Adding hidden units smooths the landscape, removing bad regions. The paper gives students a concrete picture of how neural learning really moves.
arxiv-2501-09841:
Foo, Bellamy, and Ralph present a paper from twenty twenty-five on particle paths in curved spacetime seen through quantum measures. They use weak measurements, gentle probes that barely disturb a particle. Average paths from those probes match the flow lines of chance current in curved spacetime theory. The team then show the same paths match light paths in a blended spacetime. That blended space mixes a black hole field with a warp-drive field. The triple match is the paper's core result.

The work suggests curved spacetime quantum theory can rest on defined measurements. It also supports a deterministic reading of the theory, akin to pilot-wave views. A hidden guiding metric underlies that reading. The authors present the link as a fresh bridge between fields.
arxiv-2501-11441:
Maria Taboada, Diego Martinez, Mohammed Arideh, and Rosa Mosquera match concepts across biomedical ontologies. Their twenty twenty-five paper presents a system called MILA. Matching lets data systems share knowledge across vocabularies. Language models help, but heavy use of them is slow and costly.

MILA searches in a prioritised depth-first order for likely matches. It retrieves candidate entities, identifies clear matches, and prompts the model only for borderline cases. That restraint cuts computing overhead sharply. Tests used a biomedical challenge from two recent evaluation rounds. The system topped most unsupervised tasks in that challenge. Gains over leading rivals reached notable margins on some tasks. Data teams gain accuracy without constant model calls.
arxiv-2501-12041:
Xintong Jiang wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It gives results on the birational geometry of Fano type varieties in positive characteristic, where the ground field has prime characteristic.

The paper shows three things. First, boundedness of a family stays the same when its members are normalized. Second, it gives a canonical bundle formula for fibrations of Fano type that is easier to use than past forms. Third, it proves effective birationality for some weak Fano varieties with good singularities. That last point is what the BAB conjecture forecasts. The work speaks to a field where positive characteristic has long lagged the complex case.
arxiv-2501-12441:
Ayan Chattaraj, Anirban Majumdar, and Rahul Srivastava use reactor data from the CONUS+ trial to test core physics and hunt for new effects, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The trial watches neutrinos bounce off whole nuclei, plus a second bounce type off electrons. Both signals tighten the net for odd behavior.

Within known physics the data checks a key weak-force angle with care. Beyond it, the team bounds light go-between particles from broad neutrino interactions. Limits also land on neutrino charge size, tiny charge, and magnetic pull. Readers in particle physics get fresh bounds from a compact reactor setup, with room to grow as data builds.
arxiv-2501-18041:
Riggert and seven colleagues gate semiconductor ribbons using layered materials in twenty twenty-five. Clean electrical control is vital for quantum devices. Gates built from layered van der Waals materials improved two dimensional devices greatly. The team applied that idea to indium antimonide nanoribbons, which are not layered materials.

Their gate stack used boron nitride insulation and a graphite electrode. Devices showed stable, repeatable behaviour with almost no gate hysteresis. Quantized conductance appeared and persisted to lower magnetic fields than usual. It also held over longer channels than typical nanowire devices. A split energy level varied strongly with field direction, matching the flat ribbon shape. The authors say the gating scheme should transfer to other materials.
arxiv-2502-02941:
Li and co-authors speed up diffusion-based solvers for hard combinatorial problems with a consistency trick. Diffusion solvers are strong but slow, since they denoise step by step. Their method learns to jump from any noise level straight to the best answer. Training forces samples from different paths and times to agree near the optimum. That agreement is the core training rule.

The trained model can answer in a single step. Extra steps remain available when quality matters more than speed. The design fits the training-to-testing solver frame. It offers a faster backbone for neural optimization without giving up the multi-step option.
arxiv-2502-05541:
Paul Laurain and Dorian Martino revisited a classic geometry theorem in 2025. Huber's theorem concerns surfaces and higher-dimensional shapes whose curvature is controlled, and what can be said near an isolated singularity. The authors study the second Huber theorem in two sizes and in four sizes, which behave differently and need varied tools.

In two sizes they prove a new version that allows the Gauss curvature to lie in a weak, negative Sobolev space, working through Coulomb frames. In four sizes, for a metric with a point singularity and bounds on the Bach tensor. They construct a conformal metric that stays regular across the singularity, introducing a Coulomb-type condition similar to one used for Yang-Mills links. The result broadens the 2D case and applies to singular Bach-flat metrics and certain immersions.
arxiv-2502-05841:
Jitendra Kumar Dhiman and Jainag Ambati swapped the attention inside a spoken language recognizer in a 2025 paper. Language identification starts from embeddings of a self-supervised speech model, pooled over time by an attention-based statistics layer that gathers context across frames. The pooling's vanilla self-attention is costly, and two newer attention designs, Performer and agent attention, promise similar power for less compute, motivating a head-to-head test.

Across three public speech corpora, Performer attention beat plain self-attention for language identification. Agent attention matched or sometimes topped self-attention while costing less to run. Faster pooling matters for live services that must route calls and captions by language in real time.
arxiv-2502-06441:
Leonard Constantin Gebac and Vasile Bercu simulate hydrogen squeezed inside a molecular cage, in a 2025 preprint, as a route to extreme pressures. Putting hydrogen under huge pressure changes how it behaves, and reaching metallic hydrogen is a famous prize. Lab presses struggle to reach and hold such states. A cage of carbon and hydrogen atoms, called dodecahedrane, can trap hydrogen inside. The authors ask what happens when that cage vibrates.

Their atom-level simulations squeeze the cage in a symmetric breathing motion. They track the cage's shape, energy, and heat traits as it compresses. The trapped hydrogen began to act like known high-pressure phases of pure hydrogen. The team reads this as a bridge between theory and lab work. Vibrating cages might let experimenters reach high pressure and heat in a controlled way. The results also sharpen pictures of hydrogen under extreme conditions.
arxiv-2502-06741:
Ehsan Zeraatkar, Salah Faroughi, and Jelena Tešić propose ViSIR, a method for reconstructing high-resolution images from downsampled Earth system model data. Climate models are so complex that neural networks store and emulate their outputs, and single-image super-resolution is a key task. ViSIR combines a vision transformer's reconstruction strength with a sinusoidal representation network's ability to preserve high-frequency detail.

The pairing targets the spectral bias that blurs fine structure in super-resolution. Across three measurements, ViSIR beat convolutional, transformer, sinusoidal, and adversarial baselines on peak signal-to-noise ratio, in one case by more than eight decibels. It also led on error and structural similarity metrics, the authors report.
arxiv-2502-07641:
Anastasiia Holovchak and co-authors build a method to find cause-and-effect links when hidden factors cloud the data, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Standard tools use a helper factor that shifts the cause but not the outcome directly. Most such tools estimate only an average effect.

Their method aims at the full spread of outcomes under a set cause, not just the mean. They prove when that spread can be pinned down, and show a case where an older tool fails but theirs works. Tests on fake data, an economics set, and a single-cell set all went well.
arxiv-2502-09341:
Sumantrak Mukherjee, Mouad Elhamdi, George Mohler, David Selby, Yao Xie, Sebastian Vollmer, and Gerrit Grossmann review neural spatiotemporal point processes. Point processes are models based on chance for events in space and time. They span cases from earthquakes to crime reports. Real event data shows tangled links and varied dynamics. Old models struggle to catch them. Deep learning lets these models depict such traits with more skill.

The fusion of neural methods with such point processes has become an active area that changes fast. The review sorts past paths and unifies key design choices. It sets out the tests of this data type, such as irregular sampling and linked space-time effects. The team stresses new trends and varied domains of use. They close by naming open tests and gaps.
arxiv-2502-12241:
Pavel Sekatski, Jef Pauwels, Edwin Peter Lobo, Stefano Pironio, and Nicolas Brunner show in two thousand twenty-five how to certify quantum correlations over any distance despite signal loss. Device-independent tests prove quantumness without trusting the hardware, but photons lost in transit have capped their range. That cap also limits device-independent key distribution.

Their trick uses routed Bell tests, where a particle can be measured near the source or far away. They prove that tests with only entangled qubit pairs can still certify quantum correlations under arbitrary loss on the long channel. The proof adapts ideas from self-testing and quantum steering. They then sketch a key distribution protocol that stays secure, in principle, over arbitrary distances. The routing idea sidesteps the loss barrier.
arxiv-2502-12341:
Léo Poyeton and Pietro Vanni built a many variable form of p-adic Hodge theory. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with Galois groups that come as products. To a family of p-adic images of such a group, they attach a family of special modules. This grows old results by other authors to the product case. The link uses a descent method named for Colmez, Sen, and Tate.

They also define rings of periods for the many variable case, in both crystal and near crystal forms. They show how the full theory can be read back from the module. Their frame also gives back known results on many variable Galois images. Readers in number theory get one frame for a split group field.
arxiv-2502-12841:
Zhicheng Feng, Miquel Martínez, and Damiano Rossi attack a character conjecture in twenty twenty-five. Finite group theory links a group's characters to those of smaller subgroups. A recent conjecture by Malle, Navarro, and Tiep concerns p-Brauer characters. It says the counts for a group and for a Sylow subgroup's normalizer agree exactly when that Sylow subgroup is normal.

The authors reduce the conjecture to a question about finite simple groups. They then prove it completely for the prime two. As a by-product, they prove a reduction theorem for the blockwise version of Alperin's lower bound. That bound is also proven for two-blocks of maximal defect. Readers in representation theory get a major case settled and machinery aimed at the rest.
arxiv-2502-13341:
Zane Taylor and eight co-authors build a math model of the balling defect that mars laser welding and metal 3D printing. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Balling leaves beaded, rough tracks instead of smooth seams. It is usually blamed on fluid instabilities in the melt pool.

X-ray movies of thin samples show the instability grows about as fast as the metal freezes. The team's model is the first to let those two races compete openly. Borrowed rivulet theory handles how the substrate steadies the liquid thread. The model predicts balling at longer wavelengths and shallower pools, and sharp sensitivity to the freezing front's curve. Gaps with their experiments prove that flow and heat transport also matter. The work gives printers a sharper map of when beads form.
arxiv-2502-16941:
Binbin Jiang, Rui Huang, Qingyi Zhao, and Yuxiang Zhang present a method that finds every changed object in a 3D scene, even under messy real-world conditions. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Change hunting breaks when photos lack labels, camera poses drift, or light shifts between visits. Their approach sidesteps paired photos entirely.

The method packs many images into a set of soft 3D blobs that carry time as a fourth axis. From those blobs it renders two steady image streams of the scene. Each object in view gets a fixed tag, so changed things stand out by tag mismatch. Learned maps then mark each blob as changed or not, and full change maps render from any angle. Tests beat leading rivals, above all where light varied a lot. Processing stays fast enough for field use.
arxiv-2502-19141:
Lucas Reis studies what happens when a special kind of polynomial over a finite field is applied again and again. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The polynomials at hand are additive, meaning they respect addition in a strong way. Reis tracks the size of the field needed to hold all roots of each repeat.

An older result showed that size grows in a straight line for most additive cases. Reis shows the growth is at least linear unless the polynomial has a rare special form. For prime fields he pins the growth to a neat step pattern, with constants that fit each case. A few dynamical oddballs break the pattern. The results feed counts of points that return to themselves under repeated maps. They also shape how repeated polynomials split into factors.
arxiv-2502-19241:
Sammani, Saidi, and Ahl Laamara build black holes with E6 marks in 3D pull work. The holes are BTZ forms that bear E6 marks in their build. They solve a 3D high-spin pull frame with E6 edge terms. Tits-Satake charts of true E6 forms guide the build path. Three hole forms rise from that guide in the work set. Two forms stem from splits of end nodes in one chart.

One form stems from a fold down to an F4 form in the chart. Hasse charts let the team view the high-spin ranges there. Two gauge shift types then build the hole forms from those views. Heat work on the stock BTZ hole caps the work text. A sum there ties hole parts to E6 root facts one to one.
arxiv-2503-01641:
B. Lehnert and colleagues searched for extremely rare radioactive decays of gadolinium atoms using quiet underground detectors. Gadolinium is common in large physics experiments, so leftover screening data from a neutrino project offered a ready sample. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team used samples first checked for purity before deployment in the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan. Their germanium detectors sat in an underground lab in England, shielded from background radiation. Only decays that release gamma rays could be seen with this setup.

No clear decay signal appeared for the three gadolinium isotopes studied. Combining their data with earlier results in a statistical analysis, the team set new lower limits on the decay half-lives, roughly a hundred times stricter than before. The work shows how purity screening campaigns for big experiments can double as sensitive searches for rare processes.
arxiv-2503-02741:
Bernd Prostmaier, Jan Vávra, Bettina Grün, and Paul Hofmarcher guide topic models with seed words so the themes they find match domains experts care about. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Topic models sort huge text piles into themes on their own. Left alone, though, the themes may miss the categories users actually need.

Their method, seeded Poisson factorization, tilts the starting rates toward chosen seed words. Each theme thus grows around a known anchor concept. Fitting uses a fast, scalable scheme built on sampled gradients. On Amazon feedback, product categories served as the guides. The guided model beat rival guided tools in both speed and sorting accuracy. It also held up when the seed words were imperfect. Four more data sets confirmed the edge over the unguided version.
arxiv-2503-03741:
Sistko studies a new kind of representation theory built for inverse monoids. He starts with a finite abelian group plus an added zero element. Vector spaces over this structure form a proto-abelian category. A monoid that acts in this setting is called linear over the group. Sistko then builds the category of its finite representations.

The new category looks close to the usual module category. Still, it acts in quite different ways for key classes of monoids. Sistko proves a form of the Clifford-Munn-Ponizovski theorem for it. He also sorts which monoids have every nonzero object split into simple parts. A final part weighs other ways to frame the same objects.
arxiv-2503-03841:
Sam Allen and others show that a forecasting system tuned to be honest on its own training data can be upgraded by a fixed recipe. The upgrade gives it honesty guarantees on future data. Conformal sets already wrap forecasts with coverage pledges, assuming exchangeable data. Fuller systems go further and issue whole outcome spreads. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team proves that conformal systems quietly rely on in-sample calibrated predictors, and that any in-sample calibrated method can be conformalized to inherit out-of-sample calibration. The logic extends from plain range coverage to the stronger conditional calibration notions used in forecasting theory.

Two new systems follow: one based on binning the data, another on isotonic regression of distributions, a shape-constrained method. Model tests and two case studies test them against current conformal systems. The bridge between calibration and conformal methods eases building forecasters with guarantees.
arxiv-2503-04341:
Shoesmith and four co-authors presented this work in twenty twenty-five on training brain-like networks for special chips. Neuromorphic chips copy the brain's event-based style and can run AI with far less energy. Training such spiking networks has been the hard part. The team trained networks on graphics cards with an event-based method, then moved them to Intel's Loihi 2 chip.

They tested the pipeline on keyword spotting, a task that listens for set words. Accuracy barely dropped when the network moved to the chip. Sorting one sample on Loihi 2 ran up to ten times faster than on a small edge computer. It also used about two hundred times less energy. The results support moving AI tasks from the cloud to local devices.
arxiv-2503-06741:
Penglin Hu, Chunhui Zhao, and Quan Pan propose a new reinforcement learning algorithm for pursuit-evasion games. Their twenty twenty-five paper addresses a practical problem: real pursuit-evasion tasks involve several goals that conflict with each other. A single-objective learner optimizes one goal and struggles to balance the rest.

The team builds a three-objective algorithm on fuzzy Q-learning. Its reward function covers evading pursuit, reaching the target, and avoiding obstacles. A multi-objective evaluation method and action selection strategy based on three-dimensional hypervolume handle the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Sampling the Pareto front yields the update rule for the global strategy. The authors report that the method cuts computational load while keeping exploration ability, and they verify its performance in simulations. The work offers a route to controllers that must satisfy several competing objectives at once.
arxiv-2503-09341:
Joshua Jacas, Hana Winchester, Alicia Boyd, and Brittany Johnson test how well language models spot harmful computing terms. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, uses a curated set of sixty-four terms. Each term comes with a concrete use case. Models from three design families face the same prompt.

Decoder models, led by Gemini Flash and Claude, read context with nuance. Encoder models like BERT catch surface patterns well but hedge on hard calls. Encoder-decoder models fill out the comparison. The findings sort strengths by architecture type. Better automated flags could support more inclusive technical language. The authors weigh what each design does best and worst.
arxiv-2503-10141:
Linzuo Zhang and four co-authors fly small drones through clutter with no map, using a control method that plans ahead from depth camera data. Map based flight can stack errors and slow the craft, which cuts speed and safety. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The planner takes sparse goal points and point clouds from the depth camera and gives safe moves at once. Goal points shift on the fly as blocks near the craft are sensed. Two fast search trees help, one to find the nearest block, one to seed the solver so it does not stall in a dead end. Tests in fake and real settings beat map based and learned rivals.
arxiv-2503-14141:
Yuming Fu and fourteen co-authors extend a cleaned-up quasar candidate catalog to the southern sky and merge it into one all-sky list. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A space survey offered millions of quasar candidates, but most are impostors. Earlier northern work showed that extra survey data plus machine learning can purify the list.

The team trained a classifier on sure stars, quasars, and galaxies across several surveys. For candidates with spectra, a neural net read off distances directly. A blended model estimated distances from colors for the rest. Merging south with north yields nearly two million candidates with high purity. The catalog, CatGlobe, sets up future spectroscopic campaigns. Such lists feed studies of black holes and the large-scale cosmos.
arxiv-2503-14341:
Andrew Roxburgh, Floriana Grasso, and Terry Payne predict which words a young child will learn next, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Knowing the likely next words could help boost early language acquisition. Earlier predictors used either vocabulary change over time or relationships between words, but not both together.

Their model is a spatio-temporal graph convolutional network. Words form a graph whose edges capture different linguistic relationships. The network also tracks how each child's vocabulary state evolves. This combination aims to mirror the real complexity of infant learning. The authors evaluate how each relationship type affects prediction quality. Their observations shed light on which connections matter most during early word learning.
arxiv-2503-16241:
Shantonu Mukherjee, Sayantan Sharma, and Hridis Pal study the chiral anomaly in spin-one fermion systems, a setting where a basic count rule seems to break. In clean field theory, matched electric and magnetic fields can change the count of one handed type of particle. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

In solids, the same effect shows up in Weyl semimetals with a fixed strength tied to a charge at a node. Spin-one systems break a key symmetry, though. The authors show the rule gains an extra term that is not fixed, so the strength is not locked. They trace the extra term to a split of spin-one particles into two Weyl types plus a background field.
arxiv-2503-16541:
Hanzhi Zhang and five co-authors introduce Poly-FEVER in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Large language models often state false claims with confidence, a flaw called hallucination. Tests that catch this flaw focus mostly on English. That leaves model behavior in other languages unclear. Poly-FEVER is a fact-checking benchmark built to close that gap.

The set holds nearly seventy-eight thousand labeled claims across eleven languages. The claims come from three existing fact-check sources, on general facts, climate, and science. The authors use it to test models such as ChatGPT and the LLaMA series. Their analysis shows how topic mix shifts model scores across languages. The benchmark gives builders a shared yardstick for truthfulness beyond English.
arxiv-2503-17441:
Shuai Wang and co-authors identified a new instability in hot chiral matter in 2025. Chiral hydrodynamics describes fluids, such as the quark-gluon plasma, whose particles carry handedness, and its collective waves include chiral shear waves. Re-examining those waves at second order in the theory, the authors found they can turn unstable at short enough wavelengths when dissipation is too weak to tame them. With the result set by a contest between shear thickness and an anomalous vortical term.

The instability, named the chiral vortical instability, generates helical flows. Like two earlier chiral instabilities, it converts microscopic handedness into large-scale helicity, which the authors fold into a broadened axial charge. A classic helical flow pattern turns out to solve the full nonlinear equations exactly, while plain global spin does not, evidence the effect reaches beyond the small-disturbance regime.
arxiv-2503-18241:
Sotiris Kanellopoulos, Giorgos Mitropoulos, and six co-authors design near-optimal algorithms for fair splitting problems. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies the k-subset sum ratio problem. Given a bag of positive numbers, choose k disjoint groups whose sums are as equal in ratio as possible. Perfect balance is hard to compute exactly.

Their scheme guarantees answers within any set error margin. Its runtime grows in a controlled way with group count and precision. A second problem forces the groups to cover every number. That version, tied to envy-free division, gets its own scheme. Both are the first of their kind for more than two groups.
arxiv-2503-18641:
Zou, Zhang, and Zhao survey smart tools for drawn plan work in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such tools now read plans and birth new plan bits for ads and brands. The field splits in two roads: sight reads and born work.

Inside, sight tasks span bit reads, taste reads, and lay-out reads in the tour. Born tasks span bit births, lay-out births, and whole plan builds. Big tongue tools bridge lone bits to whole plan aims in new builds. Bare snags stay: true aim reads, clear steps, and coat-stack rule. The tour maps the field's state and its next roads for peers.
arxiv-2503-19341:
Keerthy Menon, Thomas Busch, and Thomás Fogarty propose heat engines that swap the quantum nature of their particles mid-cycle. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A recent real device, the Pauli engine, drew power from changes in particle type rather than heat alone. This team asks whether mixing both kinds of steps can beat engines that use one type only.

They study a one-dimensional gas whose particles can be tuned from soft to hard-core behavior. Timed right, the extra type-swap steps lift both output and efficiency. The gains beat engines that stay with a single particle type. In the cold, dense regime their engine can even reach the top limit set by Carnot. The same cycle can also run as a fridge. The authors present particle type as a real resource for tiny thermal machines.
arxiv-2503-21241:
HyeYoung Lee and Pavel Tsoi test machine learning models that predict death in hospital, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Good predictions help teams grade risk and tailor care. Past work often covered one disease or a narrow set of inputs.

Using a large public hospital database, the team built rich inputs from vital signs, lab results, and patient traits. A forest-style model scored highest, well ahead of other learning and deep models. Careful input building was key to the score, the authors stress. They discuss clinic use and next steps, such as models tuned to single diseases.
arxiv-2503-21441:
Cameron Seth gave near-optimal bounds in twenty twenty-five for testing whether a graph hides a large sparse corner. Property testing asks if a huge object has a trait, judged from a tiny random sample. Here the trait concerns a fixed share of vertices forming a nearly edge-free set, and the test must be tolerant, accepting graphs that come close.

His algorithm inspects a random subgraph on a modest number of vertices. It separates graphs with a nearly empty large corner from those where every large corner holds many edges. The sample size matches the best known bound for the stricter, non-tolerant version, up to log factors. The key tool is a new container lemma for sparse subgraphs. It also extends classic counting results from independent sets to sparse subgraphs.
arxiv-2503-22141:
Zhang and five colleagues grade how well ChatGPT writes metamorphic relations for software testing in twenty twenty-five. Such relations state how outputs should shift when inputs change in set ways. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 drafts were scored under old criteria first. A sharper criteria set then graded GPT-4 across nine test systems.

The systems ranged from plain code to AI laden stacks. GPT-4 beat its older sibling on accuracy and use. It kept quality high even on the complex systems. A custom GPT grader was set against human judges. The team sees AI and human skills as partners in testing work.
arxiv-2503-22641:
Gabriel Pontolillo, Mohammad Reza Mousavi, and Marek Grzesiuk present QuCheck, a testing frame for quantum programs in two thousand twenty-five. Property-based testing checks that a program keeps set traits across many random inputs. A past tool did this for one quantum language but was narrow and hard to extend.

QuCheck is built on Qiskit and the wider Python world, with flexible input makers, claims, and preconditions. The team stress-tested it by planting faults in five quantum programs of two to ten qubits. More checked traits meant more faults caught, while more measurement shots cut false alarms. Top setups caught about nine in ten planted faults. QuCheck found over a third more faults than the past tool and ran far faster.
arxiv-2503-23041:
Borówka and Shatsila study coverings of genus two curves and the Prym varieties built from them in twenty twenty-five. A covering wraps one curve over another in a neat, symmetric way. The Prym variety is a companion shape that holds much of the covering's data. The pair ask if the covering can be rebuilt from that companion alone.

For coverings with a nine element symmetry group, they prove it can. That is the Prym Torelli claim for this class. They also study the map from coverings to their Pryms for any abelian symmetry group. Its general fiber is finite, save for small cyclic groups. The results sharpen a classic line of curve theory.
arxiv-2503-23441:
Mota, Sharlin, and Alim mapped a design space in this paper from twenty twenty-five for lens visualizations. A lens is an interactive window that reveals detail inside dense spatial data. Designers lacked a shared map of the choices involved. The authors analyzed forty-five papers from the past fifteen years to build one.

Their space spans seven dimensions of design choice. Each dimension is shown through real examples, with the gains and pitfalls of each option. The catalog helps designers judge old lenses and plan new ones. Some regions of the space remain barely studied. The authors close by pointing at those gaps as openings for future work.
arxiv-2504-00541:
A large team of particle physicists proposes LEP3, an electron-positron collider in the existing LHC tunnel. Their paper from twenty twenty-five responds to a call for backup plans in Europe's particle physics strategy. The top pick for a future collider is a new ring called FCC. Planners asked for ranked fallbacks in case that ring proves out of reach.

LEP3 would reuse the LHC tunnel rather than dig a new one. It would draw on much of the design work done for the FCC electron ring. The machine would study Z, W, and Higgs particles with high care. It would run below the threshold for making top quark pairs. The authors frame it as a high-output Higgs and electroweak factory. It stands as a hedge if the main plan fails.
arxiv-2504-00741:
Izumi Takahara, Teruyasu Mizoguchi, and Bang Liu put a language model in charge of hunts for new inorganic stuff, with a diffusion model as its hands. Crystal design wants set traits, but new-form search can be slow, hard to read. Their agent, MatAgent, pairs a model that draws crystal forms with one that scores traits. Notes flow back and forth, and that loop steers the hunt to goals the user sets.

The agent also bears mind-like tools: short-term and long-term memory, the periodic table, and a broad base of facts on stuff. That frame mimics how a human pro thinks. Hunts land on the traits sought each time. Forms score high on sound build, on being rare, and on being new. The frame is a sound, broad path to new stuff, from batteries to catalysts.
arxiv-2504-00841:
Bayron Portilla-Revelo and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about a planet-forming disk bathed in strong radiation. The disk circles a Sun-like star in a distant, massive star-forming region. Most disks studied closely sit near the Sun, where no huge stars shine, so they may not show how most planets form.

Using a chemistry and heat model, the team matched data from the James Webb Space Telescope and older light measures. The dust in the disk looks much like dust in nearby disks. The gas signals come from within a small inner zone. The model favors a compact disk with less gas than expected, shaped by the harsh light around it. The work helps read disks in rougher neighborhoods.
arxiv-2504-02041:
Leonardo Maggiore, Sofia Contarini, Carlo Giocoli, and Lauro Moscardini build a new pipeline to find and study empty regions of space in maps made by weak lensing. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Empty regions, called voids, can test views where gravity works in new ways, since thin places feel such shifts most. Lensing maps trace mass along our line of sight, free of some bias. The team makes true-to-life maps from fake cosmos runs, under changed gravity and with heavy ghost particles. Their tool finds tunnel-like gaps in the strength of the lens signal. The pipeline lets them read what each theory writes on the voids.
arxiv-2504-02341:
László Koltai, Alexander A. Kubasch, and Róbert Szőke work on a pure math claim about Bergman spaces, which are sets of well-behaved maps on curved shapes. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A known claim by Wiegerinck says such a space, on an open part of the plane, is either huge or holds just the zero map. Others had stretched that claim to bundles over round shapes. Koltai and his co-authors stretch it once more, to a case with rough measures tied to marked points on a curved shape. As a result, they gain forms of the claim for both closed and open algebraic curves.
arxiv-2504-03041:
Huiming Sun and a team of co-authors present VIP, a pipeline for removing humans from video in two thousand twenty-five. Real world clips are high resolution and full of hard contacts. People touch objects, carry things, and cast shadows. Fills must look right and stay steady across frames.

VIP needs no text prompt to run. It boosts a top text to video model with a motion module. A variational autoencoder denoises in steps in a latent space. A precise segment step marks humans and their belongings for masks. Reference frames and a latent fusion trick aid long clips. Tests beat top rivals on hard sets.
arxiv-2504-03541:
Mayank Kothyari and co-authors improve in 2025 how language models turn questions into programs. The model learns from examples shown in the prompt, but whole programs are big, tree-shaped objects. Their idea is to break example programs into fragments and show only the useful pieces.

The system first splits example trees, then uses a prompted model to write matching fragment questions. A diversity-seeking selector then picks a varied set of whole and broken examples for each new question. On standard tests the method raised accuracy visibly. Gains were largest for smaller models, bigger example trees, and languages with little training data.
arxiv-2504-06141:
Alexander Bukharin and eight co-authors introduced Adv-RM in twenty twenty-five, an adversarial training method for reward models. Reward models score language model outputs for alignment training, but they often give high marks to low-quality, off-distribution text. Policies then hack the reward, finding shortcuts instead of genuinely improving.

Adv-RM trains a reinforcement learning policy whose job is to craft responses that fool a target reward model — high scores for bad text. It reliably exposed weaknesses even in a very large state-of-the-art reward model. Folding those adversarial examples back into training made reward models more robust and downstream alignment training more stable. The method outperformed conventional training on both synthetic and real data.
arxiv-2504-06741:
Constantin Ulrich and colleagues pretrained a segmentation network broadly before aiming it at brain injuries in a 2025 paper. Lesions from moderate to severe traumatic brain injury vary wildly in size, shape, and tissue, which breaks general image tools and corrupts downstream steps like registration. Their entry to a 2024 segmentation challenge first trains on a large stack of datasets covering many anatomical and pathological structures, following a multi-talent strategy.

Fine-tuning on injury scans in the standard clinical MRI contrast then specializes the broadly educated network. The pretrained model beat its non-pretrained baseline by up to a couple of overlap points. Broad supervised pretraining, the result suggests, is a strong default for hard medical segmentation.
arxiv-2504-07841:
Nayesha Gandotra and co-authors improve one step planning for many moving agents in this 2025 paper. PIBT is a fast method that picks collision free next moves for hundreds of agents. It returns its first solution in under a millisecond. Greedy priorities make that solution crude, though, and spare time goes unused.

Anytime PIBT keeps improving the step after the first answer. Given enough time, it provably reaches the optimal single step. Quality rose within milliseconds in their experiments. Surprisingly, better single steps barely changed full route costs. Local polish has limits when the whole horizon matters. Still, the method upgrades a core tool inside several leading planners at no risk.
arxiv-2504-09041:
William Schupbach and Kannan Premnath build fluid solvers that borrow their collision rule from the Fokker-Planck equation. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in the lattice Boltzmann method, a grid scheme for flow. Collisions are cast as central moments relaxing toward set targets. Past targets came from the Maxwell spread. Their targets come from matching moment changes under the Fokker-Planck model instead.

Two solvers result: one for the flow equations, one for the energy equation. The targets ride on lower moments and a diffusion tensor, which sets them apart from Maxwell forms. A renormalization rule picks tensor values for thin fluids. Tests in two and three dimensions cover buoyant thermal flows. High Rayleigh numbers run cleanly. Stability beats Maxwell-based rivals, most at high Peclet numbers in mixed flows.
arxiv-2504-10741: Julio César Jaramillo Quiceno introduced a deformed Heisenberg algebra inside a doubled tensor space in a 2025 paper. The q-Heisenberg algebra twists the canonical commutation rules of quantum mechanics by a setting. Placing it on the tensor product of two spaces enriches its representations. Quiceno establishes the algebra's main traits in that setting and applies the building to non-monogenic functions, a class arising in Clifford-style analysis. The work extends known q-deformed constructions and offers tools for working analysis in non-commutative settings.
arxiv-2504-12941:
Vasileva, Mazur, Brandyshev, and Budkov study additives in tiny electrolyte filled pores in twenty twenty-five. The pores are slit like, with charged conducting walls. Additives called osmolytes carry both positive and negative charges in one molecule. The team asks how they change pressure between walls and charge storage.
