They use a modified Poisson-Boltzmann theory to model the system. Raising the osmolyte level boosted both the disjoining pressure and the differential capacitance. The two effects work together in a helpful way. The authors say such additives could improve supercapacitors on two fronts. They may raise capacitive efficiency while also extending the life of microporous electrodes. The work links double layer tuning to device design.
arxiv-2504-13441:
Anita Shahrokhian, Xinwei Deng, and Devon Lin set out ways to learn by choice for tests on screen that mix count type and kind type inputs. Such tests use hard mock models to study real things in place of real tests in labs. Most set ways take just count type inputs. But many real tasks have kind type traits too.

Their text maps key steps in design, models, and calls for such tests. The team then puts forth ways to learn by choice. Those ways aim at models, at best picks, and at lines that bound a trait. Tests with counts weigh the new ways next to old ones. Readers get both a map of the field and new step by step plans. Those plans pick the test runs that tell the most.
arxiv-2504-15441:
Xinyuan Zheng and co-authors lay out a way to simulate strongly interacting light particles in waveguide networks, in work from twenty twenty-five. Waveguide grids already mimic many light effects when particles ignore each other. Adding true interactions, needed for key quantum matter models, had stayed out of reach.

The key device is a gate that shifts phase by particle count, built from a three level atom that adds or removes photons. With it, circuits can mimic the Bose-Hubbard model and fractional quantum Hall physics. The team also shows how to shape steady states that match target ground states. The scheme keeps the platform's perks: single site control, tunable settings, and lean hardware.
arxiv-2504-15941:
Fanny Jourdan, Yannick Chevalier, and Cécile Favre wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents FairTranslate, a data set for testing gender bias when machines translate from English into French.

French forces gender choices that English can leave open, as with the singular they. The data set holds thousands of hand-marked sentence pairs about jobs, tagged with how the job is stereotyped, how vague the source is, and the right label: male, female, or inclusive. The team ran four large language models through it under varied prompts. All showed marked bias in how they cast gender. The set is public, so others can test fixes on it.
arxiv-2504-16141:
Yue Shi, Liangxiu Han, and a team of co-authors reviewed hybrid crop modeling in twenty twenty-five, joining process-based models with deep learning. Process models encode plant and soil physics, giving interpretable rigor but struggling to scale or adapt. Deep learning finds patterns in large data yet can be opaque and brittle where data are scarce.

The review sorts hybrids into two directions: networks that refine process models, and process knowledge that constrains networks. A case study on crop dry biomass compares hybrids against each parent approach across data quality, sample size, and location shifts. Hybrids won consistently, tolerating noise and generalizing to unseen places better. The authors close with challenges — interpretability, scale, data needs — and recommendations for agricultural modeling that weds domain knowledge to AI.
arxiv-2504-19941:
Fandi Oktasendra and four co-authors present a simulation method for fluids touching solids in complex shapes, in a 2025 paper. Flows with several fluids, such as droplets on textured surfaces, are hard to model where the fluids meet the solid. Their method treats the solid as one more component in a multi fluid model, shaped to match any set geometry.

The approach needs no special rule for the fluid solid border, which keeps coding simple. The team shows it working in two standard simulation frameworks. Test cases range from droplet angles on flat surfaces to capillary rise against gravity and droplet motion over wavy surfaces. The method suits the textured surfaces common in nature and engineering.
arxiv-2505-00641: Nan An derives a general formula for the expected time a random walk takes to return to its starting point on a finite graph. Writing in twenty twenty-five, An then applies the framework to bounded rectangular grids. The expected first return time is computed in several grid settings, each under different boundary conditions. The note moves from a graph-wide formula to concrete answers on the grids that model chips, boards, and lattice walks.
arxiv-2505-01041:
Xuyang Chen, Jingliang Duan, and Lin Zhao prove a learning guarantee for actor-critic methods in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Actor-critic algorithms star in modern reinforcement learning, yet their theory lags practice. Most proofs cover slowed-down or double-loop variants that nobody deploys. The authors study the plain version: one sample, one timescale, acting and learning together. Their test bed is the classic linear quadratic regulator, a control problem with endless states and actions.

They show the method reaches near-best control with a modest sample budget. The bound holds on the demanding continuous setting, not a toy grid. This narrows the gap between what practitioners run and what theory promises. The paper serves learning theorists and control researchers.
arxiv-2505-01441:
Joykirat Singh and co-authors present ARTIST in 2025, a way to teach language models to reason with tools. A plain model reasons only from memory and text, yet real problems need fresh facts, code, and stepwise checks. ARTIST lets the model decide on its own when and which tool to call, mid-reasoning.

Training uses reinforcement learning scored only on the final outcome, with no step-by-step teacher. The model learns robust habits for tool use across many turns. On math and multi-step tool-calling tests, ARTIST beat strong baselines, gaining up to twenty-two points over base models. The authors say the training yields deeper reasoning and cleaner tool use.
arxiv-2505-01541:
Thomas Blommel, Enrico Perfetto, Gianluca Stefanucci, and Vojtěch Vlček build one frame to simulate driven, lossy quantum matter in two thousand twenty-five. Light-pulse experiments watch electrons move in real time, but exact theory must juggle both interactions and energy loss, a costly pair.

Past methods, a real-time Dyson expansion and a many-body theory for lossy systems, existed apart. The team merges them into a single working code path. A test on a two-band semiconductor with long-range forces shows conduction electrons settling within their band, which reshapes the band map and shrinks the band gap by up to ten percent. Those traits hold across settings, and the frame opens wider studies.
arxiv-2505-05741:
Hu and seven co-authors presented a detection system in twenty twenty-five for finding tiny objects in wide images, a task that matters for drones, satellite views, and self-driving machines. Small targets drown in large scenes, and most detectors waste effort scanning empty ground.

Their system, Dome-DETR, first builds a rough map of where objects cluster. Attention then focuses computing power on those busy patches instead of the whole frame. A third piece spreads the system's search queries thickly where targets crowd and thinly where they do not. On two standard benchmarks the method set new accuracy records while staying small and cheap to run. The authors release the code openly. The design lesson is simple: spend the budget where the targets are.
arxiv-2505-07141: Yixuan Jia and co-authors plan in 2025 low flight paths that hug the ground, using only camera images and the craft's position. Such nap-of-the-earth flying must be planned in real time. Their training mixes imitation of an expert planner with self-supervised practice, letting the learned policy improve on the expert's paths. In simulation, the method cut average path height by about a quarter compared with plain imitation learning.
arxiv-2505-07541:
Dhruv Chouhan, Tim Schneemann, Kristof Schmieden, and Matthias Schott wrote a design report in two thousand twenty-five for an experiment hunting axion-like particles. Such particles are candidates for dark matter. They should turn into light inside a strong magnetic field when the cavity holding them is tuned to the right frequency.

The experiment, SUPAX, uses a magnet of twelve tesla and tunable superconducting cavities. Its tuning can scan up to three frequencies at once, which speeds the search. The report covers the design, early development work, and prototype results. The prototypes already ruled out a slice of dark photon possibilities that no one had probed.
arxiv-2505-08641:
Parsch wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on how thin liquid films settle into their resting shape. A thin-film equation describes the flow, with a confining force and a second-order spreading term. Without the extra term, solutions were known to relax to the single steady profile at an exponential rate.

The paper asks whether that tidy behavior survives the added physics. If the extra forces are weak enough, it does: solutions still converge globally to the steady profile, just slightly more slowly. The proof recasts the equation as a gradient flow and uses a helper energy function.
arxiv-2505-09241:
Rita Mastroianni and co-authors present a fully formula based propagator for satellites orbiting the Moon, in work from twenty twenty-five. Mission planners need fast, accurate orbit forecasts over years. Numeric propagation is exact but slow, while formula methods can run at once for any time point.

The gravity model holds the twelve top lunar harmonics plus Earth tidal pull with a precise Earth path. Accuracy matched a much larger semi analytic tool for orbits from three hundred to three thousand kilometres up. The method is valid for decades, bar thin zones near resonances. Extra gravity terms can be added with the given formulas. Open code in Python and symbolic form ships with the work.
arxiv-2505-10041:
Jianqi Huang and six co-authors release an open source program for Raman spectra in a 2025 paper. Raman scattering uses light to probe vibrations in materials, and a double resonance version gives extra detail. Their program computes these spectra from first principles, starting from standard quantum simulation outputs.

The program handles ordinary resonance spectra, double resonance spectra, and spectra changed by defects. For defect cases it uses a simple constant assumption for one scattering term. Hands on tutorials use graphene as the example material. Results agree with an earlier Raman program on test cases. All code, examples, and scripts are posted openly for reuse.
arxiv-2505-13341:
Ashish Gurung and six colleagues propose using when students start seatwork as a measure of engagement. Automated detectors built from learning software logs already track self-regulation, but start and stop decisions are underexplored. The team computed session-level measures such as delayed start and early stop from year-long Cognitive Tutor logs for 222 students in grades eight through twelve.

These measures proved reliable month to month and improved prediction of final math scores beyond prior knowledge and gaming-the-system behavior. A second analysis in the i-Ready system, with 818 seventh graders, showed the measures also predict state test scores. The authors argue such log-based measures capture motivation without extra surveys or class disruption.
arxiv-2505-13841:
Yixuan Gao, Xiongkuo Min, and Guangtao Zhai study image quality judgment through pupil size in a 2025 arXiv paper. They ask what happens in the mind when people rate image quality. Pupil size offers a window on that hidden process.

Subjects took part in two tasks: free viewing of images and scoring image quality. The team compared pupil size between the tasks. Scoring seemed to switch on a visual attention mechanism that free viewing did not. Pupil changes during scoring also tracked the quality of the image closely. The work gives theory for objective quality tools and a new way to gather honest quality impressions.
arxiv-2505-14041:
Andreas Debrouwere wrote a 2025 paper in advanced analysis about moment problems. A moment problem asks which number lists can come from averaging powers against some well-behaved function that lives only on a given region. He works with two strict families of smooth functions, the Schwartz class and the Gelfand-Shilov classes.

Debrouwere gives a shape-based test for the regions where every possible number list can be matched by such a function. A matching result holds for the second family as well. Worked examples show how the test plays out in practice. The study extends a recent result that covered measures instead of functions, and it sharpens what analysts know about these spaces.
arxiv-2505-16041:
Siddhant Agarwal and four co-authors speed up simulations of Earth's mantle convection by letting a neural network handle the hardest step. Solving for creeping flow at every timestep dominates the cost of models that run for billions of simulated years. Their hybrid keeps a conventional solver but replaces the flow solve with learned prediction.

The network predicts velocities from the temperature field while exactly conserving mass, and a finite-volume solver advances temperature with those velocities. Training needed snapshots from only ninety-four simulations. On a heated two-dimensional box with pressure- and temperature-dependent viscosity, the hybrid ran up to eighty-nine times faster. Ablations showed mass conservation, learned boundary padding, and loss scaling all mattered for stable rollout.
arxiv-2505-16941:
Jeanselme and colleagues test large pre trained models for health records in a benchmark called FoMoH in twenty twenty-five. Such models promise to work with little labeled data and to move well between hospitals. No shared test had checked if they keep those promises. The team built fourteen tasks that matter in clinics, from outlook to early warning of illness.

They tested six top models on records of more than six million patients from two sources. The best models beat older methods when labeled data were scarce. They also scored more fairly across patient groups. But they did worse on rare conditions and moved poorly to a new hospital. Score trust also fell when labels were scarce.
arxiv-2505-17341:
Dibyajyoti Nayak and Somdatta Goswami present TI-DeepONet, a method to forecast how a physical system evolves over long times. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses neural operators, models that learn maps between functions. Standard versions either jump to a fixed horizon or step forward one frame at a time, piling up error.

Their method learns the rate of change of the state, not the state itself. A classic numerical solver then steps that rate forward, with steps that can grow finer at test time. A variant learns the stage weights of the solver too. On six test equations, errors fell sharply against both older styles, and forecasts stayed stable for near twice the training span.
arxiv-2505-17441:
Can Rager, Chris Wendler, Rohit Gandikota, and David Bau tackle a new task: finding every topic a language model refuses to discuss, in two thousand twenty-five. Refusals are set during safety tuning, but the full list is rarely public. Knowing the list matters for spotting bias and hidden limits.

Their crawler uses a trick that starts the model's reply for it, coaxing out hidden refusals. On an open model with public tuning data, it found most of the known refused topics within a set prompt budget. They then scaled it to larger models. One model showed refusal patterns in line with censorship tuning, which the authors flag as a concern.
arxiv-2505-17641:
Hanze Zhang and four co-authors tackle a speed snag in split-memory computers, where lock steps can clog the network cards on memory nodes. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. In this setup, work nodes and memory nodes are apart, and many jobs must take turns through locks. Under heavy load, lock traffic alone can cut speed by a huge span.

Their fix, DecLock, splits the lock job in two. Memory nodes keep the queue of who waits, while work nodes pass the lock from one to the next by direct notes. Tests showed large speed gains over top past locks. Two real apps kept their speed under load that had slowed them badly before.
arxiv-2505-23141:
Ian Langmore, a solo author, reframes a way to measure distance between probability patterns in a 2025 paper. Such distances, built from kernels, are widely used to compare data sets in machine learning. Langmore shows they can be written as the expected variation of a random field acting on the difference between two patterns.

That viewpoint clarifies which distances allow handy estimates from finite samples. The handy ones come from fields that are spread out, steady in their increments, and unchanged by scaling. A leading example is energy distance. The paper also builds a new distance from a different field and compares signal to noise traits, giving practical intuition for choosing between distances.
arxiv-2506-00241:
Menglin Zhao and Zhuorui Yong lead a team interviewing emergency physicians about letting AI help with serious illness conversations, the hardest talks in medicine. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. These conversations align care with a dying patient's values, yet they rarely happen in emergency departments. Time, scattered information, and documentation burdens all conspire against them.

Eleven providers mapped the work into four stages, from spotting candidates to writing notes. Barriers dogged every stage of that workflow. Providers welcomed AI that synthesizes records, supports the talk in real time, and drafts documentation. They also insisted on guarding human connection and their own judgment. The authors propose ambient, peripheral AI designs that assist without intruding. Efficiency and empathy, the study argues, must be designed together. Neither can be traded for the other.
arxiv-2506-01641:
Van Puyvelde, Zareh, and Develder make heat pump control both smart and explainable in twenty twenty-five. Deep reinforcement learning can manage home energy well. Companies hesitate to adopt it because its decisions are opaque. Decision trees offer clear rules, but full trees grow too deep to read.

Their method builds soft decision trees that grow only where needed. Branches expand adaptively instead of filling a fixed symmetric shape. That saves decision nodes and keeps the tree readable. A controller is distilled from a trained learning agent into the tree. The result aims to keep performance while showing its logic. The authors target home energy management systems. Transparency could help regulators and users trust automated heating.
arxiv-2506-02641:
Charlotte Vastel and Francesco Fontani review molecules found in space in a twenty twenty-five handbook chapter. Their focus is on non-complex organic molecules in the gas phase between stars. New radio telescopes have pushed this field forward, with sharper receivers and wider bandwidth. Many molecular species have now been detected in clouds, in shells around stars, and even in other galaxies.

The first interstellar molecules were found in the nineteen thirties through light in the visible and near ultraviolet ranges. Rotational lines found from the late nineteen sixties opened the radio and submillimeter sky. Bigger molecules give more lines, each weaker, so the hunt gets harder as molecules grow. Readers get a survey of what has been seen and how.
arxiv-2506-03241:
Pablo Díez-Valle and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five linking two quantum computing methods that look alike. One, called QAOA, builds a layered circuit whose angles can be tuned. The other, quantum annealing, slowly changes a system over time. The circuit method can be seen as a sliced version of the annealing path.

The authors show formally and in data that the tuned angles of a many-layer circuit settle onto universal annealing curves. Errors in both methods act like thermal noise in a probability pattern whose temperature drops as more time or angle is invested. Both are thus cooling protocols whose target temperature can be set by scaling. Cooling power follows favorable scaling laws.
arxiv-2506-05641:
Andrey Zhmoginov, Jihwan Lee, and Mark Sandler wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with names in fuller form in its text. It shows how to stamp a small, task-tuned transformer out of a large foundation model in one shot.

Big models know much that a single task does not need, and cost too much for small devices. The method maps the big model's weights to a small one's by a task-set rule. The narrow copy thus holds just the slice of skill the task calls for. On image modeling tasks, the stamped models beat broad conditional models of like size. The work hints at cheap custom models on demand.
arxiv-2506-06841:
Xinxin Rao, Yang Liu, Mingshen Li, Teng Liu, Huabi Zeng, and Le Luo wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests in the lab a forecast that the Kibble-Zurek law for flaw counts breaks down when a system is quenched too fast.

The classic law says the count of topological flaws left after a phase change scales with the quench rate. Fresh theory says that past a set rate, the count stops caring about rate and scales with the quench range instead. With one trapped-ion qubit, the team ran fast quenches in two models. Below a threshold rate the classic law held. Above it, the new range law held. The shift point itself scaled as the theory said.
arxiv-2506-06941:
Parshin Shojaee and five co-authors test reasoning language models on puzzles whose hardness can be dialed up step by step. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Such models write out long chains of thought before answering. Scores on math and code tests show gains, but those tests are prone to contamination. They also say little about how the thinking itself behaves.

Puzzle worlds keep one logic while the size grows, so traces can be judged fairly. Past a set size, every model's accuracy fell to zero. Oddly, the models also tried less hard as puzzles grew past a point, though they had tokens to spare. Three zones emerged: easy tasks favor plain models, mid tasks favor reasoning ones, and hard tasks sink both. The title's claim is that much seeming thinking is an illusion. The results urge care in trusting long traces.
arxiv-2506-07041:
Leijie Wang and colleagues published a study in 2025 on how online communities handle user reports. Reporting systems decide what happens after harassment in private chats and messages. Gathering evidence there is hard, and users worry about fairness and privacy. The authors studied the platform Discord as their main example.

They compare these systems with two legal traditions. In one, officials lead the search for evidence. In the other, the parties control and contest the evidence themselves. Most platforms follow the first model, they find. Giving users more control could improve fairness and privacy. It could also open new paths for abuse. The paper maps design choices that balance those risks.
arxiv-2506-07241:
A polyhedron that runs off to infinity still has a boundary. George Balla, Michael Joswig, and Lena Weis ask whether that boundary can be peeled apart shell by shell in an orderly way. Because the shape never ends, they first study ways to cap it off into a finite form. The capped results then carry over to the shapes they care most about.

Their main payoff concerns tropical hypersurfaces, shapes from a branch of math where addition and multiplication swap roles. The same ideas, restated in the language of discrete Morse theory, show that a related shape called the tight span always collapses down neatly. It cannot always be shelled, though. The work links geometry, counting, and shape theory in one frame.
arxiv-2506-08441:
Nhu, Son, and Lin built a world model in twenty twenty-five that takes time step size as a part of what it learns. Most such models learn at one fixed step, which can miss fast or slow acts in a task. Their model trains on a range of step sizes at once.

That lets it learn both fast and slow traits of a task in one run. The best step rate rests on the task's own pace, a point they ground in signal theory. Across control tasks and read rates it beat plain models with the same data and runs. Gains held as read pace changed.
arxiv-2506-09841:
Rodrigo Negreiros, Jeffrey Peterson, and Veronica Dexheimer present a study from twenty twenty-five on how neutron stars cool when they hold strong magnetic fields. They use a two dimensional code that solves Einstein's and Maxwell's equations as one whole. The field in play is a poloidal one, looped through the star. Its strength sits near what is seen in real stars.

Strong core fields slow the star's heat loss in a marked way. Stars of like mass but unlike fields then cool on unlike paths. The lag grows in a non-linear way with field strength. The team ties the lag to a curb on a fast cooling path, the direct Urca process. The field's sway shows long before it warps the matter spread.
arxiv-2506-10241:
Tatsuo Kobayashi, Hironobu Mita, Hajime Otsuka, and Riku Sakuma examine what non-invertible selection rules imply for supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model. Such rules arise from fusion algebras in string-derived models. The authors find that a remnant two-fold symmetry of the fusion algebra survives at all loop orders and plays the role of R-parity.

That symmetry forbids operators violating baryon and lepton number. Combined with Standard Model gauge symmetry, the selection rules also yield baryon triality and proton hexality, protecting the proton from decay. The authors clarify which matter field assignments fit grand unified theories based on different gauge groups, and note where selection rules outperform conventional discrete symmetries.
arxiv-2506-11741:
Justin Edmondson bounds quantum resources in finite systems in two thousand twenty five. Entanglement, redundancy, and coherence each power quantum gains in practice. They also trade off against each other in hard ways. He unifies three tasks under one geometric constraint.

Teleportation, cloning, and coherence based metrology get task scores here. The squares of the three scores sum to at most one. All reachable states sit in one octant of the unit ball. The scores are measurable, so the bound can be falsified. Symmetry steps conserve the norm, while decoherence shrinks it.
arxiv-2506-13941:
Pokharel and a large team watch charge patterns shift inside a kagome superconductor as holes are added in twenty twenty-five. The metal's atoms form a woven lattice tied to both charge order and superconductivity. Swapping titanium for some vanadium adds holes. X ray scattering and magnetic scans tracked charge order and the super flow together.

In the first dome of superconductivity, two rival charge patterns fought inside the ordered state. Added holes killed them fast. In the second dome, no charge order showed at all. Vortex views stayed plain and steady throughout. Doping by site gave unlike disorder effects, the team notes.
arxiv-2506-14741:
Yueke Hu, Ian Petrow, and Matthew Young proved new bounds in 2025 on averages of values of L-functions, the central objects of modern number theory. The cubic moment, an average of cubes of values at the central point, controls deep questions about how those values are distributed. Earlier work bounded it for families of automorphic representations whose local behavior at chosen primes was of the simplest kinds; the hard supercuspidal case resisted.

Using summation formulas the authors themselves recently developed for supercuspidal families, they now prove Lindelöf-strength bounds on average in that case too. The corollaries include subconvexity bounds of Weyl strength, the gold standard of saving, in several aspects at once, depth, square-full level, and hybrids. One special case gives the Weyl bound for every cusp form of squared-prime level, where previously only about half of those forms were covered.
arxiv-2506-16141:
Yi Chen and colleagues found in 2025 that a popular reinforcement learning method can make multimodal models more accurate but less coherent. GRPO, an outcome-supervised technique, improved chain-of-thought reasoning in text models. Nobody had rigorously tested its transfer to models that also see images and video. The team built SEED-Bench-R1, a benchmark of complex real-world videos demanding both perception and reasoning, with tests escalating from familiar settings to new environments and tasks.

Standard GRPO raised answer accuracy, yet the reasoning often stopped matching the answer, with consistency under sixty percent. Rewards based only on final answers encourage shortcuts, and strict penalties limit exploration. Their fix, GRPO-CARE, adds consistency awareness to the training. The work is a caution for multimodal AI: scoring the destination while ignoring the route teaches models to bluff convincingly.
arxiv-2506-20341:
Marco Laudato, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, trained a fast stand in model for platelet shape change. Platelets are the small blood cells that help form clots. True models of clots need cell level truth at organ level cost, a gap that is hard to bridge. Laudato trained a neural operator on runs from a physics code. The runs spanned ten stiffness levels and a wide range of flow rates.

The network reads shear stress, bond stiffness, time, and start points of the membrane. It gives back the full three dimensional shape change. Errors stayed near one percent for the middle case, and speed rose by four to five orders. Readers who model clots get a near exact tool at a far lower cost.
arxiv-2506-20841:
Son, Rezaei, and Liu built a learn tool in twenty twenty-five for models that must work on new kinds of data with few marked cases. Few marks make broad skill hard to train. Their tool adds a push-apart step that uses guessed marks to keep class traits the same across kinds.

The step uses just the push-apart part of a known self-teach way, with no pull part. It can sit on top of most tools of its kind for extra gains. Wide tests span pre-trained and fresh models and sets with many kinds. The tool proves strong in that broad run, they find.
arxiv-2506-23441:
Naoki Seto wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It asks whether LISA, a planned space-based detector of gravitational waves, can pick up higher harmonic signals from close pairs of white dwarf stars.

Thousands of such pairs in our galaxy should give off near steady waves in the millihertz band. Seto shows LISA is quite likely to catch the higher mode from a small set of near pairs, even though their orbital speeds are tiny next to the speed of light. The strength of these modes can show how uneven the two masses are. That makes them prized targets, above all in pairs where one star feeds mass to the other.
arxiv-2507-04141:
Mohsen Azarmi, Mahdi Rezaei, and He Wang test vision-language foundation models for pedestrian crossing prediction in this two thousand twenty-five study. Knowing whether a pedestrian intends to cross is critical for autonomous vehicles. Conventional vision methods often generalize poorly and reason weakly about context and causes. The authors instead feed visual frames, physical cue observations, and ego-vehicle dynamics into hierarchical prompt templates for the models.

Experiments ran on three standard datasets, JAAD, PIE, and FU-PIP. Adding vehicle speed, its change over time, and time-aware wording raised accuracy by up to about twenty percent. An automatic prompt engineering framework added further gains of about twelve percent. The results suggest foundation models beat conventional vision methods on generalization and contextual understanding for this safety task.
arxiv-2507-04741:
Yasser Dahou and co-authors present a benchmark from two thousand twenty-five testing whether vision-language models notice the obvious. Humans spot a big circle among small ones at a glance. Such pop-out features, in color, brightness, or tilt, are basic to human vision, yet models that describe images fluently may miss them entirely.

Their benchmark, called SalBench, holds images with rare or odd elements that draw the eye. Three tasks ask models to find the odd one out, to follow a text pointer to it, or to ground it from a referring phrase. Even a top commercial model scored under half correct on the simplest task. The authors offer the benchmark as a step toward models whose attention matches human attention.
arxiv-2507-05041:
Jaume Cunill-Subiranas and co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper on the magnetic flux that threads the hole in a flat superconductor. Such sheets screen out magnetic fields completely. A small dipole magnet was placed on the axis of the sheet for the analysis.

The team works out the currents in the sheet with pure mathematics. They give a simple rule that links three things: the flux through the hole, the net current circling it, and the strength and position of the dipole. That rule must be combined with the basic screening equations to understand each case. They then examine four cases. Two fix the flux under different cooling styles. One is a slit sheet where the circling current is zero. One is a self-inductance case, where the flux comes from the screening currents alone. The results can serve as a check for tiny devices now being built.
arxiv-2507-06941:
Alexandra Ramôa, Raffaele Santagati, and Nathan Wiebe tested advanced statistical samplers in twenty twenty-five for calibrating quantum devices. Bayesian inference suits real-time characterization when data are scarce, but its power hinges on how the probability distributions are represented numerically. The team benchmarked a shelf of methods — sequential importance resampling, tempered likelihoods, several Monte Carlo flavors, and Gaussian rejection filtering.

The advanced methods proved more robust when distributions had many peaks or high dimensions. Applied to IBM superconducting qubits, they beat the standard quantum limit and Qiskit's default tools. In echo and Ramsey experiments, uncertainty fell tenfold and threefold at equal data, or matched quality with up to ninety-nine point five percent less data.
arxiv-2507-07141:
Dongxiao He and co-authors taught graph learning to use common sense in 2025. Graph contrastive learning trains encoders by weighing altered views of a graph, and it makes strong versions without labels, but it mostly harvests implicit numeric patterns. Graphs also carry structural commonsense, regularities about how links and traits hang, which standard methods overlook because nothing in the raw data states it clearly.

Their method, Str-GCL, writes that commonsense down as first-order logic rules, covering both the graph's topology and its traits, and weaves the rules into training without modifying the graph itself. A version alignment process then pushes the encoder to honor the rules as it learns. Showed at a leading web conference. The work is described as the first to bring clear structural commonsense into graph contrastive learning, aiming at versions that respect how the domain works.
arxiv-2507-08441:
Anlin Zheng and seven co-authors build an image tokenizer straight on a frozen vision foundation model in a two thousand twenty-five computer vision paper. Tokenizers turn images into discrete tokens that autoregressive models can generate, and they are usually trained from scratch.

Their tokenizer, VFMTok, keeps the foundation model as a fixed encoder. A region-adaptive rounding step removes redundancy in the grid features, and a semantic reconstruction objective keeps outputs faithful to the foundation model's representations. Reconstruction and making quality improve while tokens are used with less waste. On ImageNet the system reaches a making FID of 1.36, settles three times faster, and needs no classifier-free guidance.
arxiv-2507-09441:
Ankit Sanjyal, a solo author, presents a method to make high-resolution images with diffusion models more stable, in two thousand twenty-five. At large sizes, the sampling process can drift in energy and produce guidance artifacts. Those flaws lower the visual quality of the final image.

Sanjyal profiles the energy of the hidden image state as sampling proceeds. Guidance strength is then scheduled to keep that energy path steady over time. One sampler pairing, with guidance that falls in a straight line, gave the best results. The reported stability and consistency scores beat fixed guidance, with sharper and more faithful images and fewer artifacts.
arxiv-2507-10241:
Vikas Dwivedi, Balaji Srinivasan, Monica Sigovan, and Bruno Sixou propose a kernel adaptive learning machine in two thousand twenty-five. Their target is equations with sharp slopes, where past physics based learners fail. One past type is biased to smooth waves. The other is one shot and cannot adapt its shape.

Their method tunes where radial basis kernels sit and how wide they are. Search runs over a small set of clear knobs, not all weights. That lets kernels crowd where slopes are steep. Tests cover flow and heat type equations, plus a hard cavity flow case. The method matched or beat strong rivals with far fewer knobs to tune.
arxiv-2507-12241:
Arnaud Serret-Larmande, Jérôme Lambert, Stéphane Gaudry, and David Hajage wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about comparing treatments across trials when no head-to-head trial exists. Analysts reweight one trial's patients to match another's published averages. The most used method is called MAIC, but its behavior when patient groups barely overlap was little tested.

The team ran Monte Carlo simulations across eight scenarios, from ideal overlap to strong violations and odd, two-humped covariate shapes. Matching on averages alone stayed unbiased under moderate violations, while richer matching and a full-data benchmark bent more easily. All methods failed when key confounders were left out. A real example on kidney therapy in critical care matched the simulated pattern.
arxiv-2507-12541:
Kriti Kamal Gupta and colleagues ask what controls how much of a feeding black hole energy comes out as X-rays. Active galactic nuclei shine across the spectrum as gas falls in, but the disk and corona picture does not predict several features. A clue is the X-ray share of total output, which earlier work tied to brightness and feeding rate relative to the maximum. Those measures are linked, so the true driver was unclear. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team analyzed simultaneous data from ultraviolet to hard X-rays for a large sample of nearby unobscured nuclei.

The feeding rate ratio, not brightness, emerged as the main regulator of the X-ray share. As the ratio climbs, the X-ray fraction falls in a consistent pattern. The result gives model builders a cleaner rule for how accretion power splits between the hot corona and cooler disk.
arxiv-2507-13141:
Chattopadhyay, Das, Puri, and Roy wrote in twenty twenty-five about limits on hypothetical flavor-changing processes in particle physics. Charged lepton flavor violation would prove physics beyond the Standard Model. No experiment has seen it yet, despite careful searches. Effective field theory lets physicists bound new effects without knowing their source. The authors focus on operators linking two quarks with two leptons. Many low-energy processes can constrain exactly those operators.

They collect the relevant low-energy violation searches in one place. They also collect the full set of operators behind those processes. Because operators correlate with each other, joint treatment gives stronger bounds. Their goal is the strongest combined limits on this operator class. The work guides where future searches can bite hardest.
arxiv-2507-13441:
Hyerin Cho and Ramesh Narayan study variability in black hole accretion in two thousand twenty-five. Hot flows onto black holes are often simulated from small spinning tori. Those runs give stable jets with small swings. Bondi like starts, though, have shown jets that blink and spin that breaks.

The team grows the torus huge and runs far longer than past work. Big range alone does not breed strong swings, they find. Spin trims the inflow rate by clear factors in their runs. A much stronger start field, though, sparks wild swings. Jet power can range over orders of magnitude, and gas spin can flip.
arxiv-2507-13541:
Li and co-authors introduce PrefPalette, a way to model what users like by splitting taste into named traits. Standard preference models treat judgment as a black box. Yet people weigh traits like formality, humor, and cultural fit when they choose. PrefPalette builds training data that isolates one trait at a time. It then learns how social groups weight those traits as they judge. An attention design handles the shifting weights.

The frame draws on multi-attribute decision making from cognitive science. Predictions stay readable, since each trait's role is visible. The method aims to serve groups whose values differ from the average. Aggregate scores, the authors argue, wash out those differences.
arxiv-2507-14041:
Stefano Covino asked how surprising the brightest gamma-ray burst ever seen really was, in a 2025 statistics paper. The 2022 burst nicknamed the BOAT outshone all recorded rivals by orders of magnitude in brightness and total energy. Rather than assume a physical model for bursts, Covino let general extreme value statistics speak, using catalogs from two satellite instruments spanning many years.

He collected brightness, peak flux, and duration, took the extremes within equal time slots, and fitted the standard extreme value distribution, which describes record events for any large population. The fit tests whether one population of bursts can produce such an outlier by chance. Model-free checks like this discipline speculation about whether the BOAT needs new physics.
arxiv-2507-14941:
Armand Despons, Jérémie Unterberger, and David Lacoste find a simpler way to tell when a self-copying chemical network can hold its ground against decay. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Such networks must copy or maintain their parts faster than those parts break down. The balance point is a decay threshold.

For networks whose math has a helpful sign pattern, the team borrows tools from the theory of random walks. The threshold then comes from solving a straight linear problem. That is far easier than the eigenvalue hunt used before. They trace how the threshold shifts with network size, link density, and whether steps can run backward. From those trends they draw design rules for building persistent networks. The rules may guide origin-of-life research on the first self-copying chemistries.
arxiv-2507-15741:
Gabor Lugosi and Marcos Matabuena built ways in twenty twenty-five to gauge uncertainty for regression on metric spaces. In such spaces the outputs can be distributions, graphs, or shapes. They are not plain numbers. The intervals for prediction there need distribution-free guarantees. They need to adapt to local noise too. The pair first define homoscedasticity, or constant noise, for this new setting.

When noise is constant, their conformal algorithm gives finite-sample marginal coverage. It nears the ideal prediction region fast. When noise varies, a nearest-neighbor procedure adapts the width of the interval to the local case. It makes no smoothing assumptions. It gives up the finite-sample guarantee, though. A sequential extension deals with metric-valued time series. They prove consistency under mild conditions. They show the frame on personalized medicine problems. The outputs there are distributions and graphs.
arxiv-2507-16341:
Mingtao Guo, Guanyu Xing, Yanci Zhang, and Yanli Liu presented FRVD in twenty twenty-five, a video diffusion model for face reenactment under large head turns. Reenactment drives a still portrait with another person's motion. When the head turns far, warping tears the image or coarse landmarks lose the pose, breaking identity or realism.

Their pipeline first extracts implicit facial keypoints from source and driver and aligns motion by warping. A mapper then fixes warping damage by projecting the result into the latent space of a pre-trained image-to-video model. That space carries rich priors about how faces move, restoring quality and time consistency. Experiments show gains in pose accuracy, identity preservation, and visual quality, largest exactly in the extreme-pose cases that defeat earlier methods.
arxiv-2507-17541:
Vilhelm Agdur and five colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on measuring community structure in networks that change over time. Modularity scores how well a network splits into tight groups. In temporal graphs, links appear and vanish step by step, as in real social ties.

Even for still networks, modularity is NP-hard to compute well. The authors study graphs whose hidden backbone is narrow, a trait measured by treewidth. Their main result gives a multiplicative approximation for temporal modularity on such graphs. That is, the algorithm's score stays within a fixed factor of the best. Narrow backbones are common in road and contact networks, so the result has wide reach.
arxiv-2507-18441:
Zachariah Addison and Nandini Trivedi derive a local measure in two thousand twenty-five for the Hall effect in messy materials. Topological insulators carry Hall currents, but disorder breaks the symmetry that standard formulas rely on. The authors write an expression for the response at each point in such systems.

They use it to study how the Hall signal varies around disordered patches in magnetic insulators. Adding non-magnetic disorder widened the range where the system stays in its Chern phase. Splitting one big patch into many small ones, at the same total disorder, also enlarged the region of the disorder-born phase. The authors expect the results to guide local scanning tests on these materials.
arxiv-2507-19441:
Srinivas Rao and four co-authors mined satellite photometry in twenty twenty-five to refine the clockwork of V709 Cassiopeiae, an intermediate polar. In such a system a magnetic white dwarf siphons gas from a companion star. Long, rapid-cadence light curves from the TESS survey allowed a careful timing analysis of the system's overlapping cycles.

They measured an orbital period near five point three hours, a white dwarf spin just under three hundred thirteen seconds, and the beat period between them, all far more precisely than before. The pattern shows gas mostly arrives through a disk, though at some epochs the stream feeds the poles directly. Harmonics in the fastest data reveal double-peaked spin modulation: signatures of accretion onto both magnetic poles.
arxiv-2507-19641:
Yue and three colleagues use one rare particle to pin down the width of another in twenty twenty-five. Both particles may be loose pairs of two known particles bound as molecules. A collider team in Europe recently spotted the first of the two. Width tells how long a particle lasts before it breaks apart.

Treating both as molecule like pairs, the team models how each one decays. Their model matches the known width of the new particle when one decay path rules. In that same range, the older particle's width must fall in a narrow band. That band sits well below the best current upper limit. The result gives future tests a sharp target.
arxiv-2507-20041:
Daniel Manor, Mor Perry, and Moshe Sulamy present a concurrent data structure for sets that stays fast when updates dominate and range questions must be answered atomically. Most concurrent sets are tuned for read-heavy work and sag under heavy writing, while the update-tuned rivals handle range queries poorly. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team builds on a balanced (a,b)-tree design that splits nodes within a size band. Their structure guarantees linearizability, the formal promise that every operation appears to happen at a single instant between its start and finish.

In head-to-head tests on range query operations, the new set beat leading update-optimized rivals by up to double, according to the authors. The paper speaks to builders of in-memory databases and other shared-state systems where writers and range scans collide constantly.
arxiv-2507-21141:
McNair Shah, Saleena Angeline, and colleagues map the internal geometry of harmful content in language models in a 2025 study. Safety work needs to find and curb harmful behavior inside a model, not just filter its outputs. Treating harm as one blob may miss its many distinct forms.

The authors learn separate linear probes for dozens of harmfulness sub-concepts, such as racial hate, scams, and weapons. Together those probe directions span a harmfulness space that turns out to be strikingly low in dimension. Tests then remove that whole subspace from the model's internals. A compact map of harm could make steering and safety checks more precise.
arxiv-2507-22341:
Pegah Mohammadipour and Xiantao Li showed in twenty twenty-five how extrapolation can shrink the circuits needed to simulate open quantum systems. Lindblad dynamics describe systems leaking into their environment; simulating them on quantum hardware demands deep circuits whose depth grows steeply as the target accuracy tightens. The authors apply Richardson-style extrapolation across simulation step sizes.

Backward error analysis gives an expansion of the simulated state in the step size, with explicit coefficient bounds. Those bounds certify the smoothness extrapolation needs and let them control both its bias and its shot-noise cost. Their main theorem cuts the needed depth from polynomial in inverse accuracy to polylogarithmic — an exponential improvement — while sampling cost stays standard. Experiments support the practicality.
arxiv-2508-00941:
Hassan Ugail and four co-authors evaluated diffusion-based photo enhancement for forensic face recognition in twenty twenty-five. Recognition systems collapse on the degraded images typical of evidence: compressed, blurred, noisy. Their pipeline applied a latent diffusion model, Flux.1 Kontext with a face-focused adapter, to restore such faces before matching.

The test drew three thousand people from a standard face data set, with twenty-four thousand recognition attempts across seven degradation types. Enhancement lifted overall accuracy from twenty-nine percent to eighty-four point five percent, a gain of over fifty-five points. Every degradation category improved significantly, with effect sizes beyond practical thresholds. The authors conclude modern diffusion restoration can rescue forensic identification that would otherwise fail, a result with direct investigative value.
arxiv-2508-01641:
Yujian Liu and seven co-authors argue that a few sharp patches can speak for a whole microscope slide. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Pathology slides are gigapixel images with sparse diagnostic zones. Standard pipelines chop them into countless small patches. Feature extractors trained on photos then misread tissue. Self-supervised fixes still inherit the chopping problem.

Their cascaded method rebuilds slide representations at two scales. Reconstruction tasks teach features matched to histology, not photos. Only minimal high-resolution patches prove necessary. Structures stay whole instead of being shredded across tiles. Redundant and dependent patches stop dragging down the aggregator. Slide-level prediction gets leaner and sharper inputs.
arxiv-2508-06141:
Marco Bertuletti and co-authors build a fast simulator for testing many-core radio chips long before the hardware exists. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Next-generation mobile networks need baseband processors that bend with changing standards. Programmable clusters of small cores promise that bend, but testing them is slow.

Their tool translates the chip's programs ahead of time and adds a rough timing model. It links the chip model to wireless channel models for end-to-end runs. A cluster of over a thousand RISC-V cores is simulated this way. Spotting a 5G signal takes seconds to minutes on one thread. That is a thousand times faster than gate-level simulation. Spreading the work over many threads speeds it further still. Designers can now sweep design choices in hours, not months.
arxiv-2508-08441:
Yunyue Su and six co-authors teach a language model to read spectra and name the molecule, with SpectraLLM. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles structure elucidation, long chained to databases or single instruments. Their model reasons over several spectral kinds at once: infrared, Raman, ultraviolet-visible, and NMR as continuous traces, mass spectra as discrete peaks. All are rendered into one shared language space.

Pretraining and fine-tuning on small molecules precede tests on four public benchmarks. The model tops the state of the art and beats single-modality baselines soundly. It stays robust when only one spectrum is offered, and improves further as modalities join. The authors frame language itself as the universal solvent for spectroscopic evidence.
arxiv-2508-08741:
Junya Fujimoto and Masaru Kajisawa study post-starburst galaxies in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such galaxies have recently stopped a burst of star formation. The authors measured color gradients in galaxies at redshift near zero point eight, in the COSMOS field.

They compared thirty-three post-starburst galaxies with quiescent and star-forming ones, using Hubble telescope data. Color gradients fell as central asymmetry rose in all three groups. Only post-starburst galaxies with strong asymmetry showed positive gradients, hinting at young stars near the center. Those galaxies were also very small, which fits a recent gas-rich merger that lit a nuclear burst. Galaxies with weak asymmetry looked dustier and larger, and may have a different origin.
arxiv-2508-08841:
Makinson, Oman, and Swinbank present a way to model how nearby galaxies spin, in twenty twenty-five. The MHONGOOSE survey maps hydrogen gas in thirty dwarf and spiral galaxies. Each is seen at several levels of detail, with map depth varying widely. A model built from one level can show sharp jumps that are not real.

The team fits a motion model at each level, then blends the fits into one set of curves. The blend uses weights drawn from tests on fake galaxies with known spin curves and shapes. The blended tilt and angle curves are smooth and look much more real. With those shapes fixed, spin speed and spread are fit at each level and blended too. The end curves use all the data at hand and have smaller built in flaws than curves from one level alone, most of all near the core and the outer edge.
arxiv-2508-11241:
Hangjun Cho, Jiu-Gang Dong, Seung-Yeal Ha, and Seung-Yeon Ryoo studied synchronization in the inertial Kuramoto model in twenty twenty-five. The Kuramoto model describes how coupled oscillators, from fireflies to power grid generators, fall into step. Its inertial version adds mass-like lag, making each oscillator a second-order system. The team treats small inertia as a perturbation of the classic model.

They prove a quantitative Tikhonov theorem, which tracks how closely the inertial system follows the classic one. From it they derive a new synchronization result for small inertia, with strong bounds on the order parameter that measures coherence. They also probe whether phase speeds can be read off from positions alone, showing the perturbation view only holds for small inertia. The work complements their earlier phase-locking results.
arxiv-2508-12441:
Yury Grabovsky and Lev Truskinovsky broadened a classic theorem of elasticity in 2025 into a group of new integral identities. Clapeyron's theorem expresses the energy stored in a stretched elastic body through the work of forces applied at its edge. The classic result belongs to linear elasticity. The authors derive nonlinear analogs, reinterpreted as general statements in the calculus of changes.

In the nonlinear setting, the relations reflect partial symmetries of a substance's response, such as scale invariance or scaling homogeneity. When the energy is scale-free, their broadened theorem emerges, naturally joining the work of normal actual forces with configurational forces, which drive defects and links. A series of case studies shows the identities at work. For builders and mathematicians, such rules turn bulk energy into edge bookkeeping, simplifying both theory and computation.
arxiv-2508-13341:
Fathi studies the shadow of a spinning, charged black hole in a space with a pull at large scales in twenty twenty-five. A black hole's shadow is the dark patch it casts in images from radio telescopes. His model adds a nonlinear form of electromagnetism, which bends the rules for electric fields near the hole. He builds the shadow for watchers at set distances, since space here is not flat far away.

He charts how spin, charge, and the nonlinear term change the shadow's size and shape. Real images of two black holes then bound those values. He also works out how fast the hole sheds energy. Spin and the new term both shape the shadow strongly.
arxiv-2508-13841:
Colin Cleveland, Bart de Keijzer, and Maria Polukarov wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about where a new election candidate should stand on multiple issues. In spatial voting, voters and candidates are points in a space of positions, and each voter backs the closest candidate. Campaigns face this placement problem in real life.

The authors prove that computing the best spot is computationally hard even against a single rival. When the number of issues is fixed, though, exact algorithms exist, and they give two, one of them fast for the two-issue case. They also give the first approximation guarantees for races with many candidates. The geometric methods extend to scoring rules such as approval-style and Borda counts.
arxiv-2508-14641:
Jia-Kun Li and nine co-authors build a CNOT gate on a photonic rig that mimics Majorana zero modes. Their paper from twenty twenty-five encodes two logical qubits in three Kitaev chains. The chains hold Majorana modes at their ends. Braiding moves, within and between chains, carry out the gate logic.

The photonic setting lacks full topological shielding, since its parts do not interact. Still, the encoding shrugs off the main noise and decoherence at play in the lab. Gate fidelity lands above a high mark the authors report. That clears a known hurdle on the path to scalable quantum machines. The team frames the result as a step for topological computing with Majorana fermions. Light-based rigs gain credit as hosts for high-fidelity gates.
arxiv-2508-16541:
Tiago Aprigio and João Paulo Guardieiro characterize special polynomials over finite fields in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A binomial's value set is the collection of outputs it takes. Minimal value set binomials produce the fewest possible outputs, an extremal case worth pinning down.

The authors classify all such binomials completely. Building on that list, they also classify a family of curves built from separated variables. Those curves are tested for a Frobenius nonclassical property tied to a line morphism, a subtle geometric distinction. The two classifications fit together: extremal function behavior on one side, curve geometry on the other. The work adds exact catalogs to finite field theory, where examples are often found by search rather than proof.
arxiv-2508-17641:
Xun Tang and co-authors speed up entropic optimal transport under martingale style constraints, in work from twenty twenty-five. Optimal transport moves mass at least cost between distributions. Martingale constraints, common in finance, force the plan to keep certain averages fair.

Exact constraints are often infeasible, so the team uses an entropic form that finds a near satisfying plan. Their Sinkhorn style method adds sparse Newton steps that exploit the lean structure of the dual problem. In practice the method converges super fast and stays robust, with tunable caps on constraint misses. The approach also covers a broad class of transport problems with row wise structural limits.
arxiv-2508-19141:
Federico Chiariotti and Andrea Zanella build theory for goal-oriented access in twenty twenty-five. Goal-oriented communication drops the wall between data and its use. Transmission choices are tailored to what the receiver needs for its task. Encoding gains are proven for one-to-one links, but multi-node settings are barely explored.

Most multi-node work assumes a central scheduler with no collisions. The authors instead study distributed access, where agents share a wireless channel themselves. They must coordinate to avoid interference without a central order-giver. A theoretical framework for analysis and optimization is proposed. They prove the problem is non-convex and may admit certain solution forms. Readers get a first step toward a full theory of distributed goal-oriented access.
arxiv-2508-20241:
Bischoff, del Pino, and Witte wrote in twenty twenty-five about a class of singular foliations in geometry. A foliation splits a space into sheets, like pages in a book. Their structures describe vector fields that touch a submanifold to a set order. When that submanifold is a surface, the structures generalize known tangent bundles. The authors introduce and classify these objects in full.

They prove the structures are encoded by finite-order data near the submanifold. That data can be read as foliations on a thickened neighborhood. Using it, they build groupoids and apply a holonomy tool to classify the structures. The result resembles classic Riemann-Hilbert style sorting. Extending the data by one order is blocked by a characteristic class, which they identify.
arxiv-2508-20441:
Ruben Solozabal and four co-authors study hidden biases in state space models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. These sequence models are usually seeded by a framework built on polynomial approximations. Simpler diagonal versions run faster, but how their starting values bias learning was unclear.

Looking through a frequency lens, the team shows how pole placement at the start steers what the model learns. They propose a new diagonal seeding scheme defined in the Fourier domain. The insight lets them scale the models up with confidence. On a long-range benchmark, the approach reached state-of-the-art results, training from scratch even on very long sequences. The authors argue initialization deserves the same care as architecture.
arxiv-2508-20841: Araújo and Sobral study a free boundary problem from superconductivity where the governing law is nonlocal. The work extends a local theory by Caffarelli, Salazar, and Shahgholian to the nonlocal case. In these models, no equation rules the moving sets where the gradient vanishes. Test functions there only need a nonzero gradient, which shapes the whole analysis. The main results give interior gradient Hölder regularity estimates for viscosity solutions of these degenerate problems.
arxiv-2509-00041:
Takahiro Hiraki leads a team with twenty-five co-authors who extend Mössbauer spectroscopy into the optical range in 2025 using thorium-229. The classic method reads tiny shifts in gamma rays to reveal a material's inner build. Here a vacuum ultraviolet laser probes low-energy nuclear shifts of thorium set inside calcium fluoride crystals.

Four distinct sites for thorium ions are found, with their electric field patterns measured. The inner build of the two main sites is pinned down. Site-picked laser light lets the team time how long the excited state lasts and how laser light can quench it. Such base data are key steps toward solid-state nuclear clocks, which would keep time by nuclear ticks.
arxiv-2509-00241:
Douglas Coates and Katrin Gelfert study generic points for non-statistical dynamical systems in 2025 through Hausdorff dimension. A dynamical system evolves a state by a fixed rule. Generic points are those whose long-run averages sample the whole space, and a physical measure is one whose basin draws in a visible set of starts.

Their maps in one dimension have several neutral fixed points and admit no physical measures at all. Even so, they build a simplex, a full family, of measures such that each measure's basin has full Hausdorff dimension. Hausdorff dimension gauges how thick a set is at fine scales. Full dimension shows that generic behavior can be vast even when no measure is physical.
arxiv-2509-00641:
Zhipeng Yin leads a team of six authors on copyright risk in image models. Text-to-image models train on huge datasets of images. They may copy protected elements into new outputs. Prompt filters can block risky wording at input. But benign prompts can still yield infringing images. Subtle cases thus slip past simple filters.

The team proposes AMCR to close that gap. AMCR first rewrites risky prompts into safe forms. It then detects partial copying through attention-based similarity checks. Last, it adapts its safeguards during image generation itself. Quality of the image is kept in view throughout. Broad tests validate the full framework. They show it can reveal and cut hidden copyright risks. The work also offers benchmarks for safer deployment.
arxiv-2509-00841:
Michelle Elizabeth leads a team of seven authors on scoring open-ended conversations. Generative dialogue systems are growing fast in number. Judging their quality has become a crucial challenge. The work targets a Dialogue System Technology Challenge track. Models must give dialogue-level scores per dimension. All models used must stay under thirteen billion parameters.

The team pursues two strategies in parallel. One prompts language models to act as evaluators. The other trains encoder-based classification and regression models. Prompting achieves only modest agreement with human judgments. It still ranks second on the test set, behind only the baseline. The smaller trained models agree well on some validation dimensions. Their scores drop on the test set, though. Its score ranges differ sharply for some dimensions.
arxiv-2509-01141:
Gaps in atmospheric records, caused by equipment limits and harsh weather, hinder the study of how the air moves and changes. Jiahui Hu, Wenjun Dong, and Alan Z. Liu propose CT-MVP, a learning model that fills in missing values across place, time, and height. It handles several variables at once, including temperature and winds.

The model joins convolutional networks, which pick up local patterns, with transformers, which track links over long spans of time and height. Training used a thirteen-year data set from a whole-atmosphere climate model with global coverage. Tests under varied gap patterns check how well the filled values hold up. Hu and the team aim for complete records that support stronger analysis of atmospheric processes.
arxiv-2509-01241:
Object detection models are notoriously hard to picture, and RT-DETRv2, a real-time detector, is no exception. Ethan Qi Yang Chua and Jen Hong Tan set out to explain its design through eight carefully drawn illustrations. Existing diagrams, they argue, do little to show how the parts actually work together.

The article moves from the whole pipeline down to key pieces, including the encoder, the decoder, and multi-scale deformable attention. It visualizes how tensors flow through the system and unpacks the logic behind each module. Chua and Tan aim to give researchers and practitioners a clear mental model of the detector under the hood. The piece is a teaching guide rather than a new model, built to make a complex design genuinely understandable.
arxiv-2509-01341:
Pinpointing where a street photo was taken supports navigation, local recommendations, and city planning, but social media images make the task hard. Yunus Serhat Bicakci, Joseph Shingleton, and Anahid Basiri combine multimodal language models with retrieval to locate images at street level. Their method needs no costly fine-tuning of the models.

First, a vector database is built with an image encoder over two large data sets of geotagged photos. A query image is then paired with prompts that include both similar and dissimilar location hints drawn from that database. The language model reasons over those hints to name a place. Tests on three widely used benchmarks beat prior leading results. The authors present the system as a practical route to accurate image geolocation from open and public tools.
arxiv-2509-02141:
Mohit Mendiratta leads five co-authors with GRMM, a real time morphable head model built from Gaussian primitives. Morphable models enable face editing for reconstruction, animation, and virtual reality, but mesh versions lack detail and realism. Neural volumetric rivals look better yet run too slowly for interactive use. Gaussian splatting models render fast but lean only on mesh priors for expression control.

GRMM augments a base morphable model with learned residual geometry and appearance. Residuals recover wrinkles, skin texture, and hairline detail beyond the base. Separate decoders handle coarse mesh motion, per Gaussian appearance, and a final image refinement. A new dataset aligns dozens of expressions across many identities for training. The system renders in real time while beating rivals on fidelity.
arxiv-2509-02241:
Strahinja Klem and Noura Al Moubayed give a staged prompt way to ask and answer on long law docs. To fine tune models for law costs a lot, and trust plus clear logs slow take up. Their swap shapes prompts in a staged way in place of fresh training. Docs from a pact data set are split and padded to beat length caps.

A shaped prompt feeds a broad use model that gives a set of picks per query. Two rules then pick from those picks by spread of picks and a weight on pick count. Scores beat the past way by a clear share and reach the top mark on the task. Auto scores in turn show as a cap on law ask and answer work. Staged prompts are framed as a trust tool for law AI.
arxiv-2509-02541:
Guyue Hu and five co-authors wrote a 2025 medical AI paper on segmenting MRI scans when hospitals cannot pool their data. Each hospital holds different mixes of scan types, so both data and modality mixes vary across sites, breaking centralised multimodal training.

The authors define this setting as mix-modal federated learning, distinct from earlier multimodal variants. Their framework splits each modality into tailored parts, unique to that scan type, and shared parts common across types. Updates respect that split during federated training. A memory mechanism stores shared prototypes from every encoder and refreshes them over time, filling gaps where a hospital lacks a modality. The design aims for stable training and better brain tumour segmentation across sites.
arxiv-2509-03141:
Mattia Litrico and 4 co-authors proposed a 2025 diffusion model for predicting how a patient's brain will change over time on MRI scans. Such forecasts could help clinicians judge outcomes and follow disease at the level of one person. Earlier methods often ignored how change depends on the time gap, or merely blended two scans instead of forecasting.

Their three-dimensional model, TADM-3D, works on whole brain volumes rather than flat slices. A brain-age estimator guides it, checking that a generated follow-up scan looks the right number of years older. A second trick trains the model in both time directions, forward and backward, to sharpen its sense of time. The team trained on one large aging dataset and tested generalization on another.
arxiv-2509-03241:
Pujitha Mamillapalli and 5 co-authors tackled element allocation for smart radio surfaces in 2025 wireless networks. Such a surface is a panel of many small reflective elements. Tuning each element's phase can steer signals toward users. With several users competing, deciding which elements serve whom is crucial. The task also grows costly very fast as elements multiply.

Classical solvers grow far too costly at scale, and supervised learning needs labels that are themselves hard to make. The authors instead train a compact five-layer neural network with no labels. A preprocessing step trims the input size sharply. Fairness across users is enforced by a scheduling rule with a tunable balance. Simulations beat prior allocation schemes on throughput by a stated margin. The method also scaled far better than iterative solvers.
arxiv-2509-03341:
Ilana Sebag and 4 co-authors compared private generative models in 2025 through the lens of membership inference attacks. Such attacks test whether a specific person's data was used in training, a direct threat to confidentiality. Both GANs and diffusion models, the two leading image generators, can be trained with differential privacy, a formal noise-based protection.

Theory based on stability suggests GANs react less to single-data perturbations than diffusion models, hinting at a structural privacy edge. The authors test that claim with one standardized attack pipeline across datasets and privacy budgets. Results consistently showed a marked robustness gap favoring GANs, even under strong privacy settings. Model family alone, they conclude, can shape how much private information leaks.
arxiv-2509-03541:
Chong Wang and four co-authors' 2025 systematic mapping study takes up datasets used in requirements engineering for mobile apps. Requirements engineering covers how software needs are gathered and checked. Researchers in that field rely on datasets created by users, developers, or vendors, but their sources were poorly mapped.

Following established mapping guidelines, the authors screened the literature and kept 43 papers for close study. More than nine in ten drew their data from Google Play or the Apple App Store. Gathering requirements and analysing them were the activities studied most. Use of such datasets has grown since 2012, the authors find. Heavy reliance on two stores may skew what the field knows, so they urge wider and combined data sources.
arxiv-2509-03641:
Michael Updike and one co-author ask a sharp question in a 2025 physics paper. Does an exact magnetic moment exist for a charged particle in a uniform, time-changing magnetic field? Guiding-centre models track a particle's averaged orbit instead of every tight spiral, and they rely on the magnetic moment staying nearly constant. An exact version of that model can succeed where the traditional theory fails.

The authors show this moving-field case can be solved fully inside the exact model. A magnetic moment built by Qin and Davidson matches Kruskal's classic series of approximate invariants. Unlike those approximations, the exact quantity also encodes parametric resonances. Over very long times, those resonances break the usual moment's conservation. Earlier claims of invariance for all time are therefore refuted.
arxiv-2509-03841:
In a 2025 research paper, Shujun Zhao and three co-authors test whether fluid dynamics can describe proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Whether hydrodynamics applies to such tiny, short-lived systems stays controversial. The collisions studied run at thirteen teraelectronvolts, and the question is whether the debris expands collectively, like a fluid, at all.

Their tool is viscous anisotropic hydrodynamics, built to handle large differences between longitudinal and transverse pressure. It describes the measured flow signals well across a wide range of particle multiplicities, and reproduces a negative four-particle correlation signal seen in experiments. Standard second-order viscous hydrodynamics matches those measurements only with parameters implying outsized shear effects through most of the evolution. It also misses the large early pressure anisotropy entirely. The authors conclude the traditional framework fails in small systems, while the anisotropic version describes the bulk evolution and flow more reliably.
arxiv-2509-03941:
A 2025 research paper by Mathias Åsan Myhre and four co-authors asks how film thickness changes magnon spin transport in antiferromagnetic insulators. Magnons are waves of magnetic orientation that can carry spin information without moving charge. A recent report of giant room-temperature magnon conductivity in a thin ferromagnet motivates this closer look at antiferromagnets.

Their test material is hematite, an antiferromagnetic insulator with very low magnetic damping, plus two magnetic phases at different temperatures. Stochastic micromagnetic simulations track spin transport across both phases as thickness varies. A crossover appears at a critical thickness, set by the excited magnons' frequency: below it, transport turns quasi-two-dimensional instead of quasi-three-dimensional. The magnon diffusion length then grows in both phases. The rise is traced to a changed density of states, since thinner films leave less room for scattering. The work informs spintronic nanodevices near the two-dimensional limit.
arxiv-2509-04041:
Daniel Raggi and five co-authors introduce Oruga in a 2025 research paper about how machines might handle representations more flexibly. People sketch diagrams, switch between formats, and borrow analogies from other fields. The team's earlier Representational Systems Theory studies how such representations are built and changed. Oruga, named after the Spanish word for caterpillar, turns parts of that theory into working software.

Three pieces make up the system. A core holds data structures that mirror the theory's concepts. A language lets users talk to that core. An engine then produces new representations through a method the authors call structure transfer. A short worked example shows what one such change looks like.
arxiv-2509-04241:
Jaroslaw Kornowicz and two co-authors study whether people regret going against the crowd when choosing artificial intelligence tools in a 2025 research paper. Workers increasingly decide between AI help and human expertise inside teams shaped by peer and supervisor norms. Earlier work showed norms can soften dislike of algorithms, but how norms form stayed unclear. An online experiment showed participants short workplace scenarios, then asked about their feelings after matching or defying the stated norm.

Breaking the norm brought more regret than following it, as theory predicted. Picking AI over a human also raised regret on average, unless AI use was framed as normal practice. People blamed technology less than humans, which deepened regret after AI choices went wrong.
arxiv-2509-04541:
Kasymkhan Khubiev and three co-authors retrain return-prediction models with loss functions borrowed from traders in a 2025 research paper. Deep learning thrives in vision and language, but finance judges models by its own metrics, not prediction error alone. The authors build losses from the Sharpe ratio, which balances return against risk, raw profit and loss, and maximum drawdown, the worst peak-to-valley fall. Turnover regularization also caps how often generated positions flip, keeping trading costs realistic.

Against the traditional mean squared error loss, the finance-grounded losses won on algorithmic trading evaluations. Portfolio optimization benefited as well. Interpretable, domain-native objectives can beat generic accuracy chasing in markets, the study argues.
arxiv-2509-04741:
