One global model fits divergent clients poorly, most when their data skew far apart, and talk costs cap what can be shared.

FedSTAR pulls each client's style factors out of the shared content code. The server then merges class wise prototypes with a transformer attention step that weighs client inputs with care. Clients swap compact prototypes and style vectors in place of full model weights, which cuts traffic. Personal fit survives the merge. Skewed, chat shy fleets are the target.
arxiv-2511-19341:
Thomas Hughes, Michael J. Wilensky, and Philip Bull probe the Hubble tension, the mismatch between measures of how fast the universe expands. Different methods give values that disagree beyond their stated errors. Many groupings of the data have been tried to blame physics or hidden errors.

Their Bayesian jackknife study works through sixteen independent measurements, testing whether they fall into meaningful clusters. After checking the usual early-versus-late split, they try scenarios where certain subsets carry a bias, such as the local distance ladder or microwave background data. Population parameters describe each subset, letting the data itself point to the tension's origin.
arxiv-2511-19441:
Marien-Lorenzo Hanot and Kaibo Hu rewrite the linearized Einstein equations in a form that suits careful computer work. Simulating gravity is hard: gauge choices, constraints, and tensor symmetries all cause trouble. Their new form casts the ADM equations as a wave system built on a tool called the divdiv complex.

That structure makes the system well posed, meaning small changes in inputs cause only small changes in outputs. It also points to schemes that keep the physics intact on a grid. The authors build such schemes for two kinds of grids and prove error bounds under weak assumptions.
arxiv-2511-19541:
Sajjad Taravati argues that shaping dispersion is the master key for space-time metamaterials. These are materials patterned in both space and time. They can steer the frequency, size, momentum, and path of waves all at once. That goes far beyond merely breaking one-way behavior rules.

The link between frequency and wavenumber acts as a blueprint for the whole design. By mapping that link across slow, light-speed, and fast modulation regimes, the article shows how shaped change routes energy among harmonic modes. Effects include beam splitting, one-way flow, uneven frequency shifts, gain, and momentum gaps. The framework is then tied to real wave devices.
arxiv-2511-19741:
Xinran Liu and four co-authors ask whether a learned shortcut for optimal transport still works on new data. Transport plans match one distribution to another at some cost, but full computation scales badly. Sliced methods project the problem to one dimension, where the answer is cheap, and learn a good projection direction.

The open question is transfer: can a slicer trained on one pair of distributions serve unseen pairs when the data shift? The authors study the min-sliced transport plan framework with that question in focus. The answer matters wherever transport is recomputed often on related, evolving data, from shape analysis to image generation.
arxiv-2511-20041:
Petr Molodyk, Jaemoo Choi, David W Romero, Ming-Yu Liu, and Yongxin Chen present MFM-Point, a multi-scale flow matching method for generating point clouds. Direct point-based generators are cheap to train and simple, but they usually trail methods that work through latent features, meshes, or voxels. The authors aim to close that gap without losing the simplicity.

Generation proceeds from coarse to fine, which improves quality and scale at no extra training or inference cost. A structured downsampling and upsampling plan preserves the geometry of unordered point sets and keeps the resolutions aligned. In tests, MFM-Point leads the point-based methods and rivals the best representation-based ones, with strong results on multi-category and high-resolution tasks.
arxiv-2511-20541:
Ranieri, Palmieri, and Biasotti teach networks to find cracks in statues before conservators can. Their 2025 paper applies semantic segmentation to cultural heritage monitoring. Statues and monuments degrade outdoors, developing structural cracks. Manual inspection is slow, subjective, and often hard to access. Pixel-level image labeling can flag fine cracks automatically.

The study compares U-Net models with four different encoders. ResNet-50, ResNet-101, and two ConvNeXt V2 sizes were trained. Training used the OmniCrack30k dataset of crack images. Scores included overlap measures like mIoU, Dice, and Jaccard. ConvNeXt V2 Huge topped every metric on the test set. Bigger backbones and higher input resolutions helped consistently. A second test used unlabeled photos of real cracked monuments. Models generalized despite never training on heritage images. ConvNeXt variants caught hairline cracks best in that trial. Complex textures and lighting did not break them.
arxiv-2511-20641:
Tang, Wang, Zhang, Wei, and Zhang rescue rare labels in multi-label image recognition. Their 2025 paper presents CapNet for long-tailed visual recognition. Real images carry several labels, but common ones dominate training data. Rare tail classes get ignored by biased models. CLIP's design favors single-label matching over multi-label tagging.

CapNet models label correlations from CLIP's own text encoder. A graph network propagates information along those correlations. Learnable soft prompts refine the label embeddings further. A distribution-balanced focal loss reweights training toward rare classes. Test-time ensembling combines predictions for better generalization. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts vision to text cheaply. On VOC-LT, mean average precision reached 93.03 percent. That beat the LMPT baseline by over five points. COCO-LT results hit 76.36 percent, up to ten points ahead. Ablations on NUS-WIDE confirmed each component helps. Head classes kept their accuracy while tails improved.
arxiv-2511-20741:
Futoshi Hamanoue reports in 2025 a feasibility study of Aurora-DD, a method that keeps superconducting qubits from losing their phase. Qubits drift out of phase as they idle, and that drift corrupts quantum computations. Aurora pairs a fixed XY8 pulse sequence, which echoes away slow noise, with one global phase offset. The offset is tuned in advance on a calibrated emulator, not live on the machine.

Across 30 randomised trials at each of four phase settings, the emulator runs cut mean-squared error by 68 to 97 percent against an unprotected baseline. A three-run campaign on IBM's real ibm_fez hardware pointed to roughly 99 percent lower absolute error. Hamanoue stresses those hardware numbers are proof-of-concept only. A side branch adding zero-noise extrapolation proved unstable, sometimes amplifying errors badly, and now sits in an appendix as a warning.
arxiv-2511-20841:
Edmond Tong and colleagues present in 2025 OVAL-Grasp, a system that lets a robot grasp objects by the right part for the job. Grabbing a knife by the blade fails the task even when the grip is firm. Geometry-only methods struggle with appearance-defined parts, blocked views, and unseen objects. OVAL-Grasp needs no training for new objects, working zero-shot from language and vision alone.

Given a photo and a task, a large language model names which parts to grasp and which to avoid. A vision-language model then segments those parts, and builds a heatmap of actionable regions for the gripper. On 20 household objects with three tasks each, it beat two grasping baselines. On the Fetch mobile manipulator it segmented the correct part 95 percent of the time and grasped the right area in 78.3 percent of attempts. Under clutter, part selection succeeded 80 percent of the time.
arxiv-2511-21641:
Michael Ruderman shows control engineers how to tune a feedback controller without any model of the machine, in 2025. Plant models are often unavailable in practice, especially in motion control, yet PI and PID controllers still need principled tuning. His PI-Lead design revives the ultimate sensitivity idea behind the classic Ziegler–Nichols rules, extended with loop-shaping insight.

A three-step procedure sets the integration time constant, the control gain, and the Lead element in turn, using only experimental observations of the output. The design guarantees a sufficient phase margin for the assumed class of type-one stable processes. Ruderman validates the method on a noise-perturbed electro-mechanical actuator with translational motion. The tuning proves robust against feedback noise, because the ultimate oscillations it hunts appear unmistakably at low frequencies where sensor noise cannot mimic them. The result is a practical, simple recipe for engineers who cannot model first.
arxiv-2511-21741:
Conrad D. Hougen, Karl T. Pazdernik, and Alfred O. Hero build a geometric topic model that tracks how research themes drift inside co-author communities, in 2025. Topic models sort document collections into themes, but modern versions built on dense transformer embeddings tend to miss rare niche topics. They also fail to line topics up smoothly across time.

Their method, MSTML, fuses text with co-author network data. Hellinger distances, a way to compare probability distributions, and Ward's linkage build a hierarchical topic tree that holds both local detail and global structure. The experiments show the approach recovers rare-topic structure and visualizes gradual topic drift over the years. A notable lesson emerges: interpretable word-count models, paired with principled geometric alignment, beat embedding models at alignment even though transformers win on coherence. Because novelty lives in niche topics, the authors argue alignment deserves priority when mapping a field's evolution.
arxiv-2511-21841:
Bozorgnia and colleagues argue that searches for very heavy dark matter particles, particles far above a TeV in mass, need a better map of dark matter motion near Earth. The standard model assumes a smooth Maxwellian spread of speeds. The Large Magellanic Cloud, ploughing through the Milky Way's halo, should add a fast tail and bunch incoming particles into one sky patch.

The team introduces new techniques for turning simulated velocities into detector flux, then reworks limits from plastic etch detectors at the Ohya mine and aboard Skylab, which recorded no suitable tracks. Because the fastest particles arrive from a preferred direction, a detector's latitude matters. The Ohya site happened to sit near the latitude that maximizes the flux in their calculation. Bounds shift when the Magellanic boost is included, which matters for future detector design.
arxiv-2511-22241:
Borlakov and Kazakov, theoretical physicists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, revisit the oldest weak-interaction theory's bad reputation. Fermi's four-fermion theory is non-renormalizable and its scattering amplitude grows with energy, violating unitarity, which is why the Standard Model replaces it with W and Z boson exchange at high energies. The authors ask what the theory itself predicts once its ultraviolet divergences are summed properly, using recurrence relations for divergences licensed by the Bogolyubov-Parasyuk theorem's guarantee that counterterms stay local.

Checked through three loops, the recurrences yield renormalization group equations summing leading logarithms to all orders. Numerically, the outcome splits by operator: the unit operator's amplitude hits a Landau pole. The physically relevant V-A operator, the actual weak current, turns asymptotically free. So radiative corrections tame the growth and restore unitarity. In that regime the amplitude even overlaps with the gauge-boson theory's behavior.
arxiv-2511-22341:
Rosenthal, Schmidt, Graf, and colleagues at TU Munich audit the exams used to grade vision-language models, and find the formatting alone moves the scores. Multiple-choice visual question answering is a standard benchmark, but earlier work showed answers shift with choice order. This study varies three subtler prompt-formatting factors, things like separators and answer markers that change nothing semantically. Across seven multimodal models and five datasets, generating 48 distinct prompt formats for the same questions.

Accuracy is highly sensitive to these cosmetic changes, independently of order effects and of model confidence. Existing debiasing strategies fail to neutralize the formatting biases. The warning is direct: a reported score partly measures the prompt template used, so cross-paper comparisons with different formats are unreliable. The study deliberately builds on the earlier order-bias literature rather than re-litigating it, isolating formatting as a separate, uncontrolled variable in current evaluation practice.
arxiv-2511-22441:
Zhang and colleagues measure how easily artificial intelligence can work out where a social media photo was taken. Their system, GEO-Detective, imitates a human investigator. It picks strategies based on how hard an image looks. It uses tools such as visual reverse search to gather outside clues about landmarks, signs, and building styles. Ordinary users with such tools could expose locations that photo owners never meant to share.

GEO-Detective beat plain large vision-language models overall, especially on images with no obvious geographic features. On country-level guesses it improved accuracy by over 11.1 percent compared with baseline models. It kept a gain of about 5.2 percent at finer scales, while outside clues cut its rate of unknown answers by more than half. The team also tested four defences and found watermarking the most effective, warning that current safeguards are weak against this kind of agent.
arxiv-2511-22741:
Coriasco, Kirilov, de Moraes, and Tokoro determine exactly when a class of partial differential equations on non-compact spaces is globally solvable. The operators come from involutive structures, systems of vector fields closed under Lie brackets, on a product of a non-compact manifold with a torus. Global solvability hinges on the operator's range being closed, deciding whether every compatible right-hand side actually has a solution, in smooth and distributional senses alike.

The authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for that closed range, working in Fréchet-Schwartz spaces and their duals to handle the non-compact geometry. They also prove that a weaker notion of global hypoellipticity, a regularity property of solutions, already forces the range closed for operators on smooth paracompact manifolds. That extends a compact-manifold result to the non-compact setting. It completes a piece of solvability theory for involutive systems.
arxiv-2511-23041:
Nguyen and Rosseel ask whether large language models judge people from their spelling the way humans do. In online writing, a stretched or shortened word, like funnnn instead of fun, quietly signals things about the writer. The team measured those impressions on three scales, formality, carefulness, and the writer's apparent age, for both human raters and several language models.

Overall the models' ratings correlated strongly with humans' ratings, with GPT-4o reaching a correlation of 0.905 on raw scores in the paired setup. But the match broke down on the differences between spelling variants. There, correlations fell to about 0.53 for GPT-4o and nearly zero, 0.043 in the table, for Llama3-8B. Rating distributions also differed, and the size of the penalty depended on the variation type, so models share the broad human bias but not its finer shape.
arxiv-2511-23341:
Allen and colleagues ask how few edges a host hypergraph can have while containing. As a sub-structure, every member of a class of hypergraphs, the universality problem of combinatorics. For graphs the answer for D-degenerate graphs, those whose every part has a low-degree vertex, was known to be near a power of n. And the team generalizes the construction and the counting lower bound to r-uniform hypergraphs.

They prove a universal hypergraph exists whose edge count grows like n raised to the power r minus one-over-D. Multiplied only by powers of logarithms, and that this is best possible apart from those logarithmic factors, which remain the paper's open problem. The result covers every degeneracy D above one, and the authors note the tree-like case D equals one likely follows with minor adjustments. Though whether the extra logarithmic factor is needed there is unclear.
arxiv-2512-00641:
Facial expression recognition often collapses when the people or cameras change between training and deployment. Razieh Ghaedi and co-authors propose GAT-ADA in 2025, a graph-attention network with adversarial domain alignment for cross-domain expression recognition. Severe domain shift is the central obstacle.

The framework pairs a ResNet-50 backbone with a batch-level graph attention network that models relations between samples under shift. Adversarial alignment pushes the model toward features that work in both domains. Robust expression recognition supports accessibility tools and human-computer interaction that must work for new users without retraining. Batch-level graphs let the model borrow strength from similar faces in the same batch. Adversarial alignment is the mechanism that forces domain-blind features.
arxiv-2512-00841:
Du Wenzhang proposes a market-based twist on federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains one model across many devices or sites without pooling their data. For multimedia tasks, the method strains under uneven data across clients and tight communication limits, especially with large models.

Classic averaging methods send full model weights back and forth, and they can diverge when client data differ a lot. The proposed system, KTA v2, trades knowledge in prediction space instead of raw weights. Clients buy and sell predictions in a knowledge market. Trading compact predictions could cut traffic while keeping learning stable.
arxiv-2512-01141:
Akshat Bagade, Maanas Baraya, Chittebbayi Penugonda, and Muhammad Yousuf teach machines to rename variables in a 2025 paper. Developers often inherit code whose variable names are generic or misleading. Teams moving fast leave many functions undocumented, which slows comprehension for everyone who reads the code later.

Poor names raise the risk of subtle bugs. They also make it harder for large language models to reason about code, since names carry much of the meaning. Their neural variable name repair system learns to suggest readable identifiers. Automatic renaming could help teams clean legacy code and help AI coding tools understand it.
arxiv-2512-01941:
A Schrödinger operator describes a quantum particle moving through a potential landscape, and bound states appear as eigenvalues below the spectrum's edge. Jussi Behrndt and three co-authors study in 2025 what happens with complex-valued potentials, in one or two dimensions, when the coupling is weak.

Complex potentials break the usual rules, since energies need no longer be real numbers. The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the potential for discrete eigenvalues to exist in this faint-coupling regime. They also examine whether such eigenvalues are unique and how their algebraic multiplicity behaves. The results tidy a corner of spectral theory where intuition from real potentials fails.
arxiv-2512-02241:
Some systems hang between life and death. Bits branch, move, and wipe each other out, and the group as a whole lives or dies. Peter Grassberger's 2025 paper reports fine-grained computer runs of one such class: parity conserving directed percolation. It is the second most weighty class of these life-or-death phase shifts.

What sets this class apart is parity. The count of bits is kept modulo two, so a finite system splits into even and odd camps with unlike fates. Careful runs pin down the class's traits near the tipping point, in one space dimension plus time. Shared classes let one pattern forecast the acts of many unlike systems, so each sharp trait tightens a broad net.
arxiv-2512-02841:
Lechen Zhang and five co-authors test whether one system prompt can steer a language model well in many languages. System prompts condition model behavior at inference time with little cost. Most prior study covers English only, yet real deployments serve the whole world at once.

A single prompt that behaves reliably across languages is the goal. The team measures steerability cross lingually, hunting for languages where steering slips. Findings of this kind help builders write prompts that stay accurate and robust, so users get equal quality whatever tongue they type in. One prompt for all tongues cuts cost and drift, but only if each tongue gets the same grip on the wheel.
arxiv-2512-02941:
Wittawat Kositwattanarerk and three co-authors study the false codewords that can fool modern error correcting decoders. Low density parity check codes nearly reach channel capacity with iterative decoders. Those decoders sometimes stall on pseudocodewords, patterns that look valid but are not true codewords.

The authors view pseudocodewords through the fundamental cone, a geometric object that organizes decoder behavior. They cover quantum, quasi cyclic, and spatially coupled code families. Understanding these traps helps engineers design decoders for storage and communication that fail less often at low error rates. False friends of true codewords are the traps that bite at the last step. A clear view of them is worth the work it takes to draw.
arxiv-2512-03641:
B Turner and co-authors model the moment a hacker decides whether a deceptive system is worth taking on. Cyber-deception plants fake targets and false clues, but most formal models start after the attacker has already bitten. Their 2025 model moves the lens to that first judgment call.

Five parts shape the call in their framework: belief, scepticism, deception fidelity, reconnaissance, and experience. Together they describe how attackers read fake cues and price staying in. The authors have planned Capture the Flag contests, tracking moves and body signals, to test the model. No results are claimed yet; what the paper adds is the framework and the test plan.
arxiv-2512-04041:
Terhertz pulses can shove a crystal's atoms off balance and reshape the material's properties, a field called nonlinear phononics. Francesco Libbi and Boris Kozinsky supply the field with an analytical quantum theory in a 2025 materials preprint. Numerical tools could already evolve the quantum state of the nuclei, but they offered little interpretable insight into how quantum fluctuations steer the motion.

The framework handles all third- and fourth-order couplings between phonon modes. It writes forces as explicit functions of the fluctuations, allowing exact solutions for the nuclei's evolution. One theorem stands out: a strong pulse displacing a phonon mode also squeezes that mode's quantum fluctuations. This systematises an effect glimpsed in earlier work. They propose using the cooling-like effect deliberately, to drive symmetry breaking inside quantum paraelectric materials, turning a side effect into a control knob.
arxiv-2512-04341:
Tianwei Ni, Esther Derman, Vineet Jain, Vincent Taboga, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, and Pierre-Luc Bacon question a core habit in offline reinforcement learning: always playing it safe. Offline agents learn from fixed logs, with no fresh trial and error. Standard tools punish choices outside the logs or cap how far ahead the agent may plan. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks whether a Bayesian view can replace that caution.

The Bayesian agent keeps a spread of possible world models and plans for the average case. In a simple bandit test, this view won exactly where caution failed, on weak data. Scaling up, the team found long planning horizons are key once caution is dropped. Their algorithm, NEUBAY, adds design choices that tame error growth over long rollouts. The results suggest safety can come from honest doubt about the world, not from blanket bans.
arxiv-2512-04941:
Abdessamad Belfakir and Weibin Li study how energy surfaces steer coupled spin and vibration motion in a pair of trapped Rydberg ions, near a sloped conical intersection. Conical intersections are funnels where two energy surfaces touch, letting molecules switch states ultrafast. Here lasers create the intersection by coupling the ions' electronic spins to their shared vibration. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows the surface shape can be engineered with sideband transitions and dipole-dipole forces between the ions.

The crafted intersection tilts along one spatial axis only. A wavepacket starting at the lower surface's minimum stays largely frozen, held by a geometric phase effect. Starting on the upper surface, the spin and phonon states tunnel down together. The split behavior gives researchers a tunable test bed for the quantum dynamics behind light harvesting and vision chemistry.
arxiv-2512-05041:
Archana Aravindan and a large team of co-authors present the first close-up look at coronal lines in dwarf galaxies with feeding black holes. Coronal lines are faint spectral fingerprints from atoms stripped of many electrons, and only fierce light near an active galactic nucleus can make them. Using the James Webb Space Telescope's near-infrared spectrograph, the team mapped these lines in four dwarf galaxies known to blow ionized gas outward.

Sixteen distinct coronal-line species show up, and their relative strengths say the black hole's light, not shocks, does most of the exciting. The glowing region reaches a sizable fraction of each small galaxy, and its brightness tracks the strength of the outflows, suggesting the winds help the gas shine. Some lines carry a broad extra component from fast, compact, highly ionized gas — evidence that even small black holes can stir their hosts and shape their evolution.
arxiv-2512-05441:
Sindhana Pannir-Sivajothi and David Limmer show how a twist of light can magnetize a molecule's electrons. Chirality-induced spin selectivity — the tendency of chiral systems to filter electrons by spin — usually requires a chiral molecule. Here the chirality comes from the light itself: circularly polarized light exciting an achiral donor-acceptor complex. The authors map the energetic and symmetry requirements for the effect and work it out in a model metalloporphyrin with a ligand.

Excitation drives a ring current in the porphyrin, breaking the tie between the two spin states and leaving a net spin polarization. The polarization grows with the spin-orbit coupling between the metal and its ligand, and it is transient, fading at a rate set by a vibration of the molecule. The authors note the effect should be visible to spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy — a possible route to writing spin information with light alone.
arxiv-2512-05541:
Timothée Mounier and ten co-authors measure the chirp of laser pulses at the feeble energies where single quantum emitters live. Chirp — the rate at which a pulse's colour sweeps — matters for exciting quantum light sources. But standard pulse diagnostics rely on nonlinear effects. Those demand far more power than the attojoule-to-femtojoule scale of this regime allows. Their method needs no nonlinearity at all.

They map wavelength to time: the pulse's spectral slices are filtered and their arrival times recorded with a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector and a time tagger. The straight-line relation between wavelength and arrival time hands over the dispersion directly. The technique suits single-photon spectroscopy, ultra-low-power optical communication, and time-domain quantum control — anywhere dispersion must be characterized linearly and without destroying the light being measured. It is an instrument paper with a wide bench of users.
arxiv-2512-05941:
Zhiyuan Jiang and ten co-authors show that the humble zoom is a powerful tool for software that must click on the right pixel. Interface agents live or die by grounding: given an instruction, find the button or field on screen. Models trained on mountains of labeled boxes still stumble across platforms, tangled layouts, and tiny elements. ZoomClick instead teaches existing models to lean in. It is training free.

The team characterizes four properties of zoom: timing, depth, shrink size, and minimal crop. Dynamic focusing alternates between the wide scene and fine detail. The method lifted both general vision language models and specialist grounding models to state of the art results on leading benchmarks. One large model reached about seventy three percent success on a hard professional screen benchmark. A new test suite, GUIZoom-Bench, measures adaptability to zoom.
arxiv-2512-06241:
Zipeng Hu, Ke Wang, Mark Krumholz, and Keyun Su study the life story of giant gas threads that stretch across galaxies like ours. Surveys keep finding these huge strands of cold gas, yet no one was sure how they form, how they break up, or how long they last. The team made fake sky surveys from a detailed galaxy simulation, then picked out more than seven hundred such strands to track.

Shocks from churning gas, joined with the galaxy's own shear and blasts from young stars, turn out to build the strands. Magnetic churning holds each strand up against collapse while also pinching it into dense lumps, and those lumps form stars well. Crashes between gas clouds hit most strands and often tear or reshape them. A strand lives only a short span by galaxy standards, yet while it lasts it shapes where new stars are born.
arxiv-2512-06341:
Ronald Katende proposes a score for a question machine learning rarely asks in numbers. How much of what the data knows about a task survives in a human readable summary of it? A clear summary that drops the key signal is useless, while one that keeps noise is clutter. His score, Interpretive Efficiency, states the share of task relevant information that passes through a chosen summary channel.

The score is built on five stated rules, covering bounds, fair channel comparisons, and steady behavior as data grows. Katende links it to shared information measures and to the local geometry of statistical models, and proves how well it can be guessed from finite samples. On controlled image and signal tasks, the score matched the order theory predicts, exposed wasted bulk that accuracy hid, and tracked how robust a summary was. It gives designers a principled gauge for trusted summaries.
arxiv-2512-06641:
Yihan Chen, Benfeng Xu, Xiaorui Wang, and Zhendong Mao speed up how AI agents pull the useful text out of web pages. Research agents read huge volumes of pages, and their context windows fill with boilerplate: menus, ads, and footers bury the small share of signal. Older extractors generate the cleaned text word by word, which is slow, or follow fixed rules that break on new layouts, or chop pages into chunks blind to their structure.

Their method reframes extraction as index prediction. The page is split into structure aware, addressable segments, and the model outputs only the index numbers of the segments a query needs. That splits extraction time from page length entirely. Inside a question answering pipeline the method lifted accuracy, and in direct tests it matched the target content well, both for whole page main content and for query driven extraction.
arxiv-2512-07041:
Hiroki Sawada, Alexandre Pitti, and Mathias Quoy give a humanoid robot one brain for three jobs: copying movements, recognizing them, and knowing how sure it is. Their model, CERNet, is a layered recurrent network built on predictive coding, the idea that the brain constantly forecasts its inputs. A special class vector steers the system. During generation it pins the network's motion to one learned pattern family; during recognition it is adjusted live to shrink forecast errors.

The robot learned twenty-six alphabets taught by hand through physical guidance. The layered model reproduced the writing motions with far lower error than a same-sized single-layer network. It kept its form when pushed by outside disturbances. Watching a person write, it named the letter class online with respectable accuracy, and its own forecast errors rose exactly when it was unsure, giving a built-in confidence signal.
arxiv-2512-07241:
Md Srabon Chowdhury and co-authors classify brain tumors in MRI scans with a network small enough to run at the edge of a hospital network. Outlining tumors by hand is slow and varies between specialists, so automated reading support matters. Their model squeezes together two existing designs, a featherweight network and a high-performing one. And enriches them with hand-crafted texture descriptors drawn from classic image analysis: gradient directions, local binary patterns, Gabor filters, and wavelet transforms.

Training and testing used one public data set of several thousand contrast-enhanced brain scans, sorted into glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. Accuracy landed near ninety-nine percent, nudged higher when test images were read under several augmentations and averaged. All that comes from fewer than a couple of million parameters and a light computing budget.
arxiv-2512-07341:
S Tingay and co-authors listen for satellites that are accidentally broadcasting. Recent work found low Earth orbit satellites leaking unintended radio emission, a growing source of interference for radio astronomy. Whether the far higher geostationary belt leaks too was unknown, and the coming Square Kilometre Array's low-frequency telescope would suffer if it did. The team's trick exploits geometry: a wide-field telescope in Australia stares at a fixed patch where geostationary satellites hang nearly motionless for hours.

Using one night of survey data across a broad low-frequency band, they stacked images at the predicted positions of well over a hundred geostationary and geosynchronous satellites. Stacking lets faint, steady leaks rise above the noise. None convincingly appeared: the limits say any unintended emission is weaker than a milliwatt of radiated power in most cases, and far weaker in the best.
arxiv-2512-07441:
D. I. Novikov and five co-authors wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on the cosmic microwave background. That background glow carries faint patterns, summed up by numbers called multipoles. The lowest few multipoles are hard to pin down because cosmic variance limits any direct view.

The authors study a subtle distortion that arises when background light scatters off hot plasma in galaxy clusters. This anisotropic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect could yield a fresh, independent reading of the lowest multipoles. It could also split apart two effects that normally blur together in the data. They apply a component separation method called the Least Response Method. With it, they estimate how sensitive a future instrument must be. They test the plan on a simulated signal mixed with messy foregrounds. Relic spectrum distortions from related effects are folded into the test as well.
arxiv-2512-07541:
Katerina Papagiannouli, Yang-wen Sun, and Vladimir Spokoiny wrote this 2025 statistics paper. It tackles change point detection: finding the moment when data quietly change character. In high dimensions, with many streams at once, that moment is easy to miss.

Their algorithm grows out of graph-based thinking about data. It works on stored data after the fact and on live data as it arrives. The data may be plain numbers or values sitting on a graph. No one needs to know the underlying distribution in advance. Error probabilities stay under control throughout the procedure. Theory shows the method detects changes once they pass a sharp size threshold. That threshold matches the best rate any method could hope for. Tests beat rival techniques on both bell-shaped and messier data. Small observation windows still give strong detection power. Live monitoring, where a fast alarm matters most, is the natural home.
arxiv-2512-07941:
Thomas Colas, Zhehan Qin, and Xi Tong, theoretical cosmologists, posted a long study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the cosmological collider signal, a pattern in the early universe that could reveal heavy particles present during inflation. They examine where that signal comes from using open effective field theory, which allows energy and information to leak away.

Focusing on one exchange of a massive scalar field, they show the trispectrum splits cleanly into local and non local parts. Removing the heavy field leaves a theory with both unitary terms and terms tied to dissipation and noise. The local signal comes from the unitary part, while the non local signal belongs to the stochastic part. They also link that signal to entropy production and the mixedness of the quantum state.
arxiv-2512-08041: Gustavo Amilcar Saldana Moncada, a mathematical physicist, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025 on noncommutative geometry. He studies two noncommutative Laplacians with a U one gauge structure, built on the upper sheet of a two sheeted quantum hyperboloid. The paper characterizes the spectrum of both operators, that is, the full set of values they can take. Spectral results of this kind are basic tools for doing analysis and physics on quantum spaces, where ordinary coordinates no longer commute.
arxiv-2512-08141:
Alastair Kay and Christino Tamon, mathematicians who work on quantum walks, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is a counterintuitive trick in quantum transport: attach edges, only weakly coupled, to a large base graph, and quantum states can transfer across it with high fidelity. That claim circulated as folklore, but it lacked a firm mathematical treatment.

Kay and Tamon supply that treatment with elementary proofs built on the Feshbach Schur method from perturbation theory. They show the weak coupling idea really does deliver the promised transfer quality. They also show it can sidestep Anderson localization, the trapping effect that halts quantum motion in disordered spin chains. A further payoff is faster hitting times, which matters for quantum search. The paper turns a handy piece of lab intuition into a tool other researchers can apply with confidence.
arxiv-2512-08241:
Preksha Girish, Rachana Mysore, Mahanthesha U, Shrey Kumar, and Shipra Prashant, researchers in India, posted a framework paper on arXiv in December 2025. They propose a brain inspired way for machines to learn representations. It rests on two branches of math. One tracks shapes that survive across scales. The other moves data through algebraic structures called cohomology.

In their setup, computation becomes the growth of cochain maps over changing simplicial complexes. Representations can then hold steady features across time, space, and function in brain states. Tools from sheaf theory and spectral Laplacians widen ordinary gradient learning inside this landscape. The team tests the model on synthetic data with known shape signatures and on real neural datasets. They report better consistency and stronger noise resilience than graph neural and manifold based deep models. The work aims to give topology driven learning a firm base.
arxiv-2512-08341:
Thai Duong Nguyen, Ngoc Tan Nguyen, Thanh Dao Nguyen, and colleagues, wireless researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is swarms of drones acting as flying communication relays in contested settings, the kind tactical networks may need. The drones must raise total throughput, avoid collisions, and resist enemy jamming all at once, a trade off that fixed rules handle poorly.

The team poses the problem as cooperative multi agent reinforcement learning. A central critic sees the full state during training and guides the learning, while each drone actor later flies using only its own local observations. In simulations, the framework beat heuristic baselines clearly, lifting throughput by about half while collisions fell to nearly zero. The striking finding was unprogrammed: the drones invented an anti jamming strategy on their own. They learned to position themselves to blunt interference while keeping strong links to ground users.
arxiv-2512-08441:
Luca Cogo, Marco Buzzelli, Simone Bianco, and colleagues, imaging scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. New snapshot multispectral sensors, small and cheap enough for phones, capture far richer light information than ordinary color sensors. That extra spectrum should help correct colors in mobile photos, yet most pipelines throw it away early.

Their framework performs color correction end to end in one learned model, fusing a sharp color image with a small multispectral companion image throughout. To show the design is general, they rebuilt two leading image to image architectures around it. They also assembled a training set from public spectral collections, rendered under several camera sensitivities. In tests, the unified approach improved color accuracy and stability, cutting error by up to half against color only and spectral driven baselines. For phone cameras, the message is simple: keep the spectral signal in the loop throughout.
arxiv-2512-08641:
Dmitriy Kondaurov and Evgeny Polyakov study quantum Brownian motion, the random motion of a small particle coupled to a large bath. They use the Caldeira Leggett model, a standard model for that setting. Their main claim is that the exact quantum motion can be matched to a classical random process in phase space, at any temperature.

The match is exact when the outside potential is at most quadratic, and it holds for any starting quantum state of the particle. Odd states, such as superpositions, enter through their Wigner functions, which act as weights for groups of paths. The framework also handles outside control and measurement steps at set times. For smoother general potentials, the authors point to a small parameter that may support a controlled approximation.
arxiv-2512-08741:
Louis Boucherie, Yong Yeol Ahn, and Sune Lehmann present a method to cut hierarchical clustering trees at many levels instead of just one. Cutting a dendrogram at a single height is common for finding clusters or communities in networks. When the tree is unbalanced, a single cut often misses the true structure in the data.

Their adaptive cut searches over multi level cuts, guided by an objective function and a sampling method with simulated annealing. The authors also define a balancedness score that measures how balanced a tree is, and that score predicts when multi level cuts will help most. Tests cover link clustering and modularity based community finding, across more than two hundred real networks and synthetic data. The method improves partition quality over single cut baselines and works with many clustering techniques and objectives.
arxiv-2512-08841:
Mukthesh Mahadev and Marc Gerritsma propose a structure preserving discretization for inviscid barotropic fluid flow, built from a variational principle in space and time. Standard Lagrangian methods can suffer from mesh distortion as the fluid moves. A method that keeps the core conservation laws exact would be more robust for long or demanding studies.

Their method uses a multisymplectic variational formulation discretized over a full space time domain. Variables for the flow live on a staggered space time mesh, using mimetic spectral elements. Deformations are computed in a fixed reference setup and mapped to the physical domain through a standard stress based transformation. By design, the discrete versions of mass, momentum, and energy conservation hold to machine precision. The method also handles low speed flows without special preconditioning. Tests on expansion and compression flows confirm accuracy, stability, and exact conservation in practice.
arxiv-2512-09141:
Cleis Battaglia and coauthors study how binding kinetics controls two jobs of type II topoisomerase,. The enzyme resolves tangles by passing a segment of double stranded DNA through a transient break in another. How it keeps the genome simple, across other forms of entanglement, is not fully understood.

Single molecule measurements first quantify how salt concentration changes the rate at which the enzyme leaves DNA. The team then finds a striking split: faster dissociation speeds up decatenation, the unlinking of intertwined DNA rings, yet slows down torsional relaxation of supercoiled DNA. Molecular dynamics studies explain the trade off. It comes from a balance between searching for targets by facilitated diffusion and staying processive once engaged, which plays out differently for catenated and supercoiled substrates. Modulating binding kinetics can thus tune the two activities in opposite directions, with likely impact inside living cells.
arxiv-2512-09241:
Boris Bilich, Roozbeh Hazrat, and Tran Giang Nam study which algebras can be embedded inside a particular Leavitt algebra. That algebra is a ring built from a small graph with one vertex and two loops. An embedding asks whether one algebraic structure can sit faithfully inside another. The Leavitt algebra is a natural target because a simple ordering fact gives maps into it from many algebras built from commutative monoids.

Using that fact, the authors prove that Leavitt path algebras of finite graphs with a standard condition embed into it. They also find criteria for embeddings between matrix versions of such algebras. Their second main result is negative: the first Weyl algebra, defined by a famous commutation equation, cannot embed into it, because that equation cannot be realized in any Steinberg algebra. They close by showing a graded embedding exists if two copies of the target algebra are combined.
arxiv-2512-09441:
Jiantao Tan and colleagues work on class-incremental learning for image classification, where a system must keep learning new classes over time without forgetting old ones. Their approach builds on vision-language models, which classify images by matching them against text descriptions. Even leading methods still confuse classes that were learned in different rounds of training.

Their framework adds small task-specific adapters to a frozen pretrained image encoder, so new knowledge is learned without disturbing the base model. A cross-task calibration strategy, using a mixture of lightweight projectors, then pulls all learned classes into one shared feature space where they separate more cleanly, reducing confusion across tasks. At prediction time, a new strategy uses the model's own uncertainty to choose the most appropriate image feature for each decision. Experiments across several datasets and settings show the method beating existing approaches.
arxiv-2512-09741:
Frédéric Rousset and Pei Su study a rigid body moving freely inside a compressible fluid with no viscosity. The fluid sits in a bounded three dimensional region and obeys the compressible Euler equations. The body follows the conservation laws for linear and angular momentum. Fluid and solid meet at a moving boundary, where their speeds must match along the normal direction. The two halves form one coupled system.

The authors prove that a unique smooth local solution exists, at least for a short time. Their strategy first rewrites the problem in a fixed region, removing the moving domain. They then study an approximate system whose boundary is easier to handle. A fixed point argument builds the solution step by step, alternating updates of fluid and solid. Estimates independent of the approximation let them pass to the limit and recover a solution of the original problem.
arxiv-2512-09841:
Yijing Chen and colleagues introduce ChronusOmni, a large language model built to be more aware of time across video, audio, and text. Earlier systems mostly handled explicit questions about timing in vision and language, and they made little use of sound. They also missed implicit links, such as what is on screen while a character speaks, or what is said while a visual event unfolds.

ChronusOmni interleaves text timestamp tokens with visual and audio features at each time step, giving one shared timeline. Reinforcement learning with specially designed rewards then enforces correct ordering and sharper timing judgments. The team also built ChronusAV, a timing accurate, cross modal aligned dataset. On that benchmark the model improved results by more than thirty percent, and it led on most measures across other timing benchmarks while keeping general video and audio skills.
arxiv-2512-10341:
Vinoth Punniyamoorthy and five coauthors design a cloud architecture for training machine learning models across institutions without pooling the sensitive data. Their framework stacks several privacy technologies. Federated learning keeps data at its home institution while sharing model updates. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise with formal privacy budgets. Zero knowledge proofs let participants verify policy compliance cryptographically, without seeing each other's data. A governance layer, steered by reinforcement learning, adapts policies to assessed risk. The system is built cloud natively for heterogeneous, multi cloud deployment.

A full prototype runs across hybrid Kubernetes clusters. The authors report reduced membership inference risk, meaning attackers learn less about whether a specific record was in the training set. Formal privacy budgets were enforced consistently, and model performance stayed stable under the differential privacy noise. Multi institution workloads ran with minimal overhead.
arxiv-2512-10641:
Cédric Join, Emmanuel Delaleau, and Michel Fliess give control theory's workhorse, the linear quadratic regulator, a fresh algebraic foundation. Regulators steer a system while balancing effort against error, and textbooks build them on Kalman's state-space picture. The authors show that plain linear differential equations with constant coefficients are the real building block underneath.

Applying Euler-Lagrange equations to a flat output, described in module theory over the ring of differential operators, yields the regulator directly. Freeness of that module turns out to be exactly Kalman's controllability condition, as Fliess had shown. Inside this frame, the two-point boundary value problem becomes tractable, giving optimal time horizons, parameter design, and rest-to-rest paths, plus a new turnpike-like effect proved by nonstandard analysis. The feedback loop closes through the HEOL approach, and simple simulated examples carry the intuition.
arxiv-2512-10741:
Elroy Galbraith, Chadwick Sutherland, and Donahue Morgan design emergency call support that does not fail Caribbean callers. Speech recognition degrades systematically on non-standard English varieties, so a distressed caller speaking in a local register may be transcribed badly at the moment accuracy matters most. Their system, TRIDENT, supports human dispatchers rather than replacing them, structuring calls for standard triage protocols.

Three layers run in parallel: speech recognition tuned to Caribbean accents, local extraction of clinical entities by a language model, and bio-acoustic detection of vocal distress. The key insight flips a weakness into a signal: low transcription confidence, especially alongside high vocal stress, marks a caller in crisis whose speech has shifted register. And should raise their place in the queue. Calm reports of grave emergencies, which stress detectors miss, are caught by the entity layer instead.
arxiv-2512-10841:
Mohammad Mirtaba and co-authors design a controller that actively damps vibration in a flexible beam, a stand-in for aeroelastic structures such as wings that flutter under aerodynamic load. They begin with a nonlinear structural model. It includes moderate deflection and the air forces, and it is built on a finite element grid. Then they compress that heavy model into a low-order linear one. The small model is identified from its responses to random Gaussian inputs.

On the small model they synthesise an output-feedback controller in the H2/H-infinity framework, which balances average behaviour against worst-case disturbance rejection. A frequency-weighted dynamic filter aims the controller at the vibration frequencies that matter most. Simulations show the design suppressing vibration well, and the authors probe its robustness as system settings vary, including where the actuator is placed, ahead of a presentation at the 2026 SciTech Forum.
arxiv-2512-10941:
Arijit Ray and co-authors let a model think in pictures without drawing them. Reasoning is not purely verbal: space, time, and what objects afford all resist words. Existing multimodal reasoners that try to think with images are brittle, leaning on specialist tools, expensive image generation, or handcrafted reasoning traces to switch between text and image thoughts.

Their Mull-Tokens are modality-agnostic latent tokens, pretrained carriers that can hold intermediate information in either image or text form. So the model reasons in a free-form latent space toward the answer. Training first supervises the tokens with interleaved text-image traces, then fine-tunes on final answers alone. Across four hard spatial reasoning benchmarks, from puzzles to perspective-taking, Mull-Tokens beat text-only and interleaved image-text baselines, with the largest gains on a reasoning-heavy puzzle split. The paper was accepted to the CVPR 2026 findings track.
arxiv-2512-11041:
Robert Reischke and the Kilo-Degree Survey team use the survey's final data release to test the standard model of cosmology. Their cosmic shear analysis measures how gravity from intervening matter slightly distorts distant galaxy shapes. For the first time, those results agree well enough with cosmic microwave background data to combine the two reliably.

Adding microwave lensing, galaxy clustering patterns, and other probes, they test whether space is curved, whether neutrino masses vary, and whether dark energy changes over time. The standard flat model still fits well, and the key clustering measure stays robust as the model space widens. Combining every probe hints at some tension with evolving dark energy, but the evidence falls short of a clear departure from the standard picture.
arxiv-2512-11241:
Yupei Li and fellow authors find an unexpected route to detecting fake speech: train a speech encoder only to recognise emotion, then use it to spot deepfakes. Emotion cues were already known to help spotting. Earlier systems, though, fused them through complicated processes, or fine tuned encoders directly for spotting. which can damage the representations that other tasks like speaker verification rely on.

Their simpler recipe fine tunes the encoder on emotion spotting alone, freezes it, and trains a small support vector classifier for spotting on top. Detection scores rose noticeably on two standard fake speech collections while the underlying speech representation stayed intact. Swapping emotion for speaker identity in fact hurt spotting, showing emotion itself is the bridge. Analysis of a third data set also exposed speaker bias hiding in its genuine recordings.
arxiv-2512-11441:
Charles Elbar and Alejandro Fernández-Jiménez construct the first rule based particle approximation for a fourth order partial differential equation, a model connected with how cells stick to one another. Fourth order equations are known to be hard to simulate with particles, whose collective spread normally follows simpler second order laws. A reliable particle picture matters because it links individual based models to smooth bulk models.

Their route passes through a family of nonlocal equations that approach the fourth order one and are well posed. For those equations, the actual spread of the particles satisfies the equation naturally. Stability of the associated gradient flow in the Wasserstein shape then transfers the approximation to the target equation. Numeric model runs at the particle level illustrate the model. The result opens rule based particle methods to a class of higher order problems in biology and materials.
arxiv-2512-11541:
Emmanuel Katalay, David Dimandja, and Jordan Masakuna automate the retraining of cloud hosted classifiers when the data they serve begins to drift. Machine learning models decay as real spreads shift, yet in many organisations a human must notice and trigger retraining by hand. Their process watches for significant change itself and acts only when action is warranted.

Multiple statistical criteria combine to detect spread shifts robustly, avoiding both missed drift and wasteful retraining on noise. When a trigger fires, the process retrains and redeploys the neural network classifier automatically. Tests on several benchmark anomaly spotting data sets showed clear gains in hit rate and robustness over conventional retraining schedules that update on a fixed timetable or not at all. The authors frame the system as a base for dependable, self maintaining machine learning in changing real world environments.
arxiv-2512-11641:
Bruno Rodrigues, Inês Ochoa, and Agostinho Gomes work on better calorimeters, the detector blocks that weigh particle energy at colliders. Next generation machines demand sharper measures than ever. A calorimeter quality hinges on two terms: one from random sampling noise, one from uneven response.

Using the ALLEGRO detector idea for the FCC-ee collider, the team varies the thickness of absorber layers in Geant4 simulations. Thicker or thinner layers trade one error term against the other, so the best mix is not obvious. Their method maps that trade off in a planned way. It lays groundwork for a closed design loop that tests many layouts against clear physics goals.
arxiv-2512-11941:
Jingmin Zhu and co-authors present DynaPURLS, a system that names actions from skeleton data for classes it never saw in training. Zero shot action recognition usually aligns whole body motion with flat class level text, a coarse match that breaks when new classes shift the picture.

DynaPURLS builds layered text descriptions, from whole movements down to single body parts, using a large language model. An adaptive module groups joints into matching fine parts. At test time a refinement step adjusts the text features to the live motion, steadied by a confidence aware memory bank that resists noisy guesses. On NTU RGB+D 60 and 120 and PKU-MMD, it set new state of the art scores.
arxiv-2512-12141:
Subhadip Dey and Sebastian Hurtado prove a result in pure math in a 2025 paper. They work with real semi-simple Lie groups, which are smooth groups used to study symmetry. A discrete subgroup sits inside such a group, and a smaller subgroup may act in a mixing way on its boundary.

They show the larger group cannot then split as a free product of the smaller group with the integers. If the smaller group has algebraic entries, so does the larger one. One result is that certain discrete subgroups of two copies of SL2(R) cannot be free groups. An appendix links such groups to number properties of Lie groups.
arxiv-2512-12241:
Muhammad Junaid Khan and Rida Batool Sheraliyat review cavity ring-down spectroscopy with hybrid cavity designs in a 2025 paper. The method measures how fast light fades inside a mirrored cavity, rather than how much light a sample absorbs. That decay rate reveals even very weak absorption by gases or other samples.

The paper covers use with both pulsed and steady light sources. It stresses that the method is far more sensitive than standard absorption spectroscopy. Weak signals that older methods miss become easy to detect. The focus on hybrid cavity structures shows how cavity shape affects the decay behavior that users rely on.
arxiv-2512-12341:
Paul Hofman, Yusuf Sale, and Eyke Hullermeier argue that no single uncertainty measure fits all machine learning tasks in a 2025 paper. Safe use of models in high stakes settings needs honest estimates of how unsure a prediction is. Many measures claim to beat the rest, but the authors say the right choice depends on the job.

They use a flexible family that splits total, aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainty, tuned by scoring rules. For selective prediction, the scoring rule should match the task loss. For spotting out of distribution inputs, mutual information worked best. In active learning, epistemic uncertainty from zero-one loss won consistently.
arxiv-2512-12441:
Rr Nefriana, Muheng Yan, Rebecca Hwa, and Yu-Ru Lin study how leadership structure shapes online hate groups in a 2025 paper. They analyze ten years of Facebook activity by hate groups tied to the Israel-Palestine conflict, covering anti-Semitic and Islamophobic ideologies. The question is whether groups run by a few key actors behave differently from flatter groups.

Higher centralization linked to greater user engagement across both ideologies. Yet messaging differed: centralized Islamophobic groups used more uniform frames, while centralized anti-Semitic groups showed wider framing and topics. Islamophobic groups also clustered tightly in the inter-group network, while anti-Semitic groups spread more evenly. The findings may guide tailored disruption plans.
arxiv-2512-12541:
Osvaldo L Santos-Pereira, Everton M C Abreu, and Marcelo B Ribeiro match a warp drive spacetime to flat spacetime in a 2025 paper. The Alcubierre metric describes a bubble that contracts space in front and expands it behind. Joining that inner geometry to an outer Minkowski, or flat, geometry must satisfy the Darmois junction conditions at the shared surface.

They show the warp shift vector at the wall must solve an inviscid Burgers equation, in a gauge where it does not depend on the y and z coordinates. That gauge links the metric to shock waves. Some curvature components stay nonzero at the wall, depending on that solution. The warp geometry is therefore not globally flat.
arxiv-2512-12641:
Sander Land and Yuval Pinter ask which pieces Unigram tokenization really needs in a 2025 paper. Tokenization splits text into pieces for language models. Unigram offers a probabilistic method, unlike the greedy rules of Byte-Pair Encoding, but its practical implementation is complex, limiting use to the SentencePiece package and its adapters.

The authors bridge theory and practice with a clear guide to implementation and parameter choices. They also identify a simpler algorithm that accepts slightly higher training loss in exchange for improved compression. For builders who avoided Unigram over its complexity, the paper lowers the barrier, and code is available alongside it.
arxiv-2512-12941:
Siyuan Yao and co-authors present UAGLNet, a network that picks buildings out of remote sensing images. Buildings vary a lot in shape and size, so maps made this way often come out blurred or wrong. Past models also fused broad and fine details poorly.

UAGLNet mixes two kinds of layers: convolutional layers for local detail and Transformer layers for the broad scene. A fusion module joins the two views, and a decoder estimates doubt pixel by pixel to sharpen unsure areas. In wide tests, the method beat prior state-of-the-art systems for building extraction. The authors also released their code in public.
arxiv-2512-13641:
Gabriel Vitorino de Andrade and co-authors test how well neural networks diagnose disease in mango leaves when images are degraded. Real farm photos face noise, blur, and weather effects, yet few studies check model robustness for mango. That gap matters for a crop of global importance.

They built MangoLeafDB-C from an existing data set, adding 19 corruption types at five severity levels. They compared ResNet-50, ResNet-101, VGG-16, Xception, and the light LCNN model. LCNN beat larger models on defocus and motion blur and had the lowest mean corruption error. Big models fell off sharply under corruption, so light, specialized models may suit field use on edge devices better.
arxiv-2512-13841:
Eduardo Gutiérrez-Peña and co-authors present a new fitting framework for continuous-state branching processes. Such processes model groups that branch and vary in a continuous way, and their parameters are hard to estimate from partial data. Their method leans on the process's subordinator form.

By shifting the stochastic dynamics onto the associated subordinator, they recast estimation in a form that needs no extra premises. The likelihood can then be recovered by Laplace transform inversion, with numeric steps, even when no closed-form transition density exists. They also propose a simulation framework that builds discrete-time paths from the same subordinator structure. The approach gives a flexible route to parameter estimation for this class of branching models.
arxiv-2512-14041:
Mingjia Yin and co-authors propose a generative paradigm for click-through rate prediction in recommendation systems. CTR models estimate the chance a user clicks an item. Standard models are discriminative and lean on explicit interactions between raw ID embeddings, which causes embedding collapse and information redundancy.

Their Supervised Feature Generation framework has an encoder that builds hidden codes for each feature and a decoder that rebuilds all feature embeddings from them. Unlike self-supervised methods, its loss uses the click signal directly. The framework plugs into most existing CTR models, recasting them in that form. Experiments across data sets and base models show consistent gains, with less embedding collapse and wasted overlap.
arxiv-2512-14141:
Hanning Chen and ten coauthors present TorchTraceAP in a 2025 paper on slowdowns in computer vision models. Traces record each step a model runs, and hidden patterns called anti patterns can waste training and inference time. Finding them by hand takes deep skill across systems and kernels.

The dataset holds over 600 PyTorch traces from vision models for classification, detection, segmentation, and generation, gathered on several hardware platforms. The authors also propose a two step method. A light model first flags suspect trace segments, then a large language model classifies them and gives targeted feedback. Their method beat clustering and rule based methods at finding the problem regions.
arxiv-2512-14241:
Salvatore Romano, Marco Grassia, and Giuseppe Mangioni propose a new way to judge graph generative models in a 2025 paper. Such models learn from real networks and create synthetic graphs that mimic them, which helps in network science and bioinformatics.

Most checks rely on Maximum Mean Discrepancy, a metric the authors show is weak for this job. Their method, called RGM, uses a geometric deep learning model trained to classify graphs from a custom set of synthetic and real graphs. They test two leading models, GRAN and EDGE. Both capture some graph traits but miss key structural features that set graph domains apart. The authors urge better metrics for future work.
arxiv-2512-14641:
Designing health apps with older adults, rather than just for them, is the theme of one qualitative co-design study. Four adults aged sixty and over gave design feedback on a Figma prototype and a generative AI chatbot for an app that would coach physical activity.

The sessions gathered concrete insights on what the prototype and chatbot should do to earn older users' trust and fit daily routines. Co-design of this kind surfaces needs that younger design teams routinely miss. The study speaks to a wider push for health technology that older adults will actually keep using, and it records what the participants themselves asked the app to become.
arxiv-2512-14741:
Jing Cui and coauthors show that a hidden backdoor planted in a large language model can be built to survive the updates users apply later. A backdoor makes a model produce harmful output or skip safety checks when it sees a secret trigger. Their 2025 attack, P-Trojan, is designed for the rounds of fine-tuning that follow a model's release.

Normal backdoors fade as training continues, so the authors align the poisoned training signals with clean task signals on token embeddings, making the hidden mapping harder to forget. Tests on Qwen2.5 and LLaMA3 models kept the backdoor working over 99% of the time while clean task accuracy held up. The results argue that safety checks must test models after updates, not only at release.
arxiv-2512-14841:
Brian Batell and three coauthors widen a proposed answer to a fine tuning puzzle in particle physics. The puzzle is why the Higgs mass is so small next to other natural scales. Their base idea, N naturalness, posits many copies of the Standard Model, each with a different Higgs mass value.

A particle called the reheaton refills the copies with energy after the big bang, mostly favoring one copy. Past work assumed our world is the copy with the lightest Higgs value. The authors show resonant mixing between the reheaton and the Higgs can favor a heavier copy instead. That broader version still fits cosmic bounds on extra radiation and heavy relics. Future sky surveys could test much of what remains, and the many copies might ring with a shared gravitational wave hum.
arxiv-2512-15141:
Liangcai Huang and a coauthor proposed a fast numerical scheme for a tempered time fractional advection dispersion equation, a model of spreading with memory effects. The scheme was second order in time and tackled a weak singularity at the starting instant, where solutions are not smooth. The authors studied uniqueness, stability, and convergence, and claimed second order accuracy in both time and space.

Readers should know that this paper has been withdrawn from arXiv. The withdrawal note states that an error in the proof of Lemma 3.8 affects the main conclusions, and that all co-authors agree to the withdrawal. The claimed convergence results should therefore not be relied on. The entry is kept as the record of a withdrawn submission.
arxiv-2512-15441:
Gilderlan Tavares de Araujo and co authors tackle channel estimation for a new kind of smart surface in a 2025 paper. Beyond diagonal reconfigurable surfaces link their elements together, which gives more control over radio waves than older surfaces. That same linking makes the channel much harder to measure.

Instead of relying only on pilot signals, the team uses a semi blind method that also learns from the data symbols themselves. They reshape the received signal as a tensor and offer two receivers, a two stage one and a single stage iterative one. The work covers moving users with changing channels, states when recovery is reliable, and shows gains over prior methods in tests.
arxiv-2512-15741:
K. M. Belotsky, F. V. Kostromin, and M. L. Solovyov reconstruct the dark matter density profile from the cosmic positron anomaly in a 2025 paper, dated December 8. Cosmic rays show more positrons than standard sources predict, and dark matter annihilation or decay is one proposed cause. Earlier studies assumed a spatial distribution and checked the fit.

This work inverts the problem: an algorithm using linear algebra and adaptive grids searches for the distribution that matches the data. A class of solutions is formally found, though the profiles look only slightly realistic at the chosen injection spectra. The result still shows the explanatory room that spatial freedom gives, and motivates more realistic models.
arxiv-2512-15841:
Sandro Tacchella and co authors argue that galaxy evolution must be treated as a stochastic process in a 2025 white paper. Each galaxy is observed only once in its life, so time dependent physics must be inferred from single epoch snapshots of many galaxies. Descriptive scaling relations cannot reveal the regulation mechanisms behind star formation and quenching.

The authors call for samples of about one hundred million galaxy spectra with enough depth for absorption line ages and chemistry, across redshift 0 to 3. Current surveys give either depth or size, not both. At that scale, burstiness, duty cycles, and other process parameters can be pinned down. The paper outlines a future ESO wide field spectroscopic facility to deliver it.
arxiv-2512-16041:
Yuanning Feng and four co-authors question a popular AI testing method in work posted to arXiv in 2025. Many labs now use a large language model as a judge to grade other models, and even as a training reward. Most judge benchmarks rely on human-written answers as ground truth, which imports human bias and limits scale.

The team built Sage, a test suite that needs no human labels. It checks whether a judge is self-consistent on pairs of answers and logically consistent across a whole set, using 650 questions. Sage scores track known benchmarks well. Yet even top models like Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5 gave inconsistent preferences in nearly a quarter of hard cases. The authors blame a new effect they call situational preference, and note that human judges are inconsistent too.
arxiv-2512-16641:
Katrin Bolsmann and coauthors design fast three-qubit gates for trapped ions lifted to Rydberg states, highly excited states with strong long-range forces. Trapped ions are a top quantum hardware path, but standard gates that use shared motion are slow and hard to scale.

Their single-pulse plan gives a native controlled-controlled-Z gate with microwave-dressed Rydberg ions, tuned to respect the short Rydberg lifetime. Fidelity tops 97 percent under realistic terms, in about 2 microseconds at cryogenic heat levels. The team then builds a fault-tolerant, measurement-free error correction plan on the nine-qubit Bacon-Shor code, and shows by simulation that it works on a linear ion chain.
arxiv-2512-16741:
Zaheed Ahmed, Philip Makedonski, and Jens Grabowski run the first head-to-head test of whether fake faults in deep learning act like real faults. Testers use mutants, small edits to a model or its training, as stand-ins for real bugs, but that swap was unverified for deep learning.

The team scored realism with two measures, coupling strength and behavior match to real faults, across four public bug sets: CleanML, DeepFD, DeepLocalize, and defect4ML. Mutants made before training beat those made after training on both scores, across single operators too. The catch is cost: pre-training mutants take far more compute, so better post-training operators are still needed.
arxiv-2512-16941:
Eduardo Guendelman builds de Sitter space and a dark matter candidate from strings whose tension can vary. In the modified measure frame, each string can carry its own tension, and a new bulk field, the tension scalar, shifts tension along the string sheet.

With two string tensions present, a braneworld solution gives an induced de Sitter space on the brane, sidestepping swampland limits of standard string theory. Strings with tension unlike ours can also serve as dark matter. Since they share our space and compact shape, they should yield dark copies of the Standard Model, a mirror sector hinted by the setup.
arxiv-2512-17141:
Roman Firt and coauthors benchmark Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization, a quantum algorithm for ground state energies, on Heisenberg spin models in one and two dimensions. Hard cases include dense ground states where many configurations mix.

With problem-informed start states and magnetization-sector sweeps, SKQD matched ground energies and field-driven magnetization curves across anisotropy values. Checks against DMRG and exact diagonalization agreed in kind, with accuracy rising in more anisotropic regimes. Runs on real quantum hardware with 18 and 30 qubit chains gave magnetization curves that fit theory. Small 2D square lattice runs show the method works past one dimension.
arxiv-2512-17241:
Suraj Nukala and four co-authors ask how a service robot should get the attention of a customer who is busy with something else. They test three channels a robot can use: sound and speech, a visual display, and small body motions called micromotion gestures. The setting mimics a restaurant delivery task.

Twenty-four people took part, each playing a typing game to stay occupied while a Temi robot brought cups. Speech worked best at pulling attention away from the game. Yet a screen display was rated clearest for showing which cup the robot meant, with speech second and micromotion last. The split matters: grabbing attention and being understood turn out to be two different jobs.
arxiv-2512-17441:
Jiri Kvita asks whether a brand-new heavy particle would leave a fingerprint in the rain of debris a cosmic ray makes in the sky. When a cosmic ray smashes into air, it spawns a shower of particles whose depth profile telescopes record. A fast, simplified shower model lets Kvita test ideas full simulations would take far longer to check.

Into that model he inserts a made-up resonance, a short-lived heavy particle, at masses of 100 GeV and 1 TeV. Its decays bend the shower's average depth, with the bend lasting across a wide energy band. A wide resonance leaves a clear mark, while a narrow one fades toward a percent-level effect. Plotting two shower traits together, he suggests, could expose such hidden marks.
arxiv-2512-17641:
Aimé Matheron and three co-authors wire a ninety-year-old quantum prediction into the software that designs real laser experiments. Quantum theory says empty space itself should bend light very slightly when fields grow extreme, an effect called vacuum birefringence. Nobody has measured it directly in a lab yet. The best hope is firing two laser beams head-on and hunting the faint twist in one of them.

Signal formulas existed, but experiment planners lacked a tool that also models lenses, apertures, and diffraction smearing along the bench. The team adds a vacuum signal module to an established beam propagation toolkit, losses and all. Planners can now rehearse the full experiment, background glare included, before spending on hardware.
arxiv-2512-17741:
Hallmann Óskar Gestsson and Alexandra Olaya-Castro show how the flicker pattern of emitted light betrays quantum teamwork inside a light-harvesting pair. Their model unit holds two mismatched emitters, coupled so energy can slosh between them, like molecules in a leaf sharing sunlight. The quantum traits at stake, shared excitons and coherent transfer, hide from ordinary brightness measures.

The tell is in cross correlation: how often the two emitters flash in relation to each other, tracked over time. The rhythm of that pattern hands over two numbers at once, the transfer speed and how widely the exciton spreads across both emitters. The same signal also certifies lasting quantum coherence in the driven steady state. Photosynthesis researchers gain a lab-ready witness for quantum effects.
arxiv-2512-17841:
Phani Pavan Kambhampati and three coauthors built NeuRehab, a system meant to make robot guided stroke therapy adapt to each patient. Standard rehab machines follow fixed routines and struggle with changing patient behavior. They also draw too much power for mobile use away from a clinic.

NeuRehab splits the work in two. A small device at the patient's side runs low power spiking neural networks on special hardware, while a larger machine handles heavy retraining for each patient. Tested on a shoulder exercise device, the split design matched standard performance while cutting power use and response delay by over 60 percent.
arxiv-2512-17941:
Bin Xu, Ayan Banerjee, Midhat Urooj, and Sandeep K. S. Gupta compare hardware for teaching a digital twin at the edge of a network. A twin is a live math copy of a patient that updates as new data arrive. Hospitals need that learning to be fast and light, yet standard methods lean on slow repeated solving.
