The team's approach, GenCP, is a generative modeling framework for coupled physics. It aims to handle strong links between the different processes in space and time. Split-data methods tend to lose both speed and accuracy in that setting. A model that learns the coupling directly could serve engineering design better. The work speaks to fields from materials to climate, wherever physics refuses to stay separate.
arxiv-2601-19641:
Florian Bruse and Martin Lange work on a deep question in computer science: can complexity classes be pulled apart? The famous gap between P and NP asks whether fast checking implies fast solving. They study the parts of these classes that are invariant under bisimulation, a notion of sameness for processes. A theorem of Otto characterises the P part exactly, using a logic called the polyadic mu-calculus.

The authors use a known construction from model checking to shrink the problem. Definability in the big logic is reduced to definability in the ordinary modal mu-calculus. That reduction works inside a special class of structures called power graphs. The result is a new route toward separating the fragments. Even partial separations would clarify what logic can express.
arxiv-2601-19741:
Nikiforos Galanis studies how well a space mission could detect a faint background of gravitational waves. Pulsar timing arrays have hinted at such a background in the nanohertz band. The LISA mission will listen in the millihertz band from space. Finding a background hum with a single orbiting detector is hard, because the instrument's own noise is also mostly random.

The author examines how the way noise is characterised affects detection. If the noise model is off, a real signal can be missed or a fake one claimed. Careful noise modelling is therefore central to the search. The study helps set realistic expectations for LISA. It also informs how its data should be analysed when it flies.
arxiv-2601-19841:
Armando M. V. Corro, Carlos M. C. Riveros, and Jose L. Teruel Carretero study a family of surfaces in three-dimensional space. The surfaces are defined by their support function, which measures distance from a fixed plane. Here that function is quadratic and of harmonic type. These HQSF surfaces generalise an earlier class built the same way.

The authors obtain a Weierstrass-type representation for them. Such a formula builds every surface of the class from three holomorphic functions. They also classify the surfaces of rotation within the family. Representation formulas turn a geometric condition into concrete data. Classification of the symmetric cases completes the basic picture of the class.
arxiv-2601-20041:
Shih-Hsuan Chiu and Ming-Syan Chen adapt retrieval-augmented generation for personal assistants on edge devices. A phone-based assistant can personalise answers by retrieving a user's profile data. Profile data grows fast, though, as interactions and updates pile up. Edge hardware has little memory and compute to spare, so standard retrieval struggles.

Their system, CiMRAG, is aware of computing-in-memory hardware, adapts to the domain, and resists noise. It targets retrieval that stays fast as profiles swell. Personal data also stays on the device, a privacy advantage over cloud assistants. Making on-device retrieval viable matters as assistants move off the cloud. The work aligns algorithm design with the hardware that will run it.
arxiv-2601-20641:
Boaz Carmeli and four colleagues investigate whether vision-language model agents develop their own task-oriented communication. When agents must cooperate, they might invent protocols that differ from natural language. The authors focus on two properties such protocols may show: efficiency, conveying task-relevant content more concisely than natural language, and covertness.

A covert protocol is hard for outside observers to interpret, which raises concerns about transparency and control. The study uses collaborative reasoning tasks. Watching how machine dialects form, and whether humans can still read them, is central to keeping multi-agent systems accountable. The risk grows as more teams of agents are put to work side by side.
arxiv-2601-21041:
Dylan Jow and Delon Shen develop the theory of reading starlight that twinkles through interstellar gas. Their 2026 paper concerns scintillometry. Compact radio sources, such as pulsars and fast radio bursts, scintillate in the interstellar medium. Their scattered images interfere at the observer. Scintillometry extracts astrometric information from that interference. It can locate the images and measure distances to the screen and the source.

Precise astrometry from scintillation is a young art. The authors aim toward precision, laying out theory and prospects. Better distances would map the gas between the stars. They would also sharpen the positions of exotic radio sources. The paper is a roadmap for observers and theorists alike. It shows how a nuisance effect can become a measuring tool.
arxiv-2601-21241:
A 2026 arXiv paper presents a fast implicit scheme for flows made of many materials side by side. Layered fluids can act quite unlike any one of their layers alone. Taken as a whole, such a stack behaves like a new kind of fluid material.

Each layer is described by the classic Euler equations with a stiffened gas law. The scheme works in coordinates that move with the fluid itself. That choice helps track the borders between materials as they shift. The method aims at accurate results for layered flows found in engineering and physics.
arxiv-2601-21641:
Evandro S. Ortigossa and Eran Segal bring mixture-of-experts scaling to time series forecasting. Transformers have advanced forecasting, but they scale poorly to long histories. Expert layers are a proven scaling trick in language models, where each token is routed to a few specialists.

Token-wise routing fits text, where each word is fairly separate. Time series are different: nearby points form stretches with shared meaning. The authors route whole segments at several resolutions instead. Segment routing respects the local, continuous nature of signals like demand, weather, and traffic, and should let forecasters grow without losing the thread of long patterns.
arxiv-2601-21741:
Erick Pasten and Christos G. Tsagas explain why galaxy peculiar motions grow faster in Einstein's gravity than in Newton's. Surveys keep reporting bulk flows, large-scale drifts of galaxies, that look too big and too fast for the standard model. The mismatch has become a standing problem for the concordance picture of the cosmos.

The authors trace part of the gap to the theory itself. General relativity lets these velocities grow faster than Newtonian reasoning suggests. That does not settle the bulk flow dispute, but it recalibrates what counts as anomalous. Some of the reported excess may be relativity doing exactly what it should.
arxiv-2601-21841:
Robots that act in the physical world face a planning problem that text models do not. A large language model can reason in words. An embodied agent faces more. It must break a high-level goal into steps it can actually perform. Each step must fit a changing, observed environment.

The 2026 preprint behind this entry proposes task planning that is informed by graphs. The idea is simple. Let the structure of the environment guide how the model generates actions. Do not let it improvise long chains of steps unaided. Graph guidance could cut the classic failure mode of robot planners. Fluent plans that break on the third step because an object is not where the words assumed it was.
arxiv-2601-22041:
Naomi Pitzer and Daniela Mihai study how artificial agents invent ways to communicate when their senses differ. Research on emergent communication shows how agents develop shared, structured signals. Most studies, though, assume agents share the same modality or aligned representations of the world.

Real settings are messier. The authors study a multi-step binary communication game where agents differ in modality and lack perceptual grounding in a shared world. One agent's signal must cross into another's different way of sensing. Their 2026 preprint asks what shared structure can still emerge. The results speak to multi-agent systems deployed in the wild, where cameras, microphones, and other sensors rarely give matching views.
arxiv-2601-22241:
Jelle Westra and co-authors study two design choices that decide whether gradient-free optimization finds good structures. Topology optimization designs structures, such as beams, by simulation, without gradient information. It is widely used in engineering because it can discover high-performing shapes that no one would sketch by hand.

Success depends on the geometric parameterization, which defines the search space, and on the optimizer that explores it. Using a cantilever beam as a case study, the team's 2026 preprint investigates how those two choices interact. Their findings guide engineers who must pick a setup before burning simulation budgets: the best optimizer on the wrong parameterization still designs the wrong beam.
arxiv-2601-22441:
Getachew Befekadu opens a two-part study on inference when the true likelihood is out of reach. In such cases, teams simulate data and compare it to real data through summary scores. His 2026 preprint lets a learned score act as a stand-in likelihood, with a bonus: it can improve the inference as it goes.

The frame is Bayesian, so it yields full ranges of doubt, not just point calls. Learned scores can adapt to the model at hand. The work aims at fields where simulators rule, from epidemics to climate. Part one lays the base; part two builds on it.
arxiv-2601-22541:
Sean Current, Chandan Kumar, Datta Gaitonde, and Srinivasan Parthasarathy test how far neural surrogates can roll out a hard airflow on their own. Neural operators learn to step a physics field forward at great speed. Their 2026 preprint uses the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, the core rules of gas flow, with shocks and sharp fronts.

Long rollouts are where such tools tend to drift or blow up. The bench marks that drift over many steps. Honest limits help engineers know when a fast surrogate can be trusted. The work serves flight and turbine design.
arxiv-2601-22841:
Leonard Hackel, Tom Burgert, and Begüm Demir ask how much of a big Earth-observation model is really needed. Foundation models for remote sensing borrow their design from computer vision. They work well on tasks like mapping land from satellite images, but they are large and costly to run.

The authors test how far these models can be slimmed down without losing skill. Their checks question whether vision scaling rules carry over to satellite data at all. Leaner models would let more groups map crops, forests, and floods with modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-23041:
Youxu Shi, Suorong Yang, and Dong Liu steer vision-language models away from making things up. These models do well on tasks that mix images and text, but they still hallucinate and fail on safety, even at large scale. Steering nudges a model's internal state to improve behavior with little cost.

Their one-shot optimized steering vector is tuned once, then applied broadly. Prior steering traded efficiency against effectiveness in awkward ways. A cheap, reusable vector could make image-aware assistants more truthful without retraining. Steering is attractive because it is lightweight: one vector can adjust behavior without retraining the whole multimodal model.
arxiv-2601-23241:
Damien Barbier studies when a single binary neuron becomes trainable, using a statistical-mechanics lens. Binary neurons take only two states, making them cheap but hard to train. The connected ensemble framework tracks how low-loss paths form in rugged loss landscapes.

Those paths reveal when a network can learn a simple task at all. They also show which minima training should aim for. Knowing the transition point between impossible and trainable guides the design of efficient, discrete networks. Low-loss paths are the diagnostic object, revealing which minima training should target once trainability switches on.
arxiv-2602-00241: Hansol Lee and colleagues test whether algorithmic uncertainty sways human experts in college admissions. The authors define algorithmic sensitivity as how far a decision shifts when a more or less favorable score is shown for the same person. In a randomized field experiment with 19545 applicants in a selective admissions cycle, officers reviewed files alongside a score from one of two similar models. The study asks how much human verdicts move with the model shown.
arxiv-2602-00341: Grigor H. Sargsyan and team review ab initio beta decay calculations in light nuclei as probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Precision beta decay experiments test fundamental symmetries, focusing on the CKM matrix element Vud and exotic weak currents. Ab initio nuclear many body methods, based on realistic nucleon nucleon interactions and now systematically improvable approximations, have moved considerably in computing higher order corrections. The review surveys state of the art calculations of radiative and recoil order terms and weighs their significance for new physics searches.
arxiv-2602-00441: Fabian Jofre Parra and team study electron-phonon interactions in a Weyl semimetal under a magnetic field with torsional strain. That superposition of field and strain, modeled by a gauge field, produces an asymmetric pseudo-magnetic field at chiral Weyl nodes. The authors study nodal asymmetry using the Kadanoff-Wilson renormalization group and its flows. Solving those equations, they track the coupling parameters. They analyze fixed points and lattice Peierls instabilities from interactions between phonons and the chiral Landau level in strong pseudo-magnetic fields.
arxiv-2602-00641: Alain Durmus and colleagues tackle sampling from unnormalised densities on curved manifolds, where several modes defeat existing methods. Their training-free algorithm moves an easy noise sample toward the target through a deterministic flow out of equilibrium, following an interpolant shaped by the manifold geometry. It rests only on standard Monte Carlo posterior steps, so no learned model is needed, and it carries diffusion-style sampling beyond flat spaces. Theory backs the method, and tests on varied multi-modal cases, including high-dimensional and heavy-tailed targets, show it works.
arxiv-2602-01141: Shun Arai lifts shapelets for star pictures into phase space, naming the result Wigner shapelets. Old shapelets split pictures into place or wave views, while the new set reads pictures straight in four-dimensional phase space, with a symplectic frame and cell-set sharpness cap. The base comes from cross-Wigner forms of Laguerre modes, giving a band map over two kept quantities, tune energy and spin push. The paper lines up all Wigner math for star work in both astro and quantum-info tongues.
arxiv-2602-02141: J. Roman-Garza and colleagues model mass shedding when stars far more massive than the Sun merge. Such giants may form in metal poor dense crowds, and may seed mid sized black holes. With a one dimensional fluid code, the team tracks huge stars with small partners spiraling in, as drag turns orbital energy into heat. The merger throws off ten to thirty percent of the system's mass, spending most fed in energy on ejection. Merger driven mass loss matters for how such giants form.
arxiv-2602-02641:
A 2026 benchmark by Najmul Hasan and 1 co-author tests whether large language models can spot phishing URLs with little or no training examples. Deceptive links have grown far more sophisticated as criminals adopt generative AI, and phishing volume has exploded since 2022. Labeled data cannot keep pace with new tactics, which makes zero-shot and few-shot detection attractive.

The evaluation places several models under one unified prompting framework on a balanced dataset with consistent prompts. Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and two ranking metrics capture both classification quality and practical utility. Operational trade-offs between models are laid out in detail. Few-shot prompting, giving the model a handful of examples, improved performance across multiple models. The authors present the benchmark as guidance for defenders choosing models for large-scale screening, where a small success rate for attackers still means many victims.
arxiv-2602-02741:
Anmol Gupta and 4 co-authors teach robots the joint structure of unfamiliar objects by watching one human demonstration, in a 2026 paper. Articulation models tell a robot how drawers slide and doors swing, enabling later manipulation. Earlier methods needed prior knowledge of joint counts or types, missed occluded joints revealed only during interaction, or demanded many multi-view images.

PokeNet works from a sequence of point cloud observations of a person manipulating an unknown object. It predicts joint parameters, infers the order in which joints must be operated, and tracks joint states over time. Manipulation order matters for objects like dishwashers, where one joint unlocks another. Across diverse objects, including unseen categories, joint axis and state estimation accuracy improved by over twenty-seven percent on average over leading methods. Gains held in simulation and in the real world.
arxiv-2602-02841:
Jaesung Bae and 1 co-author tackle learning when labeled data is scarce in a 2026 paper. Their framework, GeLDA, creates extra training examples in a compressed latent space. A latent space is the compact set of features a foundation model extracts from raw inputs.

GeLDA uses conditional diffusion models to generate those examples. Extra feature vectors guide generation toward the right class or subdomain. Two large tests follow. One covers speech emotion recognition in a new language with no training examples. The other covers image classification with rare classes. In both, GeLDA improved results, including a new best score for rare image classes.
arxiv-2602-02941:
A swirling magnetic pattern in a quasicrystal-like material is studied by Shinji Watanabe and 1 co-author in a 2026 paper. Recent neutron data found whirling-anti-whirling order, a noncollinear layout of magnetic moments, in a gold-based approximant crystal. The authors study how a magnetic field's heading affects that order.

Their math uses exact diagonalization of a working model with uniaxial anisotropy from the crystal's electric field. Along one field heading, a metamagnetic shift and a topological shift occur at once. Afterward, the chirality of the moments creates an emergent field. The analysis predicts a topological Hall effect should appear in electrical conductivity. Turning the field toward another axis points the same way.
arxiv-2602-03441:
Severin Bunk and 3 co-authors generalize the idea of a connection to bundles of higher-dimensional objects. A connection is the tool geometry uses to compare fibers at different points. Their 2026 paper works in derived differential geometry, where spaces are replaced by richer derived stacks. The goal is a clean general definition for higher-form connections on principal infinity-bundles.

The authors build the needed differentiation and integration theory for maps into derived stacks. They define the Atiyah algebroid of such a bundle and describe p-form connections as splittings of it. The new definition reproduces the known connections on higher U(1)-bundles. The paper also connects the symmetry algebras involved to higher Courant algebroids, with applications in gauge theory and supergravity.
arxiv-2602-03641:
Synthetic data fails exactly where it matters most when the rare class is the important one, like fraud or disease. Milosh Devic and 2 co-authors introduce CTTVAE in a 2026 paper, a conditional transformer-based variational autoencoder for tabular data. The target setting is severe class imbalance, where most generators ignore the minority or produce useless samples.

Two mechanisms do the work. A class-aware triplet margin loss reshapes the latent space for tighter, better-separated classes, and a training-by-sampling strategy shows the model underrepresented groups more often. Across six real-world benchmarks, the combined system achieves the best downstream results on minority classes, sometimes beating models trained on the original data. Ablations credit both components for the gains.
arxiv-2602-03741:
The Sun rings with global inertial modes whose frequencies and strengths drift over the solar cycle. B Lekshmi and 4 co-authors track those drifts in a 2026 paper. They use two decades of observations from the GONG network and the HMI instrument. They focus on equatorial Rossby modes and one high-latitude mode, measured in overlapping four-year windows.

The two instruments agree well across their shared years. Frequency variations grow with the mode's azimuthal order, and power changes typically exceed a factor of two. The high-latitude mode's power falls as sunspot number rises, while Rossby mode frequencies generally do the opposite of their powers. One Rossby mode breaks the pattern entirely. The authors present the modes as diagnostics of the solar interior's dynamics and magnetism.
arxiv-2602-03841:
Cosmological correlators, the fingerprints of quantum fields in the early universe as it expands, turn out to have a hidden simplicity. Chandramouli Chowdhury and 5 co-authors exploit that simplicity in a 2026 paper by drawing on flat-space scattering amplitudes. Dressing rules already lift ordinary Feynman diagrams into de Sitter correlators, with helper propagators attached.

The authors show that discontinuities of the correlators, jumps across energy values, come from unitarity cuts of flat-space diagrams dressed the same way. Cuts of the helper propagators give discontinuities in the outer energies. Those facts impose simple sum rules on the correlators, strong constraints in their own right. Cases at tree level and one loop illustrate the method, and dispersion relations rebuild full correlators from their discontinuities.
arxiv-2602-04041:
Hubble's workhorse camera slowly warps its own images. Anne O'Connor and 3 co-authors tracked the geometric distortion of the WFC3/UVIS instrument from 2009 to 2022. They aligned more than seven thousand exposures against the Gaia star catalog. Their 2026 paper isolates the linear terms: shift, rotation, scale, and skew.

Scale and skew drifted only slightly over thirteen years, less than intrinsic scatter. A filter-dependent scale offset appeared at all epochs, and rotation offsets grew after mid-2017. The archive pipeline already corrects residual terms when enough stars match. The authors advise high-precision users on when extra care is still warranted.
arxiv-2602-04241:
How a tokenizer chops words decides how well models handle Uralic languages. Nuo Xu and 1 co-author compare three subword methods across six Uralic languages in a 2026 study. These languages pack meaning into long, rich word forms and often lack large training corpora.

Overlap BPE, a variant encouraging shared pieces, beat byte pair encoding and unigram methods on part-of-speech tagging. Its advantage was clearest in Latin-script languages, with less fragmentation of content words. Transfer between languages depended on the tagging architecture, training volume, and family closeness. Tokenization, the authors conclude, is a modeling decision, not a preprocessing detail, for morphologically rich languages.
arxiv-2602-04341:
Old enterprise software can be rebuilt through a model rather than by hand. Tobias Böhm and 5 co-authors report a model-driven modernization approach in a 2026 practice paper. A rich, platform-neutral middle model sits between the legacy code and the modern target platform.

Four stages carry the system across: study, enrichment, building, and transition. Applied to a large industrial application on legacy .NET and ASP.NET, core screen components moved over semi-automatically while behavior was preserved. Standard patterns moved well on their own; bespoke layout pieces still needed focused manual work. Writing design knowledge into explicit models also improved the resulting code's upkeep.
arxiv-2602-04941:
Tomas Tokar and Scott Sanner wrote this 2026 machine learning paper, due to appear at ICLR 2026, about learning from sets. Sets have no natural order, so models like DeepSets squash them with a fixed operation such as a sum or a maximum. A fixed squash can blur useful information and limits what the model can express.

The authors propose a learnable replacement: a neural version of the Kolmogorov mean, which averages values after passing them through an invertible function. Networks built around it, called QUANNs, are shown to approximate a broad class of set functions in theory. In tests they beat leading baselines across varied benchmarks, and their learned representations transferred well even to tasks with no sets at all.
arxiv-2602-05041:
Studies that watch people often group them: pupils inside schools, patients inside hospitals. Eli Ben-Michael and 2 co-authors built a single weighting scheme for that setup in this 2026 statistics paper. Grouping creates two kinds of skew to fix, gaps across groups and gaps inside them, and common methods quietly fix only one.

The usual approach, weighting by a random-effects propensity score, aims only at the across-group balance. The authors offer two fixes. Hierarchical balancing weights control both kinds of balance through one optimization task. A new Mundlak-style estimator adjusts for group summaries and copes with tiny groups where all share the same treatment state. The approaches rest on varied assumptions, spelled out in the paper. Simulations plus uses in education and health services research compare them.
arxiv-2602-05141:
Lithium metal batteries promise high energy density, but an unstable surface layer keeps holding them back. Syed Mustafa Shah and 2 co-authors simulate that layer's birth in this 2026 materials science paper. The layer, the solid-electrolyte interphase, forms when electrolyte meets the metal, and its early chemistry shapes the battery's life.

Using molecular dynamics with a neural network potential trained on first-principles data, the team compared a concentrated lithium salt electrolyte with a standard reference. Raising the salt concentration shifted the liquid's structure from separated ion pairs toward contact pairs and clusters, with the strongest anion coordination at the highest concentration. That anion-rich environment triggered earlier bonding at the interface and a denser protective layer rich in lithium fluoride and oxide, unlike the more organic layer from the reference electrolyte. Solvation structure, they argue, is a design lever.
arxiv-2602-05441:
Robots that follow language commands must learn to handle new objects that share familiar features, such as switches or dials. Dean Fortier, Timothy Adamson, and 6 co-authors present BusyBox, a hands-on test kit for measuring that skill in vision-language-action models. The kit has six modules with switches, sliders, wires, buttons, a display, and a dial, and the modules can be swapped and turned to make many new layouts.

Even strong open models did poorly when the layout changed while the parts stayed the same, which shows how hard this kind of generalization still is. To help other labs run the same tests, the team shares files for printing the parts and a list of parts for the electronics. They also share a data set of language-labeled demonstrations, gathered with a two-armed mobile robot on the standard setup.
arxiv-2602-05541:
Matrix multiplication sits inside nearly every heavy computing task, and speeding it up on quantum hardware is a long-standing goal. Jiaqi Yao, Tianjian Huang, Tonghe Zhang, and Ding Liu present a quantum algorithm for the job based on quantum kernels. They report a gate count that grows more slowly than the best known classical method, with the cost of loading data counted openly and no assumed memory oracle.

On top of that algorithm, the team builds a family of related operators for inner products, vector-matrix products, and chains of matrix products. Noiseless simulations, noise models, and runs on a superconducting quantum processor map out accuracy, resource needs, and hardware limits. They also plug one operator into neural network inference, letting features pass between layers without repeated measurement and reloading. The authors frame this as a path toward end-to-end quantum computing for matrix-heavy tasks.
arxiv-2602-05641:
Tiny devices such as ID chips and smart sensors need strong codes that run fast on weak hardware. Najmul Hasan and Prashanth BusiReddyGari study the final ten of the NIST lightweight cipher contest, which were judged by tests. A unified theory of how their running time scales has been missing, and the authors set out to supply it.

Their math model splits each scheme into start-up, data work, and close-out phases. From that split they derive time-cost rules for all ten. The results clarify how design settings drive computing cost on tight mobile and built-in hardware. Such rules help engineers predict speed before building, rather than only testing after. The authors offer the frame as a base to rank code speed across the ten. The paper appeared at an IEEE computing and communication workshop. It speaks to builders of security systems for tight devices.
arxiv-2602-06141:
Curves with special algebraic properties on surfaces in three-dimensional projective space are classified by Abel Castorena and Montserrat Vite. The curves are called ACM curves, a class defined through their coordinate rings. The sorting is done in terms of pairs of numerical data called weak admissible pairs.

For one important case, a very general smooth determinantal quartic surface, the pair give a geometric picture of these curves. They also compute the curves' classes in the surface's Picard group, which records how curves sit inside the surface. The final part extends the story to higher-dimensional hypersurfaces and subvarieties of codimension one.
arxiv-2602-06341:
A humanoid robot that walks while using its hands must keep its grip points steady in the world, not just relative to its swaying body. Zhanxiang Cao and 9 co-authors present HiWET, a hierarchical learning framework built around world-frame end-effector tracking. Body-centered commands, they note, let leg motion pile up into world-frame drift.

A high-level policy picks subgoals that balance hand accuracy and base placement. A low-level policy then carries them out while keeping the robot stable. A kinematic prior baked into the action space cuts wasted exploration and blocks impossible poses. Simulations showed precise, stable tracking over long tasks, and the low-level policy transferred to a real humanoid with no extra tuning.
arxiv-2602-06441:
Forgetting in a trained model is usually forced by gradient ascent, running learning in reverse on the data to remove. Zhuo Huang and 5 co-authors warn that reversal can collapse the model's general skill. They propose extrapolation instead. First, the original model is trained further to memorize the unwanted data while keeping its other answers steady.

That memorization model and the original then define a direction in model space. Stepping from the memorization model through the original and beyond lands on a forget model, reached without any direct ascent. Training stays in the stable descent regime throughout. The authors report cleaner unlearning and better preserved performance, with a method simple to implement.
arxiv-2602-06641:
Wenchang Sun and Weiqi Zhou work in harmonic analysis, on the question of which sampling grids a signal shape can fully support. They study a broadened family of Gaussian curves, stretched by complex parameters, and ask when shifted and rescaled copies of one such curve can frame every signal. A frame lets any signal be rebuilt from its samples.

They prove this family has the largest possible frame set: every grid whose density passes the basic threshold works. They also show a related transform of the curve has exactly one simple zero in its unit square. The proof leans on a symmetry tool from physics and on classical results about the ordinary Gaussian, plus properties of the theta function. The findings add new cases to a pattern linking frame size and transform zeros.
arxiv-2602-06741:
Gorka Muñoz-Gil and six co-authors address disentanglement, the goal of learning data representations where each internal coordinate tracks one real factor of variation. With ordinary variational autoencoders this is provably out of reach in general. Their framework instead starts from the actions or experiments that can be performed on a physical system, and builds the representation around them.

Within that action-based view, they prove that degrees of freedom can be disentangled according to how they respond to actions. Their variational model learns these action-induced representations and succeeds at disentanglement in cases where standard autoencoders fail. It also records how each underlying factor depends on the available actions, linking every experiment to the parts of the system it can influence.
arxiv-2602-06841:
Sindhuja Chaduvula and eight co-authors compare how to explain AI systems as they move from single predictions to multi-step agent behavior. A decade of explainability research has focused on attributing one output to its inputs, but agentic systems succeed or fail through sequences of decisions. It was unclear whether attribution tools built for static settings could diagnose failures in trajectories.

Their comparison finds that attribution methods rank features stably in static settings, yet cannot reliably locate execution-level failures in agent runs. A trace-based method that scores trajectories against rubrics, by contrast, consistently pinpoints where behavior breaks down. It reveals that inconsistent state tracking is about 2.7 times more common in failed runs and cuts success probability by nearly half. The authors argue the field should shift toward trajectory-level explanations for autonomous agents.
arxiv-2602-06941:
Alex McKenzie and eight co-authors discover that large language models can fight back against activation steering. When a model's internal activations are pushed off-task, it sometimes recovers mid-generation, producing explicit verbal restarts such as noting that something is not right, and continuing on-topic while the perturbation remains active. The authors call this endogenous steering resistance.

Using sparse autoencoder latents to steer, they find the largest tested model shows explicit resistance in about 3.8 percent of cases, with smaller models showing it less often. Two controls separate a detection event from a sustained-resistance component that recent on-topic tokens do not fully explain. Zeroing out 26 identified latents cut the multi-attempt rate by a quarter. Resistance can also be deliberately strengthened by prompting or fine-tuning, with a double edge: it may harden models against attacks, but also block beneficial steering.
arxiv-2602-07041:
Leeje Jang and ten co-authors offer OMNI-Dent, a dental diagnosis aid built for places with little access to dentists. Timely professional checks are scarce for many people. Old AI tools treat diagnosis as pure pattern matching, skipping the structured clinical thinking dentists use. They also demand large piles of expert-labeled data and struggle when imaging conditions vary.

OMNI-Dent works from phone photos taken from several views. It weaves diagnostic heuristics from dental experts into a vision-language pipeline, then guides a general-purpose vision-language model to judge each tooth. No dental-specific fine-tuning of that model is needed. As an early-stage aid, it helps users spot possible problems and decide when a professional check is needed, where curated clinical imaging is out of reach.
arxiv-2602-07241:
Lights Out is a puzzle where pressing a vertex toggles its own light and its neighbors', and the goal is to switch everything off.  Julien Codsi and three co-authors study extremal graphs, where pressing every vertex is the unique solution starting from all lights on.

They prove a graph is extremal exactly when it is even and has an odd number of matchings. They count labeled extremal graphs through symmetric invertible matrices over the two-element field.  They also show even graphs with no cycle length divisible by three must be extremal, and they give operations for building larger cases from smaller ones.  Combinatorialists get a complete characterization of a clean extremal class.
arxiv-2602-07341:
Teaching a dexterous robot hand by demonstration is expensive when experts must be present, so remote collection through augmented reality promises scale.  Yicheng Yang and nine co-authors build a system where a remote human-robot link via AR gathers expert demonstrations for arm-hand manipulation.

Learning runs in two phases. First comes behavior cloning from the AR demonstrations, then a contrastive reinforcement learning phase with a projection head that yields a more efficient and robust policy. An event-driven reward encourages safety.  Simulated and real validation support the design.  Robot learning teams get a scalable pipeline from remote human skill to capable dexterous policies.
arxiv-2602-07441:
Offline reinforcement learning regularizes actor-critic methods with behavior cloning to stay near the dataset. That imitation imposes a ceiling: when dataset actions are suboptimal, the actor cannot fully exploit better actions its value function suggests.  Jinzong Dong and seven co-authors analyze that ceiling formally and verify it on a controlled bandit task.

Their fix, proximal action replacement, is a plug-and-play training sample replacer that substitutes suboptimal dataset actions, letting the actor climb past the imitation ceiling, especially late in training when imitation otherwise dominates.  Offline RL users get a small, principled change that removes a structural limit of a popular method.
arxiv-2602-07641:
Generative AI, copilots, and agents now do substantive delegated work in knowledge teams, yet no method organizes daily work for hybrid human-AI teams as a coherent delivery unit. Marc Bara proposes the Human-AI Integration Framework, a protocol-based, scalable operational system for hybrid team work.

Built on four core principles, a formal delegation choice model, tiered autonomy with quantifiable transition criteria, and feedback mechanisms, it fits current Agile and Kanban workflows. It demands no new roles for small teams. Developed through design science research, it confronts the adoption paradox that more capable AI makes oversight harder to justify, even as the cost of skipping it grows. Leaders of hybrid teams get an operating system for work humans and agents do together. Tests in real teams are left as future work.
arxiv-2602-07741:
Young stars grow by pulling gas from a surrounding envelope onto a disk, but the details of that inflow shape everything that follows. Masahiro N. Machida and two co-authors simulate the process in three dimensions, starting from a calm prestellar core whose magnetic field tilts against its spin axis.

Over roughly a hundred thousand years after the protostar forms, the disk's rotation twists the nearby magnetic field and deforms the flattened pseudodisk into a complex shape. Gas then falls onto the disk mainly through narrow streams, and the inflow varies over time, making the star's own accretion flicker. Strikingly, this messiness arises with no turbulence and no lopsided outside inflow assumed, a lesson for models of star and planet formation.
arxiv-2602-07941:
The X(3915) meson puzzles physics teams: is it an ordinary charmonium state, a four-quark tetraquark, or a loosely bound compound of two mesons? Sungtae Cho and three co-authors study its structure in a quark model with color-spin interactions, treating it as a charm-anticharm plus strange-antistrange state.

Their calculation favors a separated Ds and anti-Ds configuration for the spin-zero ground state. They then compute momentum distributions and yields for heavy-ion collisions under each structural hypothesis, arguing that readings of those distributions can distinguish charmonium, tetraquark, and molecular pictures. Experimentalists at heavy-ion colliders gain a concrete test for an exotic hadron's identity.
arxiv-2602-08041:
Training language-model agents for poker by win rate alone misses strategic forces that evolve over long horizons. Boyang Xia and nine co-authors offer implicit strategic optimization, a prediction-aware method where every agent predicts the strategic context it faces now and updates its policy online.

A strategic reward model estimates the long-run value of actions, while a context-conditioned optimistic learning rule turns those forecasts into policy updates. Theory proves sublinear contextual regret and equilibrium convergence whose dominant terms scale with context mispredictions, recovering static-game rates when predictions are accurate. Tests in six-player no-limit Texas Hold'em support the approach. Game-playing agent teams gain a method for strategy that looks ahead, not just at the last hand.
arxiv-2602-08241:
Chain-of-thought reasoning helps multimodal models, but their visual attention often starts misaligned and never recovers, so errors propagate through the whole reasoning chain. Siqu Ou and four co-authors trace this to poor credit assignment for visual attention during training.

Their model, SAYO, trains with reinforcement learning using a region-level visual attention reward that ties optimization signals directly to visually grounded reasoning steps. The reward teaches the model to look at the right regions and keep looking there as reasoning proceeds. Across multiple multimodal benchmarks, SAYO improves performance consistently over baselines. Vision-language researchers gain a training signal aimed at seeing, not just talking about seeing.
arxiv-2602-08441:
Counting certain symmetry patterns in algebra is famously hard, and whether quantum computers help has been an open question. Matthias Christandl and four co-authors show that a broad family of representation-theoretic multiplicities sits in the quantum counting class #BQP. Their arXiv paper settles the plethysm coefficients in particular, previously known only in special cases.

Repeated use of the Schur transform drives the result, aided by recent improvements in its dependence on local dimension. The same argument recovers all earlier quantum-complexity results for related coefficients as special cases, unifying and extending them. The authors also place these multiplicities in GapP and give fast classical algorithms when certain parameters are fixed. Readers get a sweeping complexity map for algebraic counting.
arxiv-2602-08641:
Models trained on protein sequences define fitness landscapes, but whether they capture real change over time is unclear. Leonardo Di Bari and five co-authors compare three simulation schemes against deep sequencing data from four lab evolution tests. Their arXiv paper tests standard Monte Carlo, tree-based Monte Carlo, and population-genetics dynamics.

Standard Monte Carlo misses family-tree structure and produces unrealistic gradual sweeps. Monte Carlo on an inferred tree improves historical fidelity. The population-genetics scheme captures family-tree links, abundances, and sweeps as emergent traits, though it stops sampling the true model distribution at long times. Readers learn that family-tree links and finite-population effects shape paths decisively.
arxiv-2602-08741:
Mixture-of-experts language models activate only a few experts per token, gaining efficiency but creating new safety weak points. Jona te Lintelo and two co-authors find that safety behaviors like refusal concentrate in a small expert set rather than spreading evenly. Their arXiv paper introduces Large Language Lobotomy, a training-free attack that exploits routing dynamics.

By learning which routing patterns track refusal and adaptively silencing the most safety-relevant experts, the attack raises average success from 7.3 to 70.4 percent across eight open-source expert models, peaking at 86.3 percent. Silencing under twenty percent of layer-wise experts usually suffices while preserving general utility. Readers get a stark tension between efficient expert design and robust safety alignment.
arxiv-2602-08941:
Lab tests of memory and attention rarely look like real thinking in a rich world. Zeyu Lu and one co-author present pixelLOG, a data-collection framework for Minecraft servers built on Spigot, designed for process-based cognitive research. Unlike tools built only for AI players, it tracks real people too, in multiplayer worlds where many agents act at once.

Running at twenty updates per second or more, it mixes active state polling with passive event listening and isolates sessions cleanly. Outputs arrive as structured JSON ready for standard analysis tools. The framework lets researchers watch cognition unfold moment by moment in complex virtual settings, closing the gap between sterile lab tasks and everyday mental life.
arxiv-2602-09141:
Gauging cosmic gaps by shape, without the usual tuning ladder, is the dream behind the Cosmic Positioning System. Matthew McQuinn and nine co-authors report a NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts study of a fleet of radio dishes spread across the outer solar system, on spans of tens of AU. By timing repeat fast radio bursts across the array, gaps follow by three-point timing, like GPS on cosmological scales.

Even a handful of sightings could pin the Hubble constant to sub-percent sharpness, and 10 to 100 sources are hoped to be visible. Timing sharpness, between-star delays, craft spots, and clock stability all prove controllable with near-term technology. The nominal design uses five craft with 8-meter dishes, 3 to 6 gigahertz receivers, and GPS-like atomic clocks.
arxiv-2602-09241:
Maria Manuel Clementino and one co-author show that the group of V-groups, for V a square quantale, is locally algebraically square closed for points under the product V-group structure. Pre-set groups are a key special case. The proof notes that such points match enriched maps from a V-group, viewed as a one-object V-group, into the group of V-groups.

Also, the moves matching those points can be drawn. The result puts V-groups among groups with well-kept algebraic powering, linking quantale-enriched group theory with group moves. It is a frame step for scholars working with enriched groups and their moves.
arxiv-2602-09341:
Multi-agent language systems usually settle disagreements by majority vote, throwing away the reasoning that produced each answer. That shortcut breaks when agents share the same biases and converge on the same wrong rationale, a failure the authors call confabulation consensus. Wei Yang and five co-authors propose AgentAuditor, a 2026 system that instead organizes agent traces into a reasoning tree showing where lines of thought agree and diverge.

Conflicts are settled by comparing branch-level evidence at the exact points of divergence, turning a global judgment into a series of local checks. A training method called Anti-Consensus Preference Optimization further teaches the adjudicator to resist misleading majority cues, using supervision verified against evidence. Across four multi-agent frameworks and several reasoning benchmarks, the system beats majority voting by up to five percentage points in accuracy while staying token-efficient.
arxiv-2602-09441:
Production state-machine replication stacks are layered beasts, combining data spread, ordering, execution, and changeover. Research protocols rarely discuss changeovers, and those that do weld member-list changes to one algorithm, blocking solo upgrades and forcing costly downtime when designs change. Allen Clement and three co-authors argue modular design is the missing trait for systems that stay easy to maintain.

Their answer is Gauss, a changeover engine that treats consensus designs as swappable modules. Gauss draws a line between a design's inner log and a cleaned outer log shown to the replication node. That split lets builders upgrade member lists, failure thresholds, and the consensus design itself on their own, with minimal global downtime. An early trial on the Rialto blockchain shows the stack changing smoothly across diverse designs.
arxiv-2602-09541:
Large vision-language models hallucinate when strong language priors and misaligned attention pull outputs away from images. Ziqiang Shi and four co-authors propose Scalpel, a 2026 method that steers attention activations toward more credible regions at inference time. For each attention head, Scalpel predicts trusted attention directions, then adjusts activations to match them.

A Gaussian mixture model captures the multi-peaked shapes of attention in trust and hallucination manifolds, while entropic optimal transport maps mixture components precisely between them. Intervention strength and direction adapt dynamically to component membership and mapping relations. Across multiple datasets and benchmarks, Scalpel beats prior methods and reaches leading performance. It needs no extra compute beyond a single decoding step and works across models and data.
arxiv-2602-09641:
Steering matter through contact with field ripples is a new frontier in matter work. Chongxiao Fan and seven co-authors note that dark cavity effects have been shown for charge phases like zero-loss flow and charge order, yet a clear test for magnet systems is lacking. The focus on phase shifts demands large key light-matter coupling. Their 2026 paper offers spiral magnets instead: even a small cavity-made change in magnet links shows up as a wave length shift.

The platform is single-layer dual-order nickel iodide. It touches charge field ripples from surface waves of the para substrate strontium titanate. As substrate-matter distance shrinks, the ratio of nearest to third-nearest neighbor exchange links falls, stretching the wave length and in time driving a shift into a magnet state. The work names a real platform for seeing cavity vacuum tuning effects in magnet systems.
arxiv-2602-10041:
Heat in weakly collisional, magnetized plasma escapes simple models because microinstabilities scatter the heat-carrying electrons. A 2026 paper led by T. A. Vincent, with seventeen co-authors, presents a new experimental platform for measuring that transport. The platform creates a weakly collisional plasma with high beta expected to host the whistler heat-flux instability.

The platform will run on the Orion laser, with its design tested in radiation-magnetohydrodynamics simulations using the FLASH code. Three thermal conduction models predict conductivity suppressed more than tenfold from the Spitzer value at whistler saturation. The result shows the platform can pin down whistler-regulated thermal conductivity.
arxiv-2602-10141:
Permanents, the unsigned cousins of determinants, are known to be hard to compute, yet their distributions reveal deep structure. A 2026 paper by Igor Rivin reports a computational and experimental study using graphics hardware to speed permanent computation across complex, real, finite-field, and rational matrices. For Haar-distributed unitary matrices, the permanent follows a circularly symmetric complex Gaussian law, confirmed with tens of thousands of samples for sizes up to twenty-three.

For orthogonal matrices, the permanent looks nearly real Gaussian with excess kurtosis fading slowly. For Gaussian ensembles, it follows a heavy-tailed stable law well below Gaussian stability, and a conjecture about log-shaped tails holds for some ensembles but fails for others. Along geodesics on the unitary group, a shared scaling function emerges independent of size.
arxiv-2602-10541:
Antonin Sulc presents a system for solving partial differential rules in a single shot in a 2026 paper. FastLSQ builds on trigonometric random Fourier traits whose derivatives have closed forms at any order, allowing rule assembly without automatic differentiation. Linear problems reduce to one least-squares call; uneven ones iterate Newton steps that reuse the same assembly.

Tests on seventeen problems in one to six sizes report high scores in fractions of a second for linear cases. Uneven cases take seconds. Both are orders of magnitude faster and more exact than iterative physics-informed neural networks. Analytic higher-order derivatives also yield a differentiable digital twin, showed on inverse problems like heat-source and coil recovery, and on equation discovery from data.
arxiv-2602-10641:
Yichen Liu and Cheng-Cheng Liu prove a new multiferroic effect in a 2026 physics paper. The antiferroaxial state, in which twists counter-rotate, is rising as a notable ferroic order. The paper shows it can induce altermagnetism and enable its fixed, two-way switching.

Within a unified Landau-theory plan, the authors identify a trilinear coupling linking antiferroaxial order, the Néel vector, and magnet order. Flipping the antiferroaxial order flips the spin splitting and linked effects like odd Hall conductivity. A useful spin-group guide maps Néel-vector models to possible solids, turning abstract theory into a search guide for switchable magnets.
arxiv-2602-11041:
Fast matrix multiplication leans on tensor decompositions, but rank alone can mislead. Manuel Kauers and two co-authors exploit special structure in such decompositions to beat the exponent their rank would suggest. Their new recipe uses traits of the tensors to shave the exponent down.

For six-by-six multiplication, the exponent falls from about two point eight zero seven five to about two point eight zero one nine. The leading coefficient stays sane. The gain is small in digits but real in theory, and it shows that structure-aware methods can still squeeze speed from a problem studied for decades.
arxiv-2602-11541:
Tool-using agents under a strict money budget cannot plan naively. Hanbing Liu and six co-authors formalize budget-constrained tool use as sequential decision making with priced, random tool executions, where massive state-action spaces and high outcome variance make direct planning intractable. Their INTENT frame uses an intention-aware layered world model to anticipate future tool use.

Risk-tuned cost values guide decisions online, anticipating usage before committing budget. Across cost-augmented tool benchmarks, INTENT strictly enforces hard budget feasibility while greatly improving task success over rivals. It stays robust under moving market shifts such as tool price changes and varying budgets, offering a practical planner for agents whose tools cost real money.
arxiv-2602-11641:
Graph networks that read text and structure often fail with confidence on strange new nodes. Existing fixes tend to use one side of the data and neglect the other. Topology methods lean on neighbors but flatten text into shallow features. Language-model methods invent fake examples that drift from reality or pollute clean data. Yinlin Zhu and four co-authors propose LG-Plug, which lines up topology and text into fine node embeddings.

From those embeddings it builds consensus-driven exposure examples through clustered, iterative prompting. Light codebooks and heuristic sampling keep query costs down. The exposure acts as a regularizer separating familiar from unfamiliar nodes and slots into detectors without a custom architecture. Across six benchmarks it improves topology-driven detectors by over 7 percent on a key error metric. It also beats prior language-model methods by over 5 percent.
arxiv-2602-11841:
Neural search tools rank well but break on vague or ambiguous queries, even when relevant documents exist. Large language models rewrite queries without search-tool feedback, while token-spotting methods spot misleading tokens only after the fact. Moncef Garouani and one co-author close the loop with score-guided query rewriting. Gradient-based token attributions from the ranker guide a structured prompt to a language model, which clarifies weak or misleading query parts while preserving intent.

Evaluated on BEIR tests, the rewrites improve search quality over strong baselines, with larger gains for hidden or ambiguous information needs. The lesson for design is that feedback should flow from ranker to rewriter during rewriting, not merely from rewriter to ranker at the end. Grounding rewrites in what the ranker actually found confusing makes them clearly better.
arxiv-2602-11941:
Music retrieval has grown strong, yet it lacks high-quality benchmarks for fair comparison. Benjamin Clavié and five co-authors present IncompeBench, a carefully labeled benchmark of more than 1,500 permissively licensed, high-quality music snippets, 500 diverse queries, and over 125,000 individual relevance judgments. A multi-stage pipeline produced strong agreement between human raters and machine data.

The benchmark targets a gap: existing tests often lean on narrow catalogs or noisy labels, making it hard to tell which systems truly retrieve well. By pairing cleared snippets with many queries and judgments, it supports fine-grained evaluation of music search systems. The datasets and prompts are publicly released, giving researchers a shared, reusable testbed for the next round of music search work.
arxiv-2602-12141:
In heavy-fermion metals, electrons act together in ways that make normal metal rules break down. Soumendra Nath Panja led this study with four co-authors, using a crystal called YbRh2Si2 to test how strain changes that shared behaviour. They stretched the crystal in two directions and tracked how its resistance changed.

Most strain patterns gave almost no signal, but one symmetric pattern grew huge at low heat, reaching about minus 50. By matching that signal to heat-expansion data, the team links it to how Kondo scattering shapes magnetic entropy under strain. The result points to strain- and field-tuned quantum criticality as the sample cools toward 2 kelvin.
arxiv-2602-12841:
Cell-free massive MIMO spreads antennas across many radio units for uniform coverage, but joint transmission and cloud processing carry a steep energy bill. Zilin Ge and four co-authors propose EARL, a reinforcement-learning framework for Open RAN networks. It switches antenna elements on and off to minimise radio, fronthaul, and cloud power while meeting user data-rate demands. The controller adapts continuously as conditions change.

Numerical results show power savings up to 81% over keeping everything on, and 50% over heuristic baselines. Decisions arrive within 220 milliseconds, inside the near-real-time limit for Open RAN, and a greedy refinement halves power again at a two-second runtime. For operators chasing sustainability, the work shows that adaptive antenna control can cut energy sharply without breaking service promises.
arxiv-2602-13241:
Emergency call takers answer more than 240 million calls a year in the United States. Yet many centers face staff gaps above 25 percent, and training one new hire can take up to 720 hours of one-on-one coaching. This study reports a real rollout built with the Metro Nashville emergency communications department. It tests a training system powered by generative AI that lets trainees practice calls without pulling veteran staff off duty. Over six months it grew from a pilot to 190 users and 1,120 training sessions.

Logs from 98,429 user actions, plus notes on how the rollout was run, yield four lessons with concrete design and governance tips for safety-critical public services. The authors stress what lab tests miss: delivery, rigor, resilience, and human factors shape whether such a system works in practice. Zirong Chen leads the work with one co-author, Meiyi Ma.
arxiv-2602-13341:
Superparamagnetic layers matter for spintronic sensors and computing, but standard magnetization tests need strong perturbing fields and struggle inside working devices. This study probes a 1.1-nanometer CoFeB layer on diamond without disturbing it, reading its low-frequency near-field fluctuations with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond as quantum sensors. The dephasing time of those centers showed an unusual non-monotonic temperature pattern, attributed to thermally driven flipping of magnetic domains.

Theory and SQUID magnetization checks back the reading, and the method also yields the spectral density of the fluctuations plus distance-dependent coherence times. Together these reveal how the layer's magnetic dynamics shape its near-field environment, with implications for hybrid quantum spintronic devices. Shoaib Mahmud leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13441:
The Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph needed recalibration after model atmospheres for its three primary standard stars were updated, shifting predicted continuum fluxes by up to 2 to 3 percent. This report re-derives spectral sensitivities for the five STIS low-resolution gratings, G140L, G230L, G230LB, G430L, and G750L, spanning far-ultraviolet through near-infrared wavelengths.

Updated throughput tables delivered to the Calibration Reference Data System in April 2022 and April 2023 triggered recalibration of all historical STIS data taken in these modes. Sensitivities from the three standard stars typically agree within 1 percent, with discrepancies up to 1.5 percent where hydrogen absorption bites hardest. Amy M. Jones leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14241:
Milan Bašić, writing alone, solves a 2026 arXiv extremal problem for trees. The sigma-irregularity index sums squared degree gaps over edges, gauging shape unevenness. The paper maximizes it among trees of fixed order n with max degree Delta at least 4.

Framing the problem through edge-degree counts yields a linear plan, whose dual study gives sharp upper bounds and describes extremal degree-pair spreads. The problem is fully solved when n is congruent to 1 or 0 modulo Delta. In the first case the linear plan has a whole-number best answer and the bound is tight. In the second, a penalty from dual slack gives the exact max, with all extremal trees named.
arxiv-2602-14441:
Samudi Amarasinghe and two co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv setup for multimodal misinformation detection. New false news mixes true-looking image edits with fluent tricky text, making hard-to-check posts. Content spotters catch local clashes but cannot judge global factual truth, while lookup fact-checkers weigh outside proof but miss fine-grained edits.

D-SECURE joins both proof sources for news-style posts. It links the HAMMER edit spotter with the DEFAME lookup line: DEFAME does broad checks, while HAMMER studies left-over or unsure cases that may hide fine edits. Tests on DGM4 and ClaimReview samples mark the combo's worth, catching inwardly steady fakes that slip past single-source systems.
arxiv-2602-14741:
Christian Monch tests a plain guess about trees that grow by rich-get-richer rules: pay high-degree nodes more, and the tree should grow less tall. For the log-scale growth rates of depth and height, he shows by a set counter-case that growth-ratio lead alone proves neither trend.

Extra tail rules, drawn from the trees' branching-process view, bring both trends back when they hold. The paper thus splits a handy rule of thumb from a true claim, and marks just where the guess breaks. Tree growth gains a sharp, honest edge.
arxiv-2602-14841:
Leonardo A. M. Souza and others gauge how well gravity-made fade can be read in light-and-motion gear, with plain Gaussian probe states. A small-scale tale of gravity spread joins a Fisher score to set the sharpest read one can hope for in theory.

Gravity spread leaves clear marks on the moving part, both while it settles and once it rests. How the probe is set shapes the sharpness one can reach. The work thus fixes the outer bounds for spotting and gauging gravity-made fade. Such bounds help labs judge if a test could ever see the fade.
arxiv-2602-14941:
Wang and colleagues tackle a stubborn flaw in camera-guided video generation: scenes drift as a clip runs long. Earlier memory methods rebuild one global 3D scene from past views. Small pose and depth errors place the same surface in slightly different spots. Fusing those views yields noisy geometry that harms the result.

AnchorWeave instead keeps several clean local geometric memories. It retrieves the ones covering the planned camera path. A multi-anchor controller then weaves them together while generating. Tests reported in the paper show markedly better long-term scene consistency with strong visual quality, and ablations support each part of the design.
arxiv-2602-15141:
Alcázar-Laynez and colleagues build synthetic pre-labelled galaxies mimicking local large-scale structure. Observed and simulated sets often disagree on which ones belong to which groups. No universal classification rule exists. To supply training data for classifiers, the team builds a geometrical simulation from statistical spatial traits in structure surveys. The Sloan main sample, out to a redshift near one tenth, serves as a use case.

A parallel with Voronoi tessellation guides the design. Nodes, links, surfaces, and cells stand for clusters, filaments, walls, and voids. Void positions seed tessellation of 3D space. The structures are then filled with galaxies matching survey statistics, each tagged at birth. Each run yields six mock catalogues following SDSS behavior, with Malmquist bias and Fingers of God effects included. Tuned to SDSS but usable for any catalogue, it lets researchers adjust classifiers, train models, and benchmark methods on pre-labelled data.
arxiv-2602-15241:
Tschand surveys generative AI for systems, from software to silicon, through a cross-stack lens. Generative AI changes how computing systems are built, yet research stays split across software, hardware, and chip design communities.

Its central finding is convergence. Despite diverse domains and tools, the field keeps facing five chronic challenges. They are the feedback loop crisis, the tacit knowledge problem, trust and checks, cross-team co-design, and the shift from fixed rules to flux. It also keeps reaching five design principles as strong responses: hybrid approaches, steady feedback, splitting concerns by role, matching methods to problem structure, and building on decades of systems knowledge. The team builds these into a challenge-principle map. They argue the field needs shared methods, terms, and benchmarks, so progress compounds rather than being redone per group. The analysis covers more than 275 papers across eleven areas and three layers.
arxiv-2602-15341:
Yoshida studies monotonicity testing of real functions on DAGs. Let m and l be the edge counts in the transitive reduction and closure. For 1 at most c at most d at most 2, define u of c and d. It is the minimum of one half, c over 3, and c plus d over 2 minus 1.

Families of DAGs with m about n to the c and l about n to the d admit, for fixed epsilon, a non-adaptive tester with one-sided error. It uses about n to the u queries. Conversely, for small epsilon above 0 and pairs c and d, there are families of DAGs satisfying the edge counts. On these, every non-adaptive tester, with two-sided error, requires about n to the u queries, matching the upper bound up to small factors. The main contribution is a lower-bound technique based on Ruzsa-Szemerédi families of matchings.
arxiv-2602-15441:
Chaudhuri and Loho study gravity ripple making from ancient black holes whose fading is shaped by setting. Ancient black holes born in Universe fade by Hawking rays and form a well of random ripples. Current work on gravity ripple making from fading black holes suppose vacuum fading, missing that ancient black holes in the early Universe are bathed in plasma.

They use a thermal fading setup in which clashes with nearby plasma shift the black hole's real fade pace. This gives boosted mass loss early and a shift of fading history compared to the vacuum case. Since gravity bit output is linked to the fading history of ancient black holes, these effects play a role in setting the schedule and color traits of the ripple sea. Their findings give a setup for adding thermal effects into gravity ripple making from fading black holes and set the stage for marks.
arxiv-2602-15941:
Connes and Consani give a new geometric picture of the adele class space of the rational numbers. They treat it as a broadened version of the Picard group of the arithmetic curve built from the integers, extended to cover the whole adelic setting. Each point matches a rank one abelian group with no torsion, plus extra rigidifying data.

In the Riemann sector, that extra data takes the form of a norm, much like the metric carried by a line bundle in Arakelov geometry. For the full space, the norm is replaced by a map to the real numbers and a rule for listing roots of unity tied to the dual of the group. Multiplying adeles then becomes tensoring these groups and their extra data. The Picard group thus grows into a monoid space holding the singular layers needed for the spectral view of L-functions.
arxiv-2602-16341:
Georgios Gravanis leads a team of four coauthors comparing two explainability methods for fault detection in chemical processes. The team applies Integrated Gradients and SHapley Additive exPlanations to explain the decisions of a highly accurate Long Short-Term Memory classifier. That classifier is trained to spot faults in the Tennessee Eastman Process, a benchmark nonlinear chemical process.

The explainability methods help pinpoint the subsystem where a fault occurred. In most cases both methods flag the same features as most important, while in some cases SHAP looks more informative and closer to the root cause. Since both methods are model-agnostic, the approach is not tied to this one process and can be carried over to similar problems.
arxiv-2602-16441:
Carl Collmann, Ahmad Nimr, and Gerhard Fettweis present and validate a simple local phase calibration method for digital MIMO arrays. Channel measurements in such systems hinge on precise timing. While time and frequency synchronization methods are well established, keeping real-time phase coherence remains an open requirement for many MIMO systems. Phase coherence matters for beamforming and for precise parameter estimates such as angle of arrival and departure.

The authors compare two methods, instantaneous and smoothed, to find the best interval between sync procedures. Performance is judged by average beamforming power loss and root-mean-square cycle-to-cycle jitter. Both prove effective, with jitter from about two picoseconds to about one hundred and twenty-four femtoseconds across different software-defined radio models. That precision enables coherent transmission on commonly available platforms, opening the way to advanced MIMO techniques and beam use in practical testbeds.
arxiv-2602-16541:
Santiago de Leon-Martinez, Robert Moro, Branislav Kveton, and Maria Bielikova study click models for carousel interfaces. Carousels are the swipeable rows of recommendations on streaming and shopping platforms. Most click models were built for a single ranked list. Carousels invite richer browsing, so the authors build three position-based models for that layout. One uses observed eye-tracking signals instead of hidden variables.

Tests compare gradient-based fitting against expectation-maximization and maximum likelihood methods. Gradient methods win on click likelihood. The eye-tracking model predicts clicks best and matches viewing patterns most closely. Yet a strong click fit alone does not guarantee a true picture of browsing. Recommender researchers get new models plus a caution about click-only tests.
arxiv-2602-17041:
Conor Chandler and a coauthor wrote a 2026 methods paper on a problem in health technology assessment: how to carry trial results from one patient group to another. When no head-to-head trial exists, analysts use population-adjusted indirect comparisons to bridge trials that enrolled different people. Adjusting for observed differences, the authors argue, does not by itself make an effect portable to a new population.

Working from an estimand view, the paper separates conditional from marginal effects and shows portability turns on effect modification, collapsibility, and the scale of the measure. Marginal effects on common non-collapsible scales, such as hazard ratios and odds ratios, stay population-bound even when modifiers match. The authors map when an indirect estimate can move to a new target, when it needs extra assumptions, and when it should stay population-specific.
arxiv-2602-17241:
Anand Rai led a three-author team studying particle yields in off-center gold-gold collisions across the RHIC Beam Energy Scan. The paper studies transverse momentum spectra and elliptic flow of pions, kaons, protons, and antiprotons. The model is a growing fire-cylinder with lengthwise expansion and uneven transverse flow.

Particle yields at kinetic freeze-out come from a local equilibrium spread with a blast-wave-like fluid speed profile drawn from its growth. Model settings for collective motion are first fixed by fitting midrapidity pion spectra, then applied as-is to the other species. The model covers the spectra well and matches the broad flow pattern for every species studied.
arxiv-2602-17341:
Erik Fitzner led a four-author team detecting nonequilibrium phase transitions in quantum systems without knowing the order parameter in advance. Group behavior in such systems is usually read through order parameters, but those may be unknown beforehand, and estimating quantum states and expectation values demands many projective measurements. Open quantum systems, however, can be watched in place through their output, via heterodyne detection or photon counting, yielding space-time resolved dynamics.

The paper presents a machine learning approach that reads phase shifts from measurement time-records of continuously monitored quantum systems. Benchmarking uses the quantum contact process, a model with an absorbing-state phase transition that poses a particularly hard test for quantum simulation of off-balance processes. The method shows how watched output alone can reveal collective shifts that state estimation would struggle to expose.
arxiv-2602-17441:
T. Benest Couzinou led a three-author team on how complex organic molecules reached the Jupiter system. Lab work suggests UV irradiation or thermal processing of ammonia and carbon dioxide ices can form them.

The team modeled formation in the protosolar nebula and transport toward Jupiter, simulating five hundred particles in a two-dimensional disk evolution model. Almost none of the particles released at twenty kelvin, about twelve astronomical units from the Sun, reach Jupiter's region. Released at eighty kelvin, about seven astronomical units out, roughly forty-five percent of centimetre-sized particles and thirty percent of micrometre-sized ones form complex organic molecules by thermal processing. They reach Jupiter's region within three hundred thousand years. If the Galilean moons formed in a cold disk around Jupiter, nitrogen-bearing species inside them could have come from such molecules.
arxiv-2602-17641:
Keith Burghardt and team introduce FAMOSE, an agent system for automated feature discovery in machine learning. Feature engineering stays a key bottleneck, above all for tabular data, where the space of candidate features is vast and domain expertise is costly. FAMOSE is billed as the first agentic ReAct system aimed at this task.

The agent explores, builds and refines features on its own, while selection and evaluation tools sit inside its loop. Tests put it at or near the state of the art on classification, and at the state of the art on regression, with small average gains on both. It also proves more robust to errors than rival algorithms. The authors credit the ReAct loop: its context log of what worked and what failed steers the model toward fresher, more inventive features.
arxiv-2602-18141:
Mia Zosso and four co-authors rethink how signals travel across graphs in neural networks. Their 2026 paper starts from a known trouble. Tasks that need far-apart nodes to talk strain standard graph networks. Deep local steps blur signals, and wide attention costs too much. The team offers a lighter fix.

Their mu-ChebNet design learns a weight for each node first, then runs standard spectral filters on the reshaped geometry. The learned weights open favored routes for signals, so long-range messages dodge tight bottlenecks without stacking many layers. Tests on made-up long-range tasks and real graph benchmarks show better scores, and the weights themselves can be read for insight. The method gives a cheap, clear alternative to attention and rewiring.
arxiv-2602-18241:
Seohwa Hwang and one co-author built an online method for flagging disease signals without crying wolf too often. Their 2026 paper targets infectious disease data, which are discrete and tangled by dependence, where older online false-discovery methods assume independence or lose power. The method rests on conditional local false-discovery scores within a susceptible-infected-susceptible disease model.

Cast as a dynamic Bayesian network, the approach needs no tuning knobs beyond the sliding window width, suiting real-time monitoring. The team proves it keeps false discoveries in check under stationary, ergodic dependence, widening online testing to dependent discrete data. It also beats older methods on detection power in simulations and real incidence data, since local scores beat plain p-values. The work offers epidemic watchers a practical, proven tool.
arxiv-2602-18541:
Daniel Garcia proposes a slimmer API format for language models. His 2026 paper notes large language models increasingly consume API specifications for code generation, agent interaction, or API-assisted reasoning. OpenAPI, the de facto standard, was designed for documentation tools and generators, resulting in heavy token overhead for LLMs.

Garcia presents LAPIS, a format built for LLMs. It preserves the semantic information needed for API reasoning. Tests against five production API specifications: GitHub, Twilio, DigitalOcean, Petstore, and HTTPBin, show average token reductions of eighty-five point five percent versus OpenAPI YAML and eighty-eight point six percent versus OpenAPI JSON. Measurements use cl100k_base. LAPIS adds structural innovations: central error definitions, webhook triggers, structured rate limit notes, and operation flow notes, information OpenAPI duplicates or cannot represent at all. The format converts fully from OpenAPI 3.x via a converter and is published as an open specification under CC BY 4.0.
arxiv-2602-19041:
Cyclic preferences break preference fine-tuning. When rankings loop, no single best policy exists. Jiahao Zhang, with five co-authors, tackles that flaw in 2026. The trouble comes from two sources. Rankings can clash on one goal. Several goals can also collapse badly into one score.

The authors propose a new game-theoretic answer, the Maximum Entropy Blackwell Winner. It stays well-defined even when preferences cycle across goals. A new algorithm, PROSPER, computes it at scale. Unlike earlier self-play methods, PROSPER handles several goals at once. It never collapses them into one score.
