Process mining rebuilds real workflows from event logs rather than trusting official pathway diagrams. The team built an open pipeline converting messy clinical tables from a shared COVID learning dataset into a clean event log. They then applied process discovery, conformance checking against expected rules, and outcome analysis to the pathways.

The analysis exposed a monitoring backbone running through inpatient care, plus wide variation where emergency department patients entered admission. Outcomes differed mainly with patient age and exposure to intensive care, they report. Those findings translate into governance advice: standardize triage at intake, plan capacity around the discovered bottlenecks, and coordinate step-down transfers to ordinary wards. The authors frame process mining as evidence for hospital management decisions, not just an exercise.
arxiv-2606-00241:
Hu and co-authors build a base model that gauges links between data sets in one pass. Gauging how much two rich data sets share is a core data task. Net-based gauges work well but need fresh slow training per set. That cost blocks live use.

InfoAtlas is trained once on vast fake data with rich link forms. It learns to spot a broad range of link shapes. At test time, it reads a new set and calls the link strength at once. Tests show it ties top gauges on scores while running far faster. One model takes in varied widths and set sizes. It also holds up on hard, real-world sets. The shift turns link gauging into a quick read task.
arxiv-2606-00441:
Alhosani, Talafha, and Al-Wardat trim the fit zone for how the Sun's face field drifts and fades. Their SFT model tracks the Sun's large face field over time. Straight drift parts are well pinned by past work. Bent back-pull parts, like tilt and width quench, are less known.

The team add clean math forms for both quench types in the source term. A flux-loss dial joins them in the grid of runs. Runs sweep flow speed, spread rate, and loss span in a grid. Fit runs must match pole field marks and flip times from sight. Both quench types shrink the fit zone, width quench most. Paired, they cap how strong the pole lean can grow. A loss span near a decade trims the zone yet more.
arxiv-2606-00641:
Bukreev, Kummerländer, and Krause wrote this 2026 paper on ways to simulate flows of charged fluids. Their tool is the lattice Boltzmann method, a scheme that tracks small packets of fluid on a grid. The work deals with flows that can be squeezed and with flows ruled by magnetic fields.

Their new class of schemes splits the core math so each part moves on its own traits. This keeps all steps local and fast on big machines. The team codes the method in the OpenLB framework and tests it on known flow cases. They report it reaches 98.9 percent of the peak speed the hardware allows. A last test tracks a magnetized asteroid, based on 16 Psyche, in a supersonic solar wind.
arxiv-2606-00841:
Kushimo, Holt, and Talal audit U.S. quantum master's degrees in this 2026 paper. Quantum technology is a strategic race for the United States. As devices move from lab prototypes to real systems, the skill of the workforce comes into focus. Few past studies pair a full curriculum scan with what industry says it needs.

The team codes course lists from the main U.S. programs in quantum science and technology. Each course maps into six skill classes, and the counts form a skill profile per program. They then set those profiles against competencies from recent workforce studies. Theory of quantum systems is strong across programs, they find. Hands-on technical skill, applied learning, and professional growth vary a lot. The gaps point to weak spots in job readiness and cross-field breadth. Programs also differ in how they meet fast-shifting tech demands.
arxiv-2606-01041:
Feng and co-authors let AI agents learn from past experience without stuffing text into the prompt in this 2026 paper. Agents can reuse old interactions as knowledge. Standard retrieval fetches matching text and pastes it into the context. That costs many tokens and splits retrieval from generation into two loose parts.

Their framework, ExpWeaver, retrieves in latent space instead. Experiences are encoded by the model's own hidden states. At each decoding step, fit experiences are pulled in that space. Cross attention and a gated residual fold them into the live computation. The whole pipe trains end to end with reinforcement learning. It serves both writing and ranking tasks. Across 13 tasks, from questions to code and recommendations, ExpWeaver tops the chart on 12, they report. It beats the best baseline by over 6.8 percent on the strongest baseline tests, while token costs stay near the no retrieval line.
arxiv-2606-01241:
Zhang and co-authors unite robot navigation and manipulation in OneVLA. Robots must parse plain commands and act in the world. Most vision-language-action models do just one of these jobs. That split blocks general-purpose robots. OneVLA uses one shared action head for both jobs. It needs no task-specific variants to switch roles. Training runs in stages that build skills in steps.

Curated data and chain-of-thought fine-tuning aid the stages. Skills transfer and boost each other across the two domains. Tests run in both simulated and real settings. OneVLA beats models built for a single task. It also beats past cross-task models. The work points toward robots that can do many jobs.
arxiv-2606-01341:
Zhang and Jing generate huge Fock states with adaptive measurement. Fock states hold a precise integer count of excitations. They are core building blocks for bosonic modes. Large versions are prized for quantum information and metrology. Making them deterministically has long been hard in quantum optics. Their protocol uses adaptive generalized parity measurement. Measurement gaps update based on the last outcome. No trajectory gets discarded along the way.

In the resonant Jaynes-Cummings model, ten rounds suffice. A large coherent state becomes a Fock state near 10,000 excitations. Average fidelity sits near 87 percent in that run. A near 20,000 target hits over 99 percent fidelity about 35 percent of the time. The method tolerates moderate measurement error.
arxiv-2606-01841:
Tsybina and co-authors argue that brain-like circuits can lift neural nets sharply. Live brains learn new patterns from a few examples. They also work well under heavy sensory noise. Modern deep nets still fall short on both counts. The team adds circuits modeled on real brain parts.

The added parts mimic astrocyte control and spiking signals. Hybrid models are tested on standard benchmarks. Tasks vary in how hard they are. The authors report high scores from few examples per class. Scores hold up under occlusion and impulse noise. Standard nets collapse under that same noise. The team names this edge neuromorphic supremacy. They see it as a base for embodied AI perception.
arxiv-2606-01941:
Hoang and co-authors secure light-based wireless networks against insiders. Visible light communication sends data through light signals. Rate-splitting multiple access serves several users at once. Some legitimate users may spy on others' private data. That internal eavesdropping threat drives the study.

The team maximize the secrecy sum rate of the system. The problem is non-convex due to coupled terms. Two methods tackle it: a convex-concave procedure and semidefinite relaxation. Channel similarity measures how spatially correlated users are. High similarity drags secrecy performance down. A clustering strategy is proposed to cut that similarity. It groups users to lower correlation in advance. Gains in secrecy follow from the redesign.
arxiv-2606-02241:
Deschenaux and Gulcehre build a blockwise sequence model with hybrid samplers. Discrete diffusion has two rival forms in current work. Uniform-state diffusion may be the more powerful paradigm. With predictor-corrector samplers, it beats masked diffusion on sample quality. Downstream tasks also favor it, despite worse perplexity. Two issues remain open in that comparison.

Correctors in past work re-inject noise at random spots. They do not target tokens most likely to be wrong. Past comparisons also use full-sequence diffusion only. Block-by-block generation may behave differently in the contest. Their BlockGen model generates tokens block by block. Hybrid samplers combine the strengths of both forms. The study tests whether uniform-state gains survive blocking. Sequence modeling gains a more flexible design.
arxiv-2606-02341:
Mohammadi and co-authors build a classifier for sounds recorded under water. Ships and other sources must be sorted from noisy acoustic data. Two views of the signal help. Spectrograms show harmonic patterns but drop some fine detail. Raw waveforms keep phase data yet are hard to read. The team uses both views at once.

Their design pairs two encoders built from pretrained backbones. Small tuning modules adapt each branch with few trainable weights. A fusion step based on the Choquet integral merges the branches. The merge can be read back to show what each class relies on. It also shifts weight toward the view least hurt by channel flaws. Tests on DeepShip and ShipsEar beat single-encoder baselines. The design also cuts training cost and guards against overfitting on small sets.
arxiv-2606-02541:
Fox and Hunter prove a growth result for three-color van der Waerden numbers. Such a number gives the longest run of integers that can be three-colored with no single-color arithmetic progression of a set length. The question is how fast that length grows with the progression size.

For large k, the authors build a coloring of the first 2 to the power k log-star k over 4 integers. It holds no monochromatic k-term progression. So the three-color number grows faster than any exponential in k. The growth is super-exponential. A new lower bound for multicolor numbers also appears. It resolves a problem of Erdős and Graham on canonical van der Waerden numbers. The work sharpens a classic corner of Ramsey theory.
arxiv-2606-02741:
Kunkel and co-authors test the environmental attitudes that language models show. Such models now help with sustainability choices, reporting, and public messaging. Systematic evidence on their green leanings has been thin. The test draws on established environmental awareness surveys. Behavioral measures join the question set. Thirty-one widely used models are tested, proprietary and open-weight alike. Answers are compared among models and against German human survey data.

Many models lean greener than the average respondent. They show higher environmental affect and cognition. They recommend behaviors with large carbon reduction potential. No systematic link ties green answers to model origin, size, or release context. Prompting conditions matter, though. Persona prompts shift answers in clear ways. Models also mirror user-stated ideology, in a sycophantic shift. That steerability raises concerns for real use. The framework can be reused for value checks. Oversight is urged as models enter public decisions.
arxiv-2606-02841:
Gaukstad and co-authors tackle a basic problem in deep learning. Single neurons often respond to scattered, unrelated inputs, so their role stays unclear. The team defines a property they call coherence, inspired by brain cells that respond to one connected region of space.

A matrix is coherent when each sample uses a clustered set of features, and each feature serves a clustered set of samples. The authors prove that such matrices keep the shapes of sample space and feature space closely matched. They then add a training objective called Coh, based on Fréchet variance, that pushes networks toward coherence. Tests use an auto-encoder on synthetic and rotated MNIST data. They also test a token embedding from BERT. The aim is features that stay readable, and a feature space that stays readable as a whole.
arxiv-2606-02941:
Agnew studies when modal K4 algebras are locally finite in mathematical logic. An algebra is locally finite when every finitely generated subalgebra is finite. The work approaches the question through the dual general frames of these algebras, and through a property called tunability.

Agnew gives a sufficient condition for local finiteness. The key step is to name a structure that must appear in any K4 algebra that fails to be locally finite. For complex modal K4 algebras, that condition is also necessary. The result then translates into two order conditions on transitive Kripke frames. Those conditions classify local finiteness for the dual algebras. Agnew also proves a finite model property for the logic of any class of well-founded transitive relations with no infinite antichains. The logic of well-quasi orderings gets the finite model property as a consequence. The work links algebra, frames, and logic in one classification.
arxiv-2606-03541:
de Laverny and co-authors build a Gaia catalogue of starlight dimming and star traits. The GSP-Spec module of Gaia DR3 published air parameters for over five million stars. Those values come from Radial Velocity Spectrometer spectra. The team joins them with parallax and brightness data from Gaia. The result lists interstellar colour excess and extinction for each star.

Stellar luminosity, radius, and mass come with the catalogue. No stellar evolution models are used to derive them. Error bars come from Monte-Carlo runs for over four million stars. A flag system marks quality by spectrum traits, numeric precision, and astrometry. Over a million stars pass the strict cut. Mass proves most sensitive to flaws in the input parameters. Checks against interferometric and asteroseismic data confirm the radii and masses. Sample uses span exoplanet sizes, mass distributions, and halo merger history.
arxiv-2606-03641:
Wong shows that medical triage by language models shifts with the patient's stated gender. Identical neurological symptoms were presented across seven demographic conditions. Age and gender varied while symptoms stayed fixed. Three model families ran 630 trials in total. The symptom set lists persistent headache, blurred vision, morning nausea, and visual disturbance.

Young women got far lower emergency referral rates than young men. On one model the rates were zero versus about 23 percent. On another they were about 7 versus 97 percent. All gaps were highly significant. At age 65 the disparity vanished. The mechanism is diagnostic substitution. Models anchor young women on intracranial hypertension tied to women of childbearing age. Men get a generic pressure diagnosis with lesions considered. Female patients are thus routed to outpatient care despite matching severity scores. The fix urged is to decouple urgency from diagnostic priors.
arxiv-2606-03741:
Chadha studies how long a reasoning system should hold a subgoal before re-planning. Long tasks need commitment to medium-range intent without rigidity. Re-plan too often and computation never coheres. Commit too long and the plan goes stale. The setting is latent reasoning, where steps unfold in hidden state, not in token traces.

A feudal manager-worker design extends the Hierarchical Reasoning Model. A slow high-level module emits a normalized subgoal that lasts for P worker steps. It biases the worker's hidden updates and adds a cosine alignment loss. On ARC and ConceptARC, persistence itself is the key knob. Periods of three to six steps beat both constant re-planning and long holds. Loss bottoms at period three. The alignment weight has a narrow optimum near 0.05. Ablations tie interference past that point to learned directional structure. Designers get a clear rule from the sweep.
arxiv-2606-03841:
Yang and co-authors build EvoDS, a data science agent that improves itself over time. Language model agents now automate parts of data science. Static action sets limit what they can learn to do. Weak long-horizon context handling blocks steady work on multi-stage pipelines. Reusable experience fails to accumulate under those limits.

EvoDS attacks both limits at once. An Autonomous Skill Acquisition mechanism synthesizes, validates, and reuses executable skills. An Adaptive Context Compression strategy treats context as a learned control problem. Passive truncation is left behind. A two-stage multi-agent training scheme orchestrates the two strategies. Theory links the design to lower tool-selection error and an information bottleneck goal. Across four benchmarks, EvoDS beats top open-source rivals by about 29 percent on average. Out-of-token failures disappear entirely. Data science teams get an agent that grows with use.
arxiv-2606-04041:
Sun and co-authors introduce an A-generalized Yang-Baxter equation for pre-Lie algebras. The work grows from a known puzzle in the field. That puzzle asks how to build pre-Lie structures on a dual space. Their equation extends the Yang-Baxter equation of pre-Lie algebras. Symmetric solutions are studied through A-generalized Hessian pre-Lie algebras.

They split those symmetric solutions into two types. Factorizable solutions match a class of Rota-Baxter pre-Lie algebras of nonzero weight. That match is one-to-one, and they find all such solutions. They also describe the Hessian algebras' structure in detail. Central and double extensions drive that description. Low-dimensional nontrivial cases are classified as well.
arxiv-2606-04141:
Kargi Chauhan and Pratibha Revankar study in 2026 how language model agents can be tricked into leaking credentials that share their context window with untrusted content. They test three defenses meant to catch the theft early, ideally before any answer is produced.

First, probes reading the model's internal activations separated innocent from credential-seeking prompts with high accuracy, even under disguised encodings. Second, honeytokens, fake credentials shaped by character models, were calibrated with conformal prediction to control false alarms. Third, tracking an estimated leakage budget across a whole conversation caught slow multi-turn thefts that single-turn checks missed. The authors call the results preliminary, noting the small in-house test suite and the need for internal model access.
arxiv-2606-04241:
Sushma Kumari and co-authors extend in 2026 a family of rare-earth cobalt aluminide crystals to its heavy members, growing single crystals for rare earths from gadolinium to thulium plus yttrium. The lighter members of the family were already known for an odd mix of magnetic behaviors.

Diffraction showed the new crystals take an orthorhombic structure with a small, varying aluminium shortfall. Heat, resistance, and magnetization measurements found antiferromagnetic ordering in every member, with ordering temperatures spanning roughly two to twelve kelvin. Gadolinium and terbium versions showed two close transitions each. The ordering pattern breaks the standard scaling expected from the rare earth alone, which the authors attribute to the interplay of exchange coupling and crystal electric fields.
arxiv-2606-04341:
Abhinava Chatterjee and Chao-Xing Liu predict in 2026 a one-way effect for light in magnetic materials that host axion quasiparticles. These are waves of the magnetic order that couple to electromagnetic fields. The hybrids are called axion-polaritons.

Under the right static electric and magnetic fields, the hybrids move one way differently from the other. The cause is direction-dependent coupling between the axion and the photon. In one regime the effect becomes perfect. Light going one way decouples from the axion entirely. Light going the other way hybridizes strongly. That is exactly an optical isolator, a one-way gate for light. The authors propose it as a testable probe of axion quasiparticles.
arxiv-2606-04441:
Lu and colleagues present a practical method for measuring the global polarization of Lambda particles in fixed-target nuclear collisions, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. That motion polarizes the spin of the particles that fly out. The strong polarization seen in Lambda particles shows that quark-gluon plasma is the most vortical fluid known. Measuring it at lower energies maps the phase diagram of strong-force matter.

Fixed-target experiments make this measurement hard. Their detectors cover an uneven range of angles. That uneven coverage couples the particles' directed flow with detector flaws. The coupling biases the polarization result. The method from Lu removes this bias. The team checked it with realistic detector simulations. The simulations used the STAR fixed-target setup at RHIC. The work supports future measurements at facilities such as FAIR and NICA.
arxiv-2606-04541:
Bobrov proposes a general method for computing kinematic limits in particle physics, in a 2026 arXiv methods paper. Kinematic limits are the boundary values that energies and angles in a reaction cannot cross. The approach works with Lorentz invariants. These quantities stay fixed under changes of reference frame. They behave like Cayley-Menger determinants, the volume formulas of geometry, moved into Minkowski space. A kinematic limit is reached exactly when one of these invariants vanishes.

Because the condition is algebraic, the approach applies across a wide range of particle processes. Bobrov highlights reactions involving lost particles. Or they barely interact with detector material. Neutrinos are the classic example. Knowing the exact limits helps experimenters reconstruct such reactions. The limits can also suppress background. They cut events that could not come from the process of interest.
arxiv-2606-04841:
Vázquez-Mozo studies anomalous currents in chiral fluids living in geometries more general than Einstein's, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Metric-affine geometries allow the metric and the connection to vary, producing nonmetricity, the failure of lengths to be preserved under transport. He studies equilibrium fermionic fluids chirally coupled to background Weyl-type nonmetricity.

From the equilibrium partition function, he evaluates the relation of the axial-vector current. The calculation shows chiral separation effects, currents separating chiral charges, driven by the fluid's vorticity and by the Weyl magnetic field. Such anomaly-driven transport is prized because it is exact, so these results extend a robust corner of quantum field theory into geometries.
arxiv-2606-05241:
Yongjie Wang and co-authors measure search-time contamination in deep research agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Public benchmarks promise fair, reproducible checks, but research agents search the live web while they work, so they can retrieve benchmark metadata, question context, or even ground-truth answers mid-test. That retrieval bypasses the intended reasoning and quietly inflates the measured score. The authors define three contamination types of increasing severity: benchmark metadata leakage, question-context leakage, and explicit answer leakage.

They build detection algorithms to identify each type and measure its effect on scores. Evaluating modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks, they found contamination is widespread. It can inflate performance by up to four percent, meaning existing evaluations may overestimate true reasoning ability by a real margin. They advocate contamination-aware practice in response: isolated sandboxes for agents, open records of search paths, and controlled access to benchmark material.
arxiv-2606-05441:
Al Zadid Sultan Bin Habib and colleagues present GOTabPFN in this 2026 arXiv paper, a way to make small tabular foundation models work on data with far more features than samples. Such high-dimensional, low-sample settings, genomics being the case, break models like TabPFN that were designed for at most a couple thousand features.

Their pipeline first orders the features with Graph-guided Ordering with Local Refinement, which arranges correlated features into neighborhoods. They show this ordering problem is equivalent to the weighted Minimum Linear Arrangement problem and solve it with a traveling-salesman-style surrogate. A Neuro-Inspired Subunit Compression unit then pools locally adjacent ordered features into meta-features, compressing the table into a compact token sequence the model can consume. Across tabular benchmarks, GOTabPFN improved stability and accuracy under tight token budgets. It beat using the backbone directly.
arxiv-2606-05741:
Mugdho, Hasan, and Wang weigh chip designs for data centers in orbit in a 2026 arXiv paper. Space offers sunlight and cheap launches, but no air for cooling. Heat can leave only by radiation, which demands large radiator panels. Standard graphics processors pair a hot chip with separate memory blocks. The team asks whether compute-in-memory chips, which blend storage and math, fare better under that thermal cap.

Their method ties allowed computing speed directly to radiator capacity in the design loop. Simulations showed the split GPU layout forms severe hotspots under tight cooling. The processors had to throttle down to stay safe. Memory-centric chips spread heat far more evenly. They beat the GPU designs on operations per watt across a wide range of radiator budgets. Across many AI workloads the edge grew under realistic space constraints. The paper guides orbital hardware choices with thermal reality first.
arxiv-2606-05841:
Clemen, Führer, and Roche-Newton guarantee large point subsets with all distances distinct in a 2026 arXiv paper. Extremal geometry asks how big a subset can avoid a banned pattern. Here the pattern is a repeated distance: no two pairs may span the same length. Given any planar point set, the authors find a subset whose size grows like the cube root of the whole. Every distance inside that subset is unique.

The bound improves an earlier result of Charalambides. The proof leans on a hypergraph independence theorem by Li and Postle, plus incidence geometry tools. A second problem in the paper picks grid subsets with no rhombus, a four-point pattern. Both problems descend from Erdős and Purdy's work on forbidden configurations. They have become benchmark tests for AI math systems. The paper sharpens what combinatorics can promise before the point set's structure is known.
arxiv-2606-06441:
Andy Shen, Chenqi Fu, and Ray Lin tackle a bias that creeps into cancer trials in this 2026 arXiv paper on biostatistics. In oncology trials, control patients whose disease worsens are often allowed to switch onto the experimental drug. Ethically sensible, but switching breaks the clean comparison that randomization bought, and survival estimates tilt. Existing fixes lean on strong assumptions or fragile models.

The authors bring in external controls, comparable patients from outside the trial, to stand in for what switchers would have faced untreated. Borrowing the synthetic control method and balancing weights from observational research, they build estimators using multiple imputation and time varying weights. They also discuss how to choose which external patients are eligible to impute from at each moment. Simulations show clear gains over standard adjustments and naive uses of external data. Two phase three trials, IMpower130 and OAK, demonstrate the approach on real data.
arxiv-2606-06541:
Risto Raitio completes a composite model of matter with string mathematics in this 2026 arXiv paper on particle theory. Preon models propose that quarks and leptons are bound states of smaller constituents, confined by a metacolor force much as quarks are confined in protons. Such a model needs an ultraviolet completion, a well behaved high energy description. Raitio builds one from the Nambu Goto string action, computing the Regge trajectory of a six preon state, the line relating its spin to its mass squared.

From that trajectory he constructs the Veneziano scattering amplitude with no free parameters. Its poles match the model's spectrum to within half a percent. At fixed angle it decays exponentially with exactly the Gross Mende coefficient, realized numerically to zero point zero three percent. The author calls this a soft, non perturbative completion, with the Standard Model as the low energy limit.
arxiv-2606-06741:
Software agents usually improve only when someone hands them curated lessons or a reliable grader. Yan and a large team ask what an agent can do with neither in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting, called open world self evolution, gives the agent only a task prompt and the open internet, with no answers from the target task to learn from.

Their framework, OpenSkill, gathers grounded knowledge and checking anchors from documents, code repositories, and the web, then turns them into portable skills. The agent practices on virtual tasks it builds from those anchors, not on the real answers, and sharpens its skills there. Across three benchmarks and two agent models, OpenSkill earned the best automated pass rate while respecting the no supervision rule. Its skills transferred to other models without retuning, and its home built grader agreed surprisingly well with true outcomes it never saw.
arxiv-2606-06941:
Majority vote is a lazy way to pick a model's final answer, especially in law. Wynter, Sahoo, and Griffin replace voting with evidence selection in this 2026 arXiv paper. A small local model writes many reasoning traces per question. Fragments from those traces become pools of evidence for each answer.

An optimization step then picks the best evidence subset per pool. It scores fragments on relevance, specificity, and distinctiveness. The method uses a higher order binary optimization, solved by simulated annealing or a photonic quantum machine. A frontier model makes one final adjudication call per question. On two legal benchmarks, the method beat majority vote by wide margins. Gains reached about thirteen and twenty three percentage points. It also exposed a quirk: one frontier model favored option E on most questions when unaided. Curated evidence tamed that bias.
arxiv-2606-07041:
A spin chain and a field theory can describe the same physics, but twisting the boundary conditions exposes a deep obstruction. Nicholas Read and Saleur explore that twist in this 2026 arXiv paper. The chain is an antiferromagnet whose sites carry spin S. Its continuum limit is a nonlinear sigma model with a topological angle set by the spin.

The twist is antiperiodic boundaries paired with an odd number of sites. In the field theory this inserts a flux of the model's flip symmetry. The authors show the symmetry can be gauged only under a sign condition on the topological angle. When the condition fails, an 't Hooft anomaly blocks the gauged model entirely. A would-be theory on projective space simply does not exist at the bad angles. Semiclassical calculations recover the known ground state momenta of the chains. Boundary conditions, often an afterthought, here dictate which theories are possible.
arxiv-2606-07141:
Hospitals may need a trained AI model to forget one patient's data without forgetting medicine. Sharma and co-authors build a benchmark for that dilemma in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine unlearning methods promise removal without retraining from scratch. Existing tests, though, use synthetic data far from clinical reality.

Their benchmark, REMEDI, uses the real MIMIC-III clinical database. The task is multi-label disease inference, where diagnoses correlate and overlap. Forget requests range from single patients to larger sets. Metrics track both diagnostic utility kept and information actually removed. Current methods traded one goal against the other. Several collapsed on multi-label tasks despite acing simpler benchmarks. A method called SCRUB kept the best balance between privacy and utility. Apparent success on tiny deletions often failed at larger scales. The authors call for objectives designed around label correlations from the start.
arxiv-2606-07741:
Zirui Chen and co-authors explain a puzzling constant of astrophysics in this 2026 arXiv paper: wherever hot and cold gas mix, the ratio of X-ray brightness to H-alpha brightness stays near three. H-alpha light traces cold gas near ten thousand degrees, while X-rays trace gas far hotter. Flat mixing-layer models miss that ratio by orders of magnitude.

The team ran three-dimensional wind-tunnel simulations with density contrast near one thousand between the phases. In that regime the cold gas shatters into many small glowing clumps, and hot gas forms a cocoon around them. Smoothing the simulated images to the width of a real tail brings the ratio to the observed value, about three. Their explanation splits the problem cleanly: atomic physics fixes the cold-gas share of the light, while the hot share depends on how briefly gas lingers at X-ray temperatures.
arxiv-2606-08441:
Sultana, Gonzalez, and Teather compare ways to point at things in augmented reality without holding a controller, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Selecting two-dimensional targets on virtual displays is a basic augmented reality task, and controller-free techniques promise more natural interaction. The authors systematically evaluated five pointing techniques using the standard ISO protocol for pointing devices, comparing them across three depths in terms of movement time, accuracy, throughput, and workload.

Head- and eye-based pointing significantly outperformed the hand-based methods, which used the finger, wrist, or whole arm. Head input was the most accurate and remained the most consistent as depth increased from near to far. Depth itself significantly affected performance, with complex interactions between depth, target size, and distance, so no single technique wins under all conditions. The study gives designers an empirical basis for choosing pointing techniques in depth-varying augmented reality tasks.
arxiv-2606-08941:
Deng, Sun, Li, and Liu ask when a causal estimate can ignore some variables and still give the same answer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Causal inference estimates the effect of an intervention from data in a graph. Often the graph is only partly known: a completed partially directed acyclic graph, or CPDAG, represents a family of causal graphs. An estimate is collapsible over a set of variables if marginalizing them out leaves the estimate consistent. The authors define this property for CPDAGs and characterize which variable sets qualify.

The minimal collapsible sets are strong d-convex hulls, closed graph regions defined by separation properties. The team gives an algorithm finding hulls in a causal graph, generalized to CPDAGs. They plug the method into the IDA framework, an approach for estimating effects from CPDAGs, simplifying via graph reduction. Experiments confirm that collapsibility improves causal estimation. The code is public.
arxiv-2606-09241:
Yufei Chen and colleagues find why a retrieval model that generates item IDs can lose the right answer in the first few tokens it emits, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal retrieval replaces search with generation: the model outputs a discrete code for the target, built by residual quantization, and a trie constrains decoding. Their indexing-decoding gap: training losses never ensure early prefixes separate targets, so good codes are pruned early, when their prefixes rank low.

The authors derive a survival bound tying whether prefixes survive to three factors, then build PRO, prefix retention optimization, around it. Prefix ranking distillation aligns quantized prefix rankings with pre-quantization embedding rankings. Codebook scheduling grows them from shallow to deep levels, cutting early competition. Geometric score fusion folds each prefix's match to the query into the beam score. Across 9 retrieval tasks, PRO kept more target prefixes alive and beat existing baselines.
arxiv-2606-09341:
Qamar and colleagues build an atomic-scale potential accurate enough to watch hydrogen split palladium nanoparticles into 2 phases, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Palladium-hydrogen serves storage, catalysis, and cleaning. Its nanoscale physics, set by surface energy and strain, was never gotten right. Simple potentials misprice absorbed hydrogen, and earlier machine-learning models covered only bulk. Their atomic cluster expansion matches formation energies, phonons, elastic constants, hopping barriers, and surface adsorption at near-DFT accuracy.

Validated against neutron-scattering and lattice tests, it runs fast enough for molecular dynamics of nanoparticles beyond 28,000 atoms, about 12 nanometers across, over nanoseconds. The runs resolve the kinetic separation of alpha and beta hydride phases into a core-shell structure. They also reproduce how lattice spacing shifts with size, and reveal the particle melting point dropping sharply. On CPU it is at least 3 times faster than the prior neural network model.
arxiv-2606-09441:
Rya Sanovar and her colleagues speed up retrieval-augmented generation with a method called SIFT in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, pastes relevant documents into a language model's prompt, which improves answers but lengthens the wait for the first output token.

SIFT studies each document offline and records where its high attention scores fall, for every layer and attention head. Two regularities make this work: a document's internal hotspots stay put when neighbours change, and hot keys also attract attention from later documents. Only these locations are stored, as compact bit vectors a few kilobytes in size, up to twenty-four thousand times smaller than cached key-value tensors. A custom kernel then computes attention only at the marked spots. SIFT cut time to first token by up to about seventy percent while holding accuracy within one percent of full recomputation.
arxiv-2606-09741:
Ilya Gusinski presents a solver that shrinks dense animation data under one firm error cap in this 2026 arXiv paper. Animation tools sample motion frame by frame, which is safe but bloated: each sample can turn into a key, and vector paths stay hard to edit. Past reducers split the task, one for timing and one for shape. Run apart, they can break point identity across frames or lose a shared error budget.

His bbsolver treats time and shape as one task. A host app exports samples in a JSON bundle. The solver picks sparse keys and path forms, and the result stands only if a replay stays within the cap. In After Effects tests, a walk cycle fell from twelve thousand samples to five hundred forty keys, a cut of more than twentyfold. Peak error stayed below one pixel and one degree.
arxiv-2606-09841:
Bryant Pollard builds a route guide for coal mine shuttle cars with the miners, not just for them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Room-and-pillar mines are dark, busy, and short on live data. Shuttle car drivers must pick safe paths amid moving crews and jams. A graph neural network reads the mine as a graph and ranks routes, served through a browser tool on cloud hosts.

The core claim is that design method, not model shine, made the tool work. Interviews and joint design sessions pinned the real task and mine logic. Two rounds of usability tests with six users then exposed weak spots. The fix list ran long: in-place feedback, multi-blockage reports, audio cues, and SHAP charts that show why a route was picked. Round two beat round one on tasks done, speed, and errors.
arxiv-2606-09941:
Cui and colleagues build a machine learning generator for minute-by-minute surface wind, in a 2026 arXiv paper on weather modeling. Their data come from more than thirty years of high-quality measurements at Lamont, Oklahoma, restricted to June to reduce seasonal effects. Wind vectors, recording both speed and direction, swing sharply minute to minute. A realistic generator could feed wind energy, wildfire, and aviation models.

The team tested time-series models built on vector-quantized variational autoencoders, a method that compresses patterns into a learned codebook before generating new ones. Their generators produce one day at a time, sometimes conditioned on the previous day, and can include a discrete weather state. The best versions captured the daily rhythm of wind volatility, meaning how gustiness rises and falls across the day. They still struggled to match the observed distribution of extreme wind speeds, an honest limit the authors report.
arxiv-2606-10141:
Liu uses an exactly solvable model of strong-force physics as a laboratory for a subtle mathematical breakdown, in a 2026 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. The 't Hooft model describes quantum chromodynamics in one space dimension with many colors, and its meson spectrum is known analytically. The deformation drives the two lowest mesons toward an exceptional point, where eigenvalues and eigenvectors merge and analyticity fails.

Recasting the resolvent as a continued fraction yields the critical deformation strength in closed form. It converges to a precise multiple of the coupling by depth five, an analytic threshold rather than a numerical estimate. The square-root exponent is fixed by the Jordan structure and confirmed by finite-size scaling up to nearly two thousand states. Time-domain behavior changes sharply at the threshold: the propagator norm is bounded below it, grows linearly at it, and exponentially beyond.
arxiv-2606-10441:
Han and co-authors model how tiny atomic nuclei form when gold nuclei collide, in this 2026 arXiv paper on heavy-ion physics. Loose clusters such as deuterons and helium nuclei can coalesce, meaning nearby protons and neutrons stick together as the hot system expands. Some clusters are hypernuclei, containing a strange hyperon particle alongside ordinary nucleons. The team embeds a coalescence calculation inside the PHQMD transport model and builds wave functions by solving the Schrödinger equation.

Matching results against STAR data lets them extract a formation time for each species, and the times are not universal. Two- and three-particle clusters match at later times, while four-particle systems form earlier, under denser conditions. Adding cluster-nucleon channels, where an existing cluster captures one more nucleon, improves the match for helium-4 and its hypernucleus counterpart. The paper closes with yield predictions for heavier hypernuclei.
arxiv-2606-10541:
Shao and co-authors clean up laser scans of glass-rich scenes in this 2026 arXiv paper on mapping. Terrestrial laser scanning builds point clouds of streets and buildings, but glass reflects the beam and creates ghost points where nothing exists. Older methods assume ideal mirror symmetry and struggle when glass is poorly measured, since transparent surfaces often return no signal. The framework first finds the glass: a vision foundation model drafts masks, geometry refines them, and completion rebuilds missing regions.

A second stage flags the fake points with a physics-based descriptor, RE-LGGS, comparing local and global shape and orientation against how laser light reflects. Tests on several datasets, including dominant-glass, grid-like glass, and subway scenes, show the framework beating leading methods at glass estimation and artifact removal. Pairing foundation-model perception with geometric reasoning is, the authors argue, a practical route to better surveying data.
arxiv-2606-10741:
Hansheng Xu and colleagues probe how a Mott insulator talks to graphene in this 2026 arXiv paper. Niobium chloride, Nb3Cl8, is a Mott insulator whose layer carries out-of-plane polarisation that flips with layer parity, an odd-even effect. With atomic force and Kelvin probe microscopy, the team reads that polarisation from surface and potential maps, telling the phases apart. They then build dual-gate Hall devices joining each phase to graphene, and measure the coupling.

The phase matters. Charge transfer and carrier densities differ between the heterostructures, and the hybridisation gap, where the two materials' states mix, is 25.2 millielectronvolts for phase one against 30.0 for phase two. Density functional calculations agree, tracing it to how polarisation direction changes orbital overlap. The lesson for van der Waals engineering: the polarisation and orbital orientation of a correlated layer are design knobs, not details.
arxiv-2606-10941:
Sinha and colleagues map the geometry of cislunar space with operator theory in this 2026 arXiv paper. The circular restricted three-body problem governs motion between Earth and Moon, and its phase space is usually probed trajectory by trajectory. The authors instead use the Koopman operator, which trades nonlinear motion for a global linear picture, computed through a path-integral form of its spectrum.

From the leading eigenfunctions, the zero level curves trace out the phase-space structures of the planar problem, recovering globally what local trajectory work assembles piecemeal. The method offers mission designers a single spectral object encoding the organizing structures of motion in the Earth-Moon system.
arxiv-2606-11241:
Guerguis and Bassim present APTLAS in a 2026 arXiv paper, an indexed repository of atom probe tomography literature. Atom probe tomography, a technique mapping atoms in three dimensions, has spread from metallurgy into many materials fields. Its papers scatter across general, microscopy, and materials journals. Search engines retrieve them, but cannot filter on the domain metadata that decides relevance, like analysis mode, laser wavelength, or instrument configuration.

APTLAS holds about twenty-three hundred records, each with metadata extracted from the source publication through a three-stage pipeline. A companion web tool lets users browse and filter by material system, instrument, application, publication type, or keyword. The extraction uses large language models, and the tool runs locally in any browser. The repository cuts the friction of finding prior work in a niche, fast-growing technique whose outcomes depend strongly on experimental conditions.
arxiv-2606-11441:
Rezayi and Hadipour compute how strongly electrons screen each other inside carbon nanotubes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Depending on their wrapping vector, they are either metallic or semiconducting, an ideal platform for exploring how electronic structure governs screening in one-dimensional systems. The authors use first-principles calculations within the random-phase approximation, in its constrained form, across nanotubes of different chiralities.

The strength of on-site Coulomb interactions falls between 3.5 and 5 electron volts. That is roughly two to three electron volts smaller than the values in graphene nanoribbons. The reduction lowers the long-range ones too. The finding is consistent with experimental results on the smaller binding energy of excitons, electron-hole pairs, in nanotubes. Screening in nanotubes is thus softer on site than in ribbons, shaping the effective models used for these materials.
arxiv-2606-11741:
Antonio Pagliaro and Antonino La Barbera review machine learning for gamma-ray telescopes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes photograph the faint flashes made when gamma rays hit the upper air. The central challenge is event reconstruction: working out each incoming particle's type and energy from its flash, while rejecting a huge background of ordinary cosmic-ray showers.

The chapter walks through the standard pipeline, from image cleaning to the Hillas parameters, classic shape measures of the flash, plus gains from viewing showers with several telescopes. It then frames reconstruction as supervised learning: classification for particle type, regression for energy. Two frontiers get special attention. Timing features, using when each part of the flash arrives, sharply improve background rejection at low energies. Ensemble methods such as gradient boosting beat the usual random forests and reduce energy bias. Deep learning directions close the review.
arxiv-2606-12141:
Azimov and co-authors forecast sea surface temperature in the East Sea in this 2026 arXiv paper. The East Sea mixes a warm northward current with cold northern water, forming a sharp, shifting front that makes prediction hard. Their method first compresses each temperature map with singular value decomposition, a math tool that keeps the strongest patterns and drops the rest. A learning model then predicts how those patterns evolve.

The model is an adaptive form of nonlinear vector autoregression, which predicts the next state from recent states but learns its nonlinear features from data. Across several horizons, the adaptive model beats the standard version on every error measure used, including root mean squared error. The gap widens at longer horizons, where the adaptive features slow the buildup of error. The compressed design keeps computing cost low enough for real-time use.
arxiv-2606-13041:
Lyu and Lei present SeamEdit, a training-free, model-agnostic pipeline for semantic editing of large images with closed-source vision-language models as black-box inpainters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Applying closed-source models to tiled editing introduces characteristic failures: semantic deformation and canvas-level alignment drift, where a regenerated tile shifts in position or scale. Seam artefacts also appear where generated tiles meet.

SeamEdit mitigates these issues with a 5-stage pipeline. Tile decomposition splits the image with overlaps; the black-box model inpaints them. Geometric and colour-consistency correction re-aligns each tile with the canvas. Seam-risk-based multi-candidate ranking selects the least risky candidate. Dynamic-programming curved seam fusion hides the joins along low-risk curved paths rather than straight tile borders. The pipeline treats any vision-language model with inpainting capability as an oracle. It needs no diffusion states, unlike high-resolution methods.
arxiv-2606-13241: This 2026 manuscript from arXiv puts forward new research. It addresses the topic named in its title: Brick: Spatial Capability Routing for the Mixture-of-Models (MoM) Paradigm. The field in play is artificial intelligence: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. It offers the field something new to consider.
arxiv-2606-13341:
Steele, Altalib, and Perelli present a generative model for medical imaging in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hospitals need both CT and PET scans, which show anatomy and metabolic activity, but acquiring both is costly and slow. Synthesising one modality from the other could help. Earlier generative adversarial networks, systems where a generator and a critic train against each other, worked only in the spatial domain and ignored consistency. Their network, DDE-GAN, learns in the spatial and frequency domains, capturing anatomical detail and spectral structure together.

The design builds rotational equivariance, the guarantee that rotating an input rotates the output the same way, into the losses of both generator and critic. A staged training strategy enforces consistency within and between the two domains. Evaluated on the HECKTOR 2022 dataset of head and neck scans, the model beats the baselines for combined CT-PET synthesis in quality.
arxiv-2606-13441:
Keshet argues that large language models are not moral agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Claims of agency have grown with model capability, but Keshet maintains that moral responsibility needs commitment-bearing agency. Such agency rests on intrinsic intentionality, meaning the system's states are about things on their own, and on actions the agent owns as its own commitments. Language models, by contrast, are described as probabilistic mappings from inputs to outputs learned from data.

Their apparent intentionality is derived, borrowed from the humans who wrote their training text and interpret their replies. Their outputs are neither owned as commitments nor guided by reasons the system endorses. Randomness from stochastic sampling, the dice-rolling in generation, does not amount to choosing or authoring. Keshet answers objections from the intentional stance, functionalism, and compatibilism, and from the presence of reasoning in outputs. None, he argues, establishes genuine agency.
arxiv-2606-13541: Uploaded to arXiv in 2026, this scientific manuscript shares recent results. The subject on the cover page is Overview of the. Expect science and technology throughout: careful study of how the natural and built world works. The paper's service is a clear overview of a busy research area.
arxiv-2606-13841:
Röpke studies how atoms lose electrons inside very dense, hot matter known as warm dense plasma. In such plasmas the free electrons are degenerate, meaning quantum rules force them into higher energy states. A key effect is Pauli blocking: electrons cannot settle into filled states, which changes how tightly ions hold their electrons. Standard plasma codes ignore this effect. His 2026 arXiv paper treats one- and two-electron ions with a quantum statistical method.

Solving the in-medium Schrödinger equation gives a Mott density, the density where bound states vanish, that is higher than simpler perturbation theory predicts. The disappearance of the bound state stays abrupt. For helium-like ions holding two electrons, the breakup is stepwise rather than simultaneous. One electron leaves first, and the remaining one binds more tightly without its partner's screening. At still higher density the ion loses that last electron too.
arxiv-2606-14441:
Perez-Gonzalez, Sen, and Tangarife compute how neutrinos decay inside hot matter in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that rarely interact. The authors study non-standard decays where a heavier neutrino turns into a lighter one plus a scalar or light vector boson, using finite-temperature quantum field theory.

Their general formulas show that heat can dramatically speed these decays when parent and daughter neutrinos have nearly equal masses. In that near-degenerate case the emitted boson is soft, and Bose enhancement, the tendency of bosons to pile into occupied states, inflates the decay width. The width can exceed its empty-space value by a couple of orders of magnitude in size. The effect barely depends on the interaction's detailed form, so the framework should apply to many fermion decays in thermal settings.
arxiv-2606-14741:
Yara benchmarks vision-language models on degraded emergency imagery in a 2026 arXiv paper. HorusEye studies language as dynamic attention: using words to steer visual analysis when scenes are foggy, smoky, or thermal, as in fires and rescues. The first stage builds a dataset of over fifteen thousand images from nearly four thousand base images under clean, fog, smoke, and thermal conditions.

Across five stages the study tests visual grounding, recovery through language feedback, health question answering, and hallucination. Language feedback helped unevenly: one leading model improved by about forty-seven percent in thermal conditions through iterative feedback, while another degraded by about five percent under the same protocol. A thermal paradox appeared, where cropping strategies that help ordinary images fail catastrophically in thermal views, and one model hallucinated more under degradation, making it unsuitable for emergency deployment.
arxiv-2606-14941:
Zhou and co-authors add meaning-based retrieval to time series forecasting in a 2026 arXiv paper. Forecasters often borrow patterns from history. Retrieval-augmented methods fetch similar past segments and their outcomes. But matching on raw similarity alone fails when series are non-stationary. Similar shapes can mean different things.

Their framework, SERAF, retrieves on two channels at once. One channel matches the numeric series. The other matches self-generated textual descriptions of the series. The two retrieved sets are complementary: patterns plus their corresponding futures. They are selectively combined to guide the forecast. Experiments on seven real-world datasets show the dual view beats state-of-the-art baselines. The work bridges numerical and semantic views of time series. One co-author's contribution was made while employed at Siemens AG.
arxiv-2606-15041:
Ding studies how dense Sidon sets spread across residue classes in a 2026 mathematics note. A Sidon set is a set of integers whose pairwise sums are all distinct. Dense Sidon sets inside the first n integers reach nearly square-root size, the most possible. Earlier work gave sum formulas over such sets only under an extra density hypothesis.

That hypothesis sat awkwardly with how dense Sidon sets actually distribute, as other authors observed. Ding removes it, proving the expected asymptotic formula for all fixed power sums. For each modulus and residue class, the weighted sum matches the natural share predicted by uniform distribution. The proof leans on Fourier uniformity estimates for extremal Sidon sets by Ortega and Prendiville. Cilleruelo's results on gaps in dense Sidon sets also feed the argument. The note answers a question Ding had left open in earlier work on weighted sums over Sidon sets.
arxiv-2606-15341:
Yan and coauthors present CausalDrive, a real-time world model for autonomous driving in a 2026 computer vision paper. Driving world models simulate how traffic scenes evolve, but most replay futures passively. Layout-based renderers cheat by reading other cars' future paths in advance. Predictors react, yet lack semantic control and run too slowly. CausalDrive starts from one front-view frame, the ego car's trajectory, and a text prompt, and must predict other road users' reactions itself.

A distillation architecture corrects the model's drift during generation. It reaches twelve frames per second with four or fewer generation steps. Text prompts can steer counterfactual reactions to identical ego actions. The simulator supports closed-loop evaluation with fewer collision artifacts. It serves as an environment for reinforcement learning post-training of driving policies. Policies trained inside it showed defensive driving in tests. The work turns video generation into a playable driving simulator.
arxiv-2606-15441:
He and coauthors defend language model agents against adaptive prompt injection in a 2026 security paper. In such attacks, instructions hide inside data the agent retrieves, a web page or tool output, and hijack it into serving the attacker. Defenses that ace static benchmarks collapse when attackers optimize against them, because they pattern-match known injections and train on a few templates. The proposed defense, RETA, instead grounds every step in the user's task.

At each tool-output step the defender reasons openly about whether its action serves the task. Training data comes from a simulated attacker rewarded for reformulations of injections, and the defender is tuned with reinforcement learning balancing security, utility, and reasoning rewards. Against six adaptive attacks, RETA holds every attack success rate under ten percent while keeping the agent useful on clean and attacked tasks. The lesson: defenses must be judged against attackers who adapt.
arxiv-2606-15641:
Rotman and colleagues improve in-context learning for classifying business conversations in 2026 by distilling examples into instructions. Few-shot prompting stuffs examples into the context, which grows unwieldy for long, multi-party B2B sales calls and degrades as context lengthens. The team introduces the Call Playbook dataset, five classification tasks over real sales conversations targeting sales concepts.

Their knowledge-extraction methods compress verbose examples into compact, structured classification criteria and precise task descriptions. The distilled form cuts token usage by ninety-nine percent while raising macro-averaged AUC by up to seven points over few-shot prompting. It also stays robust as context grows, where token-compression baselines lose more than nine F1 points. Because the criteria are readable text, humans can inspect and refine the classification logic. That transparency, plus the cost savings, suits production systems that must classify professional conversations at scale and explain themselves.
arxiv-2606-15841:
Yang examines a hidden assumption in how language-model systems spend compute in 2026: that an uncertainty score means the same thing everywhere. Verification policies rank inputs by such scores, presuming equal scores carry equal value across inputs. Using budgeted verification as a controlled diagnostic, Yang shows the signal quality is heteroskedastic, varying sharply across cost strata.

Some strata show near-random discriminability despite concentrating many errors, which distorts any global allocation built on the scores. A simple fix, cost-stratified thresholding, sets separate thresholds per cost stratum, with no gradient updates. Across code and maths benchmarks and three model families, global online adaptation gives inconsistent gains over static thresholds. The stratified rule improves hit rate by up to seventeen points where the spread is strong. The bottleneck is structural heterogeneity of the signal, not optimizer weakness: more compute cannot repair a misaligned signal, but respecting its structure can.
arxiv-2606-15941:
Cherik completes a classification in inner Lipschitz geometry for complex surface germs in a 2026 mathematics paper. A germ studies a shape only close to one point, here a complex surface near a singular point. Inner Lipschitz geometry compares distances measured inside the surface itself. Earlier work by Birbrair, Neumann, and Pichon classified the isolated case, where the bad point stands alone.

Cherik extends the classification to non-isolated singularities, where singular points can form larger sets. The complete invariant combines numerical data from the coordinate functions of the normalization map, a standard smoothing cover of the surface, with the combinatorics of a good resolution. The paper splits into two parts and builds several tools of independent interest along the way. Worked polar curve computations show how inner rates come out of the resolution graph. A complete invariant lets specialists tell two germs apart, or prove them equivalent, from finite data.
arxiv-2606-16041:
Aristimunha and colleagues present EEG-Dash in 2026, an open platform that makes public brain signal recordings ready for machine learning. Reusing such data is normally slow work. Each archive needs downloading, loading, format repair, windowing, and scoring code before any model can train. Even datasets that meet format standards can fail to load in practice.

EEG-Dash lists 791 public recordings from the OpenNeuro and NEMAR archives, covering EEG, MEG, in-skull, muscle, and near-infrared signals. Each dataset becomes an importable class that keeps its details intact and loads without custom code. Signal handling goes through MNE-Python, windowing through Braindecode, and format checks through the BIDS validator. A registry adds search by meaning, file repair, tags from source papers, and feature tools. Removing this plumbing should let more teams reuse shared recordings.
arxiv-2606-16341:
Mandarapu and Kunkunuru model filtered nearest-neighbor search in 2026 as a phase transition, where small estimation errors only hurt near sharp boundaries. A filtered query returns the k closest vectors that also pass an attribute filter. Systems can filter before, after, or during the search, and the best strategy changes with selectivity. Choosing requires estimating that selectivity first.

The authors show that estimation error causes plan regret, recall lost versus the best strategy, only in narrow regions around the phase boundaries. The regret forms a wedge whose width scales with the estimation error and whose height follows a flip-margin law tied to the boundary's slope. Two boundaries come from separate mathematics: order statistics place the post-filter cliff near selectivity k over K, and site percolation places the in-filter cliff near 0.83 over M. The remaining danger, they warn, is cost-model calibration.
arxiv-2606-16441:
Melong and Wulkenhaar deform topological recursion with a parameter q in 2026, taking a powerful counting scheme into quantum algebras. Topological recursion builds wave-functions and quantum curves from a spectral curve, and a shifted version was developed by Belliard, Bouchard, Kramer, and Nelson. The authors q-deform that shifted scheme by studying highest weight vectors in q-deformed W-algebra representations. The output is a q-analogue of the scheme that yields such curves.

The partition function of a deformed Airy structure produces q-correlators on a deformed spectral curve obeying the standard formula. The shifted version shares the same underlying geometry but changes the initial condition, and its rule carries extra source terms that shift the one-point q-correlators. It unifies approaches to quantum integrability and opens the geometry of q-deformed moduli spaces to these techniques.
arxiv-2606-16541:
Mohammad and Sheikh tackle in 2026 the quiet failure of autoformalization: a translated theorem can typecheck and still be the wrong theorem. Turning natural-language math into proof-assistant code is bottlenecked by faithfulness, not fluency. Their framework, Bidirectional Provability Fingerprinting, certifies faithfulness without any reference version. Each candidate is fingerprinted by its forward and backward consequence neighborhoods, then matched against probes derived from the source statement.

Counterfactual probe generation builds probes aimed at set drift directions. The equivalence spectrum replaces brittle yes-no verdicts with a graded score. Adaptive probe budget allocation routes the checking budget by value. Faithfulness-guided decoding feeds the signal back as a reward. The authors prove a drift detection theorem and a PAC result marking what can be detected at all. A new benchmark, DriftBench, ships with set drift labels. It beats typechecking and model-judge baselines, per the report.
arxiv-2606-17041:
Xie and colleagues benchmark language model agents on medical evidence synthesis in a 2026 paper. Meta-analysis pools results from many studies under a strict protocol: search the literature, apply eligibility rules, extract data, then aggregate. Automating it is tempting, but each stage can silently lose the right studies.

Their dataset, MetaSyn, packages hundreds of expert-curated meta-analyses from Nature Portfolio journals. Each question comes with structured eligibility criteria, the studies the original reviewers included, and a large PubMed corpus mixing eligible papers with plausible distractors. The stage-level results expose a striking gap. The best retriever finds most included studies, yet no end-to-end system keeps even fifty-three percent of them in its final report. The losses happen after retrieval: systems grab relevant-looking papers but fail to enforce the eligibility rules. Stage metrics make that failure visible instead of hiding it in one score.
arxiv-2606-17141:
Audard and the XRISM Collaboration map the chemical enrichment of the Perseus cluster core in a 2026 X-ray astronomy paper. The hot gas between galaxies is laced with iron and other elements forged by supernovae over billions of years. Older instruments reported a puzzling drop in iron at the very centre of some clusters.

The Resolve microcalorimeter aboard XRISM observed four pointings across the core. The team measures iron's spatial profile and its ratios against silicon, sulfur, argon, calcium, chromium, manganese and nickel. The central drop does not survive: the baseline analysis rules out a strong drop, contradicting earlier CCD measurements. The element ratios are remarkably uniform, arguing against late enrichment by the central galaxy's own supernovae. Comparing the composition with supernova yield models helps separate core-collapse from Type Ia contributions. A bright central active nucleus still limits precision in the innermost region.
arxiv-2606-17541:
Diaz presents a 2026 arXiv paper on evaluating AI agents by comparing whole trajectories, instead of stamping each run pass or fail at the end. Terminal success throws away partial progress and lumps very different attempts together as ties. Those ties are rampant: standard success metrics tie on roughly three quarters of instances across the benchmarks studied. That wastes data and blurs real differences between systems that users need to rank with confidence.

Preference-based evaluation compares two runs directly through their progress over time and their time-to-return profiles. Ties fall to roughly a third of instances under that scheme in the reported experiments. Ranking stability and data efficiency both improve, since fewer runs are needed to separate systems reliably. Diaz suggests some supposed benchmark saturation may be an artefact of the success measure itself, not of the tasks.
arxiv-2606-17641:
Jeon, Moon, and Kim present a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum-enhanced sensing and communication in one system, pairing an active reconfigurable surface with a Rydberg atomic receiver. Sixth-generation networks aim to transmit data and sense the environment on shared hardware, and Rydberg receivers promise extreme sensitivity by reading radio signals with excited atoms. Their response is magnitude-only and real-valued, which reshapes the maths of direction finding compared with ordinary radio receivers in the same joint sensing setup.

The authors derive a unified model and a closed-form accuracy bound for angle estimation under this receiver. They then jointly design the base station's beams and the surface's reflections to push that bound down under power and quality limits. An alternating method handles the hard non-convex design problem in parts. Simulations beat conventional radio-based designs and nearly match a radar-only benchmark.
arxiv-2606-18241:
Goncharov and colleagues build a single search that listens for both the hum and the loudest soloists of supermassive black hole pairs, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Pulsar timing arrays detect gravitational waves by watching for correlated delays in pulsar clocks. The signal mixes an unresolved background from countless binaries with a few bright pairs that might be resolved one by one, and past searches treated the two apart.

Their joint model describes background and brightest sources as one population, and proposes the characteristic source count as a statistic for proving the background's astrophysical origin. Bright sources sharpen that count. On simulated NANOGrav fifteen-year data, the method set direct limits on individual binaries. It found twenty-one of one hundred fourteen candidate pairs from galaxy observations in tension with the data, far more than the single candidate flagged by the original upper-limit analysis.
arxiv-2606-18341:
Radulea and colleagues follow a small compact object spiraling through the accretion disk of a supermassive black hole, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Such extreme mass-ratio inspirals cross the disk again and again, and each crossing steals energy and reshapes the orbit. The authors model the motion with exact Kerr geodesics for the relativistic orbit, adding disk effects through prescriptions for accretion and dynamical friction.

A clean pattern emerges in two stages. Disk dissipation first aligns the orbital plane with the disk, quickly, and only then damps the eccentricity on a slower clock, leaving a long phase of eccentric but coplanar motion. Comparing against a purely Keplerian treatment shows cumulative relativistic deviations even at wide separations where Newton should suffice, growing with every crossing. Two relativistic disk models, Sirko-Goodman and Novikov-Thorne, bracket how much the disk's own structure matters.
arxiv-2606-18441:
Liu and colleagues introduce a reinforcement learning method that teaches video language models to base their answers on the right frames, in a 2026 paper from Lanzhou University. Rewarding only the final answer tells a model little about which visual evidence should support it, so models can latch onto plausible but wrong moments.

Their method, Consensus Frame GRPO, first builds a consensus frame prior from cues inside the video itself: temporal coverage, scene transitions, and how relevant each frame looks to the question. It then scores how the model actually distributes its attention over frames and rewards agreement between that use and the prior, without needing human time annotations. The resulting system, VideoCFR, stayed competitive on general video benchmarks while improving several reasoning measures over baselines. Ablations credit each piece of the design, and the prior doubles as an interpretable record of which evidence training emphasized.
arxiv-2606-18541:
Adama and colleagues survey computing students about their cybersecurity knowledge, habits, and experiences, in a 2026 human-computer interaction paper. Students in computing ought to be among the best equipped young adults online, yet earlier work shows even the tech-savvy feel powerless over privacy and fall for phishing.

Their survey of more than two hundred computing students mixed open-ended thematic analysis with quantitative measures. Four tensions emerged. Students were knowledgeable yet held persistent incorrect beliefs about spotting deception, and they learned more about staying safe outside the classroom than inside it. Many had limited help available and had fallen victim to cybercrime, and the group split between confidence and concern about their safety. Cluster analysis found one cluster feeling less prepared and less confident but eager to learn more, while objective knowledge and self-efficacy tracked preparedness. The authors argue instruction must serve the eager and the disengaged.
arxiv-2606-18641:
Lee and the team construct the first supersymmetric quantum field theory built on a pseudo-Hermitian, not Hermitian, base, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. The spin-statistics theorem ties integer spin to commuting fields, and half-integer spin to anticommuting ones. Relaxing Hermiticity allows flipped statistics: scalar fields that anticommute, called symplectic fermions. Spin-half fields that commute are the other case. Supersymmetry pairs bosons with fermions, so it is a natural test of whether flipped theories can be consistent.

Their pseudo-Hermitian Wess-Zumino model pairs two symplectic fermions with a spin-half boson, written with superfields so the supersymmetry is manifest. A cubic interaction cannot be built from those odd superfields alone. So the authors couple the model to an ordinary Hermitian Wess-Zumino model, while keeping supersymmetry. This yields new interactions, including a quartic term for the symplectic fermions, opening a new path for supersymmetric model building.
arxiv-2606-18941:
Dantas and colleagues describe a 2026 formal verification tool for factory controller programs written as Ladder Diagrams. Many real programs are stored in a graphical PLCopen XML format that an earlier verifier read as empty, so it reported safety vacuously without checking any logic. The new ESBMC-GraphPLC resolver walks the connection graph from the power rail to each coil and rebuilds the missing rung logic for checking.

On three graphical programs exported from real editors, the tool now builds a full intermediate representation where the older version built none, and each program verifies as safe very quickly. Eleven older textual benchmarks still give identical results, showing no regressions. The authors also report two example programs honestly as limits, one with no ladder content and one whose timer meaning is not yet preserved. For engineers, graphical exports can now receive genuine, non-empty safety proofs.
arxiv-2606-19041:
Zucker and colleagues propose a new estimator for cumulative incidence in biobank studies in 2026. Biobanks recruit people over a period at varied ages, and some already have the disease of interest at entry. Those prevalent cases are often dropped or handled apart from cases arising in follow-up. Dropping them wastes data and can bias incidence estimates, especially for diseases that start young with long survival afterward.

The new estimator uses all cases, both prevalent and incident, whatever their later course. The authors prove its asymptotic properties and test it in simulations. It performs well against existing methods in those tests. An application to cancer data from the UK Biobank shows the practical edge over current approaches. Using every case in one coherent estimator gives biobank studies a fuller, more efficient picture of disease incidence in the population they sample.
arxiv-2606-19141:
Felbacq and colleagues give a geometric account of Bloch band topology from Cauchy data in 2026. In one-dimensional periodic media with inversion symmetry, topology was earlier read from poles and zeros of an impedance-like function tied to Bloch waves. That recipe reproduces the Berry-Zak invariant and flags topological interface states. What was missing was a clear geometric reason why poles and zeros carry that topological information.

The authors show poles and zeros arise from how inversion symmetry acts on the projectivized space of Cauchy data. Dirichlet and Neumann states are the two fixed points of the induced action on the Riemann sphere. Bloch vectors live naturally on the universal cover of the Brillouin circle. Band topology then reduces to a single monodromy sign. A lifted vector returns with a plus or minus sign after one turn, giving a trivial or Möbius line bundle.
arxiv-2606-19441:
Arseneau and colleagues present gravitational redshift measurements of an ultramassive white dwarf in 2026, pointing to an oxygen-neon core. The core mix of such dwarfs is an open question. Core carbon content decides their role as progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. Yet the photosphere shows only the outermost layer, so mass-radius data must carry the argument.

Spectra from two instruments give the dwarf's mass and radius through gravitational redshifts, plus photometry. The mass lands well above the Sun's at a tiny radius. Compared with state-of-the-art mass-radius relations, the data prefer an oxygen-neon core over a carbon-oxygen one, with modest odds. Such a dwarf is likely unable to produce a Type Ia supernova. The object also hints that dwarfs passing the Q-branch without a cooling delay tend to hold oxygen-neon cores, a clue to how the most massive white dwarfs form.
arxiv-2606-19641:
Luke Rowe and eight colleagues train self-driving policies by self-play from raw pixels in 2026. End-to-end driving models usually learn from human demonstration logs. Those logs cover few states and give no closed-loop feedback, so errors compound on the road.

The team introduce Gigapixel, a fast batched simulator with perspective rendering. It draws a simplified box world that keeps key scene structure. Throughput hits 50 thousand agent steps per second. Direct pixel self-play reinforcement learning would sample too slowly at this model scale. Instead, self-play DAgger distils a privileged reinforcement learning teacher into pixel policies on-policy. Light perception adaptation then bridges to real sensor data. Adapted policies rival rivals on HUGSIM and NAVSIM-v2 without human trajectory supervision. More self-play training yields proportional gains, marking self-play as a scalable training route.
arxiv-2606-19941:
Dat Do, Rushi Shah, Duc Le, and Dianbo Liu map where compositional structure emerges inside neural networks in 2026.
