Weiner, Kirschner and co-authors proposed in 2007 that crawling cells are organized by traveling waves of their own skeleton protein. Actin filaments push the cell's front edge outward, and many actin regulators were known. How they coordinate into shape and movement was not understood.

The team tracked the Scar/WAVE complex, a key actin assembly trigger, in human neutrophils, fast-moving immune cells. One of its parts, Hem-1, rode in propagating waves that sweep the leading edge. The complex switches actin assembly on, while built actin in turn strips the complex off the membrane. That two-way loop self-generates waves of new actin growth. Such waves show traits of real crawling, including flowing around barriers. Cell motility, they argue, is the collective product of many self-organizing waves.
europmc-pmc2013941:
Sporns, Honey and Kötter mapped hub regions in brain networks in 2007. Cortex regions link through fibre bundles forming a complex network. Hubs are highly connected nodes thought to coordinate information flow. The team analysed cortical networks of the cat and the macaque. They combined connection counts, local pattern measures and centrality, which marks nodes on many shortest paths.

That combined approach reliably identified hub regions in both species. Many hubs were already known as multisensory or multimodal areas, which combine several senses. Hubs split into provincial hubs inside a cluster and connector hubs between clusters. Removing each type from the network had opposite effects on its small-world index, a measure of efficient wiring. The results link a hub's network position to its likely functional role.
europmc-pmc2018741:
Peirce presented PsychoPy in 2007, a free software suite for psychophysics, the study of how people sense and respond to stimuli. Most vision studies present images on computer screens and record responses. Existing tools could be costly or hard to adapt. PsychoPy was written in the Python language using only free libraries. It runs across major operating systems.

Scripts are meant to be easy to read and write, while still allowing full custom control. The package handles stimulus presentation and response collection from many devices. It also fits psychometric functions, curves linking stimulus strength to responses. Users can add support for new stimuli or hardware and share changes back. That open design lets the whole research community improve the system.
europmc-pmc2082641:
Henderson and a large group of co-authors set out in 2007 to define therapeutic misconception in medical research. The term describes patients who join a trial yet fail to see that research differs from treatment. Informed consent depends on grasping that difference. The idea dates to 1982 interviews with psychiatric patients, but no consistent definition had emerged since, blocking measurement of the problem.

Scholars from medicine, law, philosophy and other fields met at the University of North Carolina in 2005. They debated the literature for a year and evaluated draft survey questions. The paper proposes a definition with specific dimensions. It also shows how each dimension can be turned into survey items. That gives researchers a valid scale to measure the misconception and test ways to reduce it.
europmc-pmc2125041:
Albert H. Ebeling of the Rockefeller Institute reported in 1913 on connective tissue living permanently outside the body. The cultures began under Dr. Carrel on January 17, 1912, as sixteen small fragments of heart and blood vessel from chick embryos. By March only five cultures survived; technique changes then made growth vigorous.

By May 1912 some twenty-five to thirty cultures, all descended from the few survivors, were growing actively. The pieces swelled so fast that dead areas opened in their centers. Ebeling took charge on June 1, washing the tissues in Ringer solution and moving them to fresh medium again and again. His day-by-day log follows single cultures through July, noting washes of two or three minutes and the slow return of wandering cells. Readers get immortality, laboratory style, kept alive by washing and feeding.
europmc-pmc2125941:
Cecil K. Drinker, Katherine R. Drinker, and Henry A. Kreutzmann opened a two-part study of why young red blood cells still carrying nuclei appear in the general blood flow. In this first part, published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1918, they tested whether faster blood flow through the bone marrow simply washes such cells loose.

Hard exercise speeding the circulation failed to dislodge nucleated red cells from the marrow in normal, anemic, or overgrown-marrow animals. Apparent rises after exercise in some anemic animals proved, on close checking, to be only a truer sampling of cells already in the blood. Cutting the vasomotor nerves to all four limbs widened the marrow vessels and raised flow, yet freed no nucleated cells either. Faster flow alone, their results say, is not the trigger.
europmc-pmc2126341:
Irvine McQuarrie and G. H. Whipple injected dogs with a toxic proteose taken from blocked small intestines. Their paper is the second in a renal function series for the Journal of Experimental Medicine, from 1919. Proteose is a partly digested protein product, and the blocked gut makes a poisonous form of it. They measured how well the kidneys cleared urea, salt, and a test dye.

The gut proteose clearly weakened the kidneys' clearing work, matching the damage seen in bowel blockage itself. The weakness showed even when fluid and test substances were injected straight into the blood in large amounts. Kidney cells seemed temporarily injured, since the main outside factors had been ruled out. Proteoses from other sources caused no such harm. Repair followed promptly once the poisoning faded. An organ's function, the authors stress, can fail deeply for a time with no visible lesion.
europmc-pmc2128241:
H. W. Graybill and Theobald Smith fed young turkeys the developed eggs of the cecal worm Heterakis papillosa to test the worm's role in fatal blackhead. Their feeding experiments appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. Groups of incubator-hatched turkeys and chickens received worm eggs, droppings from an infectious flock, both, or neither, in changing combinations.

Droppings alone, even kept for days and fed repeatedly, produced no infection in the first trials. Worm eggs changed the outcome completely. Turkeys fed developed eggs plus flock droppings caught blackhead, and so did the healthy controls once eggs were fed to them later. In the decisive trial, three turkeys given eggs alone all caught blackhead, three given eggs plus droppings all caught it, and three given droppings only stayed free. The egg of the worm, not the droppings themselves, carries the infection.
europmc-pmc2128441:
Warren H. Lewis, of the Carnegie Institution's embryology department at Johns Hopkins, watched embryonic chick heart cells change shape in culture. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. The wandering mesenchymal cells of the culture could be followed through every stage of their transformation into flat mesothelial cells.

The two cell kinds, Lewis concludes, differ only in form, not in inner structure. Mesothelium, the lining of the body's great cavities, is therefore not a separate tissue grown from its own stock. It is mesenchyme that has changed its shape. That finding bears on wound healing: new mesothelium over a scraped cavity lining may rise from the mesenchyme beneath by this same change of form. It need not spread in from the surviving lining at the wound's edges, as skin repair does.
europmc-pmc2128541:
E. V. Cowdry and F. M. Nicholson re-examined the brain and spinal cord of animals poisoned with botulinus toxin, testing older claims of central lesions. Their histological study appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924, from the Rockefeller Institute. New work in physiology had placed the toxin's action at the nerve terminals, not the centers, which cast suspicion on older microscopic reports.

Mice, guinea pigs, and rabbits were injected with carefully graded toxin doses, producing reactions lasting from one to nine days. When symptoms stood very pronounced, the animals were etherized and their tissues taken for microscopic study. Ample controls came from the authors' parallel work on encephalitis in the same species. The graded series let them set each claimed lesion against dose and duration. Their question runs through the paper: are the literature's central lesions real effects of the toxin, or do they belong to another reading?
europmc-pmc2140341:
Selig Hecht, at Creighton University in Omaha, examined the latent period in the clam Mya arenaria's answer to light in 1919. After a flash, Mya waits before reacting, and that waiting time changes with the flash. Hecht varied the exposure length and measured the latent period that followed, to learn what the waiting period is made of.

The latent period varies inversely with the length of exposure. Its speed, the reciprocal of the period, is a straight-line function of the exposure length. Since exposure length stands for the amount of light chemistry done, the substances formed then seem to catalyze a chemical reaction that sets the latent period's length. Together with his earlier work, Hecht builds a concrete picture of how Mya receives light.
europmc-pmc2140841:
John Northrop asked why living things are not digested by digestive enzymes, in a 1926 paper at The Rockefeller Institute. Dead organisms are digested fast by pepsin and trypsin, while living ones resist. The riddle is old, first raised about the stomach's own defense, then widened to all living matter and to the cell's resistance to its own enzymes.

Pepsin and trypsin are quickly taken out of solution by dead organisms. They are not able to penetrate into living organisms at all. Yet trypsin injected into a living amoeba kills and disintegrates the cell from inside. The barrier, the results say, is the living surface itself: shut the enzyme out, and the cell stands; let it in, and digestion follows.
europmc-pmc2361241:
Simmonds and colleagues reviewed surgery for colorectal cancer that had spread to the liver in 2006. Removing the liver deposits, called resection, might cure some patients, but doctors had no agreed rules for who should get the operation. No randomised trials existed to settle the question.

Of 529 studies found, only 30 met all their quality rules, and most were case series rather than trials. Death within 30 days of surgery was uncommon, with a median rate of 2.8% across studies, and the main serious problem was bile leaking with abscess near the liver. About 30% of patients were alive five years after surgery, and two-thirds of those survivors were free of disease. Such long survival is rare without surgery, the authors noted, but picking the right patients needs more work.
europmc-pmc2409341:
Marcus and colleagues showed in 2008 that one plant wall polymer can hide another from view. Plant cell walls mix several sugar polymers, and researchers map them with antibody probes that glow where a polymer sits. Xyloglucan is the main cross-linking polymer in the walls of many flowering plants, yet probes found it in only a few cell types.

The team raised a new antibody, LM15, tuned to a seven-sugar motif of xyloglucan, and checked it on sugar arrays. In tobacco and pea stems it lit up only scattered cells. Then they stripped out a second polymer, pectic homogalacturonan, a pectin component, with an enzyme. The xyloglucan signal suddenly appeared abundantly across the stems, in distinct patterns per cell type. The authors concluded pectin masks xyloglucan, so published wall maps may need rethinking.
europmc-pmc2475541:
Meletis and colleagues traced the hidden stem cells of the adult spinal cord in 2008. Spinal cord injury usually leaves permanent disability, yet the adult cord holds cells that can grow into nerve tissue in a dish. The team used genetic fate mapping, a labelling trick that marks one cell type and all its descendants permanently.

Nearly all the dish-growing stem cell power sat in ependymal cells, the cells lining the cord's central canal. After injury these cells switched on and multiplied. Most of their offspring became scar-forming glial cells, the support cells that wall off damage. A smaller share became oligodendrocytes, the cells that insulate nerve fibres. The authors proposed steering what ependymal offspring become after injury. That could offer a homegrown alternative to transplanting outside stem cells into patients.
europmc-pmc2515341:
Blais and co-authors tested in 2008 whether culture changes the way people look at faces. Eye-tracking studies since 1965 had suggested everyone scans a face in the same triangle pattern across eyes and mouth. The team recorded where Western Caucasian and East Asian observers looked while they learned and recognised faces of both races.

Western observers followed the classic pattern, scattering fixations over eyes and mouth of faces from both races. East Asian observers instead concentrated on the centre of the face, around the nose. The difference held across learning, recognition, and race-categorising tasks. The authors conclude that extracting information from faces is not a single universal routine, but a strategy shaped by culture.
europmc-pmc2577641:
McCoy and Tansey reviewed in 2008 the double-edged role of TNF, an inflammatory signal, in the brain. TNF rises at injury sites and in diseases from stroke to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, making it an tempting drug target. But TNF comes in two forms, soluble and membrane-bound, and works through two receptors with different preferences, so blanket blocking may do harm.

The review assembles animal and clinical evidence. The soluble form, acting through receptor TNFR1, drives much of the damage in neurodegeneration. The membrane form, favouring TNFR2, supports normal functions including synaptic scaling, the tuning of connection strength, and the birth of new neurons in the hippocampus. The authors argue future therapies should block TNFR1 signalling selectively while sparing TNFR2, rather than shutting TNF down entirely.
europmc-pmc2632741:
Burak and Fiete modelled in 2009 how grid cells in the rat brain could track position accurately enough for dead reckoning, estimating location from movement alone. Grid cells fire at positions forming a regular triangular lattice, and they were hypothesised to integrate velocity signals. Existing models accumulated errors so fast they needed constant sensory resets, casting doubt on the idea.

The authors show that continuous attractor models, where activity forms a stable pattern that shifts with movement, escape this problem. Fed only velocity and heading, both periodic and bounded networks produced regular grid responses and integrated accurately. They quantify how error grows with network size and noise. With realistic variability, the networks integrate over roughly 10 to 100 metres. They hold accuracy for 1 to 10 minutes. The work sets upper bounds on accuracy and proposes discriminating experiments.
europmc-pmc2680341:
Church and colleagues, with the Mouse Genome Sequencing Consortium, reported in 2009 a finished assembly of the mouse genome and what it reveals about rodent-only biology. The mouse is the main stand-in for humans in medical research, so telling shared inheritance from mouse invention matters. The new build was assembled piece by piece from cloned chunks, the most careful kind.

The finished genome exposed a burst of recent copying in mouse DNA. Whole stretches had been duplicated lately in rodent history, expanding certain gene families. The new copies mostly code for proteins of reproduction, matching the fast evolution of breeding traits. Genes that stayed single and barely changed since the common ancestor with humans are the likeliest to have kept their old jobs, the authors argue. Those are also the safest models for human biology.
europmc-pmc2832341:
Matos, Trufelli, de Matos, and da Silva Pinhal reviewed immunohistochemistry in 2010. This lab method uses antibodies to hunt set targets in tissue slices, from single proteins to whole germ types. The method lets pathologists settle diagnoses that standard pink-and-blue staining cannot separate, and it guides prognosis and research as well.

The review walks through both halves of the craft: preparing slides, from fixing tissue through the reaction steps, and then reading and scoring the staining that results. It covers the method's history since the early nineteen forties, its strengths, and its pitfalls in interpretation. The authors close by urging pathologists and clinicians to share one language for results, so patients gain the full benefit.
europmc-pmc2877741:
Hersperger and colleagues reported in 2010 that a rare group of HIV patients who control the virus without drugs have killer T cells that arm themselves unusually fast. These elite controllers keep virus levels near zero for years. The team compared their HIV-specific CD8 T cells, the immune cells that kill infected cells, with cells from patients at other disease stages.

After brief contact with HIV protein pieces, elite controllers' cells rapidly raised perforin, the protein that punches holes in infected cells so they can be destroyed. Cells from patients with high virus levels did this weakly. Other functions, like making several signals at once, did not separate the groups as cleanly. Fast perforin loading looks like a direct weapon behind elite control.
europmc-pmc2913941:
Brancati, Dallapiccola, and Valente reviewed in 2010 Joubert syndrome and its related disorders, a family of congenital conditions united by one brain malformation. On scans the malformed midbrain and hindbrain form a shape called the molar tooth sign, the group's defining hallmark. Incidence is estimated near one in eighty to one hundred thousand births, likely an undercount.

Affected children show low muscle tone, unsteady movement, developmental delay, abnormal eye movements, and disturbed breathing as newborns. Many families add eye, kidney, liver, or extra-finger involvement, sorted into six subgroups. Ten causative genes were known by writing, and every one builds parts of the primary cilium, the cell's antenna, placing the group among the ciliopathies. Inheritance is almost always recessive, so recurrence risk shapes counseling.
europmc-pmc2939541:
Romero-Ortuno and co-authors built a frailty screening tool for older Europeans in a 2010 study based on a large survey of health and ageing. Family doctors need a quick way to spot patients at risk, and no simple measure fitted that setting.

Drawing on thousands of respondents aged fifty and over from twelve countries, they combined five survey items echoing a standard frailty definition. Statistical modelling sorted people into non-frail, pre-frail, and frail classes for each sex. The classes differed across many health and social measures and predicted death risk by the follow-up wave. Two web calculators were released.
europmc-pmc2940741:
Saeed and colleagues studied how Ebola virus gets inside cells in a 2010 laboratory study using live virus and look-alike particles. No vaccine or specific treatment existed then, so the entry step looked like a promising drug target.

In two cell lines, uptake did not depend on the usual clathrin or caveolae routes. Instead the virus triggered gulping of surrounding fluid, a process resembling macropinocytosis, along with local reshaping of the cell skeleton. Blocking key regulators of that gulping, or adding a drug that hinders it, cut entry sharply. The virus then travelled through early and late sorting compartments.
europmc-pmc2970541:
Lyko and co-authors compared DNA methylation, a chemical marking system, in the brains of honey bee queens and workers in a 2010 study. Queens and workers share the same genome yet differ hugely in body, fertility, and behaviour, a split set by larval diet.

Genome-wide maps of the marks in brain tissue showed differing patterns between the castes. The contrast supports the idea that food-triggered marking helps lock in two very different life paths from identical DNA. Because brain marks were the focus, the work also speaks to how environment shapes behaviour through molecular settings in social insects.
europmc-pmc3022541:
Chaitanya, Steven, and Babu reviewed in 2010 how one repair protein breaks apart when brain and nerve cells die. The protein, called PARP-1 in short, normally helps fix damaged DNA after cell stress. When injury is severe, cutting enzymes slice it into pieces of distinct sizes. Each cutting enzyme leaves its own characteristic set of pieces behind.

Those pieces work like fingerprints for the kind of cell death under way. The review sorts which enzymes, including caspases, calpains, and others, cut the protein during stroke, trauma, and slow nerve loss. It also covers what some pieces do after they are cut, and how they bind other proteins. Reading the fingerprints could help doctors tell death pathways apart in damaged tissue.
europmc-pmc3046141:
McGowan and coauthors reported in 2011 that a mother's care in a rat's first week of life leaves marks across a broad stretch of the brain genome. The marks reach far beyond any single gene. Earlier work had tied high licking and grooming care to chemical marks on a single stress gene in the hippocampus. The team scanned a long chromosome region holding that gene, measuring marks, gene activity, and a second chemical tag together.

Adult offspring of high care mothers showed coordinated mark changes over a wide span, with many genes in the region more active. Some genes stayed unchanged, so the response was patterned rather than blanket. A gene family involved in wiring synapses responded most strongly of all. Because cross fostering flips the pattern, the marks reflect care received, not inheritance. The study reframes early care as a genome wide programming event in the brain.
europmc-pmc3052441:
Palafox-Carlos, Ayala-Zavala, and González-Aguilar reviewed in 2011 how dietary fiber changes the fate of antioxidants eaten in fruits and vegetables. Antioxidants may help prevent degenerative disease, but the richest source in food is not always the one that delivers the most to body tissues. Fiber, the indigestible wall material of plants, travels with antioxidants through the gut and can hold onto them.

How much of an antioxidant is freed during digestion, and then absorbed, depends on the food's structure and on chemical links with fiber and other food parts. The review gathers evidence on those interactions and how they play out along the digestive tract. Fiber can delay or reduce release for some compounds while aiding others later in the gut. The authors argue that health advice and food design should count the fiber context, not just the antioxidant totals on a label.
europmc-pmc3070641:
Herberts, Kwa, and Hermsen assessed in 2011 the risks that must be weighed before stem cell therapies reach patients. Stem cells promise treatments for worn out tissues and diseases with few options, and lab made pluripotent cells have raised hopes further. The authors argue that a product's risk depends on many features at once, from cell type and growth rate to delivery route and whether the treatment can be undone.

Known and possible harms include tumors, unwanted immune reactions, and infections carried by the cell product. Cells that renew without limit carry the highest tumor concern, and no patient had yet received them when this was written. Trials with adult connective tissue stem cells have mostly been reassuring, though serious events have occurred. The authors call for risk checks built into development from the start, not added after promising headlines.
europmc-pmc3114741:
Marcus Lechner and colleagues presented a computer program for finding matching genes across species in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Matching genes inherited from a shared ancestor help researchers compare genomes and guess gene function. With genome counts rising fast, older tools needed too much memory for the job.

Their program refines a best-match search method and spreads work across the cores of ordinary computers, cutting memory needs sharply. Tested on more than seven hundred bacterial genomes, it found a small set of proteins present in nearly every one of them. Because it runs on standard hardware, labs can compute fresh matches for their own data instead of waiting for database updates.
europmc-pmc3197541:
Rebecca Wong reviewed programmed cell death in cancer, from its failure to its exploitation, in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research. Healthy cells self-destruct on cue; cancer is in part what happens when cells that should die refuse. The death machinery is intricate, with many pathways and checkpoints where faults can arise.

Defects at any step can help transform a cell, seed spread, or blunt chemotherapy, and a silenced guardian gene is one notorious example found across human cancers. Yet the same machinery is the target of many modern treatments designed to push cancer cells back over the edge. Wong surveys the mechanisms, the carcinogenic faults, and the promise and safety hurdles of death-restoring drugs.
europmc-pmc3221041:
Hélène Botella and colleagues uncovered a zinc arms race between tuberculosis bacteria and human immune cells in this 2011 study in Cell Host and Microbe. Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages, the very cells meant to kill it. Gene-activity surveys of both partners during infection showed a striking pattern of metal-related genes switching on.

Macrophages flooded the bacterial compartment with free zinc within hours of infection, apparently trying to poison the invader. The bacteria answered by switching on pump genes, especially one called ctpC, that expel heavy metals. Mutants lacking that pump kept zinc trapped inside their cells and grew poorly within macrophages. The authors propose that metal poisoning and resistance form another front in the long fight between host and microbe.
europmc-pmc3221341:
Wendy Brouwer and colleagues reviewed why people stop using online healthy-lifestyle programs, in this 2011 systematic review. Internet interventions can tailor feedback and goals to each user, yet their real reach is low and dropout is high. The team asked which design features are linked to greater exposure, meaning how long and how often people actually engage.

They gathered sixty-four studies that measured exposure objectively, through log-ins, visit length, or completion. Programs used a wide mix of techniques, with feedback, interactive elements, and email or phone contact the most common. Only a few features showed consistent links to better exposure: peer or counselor support lengthened visits, while personal contact and website updates brought more log-ins. The authors note that inconsistent exposure measures blocked firmer conclusions.
europmc-pmc3229841:
Marc Ghany and colleagues wrote this 2011 practice guideline on treating genotype 1 chronic hepatitis C, issued by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatitis C genotype 1 was the commonest and hardest-to-treat form of the virus in the United States. The guideline updates recommendations for clinicians managing these patients.

The document was formally approved by the association and endorsed by infectious-disease, gastroenterology, and viral-hepatitis organizations. Its advice rests on a formal review of the world literature published up to June 2011. They also rest on established manuals for judging health practices and writing guidelines. The authors' clinical experience plays a part as well. It offers a data-supported approach meant to make care uniform, at a moment when treatment for this infection was changing quickly.
europmc-pmc3257741:
Marco Vinolo and colleagues reviewed how short-chain fatty acids regulate inflammation in this 2011 article in Nutrients. These fatty acids, mainly acetate, propionate, and butyrate, are the chief products when gut bacteria ferment fiber. Beyond feeding the gut lining, they influence water and electrolyte absorption and, increasingly clearly, the immune system.

The fatty acids act on immune and blood vessel cells in two ways. They switch on dedicated receptors on the cell surface. They also block enzymes that remove chemical tags from histones. Through these routes they shape the signals immune cells release, their ability to migrate to inflamed sites, and their capacity to destroy pathogens. The review gathers the newest findings on isolated cells and on recruitment and activation, and highlights treatment possibilities for inflammatory diseases.
europmc-pmc3271041:
Jorja Warren and colleagues validated a blood test for colorectal cancer based on a methylated DNA marker, in this 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. About half of Americans in the screening age range skip recommended screening, leaving tens of millions untested. A simple blood draw could bring many of them in, catching cancers earlier.

The test looks for methylated Septin 9 DNA in plasma. In samples from cancer patients, healthy controls, and colonoscopy patients, the improved assay caught ninety percent of colorectal cancers while correctly clearing eighty-eight percent of people without the disease. It worked for early-stage cancers and for tumors anywhere in the colon, including hard-to-reach regions. False positives ran at about twelve percent. It also detected a small share of precancerous adenomas. The authors propose offering it to average-risk adults unwilling or unable to have a colonoscopy.
europmc-pmc3312841:
Akbarzadeh, Samiei, and Davaran reviewed tiny magnetic particles and their growing role in medicine, in a 2012 article. These particles, far smaller than a cell, can be guided by magnets outside the body and made visible on scans. The review stresses that good medical uses start with well controlled recipes for making particles that match in size and crystal quality.

Sections cover how the particles are made, how their surfaces are coated so they can carry drugs or attach to chosen targets, and how labs check their properties. The authors also explain the physics of how such small magnets behave, which differs from bulk magnets. Together the pieces frame a toolkit for imaging, drug delivery, and other biomedical tasks.
europmc-pmc3334941:
Tewarie and colleagues built agreed quality rules for eye scans used in multiple sclerosis research, reporting in 2012. The scans, called OCT, measure thinning of the nerve layer at the back of the eye, a window on nerve degeneration in MS. For such scans to serve as trial outcomes across many hospitals, readers must judge scan quality the same way.

Starting from older eye literature rules, three readers agreed only moderately on a training set of scans. Disagreements were dissected, and a new checklist was written around seven checks covering obvious flaws, signal strength, centering, software errors, other eye disease, lighting, and beam placement. Its name, OSCAR-IB, strings the seven initials together. Agreement jumped to a solid level on the training set and held on a fresh set of scans. The authors recommend the checklist for multicenter studies and trials.
europmc-pmc3348041:
Muehlenkamp, Claes, Havertape, and Plener reviewed how common self injury is among teenagers worldwide, in a 2012 article. Two related behaviors are tracked: self injury without suicidal intent, and the broader category of deliberate self harm, which includes acts with any intent. Claims that rates are climbing had outrun solid evidence, and studies used clashing definitions that made countries hard to compare.

Gathering fifty two studies published between 2005 and 2011, the team found the two behaviors reported at similar average rates, around one in six adolescents. Studies that asked a single yes or no question found lower rates than those using detailed behavior checklists. Average rates had not risen over the previous five years, suggesting a plateau rather than an epidemic curve. The authors urge the field to adopt one shared way of asking, so future comparisons mean something.
europmc-pmc3364341:
Yu and co-authors built a large-scale computational system for predicting which drugs interact with which protein targets. Reliable prediction would speed drug discovery, but interactions are many-to-many: one drug can hit several targets, and similar drugs can share targets. The team integrated chemical, genomic, and pharmacological data to feed two machine learning methods.

Models built with random forests and support vector machines agreed closely in testing, reaching specificity above ninety percent across internal and external validations. The authors then applied the validated models across enzymes, ion channels, G-protein-coupled receptors, and nuclear receptors. They mapped the predictions onto disease associations and target networks for follow-up research.
europmc-pmc3372341:
Tellier argued in 2006 that flu spreads through the air in fine aerosols far more than planners admitted. Many guidelines treated large droplets as the main route, so protection against tiny airborne particles was often skipped. Canadian and United States pandemic plans then advised surgical masks, not tight respirators, for routine care.

Reviewing decades of published findings, Tellier found the evidence for aerosol spread extensive and consistent. Reference books by leading experts already described aerosols as a key route. Given the high death rates of bird flu strain H5N1, he urged stronger protection for health workers, including N95 respirators. The paper pressed pandemic planning to take airborne spread seriously.
europmc-pmc3373041:
Ooi, Goh, and Gubler reviewed thirty-five years of dengue control in Singapore in 2006. Dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, and its four virus types mean a person can be infected up to four times. With no vaccine near approval, cutting mosquito numbers was the only prevention available.

Singapore's program, the review argues, worked because it rested on disease and mosquito data rather than habit. Earlier campaigns elsewhere, run as strict top-down drives, succeeded briefly but could not be sustained. The authors trace how Singapore sustained its effort after those earlier drives faded. Their account offers a working model for cities facing dengue's worldwide return.
europmc-pmc3383741:
Cohen and a large team followed African couples in 2012 to test whether bacterial vaginosis raises a woman's chance of passing HIV-1 to her male partner. The condition, where normal vaginal flora is replaced by other bacteria, was already linked to women catching HIV more easily. Nobody had measured the onward risk to partners.

The cohort covered more than two thousand couples in which the woman had HIV-1 and the man did not. Women with bacterial vaginosis passed the virus to partners at a markedly higher rate, with risk more than three times that of women with normal flora. The finding adds partner protection to the reasons for treating the condition. It also points prevention work toward vaginal health.
europmc-pmc3414841:
Nik-Zainal led a team that catalogued every mutation in twenty-one breast cancers in 2012 to read the processes that scarred their genomes. All cancers carry acquired mutations, and their patterns record the damage and repair failures the cells lived through. Math methods pulled apart the overlapping patterns into separate signatures.

Several distinct signatures appeared, some single-letter and some double. Cancers with broken BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes showed a characteristic mix plus a telltale pattern of deletions. The team also found kataegis, storms of local hypermutation clustered near genome rearrangements. A family of enzymes that edit DNA letters is proposed as one culprit. Most signatures still lack an explanation, marking work ahead.
europmc-pmc3418241:
Onomoto and a large team identified in 2012 the cellular meeting place where virus alarms are raised. Sensors such as RIG-I detect viral RNA inside cells and trigger interferon, the body's antiviral messenger. How the sensor actually meets viral RNA was unclear. Using a new antibody, the team watched where RIG-I gathers during infection.

It collects in granules packed with viral RNA, stress-granule markers, and other antiviral proteins, which the team named antiviral stress granules. A flu virus stripped of its alarm-blocking protein formed many granules and much interferon; the intact virus formed few. Blocking granule formation cut interferon and let viruses multiply faster. The granule, they conclude, is where foreign RNA is sensed.
europmc-pmc3461341:
Lutz and Quinn proposed in 2012 that shifting cytokine levels form a common thread tying together muscle loss, obesity, and immune aging. Aging brings frailty: muscle mass, strength, and stamina decline while belly fat grows, and the immune system weakens, raising cancer and death risk. One signal, interleukin-15, is made richly by muscle and fades with age in animal models.

That signal blocks fat deposition and insulin resistance, feeds muscle in some settings, and is required to build and keep natural killer cells, the immune patrol in question. As fat-derived inflammatory signals rise and interleukin-15 falls, all three declines advance together. The review follows the fat and muscle signals that act on killer cells and argues the shared chemistry is a target worth testing.
europmc-pmc3498741:
Crabs and their kin do far more with their gills than breathe, and Raymond P. Henry, Cedomil Lucu, Horst Onken, and Dirk Weihrauch review that organ's many jobs in 2012. Their survey runs from ecology and physiology down to the molecules that move ions across gill tissue.

Ion transport in the gill underlies salt and water balance in the blood, acid-base regulation, and ammonia excretion. The same surface is where toxic metals enter aquatic crustaceans, making the gill central to their toxicology. Cadmium, zinc, and lead slip in through calcium channels, while copper and silver compete with sodium uptake. The review gathers a century of work into one reference.
europmc-pmc3526541:
Meat demand keeps climbing, and Dennis G. A. B. Oonincx, Imke J. M. de Boer, and Gregory A. Sword test mealworms as a lighter protein in 2012. Their life cycle assessment measures greenhouse gas output, energy use, and land use for producing mealworm protein and compares it with milk, chicken, pork, and beef.

Per kilogram of edible protein, conventional sources emit more greenhouse gases than mealworms. Energy needs are similar across sources. Land tells the starkest story: mealworms need far less. Mealworms make no methane and convert feed efficiently, two of the reasons livestock footprints run high. The authors conclude mealworms deserve consideration as a more sustainable animal protein.
europmc-pmc3571641:
Matthias Wacker and Michael Holick reviewed vitamin D and supplementation in Nutrients in 2013. Vitamin D, made in skin under sunlight, keeps bones sound by helping the gut absorb calcium. Lack of it is now classed as worldwide in scale. Studies tie low levels to autoimmune disease, some cancers, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and infections, though how much is cause and how much is shadow stays debated.

Sun exposure remains the main source for most people, a fact the authors say is underappreciated. Open questions run through the review: what blood level of the storage form, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, counts as enough for bone and for wider health, and how large a supplement dose should be. The paper gathers the claims organ by organ and marks where agreement ends, giving readers the state of a fast-growing, unsettled field.
europmc-pmc3596041:
Philipp Gütlich, Ana Gaspar, and Yann Garcia reviewed iron compounds that flip their magnetic state in the Beilstein Journal of Organic Chemistry in 2013. Certain iron(II) compounds switch between a low-spin and high-spin form when heated, squeezed, or lit, a phenomenon called spin crossover. The two states differ in magnetism and color, which makes them readable, and the effect has been known for over eighty years while drawing intense recent interest.

Early chapters explain the ligand field ideas behind the switch and the chemical conditions a compound must meet to show it. Then come the ripples a flip sends through a molecule and the toolkit used to measure them, with separate treatment of light-triggered switching and of pressure. The main survey ranges over single molecules, chains, sheets, and cage-like assemblies, weighing how structure bends the switching behavior. Sensor and display uses close the case.
europmc-pmc3654441:
Flu protein change is fenced in by the need to stay folded, Gong, Suchard and Bloom show in a 2013 eLife study. Protein change is often likened to turning one word into another, one letter at a time. The team built every step on a 39-change path taken by a flu protein, and also put each change alone into the starting protein, to see which steps block others.

Several changes harmed the starting protein yet had fixed during real flu history with no ill effect. Those blocking changes loosened the protein's fold. In each case, a steadying change had come first or alongside and cushioned the harm. The blocked spots cluster where human immune cells read the virus, hinting the detours aid escape from immunity. Steadying changes open doors harmful ones cannot pass.
europmc-pmc3655441:
Vaccine helpers work by waking the body's first defences, Awate, Babiuk and Mutwiri review in a 2013 Frontiers in Immunology article. The helpers, called adjuvants in the text, are added to many vaccines, yet how they act was long murky. A decade of work had begun to clear the fog when this review took stock. It sorts the routes by which helpers lift a vaccine's effect.

Helpers may act through a mix of routes: holding the vaccine at the shot site, calling in signal chemicals, and drawing immune cells to the spot. They can boost how well target proteins are taken up and shown to defence cells, and speed their trip to lymph nodes. By firing inborn defences, helpers shape the size and kind of the learned response. Knowing the routes guides safer vaccine design.
europmc-pmc3705341:
Abdel-Aal and colleagues review lutein and zeaxanthin, two plant pigments that concentrate in the human retina, and the foods that supply them. These carotenoids form the yellow spot pigment of the macula. There they filter damaging blue light and mop up reactive oxygen. They also sharpen vision.

They have also been linked with lower risk of age-related macular degeneration and cataracts, the two major age-related eye diseases the review targets. The authors list the richest dietary sources, discuss intake levels and how well the body absorbs these pigments, and describe newly developed lutein-enriched foods aimed at older people, whose need is greatest.
europmc-pmc3722041:
Dominik Péus, Nicolas Newcomb, and Silvia Hofer published a review and proposal in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making in 2013 on the Karnofsky Performance Status. That scale, in use for over 60 years, rates how well a patient can carry out daily life, from 100 percent for no symptoms down to 0 for death. It is widely used to judge patients and to predict outcomes.

The review covers work on how reliable and valid the scale is, what it truly measures, and how it relates to quality of life and survival. The authors then propose a simple algorithm that settles a patient's score with just two or three questions. Their aim is to keep the scale accurate and quick to use in modern care, true to its creator's intent.
europmc-pmc3829941:
Mário Henrique M. Barros, Franziska Hauck, Johannes H. Dreyer, Bettina Kempkes, and Gerald Niedobitek test a tissue staining method in PLoS One in 2013. Macrophages, large immune cells in tissue, come in two broad states. One state drives attack responses, the other aids repair. Telling them apart inside tissue slices has been hard.

The team pair standard macrophage stains with stains for switch proteins that set each state. They try the method on diseases known to lean toward attack or repair responses. The repair marker cells often outnumbered the general marker cells. Some repair-marked cells also bore attack switch proteins, which blurs the neat two-state story. Counts of attack-type cells still ran higher in attack-leaning diseases. The method gives path labs a workable way to read cell states in place.
europmc-pmc3830741:
Tania F. Gendron leads a large team in a brain disease study in Acta Neuropathologica in 2013. A stretched repeat in the C9ORF72 gene is the top known gene cause of frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The gene is read in both directions, and the team study the less-known reverse read.

Reverse RNA copies formed clumps inside cell nuclei in lab tests, just as forward copies do. The reverse copies were also turned into odd proteins by a rogue process that skips the usual start signal. New antibodies let the team spot those proteins. Patient tissue showed the same clumps and proteins, proving the reverse path acts in real disease. Both read directions may thus feed the harm, a point drug plans must weigh.
europmc-pmc3898141:
Peter D. Stenson, Matthew Mort, Edward V. Ball, Katy Shaw, Andrew D. Phillips, and David N. Cooper describe a mutation database in Human Genetics, with the record dated 2014. The Human Gene Mutation Database gathers inherited gene faults that cause or track with human disease. It began as a tool to study how mutations arise.

By mid 2013 it held well over a hundred thousand distinct faults across thousands of genes, growing by more than ten thousand a year. Users span clinic geneticists, genome scientists, counselors, and drug firms. A free public version serves academic users, while a fuller licensed version serves wider users. The paper sums the store's scope and its role in diagnosis, testing, and personal genomic medicine.
europmc-pmc3906841:
H. J. Lambers Heerspink, D. de Zeeuw, L. Wie, B. Leslie, and J. List report a randomized trial in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism in 2013. Their question was whether dapagliflozin, a drug that makes the kidneys release more glucose, also acts like a diuretic in people with type 2 diabetes. They compared it with hydrochlorothiazide, a standard water pill, and with placebo.

Seventy-five adults took part for twelve weeks, and blood pressure, weight, plasma volume, and kidney filtration were tracked. Dapagliflozin lowered blood pressure modestly, reduced weight, and cut the filtration rate more than placebo, while plasma volume seemed to fall in a smaller sub-study. The authors read these results as signs that the drug has diuretic-like effects on top of its glucose control.
europmc-pmc3946041:
Jane P. Messina and colleagues map seventy years of dengue's global spread in Trends in Microbiology in 2014. Dengue comes in four distinct virus types, and catching one protects only against that type, leaving people open to the others. Where types circulate together, severe disease becomes more likely, yet the geography of each type had never been charted in full.

Drawing on records from 1943 to 2013, the team plotted where each type has been detected and where they overlap. Detection of all four types has expanded worldwide, and places hosting several types at once, so-called hyperendemic areas, have grown. The map also exposes blind spots: large parts of the world still lack type-specific information, which the authors flag as the key gap for tracking dengue's next moves.
europmc-pmc3964941:
Jun-Hao Li, Shun Liu, Hui Zhou, Liang-Hu Qu, and Jian-Hua Yang present starBase version 2.0 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014, a database for decoding how RNAs regulate each other. MicroRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, pseudogenes, and circular RNAs all interact, and some RNAs compete for the same microRNAs, yet the networks among them were poorly mapped. The team mined experiments that freeze RNA-binding proteins onto their targets, 108 datasets from 37 studies.

From millions of binding sites they catalogued about 285,000 protein-RNA relationships, some 16,000 microRNA-pseudogene pairs, and about 9,000 microRNA-circular RNA pairs, plus the most complete experimentally backed microRNA target networks then available. Roughly 10,000 competing-endogenous-RNA pairs were identified. Two companion web tools predict the functions of microRNAs and of other non-coding RNAs from these networks.
europmc-pmc3968141:
Melanie Meersch and colleagues test a urine test for early warning of kidney injury after heart surgery, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Acute kidney injury is common after operations using a heart-lung machine, but the standard blood marker, creatinine, rises only one to three days later, too late for prevention. The test measures two proteins, TIMP-2 and IGFBP7, that pause cell division, an early stress response in injured kidney cells. Fifty high-risk patients gave serial urine samples.

Twenty-six patients developed kidney injury. The urine marker multiplied rose within four hours of surgery in those patients, and its peak in the first day predicted injury with good accuracy, 92 percent sensitivity at the chosen cutoff. Falling marker values were the strongest sign the kidney would recover. The authors present the pair as an early alarm and recovery gauge.
europmc-pmc4022341:
Jelena Savović and six co-authors report an evaluation of the Cochrane risk of bias tool, in Systematic Reviews in 2014. The tool, launched in 2008, grades clinical trials in Cochrane reviews by features known to bend results. It replaced vaguer quality scores with structured judgements backed by quotes from each trial report.

The team gathered views through focus groups and an online survey that drew close to four hundred replies. Most users called the tool an advance on past practice and liked the standard form and the quote support. Grading one study took between ten minutes and an hour, which most found fair. A third disliked the extra work and found the grade labels confusing. The hardest areas to judge were missing outcome data and selective reporting. Users also wanted more help on folding grades into pooled results and conclusions. Fixes followed from the review.
europmc-pmc4033041:
David Berry and Stefanie Widder test whether maps of microbe co-occurrence can reveal true interactions, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014. Surveys often list which microbes turn up together, and such patterns are used to guess who helps or hinders whom. The method had rarely been checked against known answers.

The pair built fake microbe communities on a computer with set interaction rules, then sampled them like a real survey. Network maps rebuilt from the samples matched the true interactions only in some settings. When shared habitat taste drove co-occurrence, the maps lost their meaning. Around hub species with many partners, false links clustered thickly. The team also found shape traits in the maps that flag keystone species, the few members a community leans on. Their rules of thumb aim to keep field researchers from over-reading such maps.
europmc-pmc4058041:
Christine Mehner, Alexandra Hockla, Erin Miller, Sophia Ran, Derek C. Radisky, and Evette S. Radisky studied an enzyme called MMP-9 in a hard-to-treat form of breast cancer. Their work appeared in Oncotarget in 2014. They focused on basal-like triple negative tumors, which lack the targets used by many current drugs.

Unlike many related enzymes made by nearby support cells, MMP-9 here comes from the tumor cells themselves. Silencing it in human cancer cells reduced invasion in lab dishes and lung spread in a mouse model. MMP-9 also helped tumors grow blood vessels, though it had only a modest effect on primary tumor growth. The authors suggest blocking MMP-9 could offer a route against spread in this poor-outlook cancer type.
europmc-pmc4210641:
Timotheus Y. F. Halim, Fumio Takei, and six co-authors found a missing link in allergy in Immunity in 2014. Allergens push helper T cells toward the Th2 type, which drives allergic inflammation, but what starts that push was unclear. A newer cell type, group 2 innate lymphoid cells, reacts fast to tissue alarm signals.

Giving mice the allergen papain through the nose switched on these innate cells and then Th2 cells, causing lung inflammation and raised IgE. Mice lacking the innate cells mounted only a feeble response. The interleukin-13 those cells released proved essential, because it sent lung dendritic cells to the lymph node to train naive T cells. Interleukin-4, long assumed central, was not needed. The chain depended on the alarm signal interleukin-33.
europmc-pmc4263141:
Amy H. Buck, Simon A. Babayan, and ten co-authors found parasitic worms posting RNA into host cells in Nature Communications in 2014. Gut nematodes live for years inside mammals despite immune attack, so they must damp that attack somehow. Exosomes, tiny sacs that ferry RNA between mammal cells, suggested a route.

The mouse worm Heligmosomoides polygyrus secretes exosomes loaded with microRNAs, Y RNAs, and its own Argonaute protein. Given to mice, the sacs blunted the type 2 immune response and the eosinophil rise caused by an allergen. In mouse cells they turned down the genes Il33r and Dusp1, and worm microRNAs alone could repress Dusp1. A second worm's microRNAs turned up in the blood of infected mice, so the trick seems shared among parasitic nematodes.
europmc-pmc4270441:
Charles F. Cadieu and a team of co-authors compare deep neural networks with the primate brain on object recognition. Their study appeared in PLoS Computational Biology in 2014. Both brains and the newest networks can name objects in a flash, even when the view changes, and the team asked whether the networks match the brain's inner picture of objects.

They built a fair test that corrects for noise and sample limits on both sides. The best networks matched the pattern of responses in the brain's inferior temporal cortex far better than older models. The result makes these networks useful test beds for ideas about how vision works in the brain.
europmc-pmc4284641:
Ravishankar Sundararaman, Prineha Narang, Adam S. Jermyn, William A. Goddard III, and Harry A. Atwater compute what happens when light driven waves on metal surfaces decay into hot charge carriers. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2014. These hot electrons and holes are prized for solar energy conversion, chemical catalysis, and light detectors, but their starting energies in real metals had not been mapped in detail.

Using a model that joins the light waves with the metal's full electronic structure, the team predicts the energy spread of fresh carriers in gold, copper, silver, and aluminium. Gold and copper give hotter holes than electrons, while silver and aluminium share energy more evenly. The predictions guide the choice of metal for devices that harvest these carriers.
europmc-pmc4293641:
Neslihan Koyuncuoğlu Güngör reviews overweight and obesity in children and teenagers as a world health problem. The review appeared in the Journal of Clinical Research in Pediatric Endocrinology in 2014, and Güngör writes as sole author. Rates of childhood obesity rose sharply over three decades, and diseases once seen in adults now appear in the young.

Excess weight in childhood touches nearly every organ system. The review covers high blood pressure, blood fat problems, insulin resistance, fatty liver, and the social and mental strain that can follow, plus the added health care costs. Drug options for the young are limited, so the author stresses early detection and treatment built on sustained weight control.
europmc-pmc4310041:
Jean-Charles Preiser and eleven co-authors review how to feed patients in intensive care, marking where expert agreement holds and where it breaks down. Their review appeared in Critical Care in 2015. Large new trials had just shaken older feeding practice, prompting a fresh look at energy and protein targets for the critically ill.

Topics covered include how many calories and how much protein to give. They also include the dangers of refeeding after starvation and stomach volume checks. Adding intravenous feeding when tube feeding falls short is covered too, as is measuring energy use at the bedside. The authors also weigh special nutrient additives with drug like claims. Each section ends with the open questions that trials still need to answer.
europmc-pmc4344741:
Fabio Silvio Taccone and eleven co-authors chart invasive aspergillosis, a fungal infection, in intensive care units across eight countries. Their study appeared in Critical Care in 2015. The infection classically strikes people with weak immune systems, but reports in general ICU patients were rising with little hard data on presentation or outcome.

Thirty ICUs enrolled every patient with a positive Aspergillus culture. Of more than five hundred patients, about half were merely colonized, while the rest had probable or proven invasive disease, almost always in the lung. Proven cases died at far higher rates than colonized patients. The study gives ICUs a realistic picture of how often the fungus is a passenger and how often a killer.
europmc-pmc4384041:
The UniProt Consortium reported on its protein information hub in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. UniProt collects protein sequences with expert annotation, and it doubled in a year to 80 million sequences, most arriving from genome projects. That flood forced an expansion of its accession code space from six to ten characters, so every entry can keep a unique, stable identifier as the archive grows.

A new proteome identifier tags the exact sequence set of one species and strain assembly, helping users track where a sequence came from. The website was rebuilt using a user-experience design process. Every entry also gained an annotation score, summarizing how much is known about that protein. The score helps users pick the best-characterized proteins for comparisons. All data remain free on the web.
europmc-pmc4399441:
Robert Mans and co-authors turned CRISPR/Cas9 into a multi-tool for yeast engineering, in FEMS Yeast Research in 2015. Baker's yeast is a workhorse for industry and research, but building strains with many genetic changes was slow. Their study presents editing approaches for Saccharomyces cerevisiae plus an open web tool, Yeastriction, that finds good Cas9 target sites in a strain's genome. One approach assembles the guide plasmid inside the yeast during transformation.

A second approach, with two guides on one plasmid, introduced up to six changes in a single transformation step at high efficiency. Beyond switching genes off, the team combined adding a multi-gene construct with deleting a gene, and placed two single-letter mutations at different loci at once. Standard plasmid sets accompany the methods, aiming to make complex strain building routine.
europmc-pmc4403341:
Annelien Verfaillie and co-authors mapped the switch to invasive melanoma. Their study ran in Nature Communications in 2015. Melanoma is a skin cancer that can turn deadly. Its cells can change from a growth state to an invasive state. That change is the step that starts spreading. The team mapped gene activity in melanoma cultures. They also mapped open DNA regions and chemical marks on DNA. They merged these maps with data from tumor biopsies. The aim was to find which factors run each state.

Thousands of control regions differed between the two states. Growth-state cells were run by two factors, SOX10 and MITF. Invasive cells pointed to AP-1 plus the TEAD factors. Lowering TEAD levels weakened the invasive program. That proved a causal role for TEADs. It also changed how cells responded to MAPK drugs. Gene control, not just mutation, drives the dangerous states.
europmc-pmc4415341:
Marcello Tonelli and co-authors built a scheme for spotting chronic conditions in administrative health data, in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making in 2015. Billing and hospital records could power large studies of multimorbidity, if conditions can be identified reliably from codes. The team reviewed validated code-based algorithms for 40 conditions, grading each by how often a code truly means disease and how many cases it catches. Thirty conditions passed at high or moderate validity.

As a proof of concept, they applied the panel to records of 574,409 people in Edmonton, Canada, for one fiscal year. About a quarter had two or more of the 30 conditions, a quarter had exactly one, and half had none identified. A validated menu of conditions lets other teams study multimorbidity in routine data on the same terms.
europmc-pmc4511241:
Xiaoying Fan and six co-authors built a method to read all RNA types in single cells, in a 2015 Genome Biology paper. Standard single-cell methods catch only RNAs with a poly(A) tail, a common end tag. That misses circular RNAs, loops with no such tail, which may guide early growth. The team's SUPeR-seq method reads both kinds from one cell at a time.

Applied to mouse embryos before implantation, the method showed sound sensitivity and accuracy in the authors' checks. It found 2,891 circular RNAs and 913 new linear transcripts. The team tracked how loop abundance shifts across early stages and which genes the loops come from. The work opens a way to study how circular RNAs act in early mammalian development.
europmc-pmc4659841:
Capucine Picard and colleagues issued the 2015 update of the world list of primary immune deficiency diseases. These are inborn faults that weaken the body's defence and can also bring allergy and self-attack. A panel of the International Union of Immunological Societies keeps the list.

In the two years since the last list, thirty-four new gene faults were added. Each disease is set out with its key signs and lab marks, across nine tables. The update shows a growing overlap: weak defence on one side, poor control of the immune system on the other. More faults leave a person open to just one kind of germ, a sign of how fine-tuned defence is. Doctors use the list to guide gene tests in rare cases.
europmc-pmc4659941:
Yong Cheng and colleagues brought out a 2015 study boosting photodynamic therapy by loading its drug into oxygen-carrying nanodroplets. Photodynamic therapy uses light to turn tumour oxygen into a cell-killing form, but tumours are often oxygen-poor, and treatment itself uses oxygen up. Their droplets use perfluorocarbon, which holds much oxygen. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

The loaded drug generated the killing oxygen form faster and killed more cancer cells in dishes. Injected into mouse tumours, the treatment slowed growth. A single intravenous dose also significantly slowed tumour growth, where standard photodynamic therapy had no effect. The authors propose this oxygen self-enriching design as a way to strengthen existing clinical photodynamic treatments and future ones alike.
europmc-pmc4712841:
Daisuke Kurihara, Yoko Mizuta, Yoshikatsu Sato, and Tetsuya Higashiyama developed ClearSee, a clearing treatment for plant imaging, in Development in 2015. Seeing gene activity deep inside a whole plant is hard: chlorophyll glows on its own and plant tissues scatter light. Chemical screening produced ClearSee, a solution that makes tissues transparent quickly. It dims chlorophyll's glow while keeping engineered fluorescent proteins bright, and it evens out the tissue's light-bending properties.

Cleared samples image cleanly through whole organs and whole plants, on standard confocal and on two-photon microscopes. Several fluorescent colors can be read at once, so multiple gene patterns can be mapped in one specimen. Chemical dyes work in it too, extending the method to species that cannot be genetically engineered. Because the plant stays intact, three-dimensional form and gene pattern finally appear in the same picture. The authors expect ClearSee to speed discoveries across plant biology.
europmc-pmc479041:
Michael J. Galko and Mark A. Krasnow built a genetic test bed for wound healing in PLoS Biology in 2004. They used fruit fly larvae. A puncture in the larval skin sets off a chain. Bleeding stops within the hour as a plug forms. The plug darkens into a scab. Skin cells around it stretch toward the gap. They merge into a shared sheet. The sheet crawls across to seal the surface.

The chain's links answer to separate genes. One signal path, JNK, drives the crawling and sealing. It does not drive the scab. Flies that cannot make a scab still start healing. Yet the signal then over-fires. Sealing sometimes stalls, leaving a chronic wound. The scab steadies the site and feeds back to calm the signal. The parallels to vertebrate healing suggest an old, shared program.
europmc-pmc4817141:
Andrew J. Page leads ten authors in Bioinformatics in 2015 introducing Roary, a tool for building pan genomes fast. A pan genome is the full gene set of a bacterial species: the core genes every strain holds plus the spare genes only some carry. Modern studies sequence hundreds or thousands of strains, and older builders choked on that scale.

Roary clusters genes across strains with shortcuts that keep accuracy while slashing the compute bill. On one processor it built a pan genome of a thousand isolates in about four and a half hours on a desktop machine. Extra processors cut that further. Knowing the core tells researchers what a species cannot lose; the spare set shows where virulence and drug resistance travel. The tool is free under an open license.
europmc-pmc4844641:
Erik N. Bakker and co-authors reviewed how fluid drains from the brain in 2016, a topic still sharply debated. Unlike other organs, the brain lacks a plain lymph system. Waste such as amyloid beta, a protein tied to Alzheimer's disease, must still leave. The review weighs paths along and around blood vessels and the role of spinal fluid in that cleanup.

Sleep seems to boost brain clearance, yet the flow routes, the structures involved, and the forces driving flow stay unsettled, with studies in conflict. Getting this right matters: failed waste removal may feed nerve decay diseases, and spinal fluid tests guide Alzheimer's diagnosis. The review maps what is known and where proof is thin.
europmc-pmc4872341:
K. J. Gilhooly and co-authors carried out a meta-review in BMC Geriatrics in 2016 on stress, coping, and support in dementia and dementia caregiving. So many systematic reviews had piled up that a review of reviews was due. Searching three databases plus hand checks for work from 1988 to 2014 turned up 45 systematic reviews, 15 of them with pooled numbers.

Thirty-one reviews weighed support programs, and 14 weighed factors tied to stress and coping in patients and caregivers. Programs showed modest, mixed gains, while burden tracked with behavior symptoms and poor support. A review of reviews risks double counting, the team notes. Still, the map shows where help works and where proof stays thin.
europmc-pmc4879741:
Vincenzo Carafa and co-authors reviewed sirtuin enzymes in Clinical Epigenetics in 2016, from chemistry to clinic. Sirtuins are seven enzymes that remove gene-silencing tags using NAD+, a core cell fuel. They steer cell survival, aging, division, death, DNA repair, and fuel use, and they answer calorie shortage. Faulty sirtuin work ties to nerve decay, heart disease, and cancer.

The review covers what each sirtuin does and the small molecules built to boost or block them. Some modulators already near clinical use. Because sirtuins sit at crossing points of metabolism and gene control, one drug can ripple widely, for good or harm. Careful tuning is the field's central craft.
europmc-pmc4889641:
David J. Tomlinson and co-authors reviewed how obesity affects muscle strength and structure from adolescence to old age in 2016. Obese people tend to show greater absolute strength than lean peers, since extra weight loads the leg muscles daily like training. Yet strength per unit of body mass runs low, so tasks like rising and climbing get harder.

Lower movement, nerve changes, and altered muscle makeup may explain the relative weakness. Reports on strength per unit of muscle, called muscle quality, clash, partly due to test methods. The review sorts the proof across age bands. Keeping muscle strong, not just big, is the guard against disability in heavier bodies.
europmc-pmc4912641:
Filippo Pizzocchero and co-authors presented a hot pick-up method in Nature Communications in 2016 for stacking atom-thin materials into layered builds. Stacks of two-dimensional sheets, called van der Waals heterostructures, gain traits no single sheet holds. Dirty interfaces between sheets spoil device quality, and hand stacking is slow. Their method lifts and places warm sheets in batches with clean contact.

The team made 22 controlled stacks of one, two, and three graphene layers sealed in boron nitride, with near total yield. Electrons raced through the monolayer devices with mean free paths up to 0.9 micrometers. Fast batch assembly of clean stacks brings designer layered materials closer to real production.
europmc-pmc4950041:
Mark O. Winfield leads a large team building a dense DNA marker array for bread wheat and its wild relatives. Their paper appeared in the Plant Biotechnology Journal in 2016. Breeding lines of wheat are genetically narrow, which blocks yield gains. Wild relatives in the secondary and tertiary gene pools hold far more variety, and breeders cross them in to add traits. Tracking the imported chromosome chunks, though, lacked good markers. The team mined a large set of single letter DNA differences, called SNPs.

They validated the markers on an ultra high density Axiom genotyping array. The array typed diploid, tetraploid, and hexaploid wheats and their relatives in one run. Marker data and sequences were posted in an open database for breeders to use. The authors argue the tool makes introgression, the guided import of wild DNA, practical to follow. That in turn should speed the broadening of wheat's genetic base.
europmc-pmc4951141:
Fumiaki Imamura and six co-authors compare dietary fats and carbohydrate for their effects on blood sugar control. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2016. Advice on fat types for diabetes prevention stays disputed. The team searched many databases for randomized feeding trials where meals were provided and calories held equal. Trials had to report glucose, insulin, or related measures in adults.

Just over a hundred trials with more than four thousand adults qualified. Swapping polyunsaturated fat in for carbohydrate, saturated fat, or monounsaturated fat gave the most consistent gains. It improved glycemia, insulin resistance, and insulin secretion capacity. Other swaps gave mixed or smaller effects. The authors support favoring polyunsaturated fat in diets aimed at metabolic health. They stress that these were feeding studies, so real world diet trials remain valuable.
europmc-pmc4995441:
The Global BMI Mortality Collaboration pools individual data from many prospective studies to map body mass index against death risk. Their meta-analysis appeared in The Lancet in 2016. Overweight and obesity keep rising worldwide, but studies clash on where risk bottoms out. To cut confounding, the team restricted main analyses to never-smokers without chronic disease who survived five years. That filter left near four million people across four continents, drawn from a pool above ten million.

Death risk was lowest across the twenty to twenty-five BMI range. It rose modestly just below that band and climbed steeply at low weights, likely reflecting hidden illness the filters could not fully remove. Risk also rose steadily through the overweight range and beyond. The authors say the huge, cleaned dataset gives the fairest global read yet of how body mass tracks mortality.
europmc-pmc5041141:
Sushanto Gouda, Gitishree Das, Sandeep K. Sen, Han-Seung Shin, and Jayanta Kumar Patra review endophytes as a source of medicines in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Endophytes are bacteria and fungi that live inside plants without causing visible disease. While drug hunters have long mined the plants themselves, these inner microbes turn out to make many of the same kinds of useful compounds.

The microbes produce a wide shelf of bioactive substances: alkaloids, phenolic acids, quinones, steroids, saponins, tannins, and terpenoids among them. Reported actions run against microbes, insects, and cancer cells, and the hosts themselves gain growth help and stress tolerance from their tenants. Chemical conversion methods can turn some of these compounds into further products, from antimicrobials to antioxidants. The authors present endophytes as a dependable, still underused pool for new drug discovery in medicine, food, and cosmetics.
europmc-pmc5047041:
Jonathan D. Rohrer and a large co-author group test a blood marker for frontotemporal dementia in Neurology in 2016. This dementia strikes younger people, changing behavior or language, and trials need a way to gauge how hard the disease is running. The team measured neurofilament light chain, a protein released when nerve fibers break down, in blood from 74 patients and 28 healthy controls.

Patients carried far higher levels than controls, across the behavioral form and both language forms of the disease. Levels in people with known gene causes were also raised, though values spread widely inside every group. Higher levels tracked faster shrinkage of the frontal lobes on scans, the region this dementia hits first. The authors read the marker as a gauge of disease intensity rather than a yes-or-no test, useful for following patients and perhaps for judging treatments in trials.
europmc-pmc5052741:
Frank Hille and Emmanuelle Charpentier review CRISPR-Cas in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2016. CRISPR is the adaptive immune system of bacteria and archaea: it stores snippets of past invaders' DNA and uses them as guides to cut matching invaders on their return. Charpentier is one of the system's pioneers, and the review sums up the field's major finds.

The authors walk through how spacers are captured, how guide RNAs are made, and how Cas proteins find and cut their targets. They also cover roles beyond defense that the system plays in bacterial life. The second half turns to human use. The stripped-down Cas9 system now edits DNA in a wide range of cells and organisms, with medical aims, and CRISPR parts are being shaped into antimicrobials that kill only chosen bacteria. Gaps in understanding the immunity steps are flagged for future work.
europmc-pmc5076441:
Brian H. Chen and a large international co-author group test whether methylation-based age predicts death, in Aging in 2016. Chemical marks on DNA yield an epigenetic age that tracks the calendar closely. The excess is called age acceleration; earlier work in four cohorts tied it to mortality. This meta-analysis pooled thirteen cohorts and 13,089 people from three racial and ethnic groups.

Every version of the acceleration measure predicted time to death beyond calendar age, and the link survived adjustment for standard risk factors and held within each group examined. Versions that also fold in blood cell composition predicted most strongly of all. The pattern did not differ by sex, body mass, smoking, activity, or major chronic disease. The authors read this consistency as evidence that epigenetic age captures something about biological aging, making it a candidate tool for aging research.
europmc-pmc5155141:
Hui Song and ten co-authors found a brake on a key inflammatory switch, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. The NLRP3 inflammasome defends against microbes but causes disease when overactive, and the amount of NLRP3 protein is the rate-limiting step for switching it on. How that amount is controlled was largely unknown.

They identified TRIM31, a tagging enzyme, as a feedback suppressor: it binds NLRP3 and marks it for destruction by the cell's protein shredder. Mice lacking TRIM31 fired the inflammasome more strongly and suffered worse alum-driven abdominal inflammation. Curiously, the same lack eased a colitis model where NLRP3 protects. The authors propose TRIM31 as a drug target for diseases driven by this inflammasome.
europmc-pmc516041:
Elsebeth Staun-Ram, Shlomit Goldman, Diana Gabarin, and Eliezer Shalev studied enzymes of early placenta invasion in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology in 2004. Trophoblast cells burrow into the womb wall in the first trimester, and two digesting enzymes, MMP-2 and MMP-9, do much of that work.

Comparing cells from weeks 6 to 8 and 9 to 12 of pregnancy, plus a choriocarcinoma cell line, they tracked which enzyme dominated and how two growth signals changed output. Early cells split output nearly evenly; later cells favored MMP-9, while the cancer line leaned heavily on MMP-2. Both signals raised enzyme output and invasiveness overall, though a high dose of one signal reversed course in the cell line. Blocking MMP-2 cut invasion in all groups, while blocking MMP-9 mattered only in the later cells.
europmc-pmc5164341:
J. Christodoss David and C. Vareed, of the pharmacology department at Madras Medical College, reported early tests of two pituitary hormones in The Indian Medical Gazette, in a note the record dates to 1929. Extracts of the pituitary gland's back lobe were known to tighten blood vessels and raise blood pressure. They also contract the womb and change urine flow. But whether one substance or several did all this was disputed.

In 1928, O. Kamm and co-workers separated two active principles and concentrated them as solids, later sold as Pitressin and Pitocin. Recombining them rebuilt the original extract, proving nothing was destroyed. David and Vareed set out to examine the separated pair, noting a third gut-acting factor that Schafer attributed to histamine, which may also explain the brief pressure dip in some samples.
europmc-pmc5176441:
U. N. Brahmachari described a diagnostic blood reaction in kala-azar in The Indian Medical Gazette, in an article the record dates to 1917. Brahmachari, of the Campbell Medical School in Calcutta, observes a contrast. Human serum diluted with distilled water turns cloudy as globulin falls out of solution. But in some conditions, a heavy precipitate forms instead.

He characterizes the substance as globulin-like. It dissolves in salt solution and dilute acids, and strong salt solutions throw it down. It does not dissolve in water. Chemical analysis had yet to find sulfur or phosphorus in it. The precipitate also appears in chronic malaria, consumption, and liver cancer. So its use was unclear at first. Then he cut the water to two or three volumes of serum. After that, it showed almost only in kala-azar, including a run of twenty cases he reports.
europmc-pmc522841:
Rinaldo Bellomo, Claudio Ronco, John A. Kellum, Ravindra L. Mehta, and Paul Palevsky reported the second consensus conference of the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative in Critical Care in 2004. Acute renal failure, sudden kidney failure in very ill patients, carried high death rates. Yet the field lacked even a shared definition, with more than thirty versions in use, which made studies hard to compare.
