The group reviewed the literature, framed key questions, and met for two days in alternating small and full sessions. They reached consensus on 47 questions and produced a shared definition of acute renal failure. The report also gives guidance on animal models, fluid therapy monitoring, outcome measures for trials of new treatments, and how information technology could support the work. Where evidence stayed thin, the group marked out the questions future studies should answer.
europmc-pmc5345141:
Misako Nakashima and co-authors tested stem cell repair of tooth pulp in people, in Stem Cell Research & Therapy in 2017. The pulp is the soft core of a tooth, with nerves and vessels. In deep pulpitis, dentists must strip it out, which weakens the tooth. Animal work had shown that pulp stem cells, drawn to the site, could rebuild the whole core.

Five patients with hopeless pulpitis took part in this first pilot study. Their own stem cells were grown from thrown-away teeth under strict clean rules and checked for normal gene sets. The cells were placed into the cleaned root canal with a growth signal gel. No side effects or toxicity showed over half a year of watch. Electric tests found live pulp response within a month. Scans matched the look of normal pulp, and three patients grew fresh hard dentin.
europmc-pmc5382941:
Jun Sone and a large group of co-authors describe adult-onset neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease in a 2016 paper in Brain. The disease is a slow nerve disorder marked by small clumps inside cell nuclei. The team pulled together the clinical and tissue findings from 57 adult cases, using autopsy results and skin samples taken during life.

The cases fell into broad patterns, one led by dementia and one led by limb weakness. Symptoms could also include poor balance, nerve damage, and loss of control of body functions. Skin biopsy let doctors find the same clumps seen in brain tissue. The authors urge doctors to weigh this disease when they see white matter damage or nerve disease with no clear cause.
europmc-pmc5391241:
Yi Zhu and nine co-authors test drugs that kill worn-out cells in a 2017 paper in Aging. Such cells, called senescent cells, build up with age and at sites of chronic disease. They resist death and leak factors that inflame nearby tissue. Drugs that clear them, called senolytics, have eased many age-linked problems in animal studies, but some carry blood side effects.

The team found that fisetin, a plant compound with low toxicity, killed senescent vein cells but spared growing ones. Two lab-made drugs that block one survival protein also killed senescent cells of two types. None of the three worked on fat precursor cells. The authors say these agents may be safer picks for later human trials.
europmc-pmc5400541:
Xiongyan Wu and eleven co-authors report a study in Oncotarget on how support cells help stomach cancer spread. Support cells called fibroblasts sit in the tissue around tumors. The team took such cells from stomach tumors and found they pour out a signal protein named IL-6. Cancer cells bathed in that signal moved more and took on a loose, roving form linked to spread.

The signal works through a chain inside cancer cells known as JAK2 and STAT3. Blocking IL-6 with an antibody, or blocking the chain with a drug, largely undid the effect. In mice, cutting IL-6 in the support cells also cut spread to the belly lining. The authors propose IL-6 as a drug target that strikes the tumor's support tissue.
europmc-pmc5420141:
Kim and co-authors offer a practical guide to doing microbiome studies well. Their methods review appeared in Microbiome. Studies of microbial communities have boomed with cheap DNA sequencing. They have also produced many false findings. Small flaws in design can swamp the real signal. Low-biomass samples are the worst trap. In them, stray contamination can make up most of the DNA.

The guide follows the order of a real study. It starts with design and common confounders. Age, diet, antibiotics, and pet ownership all matter. Animal studies add sharing between cage mates. Next comes sample storage for several sample types. Controls get a full section. The authors urge positive and negative controls in every run. They share a set of lab-made DNA sequences as positive controls. The guide ends with tips on multiple comparisons and validation cohorts. New labs can use it as a checklist.
europmc-pmc5451641:
Hanlon and co-authors review reviews of telehealth tools that help patients manage long-term illness. Their metareview appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Long-term conditions are rising worldwide. Self-management can ease their burden. Telehealth promises support at a distance. The team covered five diseases: diabetes, heart failure, asthma, lung disease, and cancer. They searched seven databases for reviews of trials.

They included 53 systematic reviews. Those reviews held 232 distinct randomized trials. Results varied by disease and by study. Blood sugar monitoring with feedback helped type 2 diabetes control. It did not help type 1 diabetes. Monitoring and phone support cut deaths and admissions in heart failure. Other conditions showed mixed proof. No review found harm from telehealth. Richer, multi-part programs did best in three diseases. The authors call for bigger trials built on clear theory.
europmc-pmc5456241:
Dhifi and co-authors review the chemistry of essential oils and what those oils do in living systems. Their review appeared in Medicines. Essential oils are complex mixes of scent compounds. Aromatic plants make them in large amounts. Terpenes form the largest share. Plants build those terpenes by one main route. Phenolic compounds come by a second route. The oils are liquid and colorless at room heat. Most are lighter than water.

Their chemistry gives them wide effects. They can fight oxidation, calm inflammation, and kill microbes. The food and cosmetics trades use them heavily. Health uses draw growing interest. In plants, the oils serve clear roles. They attract pollinators and repel plant eaters. They can also stop nearby seeds from sprouting. The authors argue the oils could sit beside synthetic chemicals in more products. Better knowledge of their chemistry should unlock new uses.
europmc-pmc5465941:
Golino and Epskamp introduce exploratory graph analysis for estimating dimensions in psychological data. Their methods article appeared in PLoS ONE. Counting dimensions is a long-standing psychometric problem. Classic rules examine eigenvalues or model fit. Each has known failure modes. The new approach builds a graphical model first. A graphical lasso, tuned by EBIC, does the estimation. A walktrap algorithm then finds network communities. Each community counts as one dimension.

The team simulated 32,000 datasets to test it. Conditions varied factor count and item count. Sample sizes ran from 100 to 5,000. Factor correlations reached as high as 0.7. Six rival techniques faced the same data. EGA matched the best rivals in many situations. With four factors correlated at 0.7, it stood alone. Accuracy hit 100 percent at the largest sample size. It also assigns items to dimensions directly. An R package implements the method freely.
europmc-pmc5473941:
Zhang and co-authors report a structural study in Cell on the dynein motor protein. Dynein hauls cargo along microtubule tracks inside cells. Alone, it moves poorly, and the reason was unclear. Partner proteins such as dynactin switch it fully on. The team imaged the whole human dynein complex with cryo-electron microscopy.

The structure shows dynein folded into a locked, self-twin shape, they report. Its two motor heads grip each other and bind tracks weakly. Mutations that break the lock open the motor up. Even open, the motor still cannot move well alone. Dynactin finishes the job by twisting the heads into line.
europmc-pmc5487041:
Yan and Ajuwon report a cell study in PLoS ONE on butyrate and the gut barrier. Butyrate is a short-chain fatty acid made by gut microbes. The gut lining blocks toxins and germs while letting nutrients pass. Inflammation can weaken that barrier. The authors test whether butyrate protects it, using pig intestinal cells.

Cells were exposed to LPS, a bacterial toxin that harms the barrier. Butyrate reduced that harm in a dose-dependent way, they report. It raised levels of two tight junction proteins, claudin-3 and claudin-4. It also kept a growth pathway called Akt active despite the toxin. Energy supply in the cells may play a part too.
europmc-pmc551541:
Bard, Rhee, and Ashburner present a resource paper in Genome Biology on a cell type ontology. Databases for model organisms need shared words for cell types. Without them, phenotype and gene-expression data cannot be compared across species. Older vocabularies tied each cell type to one organism. The team built a single system that crosses species lines.

The ontology covers over 680 cell types from bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals. Terms sit in a network linked by 'is a' and 'develops from' ties. Each cell type carries a public identifier for annotation. One query can then span mouse, fly, and worm databases at once. The resource is hosted on the Open Biological Ontologies site.
europmc-pmc5534341:
Koppel and co-authors present a review in Science on how gut microbes rewrite foreign chemicals. Everything swallowed counts as a xenobiotic: food parts, pollutants, and drugs. Gut microbes transform hundreds of these compounds. Their chemistry often differs from the liver's own work. Effects can flip: drugs activate, weaken, or turn toxic.

Case studies cover the heart drug digoxin and the cancer drug irinotecan. Microbes also reshape the nutrient choline, with health fallout. Most culprit enzymes remain unknown, the authors stress. Mapping them could guide personal nutrition and safer drug design. Toxicology risk calls may sharpen as well.
europmc-pmc5535941:
Börger and co-authors present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences on vesicles shed by mesenchymal stem cells. These tiny parcels, called extracellular vesicles, carry signals between cells. Stem cells seem to heal mostly by releasing such parcels, not by settling in tissue. The vesicles calm inflammation and cut oxidative stress and scarring. Human use has already begun.

Animal studies cover kidney, heart, liver, and brain injuries, they report. The vesicles nudge immune responses toward tolerance and repair. That shift lets local stem cells rebuild damaged tissue. Production methods still vary widely between labs, though. Standard protocols are the field's open homework.
europmc-pmc5551541:
Pizzino and co-authors present a review on oxidative stress in human health. That state arises when reactive oxygen species build up past the body's defenses. These molecules arise as by-products of oxygen use. Sunlight, pollution, and some drugs can raise their levels further.

At low levels, reactive oxygen helps cell signaling and immunity. In excess, it harms proteins, fats, and DNA. The review links that harm to cancer, diabetes, and heart disease. It also covers defenses such as vitamin E and plant compounds. Medicine even uses oxidative damage on purpose against cancer. Readers get both sides of a process often shown as purely bad.
europmc-pmc5560041:
Guo and co-authors report a method in Development for resetting human stem cells. Pluripotent stem cells can sit in a primed state or a more naive state. Human cells in culture are usually primed. A naive state may be easier to guide and study.

Their protocol uses brief treatment with a histone deacetylase inhibitor. It works across many cell lines without harming chromosomes. Reset cells grow fast and need no feeder cells. Their gene activity and DNA methylation shift close to cells of the early embryo. Methylation imprints are mostly lost, though. The cells can be primed again and still form all three body layers. Readers get a simple, sturdy route to naive human cells.
europmc-pmc5583141:
Olivecrona and co-authors present a methods study in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Drug hunters face a space of molecule options too vast to test by hand. Their method teaches a neural network to design new molecules with traits set in advance. The network learns from reward, like a game player.

First, the model learned to make molecules with no sulfur in them. Next, it made close analogues of the drug celecoxib from a single starting shape. Last, it aimed at the dopamine receptor type 2. Over 95 percent of its designs were predicted to be active there. Some matched known active drugs it had never seen. Readers get a clear proof that reward learning can steer molecule design.
europmc-pmc5627441:
Slavin and co-authors review how metal nanoparticles kill bacteria in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology. Bacterial resistance keeps outpacing new antibiotics. Metal nanoparticles rank among the strongest new candidates. How they kill, though, is still being pieced together.

The review sorts the proposed mechanisms. Particles spawn reactive oxygen species that damage cells. They release metal ions that poison targets inside. Direct contact can wreck the bacterial membrane. Energy stores drain as ATP falls. Hitting many targets at once may slow resistance itself. Cell wall build shapes who suffers most. Gram-negative bacteria often take the harder hit. Gene and protein profiles shift under nanoparticle attack, and the authors map those changes too. Readers get the mechanism debate organized in one place.
europmc-pmc5633041:
Messroghli and co-authors present a consensus statement on heart imaging. It comes from the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance. A European imaging group endorsed it as well. The topic is mapping tissue traits with magnetic scans. Mapping yields T1, T2, and T2 star values. It also yields the share of space outside heart cells.

These values show how heart tissue changes. They can reveal iron overload or stored fatty substances. They can also show scarring, amyloid deposits, or swelling. Unlike plain weighted images, maps give numbers that can be compared. The statement sums up proof as of mid 2017. It gives hands-on advice for clinic and research use. Intended readers are doctors, scientists, and scanner makers.
europmc-pmc5643541:
Mijic and co-authors report a cell biology study in Nature Communications. It concerns BRCA2, a tumor suppressor gene. BRCA2 guards stalled replication forks during DNA copying. When BRCA2 fails, enzymes chew those forks back. That damage helps explain why such tumors respond to chemotherapy. The team used DNA fiber spreading and direct imaging of forks.

They report that reversed forks are the entry points for attack. The regressed arms of reversed forks get degraded first. MRE11, PTIP, and RAD52 each promote this breakdown. Turning those factors off restored fork counts and chromosome integrity. Blocking reversal stopped degradation but raised chromosome breakage. BRCA2 seems to shield regressed arms with stable RAD51 filaments.
europmc-pmc5696341:
Mack and co-authors report a vascular study in Nature Communications. It shows the NOTCH1 receptor senses blood flow in adult arteries. Vessel lining cells turn flow forces into inner signals. Those signals keep the vessel wall in balance. The team found NOTCH1 responds to shear stress directly. Its signaling scaled with the strength of fluid shear. The receptor also moved to the downstream side of cells.

Cutting NOTCH1 levels broke down cell junctions. It also triggered excess cell growth. Gene changes involved calcium control and growth pathways. Blocking the calcium rise rescued the junction defects. In mice, losing Notch1 in adult vessel lining worsened plaque buildup. High cholesterol drove that added disease.
europmc-pmc5700441:
von Haehling and co-authors present updated ethics guidelines in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle. The journal covers wasting, muscle loss, and body composition. Authors must certify the principles when submitting work. Every listed author must have approved the submission. No one with a right to authorship may be omitted. Each author must add a real, independent contribution.

The work must be original and not under review elsewhere. Prior reports on the same data must be cited. Research approvals from ethics bodies are required. All conflicts of interest and funding sources must be declared. If any statement later stops being true, authors must tell the editors. The paper then gets updated or withdrawn as needed.
europmc-pmc5703641:
Harmon and co-authors study how disordered protein linkers shape phase transitions. Their research article appeared in eLife. Multivalent proteins form membraneless bodies inside cells. They can condense into droplets. They can also form gels that span a system. The two routes interact in complex ways.

The team used coarse-grained computer simulations. Polymer theory guided their analysis. They varied linker properties in the models. Linker traits set how much gelation needs phase separation. Droplet-driven gelation needs lower protein levels. Cells seem to prefer that route. The findings link sequence to behaviour. Disordered linker sequences encode transition rules. The work aids understanding of biomolecular condensates.
europmc-pmc5797541:
Uddin and co-authors review autophagy in Alzheimer's disease. Autophagy is the cell process that clears worn proteins and parts. In Alzheimer's, harmful amyloid and tau build up in the brain. Faulty clearing may help that build-up.

The review explains how autophagy works and how it fails. It links the process to genes and pathways, including mTOR. It also surveys drugs that adjust autophagy and might aid treatment. Readers get both the basic biology and a guide to possible drug targets. Key genes named include ATG7, BECN1, and PSEN1, among many others.
europmc-pmc5800641:
Peacock reports two hydatid cyst cases from London hospital care. Hydatids are fluid-filled cysts tied to tapeworm infection. One cyst sat in the liver and burst toward the lungs. The other patient kept coughing up hydatid material.

The report follows each patient day by day. It records symptoms, drugs, and decline in close detail. For the fatal case, it adds a full post-mortem account. The cyst held pints of pus and a collapsed sac. Readers get a vivid record of how doctors in 1850 saw and treated this rare disease.
europmc-pmc5845141:
Pita and co-authors frame marine sponges as tiny ecosystems riding a changing ocean. Their review appeared in Microbiome. A sponge plus its microbes forms a holobiont. The microbes feed, defend, and steady their host.

Sponge filtering moves huge volumes of seawater. Its microbes cycle carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus for whole reefs. Heat and pollution can tip the partnership into dysbiosis and disease. Whether imbalance causes collapse or follows it stays unresolved. The review asks if the microbiome helps sponges acclimate. They urge studies that follow the partnership from microbe to ecosystem scale. Saving these partnerships becomes part of saving reefs.
europmc-pmc5864241:
Tripathi and co-authors study how soil pH shapes bacterial community assembly. Their article appeared in The ISME Journal. Communities form through chance events and through selection. Which force rules more was an open question. The team pooled six datasets from soils of different ages. In these soils, age and pH did not move together. That split let them test each factor apart.

The authors report that pH, not age, drove the pattern. Harsh acid or alkaline soils yielded clustered, selected communities. Near-neutral soils showed more random, chance-driven assembly. A global dataset, drawn without regard to soil age, agreed. Extreme pH likely sets strict limits on survival, they argue. Those limits impose strong selection over time.
europmc-pmc6011841:
Venturelli and co-authors chart how gut germs act on each other in man-made gut groups. Their study was published in Molecular Systems Biology. The forces that shape gut group growth stay murky. The team built a model-led way to guess group acts. Tests on pairs and trios feed sums for big sets. They used it on a rich man-made set of gut germs. Pair acts drove most of the group shifts, they report.

Acts of three or more germs at once counted for much less. The web held many bad links and quite a few good ones. That mix lets unlike germs live side by side. Checks of waste in the broth hinted at the food trades at play. The work names the place of key gut germs.
europmc-pmc6027441:
Blaženović and co-authors review software for naming unknown compounds. Their article appeared in Metabolites in 2018. The setting is metabolomics work with mass spectrometry. Such studies detect thousands of small-molecule signals. Many signals stay unknown, which blocks interpretation.

Named compounds can be mapped to pathways. Unknown ones cannot feed reliable models. The review covers spectral database searches first. It then covers tools that predict fragmentation patterns. Names like MS-FINDER, MetFrag, and CSI:FingerID appear. Retention time and ion mobility models add extra checks. Workflows and worked examples are included. Readers get a practical guide to identifying compounds. That step is key for clinical and translational research.
europmc-pmc6029841:
McQuin and co-authors describe version 3.0 of CellProfiler. Their software article appeared in PLoS Biology. CellProfiler helps biologists measure cells in microscope images. Users build modular pipelines without deep coding skill. Earlier versions handled flat images at large scale.

Version 3.0 adds full three-dimensional image stacks. It can also work plane by plane through a volume. The underlying infrastructure was greatly improved. A protocol supports cloud-based processing for large jobs. New plugins run trained deep learning models on images. The interface stays documented and approachable for biologists. Readers get a guide to a free, open-source tool. It supports quantitative, repeatable image workflows in many fields.
europmc-pmc6050241:
Zhang and co-authors build a water-friendly carrier for cancer drugs. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The carrier joins a covalent organic framework with a curcumin-based polymer coat. Such frameworks are porous crystals built only from organic parts. Poor stability in body fluids had kept them out of in vivo studies.

The coat lets the particles disperse in water and glow. That glow lets the team track uptake and drug release inside cells. The carrier loaded the drug doxorubicin at high levels. It circulated longer and gathered more drug in tumors. One version also reached the brain well. Readers get a platform aimed at targeted drug delivery in living animals.
europmc-pmc6054941:
Loo and co-authors test tea-made silver nanoparticles against foodborne bacteria. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. The particles were made with pu-erh tea extract. Green synthesis avoids harsh chemicals and high cost. The particles measured about four nanometers across.

Tests covered four Gram-negative foodborne pathogens. They included E. coli and two Salmonella types. Klebsiella pneumoniae completed the test panel. Low doses stopped growth of all four bacteria. Slightly higher doses killed them outright. Time-kill tests showed very fast action. Counts fell by over 99.9 percent within two hours. The authors propose such particles as new antimicrobials. Drug-resistant infections are a stated target use. Readers get clear dose data for each pathogen.
europmc-pmc6063941:
Derstine and co-authors set reference values for muscle scans beyond the usual spine level. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Doctors judge sarcopenia, the loss of muscle with age, from CT scans. Cutoffs normally come from the third lumbar vertebra. Many scan protocols skip that level.

The team measured healthy kidney donor candidates aged 18 to 40. They took muscle area and density at every level from T10 to L5. Values at all levels correlated strongly with each other. Muscle area peaked at L3, backing its standard role. When L3 is missing, L2 and L4 serve best. Sex-specific cutoffs are given for each level. Readers get a fallback map for real-world scans.
europmc-pmc6068141:
Persi and co-authors model how cell acidity shapes cancer metabolism. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Cancer cells keep an unusual pH balance. Their insides run alkaline while their surroundings turn acid. The team built enzyme activity profiles into metabolic models of cells.

In the models, alkaline interiors sped cancer growth. They boosted sugar burning and adaptation to low oxygen. Acid interiors disabled those same adaptations. The search flagged two enzymes as weak points. Blocking GAPDH or GPI should hit hardest at low pH. Tests in breast cancer cells backed the idea. Aggressive cell types suffered most. Readers get a new angle for pH-based cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc6091241:
Tschandl and co-authors release HAM10000, a large set of skin lesion images for machine learning. Their data paper appeared in Scientific Data. Training diagnosis software needs many labeled images. Earlier sets were small and narrow. This collection holds 10,015 dermatoscopic images.

Images came from varied populations and devices. Cleaning used semi-automatic workflows with neural networks. All key pigmented lesion classes appear. Over half the cases were confirmed by pathology. The rest rest on follow-up, expert consensus, or confocal scans. The set is public through the ISIC archive. Readers get a benchmark for testing human and machine diagnosis.
europmc-pmc6113241:
van Hees and co-authors present a methods article in Scientific Reports on estimating sleep from a wrist sensor, with no sleep diary. Large population studies now use wrist accelerometers that record raw movement data. Diaries are often missing or unreliable. The team built a simple algorithm to find the sleep period from movement alone.

The method uses changes in the estimated angle of one axis and basic rules about sleep breaks. It was checked against diaries from 3,752 adults aged 60 to 82. It was also checked against lab sleep studies in clinic patients and healthy sleepers. The sensor-based window matched the diary closely. The work helps big studies measure sleep at scale.
europmc-pmc6202441:
Khalil and co-authors measured world deaths from two gut germs. The germs are shigella and a toxin-making form of E. coli. Both cause diarrhoea and kill many young children. The work is part of the Global Burden of Disease study. It covers the years 1990 to 2016.

The team used death records, speech-based death reports, and health data. Models gave counts by age, sex, place, and year. They report shigella caused about 212,000 deaths in 2016. That was about 13 percent of all diarrhoea deaths. The E. coli form caused about 51,000 deaths. The authors say both germs still need far more public health focus.
europmc-pmc6328441:
Hu and co-authors review CHOP, a protein that pushes stressed cells to die. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. CHOP is a transcription factor, a gene-switch protein. It rises when the cell's protein-folding workshop is strained. That strain is called endoplasmic reticulum stress. Short stress can help the cell recover.

Long stress turns CHOP into a death signal. It helps trigger apoptosis, an orderly cell suicide. The review maps the paths that switch CHOP on. It also maps the genes CHOP switches on in turn. Newer work ties CHOP to death during infections. Viruses and some bacteria feature in that research. Knowing these paths could guide new anti-infection drugs. The piece draws stress biology and infection biology together.
europmc-pmc6338741:
van Kessel and co-authors show gut bacteria can eat Parkinson's medicine before it works. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Levodopa is the main drug for Parkinson's disease. It must reach the brain to become dopamine. Many patients respond unevenly to it. Gut microbes may explain part of that gap.

The team tested bacteria that carry a decarboxylase enzyme. That enzyme turns levodopa into dopamine in the gut. The change happened even when rival chemicals were present. It also beat drugs meant to block the human enzyme. Patients with high bacterial enzyme levels had less levodopa available. Rat tests tied the effect to the upper small intestine. Where the drug is absorbed matters most. The work suggests checking gut bacteria when doses fail.
europmc-pmc6344541:
Mainprize and co-authors test focused ultrasound to open the blood-brain barrier in patients. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. The barrier blocks most drugs from reaching brain tumors. Sound waves plus injected microbubbles can loosen it briefly. Animal work showed the trick works without surgery. This phase I study tried it in people.

Five patients with high-grade glioma took part. Ultrasound targeted tissue near the tumor. Chemotherapy was given around the same time. Surgery followed the next day as planned. Samples let the team measure drug levels in tissue. Sonicated and unsonicated regions were compared directly. The study judged safety and feasibility, not cure. It marks a first step toward drug delivery for brain tumors.
europmc-pmc6396441:
Ovadia and co-authors report meta-analyses in The Lancet on a pregnancy liver disorder. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy raises bile acids in the blood. It has been linked to stillbirth and early birth, but the risk by bile acid level was unclear.

The team pooled study-level and patient-level data from many reports. Higher bile acid levels tracked with worse outcomes for the baby. Stillbirth risk rose most clearly at the highest levels. The results help doctors decide which patients need early delivery. They also refine how the disorder should be monitored in pregnancy.
europmc-pmc6436241:
Spahn and co-authors issue the fifth edition of the European guideline on managing major bleeding and disturbed clotting after trauma. Bleeding remains a leading cause of preventable death in injured patients worldwide. A pan-European task force, founded in 2004 and drawn from six professional societies, rebuilt the advice around new evidence and shifts in practice.

Recommendations follow the patient's path in rough time order, grouped around decision points rather than single treatments. Early, individualized, goal-directed care for coagulopathy earns strong support from newer physiology research. Each recommendation carries its rationale, and the group stresses local adaptation plus education and adherence programs as the largest source of further gains.
europmc-pmc6458841:
Fransquet and co-authors review whether epigenetic clocks, gauges of body age built from DNA marks, predict disease and death beyond a person's years. They combined 23 studies with 41,607 people in all, spanning long life, cancer, heart disease, dementia, and death. Age acceleration, testing older than one's real age, was the measure of interest.

Links to disease showed up but on and off, and few studies repeated the same design. Death told a firmer story: each five-year rise in clock age carried an 8 to 15 percent higher risk of death across the two clock meta-analyses. Skew in what gets published may inflate even that, so the authors stop short of backing clinic use.
europmc-pmc6461441:
Pinsard and co-authors use fMRI pattern checks to watch how the brain's pattern for a learned movement sequence changes as the skill sets. Earlier studies tracked brain signals rising and falling, but could not split knowledge of the sequence itself from general task skill. Measuring the gaps between signal patterns gave a cleaner probe.

Well-set sequences drew out stronger sequence-tied patterns in the dorsolateral striatum, prefrontal cortex, and secondary motor areas than fresh ones did. The hippocampus and dorsomedial striatum, by contrast, stepped back from the pattern over time. Motor memory thus moves house between systems as it settles. The authors present this as the first human proof of partner patterns that shift in their own ways across the phases of learning.
europmc-pmc6472541:
Chang and co-authors build a new measure of population ageing from Global Burden of Disease 2017 data, one that counts healthy years rather than birthdays alone. They first identified 92 diseases whose incidence climbs steeply with age; together those diseases made up 51.3 percent of all adult health burden in 2017.

Each country's burden was then converted into an equivalent age, the age at which an average global population carries the same load. The spread was startling: 76.1 years in Japan against 45.6 in Papua New Guinea. Age-related burden rates ran from 137.8 DALYs per 1,000 adults in rich countries to 265.9 in poor ones, though rates fell everywhere between 1990 and 2017.
europmc-pmc6567441:
Li and co-authors ask whether a cow's genes shape the microbes in its rumen, writing in Microbiome. Rumen microbes digest plant fiber for the animal, and their mix tracks with how efficiently cattle turn feed into growth. The team profiled rumen contents from 709 beef cattle and weighed breed, sex and diet against host genetics.

Breed, sex and diet all moved the microbial mix, but genes left their own mark. The abundance of 59 of 174 microbial groups was moderately heritable, and those same features tracked with feed efficiency and fermentation products. Nineteen spots in the cattle genome tied to fourteen microbial groups; five were already known feed-efficiency loci. Breeding, the authors suggest, could select the microbes along with the cow.
europmc-pmc6604941:
Reygaert surveys how bacteria resist antimicrobial drugs. Her review appears in AIMS Microbiology. Such resistance is now a major global health threat. Germs can learn to beat nearly any drug. Four main tricks account for most cases. Limiting uptake keeps drugs out of the cell. Changing the target makes the drug's site unrecognisable. Breaking the drug down disables it. Active efflux pumps it back out. These tricks may be built into the germ. They may also be picked up from other microbes.

Drug groups are classed by how they attack germs. Cell wall blockers and protein synthesis blockers feature. Poor stewardship sped the problem up. Farm use of the drugs adds more pressure. Knowing these tricks should guide better drug design.
europmc-pmc6607541:
Ye and co-authors review liquid biopsy for liver cancer. Their article appears in Molecular Cancer. Hepatocellular carcinoma is often found late, after cure grows unlikely. Tissue biopsy is invasive and samples only one spot. Blood-based tests could catch the disease earlier and track it over time.

The review centers on two blood markers. Circulating tumor cells shed from the tumor itself. Circulating tumor DNA leaks from dying tumor cells. Both carry the tumor's genetic defects. Tests on them can flag early disease and predict relapse. They can also reveal drug resistance mutations. The authors weigh study results and remaining hurdles for clinical use.
europmc-pmc6689741:
Besedovsky, Lange, and Haack review the sleep-immune crosstalk in health and disease. Their synthesis appears in Physiological Reviews. The interaction runs in both directions. Infection makes people sleepy through cytokine signals. Tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-1 deepen slow-wave sleep. Sleep in turn fine-tunes immune defence. Lack of sleep weakens responses to vaccines. Total deprivation proved lethal in animal studies. Host defence broke down body-wide first.

Chronic short sleep links to higher disease risk. The review weighs lab and field evidence separately. Controlled sleep shows causal effects in labs. Field data cover habitual sleep problems. Remedies include recovery sleep and napping. Sleep extension and behavioural therapy also feature. Pitfalls and open questions close the survey.
europmc-pmc6794841:
Ni and co-authors found a long non-coding RNA that restrains colorectal cancer by disabling the YAP protein. YAP activation fuels many cancers, including this one. The RNA, called GAS5, binds YAP directly at a key domain. That contact drags YAP out of the nucleus and marks it for tagging and destruction. Tumor growth slowed in cells and in animals as a result.

A second player completes the circuit. YTHDF3, a reader of the m6A RNA mark, promotes GAS5's own degradation. YAP itself turns YTHDF3 on, forming a feedback loop. When YAP rises, it erodes its own brake. The three-part axis, GAS5, YAP, and YTHDF3, offers new points to attack colorectal cancer.
europmc-pmc6834141:
Soares and co-authors review drug strategies against ischemia/reperfusion injury, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. When blood flow to tissue stops, the tissue starves. Restoring flow, though necessary, causes its own wave of damage. That injury shadows heart attacks, strokes, and every transplant operation, from whole organs to small grafts.

The review gathers the newest drug approaches shown to blunt this harm. It also revisits older ideas, such as brief pre-emptive episodes of low flow that train tissue to resist. Better preservation fluids that extend safe storage time get attention too. The authors present the field as fast moving, with many promising protocols still to prove themselves in patients.
europmc-pmc6855141:
Oikonomou and co-authors present a new heart risk tool in the European Heart Journal. Inflamed coronary arteries change the fat that wraps around them. CT scans already yield one such signal, the Fat Attenuation Index. The team reasoned that the fat's fine texture holds more information, about scarring and tiny blood vessels as well as inflammation.

They trained machine learning on scan patterns, joined with gene activity data from fat samples, to build a radiotranscriptomic signature. In patient data the signature detected fibrotic and microvascular change in the fat. Added to clinical factors and the older index, it improved prediction of cardiac events. The method uses standard coronary CT angiography scans.
europmc-pmc6857441:
Schiffer and co-authors review steroid measurement in The Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology. Steroid hormones govern salt and water balance, stress responses, and sexual development. Doctors and researchers track them to study hormone disorders. Labs long measured single marker steroids. New instruments now capture whole panels at once, giving a fuller steroid metabolome.

Blood and urine, the review shows, tell different parts of the story. Serum reflects steroids in circulation, while urine shows what the body made, processed, and cleared. The authors walk through synthesis, metabolism, and excretion step by step. Knowing which sample shows what helps readers interpret panel results correctly.
europmc-pmc6873641:
Rojas-Rueda and co-authors review green space and mortality in The Lancet Planetary Health. Parks, trees, and other greenery are thought to support health through cleaner air, more exercise, less stress, and stronger social ties. Whether they actually lengthen life needed a hard look at long-term studies. The authors searched the literature indexed before August 2019.

They kept only cohort studies, which follow people over time, and combined their results in a meta-analysis. Living amid more green space was linked with lower all-cause mortality. The pooled data were firm enough to derive exposure-response curves. Those curves can feed future health impact assessments for city planning.
europmc-pmc6902641:
La Merrill and co-authors issue an expert consensus statement in Nature Reviews Endocrinology. Some chemicals from outside the body interfere with hormones. They are linked to cancer, fertility problems, learning deficits, and obesity. Studies of how they act pile up, yet no agreed system sorts them into hazards. Cancer science solved a like problem with a list of key traits.

The authors adapt that idea and define ten key traits of these hormone disruptors. Each trait names a way such chemicals act: blocking hormone receptors, changing hormone output, or altering transport. One example traces farm chemicals that raise the enzyme that turns testosterone into oestrogen. The list aims to turn scattered proof into sound hazard calls.
europmc-pmc6954041:
Zhou and co-authors map a shared switch that turns on a huge family of cell receptors. Their study appeared in eLife. Class A G-protein-coupled receptors, or GPCRs, shape nearly every body process. About a third of marketed drugs target them. Activation ends with one helix swinging outward, but the chain of changes behind that move was unclear.

The team measured shape changes across 234 structures from 45 receptors. A common pathway emerged, built from 34 residue pairs and 35 residues. It strings together scattered known motifs, linking the drug-binding pocket to the G-protein site. Targeted mutations along the path produced receptors stuck on or stuck off. The pathway also explains many disease mutations, and may guide new drug design.
europmc-pmc6974441:
Wieërs and co-authors ask what probiotics really do inside the gut. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Doctors have used these live bacteria for many years to treat all sorts of ills. The idea is old. Children with loose stools were found to lack one group of gut bacteria. Feeding that group back seemed to help them get well.

Since then, studies have linked shifts in gut and skin bacteria to many diseases. Some probiotics did seem to help. Yet most studies found no clear change in the gut mix itself. The gain, the authors argue, lies in what these bacteria share and make. They pass on genes and useful products. They back up a weak gut mix and calm the gut wall. Effects differ a lot from strain to strain, so one strain tells us little about the next.
europmc-pmc7003341:
Jin and co-authors issue rapid advice for diagnosing and treating the new coronavirus pneumonia. Their guideline appeared in Military Medical Research. Cases of a new viral pneumonia appeared in Wuhan in December 2019. The World Health Organization named the virus 2019-nCoV on January 12, 2020. No treatment manual existed.

Frontline doctors and nurses needed guidance fast. The team drafted the guideline by the World Health Organization rapid advice method, adding first-hand data from Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University. It covers how the guideline was built, the outbreak's features, screening, and protection of the public. Diagnosis and treatment follow, including traditional Chinese medicine. Hospital infection control and nursing care are detailed. A fully told case of one severe patient's successful treatment closes the document, with lessons from the rescue.
europmc-pmc7118541:
Beck and co-authors used a deep learning model to predict which existing antiviral drugs might act against SARS-CoV-2, in Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal. New drugs take years to reach the market, so repurposing approved ones offered a fast route. Their model, MT-DTI, predicts how strongly a drug binds viral protein targets.

Atazanavir, remdesivir, and the combination sold as Kaletra ranked among the predicted inhibitors. Rapamycin and tiotropium bromide also emerged as candidates. The model's rankings were checked against a physics-based docking program and agreed moderately well. Predictions of this kind are starting points for laboratory testing, not proof that a drug works in patients.
europmc-pmc7156741:
Schraufnagel reviews the health effects of ultrafine air particles, the smallest fraction of particulate pollution, in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. These particles, PM0.1, are present in air in huge numbers and slip deep into the lungs. From there they can reach nearly every organ and stay in lung tissue longer than larger fine particles.

Exposure triggers cough and worsens asthma, drives body-wide inflammation and clotting changes, and is linked to heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, and cancer. Particles can travel along smell nerves into the brain, and exposure before birth raises low birthweight risk. Traffic exhaust is the usual suspect, but the review notes high exposures from trash burning, mosquito coils, smoking, and cooking in homes.
europmc-pmc7157541:
Rabi and co-authors summarise what was known about SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19 in the pandemic's first months, in Pathogens. The opening cases were fatal pneumonias in Wuhan, China, all linked to a wholesale market selling seafood and live animals. The virus spread quickly despite China's containment effort, carried abroad by travellers.

Their review gathers the state of knowledge on the virus's origin, how the disease develops, treatments under study, risk factors, and vaccine work. It recalls the earlier SARS and MERS epidemics that framed the alarm. Written while trials of drugs such as remdesivir were still running, it captures the scientific scramble of early 2020.
europmc-pmc7203741:
Guan and co-authors present purge_dups, a tool that cleans duplicated segments from genome assemblies. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. Long-read sequencing now produces near-reference genomes quickly. In variable regions, assemblers often build two copies of one stretch. These haplotypic duplicates break the assembly and confuse gene annotation.

Earlier tools removed only some duplicate types or made errors. Purge_dups combines sequence similarity with read depth to judge each region. It then cuts the extra copies automatically. Tests across several species compared it with rival tools. It removed 96.4 percent of duplicated unique markers in one test genome. Genome projects get cleaner assemblies with less manual fixing. The tool suits the new wave of large eukaryotic genomes.
europmc-pmc7265941:
James and co-authors work out how many people in the world had herpes simplex virus in 2016. Their report is a World Health Organization study. Two types are covered. Type 1 most often causes cold sores but can also infect the genitals. Type 2 is spread mainly through sex.

They put the count for type 2 at 491.5 million people aged 15 to 49 years, about 13 in each 100 of that age group. For type 1, the count was 3752 million, about two in three people under age 50. Type 2 was most common in women and in the African region. The team notes that herpes also raises the risk of HIV, which adds to its weight for health services.
europmc-pmc7291041:
Crawford and co-authors publish a full protocol for making safe stand-in viruses dressed in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Their methods paper appeared in Viruses. The real virus requires high-containment laboratories, which limits who can study immunity. A harmless lentivirus wearing the spike can be handled at a lower safety level.

The protocol shows how to coat lentiviral particles with spike and use them to infect lab cells engineered to display ACE2, the virus's doorway. Infection is read out with a light-producing gene, giving a convenient measure of how well a person's blood serum blocks entry. Binding tests alone cannot show that. The team deposited all key reagents in a public repository so other laboratories could run the same neutralization assays.
europmc-pmc7381741:
Zhang and co-authors review sirtuin 3 in Theranostics, a protein that tunes chemistry inside mitochondria. Mitochondria power every organ, and SIRT3 adjusts the acetyl tags on their proteins, shaping how they burn fuel and handle damage. Evidence ties it to aging, cancer, heart disease, and metabolic disease.

The review sorts the intricate mechanisms by which SIRT3 protects mitochondria and influences each disease group. It then covers the growing hunt for small molecules that switch SIRT3 up or down. The sirtuin family has seven members in mammals, and SIRT3 stands out for its mitochondrial post. Readers get a case for one enzyme as a drug target, and a progress report on the chemistry aimed at it.
europmc-pmc7471641:
Zhang and co-authors show that SARS-CoV-2 can bind platelet ACE2 and boost clotting in COVID-19. Critically ill patients often enter a pro-clotting state with lethal risk. The role of platelets in the disease was unclear.

Patients with COVID-19 had larger, overactive platelets and lower platelet counts. Virus RNA in blood tracked with platelet overactivity in the sickest patients. Platelets carry ACE2 and TMPRSS2, the tools the virus uses to enter cells. The virus and its spike protein directly fired platelet clumping, secretion, and clot shrinkage in lab tests. In mice, spike protein sped clot growth through human ACE2 platelets. Blocking spike or adding ACE2 protein cut the effect. The work names a direct route to COVID-19 clots.
europmc-pmc7518441:
Peng and co-authors show that PD-L1 on dendritic cells limits T cell activation and shapes checkpoint therapy response. Checkpoint blockade helps many cancers, but how T cells switch on was unclear. Dendritic cells express PD-L1 at high levels.

Type 1 conventional dendritic cells proved essential for PD-L1 blockade to work. After taking up antigen, these cells raise their PD-L1 levels. Type II interferon drives that rise in the study. The PD-L1 shield protects the cells from killer T cells. Yet it also dampens the antitumor response they start. Blocking PD-L1 in set tumors woke tumor-infiltrating T cells for tumor control. The authors call this PD-L1 role dynamic and central. Using it well could invigorate antitumor immunity in patients.
europmc-pmc7524341:
Feng and Wang review lactic acid bacteria as probiotics. These bacteria are widely used in fermented food and supplements. Part of their benefit may come from antioxidant action.

The review focuses on tolerance to oxidative stress. It explains the pathways and signals behind that tolerance. It also covers how antioxidant capacity is measured. Stress during processing and in the gut can kill bacteria. Oxygen is a major risk for survival and product quality. The authors sum up what helps strains stay alive and active. That makes the review useful for food and feed work.
europmc-pmc7614541:
Winding and co-authors map the connectome of a whole insect brain at synaptic detail. Knowing wiring is key to grasping brain function. They chose the larva of the fruit fly Drosophila.

The map holds 3016 neurons in the brain. It also holds 548,000 synapses between them. The team characterized neuron types and hub cells. Feedforward and feedback pathways were charted across hemispheres. Links between brain and nerve cord were included. Integration across senses and hemispheres was pervasive. The most recurrent circuits served the learning center. Some motifs resembled deep learning network designs. Shortcuts and nested loops appeared in the wiring. The map grounds later circuit tests and theory.
europmc-pmc7666141:
Peng and co-authors test a plant compound against lung scarring in mice and cells. The compound is scutellarin, the main active part of breviscapine. The disease model is pulmonary fibrosis, in which lung tissue scars and stiffens. The drug bleomycin was used to trigger the damage.

Scutellarin cut inflammation and slowed the shift of lung cells toward a scar-forming state. It acted through a pathway that runs from NF-κB to the NLRP3 inflammasome. When NLRP3 was forced high, the benefit vanished. The authors say this path explains how the compound protects the lung.
europmc-pmc7746641:
Wang and co-authors review inflammation's role in keloid and raised scars. These scars grow from faulty wound healing. They show lasting local inflammation and excess collagen buildup. How strong and how long inflammation runs helps decide which scars form.

The review sorts the story into three parts. First come the immune cells drawn into the wound. Next come soluble signals that spread the response. Last come the signal paths inside cells that act on those cues. The authors list current and candidate drugs that damp inflammation to limit scar growth. They frame timing of treatment as key to success.
europmc-pmc7756241:
Edlow and co-authors study SARS-CoV-2 in pregnancy, from virus levels to antibody transfer. It included 127 pregnancies during the COVID-19 pandemic. The team checked mothers and newborns for virus. They also studied the placenta and asked if antibodies cross it well to shield the baby.

No mother had virus in her blood, and no placenta was infected. No baby caught the virus from the mother. Transfer of anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies across the placenta was weak. Flu antibodies crossed in robust fashion by contrast. The two viral entry proteins rarely sat together in placenta tissue. The authors warn that weak transfer may leave newborns at risk.
europmc-pmc7859841:
Kolberg and co-authors present gprofiler2, an R package for gene list analysis. The g:Profiler web toolset has served gene studies since 2007. It profiles what gene lists do and converts ID types. Lab teams wanted that power inside R scripts.

The package reaches g:Profiler through its web API. Enrichment tests run inside automated pipelines. Plot tools help read and publish the results. Users can map IDs between hundreds of types. Ortholog species lookups come along too. The package is free on the CRAN archive. It aims to make gene list work repeatable and scriptable.
europmc-pmc7872641:
Viau writes the life of Pierre Fauchard, the founder of modern dentistry. The talk marked 200 years since Fauchard's great book appeared. It was given at the Sorbonne in Paris in December 1922. The piece ran in The Dental Register in 1923. Fauchard lived from 1678 to 1761.

Viau paints him as a man ahead of his age. Great work power and foresight mark the portrait. Fauchard raised dentistry from craft to learned art. His book set out tooth care in full system. Later dentists built on his frame for centuries. The piece honors him as the father of the field.
europmc-pmc7889641:
Krainer and co-authors report a research study on how proteins form liquid-like droplets inside cells. These droplets, called condensates, help organise the cell without membranes. The team studied proteins that form condensates at low salt levels. They asked what happens when salt rises again.

Proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, and Brd4 dissolved as salt rose, then formed droplets again at high salt. The authors call this a reentrant phase change. Experiments and simulations pointed to hydrophobic and non-ionic forces as the drivers at high salt. At low salt, electric forces also helped hold droplets together. The work clarifies the forces behind condensate formation. That matters for understanding cell function, disease-linked clumping, and how drugs might reach these structures.
europmc-pmc7946541:
Robertson and co-authors report a study of what predicts COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy in the UK. The data come from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, a long-running survey of the population. Willingness to be vaccinated was generally high across the country. But some groups held back far more than others. Finding them early matters for a fair rollout.

Black and Pakistani/Bangladeshi ethnic groups showed higher levels of hesitancy. People with lower levels of education were also more hesitant. The authors argue that vaccine delivery should focus on ethnic minority and lower-income groups. Messages and access both need to fit those audiences. The study offers a map of where trust work is most needed. It was drawn from data gathered as the vaccines first reached the public.
europmc-pmc8039141:
Kumari and Jat review the mechanisms that lock cells into senescence. Senescent cells stop dividing for good, yet stay alive and active. Stress, damage, and developmental signals can all trigger the state. The arrest holds even when growth signals call. Senescence guards against cancer by halting risky cells. It also erodes tissue repair and drives aspects of aging.

The review centers on two tumor suppressor pathways. The p53 and p21 route, and the p16 and retinoblastoma route, enforce the arrest. The authors explain why the arrest stays stable over time. Senescent cells also pour out a rich mix of signals, the SASP. That secretory flood reshapes neighbors for better and worse. Clearing senescent cells, the authors note, can restore tissue function. Few cell states cut both ways so sharply.
europmc-pmc8142841:
Earle and co-authors ask whether antibody levels can stand in for vaccine protection against COVID-19. They compare efficacy data with lab antibody measures for seven vaccines. The studies came from varied places, assays, and vaccine platforms.

Once antibody levels were scaled to human convalescent sera, the links were strong. Neutralizing antibody levels tracked efficacy, and binding antibody levels tracked it still more closely. The authors also draw on natural history work and animal models. They conclude that antibody measures after vaccination can support a correlate of protection. That finding could speed approval of new vaccines when large trials are not feasible.
europmc-pmc8191141:
McNutt and co-authors release GNINA 1.0, a docking tool scored by deep learning. Docking predicts how a small molecule sits in a protein pocket. Scoring decides which poses look best, and weak scoring spoils results.

GNINA scores poses with an ensemble of convolutional neural networks. The team tested many settings to balance accuracy and cost. They compared it with AutoDock Vina scoring on set pockets and whole proteins. Success meant a top pose within 2 ångströms of the true pose. The release gives drug hunters an open tool with learned scoring.
europmc-pmc8201141:
Wang, Niu, and Zheng review MYB transcription factors in plant stress responses. Plants cannot move away from stress, so they adapt in place. Transcription factors switch stress genes on when signals arrive.

MYB factors form one of the largest such families in plants. They bind target gene promoters and steer growth and defence. They also help make anthocyanins, flavonols, and lignin. The review gathers work on their roles under drought, salt, and cold. It shows how one family covers many stresses. The findings matter for breeding hardier crops. Stress signals switch these factors on in response.
europmc-pmc8223641:
Bolte and co-authors link long-term diet patterns to gut microbe traits. Diet feeds gut microbes, which steer gut inflammation. The question was whether eating habits can favour a calmer gut.

The study joined 173 dietary factors to microbe data from 1,425 people. Four cohorts took part, including bowel disease and general groups. Shotgun sequencing profiled microbe mix and function. Some diet patterns tracked with pro-inflammatory microbe features. Others tracked with anti-inflammatory ones. The results sketch how daily food choices shape the gut ecosystem over time. Food frequency questionnaires captured what people ate over time.
europmc-pmc8388041:
Bergen and co-authors assess the state of RNA velocity, a method that reads cell direction from single-cell data. Single-cell RNA sequencing gives only a still snapshot of a cell. RNA velocity adds motion by comparing new and mature RNA copies.

The review walks through current modeling approaches and where each one strains. Worked cases show limits and traps that can mislead users. The authors give plain guidance on how to handle these problems. They then look ahead to wider uses. Future work may extend the idea to more kinds of systems and more data types. The piece serves as both a field guide and a warning list.
europmc-pmc8494641:
Liu and co-authors build a DNA methylation atlas of the mouse brain at single-cell level. Brain cells vary hugely in gene use, shape, and job. The DNA rules behind that variety were poorly mapped. Methylation marks are a key part of those rules.

The team profiled 103,982 nuclei from 45 brain regions, most of them neurons. They found 161 cell clusters with distinct places and projection targets. Signature genes and control elements marked each type. Excitatory neurons in cortex and hippocampus varied along smooth spatial gradients. A neural network model learned to call cell type and brain area from the marks alone. The atlas links gene control to brain geography.
europmc-pmc8594841:
Maffei and co-authors build a shared set of phages to study how these viruses interact with Escherichia coli. Phages could help treat drug-resistant infections. Yet most knowledge rests on a few old lab models. The team wanted a broad, well-tested set that others could use.

They gathered 68 new phages and added 10 classic models. Each phage was checked for its host range and genome. The team found the host parts each phage needs to enter a cell. They also tested how 11 bacterial defense systems affect each phage. The BASEL set gives labs a shared base for phage work and for picking phages with a known fit.
europmc-pmc8784641:
Moretti and co-authors review how fibroblasts, the extracellular matrix, and inflammation interact in scar formation. Fibrosis plays a part in about 40 percent of deaths worldwide. Fetuses heal without scars early in development, a trick adults cannot match. Past work studied each factor alone, but they act as one system.

The review walks through the four stages of wound healing. Adult and fetal healing are compared at each stage. Signals between matrix, cells, and immune factors get close attention. Fibroblast diversity is flagged as a lead factor. Some fibroblast types may favor scarless repair. The authors point to fresh findings that could shift healing toward that outcome.
europmc-pmc8788341:
Ai and co-authors test how well vaccine-boosted blood neutralizes the Omicron variant versus earlier SARS-CoV-2 forms. Groups included patients who recovered from breakthrough infection and people boosted with the same or a different inactivated vaccine. Lab pseudovirus tests measured blocking strength at set days after each course. Four virus forms were tested in all.

Two vaccine doses left Omicron activity below detection in 80 percent of samples. A same-vaccine booster raised clear activity against Omicron. A different-vaccine booster raised it far higher still. After boosting, all samples showed positive activity against Omicron. Levels still ran well below those for the first strain. The authors conclude that boosters restore cover, but Omicron remains harder to block.
europmc-pmc8850541:
Reyman and co-authors run a randomized trial on antibiotics given to newborns in their first week. Broad-spectrum antibiotics treat suspected early sepsis. They may also disturb the gut microbes then taking root. Resistance genes might get selected at the same time. The trial assigned 147 infants to three common drug combinations. A group of 80 untreated infants served as controls.

Stool and swab samples tracked the gut over 12 months. Both microbe makeup and resistance gene profiles shifted right after treatment. They drifted back toward normal within the year. Friendly Bifidobacterium fell, while Klebsiella and Enterococcus rose. One drug pairing shifted things most; another shifted them least. The authors conclude that drug choice matters. Gentler pairings spare the infant gut.
europmc-pmc8913741:
Bryant, Pozzati, and Elofsson test whether AlphaFold2 can predict how two proteins fit together. Knowing a complex's shape is key to knowing its function. No method could model complexes accurately. AlphaFold2 changed single-chain modeling almost overnight. The team adapted it for pairs of interacting chains. Careful sequence alignments fed the runs. A simple score then judged each model. The score estimates the model's own quality.

Models reached acceptable quality for 63% of test dimers. The predicted score separated good models from bad ones. It also separated true partners from non-partners. Using it, the team caught 51% of interacting pairs. The false positive rate stayed at 1%. The authors call this state-of-the-art accuracy. Their recipe needs no new machinery. It repurposes a famous tool for a harder problem.
europmc-pmc8943941:
Jiang and co-authors review how the stiffness of the tumor's matrix drives cancer and how to fight it. The extracellular matrix scaffolds every tissue. In tumors, it stiffens and talks to cells. Sensors such as integrins and Piezo1 read that stiffness. Signals then push growth, spread, and vessel building. Immune evasion joins the list. Stiffening also breeds drug resistance. The review gathers this fast-growing evidence.

The authors first cover what sets matrix stiffness. Enzymes and crosslinking both matter. They then trace stiffness effects on tumor growth and metastasis. A section treats resistance in depth. Cancer immunity under stiffness follows. Drug targets along the pathway are cataloged. Some aim at the matrix itself. Others aim at the sensors and signals. The authors argue softer tumors may treat better. Trials will test that hope.
europmc-pmc9007741:
Morales and co-authors describe MANE, a joint transcript set meant to standardize clinical genome reports. Two big annotation teams long kept separate gene maps. RefSeq and Ensembl each named their own transcripts. Clinics then struggled to compare variant reports. MANE makes the two converge. Each chosen transcript matches exactly in both sets. One representative transcript is picked per gene. That set is called MANE Select. A second set adds transcripts needed for known clinical variants.

Select now covers 97% of human protein-coding genes. All high-priority secondary finding genes are in. The sets sit inside major genome browsers. Reports can cite the same transcript names everywhere. The authors expect wider use to smooth data exchange. Lab interpretation should get faster and steadier. The paper is a standards announcement as much as a study. Both teams pledge to keep the sets in step.
europmc-pmc9117141:
Tseng and co-authors measure how well the mRNA-1273 vaccine worked against the Omicron and Delta variants. They used a test-negative case-control design in a large health system in Southern California. The study covered 26,683 test-positive cases with variant status known. Most of those cases were Omicron.

Two doses gave 44.0% protection against Omicron infection in the first months, and that protection faded fast. Three doses gave much stronger cover, though Omicron cover still fell with time. For people with weak immune systems, three-dose cover against Omicron was far lower. Against hospital care, though, three doses gave over 99% protection for both variants. The findings support boosters while showing the limits Omicron sets.
europmc-pmc9200641:
Tang and co-authors assemble potato genomes to trace evolution and diversity in wild and cultivated types. Potato is the world's top non-cereal food crop, yet most cultivars are complex tetraploids. Diploid hybrid breeding could transform production, but diversity was poorly mapped. The team assembled 44 high-quality diploid genomes.

The set held 24 wild and 20 cultivated accessions, plus 2 genomes from a neighboring group. Family trees disagreed widely, showing a tangled evolution. Disease-resistance genes had expanded greatly versus related crops. The team found a factor that sets tuber identity and 561,433 high-confidence structural variants. A 5.8-Mb inversion was linked to carotenoid content in tubers. The work should speed hybrid potato breeding.
europmc-pmc9630141:
Krishnamurty and co-authors show that LRRC15 positive myofibroblasts set the stromal tone that holds back tumor immunity. Single-cell studies had spotted this fibroblast group in mouse and human cancers. What builds the group was not known. Its direct effect on immune attack was also unclear.

Mouse pancreatic cancer models gave the team their test bed. TGF-beta receptor 2 signals in plain fibroblasts proved vital. Without them, the LRRC15 positive cancer fibroblasts failed to form. The team bred mice that let them kill off just this group. Removal cut total tumor fibroblast counts by a wide mark. The mix shifted back toward plain universal fibroblasts. CD8 T cells then worked with less direct suppression. Tumors shrank more when anti-PDL1 therapy was added. The authors propose trimming this group as a therapy aid.
europmc-pmc9652141:
Gormley and co-authors give a narrative review of head and neck cancer epidemiology. The disease group seems to be rising in rate. Its causes may be shifting as smoking falls in rich countries. The authors set out burden, trends, and risk factors in one place.

The search covered PubMed and Epistemonikos for prior reviews. Registry data came from UK and global sources. The cancer ranks seventh most common in the world. It brings more than 660,000 new cases and 325,000 deaths each year. Global rates rose over recent decades, driven by throat cancers. Death rates have also begun to climb in the last decade. Smoking is a lead risk factor, worse still with alcohol. Betel chewing matters most in Southeast Asian groups. The HPV virus drives many throat cases, they note.
europmc-pmc9862941:
Kumar and co-authors survey major phytochemicals, their health effects, and methods used to extract them. Phytochemicals are plant compounds such as carotenoids, polyphenols, phytosterols, saponins, fibers, and polysaccharides. Foods rich in them are sold as functional foods, and concentrated forms as nutraceuticals.

The review links these compounds to lower risk of diabetes, obesity, cancer, and heart disease. It stresses that benefit depends on purity and structural stability after extraction. Yield and purity in turn depend on the plant matrix, solvent, temperature, and extraction time. Later sections compare extraction methods in detail, including high-pressure approaches. Readers get both a health overview and a practical guide to extraction choices.
europmc-pmc9984241:
Epifanovsky and co-authors give an overview of developments in the Q-Chem software package. Q-Chem is a program suite for quantum chemistry calculations. Such software predicts molecular structure, energy, and reactivity from first principles. The overview surveys advances at the frontiers of the field.

The authors span a very large developer team behind the package. Their account covers new methods and capabilities added to the code. Quantum chemistry tools serve chemists who model reactions and materials. Faster, broader methods widen what systems can be studied. The paper acts as a reference point for users of the suite. It records the state of a major community code at one point in its growth.
fdr-day-of-infamy-1941:
Roosevelt addressed Congress on December 8, 1941, the day after Pearl Harbor. His Day of Infamy speech runs barely six minutes in full. Few addresses in the nation's history carry such concentrated weight.

A date which will live in infamy, he calls the attack's day. He lists Japan's strikes across the Pacific in a grim roll. Then he asks Congress to declare that war has been thrust upon America. The vote came within the hour, and the nation mobilized at once. Six minutes of calm fury took the United States into world war at last. The speech is still taught as a model of crisis address.
fdr-four-freedoms-1941:
Franklin D. Roosevelt gave his Four Freedoms address on January 6, 1941. The State of the Union speech named the aims worth defending. Freedom of speech and of worship lead his famed list.

Freedom from want and freedom from fear complete the four points. Roosevelt spoke as war raged abroad and America still stood apart. His phrases gave the coming struggle a clear moral charter. The speech urged aid to nations fighting Hitler's armed might. Four short phrases still sum up America's best account of itself in wartime. Painters and posters soon carried the freedoms into every American home.
fielding-shamela-1741:
Fielding's Shamela, from 1741, is the sharp little burlesque that started the novel wars. Its full title promises an apology for the life of Mrs Shamela Andrews. Fielding, writing under a comic mask, attacks Richardson's Pamela, the hit novel of the hour.

In letters like Richardson's own, Shamela lets readers see her true game: her virtue is bait to trap her master into marriage. The jokes expose the cant of the original while inventing a livelier rogue. Shamela runs to barely fifty pages, yet it launched Fielding toward Joseph Andrews. Readers still enjoy its wicked speed and its place in literary history.
frus-1861-d141:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 July 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. The dispatch is document 141 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The crossing letters again show the two ends of the Paris link at work. Dayton still lacked the full Bull Run story as he wrote. His page and Seward's, read together, mark the seam between two states of knowledge. Dayton's page and Seward's crossed in the sea mails, as so often that year. The seam between two states of knowledge is where this file's drama lives.
frus-1861-d241:
Washington's orders went out to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands in a dispatch dated 1 July 1861. Congress received it as Document 241 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d41:
George Dallas wrote from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 April 1861. The dispatch is document 41 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Early April found London unsure what the American crisis would become. Dallas reported the talk of ministers and markets as he heard it. His view from the scene helped Seward plan the handover to Adams, who would face the same men within weeks. London's stance, once set, would guide the rest of Europe in its dealings with the war. Every other court in Europe would take its cue from that stance in time.
frus-1862-d141:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 13 September 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 141 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d241:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to William Stuart on 25 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 241 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The two men exchanged letters the same day, a sign of brisk business.

The emancipation plan announced on 22 September was the talk of every capital that week. Seward had long held that foreign governments should keep hands off the war. His letters after the proclamation worked to make the new policy a reason for Europe to stay out, not step in. This exchange with Stuart is part of that argument's first week.
frus-1862-d341:
Three Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 4 November 1862, and the first is Document 341 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All three went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Early November was decision week in London on the French truce proposal, and Washington wrote Paris accordingly. A three-letter mail let Seward cover the question from several sides at once. This first letter of the set belongs to the final round of the autumn campaign to keep Europe out of the war. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d41:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 2 April 1862. Congress received it as Document 41 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d441:
Closing the year's printed exchange with the Spanish minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Gabriel García Tassara on 15 November 1862. It is Document 441 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

November 1862 found the Union army changing commanders and the emancipation order weeks from taking effect. Foreign legations measured the government anew, and Seward's notes carried a firm, even tone to each of them. For Spain, the standing concerns were Cuba, neutral duties, and Mexico. The note ends the volume's Washington-Spain file for the year, a record of friction managed without rupture, which was exactly the result the Union needed.
frus-1862-d541:
Roest van Limburg replied to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 August 1862, two days after Seward's note. His letter is Document 541 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

The quick turn-around in the Dutch file that week suggests a question both sides wanted settled. Van Limburg's government traded widely and ruled colonies near the seat of war. Its minister's duty was to keep Dutch rights clearly on the record. Seward welcomed that clarity in return: a neutral that stated its position in writing was easier to satisfy than one that brooded. The exchange is a small model of correct wartime dealing between a belligerent and a careful neutral.
frus-1862-d641:
Townsend Harris addressed this dispatch from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1861. It is Document 641 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Three Harris letters in six days close the July cluster of the Japanese file. He wrote in the last week before the armies met at Bull Run, though the fact would not reach him until autumn. His reports describe the daily substance of the Edo mission in its final Harris season. The treaty ports were working and the legation's standing was maintained. The minister himself was counting his remaining strength. The letter is part of a remarkable tail to the volume, where the Civil War's record runs out into the Pacific.
frus-1863p1-d141:
London answered Washington's same-day letter with this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 2 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 141 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, set just after a Seward letter of the same date.

Adams wrote in the week the British moved on a Southern raider in their hands, a test of the law the Union had long pressed. His reports that spring carried the facts Washington craved most. This dispatch is the London half of a same-date cross in the file. It shows the post at the heart of the season's great question: would Britain hold its own ships back from the South?
frus-1863p1-d241:
