An instruction dated 18 July 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 241 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d341: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 December 1862. It is document 341 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d41:
On 17 October 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to a Monsieur Tabouelle. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state, writing from Richmond in a busy week of letters. The letter is document 41 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, in the group of Confederate papers printed there.

The French address hints at the web of contacts the South kept in Europe, where its envoys sought money, ships, and friends. Benjamin's pen fed that web from the center. This short piece of it survives because the Union printed the other side's mail in its own book. It is a glimpse of the South's quiet work abroad, kept in the foe's record.
frus-1863p1-d441:
3 April 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d541:
F. W. Seward, the assistant secretary sent an official note to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 28 May 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d641:
A dispatch dated 17 October 1863 went from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d141: On November 18, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, as the British party also closed on Cairo. His message is Document 141 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Four days remained before the conference opened, and the letters of that week have the feel of men packing for an argument. The record supplies the date and the names. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d241:
Patrick Hurley, the President's personal representative, wrote to Roosevelt from Cairo on 20 November 1943 after inspecting the China theater of operations. He had met Generals Stilwell and Chennault, toured with air commander Stratemeyer, and spent some six hours in talks with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek.

Hurley's conclusions are warm. Chiang trusts Roosevelt fully, favors democracy and liberty, opposes imperialism and communism. He will follow Roosevelt's lead on political questions at the coming conference. He hopes it restates the Atlantic Charter and the Four Freedoms. On strategy he holds one firm line: in the China theater he must remain supreme. He will not take a subordinate place under Lord Mountbatten. Still, he praises Mountbatten and offers full cooperation in Burma.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d341:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Harry Hopkins a second memorandum at Cairo on 30 November 1943, separate from the civil affairs agreement of the same day. This one concerns a proposed joint committee for all French questions, an idea from Secretary Hull.

In his talk with Eden, McCloy had raised Hull's suggestion of a new body. It would be modeled somewhat on the combined committees. All dealings with the French would be cleared through it for the time being. Hull hoped it would end the irritation and distrust bred by the two nations' separate French policies. Eden approved promptly, and Hull cabled that the group should sit in London. McCloy pictures it as informal, a military man and a foreign affairs man from each government, drawing on other agencies as needed, and asks whether the President favors pushing it along.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d41: On October 14, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, in a message that became Document 41 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. That day was a busy one at both ends of the Atlantic, with letters crossing in both directions. The record for this item gives the date and the two leaders' names and no more. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, five days before the Moscow Conference opened.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d441: Under the number 441, the Cairo-Tehran volume prints a short editorial note. Department historians added notes like this one throughout the conference record. Their job is to fill gaps, give context, and flag related documents. The surrounding papers come from the Cairo and Tehran meetings of 1943. At those meetings the Allied leaders set the course for the war's next year. Treat the note as the editors speaking directly to the reader.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d541:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on January 7, 1944, in the opening week of the year the Tehran Conference had planned for. Churchill had recovered from the illness that struck him after Cairo. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The Roosevelt-Churchill correspondence never rested for long, and early January found the two governments converting summit decisions into the Normandy invasion plan. A Churchill letter of this date belongs to that conversion: priorities argued, resources counted, and two leaders keeping their partnership warm by constant writing. Readers see the alliance's engine room at the start of its biggest year.
frus-1944-quebec-d141:
British chiefs of staff representatives answered the American strategy paper on September 2, 1944, in C.C.S. 654/1. They proposed three amendments to the basic undertakings Washington had drafted for the coming staff conference. In all other respects, they said, the American proposals were acceptable, which makes the small wording changes the real subject here.

One amendment added coordinated action with Russian forces to the pledge of aid, noting the armies were converging. Another extended assistance beyond French and Italian forces to other co-belligerents, such as Turkey or satellites changing sides. The third softened the rush to the Pacific: moving forces east should have regard to other inescapable commitments.
frus-1944-quebec-d241:
General Wilson asked the Combined Chiefs for guidance on economic policy for Italy on September 13, 1944. As the battle line moved north, he wrote, the operational phase was ending across large areas, and the approach to civilian supply and rehabilitation had to be re-examined. His directives, built for active operations, no longer fitted the situation he faced as president of the Control Commission.

The armistice promised Italians no material assistance, Wilson noted, yet an expectation of relief had arisen from both governments' known humanitarian policies. Governing only by military necessity risked losing a reasonably prosperous, contented postwar Italy. He cited a winter clothing program: he was now asked to certify it as the bare minimum to prevent disease and unrest, though it had been designed on estimated essential needs.
frus-1944-quebec-d41:
Another Churchill message reached Roosevelt on August 31, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. It sits beside the day's other letter.

Two messages on the month's last day fit a pattern. A leader was clearing his desk before a voyage. The Quebec agenda was heavy that September. It covered the final campaigns in Europe. It covered Germany's treatment after defeat. It also covered the terms of American aid. For readers, the message shows Churchill arriving at the conference on paper. His British positions were argued in advance. The conference opened at Quebec City that September.
frus-1945-50-intel-d141:
National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 1, dated 8 February 1946, is the new board's first numbered order. It followed the authority's first meeting by three days. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

First directives from a new board turn a charter into rules the whole system must obey. Directive No. 1 set the terms on which the departments' intelligence arms would work under central direction. Readers should end the volume's core run here, with the machinery complete. A president's directive, a board, a director, and an advisory board were all in place. The board's own orders were now flowing down. The argument of 1945 had become the system of 1946, on paper, in order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d241:
Dated 25 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 241 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d341:
The Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) addressed a memorandum to Secretary of State Marshall on 8 March 1948. Readers meet it as document 341 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d41: A memorandum for information, dated 2 November 1945, is one of the slimmest papers in the intelligence volume. Papers of this kind passed facts upward without asking for a choice. They kept senior men current. Meanwhile, the shape of the postwar intelligence system was fought over in longer memos. The title gives no author and no reader. So the paper stands on its place in the run, amid the autumn 1945 argument among State, War, the Budget Bureau, and the FBI.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d141:
Had Roosevelt secretly agreed to the Curzon Line at Tehran? Harriman's memorandum of 16 October 1944 answers a Polish claim that he had. Polish Foreign Minister Romer called at Spaso House in Moscow with a letter from Premier Mikolajczyk. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Romer's letter concerned Molotov's account of the President's Tehran position. Harriman told him the account was wrong. Roosevelt had not agreed to the Curzon Line at Tehran. He had made plain he would take no stand on the boundary, in private or in public. Harriman also explained why he had not challenged Molotov at the meeting itself. He had sat there as an observer, and it was not the place to argue over what the President had said.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d241:
Iran gets a four-part treatment in this briefing paper of 6 January 1945, “Memoranda Concerning Iran.” Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary calls Iran a testing ground for three-power cooperation and for the principles of Dumbarton Oaks.

American policy backs Iranian independence and seeks to strengthen the country from within, so excuses for outside meddling shrink. On oil, Washington should clear away any Soviet notion that American hands pushed Iran to refuse the concession. Yet Moscow should be persuaded that pressure on Iran breaks the Tehran pledges on sovereignty. Wartime censorship in Iran can be eased, the paper adds. The last item weighs the President's own plan, trusteeship of Iran's railways and a free port, and finds no chance of its acceptance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d341: Could you ask him, Harry Hopkins wrote to the President at Yalta on February 5, 1945. His point: why not take all Gestapo men, Storm Troopers, and other Nazi criminals. The note breaks off there. It is a single numbered item with no second point after it, passed during the second plenary meeting with Stalin and Churchill. Even unfinished, the slip shows what pressed on the American side that day: the fate of Nazi offenders once Germany fell.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d41: Wilson Brown, the president's naval aide, wrote on 3 January 1945 to Admiral Charles Cooke, chief of staff to the fleet commander. His message is document 41 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta. Naval aides handled the movement of the president himself, so staff papers like this one connect the summit's diplomacy to ships, routes, and sailing schedules.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d441:
France is written back into the Declaration on Liberated Europe by this British amendment of February 10, 1945. The draft supplies a new last paragraph for the declaration. In issuing it, the three powers express the hope that the French Republic's provisional government may be associated with them.

France would join in the action and the procedure suggested. The copy survives attached to Page's minutes of the foreign ministers' meeting that day. The amendment is a courtesy with weight: Paris, left out of Yalta, is offered a place in carrying out its promises to freed Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d141:
Churchill forwarded to Truman, on May 27, 1945, the reply he had just sent Stalin about the German fleet. The telegram, his number 56, is document 141 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The volume now turns from arrangements to the subjects the leaders would discuss, starting with what to do with Germany's surrendered ships.

Churchill thanks Stalin for his telegram of May 23 and for the outline of Soviet views. Such matters, he writes, should form part of the general discussions the three leaders ought to hold at the earliest possible date. The short message kept the fleet question open for the summit rather than settling it by cable, while politely acknowledging that Moscow had put its opening position on the record.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d241:
Secretary Byrnes approved the Italy announcement plan in a shipboard telegram dated July 12, 1945. The one-line message, sent from the cruiser Augusta, is document 241 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers Grew's telegram of July 11, which had urged that the pledge to Italy not wait for the summit.

Byrnes concurs with the recommendation and approves the suggested approach to the British government. That was the whole text. Italy was about to declare war on Japan, and Washington meant to announce at once that it would back Italy's admission to the world security organization. The brief approval, sent while the President's party crossed the Atlantic, kept a fast-moving piece of diplomacy on schedule.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d341:
Clayton returned to German financing in a letter to McCloy dated June 30, 1945. He had studied McCloy's first reply of June 21, and he reports a meeting of June 25 in Mr. Mason's office. Officers from both departments there reached a tentative deal on a proposal about interim financing, to be put to the British and Canadians.

On imports, Clayton states the State Department's firm view. The War Department should be responsible for all imports that serve the purposes of the United States government in Germany. That decision, he argues, should be taken at the highest level, not left to quarrels between departments.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d41: Mid-July suits Stalin: Hopkins cabled the result from Moscow on May 30, 1945. At that evening's meeting, Stalin said he would be ready to meet Truman and Churchill in the Berlin area any time after June 27. The date about the middle of July was therefore satisfactory to him. The extract, sent by Navy channels, is the mission's last scheduling word in this file. With place and date agreed in principle, the Potsdam Conference existed on paper before the Hopkins talks on Poland and the Pacific had even closed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d441:
Washington's note to Prague is drafted in Grew's cable to Klieforth of July 13, 1945. Klieforth is to deliver a note acknowledging the Czechoslovak note of July 3, which concerned the transfer of the German and Hungarian minorities. The draft then restates the American position first given on January 31, 1945.

The United States, it says, fully appreciated the injuries Czechoslovakia suffered from Germany and the German minority. It stood ready to examine the question toward a satisfactory solution. But that solution must take into account broader aspects: the future peace and security of Europe, and the problems of the governments holding military rule in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d541:
Lend-lease understandings with Britain are restated in a memorandum by the British Chiefs of Staff representatives dated July 2, 1945. The American chiefs will be aware, it says, that agreements were reached between the two governments last autumn on lend-lease to the United Kingdom after the end of the German war. Those agreements, London understands, have recently been affirmed by the United States administration.

An enclosure restates the understandings in summary form. The British recommend that the statement be communicated by the Combined Chiefs of Staff to the agencies and staffs now handling lend-lease to the United Kingdom. The assignment of certain lend-lease material urgently required for operations, they note, has been held up while the recent policy discussions proceeded.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d641:
From Beirut on July 7, 1945, Minister Wadsworth reported a French pledge on the Levant forces. His confidential wire is document 641 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It follows late-night talks among the French envoy and Lebanese and Syrian leaders.

Wadsworth says a formal French statement was due that evening. It would declare that the Troupes Speciales would pass to Lebanon and Syria. The terms were to be settled within a maximum of 45 days. Envoy Ostrorog hoped the step would ease tension after clashes at Latakia on July 5 and 6. He expected no thanks from Syria, though Lebanon's Pharaon was grateful. One snag stood out: some men, notably Armenians, had enlisted on regular French army terms and might wish to leave with the French.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1041:
Economic Sub-Committee drafters set out this extract of a draft report during the Potsdam talks. It treats one clause of the Economic Principles: how Greater Berlin should draw its food and fuel. The American and British members accepted the clause only on one reading of the map. Germany, for them, means Germany within its borders of December 31, 1937.

On that reading, Berlin would draw supplies from its old source areas. If land passed to Poland, the rest of Germany would hold a first claim on surplus food and coal from that land while shortages last. The Soviet members reject the principle. Fair sharing among the zones, they hold, should govern whatever the frontiers become.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1141:
Ambassador Winant sent this dispatch from London on 1 August 1945, the day before the Potsdam Conference closed. With the summit nearly over, he reported how Britain viewed the deal taking shape in Germany. It was among the last London cables of the conference run.

For two weeks the embassy had tracked British thinking for Washington. Now the task turned to judging the result and the mood it would meet at home. This dispatch closes the London end of the record. After it, the story moves from bargaining to the work of carrying out what was agreed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1241:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the President on 20 July 1945. Stimson's letters to Truman during the summit carried the War Department's counsel in its most direct form. This one dates from the first week's close, with the talks in full swing.

The war secretary's brief touched everything the army owned: the hold on Germany, the Pacific plans, and the secret atomic work he supervised. A letter to the president fixed his advice where the decider would read it. This message is part of the steady counsel that reached Truman at Potsdam, from the cabinet's most seasoned hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1341:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam put a written proposal before the conference on 23 July 1945. Delegations used such papers to place exact wording on the table for the other leaders to accept, amend, or reject. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Proposals matter because they fix a government's opening position in its own words. Readers can compare what the Soviet side asked for with what the final conference texts later said. Papers like this one turn the summit from a story of talks into a record of drafting. Single phrases could shape the peace in Europe for years.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-141:
A second delegation memorandum dated July 30, 1945 stands in the Potsdam files beside the first. The closing days produced a flood of such papers. Teams checked language, shared news, and readied leaders for the end. This memo survived in the archive and entered the second Potsdam volume.

Two memos from one day show the breadth of the work. While plenary talks drew the eye, staff ground through the details that made deals stick. The memorandum preserves one thread of that labor. Readers gain respect for the clerks and officers whose writing carried the conference. Their papers are its true daily record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-41:
The foreign ministers agreed on July 20, 1945, to meet again at 3:45 p.m., and that sitting left no minutes. Its editorial note is the forty-first unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two. The meeting had been agreed at the ministers' morning session that day.

The ministers had resolved to meet again at 3:45 p.m. that day. Their task was the redraft of paragraph 3 of the Council of Foreign Ministers proposal. The rapporteur's report of the day indicates that the meeting was actually held, the editors note. Its outcome can be read in the text the heads of government received that afternoon. But no minutes for the sitting have been found. The note is a typical piece of editorial housekeeping in this volume, tying a known event to the absence of its record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d741:
Gerig wrote again on July 31, 1945, this time to Alger Hiss and his deputy, John Ross. Document 741 continues the United Nations thread in the Potsdam volume. The Preparatory Commission in London was turning a signed charter into a working assembly. Gerig kept Washington's special political affairs office informed.

Progress reports from London show institution-building in real time. Rooms, rules, and agendas had to be made from nothing. Readers see that labor running beside the summit's end. The letter also shows the trust placed in a small circle of planners. Their names recur wherever the new order was being sketched in 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d841:
The British delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 24, 1945, as document 841. It dates from the conference's midpoint. British drafting that week balanced loyalty to Washington with London's own aims. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A midpoint British text shows the ally thinking for itself. Readers can place it between the American and Soviet drafts of the same days. The three together map the deal's possible center. The document also catches Britain days before its election verdict. Within the week, a new team would own these lines. The paper preserves the old team's last full statement.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d941:
Edwin Pauley wrote to the Secretary of State on July 28, 1945, with fresh math on maximum reparations from Germany. His team's first estimate ran between five and six billion dollars, counting farms and foreign investments. At five billion, half would sit in the Russian zone. That leaves 2.5 billion in the western zones.

Pauley warns against naming a Soviet share in dollars. Direct war potential in the west is worth about 1.71 billion, and an eighth of it is only 214 million. Naming that sum, he says, would kill any deal. He advises speaking only of total removables, with the Russians receiving 12.5 percent of equipment the western powers remove.
frus-1964-68v06-d41: An intelligence memorandum dated January 31, 1968, and numbered SC No. 01909/68, assesses the Communist Tet offensive in South Vietnam. It sits in Volume VI of the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series, on Vietnam. The memo reads the attacks as a bid for mental impact. They aim to show that Communist forces can still strike towns, bases, and the U.S. Embassy. It warns of a major assault near Khe Sanh and in the north. It also links the campaign to Hanoi's recent offer of talks, without treating it as a last bid for peace.
frus-1969-76v41:
Volume XLI of the 1969-1976 series covers Western Europe and NATO from 1969 to 1972. A regional chapter opens the volume. Country chapters follow for Canada, France, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal, Spain, and the United Kingdom. The French chapters weigh Pompidou's wish to show an independent hand. The British chapters cover entry into the European Community and defense ties.

Analyses in the papers warn that Moscow plays Bonn against Paris. Cables track alliance debates on troops, nuclear plans, and money. The Spain and Portugal chapters deal with base rights under aging regimes. The volume gives the allied half of detente.
frus-1981-88v41:
Global Issues II is the title of Volume XLI in the 1981-1988 Foreign Relations series. Sections cover AIDS policy, human rights, and the Law of the Sea. Later sections treat the African famine, population policy, whaling rules, and protection of the ozone layer. The Law of the Sea papers record the U.S. choice not to sign the treaty. Its seabed terms were judged unacceptable in Washington. Every effort, one memo urges, should still be made in New York and elsewhere.

The AIDS section is among the earliest in the series on the epidemic. Famine relief in Africa fills the next. The ozone section closes with the first steps toward the Montreal accord.
gao-gaoreports-b-298841:
John Blood protested the Forest Service's review of bids for tree thinning work. The job protects homes and power lines from wildfire. The site lies in the Gunnison Ranger District of Colorado. GAO ruled in B-298841 and B-298841.2 on December 21, 2006.

The winner's bid said its crews would camp on site. Blood argued that plan clashed with housing law for migrant workers. GAO found no clash on the face of the bid. The bid did not state a plan to break that law. The agency had no duty to probe the point pre-award. GAO also let the panel weigh first-hand past knowledge. It denied the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-298941:
ITS Services, Inc. protested a Homeland Security task order to Bart and Associates, Inc. Customs and Border Protection ran the buy. The order covered technical and engineering services for its information office. GAO decided B-298941 and B-298941.2 on January 10, 2007.

The protester sent in the lower-priced bid. The winner scored higher on technical merit at a higher price. The terms made merit count more than price in the pick. GAO read the agency record for a sound base. It found one for the higher-priced pick. Paying more for a stronger offer fit the stated scheme. No flaw in the scoring was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299041:
Planning and Development Collaborative International protested a U.S. Agency for International Development award to The Services Group, Inc. The contract covered technical aid for the Government of Armenia. The work aimed to strengthen social protection systems there. GAO decided B-299041 on January 24, 2007.

The firm claimed talks skipped a weak point in its bid. That point, though, was weak yet still fit for award. It did not block the firm from a fair shot at the work. Talks must flag flaws that could sink a bid. A soft spot that leaves a bid in play need not be raised. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299241:
Shirlington Limousine & Transport, Inc. protested terms in a Homeland Security solicitation. The buy covered agency-wide transportation services. Terms touched secure storage, sedans, and shuttle bus lifts. GAO ruled in B-299241 on March 13, 2007.

The firm called three terms an undue curb on rivalry. One asked for electronic access control at a secure lot. One asked for sedans in the fleet. One asked that each shuttle bus carry a wheelchair lift. GAO found each term tied to true agency needs. It also backed the call not to use a HUBZone set-aside. Too few such firms were apt to bid. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310741:
Rocketplane Kistler lost its protest. That ruling is B-310741, dated January 28, 2008. NASA ran a plan to spur private space flight to low Earth orbit. It used a funded Space Act pact, not a buy deal. The pact would pay firms to build and show off space hauls. Rocketplane said the work had to run through a buy deal.

GAO denied the protest. The chief aim of the plan was a public gain set by law. It was not to get goods or work for NASA's own direct use. A pact of this kind fits NASA's deal power. A buy deal is not a must when spur, not supply, is the aim.
gao-gaoreports-b-310941:
Eisenhower Real Estate Holdings, LLC lost its protest under GAO decision B-310941, dated March 18, 2008. The General Services Administration leased office space for the Drug Enforcement Administration. It kept the past landlord on a sole-source path. A rival landlord said its site would save cash. It fought the cost test that backed the stay-put call. A move would cost much to shift and to copy the setup.

GAO denied the protest. The cost test had a fair base on its facts. The rival gave no firm proof its site would save more than a move costs. Big move costs can back a sole-source lease.
gao-gaoreports-b-311141:
In and Out Valet Co. lost its protest in GAO decision B-311141, dated April 3, 2008. The Veterans Affairs office sought valet car park work at its Pittsburgh hospital. It gave the work to Veterans Parking Management, LLC with no race. Both firms are owned by hurt veterans. The loser said the no-race path broke the rules for such deals. The price sat past a low-buy bar.

GAO denied the protest. Law lets the office pick a firm of that class with no race. The price must stay at $5 million or less. The firm must be judged fit for the work. The price must be fair as well. Each bar was met in this case.
gao-gaoreports-b-311241:
Two firms won their protests. That ruling is B-311241, dated May 16, 2008. Carahsoft Technology Corporation and Allied Technology Group sought staff services deals. The race ran through the Federal Supply Schedule. Each firm won a deal that cut out pay plan services. No clear note told why that slice was cut. The firms fought the cut as a bare act with no base.

GAO sustained the protests. The file from the time of the pick is thin. It does not show why the slice was cut from the deals. The tale told in the fight clashes with that thin file. A pick must rest on notes made at the time, not tales told later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-241:
Individual Fishing Quotas, GAO-05-241 of March 11, 2005, bills the true cost of a tool that guards fish stocks. A quota gives each boat owner a set share of the catch. That cap can keep a fish stock sound. Running the caps takes staff time for grants, watch, and police work. Law says the trade, not the taxpayer, should pay those costs back.

GAO sizes the run costs for each quota plan in fiscal year 2003. It sets those next to the costs of the old way. It asks what the fisheries service got back. Costs swung wide, and payback fell short of the law.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-341:
Defense Ethics Program, GAO-05-341 of April 29, 2005, tests the guard rails on fair play in Pentagon buying. In fiscal year 2004, the department spent more than $200 billion on goods and services. Rules bar staff from use of inside facts for gain. They bind firms that sell to the Pentagon too. Each side owes clean hands.

GAO asks how the department trains and counsels its staff on those rules. It asks if the department can tell if the lessons work. It asks what the department knows of the firms' own good-play plans. Room to firm up the guards stands clear, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-441:
Army depots that repair helicopters, combat vehicles, and air defense systems are the subject of GAO-05-441, a report dated June 30, 2005. The depot group took in about $2.6 billion of orders in fiscal year 2004. It works through a working capital fund that charges customers the expected cost of work. GAO checked price rises, how gains and losses were shared, and carryover limits.

Hourly prices rose from $111.87 in fiscal year 2000 to $147.07 in fiscal year 2005, a 31 percent rise. Higher material costs drove most of the increase, which the Army had not fully studied. Gains and losses at single depots were spread across all depots, dulling the push to price work well. Carryover work also passed its allowed ceiling year after year. A new computer system at Tobyhanna Army Depot had run into trouble as well. The report ties these faults to weak oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-141:
Equipment readiness across the services is graded in GAO-06-141, a report issued on October 25, 2005. Wars in Iraq and Afghanistan wear out key gear even as the Defense Department funds new systems. GAO built a red, yellow, green rating framework for 30 equipment items. GAO asked two things: how sound is each item, and do funding plans keep it able to meet needs?

Readiness rates fell for most items between fiscal years 1999 and 2004. The drop sharpened in fiscal years 2003 and 2004. Heavy wartime use and aging, complex systems drove the slide. Trucks, combat vehicles, and helicopters ran far past normal peacetime use. Services had not fully built near- or long-term plans for every item. Some plans lacked money in the 2006 budget or ignored known shortfalls. GAO warned that unfixed gaps risk a deeper readiness slide.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-341:
Who actually collects unemployment benefits, and why, is modeled in GAO-06-341, issued March 7, 2006. The system dates to 1935 and runs as 53 state programs. In fiscal 2004 it paid $41.3 billion to 8.8 million jobless workers. Little was known about what drives an eligible worker to claim. GAO used a national sample of workers born from 1957 to 1964. Their records span 1979 through 2002. Statistical methods linked personal traits to claiming and to spell length. State eligibility rules entered the model as well.

Past benefit receipt itself shapes later claims, the design allowed GAO to test. A worker's industry also bears on both claiming and duration. The labor department praised the study while noting some caveats. Findings like these inform debates over benefit design. They separate the system's intent from its lived pattern. A safety net judged only by its rules misses who slips through.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-541:
A tax credit that drew factories to Puerto Rico was ending, and Congress wanted the facts. GAO's May 19, 2006 report, GAO-06-541, studies Puerto Rico's fiscal ties and economy. The federal possessions tax credit expires this year. It was designed to spur U.S. corporate investment in Puerto Rico and other insular areas. A Senate finance panel requested the study. Proposals for continued aid were before Congress.

GAO compares Puerto Rico's main economic trends with those of the United States. It reports changes in firms that claimed the credit. It explains how fiscal ties differ from those with states. It makes no recommendations. The governor called the report useful for policy choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-641:
New embassy building work by the Department of State is reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-641 (June 30, 2006). After two embassy bombings in Africa in 1998, the department began a $21 billion program to replace 201 unsafe and worn-out facilities. The Bureau of Overseas Buildings Operations runs the building program. GAO had reported in November 2004 on reforms the bureau put in place.

GAO found real progress in finishing new embassy and consulate compounds. Yet planning for the cost of running and maintaining the new sites was neither complete nor open. Those future costs could strain the department's budget for years. GAO urged better planning so new buildings do not become a burden once they open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-141:
Health premiums for federal workers rose every year from 1997 onward. In GAO-07-141, dated December 22, 2006, GAO studied the pace of those increases. The Federal Employees Health Benefits Program covers federal workers and retirees. The personnel office negotiates premiums with the plans in the program. GAO compared the program with other large purchasers, including California's public retiree system.

Premium growth in the program had recently slowed, GAO found. Average growth fell from a peak of 12.9 percent for 2002 to 1.8 percent for 2007. From 2003 on, the program's growth ran below that of other purchasers. Rising costs of care and drugs drove most of the growth that remained. Growth also varied widely by plan, from 0 percent to 15.5 percent for 2007. Draws on reserves helped hold down the 2006 and 2007 increases.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-241:
Some nursing homes fix violations, collect fines, then harm residents again. GAO tracked 63 such homes in GAO-07-241, a report dated March 26, 2007. The homes sat in 4 states holding about 22 percent of homes nationwide. All had past records of harming residents. GAO studied federal sanctions from fiscal years 2000 through 2005. It also judged how the Medicaid agency runs enforcement.

Almost half of the 63 homes kept cycling in and out of compliance, GAO found. Eight homes cycled 7 or more times. Fines were used more often than before: their use rate rose from 32 percent to 86 percent. But the median fine was only $350 a day in fiscal years 2003 through 2005. The allowed range runs from $50 to $3,000 a day. In 15 of 69 cases needing instant sanctions, none were imposed at once. Closures stayed rare and often delayed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-441:
Freedom of Information Act backlogs and uneven data are charted in GAO-07-441, a GAO report issued March 30, 2007. The act lets the public see agency records. Agencies must report each year on requests and processing times. A recent executive order told each agency to plan cuts to its backlog. GAO checked 25 major agencies.

GAO compared yearly reports and read each improvement plan. Trends showed heavy use of the act and slow handling at many shops. The data itself had flaws. One farm agency could not vouch for its own numbers. Median times alone hid the full spread of waits. GAO said averages and ranges would sharpen the picture. Clear totals across government would help too. The plans are a chance to fix both speed and record keeping.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-541:
Running the federal workers' retirement plan costs little, and GAO-07-541, issued May 14, 2007, verifies the thrift. The Federal Retirement Thrift Investment Board runs the Thrift Savings Plan. The plan is a core savings tool for federal staff. GAO reviewed the board's running costs as part of a wider oversight request.

Costs had in fact fallen. Fiscal year 2006 expenses sat near a 7-year low. GAO checked the board's habits against federal rules and peer agencies. It found practices that hold costs down, from tight budgets to phone-in board meetings. One idea: meet by phone each month and in person each quarter to trim travel. GAO's main push was wider benchmarking. Rather than compare only the total cost savers pay, the board should price its own tasks one by one against outside norms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-641:
Base closure orders hit Air National Guard flying units hardest, and GAO-07-641, issued May 16, 2007, tracks the scramble. The 2005 closure round touched 62 percent of the Guard's flying units. Fourteen units lose their flying mission outright. Others swap aircraft types or gain and shed planes. In all, hundreds of aircraft must move, and about 15,000 people must retrain or be recruited by 2011.

GAO worked at Air Force and Guard headquarters and in 11 affected states. It traced how spare missions get found for units that lose theirs. Plans exist at each step, but the steps chain tightly: one slip delays the next. No shared strategy yet covers risk control or plain word to the units. Savings hopes also dimmed; the study finds no yearly recurring savings for the Guard's part. GAO urged a single management strategy, shared with every stakeholder.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-141:
Tanker security against terror attacks is reviewed in GAO report GAO-08-141, dated December 10, 2007. Tankers bring in 55 percent of the nation's crude oil supply. They also carry liquefied gases and refined fuels. Attacks abroad have shown this supply chain can be hit. A 2002 suicide boat strike on the tanker Limburg killed 1 person and spilled 90,000 barrels of oil.

GAO mapped the main threats, from suicide strikes to standoff attacks. It weighed steps taken to guard tankers and the hurdles agencies face. It also reviewed plans for responding to a hit. GAO urged a national plan to balance new tanker duties with other Coast Guard work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-41:
With its report GAO-08-41, dated December 10, 2007, GAO turns to Postal Service facility management. The Postal Service runs about 34,000 facilities under money pressure and rising competition. GAO visited 58 facilities and checked how the agency tracks, maintains, and sizes its estate.

The agency's Facility Database held duplicate and conflicting records, lacked the data to track performance over time, and was not used as a shared source by major departments. An inspection of 651 sites chosen at random found two-thirds in less than acceptable shape, yet the full repair backlog was undocumented. Money limits pushed the agency toward emergency fixes over cheaper preventive care. GAO recommended fixing or replacing the database, ranking repairs with care, and using clear tests to close unneeded retail sites. The Postal Service agreed with only part of the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-541:
A special counsel's spending is audited in GAO financial audit GAO-08-541, dated March 31, 2008. Federal law requires statements of expenditures from independent counsels every 6 months, with GAO auditing them. No independent counsels were active in this period, but the audit covers the office of Special Counsel Patrick J. Fitzgerald.

GAO audited the statement for the 6 months ended September 30, 2007. It found the statement presented fairly, in all material respects, on the cash basis of accounting described in its notes. The office also kept effective internal control over financial reporting and followed the laws and rules that apply. GAO did not judge whether any single expense was reasonable or proper, a point the report states plainly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-641:
Big science builds, from labs to light sources, test whether the Department of Energy can manage projects well. GAO-08-641, dated May 30, 2008, grades the Office of Science on 42 projects. The office had set a 20-year plan in 2003 to build and upgrade research sites.

Of 27 finished projects, 24 stayed within the cost first promised. A full 21 finished on time or early. Strong leadership, skilled staff, and strict outside reviews got credit for the record. Of 15 projects still under way, 9 looked on track. GAO urged the wider department to copy the review habits that worked here.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-741:
College costs rose 20 to 38 percent over a decade, by school type. Veteran students mix grants, loans, and GI benefits to pay those bills. GAO-08-741, dated June 20, 2008, compares the aid of first-year veteran and nonveteran students in the 2005 to 2006 school year.

Veterans got about the same federal student aid as peers like them in income and school type. Once GI benefits are added, veterans came out ahead on total aid. Tables break the sums down for public 2-year schools, public and private 4-year schools, and for-profit schools. The study helps weigh how GI aid stacks with normal student aid.
guide-to-self-knowledge-the-fundamental-:
T. H. Pons published his Guide to Self-Knowledge at Boston in 1841, from the general phrenological depot on Washington Street. Its full title sets out the system: the fundamental powers of the human mind, practically applied, as manifested through the brain, in seven degrees of development. Introductory remarks commend phrenology, in its advocates' claim, as the only true and practical science of the human mind.

Pons teaches the reader to read character from the shape of the head, organ by organ. Faculties, feelings, and intellect are mapped and graded, with advice on turning the knowledge to use in education and self-rule. Phrenology is now a dead science, but in 1841 it drew crowds and filled depots. The book is a neat, earnest manual of that science at its American height, and a window on how people then sought to know themselves.
hawthorne-grandfathers-chair-1841:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Whole History of Grandfather's Chair in 1841, a history for children. The book tells New England history, from the Puritans to the Revolution, through one old chair. Hawthorne wrote it for young readers in the days before his fame as a romancer grew.

Grandfather, in a Boston parlor, traces his chair's owners through persecutions, wars, and witch trial years. The chair hears of Endicott, King Philip's War, and the Boston Tea Party in its long life. Children Laurence, Clara, and little Alice question, doubt, and dream over the tales by the fireside. Hawthorne makes dry annals into scenes a child can feel, without hiding the era's harsh deeds. It was a pioneer work of American history written for the young at home.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
The third part of chapter five in John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands defends Sainte Aldegonde. Marnix of Sainte Aldegonde, Antwerp's burgomaster, stands discouraged and calumniated after the city's surrender. Motley prints his appeal: he claims his honour shall be protected against his calumniators. All men in public affairs, the letter argues, face such hazards.

Aldegonde submits himself to Him who knows all hearts. He swears he sought God's glory and the people's welfare in the affair of Antwerp. Motley builds the chapter around such documents, letting the accused speak. The fall of Antwerp ruined reputations as well as walls. This portion is a small courtroom drama inside the great history, weighing treason charges against a patriot who negotiated with Parma because his city was starving.
international-weekly-miscellany-of-liter:
Tea-smuggling in Russia heads the International Weekly Miscellany for July 29, 1850, at New York. That was volume one, number five. The article says the Russian-German frontier trade was large but lacked romance. Corrupt officers there were often partners with the smugglers they should catch, it reports.

An essay inside asks where a man of positive ideas can be found in these days. Priest, lawyer, litterateur, and politician are each dismissed as phrase makers. Poems, tales, and reviews fill the rest of the number. Each issue in this run gives a different lead, by design of the weekly form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-or-raba-ra: Abba bar Jeremiah, also called Raba or Rabbah, was a Babylonian amora of the third century. He was the son of Jeremiah ben Abba and a pupil of Rab. He lived at Sura and passed on the sayings of Rab and of Samuel. One saying of his reads Proverbs, chapter 9, as a picture of the Messianic age. Its house is the new Temple, its seven pillars the seven years after the fall of Gog and Magog, and its feast the feast in Ezekiel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-hay:
Rabbi Abraham ben Hayyim lived at Narbonne in the first half of the thirteenth century. He was a brother of Reuben ben Hayyim and a teacher of Menahem Meiri. About 1240 he left home and settled at Villefranche-de-Confluent in Roussillon.

His son Levi ben Abraham, a philosopher, was born there and later joined the religious debates of 1303 to 1306. Meiri praised Abraham in the highest terms and ranked him among Narbonne's famed rabbis. The entry also links him to four liturgical poems used at Carpentras. One bears his name in acrostic form, and another his fuller name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-mus: Abraham ben Musa was a Moroccan rabbi and cabalist of the first half of the seventeenth century. He studied the Cabala with Abraham Azulai. He wrote commentaries on several treatises of the Talmud. His commentary on Nazir was printed in the collection Berit Ya'akob at Leghorn in 1800. His commentaries on Yoma and Sotah rest in manuscript in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. The entry lists no birth or death year for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adonai-adonai-8: Adonai, Adonai is a hymn on the thirteen traits of God. It sits in the prayers of the fifth middle day of the Ten Days of Penitence. In the north rites it is sung in full in the last rite of the Day of Atonement. Its five verses bear the acrostic Amittai, the author's name. Its chorus is built from Exodus xxxiv. 6 and 7. A plain, sad tune goes with it. The tune uses a Polish form of an Eastern scale. It is not of great age, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-of-irak-941:
Aha of Irak is a shadowy figure in the history of Hebrew writing. He is said to have invented the Assyrian or Babylonian system of vowel-points and accents. That system sets its marks above the line. Yet he is known only from Karaite sources, which the entry calls somewhat unreliable.

Scholars named in the entry place him in different centuries. Pinsker linked him to Nissi ben Noah, a link later work rejects. Furst puts him in the first half of the sixth century. Furst also suggests he may be the Saborean Aha bar Abbuhu, who died in 511.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-of-ha:
Alexander of Hales was an English theologian of the Franciscan order. He was born in Gloucester and died in Paris in 1245, where he taught. The entry calls him the founder of the new scholasticism of that century. In his "Summa" he first made wide use of Aristotle's Logic in Latin. Scholars named him the irrefutable doctor.

Toward the Jews he showed rare fairness. Jews, he argued, must not be lumped with pagans or Saracens. They should be borne with, since Christians got the Law through them. Jesus was of their race, and Scripture bids they be preserved. Jews did no wrong, he held, by writing their beliefs in the Talmud. Public blasphemy could be punished, but no more harshly than a Christian's. He opposed forcing Jews into the faith by threats. And Jewish property must never be seized, since men allowed to live must keep their livelihood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alvarez-or-alva:
Alvarez is the name of a Hispano-Portuguese family. Its members include scholars, rich men, and martyrs. Branches of the family settled in four lands. They made homes in Holland, France, England, and America. The entry gives short lives for more than a dozen members. Some died at the stake for their faith.

Isabel Nunez Alvarez kept a synagogue in Madrid. She was burned on July 4, 1632. Juan Alvarez was the first Lima victim of the Inquisition. He was burned with his whole family about 1580. Two men of the name wrote verse in Amsterdam. A Moses Alvarez was an early settler in Newport.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anschel-1441:
Anschel was a rabbi at Cracow who flourished in the first half of the sixteenth century. He wrote Mirkebet ha-Mishneh, The Second Chariot, a Judeo-German concordance to the Bible, with a long introduction. The now rare book first came out at Cracow in 1534.

It was reprinted there in 1584 under the title Sefer R. Anschel. The entry spends much of its space clearing up a mix-up in Wolf's bibliography. Wolf confused Anschel with a later namesake from Posen who turned feast prayers into German. Zunz separated the two men, the entry reports, and raised a further guess about the later man's family link to Rabbi Meir Lublin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apion-1641:
Apion was a Greek grammarian and sophist of Alexandria famed for his bitter hatred of the Jews. Born in Egypt's Great Oasis between 20 and 30 B.C., he died probably at Rome between 45 and 48. His very name, drawn from the bull-god Apis, points to Egyptian birth.

Trained in the house of Didymus the Great, he took over Alexandria's Homeric grammar school when Theon died. He preferred fancy word-roots and allegory to strict method, the entry notes. His real fame came as a traveling lecturer on Homer, popular across the Greek world. The entry then turns to his attacks on the Jews and the answers they drew, above all from Josephus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archon-archonte:
Archon was the title of a member of the governing body in free Jewish communities across the Roman empire. The entry names Alexandria, Antioch, Berenice in Cyrenaica, Rome, and Tlos in Lycia among such cities. At Alexandria the archons formed the gerusia, the council Augustus set in place of a single ethnarch.

At the end of the first century, nine archons headed the community at Berenice, while Alexandria had more than thirty-eight. Rome had several communities, each with its archon, as their tomb inscriptions show. Archons were chosen at set seasons, some for a term and some for life. The bare title was sometimes even given to women and children, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aruvas-arovas-i:
Isaac Aruvas, a rabbi and author of the seventeenth century, was a son of Hananiah Aruvas. He held rabbinical posts in several African communities and later settled in Venice. His name rests on two books printed there. Emet we-Emunah, Truth and Faith, came out in Hebrew and Italian in 1672 as a religious school book.

That book sets out the 613 commandments in the order of Maimonides, adds his thirteen articles of faith, and gives ritual laws modeled on Joseph Caro. Moses Zakut and others praised it warmly. His second book, Zibhe Zedek, Thank-Offerings of Righteousness, printed in 1662, is a rhymed alphabetical poem on the laws of slaughtering animals, with notes appended.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-zebi-ben-:
Asher Zebi ben David was a Hasidic rabbi of Koretz in Volhynia and later a maggid, a preacher, at Ostrowo in Russian Poland. He flourished at the start of the nineteenth century. He had studied under Baer of Meseritz, the successor of Israel Baal-Shem, founder of Hasidism. His book Ma'yan ha-Hokmah, Spring of Wisdom, came out at Korets in 1817.

The book holds cabalistic sermons on the Pentateuch and other Bible books. Zweifel, writing in defense of Hasidism, quotes sayings from it with praise. Yet Zweifel fairly ends with one saying that shows Asher's contempt for men who study the laws of nature or secular science. The entry thus gives both sides of the preacher: honored voice of his movement, and open foe of outside learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assing-ludmilla:
Ludmilla Assing was a German author. She was born in Hamburg on Feb. 22, 1821, and died in Florence, Italy, on March 25, 1880. She was the daughter of Dr. David Assing and Rosa Maria Assing. After her parents died, she lived in Berlin with her uncle Varnhagen von Ense. In his house she met Humboldt, Prince Pückler-Muskau, and Bettina von Arnim.

From 1861 Assing lived in Florence, where she founded a public school with required German teaching. Her writing leaned toward biography, in the manner of her uncle. She translated Mazzini and Piero Cironi from Italian, and she wrote lives of Sophie von La Roche and Prince Pückler-Muskau. Prussia sentenced her in 1863 and 1864 for editing her uncle's papers, which aired court scandals. Living in Italy, she escaped the punishment and was pardoned in 1866.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-augustus-iii-21:
Augustus the Third was elector of Saxony and king of Poland. He was the son of Augustus the Strong. He was born at Dresden in 1696 and died there in 1763. Raised a Protestant, he secretly became a Catholic in 1712 and owned it openly five years later. He lacked his father's gifts but shared his taste for splendor.

He kept the privileges of the Jews on paper, but they became a dead letter in practice. Soon after taking the throne in 1733 he laid a special body tax on nearly every Jew passing through Dresden. Only children under ten were freed later that year, after a petition from Dresden Jews. In Poland, blood charges and attacks on Jewish property and synagogues were frequent. Agents of the pope tried for two years to stop the charges, with little effect. The Frankist movement also broke out under his rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-hanan-2241:
Baal-hanan is the name of two men in the Bible. The first was a king of Edom, listed in Genesis among the kings who reigned there before Israel had a king. He is called a son of Achbor, but his home city is not given. A scholar cited here thinks the entry in Genesis is tangled. On his reading, Baal-hanan was in truth the father of the next king, Hadad.

The second Baal-hanan was a man of Geder. King David put him in charge of the olive trees and sycamores in the low plains of Judah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-dob-ben-sh: Dob ben Shraga Baer was an author who lived in Berlin at the start of the nineteenth century. This entry is only two sentences, and it tells a single fact about his work. He wrote "Naḥale Debash" (Streams of Honey), printed at Berlin in 1832. The book holds many extracts taken from various Hebrew books. Those extracts deal mainly, the entry says, with philosophical and ethical subjects. Nothing is given here about his birth, his training, or the rest of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-banishment-or-h:
Banishment, in ancient Israel, meant being shut out of one's native land, for a time or for good, as a divine punishment. Adam's driving from Eden and Cain's from the Lord's presence are its first cases. In ancient times it came only from God, never from men. To be driven from the land of Yhwh seemed as much as being told, "Go, serve other gods," since worship at the sanctuary was cut off.

Hope softened the doom: God would gather the exiles back to the land of their fathers. A rabbinic half compares Israel's exile to Adam's, as a divorce after faithlessness. "Galut" also names the flight of an unwitting manslayer to a city of refuge. The rabbis list the sins that bring banishment on men: idolatry, incest, murder, and neglect of the year of release. Leaving the Holy Land of one's own will counts as a great sin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnett-john-fr:
John Francis Barnett, an English musician, was born at London on October 16, 1837, nephew of the composer John Barnett. A pupil of Dr. Wylde, he won the queen's scholarship at the Royal Academy of Music in 1850 and again in 1852. He made his début as a pianist in 1853. From 1856 he studied three years at the Leipsic Conservatory under Moscheles, Plaidy, and Hauptmann.

In 1860 he played at the Gewandhaus and returned to England as teacher, concert-pianist, and composer. In 1883 he became a professor at the Royal College of Music. His works include the oratorio "The Raising of Lazarus" (1876). His cantatas include "The Ancient Mariner" (1867), "Paradise and the Peri" (1870), and "The Building of the Ship" (1880). He also wrote a symphony, a piano concerto, and many smaller pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassani-jehiel-: Jehiel ben Hayyim Bassani was a legal scholar and rabbi at Constantinople in the seventeenth century. His book of rulings came out there in 1737, after his death. The entry praises those rulings for keen analysis and a terse style. Bassani traded learned letters with leading teachers of the East. Other men's books of rulings cite him, and Judah Lerma of Belgrade was his pupil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bastard-10341:
Bastard, in Jewish law, centers on the Hebrew term mamzer, which the entry says is worse than a child born outside wedlock. A mamzer is the child of a union that could never be a lawful marriage, such as adultery or incest within barred degrees.

The entry works through disputes among early and later teachers over hard cases. It notes the rule that kept such a child and his line from marrying into the congregation. It also shows how teachers narrowed that harsh rule over time. Cases on inheritance, proof, and a mother's word close the account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-bernhard-2:
Bernhard Beer was a German author born in July 1801 at Dresden, where he died on July 1, 1861. Barred in practice from public schools by the narrow spirit of Saxony, he learned from private teachers and his own study. The classics, Herder, and Mendelssohn shaped him.

Beer was the first to bring German sermons into synagogue use at Dresden, though a layman. He taught poor Jewish children without pay and in 1829 helped found a society to spread trades, art, and science among Jews. He also fought in print for Jewish rights and built a rich library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmonte-moses-:
Moses Belmonte was a poet and translator, the eighth child of Jacob Belmonte. Born in 1619, he died at Amsterdam on May 29, 1647. He learned under Saul Morteira and helped edit that teacher's sermons, printed in 1645.

Belmonte rendered the Song of Songs into Spanish, printed in Hebrew letters at Venice and Amsterdam. He also turned the Sayings of the Fathers into Spanish, issued at Amsterdam in 1644. A poem of his against false converts has been reprinted. In 1639 he founded a charitable society. De Castro later reprinted that poem in his book of tombstones from the Dutch Jewish graves at Oudekerk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-judah-eliez:
Eliezer Ben Judah, born at Luzhky on Jan. 7, 1858, was the son of Judah Perlman. Educated in Talmud at Polotzk and later in Paris, he settled in Jerusalem in 1881. There he pushed the idea that Hebrew could live again as a spoken tongue, starting in his own household.

As editor he worked on the paper Ḥabaẓelet and then founded Ha-Ẓebi in 1885, sold cheaply in Jerusalem streets. The entry lists his books on the land of Israel, on Jewish history, and a full Hebrew dictionary with French and German renderings. It also notes the paper's halt and his arrest after sharp attacks on opponents at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benfey-theodor-:
Theodor Benfey, a German Sanskrit scholar, was born at Nörten, in Hanover, on Jan. 28, 1809, and died on June 26, 1881. The son of a Jewish merchant well read in the Talmud, he trained at Göttingen and took his degree in 1828. He later turned from the classics toward Sanskrit study.

At Göttingen he taught a wide range, from Indian antiquities to the Avesta and the tongues of India. His Greek root lexicon won the Volney prize. He edited the Sama Veda in 1848 and wrote full and short grammars of Sanskrit. In 1848 he became a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berechiah-ben-n:
Berechiah ben Natronai ha-Nakdan was a fabulist, grammarian, and writer on ethics. Scholars long placed him in Provence about 1260, but fresh proof put him in England late in the twelfth century. A line in his own preface points to the English massacre of 1190.

He is known chiefly for his Fox Fables, a set of more than one hundred tales in rhymed prose. They retell the beast tales that went under Æsop's name in the Middle Ages. Some match the fables of Marie de France, and the entry weighs how the two sets relate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-ignac: Ignacy Bernstein, a Polish book lover and writer on proverbs, was born on Jan. 30, 1836, at Vinnitza, in Podolia. His father ran a large banking house there, and learned tutors raised the boy. In 1858 he moved with his parents to Warsaw, where he ranked high in the Jewish community. At his urging a Jewish library was founded at the Great Synagogue in 1881. His great work was a catalogue of his own library of some 4,800 works on proverbs and folk lore, printed in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezalel-b-josep: Bezalel b. Joseph, called Yosel, was a Russian Talmudist. He served as rabbi at Orlo, in the government of Grodno. His work fell at the start of the nineteenth century. The entry gives one main fact about him. He wrote a collection of responsa. He published it in 1807 at Byelostok. Two catalogues are cited as sources. The entry offers no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bithiah-3341:
Bithiah was Pharaoh's daughter in First Chronicles. Mered of Judah married her, the verse says. The Midrash calls her Moses' foster-mother. Rabbinic lore explains her name in a wordplay. God called her His daughter, bat Yah. She had called Moses her son. She is also read as a convert. She gave up her father's idolatry, tradition says.

Legends crowd around her Nile bathing scene. Her skin disease vanished when she touched the casket. Her arm stretched miraculously to reach it. Gabriel slew attendants who protested. Through Moses' prayer she escaped the first-born plague. She is counted among those entering paradise alive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boas-eduard-344:
Eduard Boas was a German author and traveler born at Landsberg-on-the-Warthe on Jan. 1, 1815. He died there in June, 1853. His parents meant him for trade and sent him through southern Europe to learn it.

Boas turned the trip into sketches, novels, and verse instead. His first book came out in 1837. He wrote addenda to the works of Schiller and of Goethe. Later books drew on Italy and Scandinavia. His last named work, on Schiller and Goethe, came out in 1852. Among his other books was a comic romance of travel in Italy. Verse and tales from India and Scandinavia followed in later years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonn-jonas-ben-: Jonas ben Moses Bonn was a physician in Frankfort-on-the-Main in the seventeenth century. He was not employed by the community. Still, his name stands on the articles of 1656 between the congregation and its physicians. Those articles bound Jewish doctors to visit the poor free of charge. They must answer calls day and night. They could not treat patients outside the Jewish quarters without leave. Nor could they head the congregation before the age of sixty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandon-jules-b:
Jules Benjamin Brandon was a French officer from an old Sephardic family. He was born on Sept. 24, 1833, at Paris and died on May 22, 1871. His family had come to France from Spain after the exodus of 1492.

Brandon entered the artillery from the Ecole Polytechnique in 1853. At the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian war he asked for active service at once. He was captured at Sedan and held in Germany till the armistice. He hurried back to serve the army of Versailles against the Commune. On entering Paris he was killed by a stray ball from a window. His general placed his name first on the daily roll as a lasting honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brother-3741:
Brother first means a son of the same father and mother, or of either parent. The entry works through Bible passages on what brothers owed each other. A brother gave consent to a sister's marriage. Mosaic law barred marriage between brother and sister, yet required a man to marry his childless brother's widow. That duty, and the rite for refusing it, are set out from Deuteronomy.

Beyond family, the word widens step by step. It can mean a kinsman, a tribesman, or a fellow member of the nation. Kindred tribes and covenant friends also count as brothers. Later uses point to fellow men as children of one God. The entry closes with polite and figurative senses, such as companion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calno-3941: Calno was a city named in Isaiah beside Hamath and Samaria and set against Carchemish. Amos calls it Calneh, but the entry warns not to mix it with the Babylonian Calneh of Genesis. That older city has been matched with Niffer or with Ctesiphon. Since the Isaiah towns are Syrian, a Babylonian site cannot fit. The Greek version even blurs the two names. Assyrian tribute lists offer a better match in a place called Kulnia. Several scholars cited here back that match or one close to it, near Arpad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carlos-david-co: David Cohen Carlos was a Spanish writer who lived at Hamburg in the first half of the seventeenth century. He translated the Song of Songs into Spanish. His version appeared at Hamburg in 1631 with a title stating that it was rendered from the Chaldaic tongue into Spanish. The bibliographer Wolf reported that the work also appeared as a manuscript in a catalogue issued at The Hague in 1728, a note the short entry passes on without more detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catalan-catalan: Abraham Catalan, also called Catalano, was a physician in Padua who died in 1642. He wrote Olam Hafuk, a treatise on the plague of 1630-31. That work stayed in manuscript and was never printed. During the plague years he was very active in his city, the entry notes. No other work, post, or family detail is given in the short text. Two later books on the Cantarini family and on Hebrew bibliography are cited as its sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-characa-4241: Characa was a city about 750 stadia distant from Caspis. It was the seat of the Jews called Tubieni. Judas Maccabeus went to that place after his conquest of Caspis, as II Maccabees xii. 17 reports. The hosted entry runs to three short sentences. It gives the distance, the Jewish group seated there, and the visit by Judas. It names no ruler, no battle at the city itself, and no later fate for Characa or its Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chios-4341:
Chios, an island in the Aegean Sea held by Turkey, held a small Jewish community whose early start the entry cannot date for sure. Local legend ties its cemetery to Jacob Ben Asher, author of the Turim, said to have died there in 1340. His supposed tomb drew pilgrims, and the synagogue bore his name.

Under Ottoman rule from 1595 the community slowly grew, led in later years by named chief rabbis. The entry dwells on the earthquake of April 4, 1881, which killed 21 Jews and destroyed the ghetto. It closes with communal offices, a meat tax, and two schools aided by the Alliance Israélite Universelle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-4441: Coen, whose given name and dates are unknown, served as physician-in-ordinary to Prince Vassile Lupu of Moldavia. Lupu ruled from 1634 to 1654. When enemies plotted to topple the prince, Coen shielded him. He also stood high with the Sultan of Turkey. The Sultan trusted him to carry Lupu secret papers. They told of a planned Swedish-Russian attack on Turkey. Venice sought his counsel too, two letters show. His sway likely won Lupu's rulings in favor of Moldavia's Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coponius-4641: Coponius was the first procurator of Judea, in office about 6 C.E. He held knightly rank and had the power of life and death. His term saw the revolt of Judas the Galilean. The revolt grew from the Roman census under Quirinus. During Passover, Samaritans slipped into the Temple and scattered human bones along the colonnade. Soon after, Coponius was recalled to Rome. Marcus Ambibulus replaced him. One Temple door bore his name, while his own stance toward the Jews is not clearly known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremieu-4741: Crémieu is a town in the ancient province of Dauphiné, France. By the fifteenth century it had an important Jewish community. In 1441 the governor renewed the Jews' privileges for seven years. The price was fifty florins, to be gathered by two named Jewish collectors. The Jews refused to pay and left in large numbers. The dauphin Louis recalled them in 1449. He promised lighter terms if they would reopen their banking houses. The tax would drop to one ounce of fine silver.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-d-da-de-in-the-: Dabbasheth is the town this short entry describes. It lay on the border-line of Zebulun. The one Bible reference given is Joshua, chapter nineteen, verse 11. Conder identified the place with Dabsheh. Those ruins stand near the hills east of Acco. The Septuagint reading of the name is given as Baitharaba. The entry states nothing more: no size, no later history, and no other source. Readers get a border town's name, its tribe, its Bible verse, and a modern guess at its site.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ferdinand:
Ferdinand David was a violinist and violin teacher born at Hamburg on January 19, 1810. After only two years of study with Spohr and Hauptmann at Cassel, he made his début in 1825 at the Gewandhaus in Leipsic. He played in Berlin, then spent 1829 to 1835 in Russia, touring cities such as Riga, St. Petersburg, and Moscow.

In 1835 Mendelssohn chose David as concert-master of the Gewandhaus concerts, a post he kept until his death on July 19, 1873. Pupils such as Joachim studied with him. He edited nearly the whole classical violin repertoire for study, above all the collection "Die Hohe Schule des Violinspiels." He also composed five concertos and many smaller pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-gotthar:
Gotthard Deutsch was a theologian born at Kanitz, Austria, on January 31, 1859, the son of a Talmudist and heir of a rabbinical family. He trained early in rabbinical books, entered the gymnasium of Nikolsburg in 1868, and graduated in 1876. He then studied at the Breslau seminary and university and took his rabbinical diploma in Vienna in 1881.

Deutsch taught religion at Brünn, then held a state post teaching religion in Moravian high schools. In 1891 he gave up a rabbinate at Brüx to become professor of Jewish history and philosophy of religion at the Hebrew Union College of Cincinnati. He still held that chair in 1903. He wrote widely for Jewish and general papers in Europe and America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eduyot-evidence:
Eduyot, meaning Evidences, is the seventh treatise of the Mishnah's order Nezikin. It is also called Behirta, the Choice of laws. After the Temple fell, religious questions had to be settled by majority vote. Teachers then gathered unshakable traditions as a firm base. That gathering grew into this treatise.

The entry stresses that Eduyot has no single subject. Its rulings touch purity, tithes, marriage, and much more. Only the sages' names loosely bind it together. Chapter one reopens old fights between Hillel's and Shammai's schools. Later chapters give space to Hanina, Akiba, and Dosa ben Harkinas. Space given to each teacher matches, the entry says, his weight in the debates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-b-azriel: Elijah ben Azriel of Wilna was a grammarian and author. He died after the year 1748. The entry lists five books from his hand. Two give rules for reading Hebrew aloud. One is a full set of rules for Hebrew grammar. Another glosses a work by Menahem di Lonsano. He also wrote a tale in verse form. A last book gives fresh notes on a code of law. The books came out in towns across Germany and Holland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-empereur-consta: Constantin l'Empereur was a Dutch professor of theology. He also taught the tongues of the East at Leyden. He was born at Bremen in July of 1591. He died at Leyden on July 1, 1648. His father had fled home for reasons of faith. Constantin took a chair at Harderwijk in 1619. In 1627 Leyden called him to a new post. That chair was set up for debate with the Jews. Its aims were defense of the faith and winning converts. He did the work with tact and calm, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-erub-5841:
Erub means a mixture, or the joining of things kept separate, and the entry explains its uses in Sabbath law. Carrying goods between private and public ground is barred on the Sabbath. An erub softens that bar. A rod or wire across an open gap can complete a fence. The space then counts as enclosed, and carrying inside it is allowed.

One form joins the homes around a court. Each household adds food to a shared meal, so the court counts as one home. Another form shifts a person's Sabbath base by placing food 2,000 cubits away. That lets him walk a fresh 2,000 cubits from the new base. The entry cites Maimonides and the Shulhan Aruk for the rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fayer-ladislaus: Ladislaus Fayer was a Hungarian jurist born at Kecskemet in 1842. He took his law doctorate in 1870 and became a lecturer at Budapest three years later. In 1886 he won the chair of criminal law, which he still held when the entry was written. He founded the university seminar for penal law. His books treat the reform of criminal process and court practice from 1884 to 1894. He edited two law journals and served the Society of Hungarian Jurists as secretary. The academy elected him in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-freimann-aaron-:
