What decides whether a stem cell renews itself or becomes a specialized cell is a core question in biology. The team looked at two receptors, CB1 and CB2, and the cannabinoid signals that bind them.

They report where these receptors are expressed and what they do as stem cells form embryoid bodies and turn toward blood cell lines. Cannabinoids are best known from cannabis and from adult tissues. Finding their machinery at work in early embryos opens a new angle on how cell fate is steered.
plos-pone-0000741:
Mohammed Bakkali studied short bits of DNA that some bacteria go out of their way to take in. Many bacteria can absorb DNA from their surroundings and add it to their own genome. That uptake has real medical and money stakes, since it can spread drug resistance genes. Two bacterial families, Pasteurellaceae and Neisseriaceae, prefer DNA that carries certain short sequences.

Those favored sequences appear far more often in the bacteria's own genomes than chance would explain. Bakkali asks how such short sequences build up, move, and persist over time. One idea is self-recognition: by favoring their own sequence marks, bacteria trade genes mostly with kin. The study maps the pattern and weighs what could keep it in place.
plos-pone-0000841:
John P.A. Ioannidis, Nikolaos A. Patsopoulos and Evangelos Evangelou asked why pooled gene studies so often disagree with each other. A meta-analysis pools the results of many studies into one sum, and checks how much the parts differ. Such pooling was used more and more on genome-wide association studies. There, teams hunt the same gene effects and try to copy each other's finds.

The team's subject is heterogeneity: real gaps between study results. Some gaps are noise. Others are signs that groups, designs, or biases truly differ. Gene hunters who know how much gap to expect will not cheer too soon, or drop a true find too fast. The study is a guide to reading pooled claims with care.
plos-pone-0000941:
Biju Parekkadan, Daan van Poll, Kazuhiro Suganuma and colleagues tested whether molecules from stem cells can rescue a failing liver, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fulminant hepatic failure is sudden, severe liver collapse. Calming the immune system may offer a way out that avoids needing donor liver cells.

Mesenchymal stem cells, taken from bone marrow, are known to temper immune responses. The team asked whether the molecules these cells release, rather than the cells themselves, could reverse the failure. A cell free treatment would be easier to store, dose and approve. The study is an early step toward that idea, tested in a severe disease model.
plos-pone-0001041:
S. Hoyt Peckham, David Maldonado Diaz, Andreas Walli and colleagues documented turtle bycatch in small scale Pacific fisheries, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Industrial fishing bycatch, animals caught by accident, is known to harm seabirds, mammals and turtles. The impact of small scale coastal fisheries had been largely overlooked.

The team show that such fisheries jeopardize endangered Pacific loggerhead turtles. Small boats working close to shore can meet turtles where they feed and breed. Counting that harm changes the conservation ledger: protecting turtles means working with local fishers, not just fleets. The paper pairs the finding with the scale of coastal fishing worldwide.
plos-pone-0001141:
Northeast India is the only land bridge between the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It may also have been a corridor for early human migrations into East Asia. B. Mohan Reddy and co-authors present genetic evidence on that route in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their focus is the Austro-Asiatic speaking tribes of the region.

The Austro-Asiatic language family is considered among the oldest in this part of Asia. The authors argue that these tribes supply a genetic link between South and Southeast Asia that had been missing. Their data bear on how the first peopling of East Asia unfolded.
plos-pone-0001241:
In some animals, RNA from mitochondria, the cell's power plants, turns up outside them, positioned in the egg at the spot that seeds germ cells. Youichirou Ninomiya and Shizuko Ichinose checked whether mammals do the same, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The phenomenon had been reported in several non-mammal groups but not in mammals.

The authors examined the expression and distribution of mitochondrial ribosomal RNA in the mouse oocyte and zygote. Whether the RNA localizes to a germ cell determinant in mammals bears on how universal that mechanism is. Their study brings the mammal case into an otherwise broader story.
plos-pone-0001341:
Two groups of tiny cyanobacteria, Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus, carry out much of the ocean's photosynthesis. Christophe Six and colleagues studied how they divide the ocean's light environment between them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Phytoplankton cells are entrained in the water column and so are often exposed to rapid changes in irradiance within the upper mixed layer.

The authors report that light variability illuminates niche-partitioning among marine picocyanobacteria: the groups specialize on different light regimes. Who wins where determines how much carbon the ocean fixes. Their work links a physical variable, flickering light, to global primary production.
plos-pone-0001441:
Farba Karam and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a blood test for hidden TB in people with HIV. Finding and treating hidden TB in this group can cut illness and death. The team tested a home built blood test that reads a key immune signal. They asked if the test stays sound as HIV gets worse.

They report the test kept its power to spot hidden TB in HIV patients. But its readings did shift with how far HIV had gone. That caveat matters for how results are read in clinics. The work supports use of the test, with care, in places where both ills are common.
plos-pone-0001541:
Phillipa Hay and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eating disorder acts in South Australia. Proof on whether such ills are rising had been mixed. The team used two matched community surveys ten years apart. Both asked the same questions on eating acts in the general public.

They found that eating disorder acts had in fact risen over that span. A matched design makes the trend claim much firmer than loose reports. A real rise urges more funds for early care and school based guards. It also prompts work on what drove the rise in that decade.
plos-pone-0001641:
Arnaud Muller, Elise Glattard, Omar Taleb, and their co-authors measured morphine made by the body itself in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Morphine is best known as the main active drug in opium from poppies. Yet it also turns up in animal tissues and cell types, including the mammalian brain. Its making pathway had already been traced in a human nerve cell line.

The team studied a human cell line called SH-SY5Y and the cerebellum of mice to pin down where this in-house morphine occurs. The full text gives the detection methods and the amounts found. It also covers what the pattern suggests about why nerve cells would make a pain drug of their own. The work adds to the view that morphine-like signals form part of the brain's own chemistry, not just plant medicine.
plos-pone-0001741:
Vikram Paruchuri, Anil Prasad, Kevin McHugh, and their co-authors studied a calcium-binding protein in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. S100A7 is a small protein first noted in psoriatic skin lesions and later in squamous tumors of skin, lung, and breast. Its expression tracks with high-grade HER-positive tumors and a high risk of progression.

The team reports that lowering S100A7 inhibits signaling from epidermal growth factor in breast cancer cells. It also blocks the formation of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. The full text gives the cell experiments and pathway readouts. Bone is where breast cancer often spreads, so a protein linking tumor signals to bone-eating cells is a target worth attention.
plos-pone-0001841:
Jordi Moya-Laraño, Dejan Vinković, Eva De Mas, and their co-authors modeled spider body evolution with pendulum physics in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Animals were thought to gain from pendulum mechanics as they hang and swing, trading height for speed. Convincing evidence was lacking.

The team shows the shape evolution of spiders is predicted by pendulum mechanics. Leg and body proportions match what good swinging needs. The full text gives the model and the species data. A law of physics that predicts anatomy across species is a rare result. It explains why hanging spiders evolved their marked long legged build.
plos-pone-0001941:
Nita Bharti and co-authors modeled how measles spreads along coasts in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Models help map how epidemics move through space and time, and what control steps might do. A leading model for spread between places, the gravity model, weighs both distance and the size of towns.

The team asked whether the mix of land and sea at coasts warps that spread in ways plain models miss. Coastal areas bunch people in lines and ports rather than even spreads. If models ignore that shape, they may misjudge where measles goes next. Better maps of spread help aim vaccines where they count most.
plos-pone-0002041:
Karine Bagramyan and co-authors built a test that spots botulinum toxin at vanishing levels, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Botulinum neurotoxin is among the most potent poisons known, a threat in spoiled food and a feared bioterror agent. A fast, cheap, and highly sensitive test for the active toxin in foods or blood was badly wanted.

As the title states, their method detects toxin type A at attomolar levels. That is a billionth of a billionth of a mole per liter, even in complex samples. Such sensitivity could flag tainted food early and let doctors track the toxin in patients.
plos-pone-0002141:
Amanda Dixon-McIver, Phil East, Charles Mein, and co-authors profiled small RNA molecules in leukemia patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Acute myeloid leukemia is the most common acute leukemia in adults, yet the gene changes behind it are still not fully mapped. The team measured 157 mature microRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune how genes are used.

Their samples came from 100 patients whose chromosome patterns, called karyotypes, covered the known range of the disease. Certain microRNA patterns matched certain karyotypes. Links like these can help sort patients into groups, which is a first step toward care and trials matched to each group's biology.
plos-pone-0002241:
Massimo Giuliani and co-authors grew a new kind of regulatory immune cell from blood stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells are known as killers of virus-infected and tumor cells. They can also regulate the immune system, but whether a defined NK subset does the regulating was in doubt.

The team used membrane-bound IL-15, a growth signal fixed to a surface, to guide blood CD34 progenitor cells into a novel regulatory NK subset. A lab source of calming immune cells could one day help control unwanted immune attacks, in transplantation or autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0002341:
Benjamin Elder and Kyriacos Athanasiou combined pressure and growth factors to grow tissues in the lab, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hydrostatic pressure is a real force in many tissues, including cartilage, the knee meniscus, the jaw joint disc, the spine's discs, bone, bladder. Blood vessels. Engineers growing replacement tissues need to know how pressure shapes growth.

The team tested hydrostatic pressure together with growth factors, the chemical signals that urge cells to build tissue. They found the two work together with synergistic and additive effects on tissue formation. Combining physical and chemical cues gives tissue engineers a stronger recipe for growing cartilage and like tissues.
plos-pone-0002441:
Peterson and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names A. Townsend Peterson, Aimee Stewart, Kamal I. Mohamed, among others. Its subject is shifting Global Invasive Potential of European Plants with Climate Change. Global climate change and invasions by nonnative species rank among the top concerns for agents of biological loss in coming decades.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002541:
Li, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Weijiang Li, Hiroyuki Kurata, among others. Its subject is visualizing Global Properties of Large Complex Networks. For complex biological networks, graphical representations are highly desired for understanding some design principles.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002641:
Amol Pawar and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of finite size effects in simulations of protein aggregation. The catalog record names Amol Pawar first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. It is becoming increasingly clear that the soluble protofibrillar species that proceed amyloid fibril formation are associated with a range of neurodegenerative disorders such. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002741:
In 2008, Anton L. Beer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about a motion illusion reveals mechanisms of perceptual stabilization. Authorship is credited in the record to Anton L. Beer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Visual illusions are valuable tools for the scientific examination of the mechanisms underlying perception. A further point appears in the abstract. In the peripheral drift illusion special drift patterns appear to move although they are static. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002841:
In 2008, Maria Öström and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was retinoic acid promotes the generation of pancreatic endocrine progenitor cells and their further differentiation into β-Cells. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Maria Öström, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The identification of secreted factors that can selectively stimulate the generation of insulin producing β-cells from stem and/or progenitor cells represent a significant step. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002941:
Ursula Mager, Tatjana Degenhardt, Leena Pulkkinen and co-authors checked ghrelin receptor gene variants in people with poor glucose tolerance in 2008. Ghrelin helps control appetite, energy balance, and body weight. Its effects run through the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, the GHSR gene product.

The team typed seven variants in that receptor gene and tested links to obesity and glucose handling. Participants already had impaired glucose tolerance, a step toward diabetes. Published in PLOS ONE, the study adds human data on a hunger hormone pathway often targeted in obesity drug research. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003041:
Zulfeqhar Syed, Torleif Härd, Anne Uv and co-authors surveyed mucin proteins in the fruit fly in 2008. In vertebrates, vital organs are shielded by barriers built largely from mucins. These proteins carry repeated stretches rich in proline and sugar-bearing amino acids, and their sequences are poorly conserved.

Whether fly mucins play comparable roles was the open question. A potential role for Drosophila mucins in development and physiology is the paper's claim, stated cautiously. Published in PLOS ONE, the fly offers a fast genetic model for mucus barrier biology tied to gut and lung health.
plos-pone-0003141:
Gerald Kastberger, Evelyn Schmelzer and Ilse Kranner study a striking defence by giant honeybees in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Apis dorsata nests in the open and has evolved many defence behaviours. Against wasps and hornets the bees show coordinated cascades like Mexican waves across the nest surface, a behaviour called shimmering. It starts at distinct spots on the nest.

The title states what the waves achieve: they repel hornets. Readers watch a colony act as one unit to drive off a predator without each bee having to fight. The study is a vivid case of group defence in social insects.
plos-pone-0003241:
Nicole C. Grieder and co-authors study a cell transport protein in the fruit fly in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. More and more work shows that tweaks to basic cell jobs shape how tissues form and how disease starts. The team made loss-of-function cases to learn what COPI coat transport does as the fly develops.

The title reports that one part, gammaCOP, is needed for protein release at the cell's top surface and for shaping epithelial sheets. Readers see a housekeeping job prove vital for building tissue. Flaws in basic transport can thus lie behind flaws in growth.
plos-pone-0003341:
Sandro Alves, Isabel Nascimento-Ferreira, Gwennaëlle Auregan and colleagues test RNA silencing for a brain disorder in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recent studies showed that RNA interference is a hopeful approach for treating autosomal dominant disorders. But wild-type and mutant transcripts must be told apart. The wild-type copy's expression and function must be preserved. A single nucleotide polymorphism is present in the target gene.

The title reports allele-specific RNA silencing of mutant ataxin-3 brings neuroprotection in a rat model of Machado-Joseph disease. Readers see gene therapy aimed at only the faulty copy. That precision is the key hurdle for dominant inherited brain diseases.
plos-pone-0003441:
Alain Medawar and co-authors hunted the switch that starts skin formation in this 2008 paper. A protein called p63 guides the growth of layered skin-like tissues. Its exact job, and which form does it, stayed disputed. The team tested p63 in embryonic stem cells as they began to change.

One form, named ΔNp63, proved essential for the first step. Without it, stem cells could not commit to becoming epidermis, the outer skin. With it, the skin program could begin. The finding defines a master switch for growing skin from stem cells.
plos-pone-0003541:
Mauricio H. Pontes and co-authors studied a fly's resident bacterium in this 2008 paper. Sodalis glossinidius lives inside tsetse flies and passes from mother to young. It senses its own density with chemical signals, a system called quorum sensing. Those signals tune its gene expression as numbers grow.

Quorum sensing primed the bacterium's defense against oxidative stress. The cells braced for damage before it arrived. Even a friendly endosymbiont prepares for hostile chemistry. Counting neighbors lets it time that preparation well. Tsetse flies spread sleeping sickness, so their resident microbes draw study.
plos-pone-0003641:
Xiaoxue Fan, Skylar Martin-Brown, Laurence Florens, and colleagues published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Actin filaments give yeast cells their shape and drive their movement. The strands are built and taken apart at a fast rate. The team studied the protein cofilin, which breaks filaments down.

They found that budding yeast cofilin can, on its own, drive turnover of filaments bound by tropomyosin. Tropomyosin coats and guards these strands, so the result was not a given. It shows a core renewal step in the cell's skeleton needs no extra helpers, at least in yeast.
plos-pone-0003741:
Patricia C. Lopes, Élio Sucena, M. Emília Santos, and colleagues published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Pesticide resistance spreads fast in the wild and offers a clean model of adaptation. How quickly it evolves, and what it costs the organism, were still open questions. The team ran experimental evolution in the worm C. elegans.

Lab populations evolved pesticide resistance rapidly under selection. The resistance came with no apparent fitness costs in their tests. The mating system of the worms also shaped how the process played out, a warning that resistance can arise easily when adapting is cheap.
plos-pone-0003841:
Ya-li Li, Guang-zhi Wu, Gavin S. Dawe, and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The sugars coating a cell's surface shape how it interacts with its neighbors. Two such coatings, sialylation and fucosylation, add sialic acid and fucose sugars to surface molecules. What controls them in nerve cells was the question.

The team found the adhesion molecule L1 regulates both coatings, acting through phospholipase C gamma. The sugar changes cooperate to tune neurite outgrowth, cell survival, and migration. The work links one surface protein to the chemistry that helps young neurons grow and move.
plos-pone-0003941:
Jérôme Beaufays, Benoît Adam, Yves Decrem, and co-authors catalogued proteins from tick saliva in 2008. Ticks feed on blood for long stretches without being rejected. Their saliva carries many proteins that blunt the host's defenses. Lipocalins among them help calm inflammation at the bite site.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies lipocalins from the tick Ixodes ricinus. The team cloned the genes and charted how the proteins relate. They also tested what the proteins do at a chemical level. Tick proteins of this kind are targets for anti-tick vaccines. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004041:
Kentaroh Takagaki, Michael Thomas Lippert, Benjamin Dann, and co-authors improved a brain imaging measure in 2008. Voltage-sensitive dyes let scientists film activity across brain tissue. Signal size is usually scaled by total fluorescence, the delta-F over F method. That scaled signal measures population activity in tissue.

Their PLOS ONE article proposes normalizing dye signals with functional activity measures. Better scaling makes maps from different sessions comparable. It also sharpens estimates of how space is represented. Imaging labs can adopt the fix without new hardware. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record.
plos-pone-0004141:
Craig McClain and colleagues published this deep-sea study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The deep ocean below one kilometre covers most of Earth's surface. Scattered across its plains and slopes stand about 14,000 seamounts, underwater mountains rising at least a kilometre off the seafloor.

Ecologists have long debated what seamounts do for sea life: whether they host unique species found nowhere else, and how their animal communities are built. The team surveyed one seamount in the northeast Pacific, recording which species live there and how the community is structured. Their data test long-standing ideas about seamounts as islands of unique life in the deep sea.
plos-pone-0004241:
Sandra Diaz and colleagues published this detection study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Humans cannot make Neu5Gc, a sialic acid common in other mammals, but we absorb it from food, especially red meat and milk. The absorbed molecules end up in human tumours, fetuses, and some normal tissues, and in biotherapeutic products made in animal cells.

The team present a sensitive and specific method for detecting Neu5Gc in human tissues and products. Reliable detection matters for judging the safety of animal-made medicines and for studying what dietary molecules do inside us. That makes the test useful for checking such medicines before they reach patients.
plos-pone-0004341:
Hilkka Turakainen and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Conditional gene targeting, switching genes off in chosen tissues or at chosen times, is progressively used to study gene function. Every such strategy needs a targeting vector, a DNA construct built to order, and any method that streamlines building them would be valued.

The authors present a transposition-based method for the rapid generation of gene-targeting vectors. The resulting vectors can produce Cre and Flp modifiable conditional knock-out mice. Faster vector building removes a notorious bottleneck between a research question and a mouse that answers it.
plos-pone-0004441:
Cows may know each other's faces, a claim tested by Marjorie Coulon, Bertrand Deputte, Yvan Heyman, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Social animals need to read social cues well to keep their groups together. True recognition of individuals by sight had been shown in only a few mammal species.

The team showed cattle flat images of heads from different breeds and watched how the animals responded. They looked for proof that a cow treats one known individual as itself, not just that it can tell two pictures apart. Evidence of face-based recognition would change how farmers think about herd life. It would also place cattle higher on the scale of social smarts than many assume.
plos-pone-0004541:
Natural background radiation in Kerala, India, may have left unique signatures on the male Y chromosome, report Sanjay Premi, Jyoti Srivastava, Sebastian Padinjarel Chandy, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ionizing radiation most often causes chromosome lesions and cancers, though the whole genome may be affected. The Y chromosome is a good place to look for such effects.

Because the Y is passed only from father to son and does not swap parts with a partner chromosome, changes in it accumulate in a clean line. Kerala has areas of unusually high natural radiation. Comparing Y chromosomes there with those from low-radiation areas can reveal long-term, low-dose effects that lab studies cannot. The work speaks to radiation safety for whole populations.
plos-pone-0004641:
The full genome of a pig gut pathogen reveals how it is built for life in the large intestine. Matthew Bellgard, Phatthanaphong Wanchanthuek, Tom La, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium is Brachyspira hyodysenteriae, an anaerobic intestinal spirochete. It colonizes the large intestine of pigs and causes swine dysentery, a disease of significant economic importance.

The team determined the genome sequence of strain WA1, the first representative of its group to be sequenced. Reading the whole genome reveals adaptations to its lifestyle in the porcine gut. Genes for feeding, attaching, and surviving without oxygen can now be listed and studied. That list supports vaccines and tests for a disease that costs pig farmers heavily.
plos-pone-0004741:
Anna Abraham and Yves von Cramon asked if brain response to fiction rests on how relevant it feels, in PLOS ONE in 2009. People slip into made up worlds each time they read a novel or watch a film. Yet little was known about how the brain keeps real and made up apart without effort.

Their study was the first brain scan work on that split. They tracked the brain default network as people judged real versus fiction. Shifts in that network tracked how close or relevant scenes felt. The work links self thought networks to how we enter stories.
plos-pone-0004841:
Mara Almog and Alon Korngreen marked voltage gated calcium conductances in layer 5 neocortical pyramidal neurons from rats, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuronal voltage gated calcium channels are involved in electrical signaling and converting signals into cytoplasmic calcium changes. One key function is generating regenerative dendritic calcium spikes. Yet calcium dependent steps in pyramidal dendrites remained incompletely defined despite their role in synaptic integration and plasticity.

Detailed conductance profiles clarify dendritic computations. Layer five neurons are major cortical outputs. Their calcium signals shape learning and perception. Pharmacology can now target specific channels. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004941:
Cancer cells often lose methyl tags from their DNA across the genome. This change is called hypomethylation. It tracks with an unstable genome. Kristy Richards and co-authors compared head and neck cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked how tag loss differs by tumor type. Some of these tumors are linked to the virus HPV. Others are not.

Hypomethylation was more pronounced in HPV-negative tumors. The degree of tag loss also matched genomic instability. The pattern may help explain the behavior of HPV-negative tumors. It could also help sort patients by how unstable their tumor genomes are.
plos-pone-0005041:
The nucleus is crowded with tangled DNA. Scientists wondered whether that crowding slows small proteins down. Nicolas Dross and colleagues mapped the movement directly. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used glowing eGFP proteins in living cell nuclei. They varied the proteins' size by linking copies together.

The team measured how oligomer mobility changes with chromatin density. Movement can be slowed by viscosity, flows, transport or obstacles. Their map separates those effects. It gives a baseline for how molecules travel inside the nucleus. Such baselines matter for models of gene regulation. They tell modelers what simple diffusion can explain, and what it cannot.
plos-pone-0005141:
The gene doublesex sits at the bottom of the sex-determination cascade. It makes a female protein in females and a male protein in males. Mercedes Alvarez, María Fernanda Ruiz and Lucas Sánchez tested it across species in PLOS ONE in 2009. They took doublesex from Anastrepha, a fruit fly genus. They put it into Drosophila, the classic lab fly.

The foreign gene steered Drosophila's somatic sexual development. Its instructions were still readable in a distant relative. The swap test reveals how the sex switch evolved. Master switches can stay conserved while species diverge. The work compares the bottom of the cascade across flies. It shows evolution tinkering around a stable core decision.
plos-pone-0005241:
A popular method called ChIP-seq maps where proteins bind DNA across the genome. Every such study needs control libraries to separate real binding from background noise. Vega and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that those controls carry signals of their own.

If controls are not neutral, they can create false binding peaks or hide real ones. The study dissected the inherent signals inside sequencing-based control libraries. Knowing the background's shape helps researchers clean their data and trust the peaks that remain after correction. Labs that use this method can now check their own control data with fresh eyes and fix the flaws they find before they publish.
plos-pone-0005341:
Embryonic stem cells can divide without limit and can become many cell types, making them prized for therapy. That endless growth rests on an unusual cell cycle and its controlling signals. Abdelalim and Tooyama identified one crucial signal in PLOS ONE in 2009: BNP.

BNP is a peptide best known from heart biology. The study found BNP signaling is crucial for embryonic stem cell proliferation. A defined growth signal helps labs grow stem cells reliably, a basic need for any future cell-based treatment. Stem cells are held back by cost and scale, since they die or drift in poor culture. So a clear growth cue is a base each lab can build its own recipes on.
plos-pone-0005441:
Manuel Forero and colleagues built a tool to count dying cells in fruit flies for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Cell death shapes growth, cancer, nerve disease, and the effects of drugs. Yet counting dead cells by hand is slow and often rough.

Their program, DeadEasy Caspase, counts cells marked by a key death enzyme in fly tissue images. It does the count on its own, in a fast and even way. A reliable count helps workers compare drugs, genes, and disease states without the bias that creeps into hand counts. Counts from the program can be compared across flies and treatments in minutes rather than hours.
plos-pone-0005541:
Frantz Depaulis, Ludovic Orlando, and Catherine Hänni warned about timing in population genetics in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. New data sets mix DNA from samples of very different ages, thanks to ancient DNA work and fast-evolving microbes. Classic analysis tools assume all samples come from one time.

The authors showed that ignoring the age spread can warp the results. They set out how to handle samples drawn from different times. Their guidance matters for anyone reading the history of species, farms, or germs from DNA of mixed ages. The same caution applies to farm animals and microbes sampled across long spans of time.
plos-pone-0005641:
Ingrid Olsen and co-authors isolated T cells from the gut of Crohn's disease patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Crohn's disease is a long-lasting inflammation of the intestine whose cause is unknown. An overreaction to gut bacteria in people with the wrong genes is the leading idea.

The team fished out T cells from gut samples that react to a bacterium suspected of a role in a similar animal disease. Finding such cells in patients supports the bacterial overreaction idea. It also names a target for tests and treatments. Such reactive cells in the gut wall are hard to reach, which is why isolating them at all is a step forward.
plos-pone-0005741:
Benjamin Myers, Yaron Sigal, and David Julius compared a cold-sensing channel across species in 2009. The channel, TRPM8, opens in the cold and gives the cool feel of mint. Animals that keep a steady body heat and those that drift with the weather both use it.

Yet the channel answers heat very differently in different species, the team found. They traced those gaps to the channel's evolution. How a frog and a mammal sense cold need not match, even with the same part. The study shows evolution tuning one sensor to many climates and ways of life.
plos-pone-0005841:
Pär Comstedt and co-authors mapped the tangled population structure of a Lyme disease bacterium in 2009. Borrelia garinii causes Lyme borreliosis across Europe and Asia. Birds carry it in two great cycles, one marine with seabirds, one land-based with songbirds.

Sampling across subarctic Eurasia, the team found a complex mix of strains tied to those cycles. Migrating birds can move strains vast distances, blurring local patterns. That mixing complicates tracking which strains infect people. The map helps health agencies read Lyme risk in northern regions where the disease is spreading with warming climates.
plos-pone-0005941:
Trophy hunting of lions and other big predators brings in money that can fund their protection. Craig Packer, Margaret Kosmala, Hilary Cooley and colleagues weighed that bargain in PLOS ONE in 2009. They also looked at predator control, the killing done to stop attacks on livestock and people, which adds pressure on the same animals.

Hunting is a risky tool, the authors stress, because predator numbers can drop fast when too many are taken. Managers thus face a hard balance between income, safety and survival of the species. The paper gives that debate hard terms: what hunting earns, what it costs, and why control programs need tight limits to stay safe.
plos-pone-0006041:
Amyloid diseases spread when clumped protein seeds more clumping, much like a crystal growing. Per Westermark, Katarzyna Lundmark and Gunilla Westermark asked in 2009 whether seeds must come from the disease protein itself. Their PLOS ONE paper tests fibrils built from designed synthetic peptides with no link to amyloid, given to mice during inflammation.

The foreign fibrils induced AA-amyloidosis, the title reports. A seed need not match the protein it seeds, at least in this animal model. That finding widens the safety questions around peptide materials and deepens the puzzle of how amyloid diseases start, since stray fibrils in an inflamed body might light the fuse.
plos-pone-0006141:
Blood agar is the daily bread of the diagnostic lab, but good blood is costly where labs are poorest. Ellen Yeh, Benjamin Pinsky, Niaz Banaei and colleagues tested a cheaper source in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper checks hair sheep blood, citrated or defibrinated, against every requirement of blood agar for identifying bacteria and testing antibiotic susceptibility.

In much of the developing world, labs fall back on human blood because wool sheep and horses are costly to raise. Hair sheep are hardier and cheaper, and their blood fulfilled all requirements in these tests. A small change of ingredient can thus raise the quality of diagnosis for whole regions, without new machines.
plos-pone-0006241:
An egg cell must deliver the right messages to the right end to set up the future body. Musa Mhlanga and colleagues imaged oskar messenger RNA inside the fruit fly oocyte in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Oskar marks the posterior end, but its multi-step journey with partner proteins was poorly seen.

Live imaging showed where the RNA and its trans-acting protein partners sit together during transport. Quantitative pictures replace guesses about timing and place. The map helps explain how cells move cargo with such precision. Faulty delivery scrambles development, so the transport rules matter widely.
plos-pone-0006341:
Most classical Hodgkin lymphoma patients are cured, but a significant minority fail first treatment. Danielle Canioni and colleagues tested new immunohistochemical markers in fifty-nine refractory cases in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. No consensus exists on biological markers that add value beyond usual clinical parameters.

Stains that reveal proteins in tumor tissue were checked for prognostic significance. A reliable marker could flag high-risk patients for stronger or experimental therapy early. It could also spare low-risk patients excess toxicity. The study weighs candidate markers in the hardest cases. More work will be needed to prove which marks hold up in new groups of cases.
plos-pone-0006441:
Jiayuan Quan and Jingdong Tian presented a simpler way to clone genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Modern genomics and synthetic biology need fast, cheap ways to assemble genes, gene libraries, and whole pathways. Existing methods can be slow or costly. The authors set out to build a method that avoids those limits.

They describe circular polymerase extension cloning, a technique the title calls extremely simple. It aims to join complex gene sets in a streamlined process. A method like this can speed up building test genes and synthetic pathways. Lower cost and effort also put advanced cloning within reach of more labs.
plos-pone-0006541:
Rachel Kendal, Jeremy Kendal, Will Hoppitt, and colleagues offered a new method to spot social learning in animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studies of natural populations reveal widespread evidence for diffusion of novel behavior patterns. They also show variation in behavior within and between populations. But telling social learning from individual discovery is hard.

Their 'option-bias' method offers a statistical way to identify social learning. It asks whether animals disproportionately choose the option their group favors. A reliable method can settle debates about animal culture. It applies to wild populations where experiments are impossible.
plos-pone-0006641:
Julius Halaschek-Wiener and co-authors surveyed genetic variation in the healthy oldest-old in PLOS ONE in 2009. Individuals who live to eighty-five and beyond without developing major age-related diseases are special. They may achieve this, in part, by lacking disease susceptibility factors, or by possessing resistance factors. The team studied genetic variation in such healthy oldest-old people.

What the exceptionally healthy lack can be as informative as what the sick carry. Their genomes are a natural experiment in successful aging. Comparing them with general populations may reveal protective variants. Protective factors are attractive drug leads, since mimicking them should be safe.
plos-pone-0006741:
Kevin Drace, Stephanie McLaughlin, and Creg Darby studied a worm protein that lets bacterial films stick in PLOS ONE in 2009. The worm is Caenorhabditis elegans, a standard laboratory animal. Its cuticle is a layered outer skin facing the environment. Biofilms made by Yersinia bacteria attach to that cuticle. Attachment gives scientists a handle on surface properties.

The protein BAH-1 sits in seam cells of the worm. It belongs to the DUF23 protein family. Without BAH-1, microbial biofilms could not bind properly. Identifying a required host protein turns attachment into a genetics problem. That opens the way to study how surfaces invite or resist bacterial films.
plos-pone-0006841:
Lori-Ann R. Sacrey, Callie A. M. Clark, and Ian Q. Whishaw tested music's effect on reaching in Parkinson's disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Parkinson's impairs movement and sensation. Familiar music can reduce some of those impairments. Patients also lean too heavily on vision to guide reaching. Whether music eases that visual dependence was unclear.

Music attenuated excessive visual guidance in advanced disease. It did not do so in mild disease, as the title states. The stage difference matters for therapy design. Music may compensate only once internal guidance is badly weakened. The result refines when music-based rehabilitation should be offered.
plos-pone-0006941:
Maura Manganelli, Francesca Malfatti, Ty Samo, and colleagues measured ocean microbes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study site was the southern Drake Passage during the austral winter. Carbon cycling in the Southern Ocean is a major climate question. The region has strong seasons, with long dark winters.

The team measured how carbon moved through the food web in that dark season. They found microbes playing the major role in winter carbon fluxes. Winter data are rare because conditions there are harsh. Knowing who drives carbon flow year-round improves the models used to predict ocean uptake of carbon.
plos-pone-0007041: Ravi Barabote, Gary Xie, Thomas Brettin, and colleagues published the complete genome sequence of a tularemia bacterium strain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The strain is Francisella tularensis subspecies holarctica FTNF002-00. A full genome sequence gives the complete DNA record of this strain. Such records let researchers compare strains, trace outbreaks, and find genes behind virulence and drug response.
plos-pone-0007141:
Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus and Zvia Breznitz tested memory training in dyslexic adults in PLOS ONE in 2009. Error detection while reading leans on working memory. The team asked whether training working memory could sharpen that error monitor. They compared twenty-seven dyslexic readers with thirty-four controls, all university students. Brain responses were recorded with ERP methods.

Training changed the dyslexic readers' working memory capacity. It also affected their error detection system. If a trainable skill lifts reading accuracy checks, therapy gains a new lever. The comparison with controls shows which gaps training can close and which it cannot.
plos-pone-0007241:
Scott A. Hocknull, Philip J. Piper, Gert D. van den Bergh, and colleagues traced the history of giant monitor lizards in 2009. The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard. It survives on a few isolated islands in eastern Indonesia, where it is the dominant land carnivore, and it is vulnerable to extinction.

The authors study fossils and past ranges of the largest terrestrial lizards in the Varanidae family. They reconstruct where these giants lived, how they evolved, and why they vanished. Their title calls the story a paradise lost for dragons. The work informs protection of the last survivor.
plos-pone-0007341:
Jennyfer Zerbib, Johanna M. Seddon, Florence Richard, and colleagues tested an eye disease gene variant in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Age-related macular degeneration is a leading cause of vision loss in older adults. Major genetic risk factors had recently been identified, including variants in CFH and in the ARMS2 and HTRA1 region.

The authors run a case-control study in two populations. They examine a variant called rs5888 in the SCARB1 gene. They report it as a possible susceptibility factor for macular degeneration. Their result adds a lipid transport gene to the disease's genetic picture.
plos-pone-0007441:
Jedrzej Szymanski and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was how the bacterium E. coli reshapes its chemistry when conditions change. Cells respond to stress by adjusting their metabolites, the small molecules of daily metabolism. Some responses are shared across stresses, while others are specific. The team took a broad view of how metabolite levels move together.

They measured the links between metabolites under varied conditions. Some links stayed stable no matter what the cells faced. Others shifted with the stress at hand. That mix shows a metabolism that is part fixed backbone, part flexible response. Knowing which links hold steady helps predict how bacteria adapt. The map is useful for anyone engineering microbes or fighting infections.
plos-pone-0007541:
Soledad Galli and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 proposing a new view of ERK1, a famous signaling protein. ERK1 and ERK2 belong to the MAPK family, which relays outside stimuli into cell responses. Their long-term effects run through gene expression in the nucleus. Fast responses were known to happen elsewhere, but the details stayed vague. The team studied ERK1's interactions in HeLa cells.

They found ERK1 in structural association with mitochondria. That location is a surprise for a signal usually pictured in the cytosol and nucleus. A kinase parked at the cell's power plants could coordinate energy with growth signals. The authors frame it as a new paradigm for MAPK biology. If the pathway has standing business at mitochondria, many old results gain a new reading.
plos-pone-0007641:
Yuanbiao Guo and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the fetal liver's double life. Before birth, the liver both builds blood and matures into a metabolic organ. Blood-making and liver-building coexist there in mid-pregnancy. The switch between the two roles is thought to be a critical moment in development. The team profiled gene and protein activity in the midtrimester fetal liver to characterize that relationship.

The dynamic profiles capture an organ in mid-transition. Hematopoiesis wanes as hepatogenesis takes over, and the molecular data show the handover in motion. Understanding that timing matters for developmental biology and for medicine alike. Liver transplants and cell therapies both dream of replaying fetal programs. A map of the real transition tells engineers what to copy. The study records a rare moment when one organ does two jobs at once.
plos-pone-0007741:
Camille Szmaragd and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It builds a model of bluetongue virus spread among British farms. Bluetongue is a livestock disease carried by biting midges. Recent outbreaks pushed officials to plan for its return.

The framework describes how the virus moves within a single farm. It also tracks spread between farms across the country. Models like this let officials test control options before an outbreak hits. They can compare vaccination, movement bans and other steps on a computer first. That preparation can save animals and money.
plos-pone-0007841:
Steve Crampton and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It connects two major signaling systems inside cells. The Wnt pathway, driven by the protein beta-catenin, guides growth and development. Integrin signaling reports on a cell's grip on its surroundings.

The authors show the two systems are integrated through an adaptor molecule, Grb2. Adaptors physically link one pathway's parts to another's. Through Grb2, matrix and growth signals can tune the Wnt response. Such cross-talk helps explain how cells weigh several cues at once. It also adds detail to pathways often hit in cancer.
plos-pone-0007941:
Nicholas Delihas wrote a solo study of jumping genes in Lyme disease bacteria for PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacteria, Borrelia, carry small DNA rings called plasmids, crowded with copied and fused genes. One jumping element, IS605, leaves short stem-loop marks in the DNA near its landing spots.

Delihas found those marks linked to genes for lipoproteins, proteins that sit on the germ's surface. That link hints at how the germ shuffles the surface it shows to hosts. Shuffling its coat helps it dodge immune attack, so the marks point to a trick behind its staying power.
plos-pone-0008041:
Bernard La Scola and Didier Raoult sped up the naming of germs in blood infections for PLOS ONE in 2009. Blood cultures are the standard test, but they take days while patients wait on broad drugs. A mass spectrometry method can name germs from their protein fingerprint in minutes, once colonies grow.

The team showed the fingerprint method works straight from positive culture bottles, skipping a day of waiting. Faster names mean faster switches to the right drug. In blood poisoning, hours count, so a shortcut of this size can save lives.
plos-pone-0008141:
Zhida Su and colleagues found that a spinal scar calls in repair cells even as it blocks regrowth in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. After cord injury, a glial scar walls off the damage. Olfactory ensheathing cells, which support smell nerves, are transplanted to help repairs, and they migrate toward the scar.

The call turned out to be TNF alpha, a signal shed by the scar's reactive astrocytes. A scar that both blocks and beckons is a mixed blessing. Boosting the call while easing the block could draw more repair cells to the right place after injury.
plos-pone-0008241:
Peter I. Duncan and colleagues revisited sialic acid in newborn rats in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Milk is the only food of newborn mammals. It is thought to have evolved alongside the needs of the suckling young. Sialic acid is a conserved part of milk found on many sugar-coated molecules. The brain and colon are among the tissues where it matters.

The authors reviewed how newborn rats use and make sialic acid. Knowing whether pups rely on milk or their own synthesis guides nutrition research. The work connects milk chemistry to early brain and gut development. It updates an older picture of this nutrient.
plos-pone-0008341:
Dang Thi Minh Ha and colleagues evaluated a tuberculosis test for children in PLOS ONE in 2009. The MODS assay is a liquid culture method for detecting tuberculosis. It had been shown effective and rapid for early diagnosis in adults. Diagnosing tuberculosis in children is notoriously hard. The team evaluated the assay in Viet Nam with consecutive samples.

Samples included sputum and gastric fluid from children under evaluation. A faster diagnosis means treatment starts sooner for sick children. Culture-based proof also confirms which drug regimens will work. The study tests a practical tool where the need is great.
plos-pone-0008441:
Xin Liu and co-authors present a way to predict protein change in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Many diseases stem from proteins that fold the wrong way. The first step is a shift in a region that keeps the normal shape stable. That shift weakens the shape and exposes parts that should stay hidden. The authors call the key region a switch region.

They build a method to find such regions in a protein. Finding them could help predict which shifts cause disease. It could also help design drugs that hold the shape in place. The paper tests the method and shows how it can be used.
plos-pone-0008541:
Slavica Pecioska and co-authors test diabetes genes against fatness in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Type 2 diabetes disturbs carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism. It also involves insulin resistance. Most patients with the disease are obese. Obesity by itself may cause insulin resistance. The team ask if known diabetes loci act through measures of fatness. Loci are the genome positions where diabetes risk variants sit.

They evaluate associations between those loci and body fat measures. Some loci link to fatness, others act independently of it. Splitting the paths helps explain how each variant raises risk. That knowledge can refine prevention aimed at weight versus other mechanisms.
plos-pone-0008641:
Christopher Uhde and co-authors identify a marker RNA in mouse brains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Specific markers for regions of the developing nervous system are useful tools. They illuminate development, regulation, and function of those regions. By expression profiling, the team identify a putative non-coding RNA called Rmst. It shows a striking, restricted expression pattern in embryos. It marks the ventral mesencephalic floor plate, where dopamine neurons are born.

Rmst also marks anterior dorsal midline cells of the brain. As a novel marker, it lets researchers isolate and study those populations. The floor plate is central to Parkinson-relevant neuron development. A non-coding RNA marker may itself play a regulatory role.
plos-pone-0008741:
Rick Shin, Junran Cao, Sierra Webb, and colleagues tested how a stimulant sharpens rat interest in cues. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Amphetamine makes animals respond more to signals tied to reward. Many such signals are learned through pairing. The team instead used plain visual signals with no training history. They placed the drug in the ventral striatum, a motivation hub.

Treated rats interacted more with the unconditioned visual signals. The boost happened without any learned reward value. That result widens theories of how stimulants capture attention. It also informs work on addiction and attention disorders.
plos-pone-0008841:
Nicole Cadieu, Stéphane Fruchard, and Jean-Claude Cadieu watched canaries try new foods and teach each other. Their bird study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Feeding innovation means eating something new or learning a new feeding skill. Adult canaries eat many seeds but avoid large ones. A bird that cracks the large-seed problem becomes a demonstrator. Whether flock mates copy the innovator was the question.

Some innovators spread their habit through watching flock mates. Others, though, were poor teachers despite their skill. Being first does not guarantee being influential. Social learning research must weigh personality alongside innovation.
plos-pone-0008941:
Tsufit Gonen-Gross and colleagues examined how a mother's immune cells read a special pregnancy protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, HLA-G, appears where the placenta meets the womb. It helps the mother's immune system tolerate the baby, who is genetically half foreign. Natural killer cells, a front-line immune cell, carry receptors that can bind HLA-G.

The team pinpointed which contact points on the receptor and protein do the binding. They also checked which cells display the protein at the fetal-maternal border. Small changes in the contact surface changed how strongly the cells responded. The work clarifies one way pregnancy keeps the immune system calm.
plos-pone-0009041:
Mahamadou Thera and co-authors gave a malaria vaccine its first test in Malian children, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The vaccine, FMP2.1/AS02A, is built on AMA1, a protein the malaria parasite needs to enter blood cells. Children in Bandiagara, Mali, face seasonal falciparum malaria every year. A phase 1 trial asks first whether a vaccine is safe and stirs immunity.

The trial was randomised, double-blind, and raised the dose step by step. Children's reactions and antibody responses were followed closely. Testing in children who truly face malaria gives the most honest early read. A safe, immune-stirring result would justify larger efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0009141:
Yan Zhao and co-authors traced a stress peptide's nerve cells in the fruit fly brain, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Every animal must answer stress to keep its body in balance. Hormones coordinate the changes in behaviour and body that follow. In flies, a peptide called corazonin is one such stress-linked signal.

Corazonin neurons wired into different circuits in male and female flies. That sex-based wiring shaped how each sex responded to stress. The same hardship thus triggered different behaviour in males and females. A simple fly brain shows how stress circuits get tuned by sex.
plos-pone-0009241:
Johan Lind and Patrik Lindenfors published this chimpanzee study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chimpanzee communities differ in their cultural traits, like tool use and grooming customs. Why some groups keep more traditions than others was poorly understood. In humans, models predict that bigger populations hold more culture.

The authors tested a version of that idea split by sex. They found the number of cultural traits rises with female group size. It does not rise with male group size. That pattern fits females being the main carriers of chimp culture, since young chimps learn most from their mothers and females move between groups.
plos-pone-0009341:
Judith Booij and co-authors published this eye gene study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The retinal pigment epithelium is a cell layer that keeps the eye's light sensors alive. Its failure drives diseases like age-related macular degeneration and retinitis pigmentosa. To study it, researchers need the list of genes this layer uses that others do not.

The team isolated RPE cells, photoreceptors, and choroid cells from fresh human eyes. Comparing the three gave a new strategy for spotting RPE-specific gene activity. They then annotated what those special genes do. The catalogue supports work on diseases that blind millions of older people.
plos-pone-0009441:
Diane Brown and colleagues used mice to model a rare immune crisis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The crisis is called HLH. In it, the immune system runs out of control and harms the body. It can follow infections, cancers, or immune diseases. A good animal model of the full syndrome had been lacking.

Mice with a long lasting typhoid like infection grew the full set of HLH signs on their own. No extra trigger was needed. That makes the model close to how the syndrome can arise in people. Researchers can now follow its course in mice and test ways to calm it.
plos-pone-0009541:
James Stevens and co-authors issued a caution about a common lab tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in the enzyme SOD1 cause some cases of ALS, a disease that kills motor nerve cells. To study SOD1, many labs attach a glowing tag called GFP to it. The tag lets them watch the protein in living cells. The team asked whether the tag itself changes the protein.

They found that the GFP tag does alter how SOD1 behaves. Its traits in tests shifted when the tag was present. That means some past results may reflect the tag, not the disease protein. The paper urges care in how tagged proteins are used across ALS research.
plos-pone-0009641:
Victoria Wang and co-authors traced a low oxygen response gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. When oxygen runs short, cells switch on hypoxia inducible factors. Two main forms exist, HIF-1 and HIF-2, and they prefer different genes. One gene favored by HIF-2 makes a protein called PTPRZ1, a receptor type phosphatase. The team characterized how HIF-2 alpha turns that gene on.

Detailing the activation shows how the cell tailors its reply to low oxygen. Different HIF forms may ready the cell for different stresses. PTPRZ1 is of interest in brain tumors, which often face low oxygen. The work links a tumor relevant gene to the oxygen sensing system.
plos-pone-0009741:
Marion David and co-authors published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks what role autotaxin, a protein made by breast cancer cells, plays when cancer spreads to bone. Autotaxin controls the level of a fat signal called LPA in the blood.

Breast cancer cells forced to make autotaxin formed more bone-eating spread in mice, with more bone loss and more active bone-eating cells. Silencing autotaxin in a second cancer line cut the bone damage down. In dishes, LPA drove the growth of the bone-eating cells, and a blocker of autotaxin stopped that effect.
plos-pone-0009841:
Short DNA words recur across genomes, but some appear far more often than chance allows. Colin Davenport and Burkhard Tümmler cataloged such words shared by most bacteria. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Oligonucleotides are short stretches of DNA letters. The abundant ones turn up again and again across very different bacteria. Shared abundance hints that these sequences do jobs cells cannot skip. A catalog of them gives researchers reference points for comparing genomes. It can also help spot contamination or mislabeled samples in sequencing work. Most bacteria share more of their DNA language than expected.
plos-pone-0009941:
Stony corals build reefs, but their diversity is not spread evenly across the sea. Assaf Zvuloni, Robert van Woesik, and Yossi Loya measured how coral diversity divides across space around Zanzibar Island. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Diversity partitioning splits total variety into shares at each spatial scale. The scales ran from small patches to the whole region around the Tanzanian island. Knowing where variety concentrates tells protectors where reserves do most good. The method applies to any habitat split across scales. Zanzibar sits off the coast of Tanzania in the Indian Ocean.
plos-pone-0010041:
The authors were Philippe Colson, Hervé Richet, Christelle Desnues, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study chased a plant virus found in human stool. Pepper mild mottle virus infects peppers, yet living virus had turned up in healthy people. Where it came from and whether it harms people were both unclear.

The team tested pepper food products and hundreds of stool samples from adults and children. They linked the virus to specific immune responses, fever, belly pain, and itching in some people. A plant virus troubling humans would be an unusual finding worth careful follow-up.
plos-pone-0010141:
The authors were Fangqing Zhao, Jie Bai, Jinyu Wu, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sequenced plasmids from Klebsiella pneumoniae, a hospital bacterium. Plasmids are small DNA circles that bacteria trade with each other. Some carry genes for resisting many drugs at once, a growing problem in treating infections.

By sequencing these plasmids and comparing their genetic variation, the team traced how resistance spreads. Plasmids can cross between strains and even species, carrying their cargo along. Knowing their structure helps hospitals and scientists track and slow that spread. The paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010241:
Laura Bianchi and Ana Díez-Sampedro changed one building block in a protein in 2010. The protein family, SGLT, moves sugar across cell membranes together with sodium. One member, SGLT1, absorbs glucose in the gut. Another, SGLT3, was known only as a sugar sensor, not a transporter, until this PLOS ONE study.

A single amino acid change converted SGLT3 from sensor into a working sugar transporter. That tiny switch shows how closely sensing and transport are related in this family. The insight may help design drugs that fine-tune sugar handling in diabetes and gut disease.
plos-pone-0010341:
Kai Li, Rui Wang, Enerlyn Lozada and co-workers examined a DNA repair protein called WRN in PLOS ONE in 2010. WRN helps cells copy, swap, and fix DNA. It can gain a chemical tag called an acetyl group, and that tagging matters when DNA is damaged. The group had earlier shown tagging changes what the protein does and where it sits in the cell.

Here they asked whether tagging also controls how long WRN lasts. Their results show tagging protects WRN from being marked for disposal. That disposal mark is called ubiquitin, and blocking it keeps the protein stable. A stable repair protein can stay on duty longer after damage. The finding adds a control knob to a system cells need for genome care.
plos-pone-0010441:
Minseok Kim and colleagues built a tiny device to diagnose breast cancer from tissue markers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Doctors read cancer markers with a staining method that reveals proteins in tissue slices. Testing several markers at once improves diagnosis and prognosis. The standard method, though, is slow and uses much sample. The team shrank it onto a microfluidic chip, where fluids move through hair-thin channels.

Their platform ran many marker tests in parallel on small samples. Faster, cheaper marker panels could reach more hospitals. They could also guide treatment choices that depend on marker patterns. Breast cancer care already turns on such patterns, like hormone sensitivity. This device aims to deliver those answers with less tissue and time.
plos-pone-0010541:
Anton Formann examined how the Newcomb-Benford law behaves across common statistical distributions in PLOS ONE in 2010. The law notes a strange pattern: in many data sets, numbers starting with 1 occur far more often than other first digits. The pattern is striking and keeps surprising newcomers. Formann asked how the law relates to familiar distributions used in statistics. Some distributions follow it naturally; others do not.

Knowing which is which makes the law a sharper tool. Auditors use first-digit patterns to flag cooked books and faulty data. A tool misapplied, though, accuses the innocent. This analysis sets the law's proper boundaries. It is pure mathematical groundwork with practical uses in fraud detection.
plos-pone-0010641:
Nikodem Poplawski and colleagues simulated growing tumors in three dimensions, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early tumors have no blood vessels of their own. They live on nutrients that seep in from nearby tissue, which limits their size and shape.

The computer tumors did not stay smooth. Under some settings their edges buckled into rough, invasive fronts. Limited nutrient supply and surface forces drove the buckling. Rough fronts let real tumors invade tissue earlier than smooth growth would. Physicists and doctors together can use such models to predict which tumors will turn aggressive.
plos-pone-0010741:
Neelakanteswar Aluru and colleagues studied a plastics chemical passed from mother trout to eggs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is used to make many plastics and leaks into water widely. Fish absorb it, and it can lodge in their eggs before spawning. The offspring then start life already exposed.

Young rainbow trout from BPA-laden eggs grew more slowly than controls. Their stress responses were also blunted when challenged. Harm arriving through the egg means pollution effects can skip a generation's own exposure. Water standards based only on direct exposure may therefore understate the true cost to fish stocks.
plos-pone-0010841:
Andreas Androutsellis-Theotokis, Stuart Walbridge, Deric Park and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neural stem cells can renew themselves and later form brain cells, so learning what controls their growth matters for repair medicine and for cancer research. The team found that cholera toxin, a bacterial protein, switches on two known stem cell markers.

In rodent brain stem cell cultures, the toxin raised levels of the Tie2 receptor and quickly moved the Hes3 factor into the cell nucleus. After that, the cultured stem cells expanded strongly and kept dividing even without the usual growth signals. Androutsellis-Theotokis and colleagues propose a new control route for stem cell renewal. Such a route could give researchers a cleaner way to grow these cells and a fresh target in stem-like cancers.
plos-pone-0010941:
David Lucas, Lapo Alinari, Derek West and co-authors published this blood cancer drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drugs that block deacetylase enzymes, which control how tightly DNA is packed, show promise against B-cell cancers, but early versions were weak or caused harsh side effects. The team tested a new entrant, AR-42, across several B-cell malignancies.

In lymphoma and leukemia cell lines, low doses of AR-42 halted growth within two days, and it killed patient leukemia cells at similar levels. The drug raised chemical marks on both DNA-packing proteins and structural proteins, and triggered the cell's self-destruct machinery even when protective support cells were present. Lucas and colleagues also report activity in living animals. Their results make AR-42 a candidate worth carrying toward clinical trials.
plos-pone-0011041:
Khyati Kapoor, Mohd Rehan, Andrew Lynn and co-authors published this antifungal study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mdr1p is a pump that Candida albicans, a pathogenic yeast, uses to expel antifungal drugs, and its family of transporters shares a common design. The authors wanted the specific residues, the individual building blocks, that make this pump an antiporter rather than a sugar carrier.

They applied information theory measures comparing the antiporter family against a sugar porter family, flagging the thirty positions where conservation patterns differ most. Nineteen top candidates were then mutated one by one to test their role in drug transport. Kapoor and colleagues blend computation with bench verification to map a resistance pump's working parts. Such maps can guide drugs designed to jam the pump and restore antifungal power.
plos-pone-0011141:
Sambo, Trovoada, Benchimol and colleagues studied sick children in Angola for PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria can turn deadly when it reaches the brain. The team asked whether two genes, one shaping immune signals and one handling iron rich protein breakdown, change a child's risk.

Variants in both genes were tied to higher risk of the brain form of malaria. That genetic pattern could help explain why some children fall gravely ill while others recover. In time, risk knowledge might guide closer watch or early care for the most at risk children. The study centers African children in research where their burden is greatest.
plos-pone-0011241:
Spinella, Rosano, Del Duca and colleagues studied melanoma cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Skin cancer cells can turn on a low oxygen program even when oxygen is present, helping them survive. The team traced how a vessel signal called endothelin switches that program on in melanoma.

The signal blocked an enzyme that normally tags the program's master protein for removal. With the tag withheld, the program stayed active. Interrupting that chain could starve tumors of their adaptation to stress. The study names clear steps in the chain as targets for new melanoma drugs.
plos-pone-0011341:
Heath Kelly and colleagues reconstructed the start of the 2009 flu pandemic in Australia in their 2010 paper. By mid-June 2009, the state of Victoria seemed to have the highest reported rate of the new H1N1 flu anywhere in the world. That odd lead raised a question: was Victoria truly hit hardest, or had the virus arrived there earlier than anyone realized?

The team argued that spread within local communities was already well established in Victoria when the virus was first identified in North America. In other words, the pandemic was moving quietly before surveillance caught up. The lesson reaches beyond one state and one year. Early case counts can badly lag real spread, so plans for the next pandemic should assume the virus is already wider than the first reports suggest.
plos-pone-0011441:
Vojtech Adam and co-authors presented in 2010 an electrochemical test sensitive enough to detect vanishingly small amounts of metallothioneins. These small proteins soak up toxic metals in the body, and their levels matter for tracking metal exposure and some diseases. Older methods could not measure them when only trace amounts were present in a sample.

The new method reaches down to the zeptomole scale, far below what routine tests can see. Sensitivity at that level lets labs find the proteins in tiny or dilute samples that once read as blank. That opens studies of early exposure and subtle change that were previously impossible. For environmental and medical testing, the paper supplies a tool whose main virtue is simple: it sees what other methods miss entirely.
plos-pone-0011541:
Mingzhou Li and co-authors catalogued in 2010 the full set of microRNAs at work as pigs develop before and after birth. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that fine-tune gene activity, and their cast changes as an embryo grows into a newborn. Pigs are a key model for human biology and a major farm animal, so a developmental atlas of their microRNAs serves two fields at once.

Their microRNAome spans the pre- and postnatal periods, giving researchers a baseline of which regulators are present at each stage. Deviations from that baseline can then be spotted in disease, poor growth, or breeding lines. For developmental biology, the atlas turns a fast-moving cast into a reference chart. It also supports pig farming directly, since growth and health traits that breeders select on are steered in part by these small regulators.
plos-pone-0011641:
Glen Borchert and co-authors studied how the immune system targets its own antibody genes for change, in PLOS ONE in 2010. To improve antibodies, the enzyme AID deliberately alters DNA in the variable regions of antibody genes. How AID is aimed so precisely at those spots, and spared elsewhere, is not fully understood.

The team found that histones H2A and H2B carry a single ubiquitin tag at the loci AID targets. Histones are the spools DNA wraps around, so their tags may flag where mutation should happen. The finding adds a signpost to the map of how controlled mutation strengthens immunity without wrecking the genome.
plos-pone-0011741:
David McMillan and co-authors charted the family structure of a rising strep germ, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus dysgalactiae subspecies equisimilis can live in and infect humans and is gaining notice worldwide. Its strains are sorted by surface markers, which reveal a complex clan.

Their world survey found far-flung clones side by side with much DNA swapping between strains. That open mixing makes tracking and vaccine design harder, since the germ's make-up shifts across borders. The portrait shows a germ with a fluid genome that health teams must keep following over time.
plos-pone-0011841:
Alexander Bloemendaal, Ellen Brouwer, and Ad Fluit reported in 2010 a case where drug resistance moved between bacteria inside one patient. The resistance at stake was to methicillin, carried on a movable chunk of DNA in staphylococci. One species, Staphylococcus epidermidis, commonly lives on skin, while its cousin Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent cause of serious infection.

During the patient's antibiotic treatment, evidence pointed to the resistance element passing from the skin species into S aureus that had previously been treatable. A transfer caught in a real hospital course, rather than a lab flask, shows how treatment itself can set the stage for resistance to spread. It is a warning for how antibiotics are chosen and monitored.
plos-pone-0011941:
Matthias Rinderknecht and co-workers built in 2010 antibody fragments aimed at a vessel growth signal linked to cancer spread. VEGF-C drives the growth of lymphatic vessels, and tumors rich in it show more vessel density, more invasion into those vessels, and more spread to lymph nodes. The signal works through two receptors, VEGFR-2 and VEGFR-3.

Using phage display, the team produced fully human antibody fragments that block VEGF-C from engaging either receptor. Blocking the signal at its source could slow the lymphatic route that many tumors use to spread. Human fragments are attractive drug material because the body is less likely to react against them.
plos-pone-0012041:
Fabio Cafini and co-workers tested in 2010 whether prior immunity makes an antibiotic work better against resistant pneumococcus. People usually carry some antibodies before a Streptococcus pneumoniae infection begins. The team studied the antibiotic cefditoren in a mouse sepsis model, tracking how long drug levels stayed above the amount needed to stop the germ.

In pre-immunized mice, cefditoren showed enhanced activity against penicillin-resistant strains of serotypes 6B, 19F, and 23F. Drug and immune system working together is easy to say and harder to dose. Quantifying the boost helps design regimens that count vaccination and immunity as part of the treatment, not background luck.
plos-pone-0012141:
Yu Luo, Cameron Good, Oscar Diaz-Ruiz, and co-authors studied cocaine's effects on the mouse brain for PLOS ONE in 2010. Repeated cocaine use makes animals ever more reactive to the drug, a change rooted in altered connections in the brain's reward circuit. A receptor for the signal chemical glutamate is thought to drive that rewiring, but which cells need the receptor was unsettled.

The team focused on cells in a key reward hub that do not themselves use dopamine. Those cells' receptors still supported the growing response to cocaine. The result narrows where in the circuit addiction-like change begins, a map that later drug research can use to aim at the right cells.
plos-pone-0012241:
Aurore Gelin, Modesto Redrejo-Rodríguez, Jacques Laval, and co-authors dissected a human DNA repair enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. APE1 is a central repair worker: it cuts DNA at sites where a base is missing, serving one repair pathway, and nicks damaged DNA to start another. Mutant versions missing the second skill let the team ask what that skill is really for.

Their characterization of these mutants separates the enzyme's two repair jobs cleanly. Human cells juggle several overlapping repair systems, and knowing which enzyme covers which damage decides how cells survive radiation and some chemotherapies. Precise mutant tools like these are how such maps get drawn.
plos-pone-0012341:
Danupon Nantajit, Ming Fan, Nadire Duru, and co-authors reported a survival role for p53 in irradiated cancer cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The p53 protein is famous for ordering damaged cells to die, guarding against cancer. Yet under DNA damage, p53 also seems to give tumor cells a survival edge, a contradiction that matters directly for radiation therapy, where doctors count on p53 to help kill the tumor.

The team traced the survival effect to p53 sent into the mitochondria and chemically tagged there by a cell-cycle kinase, switching it into an anti-death mode. Knowing how a tumor converts its own guard into a shield suggests blocking that conversion during radiotherapy. The paradox resolved is a treatment idea gained.
plos-pone-0012441:
Dan Close, Stacey Patterson, Steven Ripp and colleagues made mammalian cells glow on their own, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Bacteria can make light with a five-gene set called lux, needing no added chemicals. Until now the full set worked only in bacteria, so animal cell imaging required feeding cells a substrate each time.
