They adjusted the sums for other factors that could skew the link. High omega-3 intake tied to far lower diabetes odds.

A high ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 tied to higher diabetes odds instead. Omega-6 intake alone showed no clear link either way. The authors say the balance of these fats may matter more than one fat alone. They stress the study is a snapshot, not proof of cause.
pmc-11607441:
Dean Kareemo and a large team build, in twenty twenty-four, genetic tools to tag and control AMPA receptors in living neurons. AMPA receptors carry nearly all fast excitatory signals in the brain. Watching and moving them in live cells is key to understanding synapses. The team turned published antibody sequences into affinity tags. Cells can make these binders, called intrabodies, inside neurons. The intrabodies grab receptors in the cell's shipping center and ride with them to the surface. There, dyes that cannot enter cells light them up.

The probes did not disturb receptor traffic, function, movement, or recruitment during plasticity, the team reports. They also adapted the tools to trap receptors inside the cell, draining them from the surface. That gives a simple way to cut excitatory transmission.
pmc-11607941:
Sampieri and four colleagues published a randomised trial in two thousand twenty-four on how long a daily fast should be. Time-restricted eating limits food to part of the day without dictating the menu. Its effects in healthy, non-training adults, and the best fasting length, were unclear.

Forty-one volunteers were split into four groups for eight weeks: fasts of sixteen, fourteen, or twelve hours, or normal eating. Body measures and blood tests tracked fat, cholesterol, sugar, and hormones. The longest fast cut body weight and fat mass clearly, with muscle preserved. Shorter windows showed weaker effects in the reported analysis. The authors compare both strict and real-world adherence views of the data.
pmc-11608641: An eighty-nine-year-old man's urinary retention led to a rare cancer diagnosis, reported by Mohammed Abusuliman and eight colleagues in twenty twenty-four. Imaging found a mass near the heart's great vessels and a small lesion in his liver. Further scans and biopsy supported metastatic type B2 thymoma, a thymus tumor spread to the liver alone. Isolated liver spread of thymoma is exceedingly rare. The authors say he is the oldest patient reported with this diagnosis, and they urge evaluating mediastinal masses for malignant spread.
pmc-11609141:
Latifi-Pakdehi and co-authors review circular RNAs as possible blood or tissue markers for colorectal cancer. These RNAs form closed loops and can aid cancer growth. Their stable shape makes them promising for non-invasive tests. The team searched three databases for studies up to September 2022. Rules for entry narrowed the field to 55 papers. Patient group sizes ran from 12 to 212.

Most of the circular RNAs studied, 47 of them, ran high in patients. Those likely act as cancer promoters through downstream paths. Others ran low and may play a brake role. The review weighs which markers look ready for firmer testing as diagnostic tools.
pmc-11611541:
Jinger Lin and co-authors pool trials of a targeted drug for severe eczema, in a review from two thousand twenty-four. The drug calms a key immune signal tied to the skin disease. Five studies with over fifteen hundred patients were pooled.

Scores for rash area, itch, sleep loss, and life quality all improved more on the drug than on dummy care. Overall side effects matched dummy care, and grave side effects did too. One dosing plan, a mid dose every two weeks, looked best. The authors judge the drug both effective and safe for teens and adults with hard eczema.
pmc-11612841:
Nathan Klett and co-authors report a mouse study from two thousand twenty-four on the brain's master clock and the signals that keep it in sync. The clock sits in a small brain region and its neurons must fire in step to drive daily rhythms. Those neurons use the chemical messenger GABA, but its role in live animals was untested.

The team deleted GABA signaling locally in the clock region of adult mice. Over time, the animals' body and behavior rhythms broke down. Cells from the region also lost their shared timing in the dish. The authors conclude that GABA signals between clock cells are essential for coherent daily rhythm, a basic insight into how the brain tells time.
pmc-11614541:
Matthew Muzzatti and co-authors work out in 2024 what farmed crickets should eat. Crickets are raised for food and feed, and diet drives survival, growth, and body size. The team raised tropical house crickets one by one from hatching to adulthood, each on a fixed mix of protein and carbohydrate.

Yield peaked on a diet of three parts protein to one part carbohydrate. Crickets on that mix most often reached adulthood and grew largest. Given a free choice, crickets instead picked a near-even mix, and males ate more protein than females. The authors say the results are a first step toward a standard feed that maximizes farm yield.
pmc-11615541:
Ghadah Alnooh and three co-authors test, in two thousand twenty-four, whether a phone app can help people with high blood pressure follow the DASH diet. That diet, built to lower blood pressure, can be hard to track by hand. The team chose a well-rated commercial app for use in Saudi Arabia.

Fourteen adults in Riyadh used the app for eight weeks and logged their meals. Most logged on three to five days a week, and logging grew over time. Talks after the trial found the app easy to fit into daily life and its food list simple to use. Users still hit slow screens and missed local dishes in the list. Scores for confidence and diet fit rose a little, but not by a clear margin.
pmc-11618341:
Ruixia Liu and six co-authors make a wood-based gel that glows after light at room heat, with strong stretch strength. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Past glow gels were weak and their glow could not be tuned, which blocked real use. The team grew a stretch polymer inside wood stripped of its dark lignin part.

Bonds twixt wood parts and the polymer made the gel both strong and lit with a green afterglow. A soak in spirit stretched both strength and glow span a lot. Swaps of spirit and water switched both traits back and forth. The gel also fed glow to a dye to make red afterglow, for new lit goods.
pmc-11622641:
Ma revisits the microgenderome, the study of how gut microbes differ by sex. Sex shapes disease risk, mainly for autoimmune illness, so microbe gaps may matter for care. An earlier report used Human Microbiome Project data but missed species-level detail.

Older methods lean on species counts alone and miss how species spread across samples. Both counts and spread shape microbe communities, the author argues. The new work aims to find and list species found only in one sex, plus those enriched in one. That catalog could sharpen how sex-linked microbe patterns are read in health and disease.
pmc-11626441:
Mottelson and seven co-authors followed Danish adults with an iron-overload gene variant in twenty twenty-four. People with two copies of the HFE C282Y variant can develop haemochromatosis, where iron builds up in organs. The team asked whether risk stays high even when blood iron measures look normal.

Three population cohorts held over one hundred thirty-two thousand genotyped people, including four hundred twenty-two with two variant copies, followed up to twenty-seven years. Double carriers had roughly double the risk of diabetes and liver disease, but no extra heart disease risk. Diabetes risk was elevated even when transferrin saturation and ferritin, the standard iron markers, were normal. Double carriers who developed diabetes also died sooner. The authors argue gene status matters beyond blood iron readings.
pmc-11629541:
Yang Jiang and eight co-authors published a pharmacology study in twenty twenty-four dissecting how Sijunzi decoction, a classic Chinese herbal formula, might act against Parkinson's disease. Rather than testing one molecule, the team mapped the whole formula computationally, then checked key predictions in cells.

Databases yielded one hundred eighty-eight active compounds and hundreds of targets shared with Parkinson's. Network analysis, docking, and molecular dynamics simulations ranked the likeliest interactions and pathways. Cell assays and protein blots then verified that predicted effects occur in living systems. The layered evidence chain, computation first and bench last, is the method's signature. The authors offer the target map as a hypothesis engine for future Parkinson's drug work.
pmc-11631441:
Tack and a large Belgian team follow people born with both testes regressed before birth. Their large series from twenty twenty-three examines causes and long-term outcomes. The rare condition leaves no working gonads at birth. A blood vessel accident was the classic suspected cause.

Genetic variants in one gene also explain some cases. Growth and puberty progressed well on hormone replacement. Dose increases followed a standard schedule through childhood. Penile growth often stayed below target despite treatment. That shortfall was worst with genetic causes or small size at birth. Tissue studies added detail on what remains of the gonads. Families gain realistic expectations for long-term care.
pmc-11631741:
Huang and colleagues test in twenty twenty-four whether a robotic radiation system tracks the skull well when a patient's head is not in the standard lying position. The system treats brain lesions and follows skull position in six dimensions using two X-ray panels. Staff worried that tilted or turned heads might throw its tracking off.

Using a skull model with varied tissue density, the team set the head at many angles. They compared skull tracking against marker tracking, a method that does not depend on head pose. Gaps between the two methods were tiny and not meaningful at any angle. Dose checks also passed clinical limits in all cases. Patients, they conclude, need not hold a strict pose for accurate treatment.
pmc-11633941:
Michelle Casagni and colleagues described in 2024 a project to pull usable research data straight from hospital records in cancer care. Clinical trials need outcome data that often sits locked in everyday electronic health records. The ICAREdata project tested whether record data, written in one standard structured format, could be extracted and sent for research use.

Standard cancer data elements were collected from records across ten sites. The team reports that the approach worked and draws lessons about standard forms for capturing and sending data in trials. Readers get a practical step toward routine research use of real-world records, which the authors link to better research and better care delivery.
pmc-11637441:
Jayakody and five co-authors review gut worm spread in Sri Lanka over the past one hundred years in this twenty twenty-four paper. Worms once spread widely on the isle, but deworm drives cut rates a great deal. Hard facts on where worms still spread and how rates moved were thin.

Inside, the review pools one hundred five past studies from print and gray sources. A first isle-wide count long ago found hookworm in most folks checked, while a late count found soil worms in under one percent. Rates stay much higher in farm-estate zones and in slum zones than in the broad public. The authors flag weak stool tests and poor hygiene as gaps that still need work.
pmc-11642041:
Caner Yesiloglu leads a team on psychiatric disorders and shingles rates in Turkiye. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses five years of hospital data. Records came from emergency and outpatient visits at one center.

Psychiatric ills are known to weaken the immune system in past work. That can raise the risk of infections like shingles. All adults seen at the hospital in the span were screened. Folks on immune suppressing care were left out of the study. Folks with mental ills had more shingles than those sans. Subgroup splits by diagnosis type were also checked.
pmc-11643541:
Frédéric Jeanroy and four co-authors sharpen mass spectrometry for tiny samples of sulfated sugar chains. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. These chains, called glycosaminoglycans, carry many charges and shed sulfate groups easily, which scrambles their spectra.

Sample preparation is the lever. Home-made capillary exchange columns tamed the extra ion attachments in one setup. For the laser-based method, though, a commercial resin treatment won out. Traces of that resin left in the water unexpectedly cleaned the spectra further. A model drug chain served as the test case throughout. The authors map which preparation suits which instrument when only miniaturized samples exist.
pmc-11644141:
Luo and colleagues analyzed genetic diversity in a Chinese oil tree and bred doubled-chromosome versions in twenty twenty-four. Idesia polycarpa from Sichuan has strong economic potential but few varieties. One line stood out for high oil content, near thirty-nine percent, and red fruits, making it a promising parent.

Treating seedlings of that line with colchicine, a chromosome-doubling chemical, produced over five hundred mutant seedlings. Flow cytometry screening flagged suspected triploids and tetraploids, plants with three or four chromosome sets. Fluorescence probes confirmed chromosome counts and identified eighteen true polyploids. The doubled plants differed clearly from normal ones in leaf shape and physiology. The authors say the work establishes a polyploid breeding system that widens the species' genetic base.
pmc-11644341:
Hong Yin and eight co-authors devise a better way to measure electric charge on spacecraft, in this twenty twenty-four paper. In orbit, plasma can charge a satellite's surface unevenly, which is a prime cause of faults and failures. Storms in Earth's magnetic field make the charging worse.

Their method splits voltage through capacitors to read very high and very low charges with fine accuracy. The team studied where errors creep in and how to design against them. A new zeroing trick clears drift that builds up from small errors over time. Precise charge readings help keep satellites safe in harsh space weather.
pmc-11644641:
Chuen-Lin Tien and colleagues built a fiber optic soil moisture sensor in 2024. The sensor starts with a standard light-carrying fiber. One side is polished flat, giving a D-shaped cross-section. A thin tin oxide film coats the flat side. Light inside the fiber then interacts with the coating. Soil moisture seeps into the film's fine structure. That seepage shifts a resonance peak in the light spectrum. The shift reveals soil humidity.

The team compared their sensor with a common electronic module. Soil humidity ranged from dry to very wet in the tests. One build, with set fiber and film thickness, gave the best sensitivity. Its response was fast, and repeat tests agreed well. The authors present the design as a precise tool for soil checks. Such sensors could serve farms and field research. They add no electronics at the sensing point itself.
pmc-11652841:
Weifeng Jin, Ping Lin, and six co-authors sum up the body effects of a schizophrenia drug. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, covers olanzapine. The drug eases symptoms for many patients. It can also shift weight and blood fats, which raises long-term health risks.

The team pooled twenty trials with more than eighteen hundred patients. Users gained clear weight on the drug. Blood fat measures, though, showed no firm change as a group. The review links dose and blood levels of the drug to how well symptoms ease. Symptom scores from standard scales fell. The balance of gain and risk can guide dose choices for each patient.
pmc-11653841:
Zi Guo and Natascha Heise published a medical education study in twenty twenty-four on rescuing anatomy teaching from the squeezed modern curriculum. Their nine-and-a-half-week gross anatomy course replaced some passive review with collaborative quizzes. Student groups rotated through twenty dissected donor stations, each posing a board-style question.

At every station, students answered alone first, then debated to a group answer, a design that forces both retrieval and peer teaching. Outcomes on the collaborative quizzes and the national board-style unit exams were compared to test the hypothesis of better preparation. The authors present the format as collective discourse doing the work that vanished lecture hours once did. Time pressure, reframed, becomes the pedagogy.
pmc-11656841:
Haoyun Su and Kannie Chan review how to design imaging contrast agents and nanocarriers for a label-free MRI technique that tracks proton exchange in the body. Their 2024 review explains design factors for making weak molecular signals visible.

The technique images compounds with exchangeable protons without metal or radioactive labels, following events like protein build-up in brain tumours or drug arrival at targets. Exchange signals are sensitive to local conditions, so carriers that concentrate agents locally can strengthen contrast. The authors cover tuning exchange rates and exploiting molecular interactions. Disease progression and treatment monitoring applications are surveyed, along with carriers doubling as drug delivery vehicles for evaluating therapy.
pmc-11657941:
Yuki Amano and co-authors report a multi-year study from two thousand twenty-four on microbes living deep underground in Japan. Two research laboratories, one in sedimentary rock and one in granite, open a window on life far below the surface. Such microbes could affect stored nuclear waste, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen, so their habits matter.

The team sampled groundwater at depths down to four hundred meters over four years. They rebuilt genomes for nearly all organisms found. The two sites held unlike communities, shaped by rock type, yet shared core functions such as hydrogen use and carbon fixing. Change over time was limited, and about a third of the organisms at one site kept near-identical genomes across depths, despite slow growth in place.
pmc-11658941:
Sureka Bhola and five co-authors study the vitamin D receptor gene in Black South Africans with type 1 diabetes, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Variants in this gene, and low vitamin D levels, have been linked to the disease in other groups. Results have been mixed, and this population had not been studied.

The case-control study genotyped one hundred eighty-two patients and one hundred fifty-one healthy controls for four variants. Vitamin D levels did not differ significantly between the groups. One variant form, the TaqI TT genotype, was linked to diabetes status in their adjusted analysis. It was also linked to higher vitamin D levels. The authors suggest the link to diabetes may act through a path that does not depend on vitamin D.
pmc-11659941:
Ian M. Rimer and Scott A. M. McAdam tested a drought idea in 2024 about compound leaves, whose blades split into leaflets on a stalk. In two tree species, leaflets blocked their water vessels sooner than the stalk during drought, acting as a cheap sacrifice that protects the stem. The team asked whether that pattern holds widely. Using an optical method that watches vessels block in real time, they measured six herb species and one tree, including forms with joint-like bases under each leaflet.

Resistance varied a lot between species, but within each leaf it stayed even. Leaflets and stalks blocked at the same water stress. In species with joint-like bases, major blockages crossed straight through those joints instead of stopping there. The authors conclude that a within-leaf sacrifice zone is not a general rule for compound leaves, and the small joints do not seal off spreading damage.
pmc-11662641:
Kfir Lavi leads a team with cases of acute lobar nephronia in children. Their series from twenty twenty-four deals with a focal kidney infection. The ill was long seen as rare in children.

Five young patients were described with a literature review. Ages ran from one to eleven years old. Fever was the main complaint in every case. Swelling marks in blood were notably high in all. None had pus in urine at presentation. Cultures of blood and urine came back sterile. Scans of varied types made the diagnosis instead.
pmc-11664441:
Correia and four colleagues present a case of sciatica like pain from a torn hamstring in twenty twenty-four. A thirty-six year old man tore his hamstring in an amateur football match. Two weeks later, leg pain mimicked sciatica, hinting the nerve was irked. Ultrasound found a partial tear of the biceps femoris head right by the sciatic nerve.

A five week rehab plan eased pain and rebuilt strength and flexibility. The case shows early, targeted rehab can head off hamstring syndrome. It also backs ultrasound as the diagnostic tool of choice here. Muscle tears can plainly bother the nearby nerve, they note.
pmc-11668941:
Natalya Slepneva and colleagues studied brain stimulation for severe OCD in two thousand twenty-four. Electrodes were implanted in a capsule deep in the brain. Five patients with treatment-resistant illness took part. Scans ran while stimulation cycled on and off. Several electrode settings were tested per person. Brain wiring maps linked contacts to networks.

Helpful settings quieted activity across many regions. Frontal and midline areas showed strong suppression. Many quieted spots belonged to the default mode network. That network supports self-focused inner thought. Unhelpful settings lacked this broad pattern. Network suppression may explain how stimulation relieves obsessions. Responders and non-responders differed in this signature.
pmc-11671241:
Hangxing Ren and ten co-authors investigate how Hu sheep tolerate hot, humid summers at the level of DNA methylation, in a two thousand twenty-four animal genetics paper. The breed is famed for fertility and adaptability, and its coping strategy turns out to be unusual.

Blood hormone and antioxidant measures in spring and midsummer showed only three of ten indices shifting significantly: the sheep lower metabolic rate and total antioxidant capacity rather than fighting heat head-on. Genome-wide methylation sequencing highlighted four genes whose methylation changed between seasons, each tied to hormone secretion or heat production pathways. The authors offer the epigenetic signatures as breeding markers for climate-resilient livestock.
pmc-11671941:
Ruurt Jukema and co-authors pool past trials to ask how well scans find blocked heart arteries in people who have had heart disease before. How well each scan works in people with a past heart attack or stent had not been summed up. The team searched four databases for blinded prospective studies where at least half the patients had prior disease, with invasive angiography as the yardstick.

Eighteen studies covered 3,265 patients, and 64% had obstructive disease. CT angiography, CT plus perfusion, and MRI all caught more than nine in ten cases. SPECT caught far fewer, near six in ten, though it was more specific than CT alone. The rank order guides care. When chest pain comes back after treatment, CT and MRI can rule disease out with trust. The older nuclear scan misses too much to give peace of mind.
pmc-11673541:
Sahar Jafari Nivlouei, Renato Natal Jorge, and six co-authors built a math model of new blood vessels, in work from twenty twenty-four. New vessels sprout from old ones as wounds heal, but live tests cannot track blood flow, pressure, or vessel width well. The team modeled a chick membrane system, a common stand-in for vessel growth.

Their model mixes two styles of math to track single cells and the whole web at once. It matched real growth to within fifteen percent on vessel volume. It also mapped pressure and the rub of blood on vessel walls. The web can widen or narrow in response to flow and food needs, much as real vessels do.
pmc-11674941:
Suresh and Temple link pop and buzz drink use to teen risk acts in this twenty twenty-four study. Buzz drink use climbs in kids, yet its health ties stay dim. Teen files from three states gave the pair a wide test base.

Inside, more than ten thousand high school teens fed the risk checks. Day pop or buzz use tied to far high drug use odds. Mind health grades ran poor for day users of both drinks. Fast food feast odds also ran high in day users of each. Sex bent each tie, with boys and girls split in the marks.
pmc-11675741:
Peng and co-authors report survey findings on Canadians who care for older relatives or friends while holding a job. More adults now juggle unpaid care with full- or part-time work. A national survey in 2022 asked who these carers are and why they give care. It also asked about the social, money, and health costs they carry. Many respondents held jobs alongside their care duties.

Past research mostly finds that women carers suffer worse mental and physical health. The new findings are more mixed than that pattern. The authors set the Canadian results beside earlier work at home and abroad. They close with policy options for governments and employers who want to support working carers.
pmc-11677541:
Yuheng Li and co-authors present a computer vision model, published in twenty twenty-four, that grades powdery mildew on rubber tree leaves. The disease shows first as pale patches on leaves and spreads fast, cutting yield and quality. Hand checks are slow and take much labor, so the team built an automatic tool.

First they built a data set of thousands of leaf images with tens of thousands of marked spots. Their model, named PM-YOLO, adds parts that help it spot small patches in messy scenes. It also grades how bad the damage is on each leaf. In tests it beat the base model it grew from on both hit rate and recall. The authors offer it as a fast way to catch the disease early.
pmc-11678341:
Sylwia Stączek, Magdalena Kunat-Budzyńska, Małgorzata Cytryńska, and Agnieszka Zdybicka-Barabas review proline-rich defense peptides, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. These short proteins help invertebrates fight germs as part of their inborn defense. Many carry extra domains rich in cysteine or a whey-like part.

Inside bacteria, the peptides strike the protein-making machinery and a folding helper. That grip stalls protein output and piles up broken proteins. Because the target sits deep inside the cell, germs resist them slowly. Lab-made copies are now being built as new drugs. The review maps the family's range and promise.
pmc-11679641:
Aleksandra Bojarczuk and five co-authors review gene variants tied to weight gain in a 2024 paper. Obesity depends on genes, environment, and lifestyle together. The review focuses on variants in six interleukin genes, which control immune signaling, and pools data in depth for one variant in the IL-6 gene and obesity risk in men.

Thirty studies with nearly thirty thousand people were included, drawn from studies published between 1998 and 2023. The authors checked study quality and signs of publication bias. Results were combined into pooled odds figures for each variant. The IL-6 gene was singled out because its effects are broad and its link to obesity was unclear.
pmc-11683141:
Liping Shi and co-authors study how the genes of Panax notoginseng, a valued medicinal ginseng, shape the microbial community round its roots. A healthy root-zone community guards plant health and yield. The team tracked two groups across the plant's growth stages: helpful bacteria and fungal pathogens, against plain farmland soil.

Both groups were richer and more diverse in the root zone than in farmland soil. The helpful bacteria thinned out after planting, while the pathogens followed a different path. The two groups pulled against each other: where helpful bacteria thrived, pathogens waned, above all for the biocontrol subgroup. Assembly of the helpful community was most strongly guided, least left to chance, in the third-year root growth stage. The plant's own genes, for protein export and for making alkaloids and amino acids, emerged as drivers of that guided assembly.
pmc-11683641:
Fan Li, Yin-Cong Kong, Zi Yang, and Chen Wang report a two thousand twenty-four synthesis study of lanthanide complexes designed as single-molecule magnets. The best molecular magnets pair ring-shaped ligands with carbon-based clamps around dysprosium. A neutral combination of both ligand types was hypothesized to sharpen magnetic behaviour.

The team instead isolated yttrium versions bearing one ring ligand and one methanediide clamp, the first of their kind. Structures were confirmed crystallographically across three ring variants. Reaction routes and characterization are detailed. These complexes set the structural stage for chasing the dysprosium magnets the design promised.
pmc-11688341:
Beatty and five co-authors wrote a review in twenty twenty-four on tracking the body to stop diving harms. Diving can strain the body on the way down, at depth, on the way up, and for hours after. Strict rules make harms rare, but they still occur, often with unclear causes. The review first lists the most common diving harms. It gives rates for fun divers and for United States military divers.

It then names body signs that could warn of trouble early. Those signs include heart rate, blood pressure, breath rate, body heat, and blood oxygen. The authors say much more testing is needed in real dive settings. Still, they see a clear path to a warning system for divers.
pmc-11691941:
Tuo Yu Chen and six co-authors published a study in 2024 on persistent pain, sleep health, and frailty among community-dwelling older adults in Taiwan. Persistent pain is known to contribute to frailty. Sleep health is closely related to both pain and frailty, yet the three-way relationship was not fully understood.

The researchers used a national longitudinal aging survey with 2,562 adults, followed from 2011 to 2015. Frailty was measured with an index built from thirty-seven items covering function and physical and mental health. Pain was graded in levels from none to severe and persistent. Sleep health was scored across five dimensions, from satisfaction with sleep to its duration. Higher grades of persistent pain at baseline raised the risk of frailty four years later. Poor sleep health did the same. The study also tests whether good sleep health can soften the impact of pain on frailty.
pmc-11692341:
Brianna Margulis and five co-authors describe a Columbia University workshop that trains future clinicians to communicate with older adults. Their report appeared in twenty twenty-four. Northern Manhattan holds the city's largest share of residents over sixty-five, so the skill is local and urgent.

Graduate students from ten programs, from dentistry to social work, mixed into small cross-field groups. They practiced spotting low health literacy and clearing barriers to understanding. Case scenarios let them use the tools together. Surveys before and after showed students felt readier to talk with elders facing sensory, cognitive, or physical change. They also learned what their future colleagues actually do. The authors note the small sample as the main limit.
pmc-11692941:
Daniel Gan, Adam Hoverman, and Kate Mulligan explore a lighter form of social prescribing in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Digital tools that refer patients to community support often fail because communities are not engaged, so referrals go unused. The team asked users and staff what blocks the system.

Work in Metro Vancouver with over seventy stakeholders surfaced twin strains: scarce resources and staff burnout. Funding came in fits and starts, referral steps ate time, and information went stale. The authors propose starting with social isolation, using an automated platform that handles routine prevention and flags complex cases. A place-based wellness model was built into a web app. The lite design aims to scale preventive care without crushing clinicians.
pmc-11693941:
Phillips and five co-authors scope sex and kind gaps in sickle trait harms in this twenty twenty-four review. The trait is oft cast as mild, yet ill fruits do fall on its bearers. If those fruits split by sex was a bare spot in the lore.

Inside, five banks gave three score works from a six-year span for the pool. Most works were band hunts in one state, on mixed ill fruits. A third told fruits split by trait and sex side by side. A third more held sex still in math; none touched kind at all. The team calls for sex-and-kind reads in all trait work next.
pmc-11695041:
Rita Ortiga, Maria Couto, Elisa Lopes, and João Fonseca describe a woman whose tongue turned black and hairy while on a mind drug. Their case report, with a short literature review, was published in twenty twenty-four. The condition is harmless and fades on its own, caused by overgrown taste buds on the tongue surface.

The patient had a form of schizophrenia and was treated with olanzapine during a relapse. The tongue change appeared as the dose rose to a daily level, hinting at a dose-linked cause. Dry mouth from such drugs and from cannabis is a suspected pathway. Better mouth hygiene plus stopping the drug and cannabis cleared the condition. The report alerts prescribers to a rare, visible side effect.
pmc-11703641:
Robert Buntyn and four colleagues published a case discussion in two thousand twenty-four on a patient who refused a pacemaker for complete heart block. Pacemaker implantation is the standard, potentially lifesaving answer when the heart's electrical relay fails fully. The patient declined repeatedly over years.

His conduction disease had crept from mild first-degree block through an intermediate stage to complete block, an unexpected path. Cardiology staff laid out the benefits in multiple discussions. He still chose to forgo the device. The authors use the case to examine patient-centred care and shared decision making. The tension between doing good and respecting autonomy frames their discussion.
pmc-11709341:
Anuradha Korukonda, Jake Atallah, Margaret Tish, and David Weinshenker published a 2025 mouse study of tau damage in the locus coeruleus. This small brainstem area supplies norepinephrine, a chemical that shapes mood, stress, and arousal. It is also the first place where abnormal tau appears in the human brain.

The team placed a disease form of tau only in this area of mice, then tested behaviour three months later. The tau mice fell asleep faster after handling, showing a sleepiness pattern. They also hesitated longer before eating in a new arena, an anxiety sign, and shredded nesting material under stress. Memory for shocks stayed normal at this stage. The results link early tau in this one area to early non-memory symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease.
pmc-11725341: Alexa Lum and Mitchell Brady describe a rare palm variant of a common blistering disease, in a case report from twenty twenty-four. A woman aged eighty-seven had an itchy red rash over most of her body for a month. Tense blisters then formed on her palms, the hallmark of dyshidrosiform bullous pemphigoid. The variant mainly affects elderly patients and can mimic other blistering diseases. A direct immunofluorescence test helps confirm the diagnosis. Treatment rests on oral corticosteroids plus an immunosuppressant. Newer antibodies show promise for stubborn cases.
pmc-11728041:
Karol Ulatowski, Patryk Szczygielski, and Paweł Sobieszuk test whether water purity and gas choice change how well microbubbles clean steel. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Bubble cleaning without harsh agents appeals to food, drug, and medical makers.

Steel plates fouled with a polymer solution were cleaned in three waters: ultrapure, reverse-osmosis, and tap. Bubbles were made from air, oxygen, or nitrogen. Infrared scans and droplet angle measures judged the clean. Results repeated well between plates. Both water grade and gas shifted the effect, so the pairing matters, not bubbles alone. The work gives process designers a firmer recipe for agent-free cleaning.
pmc-11731641:
Julie-Anne McCarthy and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-four on relationships during the pandemic among youth with a history of child maltreatment. Lockdowns and stress strained family and partner ties for many young people. Those who had faced maltreatment in childhood may have carried extra load into that period, with lasting effects on their relationships.

The team used a Manitoba cohort that followed one thousand youth and parent pairs from two thousand seventeen. Pandemic questions ran through three yearly waves, with nearly six hundred youth aged eighteen to twenty-one by the last wave. They tested whether a maltreatment history raised the odds of reporting more conflict with parents, siblings, or partners. The design centers the youths' own reports.
pmc-11740641:
Aikaterini Toska leads a team on computer and internet addiction in Greek youth. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set in the Megara region. Digital life has changed fast for kids and teens most of all.

Parents of school age kids filled a survey for the study. A parent form of a teen addiction scale was used. Most parents were mothers, and the kids spanned school ages. Just a small share of parents gave high addiction scores. Boys made up most of that high score group in reports. Mean scores and traits of the group are set out.
pmc-11784041:
Aswin Rafif Khairullah and a large team of co-authors published a 2024 review of a poultry disease bacterium called avian pathogenic Escherichia coli, or APEC. The bacterium causes colibacillosis, a costly infection of chickens that spreads through flocks and farms. Unlike other disease groups of the same species, APEC cannot be recognized by one single trait, which makes it harder to track.

The review covers how the bacterium spreads, the tools it uses to attack, and how infection is diagnosed. Its weapons include surface parts for gripping cells, shields against the immune system, systems for stealing iron, and toxins. Contaminated hatching eggs are a main route into new flocks, and poor waste handling helps it persist. Vaccines exist, but the authors note they still do not protect well enough against the range of strains in the field.
pmc-11808141:
Qila Sa and seven colleagues model which of three parathyroid operations gives Chinese dialysis patients the best value over ten years. Secondary hyperparathyroidism forces a choice among subtotal removal, total removal, and total removal with a fragment reimplanted. Their Markov model ran on a baseline cohort drawn from China's million dialysis patients.

Total removal cost more than subtotal surgery but bought substantially more quality-adjusted life years, at a cost per healthy year far below the willingness-to-pay threshold. The reimplantation variant cost most without extra benefit. Sensitivity analyses did not overturn the ranking. The authors conclude total parathyroidectomy is the most cost-effective option in the Chinese system.
pmc-11879541:
Susan Pickard and a team of co-authors explore what aging well means in minority ethnic groups, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The usual idea of successful aging reflects values most open to white, middle-class older people. The authors sought other views of a good old age.

The work draws on a longitudinal project with five minority ethnic groups in a diverse United Kingdom city. Participants used photovoice methods, sharing images and stories about their lives. Analysis read their accounts through both intersectionality and the lived feel of old age. Participants turned deficits into assets and built meaning and purpose in hard circumstances. The authors offer these accounts to help clinicians support diverse older people.
pmc-12490441:
Lucija Pavljak, Krešimir Bulić, Maksimilian Mrak, and Anko Antabak published a hand surgery study in twenty twenty-four tracking skin temperature around carpal tunnel release. The trapped median nerve also carries fibers controlling skin blood flow, so temperature should shift when the nerve is freed. Sixteen patients were measured before surgery and across six months after.

Temperature in the median nerve's skin territory rose after decompression, peaking at two months before settling above the starting level. Neighboring nerve territories moved on their own curves, and even the healthy hand's temperature crept up at every visit. The patterns suggest sympathetic function recovers gradually after release. Temperature mapping could become a simple, painless progress check.
pmc-12663541:
Lopatin and four colleagues wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It rebuilds the landscape where a saber-toothed cat cub lived in Ice Age Siberia, using tiny plant remains found near the cub's frozen body.

The mummified cub of Homotherium latidens was dug from permafrost on the Badyarikha River in northeast Yakutia. The team studied pollen, spores, plant scraps, and silica grains from soil taken at the find site. These microfossils record the plants that once grew there. The picture that emerges is a river floodplain with mature larch forest, ringed by damp meadows of sedges, grasses, and flowering herbs. That setting helps explain how the young predator's family lived and hunted.
pmc-12664241:
Jing Li, Longzhu Song, Dongzi Song, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It tests a broth brewed from human fat tissue, made without serum, as a way to slow aging in stem cells and keep tissues in balance.

Stem cells tire and age over time, which weakens both natural repair and stem cell therapies. The team bathed fat-derived stem cells in their tissue broth, in models of both stress-driven and wear-driven aging. Treated cells showed fewer aging markers, grew and moved better, and kept their ability to turn into other cell types. Skin cells aged in the lab responded well too. In mice, injections eased aging signs across skin, fat, muscle, and kidney, with no harm to liver or kidney seen. The broth worked partly by damping a known inflammation pathway.
pmc-12664841:
Sarri and a large team laid out in twenty twenty-five a plan for strong-field quantum tests in Europe's particle physics path. At fields near a vast named cap, light and charge act in ways never yet seen in labs. Pair birth from light, bent vacuum light, and odd photon bounce sit on that list.

Top laser sites in Europe now near the needed strength. The team wants high-count, fine tests in place of first-look runs. That shift needs big teams plus work on detectors, beam steadiness, and lasers. The runs also feed plans for future high-energy colliders.
pmc-12669241:
Zejian Liang, Yunxiang Zhao, Haiwen Xu, Hong Huang, and Luning Chen built a hybrid model to sort medical search queries by intent in twenty twenty-five. Sorting queries well is key to good medical search, but shallow word-count models miss context, while deep language models can miss keyword weight and class cues. Their model fuses three branches with an attention step that weighs each branch per query.

One branch uses a pre-trained language model for deep meaning. Two more use term-weight scores, one for the query as a whole and one built from class centers, which serve as anchors that help rare classes. On a public medical query data set, the model reached point eight two four accuracy and a macro F-score of point eight zero zero. It beat every baseline tried, with the clearest gains for the rare classes that other models tend to miss.
pmc-12692341:
Yaerin Wallenberger and co-authors review how depression builds in autistic people and offer a joined-up model, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Depression is common in this group and ties to grave outcomes, the authors note. How it may look unlike in non-autistic people gets early play.

Mind, growth, and clinic factors shown to feed low mood are gathered and sorted. Core autism traits and shared mind habits both enter the web. Links among the factors are spelled out as a testable pattern. Ways to test and refine the model follow, with stakes for care and policy. Readers get a map that treats the factors as a system, not a list.
pmc-12694041:
Pengliang Tang, Yu Wang, Aidong Men, and Yun Zhang propose, in two thousand twenty-five, a new way to brighten dark photos with diffusion models. Dark images need repair across wide areas, but adding heavy global tools inside each denoising step costs too much compute. Their design moves that work outside the main loop.

A side network reads the full image once and builds context cues at several scales. Those cues then guide each step of the diffusion process at low cost. A colour loss, set in a light-and-colour space, also guards against a cool tint in dark areas. Tests on paired and unpaired photo sets beat recent rival methods on sharp and loose quality scores alike. The extra path added only modest cost.
pmc-12707441:
Anja Yvonne Bischof and eight colleagues published a cohort study in two thousand twenty-five on a game-like breathing app for people with cancer. Stress is common in cancer, and short digital exercises can bring momentary calm. How a breathing game holds up over months was untested.

Breeze was one of seven relaxation techniques in the CanRelax 2.0 app, offered over ten weeks in Switzerland, Germany, and Austria. The study tracked how often users picked Breeze, how closely their breathing matched its guiding pattern, and how relaxed they felt right after sessions. Session length was also examined as a factor. The authors report on long-term use patterns for gamified breathing in real app conditions.
pmc-12712541:
Moushumi Suryavanshi led a large team validating a DNA test for leftover leukemia in a 2025 paper. Tracking tiny residual disease guides treatment in a childhood blood cancer, but the standard cell-sorting method misses very low levels. Their adapted sequencing assay was tested on archived slides, preserved tissue, and fresh marrow samples from dozens of patients. Dilution runs set its detection floor, and repeat runs checked stability.

The assay found starting fingerprints in most patients and detected disease down to one cell in a million. It agreed with the standard method in most cases and caught leftover disease weeks earlier in several. Results supported broader clinical use.
pmc-12712641:
Kucinic and a large team catalogue caddisflies in Croatia in twenty twenty-five. Caddisflies are insects whose young live in water and build small cases. The team reviews the history of research on them in the country. They also map where each species lives across regions, river basins, and ecological zones.

In total, they record two hundred twenty-five species in eighteen families and seventy-four genera. Most species were confirmed as adults, and two were found only by DNA barcoding of larvae. Counts differ by region, with the Black Sea basin holding more species than the Adriatic basin. A global barcode database holds samples for most of the Croatian fauna. The work gives a full faunistic and taxonomic reference for the country.
pmc-12713041:
Daniela Mestre and seven co-workers, with a Basque lung health group, checked a Basque form of a form on inhaler use. The Test of Adherence to Inhalers helps staff spot why patients miss doses. No Basque form yet served the many Basque speakers in the zone. The 2025 study took in 249 asthma patients and 149 patients with a long term lung ill called COPD. Staff turned the form into Basque, then back to check it was right.

Talks with patients proved they grasped the Basque words well. Trust in scores was gauged with a score called Cronbach's alpha. Form shape was checked with factor tests. Scores were also set next to ill depth and counts of other ills. Mean scores split asthma and COPD patients. A checked form in their own tongue lets Basque clinics gauge inhaler use in the tongue patients like best.
pmc-12714741:
Seung-Jun Lee and colleagues check an Antarctic station's satellite navigation gear for a global network. Their study from twenty twenty-five evaluates King Sejong Station. The International GNSS Service demands strict data quality from member stations. Remote polar sites face harsh conditions and few nearby structures.

Observations from two epochs, fourteen years apart, were reprocessed. The station moves slowly north-northeast with the crust there. Data completeness and signal slip rates met network thresholds. Reflections from nearby buildings raised one quality concern. A new tide gauge benchmark replaced a lost original marker. Level surveys tied the height references together in twenty twenty-three. The station looks nearly ready for network contribution.
pmc-12717241:
Tae Kim, Rohith Bhat, and Temesgen Yimer design a privacy-preserving learning system for health records. Their paper from twenty twenty-five combines federated learning with secure computation. Hospitals hold records for different patient groups. Privacy rules block simply pooling that data for analysis.

Their framework lets hospitals learn together without sharing raw records. Transfer learning carries knowledge between sites with different populations. Stronger multiparty computation guards the exchanges between participants. Smart record systems could then train better models safely. Personalised care stands to gain from larger combined evidence. The design targets trust problems that stall hospital collaboration today.
pmc-12720141:
Stein, Jerosch, Pause, and Fischer published in twenty twenty-five a field study of the endangered common hamster in a simple German farm landscape. The team mapped hamster burrows across Saxony-Anhalt farmland. Local factors included a protective high-cut harvest method and vole numbers. Satellite vegetation indices were tested as predictors as well. Landscape factors covered crop mix, field size, and distances to forest and towns. Hamster density fell where voles were abundant in their data.

High-cut harvest showed a slight positive but non-significant effect. Vegetation indices showed no effect on hamster presence. Winter cereal share around fields raised the chance of hamsters occurring. Other landscape measures showed no clear effects in this simplified landscape. The authors advise adapted vole management to avoid harming hamsters. Single local measures cannot stabilize populations alone, they conclude. Landscape-level farm schemes are needed in such plain regions.
pmc-12730141:
Nozima Razakova, Dace Priede, and Surayyo Artykova compared smiles and smile satisfaction among young adults in Latvia and Uzbekistan. How a smile looks shapes judgments of facial attractiveness, and tastes may differ between cultures. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team photographed smiles from half of their two hundred volunteers and measured traits such as smile type, symmetry, teeth shown, and smile arc. The other half answered a questionnaire about how they see their own smiles and how satisfied they feel with them.

The two national groups differed clearly in smile type and in how many teeth a smile displays. Uzbek participants reported higher satisfaction with their smiles than Latvian participants. Both groups most preferred an average smile line and a smile arc that runs parallel to the lower lip. The authors conclude that both physical traits and satisfaction vary across cultures.
pmc-12730241:
Eight researchers led by Siqi Liu asked how coumarin, a plant compound that slows root growth in many species, does its work. They screened mutant forms of a small lab plant for ones that shrugged off the compound. Two mutants pointed to a protein-tagging system called neddylation, which also steers the plant growth hormone auxin.

Plants with extra copies of the tag gene were extra sensitive, and a drug that blocks the system stopped coumarin cold. Coumarin made one auxin-response protein build up in roots. The team concludes the compound halts main root growth by twisting auxin signals through the tagging path.
pmc-12731141:
Lejla Pašić and a team of co-authors ask whether a mother's gut microbes link to oversized babies in diabetic pregnancy, in two thousand twenty-five. Diabetes in pregnancy raises the chance of a large baby. Whether gut microbes add to that risk beyond blood sugar control was unclear, so the team followed eighteen women across pregnancy.

Mothers of large babies showed lower microbe diversity and fewer microbes that make helpful short-chain fats. Some pro-swelling microbes were enriched in those mothers. One candidate marker lost its link once body size and weight gain were weighed. A few other microbes kept a negative link after those adjustments. The authors frame the work as a pilot.
pmc-12736141:
Raluca Pele and colleagues created new candidate cancer compounds in two thousand twenty-five. The compounds belong to a ring family called quinazolinones. Three variants were synthesized and fully characterized. Lab tests measured their effects on cells. One test line was normal skin tissue. The other was human liver cancer cells.

One variant hit liver cancer cells hardest. Another spared normal cells better than the reference drug. The reference drug still beat all new compounds overall. Computer studies checked fit against a growth receptor target. Fat solubility testing rounded out the profiles. Chemists gain a starting scaffold for refinement. Stronger, safer versions remain the goal.
pmc-12736441:
Krzysztof Chmielowiec, Aleks Piszczek, and Łukasz Topolski test solar inverters in a 2025 paper. Rooftop solar units must notice when they get cut off from the main grid, a fault called islanding. If they keep feeding power into a dead section of grid, workers and gear face danger. Current tests mostly check one unit at a time.

They tested seven shop-bought inverters under two safety standards. All units with active protection spotted islanding inside the time limit, though speeds varied widely. Running units side by side slowed detection, and one unit with protection off could sustain an island on its own. The authors urge standards that test units running together.
pmc-12737141:
Giovanni Forte and co-authors published a 2025 study of metal levels in the urine of people who live near the most active volcano in Europe, Mount Etna in Sicily. The mountain releases gas and ash almost without pause, and its lava flows send metals into the air. The team asked whether years near the mountain raise the dose of such elements inside the body.

They collected urine from 167 adults in the city by the mountain and from 193 adults in distant parts of the island. Five metals ran high in the city group: two that nourish crops yet harm in high doses, two more known poisons, and one used in medicines. The remaining levels traced to food, drink, and habits more than to the mountain. All levels sat well within safe ranges. The team reads a real but small increase in dose, with no serious risk.
pmc-12739141:
Barbara Poniedzialek and four co-authors ask whether a prior COVID-19 infection makes a later chest infection worse in young children, in a 2025 study. The second virus, called RSV, is a leading cause of hospital stays for small children. The team studied one hundred thirty nine children aged five and under during one winter season.

Blood tests at admission sorted the children into prior infection, recent infection, and no infection groups. About two thirds showed signs of a past COVID-19 infection. The groups did not differ in hospital stay length, inflammation levels, or treatment needs. More children with recent infection needed oxygen, but the gap was not firm. The authors conclude prior infection did not clearly worsen RSV illness.
pmc-12739941:
Weizhen Wu and colleagues describe eye damage seen in a severe immune disorder. Their clinical analysis from twenty twenty-five covers hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, or HLH. Retinal lesions in this condition are poorly described so far. Better description could guide eye care for these very ill patients.

Fifteen patients with retinal lesions received full eye examinations. Imaging included fundus checks and cross-section scans of the retina. Bleeding inside the retina appeared in most eyes studied. Outer retinal thinning and layer disruption were also common. Bright spots in the outer retina showed in some eyes. The pattern suggests poor blood flow starves the retina. The authors call for larger studies to confirm that mechanism.
pmc-12745241:
Mengyao Dao and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-five on simple blood scores that predict high uric acid in Yi residents of Yunnan, China. High uric acid is common and can lead to gout. Insulin resistance helps drive it, but which cheap surrogate score works best in this group, among people without diabetes, was unknown.

The team studied seven hundred sixty-five adults and split them by uric acid status. Four scores built from triglycerides, glucose, body mass, and cholesterol were compared as predictors. All four scores ran higher in the high uric acid group, along with smoking, drinking, blood pressure, and weight. Statistical curves judged which score separates the groups best, to guide screening in this population.
pmc-12746341:
Amena Almubarak and three co-authors report a limb-saving case in a 2025 paper. A man of sixty with diabetes developed chronic bone infection in the lower third of his shin after an injury. That spot is hard to rebuild because soft tissue is thin and blood flow is poor. His care came in stages, from deep cleaning of the wound to treatment matched to lab cultures.

Bone graft from his own body filled the gap, and a muscle flap from a nearby leg muscle covered it. The flap is turned from a base near the ankle, avoiding complex microsurgery. Healing was complete, full limb function returned, and the infection did not come back.
pmc-12747541:
Cronshagen and a large team of colleagues build a lab rig to study the main harm tool of malaria germs in this twenty twenty-five paper. The tool is a coat the germ shows on red cells it has seized in the blood. It lets the sick cell cling to vein walls, a root of grave malaria.

Inside, each germ holds scores of coat types yet shows just one at a time. Their rig forces a whole brood to show one set type, which past work could not do. Gene cuts can then be made at that live coat spot for clean tests. New rig lines bind the most common vein locks, as sick cells do in the body. The rig found fresh parts the germ needs to cling and hide.
pmc-12748241:
Magdalena Karasek, Izabela Kubiszewska, and Marta Sobas review a rare and mixed form of acute leukemia. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In this disease, the cancer blasts bear marks of more than one cell line at once. That mix makes it hard to name and hard to treat, and results are poor on the whole.

They sum up how the disease is defined, split by gene marks, and treated. Two mixes rule: one joins B-cell and myeloid marks, the other T-cell and myeloid. Gene faults are found in most cases. No standard care path exists. Plans built for lymphoid leukemia give the best results so far, and stem cell transplants stay key. New targeted drugs are in view.
pmc-12748741:
Prathum and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a trial of mild electric brain stimulation in healthy adults. The method sends a weak current through the scalp. It can affect how the two sides of the brain hold each other back during hand moves. The team tested three current levels and a sham, or fake, session. Twenty right-handed adults each took part in four sessions.

During each session, people did a timed reaction task while stimulation was applied. Brain waves were recorded before and after. The strongest current gave the largest change in a brain symmetry measure. Reaction times also improved most at that level, and the two changes moved together. The authors suggest that measure could help guide dose choice in later work.
pmc-12749641:
Zahabi, Nayebi, and Shojaei load three drugs into metal frame carriers. The frames are porous crystals built from metal and carbon links. A fast ultrasound method made them at room heat. Two frame types used copper or zinc as the metal.

Tests proved the frames were porous and held the drugs well. The zinc frame loaded one drug at more than 60 percent. Copper frames loaded each drug at lower rates. Release was tracked in a buffer at body heat. That buffer mimics fluids the drug would meet in the body. Frame choice thus shapes dose and release pace.
pmc-12752041:
Ari August and a team of co-authors test whether eye scan rings are light artifacts, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Three patients with underdeveloped central retina gave six eyes for study. Rings on laser photos and ripples on scans are used as signs of the condition.

The team measured dark fringe widths under red, green, and blue laser light. Fringe size grew in neat linear step with fringe order at every color. Scan ripples matched the same pattern closely. Ratios strayed a bit from pure theory. Still, the match backs light interference, not tissue change, as the cause.
pmc-12753741:
Yutong Guo and eleven co-authors published a cardiology study in twenty twenty-five on an epigenetic switch that pours fuel on inflammation after a heart attack. A chemical mark called succinylation, placed on histone H3, surged in monocytes from patients and mice after infarction, tracking stronger inflammatory responses. The writer of the mark turned out to be an enzyme known for a different one.

Histone acetyltransferase 1 doubles as the succinylation enzyme here. Mice lacking it had smaller infarcts, better heart function, and calmer inflammation. The enzyme opens chromatin at inflammatory genes and decorates them with the mark. Blocking it becomes a candidate strategy for the dangerous first days after a heart attack.
pmc-12764341:
Sangjoon Choi and seven colleagues published a 2025 study on a simple count that may foretell liver cancer's return. The count is the mitotic index, the number of dividing cells seen in a tumor sample. Their focus is very early stage liver cancer, where two cures compete: cutting the tumor out or burning it away.

The team counted dividing cells in slides from 942 removed tumors at one Korean medical center. They asked whether a high count tracks early return of the cancer. If it does, high-risk patients could be steered toward surgery over ablation. A cheap slide count that sharpens that choice would be prized in liver clinics.
pmc-12772541:
Wanglian Peng and six co-authors examine which home hospice patients with advanced cancer end up on high-dose opioids, in a two thousand twenty-four retrospective study from central China. Dose escalation raises questions about both need and safety.

Records covered four hundred sixteen patients; eighty, about nineteen percent, received high-dose opioids at home. Male sex, higher preadmission morphine-equivalent dose, and morphine as the drug at peak dose each predicted high-dose use. Survival did not differ between high-dose and very-high-dose groups. The authors advise anticipating dose needs in men arriving on substantial opioids, and reassure that regulated adequate dosing does not shorten life.
pmc-12779441:
Bai and a large team test in twenty twenty-five whether a metabolic index predicts overactive bladder in United States adults. Overactive bladder is a common urinary problem tied to weight gain and diabetes. The index blends body size, blood sugar, blood fats, and a liver enzyme ratio into one score. The team used national survey data for well over fifteen thousand adults.

Higher scores linked to higher rates of overactive bladder in a curved pattern. The link was clear in women but not in men. The authors propose the index as a possible early warning tool, above all for women. They call for more work to confirm the link and find its mechanism.
pmc-12780441:
Jared Beller leads a team that compares two ways to remove the thymus. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with myasthenia gravis sans thymus tumor. Chest split surgery was the old standard for this care.

Data from four centers over near a decade were pooled. Half the folks had small cut surgery, half had chest split. Nerve outcomes were checked each three months for two years. A nerve doctor read the follow up from the charts. The ask is if small cuts give the same nerve gains. Such gains would spare folks a large chest cut.
pmc-12781441:
Xuena Zhang and seven co-authors tie vitamin D levels and a diet-and-habit score to death risk in people with metabolic syndrome, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The data came from a United States health survey run from two thousand one to two thousand eighteen, with just over twelve thousand adults who had the syndrome. Deaths were tracked through national records to the end of two thousand nineteen.

Over the follow-up, more than two thousand deaths occurred. People with vitamin D at or above a set level died less often from all causes and from heart disease than those with low levels. The benefit curve leveled off at the top. A higher oxidative balance score, which credits antioxidant-rich habits, also went with lower death risk. The two helped most when combined, the joint study showed.
pmc-12786841:
Kamata, Okada, and Ohta track in twenty twenty-five how bitter compounds in lettuce change after harvest, across hours and days. Lettuce's bitterness comes from a family of compounds in its milky sap, some linked to calming and anti-inflammatory effects. Reports say picked lettuce grows more bitter on the shelf, but the core's chemistry was little known.

The team refined a method to measure these compounds in the core and followed sugar and antioxidant levels in leaves. One compound proved the main bitter presence in the core, rather than the sap compounds usually blamed. Levels varied with harvest time of day and storage length. The authors say such measures could ground freshness checks for stored lettuce.
pmc-12788441:
Yunus Khader, Sana Mehek, and Shubhanshu Gupta published a children's fluids study in two thousand twenty-five. Hospitalised children often get fluids by drip. Standard salt water can push blood chloride too high, which may strain the kidneys. Newer balanced fluids are offered as a gentler choice.

Ninety children each received one of three fluids: salt water or one of two balanced types. Blood chloride was checked before the drip and after a day. Children on salt water ended with clearly higher chloride than both balanced groups. Their blood also leaned slightly toward acidity. The balanced fluids differed little from each other. The authors suggest balanced fluids keep blood salts steadier in children.
pmc-12795541:
Bishoy Manqaryos, Michael Shakhloul, and Ahmed Amer described in two thousand twenty-five a man whose brain lymphoma first appeared as behavior change. Brain tumors usually announce themselves with headaches, sickness, seizures, or weakness, but tumors in the front or side lobes can alter personality first. Their patient, nearing seventy, saw his doctor repeatedly for worsening behavior and occasional headaches.

Early checks found nothing, and talk therapy did not help. Later face and limb symptoms prompted a head scan revealing a large tumor, confirmed as primary brain lymphoma by tissue sampling. Doctors learn to image the brain when behavior changes persist without explanation.
pmc-12799641:
Othman Iskander and co-authors published a 2025 study of how weight-loss surgery affects leaks of urine and stool in women with severe obesity. Both leaks are leading troubles of the pelvic floor, and both run high in such women. The benefit of the surgery for stool leak was in debate. The team studied the year after the operation.

Over two hundred women at one hospital took questionnaires before and after the operation. Over two in three lost over a fifth of their weight in the year. Of them, a third completed all the questionnaires in full. Their median weight score fell from the low forties to the high twenties. Stress urine leaks fell by a third share. Stool leak turned the other way: moderate cases doubled, and loose stool and gas troubles rose too.
pmc-12816241:
Seven authors wrote a review, published in two thousand twenty-five, on irregular heart rhythms in animals and what they teach doctors. Heart rhythm problems in other species are well known to vets but less so to human cardiologists. The authors see a missed chance to learn across species lines.

Veterinary cardiologists summed up common rhythm problems in dogs, cats, horses, and birds. They compared gene risk, disease course, treatment, and spread with the human versions. Common human problems, such as atrial fibrillation and fast ventricular rhythms, occur in these animals on their own. Differences in how the diseases show up can reveal how the rhythms work.
pmc-12817641:
Andrews and a large team studied rollout of Australia's Safer Baby Bundle in twenty twenty-five. The bundle bundles five care practices, from quitting smoking to side sleeping in pregnancy, to cut stillbirth. Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria adopted it first, ahead of national rollout.

The team surveyed forty-five site leads in twenty twenty-two and interviewed twenty. Hospital leaders backed the bundle strongly, most leads said. Yet only a third felt their service had enough resources, and fewer had time for improvement work. Two practices, responding to reduced fetal movement and side sleeping advice, took hold almost everywhere. Smoking cessation support lagged below half. Themes included consistent national training, teamwork, and access to data. The authors call for tailored support and stronger infrastructure.
pmc-12820241:
Kou and coauthors probe a cell cycle gene that drives prostate cancer growth. The gene, called PKMYT1, links to cycle control and cancer. Its exact role in prostate cancer had not been clear. The team mined cancer databases for its patterns first.

The gene was high in prostate tumors in those data. High levels tracked with worse patient outlook as well. One gene switch that raises it was also found. Lab prostate cells with the gene cut grew more slowly. Motion and invasion of those cells fell too. A fat signal path rose when the gene was cut.
pmc-12822141:
Eight researchers led by Jieun Oh built computer models that predict pain after surgery from body signals in the recovery room. Signals came from heart and pulse traces of over twenty-four thousand patients at two Korean hospitals. The team drew features such as heart rate wobble and a pain-linked pulse index, then trained five kinds of models.

The best model called pain presence with about eighty-five percent accuracy at the home hospital. It held up nearly as well at the second hospital. Pulse index measures drove the calls most, and adding age and sex helped. The authors see signal-based forecasts guiding pain care tuned to each patient.
pmc-12827241:
Vahid Hemmati, Gholamreza Karimi, and Dariush Mowla published a water treatment study in twenty twenty-five on nanofiber mats that strip orange dye from wastewater. The team electrospun tough polyimide fibers, then coated them with a chitosan composite carrying molybdenum disulfide sheets and a porous framework. Each ingredient covers another's weakness.

Adsorption of methyl orange depended on acidity, dose, concentration, and temperature, peaking at a high capacity per gram. The process fit the classic monolayer model and released heat as it ran, marking it spontaneous and exothermic. Three reuse cycles left performance largely intact. The authors pitch the hybrid mat as a practical answer to dye-laden effluent from textile and printing works.
pmc-12831241:
Tekdemir and co-authors compare three rinses for clearing calcium hydroxide from root canals. Thirty-two pulled human premolars served as the test teeth. Canals were shaped, filled with the paste, and left seven days. Micro-CT scans read fill and remnant volumes per tooth. Four groups split by rinse and sonic use.

EDTA with plain rinse formed the first group. Other groups paired EDTA, phytic acid, or NAC with sonic shaking. No rinse cleared the paste in full from any canal. Remnant shares were compared by scan after cleaning. The authors weigh phytic acid and NAC as EDTA rivals.
pmc-12831341:
Almeda-Luna, Luna, and Ventura compare free tools that pull trait scores from medical scans. The field, called radiomics, turns scan views into counts that can aid care choices. Each tool counts scans in its own way, so scores can shift by tool. No past work had set many free tools side by side across cancer types. The team tests the tools on more than one cancer data set. Each tool feeds a full learn pipe with trait picks and a sort step.

The work checks how much the pulled traits vary from tool to tool. It also tests blends that fuse scores from more than one tool. The authors argue a fused set beats a pick of just one tool. Their checks span more than one cancer type, not a lone case.
pmc-12837241:
Florian Sestak and five co-authors present VN-EGNN, a neural network that locates binding sites on proteins by respecting three-dimensional geometry, in a two thousand twenty-five machine learning paper. Drug discovery depends on finding the pockets where molecules attach.

The method adds virtual nodes to equivariant graph neural networks and extends their message passing, letting the model represent pocket shapes that ordinary graph networks handle poorly. It also produces neural representations of the binding sites themselves. On three standard benchmarks, COACH420, HOLO4K, and PDBbind2020, the system set new state-of-the-art results for finding binding site centers. The authors pitch it for drug discovery and protein-ligand interaction studies.
pmc-12838841:
Ergun Tarim, Michael Mauk, and Mohamed El-Tholoth review chip-based plasma separation for bedside diagnostics. Their review from twenty twenty-five seeks alternatives to centrifuges. Spinning blood is effective but needs labs, power, and trained staff. Remote clinics often lack all three at once.

Tiny fluid devices separate plasma from small blood volumes quickly. Finger-prick amounts can suffice for these systems. Designs differ in separation principle and target application. Integration with later test steps on one chip is the goal. Costs fall and results arrive faster at the point of care. Self-testing becomes realistic for more blood markers. The review charts the field toward commercial devices.
pmc-12842641:
Nebioğlu and coauthors ask if blood counts forecast bladder cancer course. The cancer type stays in the bladder lining without muscle spread. Blood counts before surgery are cheap and routine to get. Their link to cancer return and growth is worth a full check.

Records held 551 patients treated from 2007 to 2024. Counts came from tests in the 30 days before surgery. Full data were on hand for 548 of those patients. Mean age in the group was near 66 years. The team weighed each count against return and spread. Cut points for high risk were also derived.
pmc-12842941:
Abdulrahman Saud Almalki and nine co-authors shared a review in twenty twenty-five. It is about probiotics for irritable bowel syndrome. The review splits the cases by subtype. Patients and doctors need to know which strains help which pattern. The patterns are constipation, diarrhea, mixed, or unclassified. The review followed PRISMA rules. Its protocol was registered in advance.

Sixteen trials survived screening. All were double-blind and placebo-controlled. They covered two thousand eight hundred twenty-three patients. Probiotics cut gut discomfort scores and overall severity by a clear amount. Patients' odds of global improvement were clearly higher than with placebo. Side effects were no worse than with placebo. That held for single strains and mixed strains alike. The synthesis backs probiotics as a safe choice that helps a fair amount. It calls for strain-specific precision in future work.
pmc-12849241:
Kanji Itami and co-authors report a brain tumor case with psychotic symptoms in this 2025 paper. The patient was a 16 year old boy with autism spectrum disorder. From age 13 he had hearing voices, false beliefs, and disordered thought. Such symptoms are rarely linked to tumors in the cerebellum, the back part of the brain.

Scans found a pilocytic astrocytoma in the cerebellum. That tumor type is usually slow growing and benign. Care of the tumor was followed by full remission of the psychotic symptoms. No antipsychotic drugs were needed to reach that result. Follow up lasted three years. The case supports the view that the cerebellum also shapes thought, emotion, and social behavior.
pmc-12852741:
Daniel Melese and co-authors map how climate shifts will shrink the homes of two overused Ethiopian trees, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Seven model types, each run ten times, charted fit ground now and under two climate paths. Both trees serve many local uses.

Fit land now covers about a fifth of the country for each tree, in unlike zones. By the twenty-seventies, fit land may fall to near nine percent for one and two percent for the other. One tree's refuges shift uphill, and the two barely overlap. The authors call for guarded refuges, harvest rules, and local forest care. Readers get a species-by-species survival brief.
pmc-12866041:
Shuang Liang and co-authors study a small RNA in bone fracture healing in a 2025 paper. Pilon fractures are severe ankle injuries that often heal slowly. The RNA, called miR-3651, was little understood in this setting.

The team measured miR-3651 and its target gene KRAS in patient samples. Levels of the RNA ran high in the slow-healing group, while KRAS ran low. The RNA separated slow from normal healing well and counted as a risk factor. Blocking it in cells cut bone-eating cell activity and aided bone-forming cells. A reporter test confirmed the RNA targets KRAS directly.
pmc-12870941:
Elizabeth Wallace-Anthony and seven co-authors study how a newborn rat brain reacts to bleeding inside its fluid spaces, a harm common in early birth. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. They ask whether the age of the brain at the time of the bleed changes the response.

The team read gene activity one cell at a time, one day after bleeds at two ages. They found forty-two cell types. The older brains mounted a much stronger immune response, with three times as many genes changing. Microglia, the brain's immune cells, were the most shaken type at both ages. Signals leaned toward repair in the younger brains and toward inflammation in the older ones. The results suggest treatment may need to match the brain's stage.
pmc-12872541:
Shuang Liu and co-authors read the full gene sets of four tick species for the first time, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Ticks spread disease germs and rank second only to mosquitoes as carriers. Yet tick gene sets of this kind are still scarce, and family links stay unsettled.

The four sets were compared with those of many other hard ticks. All showed a strong lean toward two of the four DNA letters. A family tree built from thirteen shared genes placed the tick family as one clean branch. The order of genera in the tree is spelled out for future work on tick control.
pmc-12882241:
Naiara Carla Manhães, Hozany Praxedes, Alisson Amaral Da-Rocha, and nine colleagues set up a safer infection model in this two thousand twenty-five paper.
