Leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania protozoa and common in Brazil, is passed by sand flies placing parasites in skin. Needle infections, into or under the skin, mimic that poorly and risk accidents. The team tested microneedle cartridges for infection through mouse-ear skin with Leishmania amazonensis, against needle injection.

Skin infection produced sore growth and parasite loads much like the needle method. Cartridges with fewer needles caused more tissue harm than the twelve-needle cartridge. Infection worked at every depth from a quarter millimeter to one millimeter, with much the same sore thickness across groups. Tissue study and flow cytometry thirty minutes after infection described the earliest tissue response. The authors offer microneedles as a more natural, safer lab route to leishmaniasis.
pmc-12884041:
Yong Joo Park and colleagues weighed whether a humidifier disinfectant chemical caused lung inflammation in South Korea, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. The chemical, known by its initials PHMG-P, was withdrawn in the early twenty tens after a lung injury crisis. Rather than rely on one study type, the team combined population data, animal and cell studies, and known steps of biological harm. They checked each line of evidence for quality and for how well the lines agreed.

Population analyses showed lung inflammation rising while the disinfectant was in use and falling after withdrawal, with children and women of childbearing age at higher risk. Lab studies showed the chemical injuring airway tissue. Taken together, the authors judge the evidence strong enough to support a causal link, a finding that matters for policy and for affected families.
pmc-12946041:
Giulio Contemori, Marianna Musa, Deniz Demirkapi, and a wider team wrote this study in 2026. It asks if the brain's response to mirror symmetry needs a long look. The team flashed symmetric shapes for just 20 milliseconds. They recorded the scalp's electrical signals as they did so.

People spot symmetry fast. A sustained negative wave at the back of the head is its known brain mark. The shapes were irregular octagons. Some were symmetric and some were not. Responses were delayed and shuffled. So no motor planning could skew the signal. Signals from 64 electrodes still showed the known wave. It had the right pattern in both checks the team ran. People also judged the brief flashes well. The authors say the symmetry system fires on a brief glimpse. No long look is needed.
pmc-12998241: Salem and four co-authors report a rare prostate case in a man aged seventy-eight. The illness looked like prostate cancer. He had high PSA and an abnormal rectal exam. Tissue tests pointed to xanthogranulomatous prostatitis, not a tumor. Scans and PSA alone could mislead the care team. The authors urge joint review of symptoms, scans, and tissue results. That joint check helps avoid a wrong cancer diagnosis.
pmc-13033741:
Miriam Richter and colleagues run a structured activity programme for preteens with high-functioning autism. Their exploratory study from twenty twenty-six measures thinking and sleep changes. Autistic children often show unusual cognition and poor sleep. Exercise may help both domains at once.

Sixteen children aged ten to fourteen completed the programme. It ran for about ten to twelve weeks. Parents reported better executive function afterwards. Computer tests measured thinking skills directly at both ends. Wrist devices tracked sleep patterns objectively through the study. Sensory processing also improved per parent reports. Small, single-group design limits firm conclusions. A controlled trial is the clear next step.
pmc-13115741:
Melnikova and a large team build a machine learning pipeline to measure scar forming cells around brain implants in twenty twenty-six. Implants can treat severe brain and mind disorders, but the body's scar response dulls them over time. Star shaped support cells drive much of that scar. Their shape is hard to score the same way twice by hand.

The pipeline segments stained cells and measures their size and branch length. Scar zone cells showed more stain, larger area, and longer branches than far cells. How the classifier was taught shifted the results a lot. Rule based teaching matched hand truth best. The team offers the pipeline as a shared standard for implant studies.
pmc-13141441:
Wolfgang Schulz and co-authors track German families for eighteen years. They ask if early child care outside the family shapes later mental health, risk habits, and school results. Their 2026 study tracked two hundred twenty-five families over that span.

Set next to care by parents, early care outside the home was linked to higher risk habits in young adulthood. Those habits took in risky sexual behaviour, abuse of alcohol, and use of tobacco. Quality of close relationships was lower. Yet the chance of a high-level qualification for a job was higher. A young age at first entry was linked, in a weak way, with more mental health problems. Background in migration shaped some effects, in analysis that was meant to probe. The team says parents should weigh age at entry, how good the care is, and the social and economic place of the family when they choose.
pmc-13155241:
Yan Cai and four co-authors study kidney disease in older patients in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. IgA nephropathy is a common glomerular disease, and aging may change its course. The team asked whether podocyte aging marks worse disease in the elderly.

Over one thousand biopsy-proven patients were split into elderly and younger groups. The elderly had heavier protein loss, worse kidney function, and more scarring. Severe fusion of podocyte foot processes independently predicted poor outcomes only in the elderly. A sensing pathway tied to cell aging was highly active in elderly podocytes, alongside aging-related signals in blood. The authors propose that pathway as a treatment target for older patients.
pmc-13182241:
Lingyu Bao and co-authors show in 2026 that a gut transporter protein is needed to keep the mouse intestine in balance. The protein, LAT1, ferries large amino acids into cells and can switch on a growth signal. It sits in the crypts where new gut lining cells are born.

When the team knocked the gene out in gut lining cells, a surprise followed: mature Paneth cells, a secretory cell type, dwindled, and cell division rose. The Paneth loss came first, in both adult-induced and lifelong knockouts. The pattern suggests the transporter steers secretory cell development, and that this steering, in turn, keeps cell growth in check.
pmc-13190341:
Othmar Moser and a large panel of co-authors issue joint German and Austrian guidelines on automated insulin delivery and exercise in type one diabetes, published in two thousand twenty-six. Insulin pump systems that dose automatically help users hit glucose targets, yet exercise still destabilizes glucose.

The guideline, written in German, builds on European and international children's place statements. It reviews the evidence for automated delivery around physical activity and gives useful management advice for children, adolescents, and adults. Each system sold in Germany and Austria gets device-certain guidance for sport. The authors also map typical glucose responses to exercise and plans for staying in range.
pmc-13191241:
Mary Cathleen McKinney, Jason Morrison, Frederick Mann, and a wider team wrote this protocol paper, published in 2026. It gives step-by-step instructions for fishing a chosen cell type out of a planarian flatworm and reading its genes, using a fluorescent RNA tag as the hook.

Rare cell types in unusual model animals are hard to isolate. The protocol breaks the worm into single cells and fixes them in one step that skips formaldehyde, which chews up RNA. A hybridization method then lights up cells carrying a chosen RNA. A flow sorter pulls the glowing cells out, enriching the gene reads from just that population. The authors point to their earlier study for the full worked example. Labs studying regeneration in planarians can adapt the method to other target cells.
pmc-13194341:
Kristin Riedel is first author on a 2026 rat and human tissue study of how estrogen shapes blood vessel tone. Women's vessels relax more through beta receptors, a class of adrenaline response proteins, than men's. But the role of estrogen receptors in keeping that pattern was unclear. Arteries from rats were tested after blocking estrogen receptors or giving cross-sex hormones.

Blocking estrogen receptors made vessels squeeze harder and relax less, in both large and small arteries. Two beta receptor types also showed about half the gene activity, while a third did not change. Estrogen given to males shifted their vessels toward the female pattern. Testosterone in females did nothing. Human arteries likewise showed higher levels of those receptors in women, suggesting a shared mechanism.
pmc-13195041:
Joy Ku and co-authors scope the use of machine learning on liquid biopsies for early pancreatic cancer detection, in a review from two thousand twenty-six. The cancer is usually caught late, which drives its poor outlook. Liquid biopsy reads cancer traces in body fluids, but samples vary so much that pattern-finding algorithms are called in.

Eighty-five studies were screened and eighteen kept. Blood was the fluid in most, with urine, bile, and cyst fluid behind. Random forests and support vector machines were the favorite models, and deep learning appeared twice. Small cohorts and uneven reporting limit the field, the authors note.
pmc-13195441:
Reham M Hashim leads a 2026 randomized trial on numbing the airway for awake intubation in bariatric surgery patients. Placing a breathing tube while awake is safest when a difficult airway is expected, common in obesity, but patients need good numbing. The trial compared ultrasound-guided airway nerve blocks against topical lidocaine spray, using a video laryngoscope.

Eighty obese patients were split evenly between the two methods, with light sedation for both. The nerve block group had less coughing and gagging, more first-attempt successes, and shorter intubation times. Comfort was better, with lower pain scores and no recall, and heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen dips were fewer. Blocks, the authors conclude, beat spray here.
pmc-13196741:
Yan Jin and colleagues describe a 2026 light-based computer for hard choice problems. Their machine uses tiny pulses of light called Kerr solitons, which circle inside small glass rings. The goal is to solve logic puzzles that grow too large for normal computers.

Each soliton acts like a switch that can settle in one of two states. Links between switches can be set freely through an electronic feedback loop. The team ran more than ten thousand trials on over one hundred random logic puzzles. The machine matched or beat standard software solvers in their tests. It used very little power per pulse and took about a millionth of a second per feedback step.
pmc-13197841:
Seven authors present a global survey dated two thousand twenty-six on antibiotics sold without prescription. Resistance to antibiotics is a critical public health threat, and easy over-the-counter sales feed it. National plans exist on paper, yet hard data on worldwide availability stayed scarce.

The team surveyed a network of ambassadors across thirty-seven countries. Sixty-five percent said antibiotics could be bought without a prescription in their country. Pharmacies were the main source, with internet sellers next. Alarmingly, some last-resort drug classes were also reported as available. The authors call for real enforcement and better tracking of sales.
pmc-13200541:
Yexuan Mao and ten co-authors give GCAST, a tool that finds the zones of a tissue from gene reads that keep place. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-six, joins gene data with tissue images.

Reads that keep place let labs map gene use across a slice of flesh. But past tools used the image side too thinly, and lacked ways to learn across the two kinds. GCAST learns by itself: it draws sound marks straight from the tissue images, when they are there. It builds twin webs over the data and learns by match-and-part across kinds. The aim is zones that hold across batches of reads.
pmc-13201941:
Plant flavonoids are being refined into cancer drug options, and a 2026 virtual study led by Precious A Akinnusi asks how small chemical changes affect their grip on a breast cancer target. The research article models methylated flavonoids binding to HER2, a receptor that drives an aggressive breast cancer subtype.

Docking scores ranked eupatolitin, rhamnetin, and three other flavonoids as the best forecast binders. Comparing parent compounds with modified versions showed that adding methoxy groups at two specific positions strengthened forecast binding in every case, while changes elsewhere did not help. Simulations backed complex stability, and the authors frame the pattern as a design rule needing lab confirmation.
pmc-13203741:
LaBreesha Batey and co-authors run a small pilot on foot orthoses made with auxetic foam for people with nerve-damaged feet. Auxetic foams grow wider when stretched, the reverse of normal foam, a trait that can spread pressure. Whether such foam can be built into custom insoles, and how feet load on it, was largely untested across mixed causes of neuropathy. The work was done with NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center.

Six people took part: five with varied neuropathic conditions and one healthy control. Each walked barefoot, in shop-bought insoles, and in custom auxetic prototypes. Ground reaction force was scaled by body mass. A global test found no significant difference between the three, though the auxetic foam showed a large descriptive effect against barefoot walking. The spread of the data was wide, so no firm claims can be made.
pmc-13205541:
Cancer immunotherapy can bleach patches of skin, and a 2026 report led by Thomas Breakell presents treating that side effect with a targeted cream. The article presents three patients with melanoma who developed facial vitiligo during or after immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and received topical ruxolitinib.

Repigmentation and quality of life were measured with clinical photographs, a semi-automatic assessment tool, and surveys. The authors report marked facial repigmentation alongside improved quality of life for the treated patients during follow-up. No side effects were observed in this small series, and the team proposes the cream as supportive care for a distressing, visible complication of treatment.
pmc-13209141:
A published study of new intensive care nurses draws constructive criticism in a 2026 letter by Xu Liu. Writing to the editor, Liu and Li Ning comment on a qualitative study of stress coping and resilience in newly licensed ICU nurses. They praise its challenge-adaptation-growth framework before raising methodological points.

The letter notes an apparent contradiction: one section describes a strong trust relationship between researchers and participants as fellow ICU staff, while another states no prior relationships existed. It also asks whether member checking was used, what transcription style was chosen, and flags nurses being called patients once in the results. Future research directions close the letter.
pmc-13212041:
Why adults lose permanent teeth in Baghdad is counted tooth by tooth in a 2026 study by Falah Hasan Jumaah at Mustansiriyah University's dental teaching hospital. The prospective cross-sectional study recorded every extraction in the oral surgery clinics between October 2024 and May 2025, along with each patient's age, sex, and health background.

In total, 1,096 patients lost 1,408 teeth during the study window. Dental caries overwhelmed every other cause, accounting for the vast majority of extractions, while gum disease explained only a small share in this population. Age mattered for gum-disease extractions but not for caries, and patients with systemic disease were less likely to lose teeth to decay.
pmc-13212741:
Eduardo Soares and co-authors review in 2026 how inflammation unfolds after an ischemic stroke, when a blocked vessel starves part of the brain. Reopening the vessel saves tissue, yet returning blood flow can itself trigger further immune-driven damage.

The review traces immune events over time across the brain, blood, and other body compartments, setting harmful and protective pathways side by side. Regulatory T cells receive special attention for their calming, tissue-protecting potential. By mapping which immune steps happen where and when, the authors aim to show where timed immune therapies might limit secondary injury. Such treatments could extend help to patients whom clot removal cannot reach.
pmc-13214341:
L. S. Boers and colleagues review in 2026 how the lung's air sacs mishandle immune defence in pneumonia and in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Blood tests miss much of this local story, yet events inside the air sacs decide clearance, injury, and recovery.

Across community, hospital, and ventilator-linked pneumonias, germs often die quickly while local inflammation burns on, fed by injured lining cells, neutrophils, and faltering macrophages. Ventilation itself can weaken defences and invite new infection. Patients diverge toward stubborn over-inflammation or immune exhaustion, steering them toward healing or scarring. Weakened local defences also let dormant viruses wake and fungi invade, prolonging ventilation.
pmc-13214541:
Adouni, Gouissem, and Dhaher modeled cartilage mechanics in this study from twenty twenty-six. Cartilage cells, called chondrocytes, sense pressure and keep joint tissue in repair. Each cell sits in a small matrix pocket rich in collagen types six and nine. How those minor collagens shape the forces a cell feels was largely unknown.

The team built a computer model linking whole-tissue load down to single cells. Changing collagen six altered the force the whole tissue pushed back with. Collagen nine barely moved the tissue-level response. Both collagens still shifted cell volume, load share, and the cell's local force climate. The authors suggest these minor collagens as markers in early joint disease.
pmc-13215541:
Hye Young Hong and co-authors report a 2026 cohort study of Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, a chronic infection needing more than a year of combined antibiotics. The study asks how often patients stop treatment early and what that stop costs.

Among 420 patients treated between 2010 and 2023, thirty percent stopped before twelve months. Serious drug side effects sharply raised the odds of stopping, and a low nutritional index score, built from albumin and lymphocyte counts, also played a role. Patients who stopped early died at nearly three times the adjusted rate of those who continued. The authors urge close side-effect monitoring and nutritional support to keep patients on therapy.
pmc-13216341:
The editors of Scientific Reports issued a 2026 retraction of an article by Qasem M. Tawhari and co-authors that modelled breast cancer drugs mathematically, using graph indices to estimate physical properties. The retraction notice explains why the journal lost confidence in the work.

After publication, readers raised concerns about references the article used to support its claims on cancer care and on what the drug daunorubicin does in the body. The editors could not verify the sources behind references 31 to 35 and 37 to 43, and on that basis withdrew the article. The notice adds that the authors did not respond to the editors' correspondence about the retraction.
pmc-13216441:
Joanna Pogorzelska-Dyrbuś and co-authors present a 2026 imaging study on telling two look-alike facial lesions apart: harmless dermal moles and basal cell carcinoma, the common skin cancer. High magnification dermoscopy, up to 400 times, claims to reveal structures invisible at standard settings, and the team put that claim to a blinded test.

Seventy-three biopsy-confirmed lesions were scored under both standard and magnified dermoscopy. Roundish structures appeared in about nine of ten moles and in no cancers, giving near-perfect discrimination for the benign side. Polygonal structures also favoured moles, while branching, irregular, and looped vessels pointed to cancer. The authors conclude that magnification adds genuine diagnostic value beyond the standard view.
pmc-13216541:
Heng Shen and co-authors present a 2026 letter analysing mutations in the RAS signalling pathway across 2,500 patients with acute myeloid leukaemia treated at one Chinese centre. Whether these common mutations worsen prognosis has been disputed, partly because older studies were small.

Just over a third of patients carried at least one RAS pathway mutation, with NRAS the most frequent, followed by KRAS, PTPN11, CBL, and NF1. Mutated groups showed higher white blood cell counts, fitting the pathway's growth-driving role. Risk class distribution differed by gene: KRAS and NF1 clustered in adverse-risk disease, NRAS in favourable-risk. The mutations also kept characteristic company, with NRAS excluding other RAS mutations while PTPN11 travelled with NPM1 and DNMT3A changes.
pmc-13216641:
Qingyu Lin and co-authors present a 2026 cancer immunology study naming a long non-coding RNA, LISS, that helps colorectal tumours hide from the immune system. Checkpoint immunotherapy fails most colorectal patients, including many whose tumours look immunologically promising, so new brakes are worth hunting.

LISS runs high in colorectal cancers and predicts poor survival. In experiments it blunted T cell killing regardless of the tumour's microsatellite status. Mechanistically, LISS grips the enzyme CamKIIγ and stops it phosphorylating STAT1 at a key site, which lowers production of the MHC-I molecules that display tumour fragments to T cells. Silencing LISS with antisense drugs restored MHC-I and improved checkpoint therapy responses in mice. Patient samples showed the expected inverse pattern.
pmc-13217441:
Shengbo Ye and co-authors present a 2026 review of neutrophil extracellular traps, the web-like DNA structures neutrophils throw out to catch microbes, as drivers of heart failure. When these traps form excessively or clear poorly, they injure the very tissues they defend.

The review traces how traps feed the failing heart's core problems: clotting inside small vessels, death of heart muscle cells, and activation of scar-forming fibroblasts, alongside chronic sterile inflammation. Traps also link heart failure to its common companions such as diabetes, hypertension, and kidney disease. Treatment ideas surveyed include blocking the PAD4 enzyme that enables trap formation, digesting traps with enzymes, repurposing existing drugs, and nanoparticle delivery. The authors frame traps as a precision target for immunotherapy.
pmc-13218141:
Parisa Naseri and colleagues follow weight trajectories of married couples in Tehran and link them to quality of life, in a 2026 longitudinal cohort analysis. Obesity lowers health-related quality of life, but most studies look at one person's weight at one moment. Because spouses share meals, habits, and households, the authors ask whether a partner's weight path shapes well-being.

The study drew 773 couples from the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study, followed for an average of fifteen years between 2001 and 2018. Group-based modeling found four body mass index trajectories in each sex, running from stable healthy weight to steadily climbing obesity. Women and men on steep obesity paths reported significantly worse physical quality of life than leaner groups. At the couple level, pairings where both partners' trajectories carried higher risk showed the lowest physical quality of life. Weight change, the authors suggest, is partly a shared household phenomenon.
pmc-13221441:
Dilsad Mungan and co-authors gather expert consensus on single-inhaler triple therapy for uncontrolled asthma, in a 2026 multinational Delphi study. Twenty-seven respiratory specialists from nine countries answered two survey rounds and met as a panel. Many patients stay uncontrolled on standard steroid and bronchodilator pairs, and add-on choices vary widely.

Panelists agreed that better symptoms and fewer flare-ups define good control. Nearly all endorsed adding a long-acting muscarinic drug to the standard pair in one inhaler for uncontrolled patients. Agreement broke down over antibiotics, leukotriene drugs, and biologics. The consensus gives clinicians shared ground for stepping up therapy while flagging where opinion still splits.
pmc-13223341:
Nehad Jaser Ahmed charts antimicrobial resistance across the Eastern Mediterranean Region from 2013 to 2023, in a 2026 ecological analysis using Global Burden of Disease estimates. Resistance mortality, burden rankings, and progress toward reduction milestones were compared country by country. The region mixes wealthy Gulf states with war-torn, low-income nations where surveillance runs thin.

Resistance death rates ranged from four to seventy-five per hundred thousand people. Gulf countries sat lowest, while Pakistan, Afghanistan, Somalia, Yemen, and Djibouti sat highest. Twelve countries made no progress in the last four study years, and nine reduced mortality. In several high-burden states, resistance ranked among the top ten causes of death. Laboratories, stewardship, and surveillance need strengthening first.
pmc-13223941:
Carl Marincowitz and co-authors set out a qualitative study plan for exploring why a care homes health plan lands in patches across England, in a 2026 protocol paper. Care home residents visit emergency departments at more than twice the rate of peers at home, and many admissions need not happen. The 2023 Enhanced Health in Care Homes framework aims to join up their care and cut those admissions.

Six districts inside three regional health boards, chosen because their adjusted admission rates differ widely, will form comparative case studies. Interviews will span planners, care deliverers, care home staff, older residents, and families. A structured analysis will compare care elements within and across cases to explain variation in hospital use.
pmc-13224041:
Xiaojia Ma and co-authors examine a 2026 laboratory study of Rubia yunnanensis, a traditional Chinese medicinal herb, against breast cancer. The herb had shown anti-tumour effects elsewhere, but its role in breast cancer was undefined. The team mixed cell and animal experiments with database mining and computer modelling of molecular binding.

In culture, the herb lowered survival of two breast cancer cell lines, slowed their movement, and pushed them toward cell death, with stronger effects at higher doses. Tumour growth also slowed in mice. Chemical analysis found 26 active components and hundreds of possible targets, with core targets including TP53, AKT1, and TNF. Enrichment results pointed to the PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways.
pmc-13224341:
Rebecca Marie Ellul and six co-authors hunt for vaccine targets in a bacterium that sickens farmed Atlantic salmon. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The disease, pasteurellosis, hits salmon welfare and Norway's fish farming industry hard.

The team sequenced a disease isolate's genome and used computer prediction to find surface proteins that help the germ grip host cells. Sixteen candidate adhesins emerged. Two were tracked as the bacteria grew at three temperatures. Both rose during fast growth at warmer settings, matching field reports that outbreaks follow warm-water lice treatments. Such grip proteins are classic vaccine material. The work shortlists targets for a vaccine the industry lacks.
pmc-13227541:
Xiaoqing Li and co-authors build a 2026 nutrition-based risk index for sepsis patients in intensive care, where inflammation drives muscle wasting and poor outcomes. Existing nutrition scores were not designed for sepsis, so the team first compared four of them in 1,915 patients. They then used machine learning to improve the best-known one by folding in blood lactate, a marker of metabolic stress.

Among standard tools, the mNUTRIC score predicted intensive-care death most accurately. The new lactate-modified index beat them all on discrimination tests. Patients scored as high risk by the new index died at more than triple the rate of low-risk patients after adjustment, in both shock and non-shock subgroups. The authors propose it for sharper bedside risk sorting.
pmc-13227741:
Wei Zhang and colleagues run a 2026 clinical and laboratory study of smell training built on traditional Chinese medicine herbs for people who have lost olfactory function. Standard smell training with simple odorants helps only modestly. Thirty-six patients trained for three months with six complex-smelling herbs, while thirty-seven controls used a steroid nasal spray, and smell was scored before and after.

The herb group improved significantly more on the main smell-identification test, with younger patients benefiting most. Subjective ratings favoured the herbs too, though not decisively after statistical correction. Chemists profiled the herbs' volatile compounds, then screened major odorants against roughly four hundred human smell receptors. Herb odorants proved more chemically diverse and engaged receptors differently, suggesting a richer training signal.
pmc-13228541:
Erqing Gao and colleagues create a 2026 living sensor that lights up mitochondria whose membranes have been catastrophically torn, in the worm C. elegans. Cells had no known way to flag this worst kind of damage to their power plants, distinct from ordinary energy failure. The team found a protein, MAI-1, that normally floats in the cell fluid because it lacks the usual mitochondrial address tag.

When membranes break, MAI-1 rushes onto the damaged organelles within moments and stays there, making it the first genetically encoded reporter of severe mitochondrial membrane damage. Watching labelled mitochondria showed they are cleared through a lysosome pathway that bypasses the famous PINK1 and Parkin machinery entirely, revealing a separate surveillance route.
pmc-13229841:
Andrey Kormilitzin and colleagues describe in 2026 a local language model that flags self-harm in mental health records without sending data outside the hospital. Notes came from an Oxford health trust in the United Kingdom, where self-harm is often buried in free text. Experts labeled more than a thousand sampled notes for whether self-harm was present and when it happened.

The locally run Gemma model beat a RoBERTa classifier on every category the team measured. It identified notes with self-harm and notes without it with high precision and recall in the test work. Sorting recent harm from older harm proved harder, with lower scores for the recent group. Keeping the model inside secure systems offers a path that protects sensitive patient data.
pmc-13231241:
Olufemi Pirisola describes a frail elderly man carrying two urinary infections at once, found almost by accident, in this solo case report from twenty twenty-six. Prostate abscess, a pocket of pus in the prostate, is a rare and dangerous turn of urinary infection. It can hide alongside kidney infection, especially in patients who cannot describe symptoms.

His patient, a man of eighty-four with dementia, arrived after a fall, feverish, with tenderness low in the belly and raised infection markers. Trauma scans meant to check for injury revealed both: an inflamed right kidney and the prostate abscess. He was too frail for surgical drainage, so doctors cycled long courses of strong intravenous antibiotics. Slowly the abscess resolved. Pirisola draws the general lesson: in atypical, slow-to-improve, or frail patients, image early, because the hidden second infection changes the plan.
pmc-13232341:
Matthew B Pomrenze and colleagues find in 2026 a small set of reward-center neurons that control the misery of opioid withdrawal. Avoiding withdrawal drives much opioid addiction, and its body aches may not share machinery with its emotional pain. A rare neuron group carrying opioid receptors and a marker gene called Tshz1 sat at the center of their mouse work.

Activity in those neurons proved necessary for learning to dread places linked with withdrawal. Deleting their opioid receptors kept dopamine from crashing during withdrawal and erased the dread, while body symptoms stayed untouched. A drug that switches on a receptor rich in those neurons also softened the dread. Splitting mood symptoms from body symptoms opens a focused treatment target.
pmc-13232541:
Yu-Hua Fu and colleagues pilot in 2026 a choice study on what caregivers value in antipsychotic medicines for young people. These drugs can calm severe behavior yet carry weight and metabolic risks for children and teens. Twenty-six caregivers near Baltimore weighed profiles that mixed three benefits against three harms across nine choice tasks.

Cutting hospital stays ranked as the most valued benefit, ahead of fewer aggressive days and fewer self-harm episodes. Among harms, diabetes risk mattered most, while cholesterol changes mattered least. Caregivers accepted extra hospital time in trade for halving a stated diabetes risk rise. Two thirds of chosen profiles were ones caregivers said they would actually use for their child.
pmc-13232841:
Bismark Ofori-Manteaw and colleagues interview in 2026 frontline doctors in Ghana about coping with too few radiologists to read medical images. Scans guide diagnosis and treatment across medicine, yet specialist readers are scarce in many lower-income health systems. Eight doctors from public and private facilities described their daily experience in depth.

Doctors called imaging vital, then described reports arriving late or never, forcing guesses or delays. Too little training in reading images themselves fed the strain, and burnout surfaced as a theme. Their fixes included expanding specialist training, teaching image skills in medical school, letting trained radiographers give first reads, and using remote reporting with computer help. Patient care quality rides on closing this reading gap.
pmc-13234041:
Nashra Khan and colleagues published a 2026 cadaver study mapping where the posterior tibial artery splits inside the tarsal tunnel of the ankle. Surgeons decompressing that tunnel or harvesting tissue flaps nearby need to know where the artery divides into its two plantar branches, since anatomy varies. The team dissected twenty-five preserved adult limbs and measured the split against a standard reference line drawn between ankle bone and heel.

The artery divided above the line in just over half of cases. It split at the line in about a quarter and below it in a fifth. The average branching angle sat near twenty-three degrees. Rare variants, including a three-way split and an early connecting branch, also appeared. The measurements define safer zones for medial ankle surgery.
pmc-13234241:
Asep Santoso and colleagues reported in 2026 on a neglected fracture of the talus, the ankle bone that carries body weight. Their patient was a 30-year-old man with four months of worsening pain in his left foot while walking. The injury dated from a motorcycle crash years earlier and had not received early care. Imaging supported reconstruction combined with fusion of the ankle joint.

Surgeons used a piece of the patient's own fibula, taken without its blood supply, as a graft during the fusion. Follow-up at one year showed the bones had joined fully on X-ray. No nerve or blood vessel problems were reported. The case presents graft-assisted fusion as a workable option for badly broken, untreated talus injuries.
pmc-13235141:
Nagah Abd El-Fattah Mohamed Aly and colleagues surveyed in 2026 four hundred female nursing students at Matrouh University about climate stress and monthly symptoms. Questionnaires measured climate knowledge, awareness, perceived stress, worry about the environment, and premenstrual syndrome. Data collection stretched over several years and used statistical models that test mediation and moderation. Nursing students may face added exposure through climate-related activities in their training.

Students showed satisfactory climate knowledge paired with high awareness in the survey. Moderate to severe climate-related stress affected a large share of the group. Eco-anxiety, meaning distress about environmental change, appeared at moderate or severe levels in over half. Awareness sharpened the link between climate stress and eco-anxiety in the models. Eco-anxiety in turn carried part of the link from climate stress to premenstrual symptoms.
pmc-13235441:
Lisha Li and colleagues compared in 2026 two doses of an antibody injection for seasonal hay fever caused by cypress pollen. Participants had low total levels of the allergy antibody IgE, a group where standard dosing guidance is uncertain. Sixty patients entered the randomized, double-blind trial at one centre. Each received a single injection shortly before pollen season, at either the higher or lower dose.

Fifty-four patients completed the analysis, split evenly between the dose groups. The higher dose produced clearly better combined symptom and medication scores during the season. Daily symptoms and eye symptoms also favoured the higher dose in the results. Quality of life scores and a rhinitis control score improved more with the higher dose at peak season. Nasal airflow resistance fell more in that group as well. No drug-related side effects appeared in either arm.
pmc-13236641:
Metin Çınaroğlu and co-authors randomized in 2026 earthquake survivors in Türkiye with post-traumatic stress disorder to remote therapy or a waiting list. Eighty-nine adults who lived through the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes met diagnostic rules for the disorder. Treatment groups received twelve sessions of either eye motion therapy or mental behavioural therapy by remote delivery. Symptoms were measured before, midway through, and after treatment.

Both therapies produced large drops in trauma symptoms compared with the untreated control group. Depression and anxiety also improved greatly under both active treatments in the trial. Direct comparison found the two therapies broadly equal overall, with overlapping uncertainty ranges. Eye motion therapy leaned stronger on core trauma symptoms, while mental therapy leaned stronger on depression. Nobody in the waiting list improved spontaneously, underlining the need for structured help after disasters.
pmc-13236741:
Ghani and Ferrer develop a quick test for unwanted microbes in wine. Wine is made when yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol, a craft thousands of years old. The wrong microbes spoil that process, so catching them early is crucial for makers who cannot wait days for lab cultures to grow.

Their method joins two tools. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification copies a microbe's DNA at one steady temperature, with no cycling machine. A lateral flow dipstick, like a home test strip, then shows the result by eye. Together they promise fast, cheap checks in the winery itself, so a bad batch can be caught before spoilage takes hold.
pmc-13237141:
Mayer and colleagues test how explaining success and failure shapes what people come to believe about their own new abilities. Healthy people usually credit success to themselves and blame failure on outside forces. People with depression or low self-esteem often reverse that pattern, and learn about themselves in a harsher, biased way.

The study asks whether those habits of explanation actively build new self-beliefs, not just colour old ones. Volunteers formed beliefs about a fresh ability while their attributions were tracked. Showing cause and effect here matters for therapy: if blaming oneself for failure writes new, durable self-doubt, then retraining explanations could protect self-esteem.
pmc-13238241:
Lihe Pang and colleagues built a prognostic index in 2026 for bone cancers, drawn from the gene activity program that lets tumor cells change shape and spread, called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Single-cell and bulk data from several cohorts covered osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and giant cell tumor of bone. Statistical factorization isolated one transition-driven program inside the malignant cells.

From that program's key genes, survival models distilled an eight-gene bone score. High scores tracked with shorter survival across three independent cohorts, with tumors showing fewer immune cells, weaker checkpoint signals, and predicted resistance to nine chemotherapy drugs. The authors offer the score as a biologically grounded tool for sorting patients by risk. It captures, they argue, the tumor-stroma conversation behind treatment failure.
pmc-13239141:
Ryan S. MacLeod and colleagues reported in 2026 a 62-year-old woman with lupus whose bone drug timing had to be choreographed around parathyroid surgery. Years of prednisone had thinned her bones, and she had taken denosumab for three years after an earlier drug failed. Rising calcium and parathyroid hormone then revealed primary hyperparathyroidism from a single gland tumor, changing the plan.

Stopping denosumab late risks rebound bone loss and spine fractures, while giving it near surgery risks dangerous post-operative calcium crashes. The team operated six months after her last dose and restarted the drug eight weeks later. Her calcium settled to normal and her course was uncomplicated. The authors offer the schedule as practical guidance where the literature is silent.
pmc-13239341:
Elizabeth D Paratz and a large Timorese and Australian team describe, in 2026, the founding of the Cardiac Society of Timor-Leste. The new society joins the World Heart Federation and sits alongside a national heart health strategy running from 2025 to 2035.

Heart disease places a heavy burden on the young country, where rheumatic heart disease is common and many children are born with heart defects that go unrepaired. The country still has no heart catheter laboratory or heart surgery service, and trained cardiac nurses and technicians are lacking. The society aims to build skills at personal, organisational, and system levels so care can grow locally.
pmc-13239841:
Berkan Acar and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six clinical series on treating pilonidal sinus disease with crystallised phenol. The condition forms infected pits near the tailbone. Phenol treatment is a low-key alternative to cutting surgery.

Forty consecutive patients were treated and reviewed at set follow-ups. Most were young men, and many smoked. Records covered pit counts, session numbers, and total treatment time. Some patients needed two sessions and others three. Abscess and recurrence during follow-up were noted. Comparing session groups shows how pit burden drives treatment effort in this simple clinic approach.
pmc-13240241:
Yosuke Iijima and co-authors report a doubled jaw joint surface found during treatment of a dislocated jaw in a 2026 case paper. A bifid mandibular condyle splits the knob that hinges the jaw into two heads, a variant found in roughly one percent of imaging studies and usually noticed only by chance.

Their patient, a 50-year-old man, dislocated his right jaw joint while yawning, and a local clinic could not push it back. Symptoms suggested the joint disk had slipped backward. Computed tomography then revealed the split condyle. Most people with the variant feel nothing, though clicking is the commonest complaint. The authors suggest the extra head can complicate joint mechanics.
pmc-13240941:
Luke Heirene and colleagues present a 2026 study of how antibody two-armed binding shapes treatment performance. Antibodies can grip two targets at once, a property called avidity. Strong gripping helps block a target, yet it can leave fewer antibodies spread across each cell when cell killing is the goal.

The team built a math model of binding, then tuned it against lab assays using matched one-armed and two-armed anti-PD-1 antibodies. Testing revealed a gap between measured and predicted binding that depended on binding strength. The authors attribute the gap to assay limits and used the model to correct the estimates. Their predictions can guide antibody design and dosing choices.
pmc-13241441:
Mohd Aji's team in Malaysia modeled whether citrus-born D-limonene can green up shale fracking fluids. Low surface tension between fluid and trapped gas aids yield but standard surfactants pollute. Atom-level modeling tracked methane, water, and limonene across mild and reservoir-like extremes. Free-energy math anchored the tension figures.

Heat slashed surface tension sharply in mild conditions, far less under deep pressure. Pressure itself barely mattered across the tested range. More limonene always lowered tension, though hot squeezed systems needed higher doses. The team frames limonene as a workable, if dose-hungry, green additive.
pmc-13242441:
Nanor Karageozian wrote a conceptual review on how time itself is treated in refugee studies. The article appeared in the Journal of International Humanitarian Action in 2026. Migration research has lately paid more attention to timing, waiting, and speed, but refugee studies has rarely made time its central concept. Karageozian surveys social theory on time and checks how selected refugee research uses, or misses, those ideas.

The review sorts time into timing, sequence, rhythm, speed, duration, and the pull of past, present, and future. Each dimension plays out at personal, community, and policy levels in forced displacement, from asylum waiting rooms to camp routines. Karageozian argues the levels intertwine and should not be studied in isolation. The paper closes by urging balance between movement and stuckness, and between refugee agency and the structures around it. It gives researchers a shared vocabulary for temporality.
pmc-13242841:
Junda Jiang and co-authors report a 2026 comparison of vision screening devices for schoolchildren. Two new self-contained darkroom screeners were tested against a standard tabletop autorefractor, with drug-dilated retinoscopy as the reference. Over thirteen hundred children and teenagers took part.

All three devices tracked the reference closely for overall focusing error. The tabletop unit matched best overall and led on farsightedness and astigmatism detection. One new device came closest on cylinder power. Every device detected nearsightedness excellently. The portable units were fast and sensitive, suiting mass first-pass screening. The authors recommend a two-level system: portable screening first, then precise confirmation for children who flag positive.
pmc-13243141:
Wei Huang and colleagues present a 2026 design for a tiny drug carrier that makes radiation work harder on tumors. Some cancers survive radiation by blocking ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron. Their carrier holds an iron-based frame plus two drugs that shut down separate defense paths in cancer cells.

A coating on the carrier breaks apart where reactive oxygen is high, and X-ray exposure speeds the release. Freed iron then drives a chemical reaction that harms DNA and drains a key cell protectant. Tests in cells and animals showed strong tumor control and clear scans with magnetic imaging. The design points to a way past radiation resistance that uses several attacks at once.
pmc-13243441:
Qingdong Yang, Zhongfu Li, and Xinhua Wen built a material that makes light behave as if the material were racing along, though nothing moves. Their paper appeared in Light: Science and Applications in 2026. In a real flowing liquid, light traveling with the flow is delayed differently from light fighting upstream, but the effect is tiny because flows are slow. Their metamaterial, a lattice of metal structures and gyromagnetic parts, engineers the same coupling artificially.

The measured response was enormous: an effective velocity of three-tenths the speed of light, the first demonstration of its kind. The effect is purely one-directional in character, which is exactly what device designers crave. Such non-reciprocity underlies components that pass light one way and block it the other, including gyrators and isolators that work regardless of polarization. The authors present the design rules, rooted in symmetry, that made the giant response possible.
pmc-13243741:
Soren A Christensen and Evan M Shipp introduce a free web tool that guards dental drug doses in 2026. Dentists often mix several numbing drugs, and the combined safe limit is easy to misjudge. Children face the highest risk when the math goes wrong.

Their tool, MaxSafe, takes the patient's weight, age, and health flags as inputs. Dentists enter doses by cartridge count for five common numbing drugs. The app adds up the share of each drug's limit and tracks the adrenaline dose on its own. Checks against 23 hand-worked cases matched exactly, including child cases. Warnings for liver or kidney problems add a further safety net.
pmc-13244341:
Feng Xu, a hospital pharmacist in China, wrote a personal essay on rediscovering the human side of a job being squeezed by policy and software. The piece appeared in Palliative and Supportive Care in 2026. National bulk purchasing has crashed drug prices so far that colleagues joke pharmacies have become worthless, while mandatory barcode scanning adds clerical load. AI agents now review prescriptions, counsel patients around the clock, and digest research faster than any human.

Against that backdrop Xu traces a personal shift from technical focus toward pharmaceutical humanistic care. The essay argues that what software cannot supply is presence: reading a dying patient's fears, weighing dignity alongside dosage, and staying answerable as a person. Technical excellence remains the floor of the profession, not its ceiling. The piece is a quiet manifesto for pharmacists to defend the relational core of their work.
pmc-13244841:
Vanessa Zwaans and colleagues describe a salvage heart operation for a prosthetic valve infection that had eaten into the aortic root. Their case report appeared in the Journal of Cardiothoracic Surgery in 2026. A seventy-one-year-old man returned eight weeks after an aortic valve replacement with a vegetation and a leaking, partly torn-out prosthesis. A standard risk score put his chance of dying in a redo operation at about one in two.

Surgeons found a ring of infection with an abscess tunneling into the left atrium and destroying its roof. They cut away all infected tissue up to the fibrous skeleton between the valves, rebuilt the sacrificed structures with biological tissue and a custom-made component, and replaced the aortic valve. The modified approach spared his mitral valve, which the standard operation would have sacrificed. He survived. The case argues radical cleaning need not always mean maximal replacement.
pmc-13244941:
Emmanuel Uwambajimana and colleagues examined why babies born too early die in two rural Rwandan hospitals with rates triple the national average. Their retrospective study appeared in Maternal Health, Neonatology and Perinatology in 2026. Records of every preterm baby admitted to the Kiziguro and Ngarama units from 2020 through 2024 were mined for what predicted death.

Roughly a fifth of the preterm deaths clustered at Kiziguro. The strongest predictors were the earliest gestational ages and newborn sepsis, which roughly tripled the odds of death. Infections in the mother, too little kangaroo mother care, and inadequate breathing support also raised risk. Overall mortality ended near national figures once case mix was considered, but the drivers are plainly fixable. The authors prescribe staff training, better infection control, reliable breathing support, and serious promotion of skin-to-skin care. Their message: in these wards, deaths follow resources and routines more than fate.
pmc-13245641:
Widhani and colleagues tested how well three artificial intelligence chatbots answer patient questions about lupus, in this 2026 JMIR Formative Research study. Lupus is a complex, flaring disease, and patients often search online for answers. The team posed twenty-two frequently asked questions, written in Indonesian, to ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

Five clinical immunologists, blinded to which bot wrote what, graded the answers for accuracy, and the researchers also scored readability. Gemini earned the best accuracy marks, though all three bots were judged satisfactory overall and the gaps between them were small. Every bot wrote at a hard reading level, which the authors flag as a real barrier for patients.
pmc-13246341:
Mengyue Hu and co-authors review lung cancers that grow around cystic air spaces in a 2026 synthesis. These tumors pair hollow pockets with solid or hazy parts on scans. They make up a large share of lung cancers found late or missed outright.

Wider screening now catches more of these cases, which raises the stakes for reading scans well. The review covers how the subtype is defined, how it may form, and how imaging guides each care step. Scans inform diagnosis, grouping, spread checks, stage, and outlook. Past studies are small and mostly backward-looking, which limits firm rules. The authors map gaps that future studies should close.
pmc-13246941:
Alakmeh, El-Hajj, and Nordquist evaluated a hands-on training course in neck-spine surgery in this 2026 Acta Neurochirurgica study. Cervical spine operations are high-risk, and practicing on cadavers offers a realistic but safe classroom. Twenty-four surgeons and trainees completed a three-day course in Sweden covering front and back approaches to the neck, with supervised practice on anatomical specimens. Answered questionnaires before, after, and six months later.

Every respondent said the course met expectations. Six months on, most participants reported operating more independently, especially in the standard front-of-neck fusion operation and in laminectomy. Participants valued the cadaver practice itself far above any other element. The authors present such courses as a valuable bridge between training and independent operating.
pmc-13247141:
Garvetto and co-authors explored a crop disease after dark in this 2026 Plant Direct study, asking what clubroot does at night. Clubroot, caused by Plasmodiophora brassicae, swells the roots of cabbage-family plants into tumor-like galls, hijacking the plant's metabolism and hormones. Because plant energy and defense run on a day-night clock, the team sequenced gene activity in infected Arabidopsis roots during the night at two infection stages.

Night changes were stronger in younger, mid-stage infections than in late ones. Some disrupted processes appeared only at night, and RNA modification stood out as the most clearly boosted night process. Infection also warped the rhythm of the plant's central circadian clock parts. The authors read this as the pathogen manipulating defense and metabolism around the clock.
pmc-13247641:
Park and Kim report the newest Visible Korean anatomy dataset in this 2026 Journal of Korean Medical Science article. The long-running project freezes cadavers and mills them into serial slices, photographing each surface to build a digital body that can be dissected endlessly on screen. Their 2024 female cadaver dataset, shot with a larger medium-format sensor, was compared slice by slice with the 2023 dataset.

Pixel size shrank from five hundredths of a millimeter to three, nearly tripling pixel density. Fine structures such as brain nuclei, fiber bundles, vessel walls, and facial ligaments became clearly traceable across planes. Real pathology, an enlarged heart, atherosclerosis, and a uterine tumor, showed plainly too. With twelve cadavers now accumulated, the authors claim the images rival physical dissection and suit clinical anatomy research.
pmc-13247741:
Kazuki Maeda and a large team compare two anti-nausea drugs in harsh chemotherapy in a 2026 matched study. Vomiting days after treatment can wreck quality of life. Two long-acting blockers are used to prevent it, but they had never met in this drug pairing.

Records from Tokushima University Hospital covered patients on two strong regimens from 2018 to 2024. Matching produced 68 balanced pairs. The fosnetupitant group stayed free of vomiting more often in the late window, days six and seven. Time to first vomiting also ran longer with that drug. Nausea rates, though, matched between groups. The edge was narrow but consistent for vomiting control.
pmc-13249541:
Kőmüves and a Hungarian team asked whether body chemistry colors a baby bird's feathers, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Collared flycatcher nestlings grow two wing markings, one dark with melanin and one pale stripe with porphyrin pigment. The researchers measured oxidative stress in nestlings' blood, weighing damaging byproducts against antioxidant defenses, and photographed wing feathers with a spectrometer.

Stress rose as the breeding season wore on and in crowded broods, especially for females. Chicks with the worst balance, high damage and low defense, showed shifted ultraviolet color in their dark feathers, hinting at more of one melanin type. Neither stress measure repeated reliably within nests, suggesting diet and chance shape them strongly.
pmc-13249741:
Kristóf Kádár and co-authors use a lab-grown cell model to study tooth enamel in this 2026 paper. Enamel hardens only if calcium crosses a layer of cells called ameloblasts, but the route calcium takes, and which side of the cell does what, was unclear.

The team grew rat-derived enamel cells as a flat sheet and tested calcium entry from each side. Two entry routes split the work: one worked mainly on the inner side, the other mainly on the outer side. Acid on the inner side reduced calcium entry, while acid on the outer side did not. The setup offers a working model for how enamel matures.
pmc-13250341:
Abdisalam Ismail Hassan led this 2026 case report of a rare surgical emergency. A 23-year-old man arrived with belly pain, vomiting, swelling, and no bowel movements, and he had never had surgery before, which made a blockage unusual.

Scans showed swollen small bowel loops, an inflamed appendix, and twisting deep in the belly. At emergency surgery, the appendix had looped around a bowel segment like a knot, blocking it, and was itself inflamed. Surgeons freed the bowel and removed the appendix, and the man recovered fully. The authors urge doctors to suspect this rare knot in young patients with unexplained blockage.
pmc-13250641:
Wu and co-authors map how baicalein, a plant flavonoid, acts inside non-small cell lung cancer. Their 2026 Translational Oncology study combines single-cell sequencing, tissue-location mapping, bulk gene data, and machine learning. Lung cancer of this type remains a leading cause of cancer death, and baicalein's exact targets were unclear.

Single-cell data resolved twenty-one cell populations in tumors and pointed to a core set of baicalein-linked genes. Machine learning narrowed the signal to a ten-gene signature that separated tumor from normal tissue with high accuracy. All ten genes ran higher in tumor areas on tissue maps, and docking tests suggested baicalein binds several of their proteins tightly. In dish tests, the compound slowed cancer cell growth in a dose-dependent way.
pmc-13251341:
Antonio Gallardo-Pizarro and colleagues track infections after CAR T-cell therapy in this 2026 study. The treatment retools a patient's own immune cells to fight cancer, but its two big side effects, a fever storm and brain toxicity, are treated with immune-damping drugs that invite infection.

Among 152 treatments from 2020 to 2023, about three in four brought on those side effects. Infections were proven in about a quarter of those episodes, split between bacterial, viral, and fungal kinds. Risk climbed steeply when several damping drugs were combined. Fever and a common inflammation marker proved unreliable at spotting infection, so the team urges sharper early checks.
pmc-13251641:
Feng Jing and colleagues test financial navigation for breast cancer patients in China in a 2026 randomized trial. Financial toxicity, the economic harm that treatment costs inflict on patients, is common but rarely addressed inside Chinese clinics. Navigation programs pair patients with trained helpers who explain costs, insurance, and aid options.

Eighty-two patients were randomized by cluster into navigation or usual care, with forty-one in each arm. Outcomes were checked at discharge and again one and three months later. Patients who received navigation reported lighter subjective financial strain over time and stronger cost-related health literacy, their grasp of medical costs and coverage. Shared decision-making ability and perceived stress, however, did not differ between groups. Material and behavioral sides of financial hardship also stayed unchanged. The authors call the results early support for adding navigation to routine breast cancer care.
pmc-13252741:
Arshad Khanani and colleagues report the COOL-2 trial in this 2026 eye study. Injections into the eye are the most common office procedure for retina specialists, yet numbing them usually means a numbing injection of its own, so the team tested freezing instead.

Eighty patients who needed repeated injections were assigned to four cooling settings, mixing two temperatures with different contact times. The winning setting, the colder temperature held for ten seconds, gave the lowest pain scores, clearly beating a fifteen-second hold. Pain also eased slightly with each visit. A mild, short-lived surface scratching appeared in about a third of eyes at one setting. The authors call cooling workable, with care.
pmc-13252841:
Maria Londono-Mendez and colleagues compare efficient and inefficient grazing heifers across seasons in this 2026 animal study from western Canada. Feed efficiency measured indoors may not hold on pasture, where summer heat and deep winter cold stress cattle differently.

Forty-one heifers were classed by how much feed they needed for their growth, then tracked on pasture from about 14 months of age. Rumen temperature was logged every ten minutes, and blood samples were taken every few weeks. Efficient heifers showed calmer stress and inflammation markers in summer, while inefficient ones carried more of a fat hormone in winter. Growth itself did not differ between groups in either season.
pmc-13253141:
Xiaoxue Yang and colleagues engineer stem cells that donate their mitochondria more effectively to heal diabetic wounds in a 2026 study. High blood sugar damages blood vessels and mitochondria in wound tissue, pushing vessel-lining cells into an iron-driven death called ferroptosis. Stem cells can hand healthy mitochondria to struggling neighbors, but sugar-rich conditions weaken the donors themselves.

The team grew stem cells from shed baby teeth on tiny carriers made from a modified chitosan material. The carriers respond to glucose by breaking down and releasing antioxidant protection, sheltering the cells while mimicking the clustered state that boosts their natural potency. The resulting cells carried stronger mitochondria and transferred them more readily. In diabetic animals, treatment curbed ferroptosis in vessel cells, encouraged new blood vessel growth, and sped wound closure. The authors offer the platform as a general way to amplify stem cell therapy through mitochondrial donation.
pmc-13253441:
Xue-Qing Liu and co-authors recount a 2026 case of toxic epidermal necrolysis caused by a chemical exposure rather than a drug. This rare reaction peels the skin from the body like a burn and is usually triggered by medicines. Their patient was exposed to a compound called DCT, used industrially, and arrived with about sixty percent of the body surface detached or blistering.

Treatment combined systemic glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, intravenous immunoglobulin, and a single dose of infliximab to shut down the immune attack. Nursing care was equally intensive, centered on protecting broken skin and mouth lining, managing pain with a multidisciplinary team, and supporting nutrition and fluids. After twenty days of this combined regimen, the skin lesions had nearly healed. The patient improved enough to leave hospital. The authors present the case as a template for personalized treatment and nursing in chemically induced cases of this emergency.
pmc-13253941:
Yosri Fahim, Ibrahim Hasani, and Samer Kabba review tiny particles in cancer care in a 2026 paper. Standard cancer drugs often harm healthy tissue and face resistance. Nanoparticles, extremely small carriers, can deliver drugs to tumors, release them on cue, and combine diagnosis with treatment in one platform.

The review covers how particles are made, measured, and aimed at tumors, plus many carrier types from fat-based to metal. Some products, like Doxil and Abraxane, already help patients. Yet uneven tumor uptake, long-term safety, and factory and approval hurdles keep many designs from clinics, the authors warn.
pmc-13254741:
Aziz Lamghari and colleagues report tuberculosis found through a scrotal abscess in a 2026 case report. A 36-year-old man had two months of growing left scrotal pain with fever. Drainage and standard antibiotics did not help, so a second operation cleaned the area again.

Tests on the pus found acid-fast bacilli, and culture and PCR confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Tissue samples showed granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis, the cheese-like dead tissue typical of TB. The infection sat in the epididymis, a sperm duct. The authors urge TB testing for chronic scrotal abscess in endemic regions.
pmc-13255941:
Arifa Zahir and co-authors screen for Parkinson disease from voice recordings in a 2026 diagnostic study. Parkinson often weakens the voice early, making speech a cheap screening signal. The team recorded 203 people, 121 with Parkinson and 82 healthy controls, and fed three kinds of sound spectrograms into parallel neural networks.

The three-view model reached a mean accuracy of about eighty-seven percent. Adding a feature based on how well speech recognition software agreed with the recordings lifted accuracy to about ninety-seven percent and cut missed cases sharply. The authors say the method suits structured screening settings, while wider real-world testing is still needed.
pmc-13256141:
Franco da Silveira and a large team present a 2026 exploratory survey of barriers to Agriculture 4.0 technology adoption in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Digital tools promise better farm decisions, yet uptake lags unevenly in developing regions. Farmers rated twenty-five literature-based barriers spanning technology, cost, policy, society, and environment in a 2024 online survey.

Economic barriers scored most severe overall, led by unaffordable equipment, high maintenance costs, and weak infrastructure. Looking at which barriers were rated highly together revealed different patterns by farm size. Small farms showed segmented clusters tying price and technical access to institutional limits, while medium farms showed the most interconnected pattern. The authors stress these are co-perception maps, not causes. They argue policy should attack bundles of barriers sized to each farm class.
pmc-13256541:
İnce-Palamutoğlu, Palamutoğlu, and Baş tested how three yogurt styles weather a mock digestive tract. Yogurts made with probiotic starter cultures, standard cultures, or a probiotic sachet stirred in were run through a dynamic in vitro system copying mouth, stomach, and small gut. Nanopore gene reads tracked which microbes survived each phase.

The sachet yogurts started with richer, more even communities than either starter yogurt. Digestion squeezed every sample toward a core ruled by Firmicutes, yet the sachet yogurts' post-digestion mix stayed clearly distinct from the others. The authors conclude sachet use yields a hardier, more diverse product that better withstands digestive stress.
pmc-13257341:
Teodora Biciusca and a large team integrate imaging, microbe, and host factors in pneumonia in a 2026 review. Pneumonia still burdens older and immune-weakened people heavily, and its scan patterns vary widely by cause. Studies from 2000 onward across three databases were structured by pathogen group.

Where infection settles in the lung reflects entry route, lung anatomy, host defenses, and exposures together. Lobar, bronchial, interstitial, and cavity-forming patterns each hint at likely organisms and severity. Matching scan pattern with symptoms and personal risk can speed early guesses about cause and guide first antibiotics. Radiologists and admitting teams share the intended audience. The authors argue that pattern reading works best as one leg of a three-part judgment, never as a stand-alone diagnosis from images alone.
pmc-13257441:
Hilmi Erdem Sumbul leads a 2026 real-world study of semaglutide dose increases in type 2 diabetes care in Türkiye. Five hundred patients in the Çukurova region who started the drug during 2024 and 2025 were grouped by their highest dose. Blood sugar, weight, lipids, and insulin use were tracked for thirty weeks.

Average HbA1c, the long-term blood sugar marker, fell by about one percentage point overall. Higher final doses brought larger drops, rising stepwise across the three groups. Insulin dose cuts also grew more common at the top dose, reaching about half of patients. Nearly a quarter stopped treatment early, which tempers the gains. Diabetes clinicians gain Turkish practice data that mirror trial patterns. Dose escalation helped, yet persistence remains a real-world weak point.
pmc-13258641:
Li Sun and colleagues study corrosion of a nickel phosphorus catalyst used in a seawater fuel cell during 2026 work. The catalyst layer sits on copper and helps release hydrogen from a borohydride fuel. Voltage, time, and temperature during plating were varied to find durable settings.

Corrosion resistance peaked at a middle voltage where the layer formed most completely. Longer plating or hotter baths opened holes and cracks that weakened protection. Mild settings of thirty degrees and three minutes worked best. In service tests, chloride in seawater drove corrosion faster than heat did. Damage stayed local, with pitting and surface loss as the main pattern.
pmc-13258741:
Rakan Hamad and colleagues review a child dental appliance called the distal shoe in a 2026 clinic records study. The device holds space after early loss of a baby molar until the adult molar arrives. Records from a specialist clinic covered placements between twenty fourteen and twenty twenty two.

Most appliances went in under general anesthesia for very young children with heavy decay. Falling out after cement failure was the most common problem. About five in six appliances succeeded over an average follow up near seventeen months. Estimated average survival passed three and a half years. Pediatric dentists gain real world survival figures for a device with little prior outcome data.
pmc-13259041:
Marek Kucbel and coauthors dissect the chemistry of recycled milk bottle plastic in a 2026 study. Used high density polyethylene packaging was heated and analyzed to identify over one hundred organic compounds. Each compound was sorted by origin, from product residue to polymer breakdown.

Decay products formed the most varied group, signaling heavy reprocessing history. Additive leftovers added to the pool of unintended substances in the recyclate. Fluoropolymer residues appeared in most samples tested. Samples grouped by degradation and contamination patterns rather than by product type. Recyclers learn that chemistry aware sorting beats category based sorting for quality control.
pmc-13259241:
Luqing Yang and colleagues dose potted soil with polyethylene microplastics in a 2026 crop study. A leafy amaranth vegetable grew across plastic levels from trace amounts to five percent of soil. Growth, leaf chemistry, soil traits, and bacterial diversity were measured.

Shoot and leaf growth fell as plastic dose rose, with fresh weight losses reaching about three fifths at the top dose. Leaf greenness dropped while a damage marker climbed. Soil pores and available phosphorus shrank from the mid doses upward. Plant phosphorus content fell by roughly a quarter to a third. Bacterial diversity narrowed and community makeup shifted. Vegetable growers get dose based warning signs for plastic laden soils.
pmc-13259841:
Vlatko Karanfilovski and colleagues described in 2026 the first use of enzyme replacement therapy for Fabry disease in North Macedonia. Fabry disease is a rare inherited disorder in which a missing enzyme lets fatty material build up in many organs. Their case series followed two men with advanced disease who had already received kidney transplants.

One man received agalsidase beta and the other agalsidase alfa, with checks on blood markers, heart, nerves, and graft function. Both men showed large, lasting drops in Lyso-Gb3, a blood marker of disease load, while graft and heart function stayed stable. Pain and daily life improved clearly for the first man, but nerve problems persisted for the second. The authors urge earlier diagnosis and family screening, since late nerve damage may not reverse.
pmc-13260541:
Humaira Yasmin and co-authors present a 2026 numerical study of heat transfer in a special fluid flowing between two rotating disks. The fluid is a Casson hybrid nanofluid, a liquid with non-standard flow behavior carrying two kinds of nanoparticles, moving through a porous material of varying resistance. The model includes electrical Joule heating, friction heating, and time-varying heat generation and absorption. Equations were solved with a semi-analytic method and checked against standard numerical solutions.

Velocity and temperature profiles shifted in clear patterns as parameters changed. Axial velocity rose with the lower disk's stretching parameter, Reynolds number, and suction, but fell as the upper disk stretched more. Temperature profiles rose with the Eckert number, heat source parameter, and suction. The two solution methods agreed closely, with percentage errors near zero. The authors link the results to cooling rotating surfaces, reactor design, and filtration.
pmc-13260941:
Rosa Lisset Salazar Herrán leads a 2026 study of postpartum depression in mothers in a kangaroo mother care program in southern Colombia. Kangaroo care involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact for fragile newborns, and mothers in such programs face added emotional demands. The study surveyed 140 mothers using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and a structured survey covering social, obstetric, and mood factors, to find the rate of depression and its linked factors.

The rate of postpartum depression was 23.5 percent of the mothers surveyed. No clear differences appeared across social factors. Higher rates were linked to vaginal delivery, previous live births, having three or more children, domestic abuse during pregnancy, and lacking support for infant care. A mother's irritation at infant crying was the strongest signal, with an odds ratio of 3.64, the strongest link found. Family support during infant care protected mothers, with an odds ratio of 0.19 for those mothers.
pmc-13261041:
Yoshiyasu Aizawa and Takumi Matsumoto present a 2026 case report of persistent ST-segment elevation mimicking a heart attack. ST elevation on an electrocardiogram usually signals acute myocardial infarction and prompts urgent invasive checks. Their patient was a 95-year-old woman admitted with COVID-19-associated pneumonia and aspiration pneumonia. Her admission tracing showed ST elevation with T-wave inversion in the lateral chest leads, a pattern that looks like an ST-elevation heart attack.

She had no chest pain, no rise in cardiac biomarkers, and normal heart pumping function without regional wall motion problems. Record review showed the same tracing pattern had been present consistently for more than a decade. The authors attribute it to chronic localized heart muscle remodeling, possibly from unrecognized scarring not visible on routine imaging. The case stresses integrating symptoms, biomarkers, and old tracings before assuming a blocked artery.
pmc-13261441:
Norio Sakai and co-authors reported in 2026 a one-pot route to two families of nitrogen ring compounds valued in drug research. Aminoquinolines appear in antimalarial and antitumor agents, yet joining them with plain alkynes had proved stubborn. Their team used gallium or indium salts, group thirteen Lewis acids, to drive the ring-forming reaction.

With these promoters, 2-aminobenzonitriles combined with many terminal and internal alkynes to give 4-aminoquinolines in moderate to good yields. Halogen, ester, and silicon-bearing partners all survived the conditions. Switching to gallium chloride alone pushed a different path: two molecules of the starting nitrile paired up instead. That dimerization delivered 4-amino-2-arylquinazolines in good yield. The authors present both reactions as practical entries into scaffolds that medicinal chemists reuse often.
pmc-13262641:
Pushpam Kumar argues in a 2026 commentary that putting a money value on drug resistance can drive action. Antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs, harms human and animal health together, the focus of the One Health approach. Kumar says clear cost figures remove haze from policy choices and make the case for spending on control.

The piece cites projections of up to one trillion dollars a year in extra health costs by 2050 if resistance grows unchecked. It also cites a global plan costed at about 46 billion dollars a year, with an estimated return of seven to thirteen dollars per dollar spent by 2050. Many side costs, such as harm to animal health and farming, were left out of those sums.
pmc-13262741:
Abraão Santos and colleagues take the first census of leafhoppers in the Eastern Canadian Arctic, from insects a pollinator program caught by accident, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The Nunavik Sentinels community science network monitored bees and kin across Quebec and Labrador from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-three. Leafhoppers, plant-juice specialists, came up in the nets as bycatch.

Identified material held twenty-five species plus seven more sorted to genus. Fourteen were new records for the region. Richness faded with latitude, from twenty species in the subarctic Taiga Shield to a pair of hardy species persisting in the coldest Arctic ecozones. The authors frame the haul as a baseline: without such community-collected records, nobody could tell how northern insect communities shift as the North warms fastest on Earth.
pmc-13262841:
Alfonso C Hernandez-Romieu leads a comparison of two disease watch systems in Puerto Rico in a 2026 journal article. A sentinel system tests patients systematically at set sites, while the island-wide passive system relies on routine reports. The team compared trends for dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and COVID-19 from 2012 to 2023, checking whether the sentinel system matched and led the larger one.

Sentinel trends matched island-wide trends for every disease studied. The sentinel system reported rises up to three weeks earlier for epidemic dengue, eight weeks for Zika, and two weeks for early COVID-19. Chikungunya rises appeared at about the same time in both systems. Agreement was weaker for dengue outside epidemics. The authors back sentinel systems as early warning tools.
pmc-13263641:
