Lilian Marques de Freitas and co-authors report a 2026 journal article mapping drug-processing gene variants in Indigenous peoples of the Brazilian Amazon. The CYP gene family makes enzymes that break down most medicines, so variants change how people respond to drugs. These populations are rarely included in genetic studies. The team sequenced the protein-coding DNA of 64 people from twelve ethnic groups.

They found 506 variants across 63 CYP genes. Most were predicted to modify protein function mildly, but 21 had high predicted impact. Eleven variants appear entirely new, absent from public databases. Their distribution differed from global reference populations. The authors offer the data as a foundation for fairer, better-matched precision medicine in the region.
pmc-13263941:
Samy A. Azer and co-authors argue in a 2026 editorial that research philosophy decides whether a study on AI in medical education is sound. They note that papers are most often rejected for design problems: mismatched aims, methods, and conclusions, weak questions, and unvalidated tools. In their experience, these flaws usually trace back to an unexamined research stance.

They urge authors to spell out their assumptions about reality, knowledge, method, and values. Authors should also name their paradigm, be it positivism, interpretivism, critical theory, or pragmatism, in the methods or an appendix. Doing so, they argue, improves a study's logic, transparency, and chances of surviving peer review, especially in fast-moving fields like AI in health education.
pmc-13264441:
Zhi-Ping Zhang wrote a 2026 case report on a burst blood vessel swelling that was first read as a harmless cyst. The vessel was the splenic artery, which feeds the spleen, and its rupture can kill if missed. A plain CT scan, done without dye, caused the error.

The patient was a 49-year-old man with high blood pressure and sudden pain in the upper left belly. The first scan suggested a pancreatic cyst, a fluid sac near the pancreas. He then collapsed as blood leaked in two stages. A dye scan showed the burst swelling, over five centimetres wide. Emergency surgery removed his spleen and saved him. Zhang urges a low bar for dye scans in such pain.
pmc-13264541:
Gretchen Holtgrefe and Patricia A Wight published a 2026 study using optical genome mapping, a way to picture long DNA stretches, on a new mutant mouse line. The mice carry a reporter gene tied to a brain myelin gene. Mutant mice were small, with odd paws and faces, and every carrier showed the traits.

The mapping showed the added gene sat where chromosomes 1 and 2 had swapped parts in an uneven trade. Chunks of DNA were lost from both chromosomes, removing dozens of genes in all. Exact break points were confirmed by targeted sequencing. The authors note the lost region matches a human condition, 1q24 deletion syndrome, so the mice may model it in future work.
pmc-13264641:
Shritesh Bhoyar and Anil Pethe wrote a 2026 review of nanotechnology creams and devices for psoriasis, a long-term immune skin disease that affects more than 40 million people. Normal creams cross the thickened skin poorly, and strong body-wide drugs carry cost and safety limits. Tiny carriers promise better entry and slower release.

The review covers lipid carriers, polymer systems, microneedles, nanoemulsions, nanosponges, and nanofibers. Studies report better skin scores, more drug kept in the skin, and good tolerance for nano forms of three common drugs. Yet hurdles remain: making batches the same each time, scaling up production, meeting quality rules, and cost. The authors map what must be solved before these products reach wide clinical and market use.
pmc-13264941:
Aaron Siong Fatt Tsen and colleagues compare autism screening tools for toddlers, in a 2026 systematic review. Early screening matters because early support improves outcomes. The M-CHAT-R/F checklist is widely used around the world. A fresh synthesis of its accuracy against other tools was missing.

Six high-quality studies covering 12,633 children aged 12 to 48 months were analysed. The checklist reliably cleared children who screened negative. Its ability to confirm likely cases was weak, with many false positives. Performance also fell outside the ideal age window of about 16 to 30 months. The authors caution against relying on this tool alone.
pmc-13266141:
Jie Zhao and colleagues review wrist-ankle acupuncture for post-stroke shoulder-hand syndrome, published in 2026. The syndrome brings pain and stiff wrist and hand movement after stroke. Nurse-led use of this technique is common in China. Seventy-nine candidate studies were screened from eight databases.

Only four trials, all from China, entered the pooled analysis. Compared with usual care, acupuncture may reduce shoulder pain. Upper limb function and daily living scores also improved. Evidence grading and acupuncture reporting checks were applied. The authors note the technique can be delivered independently by nurses, while stronger trials would firm up the optimal dose.
pmc-13267041:
TingLan Ma and colleagues report a 2026 survey study on mistreatment of doctors in training. Mistreatment in residency is linked to burnout and people leaving medicine. The team surveyed trainees at three large United States teaching sites, asking about program openness, belonging, mistreatment, burnout, and support.

Of 675 eligible trainees, 266 replied. Both an open program climate and a personal sense of belonging guarded against reported mistreatment. Mistreatment was strongly tied to burnout, while belonging was tied to lower burnout even after support was counted. Openness helped most for trainees who felt they belonged least. The authors urge programs to build both openness and belonging as core supports.
pmc-13267541:
Arne Astrup and seven co-authors argue that food guides should stress whole foods, not a firm cap on saturated fat. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. Diet and life shape long health, span of life, and risk of heart, blood, and tumor ills. The cap at issue sets fat of this kind at ten percent of food power.

The team note new US guides now let full-fat dairy in, yet keep the ten percent cap for all foods. Fat kinds in this class act in distinct ways in the body. A food's health mark comes from its whole build, not one fat part. They urge the cap be dropped for food-based rules.
pmc-13268141:
Louisa-Jane Burton and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for studying hospital green spaces in stroke recovery. Hospital stays after stroke are a key recovery window, yet patients often stay inactive and low in mood. Gardens and green areas might offer activity, company, and a lift, but their role after stroke is little studied. The planned study covers three hospital sites with different kinds of green space.

Data will mix site documents and maps, ten days of watching how spaces are used in two seasons, and interviews. About 45 patients and visitors and 30 staff will share their experiences. Stroke survivors and carers in three other places will help refine the resulting theory. The protocol paper sets out the plan; findings will follow. The team aims at practical design advice for stroke units.
pmc-13268641:
Jasper Garay and colleagues publish a 2026 plan for co-designing a virtual reality wellbeing app with an Aboriginal community in Sydney. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples face deep wellbeing gaps rooted in colonization. Their own frameworks center culture as a source of strength and healing. The study partners with an Aboriginal community-run group and Aboriginal-led creative studios.

The three-phase plan uses Indigenous research methods and community action research. About 35 staff and community members per phase will join yarning circles, a group talk method grounded in culture. The last phase adds a survey on cultural fit, acceptability, and feasibility. The finished app will run inside the partner's existing community programs. The authors hope it widens access to wellbeing support that fits the culture it serves.
pmc-13269841:
Shengsheng Liu, Yuanyuan Zhang, Xiaogui Zhao, and Bangtao Yao published a case report in 2026 about eye disease from syphilis in a patient also living with HIV. Syphilis is rising worldwide, yet this pairing of eye conditions is extremely uncommon. One eye showed a rare placoid inflammation of the retina, while the other showed optic nerve disease.

Eye syphilis can be the first sign of the infection, and the retinal condition can lead to blindness if missed. The authors report that their treatment protocol brought complete resolution of both eye problems. They advise screening for sexually transmitted infections when such eye disease appears. The case is presented as a guide for spotting and treating this rare combination.
pmc-13269941:
John Cowgill and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on the structure of a human brain receptor that calms nerve activity. This receptor, built from alpha5 and beta3 parts, sits in the hippocampus, a memory center, and is a target of anesthetics and seizure drugs. Its exact assembly and opening steps were poorly understood.

Using frozen microscope imaging and electrical recordings, the team found most receptors assemble with two alpha and three beta parts. A minority used one alpha and four beta parts. In the resting state, a gate and a zinc lock blocked ion flow. When the natural signal bound, the lock released and the gate opened. Two drugs bound without changing the open shape.
pmc-13271141:
Tien Zubaidah wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a study mapping the symptom and needs journey of cervical cancer patients around the time of surgery. That study followed patients over time with interviews, moving beyond clinical measures to their fears, struggles, and hopes at a vulnerable stage of care.

Zubaidah praises the work, then raises two cautions. First, the study justifies its 14 participants by claiming information saturation, but never states when saturation was reached or how it was judged. Second, using Maslow's hierarchy of needs may force linked themes, such as shame, lost self-worth, and wanting yet drowning in information, into a strict order. Other frameworks centred on relationships and meaning might fit better.
pmc-13271241:
Arindam Debbarma and Bryan E. Dowd wrote a 2026 review of dynamic copay health plans, a new design in United States employer insurance. In these plans, the fixed amount a patient pays varies by provider and service. It is shown before care, often in an app. It uses price data that new transparency rules and artificial intelligence tools make available.

Using UnitedHealthcare's Surest plan as an example, the authors trace plan design from broad networks to narrow, tiered networks and reference pricing. They weigh likely gains in predicting out-of-pocket costs against limits: low insurance literacy, little truly shoppable care, and steering effects that fade. They propose layering dynamic copays onto reference pricing and tiered networks.
pmc-13271441:
Natsuhiro Takahashi is lead author of a 2026 journal article on how high gravity affects osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. Bone loss in astronauts shows the skeleton senses gravity changes, and stronger-than-normal gravity, made with a centrifuge, offers a way to test how bone-eating cells respond to mechanical force.

Mouse bone marrow osteoclasts were exposed to gravity up to thirty times Earth's, for as little as thirty minutes. High gravity damaged the actin rings these cells use to seal onto bone, dimmed their structure, and moved cell nuclei, while other supports stayed unchanged. Resorption pits in dentine shrank in step. Protein tagging analysis showed wide changes across cell structure, signalling, and control pathways.
pmc-13271541:
Harshal Sahare and H Anupama comment in 2026 on a study of interferon alfa-2B injections for recurring inflammatory macular edema, a swelling at the center of the retina. Steroid treatment works but can raise eye pressure and cloud the lens over time. A steroid-sparing option would help patients who need repeated care.

The letter welcomes the reported drop in retinal thickness and better vision one week after a single injection behind the eye. Delivery through the wall of the eye can carry large drug molecules to the back segment. The writers then raise points needing care before wider use of the approach.
pmc-13271941:
Abhisek Sahu and colleagues apply in 2026 network analysis to gene activity in Indian zebu cattle with chronic Johne's disease. The disease, caused by a hardy Mycobacterium relative, inflames the gut and drains dairy income worldwide. Its molecular course in desi cattle had not been mapped in depth.

Gene sequencing of sick and healthy cows found about nineteen hundred protein-coding genes with changed activity, plus thousands of long non-coding RNAs. One network module of co-active genes tracked closely with clinical signs and centered on defense and inflammation. Key hub genes were confirmed by a second lab test, giving breeders and vets candidate markers for the disease.
pmc-13272041:
Shiyang Niu and coauthors grade in 2026 dry eye education videos on the Chinese social platform Xiaohongshu. The public increasingly learns eye care from short videos, yet quality by uploader type had not been measured. The team sampled the first two hundred videos returned for the Chinese term for dry eye.

After exclusions, 136 videos remained, most from non-medical individual accounts. Content leaned toward lifestyle tips and treatment, while definitions and diagnosis were rarely covered. Videos from non-medical uploaders carried incorrect or misleading claims far more often than those from medical users. Standard quality tools were applied to judge clarity and reliability for viewers.
pmc-13272341:
Csaba Pajor and Kalman Czeibert report in 2026 the surgical stabilization of a skull-to-spine malformation in a five-month-old Miniature Dachshund using a custom titanium implant. Malformed joints where skull, atlas, and axis meet can compress the spinal cord and unsteady a puppy's gait. Each case differs anatomically, so planning must be individual.

Scans showed a severely malformed first neck vertebra, flattened skull joints, a missing dens, and slippage at two joints. Surgeons planned the repair virtually from CT data and printed a drilling guide plus a patient-specific locking plate. The dorsal operation stabilized the junction to relieve cord pressure and pain.
pmc-13272541:
Kristina Ballestad Gundersen leads a 2026 study comparing odd changes in the sense of self across three groups. One group was at high clinical risk for psychosis, one had autism spectrum disorder, and one was a control group. The authors asked whether these self changes link to social thinking and daily social life.

The study included 39 people at risk for psychosis, 39 with autism, and 30 controls, with a mean age near 24. Self changes followed a graded pattern, highest in the risk group, then autism, then controls. Both clinical groups showed more social bias and poorer social function, but self changes linked to social bias only in autism.
pmc-13272941:
Doaa Deabes leads a 2026 study packing an extract of Swiss chard leaves into tiny coated carriers to boost its germ-fighting and antioxidant power. The carriers are novasomes coated with hyaluronate, a natural gel-like substance. The team first profiled the plant chemicals, then built and tested two formulations.

Chemical analysis found fatty acids in one fraction and 33 metabolites, mostly flavonoids and phenolic acids, in another. The raw extract worked only against a yeast, but the best carrier form showed trends against all microbes tested, including two bacteria. It also beat the raw extract on antioxidant tests, supporting novasomes as a stronger delivery vehicle for this plant extract.
pmc-13273041:
Caiquan Zhao and co-authors purified and tested plant compounds from Allium polyrhizum in a 2026 study. This wild onion relative may protect blood vessels, yet its active compounds had not been purified in a systematic way. The team set out to build a reliable method and test the product.

They tuned a resin based method and reached a high recovery rate. The purified mix fought free radicals strongly in chemical tests. In rats with a blood stasis condition, treatment improved blood flow measures, restored vessel lining function, and reduced clotting tendency. Advanced profiling found 309 compounds of the flavonoid class in the mix. The authors see promise for vascular health products, with more work planned on safety and use.
pmc-13273141:
Aya Gamal leads a 2026 study of a novel octagonal greenhouse solar dryer with a solar chimney for preserving farm produce. Standard solar dryers often have uneven airflow and unstable heat. The eight-sided design aims to improve air circulation, spread heat evenly, reduce stagnant zones, and stand up better to wind.

The dryer was tested in March, June, September, and December on leafy mint and molokhia and on tomato and onion. Average thermal efficiency was about 50 percent, with best results in June and worst in December. Leafy goods dried within one day, tomato took 1.5 to 2 days, and onion 2 to 3 days. Predicted and measured results agreed closely in a March check.
pmc-13273441:
Dongling Pei leads a 2026 illustrative case removing a small meningioma inside a brain ventricle in a 13-year-old boy, using a basket retriever through a single burr hole. The boy had obstructive hydrocephalus, a blockage of fluid flow in the brain. Round, mobile tumors are hard to grasp with standard endoscopic tools.

Surgeons used a flexible helical basket, designed for removing urinary stones, during a procedure to relieve the blockage. The basket captured and held the tumor, which was then fully removed and retrieved. The authors say the device's small size and maneuverability suit endoscopic work and may help with similar small, mobile lesions inside the ventricles.
pmc-13273541:
Claudia Brandt and co-authors argued in a 2026 article that infection diagnostic skill is a core competence medical students must gain through hands-on teaching. Courses in microbiology, virology, and hygiene are costly and compete with other subjects, yet the authors hold that they cannot be replaced by self study.

They stress that infectious diseases spread between people, animals, and ecosystems, so doctors need linked knowledge of epidemiology, prevention, diagnosis, and therapy. Fast and correct diagnosis guides sensible antibiotic use, which fights the rise of drug resistant pathogens. It also helps stop outbreaks early. Reading results demands judgment about timing, prior illness, and vaccination. Sample taking, test choice, and critical reading of findings must therefore be practiced in structured courses.
pmc-13273841:
Sato and colleagues examine eight lymphoma-like cases whose gene patterns resemble cold agglutinin disease. Their 2026 journal article questions how these cases fit the current WHO classification. Cold agglutinin disease is a rare blood disorder driven by antibodies.

All eight patients showed restricted use of one antibody gene, IGHV4-34. Their tumors carried changes in the KMT2D and CARD11 genes. Two common markers were absent. The MYD88 L265P change was not found. CXCR4 changes were also absent. This pattern differs from typical related lymphomas. The authors argue these cases form a distinct group. They suggest the classification should make room for them.
pmc-13274041:
Mia Stråvik and colleagues report a 2026 journal article from a Swedish birth cohort on when babies first eat certain foods. Diet in the first year may shape the immune system and later allergy risk. Parents in the NICE cohort filled in monthly web questionnaires about eighteen foods.

At age six, 430 children were checked by an allergy specialist for food allergy, eczema, and allergic asthma. Each month earlier that meat was introduced was linked to about twenty-four percent lower odds of food allergy. Egg showed a weaker hint that faded after adjustment. Food timing showed no link to eczema or asthma. Only twenty-seven percent of children got peanuts in their first year, so guidance was poorly followed.
pmc-13275541:
Saskia P M Truijen and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study comparing physical function in older adults with rheumatoid arthritis and population controls. The STAR study enrolled 207 patients and 214 controls aged fifty-five to eighty-five. Function was measured by two questionnaires plus, in a subgroup, grip strength, walking speed, and a sit-to-stand test.

Aging itself worsened function only modestly in both groups, and the age pattern was nearly identical, with one small exception on the sit-to-stand test. Arthritis independently brought worse self-reported function, about forty percent higher hand disability scores, and grip strength lower by 3.2 kilograms, but not slower walking. Fatigue and pain explained much of the gap, suggesting shared aging processes more than arthritis-specific decline.
pmc-13276741:
Monami Dai and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a calcified clot that sabotaged a stroke procedure. Calcified cerebral emboli, hardened fragments blocking brain arteries, resist the devices used to pull clots out. They are uncommon but likely under-recognized as a cause of stroke.

Their patient was a woman in her eighties who first arrived with speech loss and scattered tiny strokes, but no large blockage. A week later her speech failed again, this time with her main neck artery blocked. A clot-removal procedure made several passes yet restored only partial flow. A scan afterward showed a new, dense, well-defined spot matching a calcified embolus that earlier scans had missed. The authors stress that spotting such emboli, best with thin-slice scans, explains stubborn procedures and should guide strategy and the search for the stroke's source.
pmc-13276841:
WanTing Wong, Mingyang Hu, and Rivka L Isaacson review a reversible protein modification called S-palmitoylation, in a 2026 article. The change attaches a sixteen-carbon fatty chain to a cysteine building block through a sulfur bond. Because it can be added and removed, it acts like a switch for protein behaviour.

The modification steers where proteins sit in the cell, how stable they are, and which partners they bind. Roughly a tenth of human proteins may carry it, spanning receptors, enzymes, and adhesion molecules. Faulty control is linked with cancers and immune and brain disorders. The review covers the enzymes involved, recent examples, and hurdles facing drug development.
pmc-13278141:
Tharindu Ruwanpathiranage leads a 2026 case report of a rare, fast-moving form of raised pressure inside the skull in early pregnancy. The condition, fulminant idiopathic intracranial hypertension, has no clear cause and can destroy vision quickly. A 29-year-old woman arrived with two weeks of worsening peripheral vision loss, headache, dizziness, and unsteady walking.

Exams showed loss of the outer vision in both eyes and severe swelling of the optic discs. That pattern usually points to pressure on the visual pathway junction, but scans found no mass. A spinal tap confirmed very high pressure with normal fluid. Repeated drainage, a pressure-lowering drug, and finally a shunt brought major improvement in vision and gait.
pmc-13278241:
Xueying Cheng leads a 2026 animal study of a protein called Pirt in cancer-induced bone pain, the severe pain that follows cancer in bone. Pirt sits in pain-sensing nerve cells and boosts a heat-sensing channel. The team asked whether Pirt also drives release of substance P, a pain-signaling peptide, using mice with and without the Pirt gene.

Pain behavior tests and molecular measures showed that Pirt promotes substance P release and worsens this bone pain, in the study's stated finding. That upstream role was the missing link the team set out to test, since substance P was already known to shape pain and immune cell movement in this setting. Blocking Pirt is proposed as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13278441:
Janet Kobusinge Lubega leads a 2026 study of low-level viremia, small amounts of virus in the blood, among Ugandan children and teens living with HIV. Low levels can warn of coming treatment failure. The team analyzed nearly a million viral load tests from the national laboratory system for ages zero to nineteen, from 2014 to 2023.

Low-level viremia made up fourteen percent of tests and rose from about ten point five percent in 2014 to about sixteen percent in 2023. The steepest rise was in infants. Increases appeared even among children with good adherence and long treatment history. Five of fifteen regions passed twenty percent in 2023. Stronger monitoring and tailored adherence support are needed to protect long-term outcomes, the authors warn.
pmc-13279041:
Chao Guo and colleagues published a 2026 network meta-analysis comparing physical therapy options for pain in the first days after total knee replacement surgery. Searching seven databases, they gathered 42 randomized trials with 3,165 participants covering eight approaches, from cold therapy and kinesio taping to electroacupuncture and manual lymphatic drainage. A network meta-analysis ranks treatments against each other even when trials tested them only against controls.

Cold therapy, called cryotherapy, ranked highest, with an 88 percent probability score for being among the most effective options, followed by kinesio taping and electroacupuncture. Four approaches beat control care clearly, and three of them also outperformed continuous passive motion machines. Effect sizes were moderate rather than dramatic. The authors warn that certainty across most comparisons was low to very low, so the ranking is a guide for practice and future trials, not a final verdict.
pmc-13279241:
Soo-Bin Lee and colleagues report a 2026 large study of bladder trouble in worn spine disease. Wear in the neck and low back spine is a top cause of disability in older adults. Bladder trouble is a known side issue, yet its true rate was unclear. The team used Korean national health claim data from 2009 to 2016.

Each yearly data set sampled three percent of the whole nation, with an average near four hundred fifty five thousand people. Bladder trouble rates were about nine percent in neck disease and about nine percent in low back disease. Rates rose to near fourteen percent when both sites were worn. Risk stayed high after checks for age, sex and other illness, so spine clinics should ask about bladder signs.
pmc-13279441:
Beatrice Foglia and colleagues published a 2026 review of the metabolic tug-of-war between tumors and immune cells, and how that contest might be turned into treatment. Cancer cells rewire their chemistry to grow fast where oxygen and nutrients run short. They grab glucose and glutamine that immune cells also need, and release altered metabolic products that dampen immune attack. The result is a setting where anti-tumor immunity weakens and therapies lose effect.

The review walks through the rewiring on both sides: tumors imposing their metabolic program on nearby immune cells, and immune cells adapting or succumbing. Nearly 20 million cancer cases were recorded in 2022, which is why the stakes extend beyond the laboratory. Treatment ideas include blocking the tumor's metabolic advantages and restoring immune cell fuel at the same time. The authors frame metabolism not as background chemistry but as a lever for future combination treatments.
pmc-13279741:
Giulio Peroni and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of whether temperature alters brain stimulation measures in a warming climate. Transcranial magnetic stimulation probes the cortex by prompting muscle responses or brain signals. Under standard review guidelines, the team found studies that cooled or warmed healthy people, or people with heat- and cold-sensitive conditions. The search covered four databases through late 2025.

Twenty-one studies in healthy people (360 participants) qualified, along with a single study in multiple sclerosis. Most reported no effect of temperature on response size, timing, or inhibition measures. Roughly three quarters of results were null, and where effects appeared they did not agree. The lone multiple sclerosis study stood apart: heat worsened thresholds and responses, unlike in controls. The authors argue lab setups change brain temperature too little to mirror real heat exposure. They call for designs with sustained warming and direct brain readouts.
pmc-13280441:
Sheila O Martins and colleagues published a 2026 review of stroke prevention across the Americas, on why proven measures reach populations. Stroke remains a top cause of death and disability in the region, and the burden hits lower-income countries and underserved communities hardest. The authors survey the gap between what prevention science recommends and what health systems deliver, with attention to rural populations, ethnic minorities, and poorer patients.

Programs modeled on the World Health Organization's HEARTS package show that prevention can be reshaped for local conditions, the review argues. Telehealth and digital tools earn a role for coaching patients, teaching communities, and supporting workers. Obstacles include unequal access, policies that never become practice, and low investment. The authors tie prevention to the United Nations goal of cutting early deaths from these diseases by a third by 2030. They lay out strategies built on healthy lifestyles, risk detection, and system change.
pmc-13280741:
Yi-Chou Hou and colleagues published a 2026 comparison of surgery versus medication for severe secondary hyperparathyroidism in dialysis patients, looking beyond the usual bone and mineral outcomes. Overactive parathyroid glands plague people with end-stage kidney disease, and both removal and calcimimetic drugs control them. Drawing on a research network covering 2010 to 2024, the team matched 11,290 surgical patients with 11,290 drug-treated patients on background health and lab values. They followed outcomes for up to seven years.

Surgery was associated with lower all-cause mortality, with a hazard ratio of 0.914, and with lower risks of mild cognitive impairment and of sepsis. Heart and cardiovascular event rates, fractures, and cognitive impairment did not differ between strategies. The authors suggest gland removal may deliver systemic benefits than drug therapy in selected patients. Because the data are observational, they present the advantage as an association that selection effects could partly explain, not proof of cause.
pmc-13280941:
Medha Shekhar and colleagues studied how sure people feel about choices in a 2026 set of tests. Past work used simple dots and shapes, not real-life scenes. Here, people watched short film clips and typed answers about what they saw. They also rated how sure they felt, from zero to one hundred. The team varied the mood of the clips, the order of scenes, and the number of people shown.

Strong feelings bent accuracy in a curve, first helping and then hurting. Feelings bent sureness in the flip pattern. Crowd size, scene order, and past clips from the same film shifted sureness but not accuracy. A second test with set answer choices found the same pattern, bar one. The authors say sureness and accuracy draw on unlike clues.
pmc-13281241:
Jiawei Li and colleagues taught a computer vision model to read hip X-rays in a 2026 study. After hip replacement surgery, doctors must check how the new joint sits. Hand measures take time and vary by doctor. The team gathered X-rays from five hospitals in Inner Mongolia, China. More than one thousand images trained and checked the model. A fresh set of about one hundred images tested it.

The model placed most key points within three millimeters of expert marks. Its measures matched expert values closely across all checks. It also agreed well with senior X-ray doctors. Speed was the stark gap. The model read an image in about three seconds, while hand work took more than twelve minutes. The authors say the tool could speed follow-up care.
pmc-13281341:
Yanan You and colleagues published a 2026 study comparing how athletes and non-athletes use their hamstring and trunk muscles during two eccentric exercises. Twenty-five men, ten athletes and fifteen active adults, did the inclined Nordic hamstring exercise and a bilateral hip extension while electrodes recorded muscle activity. The analysis covered signal size and frequency, and the balance between the two hamstring muscles, biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus.

Athletes drove the biceps femoris harder during hip extension and leaned toward dominance of that muscle, though the ratio gap between groups was not significant. Non-athletes showed higher frequency values in muscles and used trunk muscles more under some conditions, while relying more on the semitendinosus. The authors stress these are descriptive links, not proof that training rewired the muscles. Still, similar activity levels hid different coordination strategies, which coaches may weigh when prescribing the same exercise to different groups.
pmc-13282041:
Xiaoqiong Yang and co-authors describe a 2026 study on spotting sepsis early, a dangerous body-wide response to infection. Most prediction tools need lab results that arrive late. The team built a model that uses only six vital signs, such as heart rate and temperature, which staff can read at the bedside. Their method learns patterns over short and long time spans and compares patient paths that did or did not lead to sepsis.

The model was tested on more than four hundred intensive care patients, with and without sepsis. It sorted cases well, catching most sepsis cases while using records of uneven length. Its low cost and fast running suit live ward monitoring and clinics with few resources. The authors present the approach as a practical aid for early warning, not as a stand-alone diagnosis. Further checks in real hospital use would still be needed.
pmc-13282441:
Antonio R Fernandez and colleagues published a 2026 national study of Americans' 911 emergency medical services use, built from 9,508,809 ambulance encounters involving 6,604,938 patients in a 2024 data collaborative. Repeat callers expose where the wider health system fails people. A name-matching technique linked each patient's encounters, and use was banded from one encounter up to twelve or more in the year.

Three percent of patients generated 16 percent of all encounters. The heaviest users were disproportionately insured by Medicaid and lived in vulnerable communities, and chronic conditions dominated their call reasons. Although ambulances transported them more often, they were 40 percent less likely to be admitted to hospital than one-time patients, and their median gap between encounters was ten days. The authors read frequent use as a symptom of access failure and unmet social need rather than patient misbehavior. They propose EMS data as an early-warning map for targeting care coordination.
pmc-13282741:
Yuanhao Peng and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, a cell sensor for chemicals from the environment and food, affects cancer. The receptor switches genes on or off once a matching chemical binds it. Early work focused on how it handles pollutants, but its reach now looks much wider.

The review covers the receptor's structure, its gene control routes, and its effects on cell energy use, cell death, and tumour immunity. It also surveys drugs in development that target this receptor. Readers get a map of how one sensor links outside exposures to tumour behaviour, plus a case for testing it as a point of attack in cancer therapy.
pmc-13283141:
Guinea pigs in histamine shock respond to a lab-built enzyme in experiments Felix Kosta and associates ran in 2026. Histamine drives severe allergy attacks, and levels track symptom strength. Adrenaline is first-line care but does not remove histamine and can cause side effects.

Guinea pigs got histamine shots with or without adrenaline or the enzyme. Histamine alone caused shock in all animals and death in many. The enzyme broke down histamine fast when given before or after the shot. At top doses, shock fell to zero and survival improved in the tests. Oxygen levels rose and fast heart rates eased sooner. Adrenaline by muscle shot did not help in this model.
pmc-13284341:
Tatsuya Suzuki and colleagues reported five cases in 2026 of emergency hernia surgery done by keyhole methods alongside bowel removal. A strangulated femoral hernia traps bowel in the groin until its blood supply fails, forcing surgeons to remove dead gut. Whether synthetic mesh is safe in that contaminated setting, through a camera approach, has been debated. The cases were treated at one Japanese hospital between 2015 and 2024.

Surgeons freed the trapped bowel by widening the hernia opening with gentle traction and pressure. They placed mesh from inside the abdomen. They also removed the damaged small bowel through a small outside cut in the same operation. No case converted to open surgery, and no infections followed. The authors call the combined approach feasible, while asking for larger studies.
pmc-13284541:
Maria Ritha Veiga Colognese and colleagues report a 2026 dental trial on gels to ease pain after tooth bleaching. The split-mouth trial enrolled 30 adults, giving each person both gels on different sides: ibuprofen with arginine on one side, and potassium nitrate with fluoride on the other. Pain was scored during bleaching and for seven days after.

Both gels cut sensitivity during and after bleaching, with no clear difference between them in the authors tests. Tooth color gains were also alike, so neither gel blocked bleaching. The ibuprofen gel cost far less while matching results. The authors present it as a safe, cheaper option for dentists managing post-bleaching pain.
pmc-13285041:
Rewaa G. AboElhassan and Alaa M. Eltaweel report a 2026 laboratory study on cleaning root dentin before cementing fiber posts. Leftover smear layers and bleach traces can weaken the bond. Forty-five pulled single-root teeth were split into five groups and treated with chitosan, apple vinegar, two dental lasers, or saline as control.

All treatments beat the control on push-out bond strength in the tests reported here. The erbium laser group scored highest, followed by chitosan. Microscope views showed the best smear removal with that laser and with chitosan, while other groups cleared only in part. Mixed break types ruled in treated groups. The authors say pre-treatment choice shapes bond quality.
pmc-13285441:
Yonggui Li and co-authors find that an enzyme called myeloperoxidase protects the liver and spleen during low oxygen stress, in work from twenty twenty-six. Thin air at altitude inflames tissue and stirs oxidative stress. The enzyme's part in that harm was unclear, and many expected it to worsen damage.

In a three day mouse model of low oxygen, mice lacking the enzyme fared worse, not better. Their liver and spleen tissue showed heavier injury and more immune cell influx. Signals that recruit immune cells and drive inflammation ran higher. Key stress pathways in the spleen also rose. The authors read the enzyme as a brake that keeps immune response in balance.
pmc-13285741:
Bilge Eraydin and colleagues compare eye surgery outcomes in a 2026 retrospective study of open-angle glaucoma. Some patients had a drainage operation alone, while others had the same operation combined with cataract removal. The team asked whether adding cataract surgery changes how the choroid, the vessel layer under the retina, responds.

Scans taken before surgery and one month after covered 55 eyes that had failed full drug treatment. Pressure inside the eye fell sharply in both groups after surgery. Beyond that, the choroid behaved in unlike ways, with broader growth in thickness and vessel area after the combined operation. The authors link the extra change to pressure drop plus swelling from cataract work, and they call for longer follow-up.
pmc-13286141:
Abel Sefasi and colleagues test cheap ways to multiply banana planting stock in Malawi in a 2026 field study. Disease passed through shared suckers has wiped out much of the country's banana crop, and lab-grown plants cost more than small farmers can pay. Macro-propagation, where cut corms sprout new shoots under cover, offers a low-cost path if the setup is tuned right.

Trials crossed three cover types with three bedding materials for the Williams variety. The standard covered chamber grew the tallest plants and the most suckers of any setup. Sawdust and plain loam soil led the bedding race, while rice husks grew the longest roots instead. Pairing the chamber with sawdust topped every other mix by a wide margin. Cutting the head off a first sucker also strongly boosted the next flush of shoots, a free trick farmers can use.
pmc-13286841:
Xu Li and co-authors compare China's coronary heart disease research output with its clinical drug trial activity, asking whether investment matches treatment priorities. The 2026 analysis screened thousands of publications and over a thousand registered drug trials, classifying drugs and traditional Chinese medicine ingredients with standard systems.

Publications grew steeply over two decades. Yet more than three quarters of trials merely proved that generic copies match originals, and chemical drugs dominated over traditional medicine entries. Genetic research clustered on inflammation markers while lipid targets, central to standard therapy, were neglected. High-prestige journals carried a minority of the work. The authors call the landscape policy-driven and urge rebalancing toward novel drugs and lipid genetics.
pmc-13287041:
Ming-Rong Xie, Yan-Jun Chen, and Hui Yuan map past work on sphingolipids in Alzheimer's disease. The 2026 study counts 623 papers from two large databases. Sphingolipids are fatty parts of cell walls. Their balance has been tied to the brain harm seen in this disease, so the shape of the field guides new work.

The United States and China led in paper counts. One United States school, Johns Hopkins, topped the list of sites. A journal named for the disease ran the most papers. Two lipid types, ceramides and sphingomyelins, drew the most study. Fresh hot terms point to lipid-wide scans, cell maps of fats, and the brain's guard cells as fields to watch.
pmc-13287141:
Xueliang Chen and colleagues build a deep learning system that flags advanced kidney dysfunction linked to uremia from routine admission blood tests in intensive care patients. The 2026 study uses a large critical care database, taking laboratory values from the first day and counting only each patient's first eligible stay to prevent leakage between training and testing.

The network groups laboratory variables by clinical domain and records which tests are missing, a pattern that itself carries information. On a held-out patient set it discriminated better than standard machine learning and a rule based on filtration rate alone. Taking the model apart showed that the clinical grouping, more than a fancier interaction module, drove performance. The authors frame it as decision support, not a diagnostic replacement.
pmc-13287241: Drug Design, Development and Therapy retracted a 2015 study of alisertib in human pancreatic cancer cells in 2026, after concerns were raised in 2025 about three figures. Checks found blot images matching data in a companion article yet presented as different proteins or conditions, with added problems in other blots. When asked, the authors reviewed their data, confirmed basic errors, and agreed to withdrawal. The short notice adds no new results; it states that the article stays online with a retracted marking to keep the record clear.
pmc-13287441:
Zhengui Zhou and co-authors used a physics-guided learning model in 2026 to design smart window layers based on vanadium dioxide that darken with heat and can shield privacy in a chosen direction. Layer thickness and particle size were tuned together rather than by trial and error.

The finished window kept visible light passage very low while still shifting infrared transmission and heat emission strongly. Values beat commercial products and earlier best reports in the authors' tests. Trials on vehicle and building glazing showed better heat control. The authors present the design loop as a template for windows built for a specific job rather than general use.
pmc-13287541:
Hideki Nakajima and colleagues reported in 2026 a woman aged 81 who had used a dialysis access vessel in her left arm for fifteen years. Backflow of blood into head veins was found by chance seven years earlier, when she had no symptoms.

Over six months her thinking scores fell sharply, from 26 to 16 on a standard test. Scans showed backflow now reaching surface brain veins, fed by a narrowed large vein in the chest. Balloon widening barely helped. Tying off the dialysis vessel in stages cleared the backflow, and her score rose to 22. The authors warn that vein backflow in dialysis patients can progress quietly into memory loss.
pmc-13287841:
Hye Ah Joo and a large team surveyed 51 Korean patients with facial nerve palsy in mid-2025, reported in 2026, about what they want from care and what they fear most. A 21-question survey at a referral clinic covered testing, drug choices, surgery, team care, and how doctors communicate.

Patients favoured objective tests and honest forecasts of recovery. Most backed active steroid treatment, and three quarters liked adding antiviral drugs. Surgery was a last resort for most, even when palsy lasted past six months. Fear of lasting facial marks dominated worries, at 64.7% of patients. Team-based care and plain, detailed talk were strongly prized.
pmc-13288041:
Sydney M McSweeney and colleagues report in 2026 a rare body variant. It was found during routine teaching dissection of a donated body. Saliva glands of the under-jaw type sat on both sides of the neck. Their usual spot is under the jaw bone. Such misplaced glands are uncommon, and paired cases are rarer still.

The glands sat near the carotid triangle at tongue-bone level. They drew blood and nerve supply like normal glands and each had a duct aimed toward the mouth, suggesting they worked. Microscope checks showed normal gland tissue with no tumour. The authors present the find as a teaching case for future clinicians.
pmc-13288141:
Luana Zagami and co-authors swapped the centre atom of a four-armed molecule in 2026. They put the heavy metal osmium where carbon or silicon usually sits. Their aim was to see whether electricity flows better through single-molecule wires. A scanning probe repeatedly formed and broke tiny junctions to measure current.

In plain solvents the osmium wires lost far less current as length grew than their carbon cousins. In charged solvents their flow could be dialled up to eighty times that of the silicon version. Spectra and first-principles maths point to spread-out electron clouds and a smaller energy gap. The authors propose metal-centred arms for future molecular circuits.
pmc-13288441:
Emilie Vansant and co-authors argue in 2026, working with practitioners in Malawi, that tree restoration projects across Africa should plant native food trees rather than defaulting to fast-growing foreign species. Native fruits, leaves, nuts, and seeds are rich in micronutrients that local diets often lack.

Three weak points block wider use: nurseries struggle to raise the species, young trees die at high rates, and markets for tree foods stay thin. The authors call for training and support on those three fronts. Done well, they say, restoration could fight biodiversity loss and malnutrition together instead of treating them as rival goals.
pmc-13288541:
Jianhui Wei and co-authors examine gene and environment together in a 2026 hospital-based case-control study of congenital heart disease in China. They compared 585 affected infants with 600 controls, testing variants in three heart transcription factor genes, NKX2.5, GATA4, and TBX5, alongside mothers' exposures around conception.

Some variants in each gene raised risk while others lowered it, and combinations among the loci shifted risk further. Maternal diabetes before or during pregnancy, a troubled pregnancy history, certain medicines, and lifestyle factors also tracked with higher risk. A few gene and exposure pairings looked suggestive, though some lost significance after correction for many tests. The authors call for larger studies to confirm the patterns and explain how they act.
pmc-13288941:
Matthew Henry Iveson leads a 2026 study of hidden brain vessel disease. Software read scan reports for all of Scotland. The cohort held 367,988 people with brain scans. None had past stays for brain disease. The team tracked stroke and memory loss later.

Each hidden sign raised later stroke risk. Pale white matter patches raised it least by type. Small deep strokes and surface strokes raised it more. Shrinkage of the brain tracked most with dementia. Links to two control diseases sat near zero. That pattern supports a real effect. The authors urge prevention for these patients.
pmc-13289141:
Suhana Jawahir and colleagues study hospital stays by wealth in Malaysia in 2026. Their study uses the Malaysia Ageing and Retirement Survey. It holds 5,612 adults aged 40 and up. A model tested wealth, aids, and health needs. The aim was to see what drives admissions.

Wealth did not predict hospital stays. Richer adults had less body impairment. They also had sharper thinking scores. More schooling also lifted thinking scores. Worse body function raised admissions a lot. More chronic diseases also raised them. Sharper thinking cut admissions instead. Outlook on life linked wealth to stays. The authors back disease prevention first.
pmc-13289241:
Julia Schulten-Baumer led a 2026 multicenter review of timing for EKOS treatment in risky pulmonary embolism. Pulmonary embolism is a clot blocking lung arteries, and the intermediate-high risk form strains the right side of the heart. EKOS uses ultrasound plus a catheter to deliver clot-dissolving drug right at the clot.

Records covered 152 patients at three major centers, split into care within 12 hours of scan proof and care after 12 hours. The early group held 106 people and the delayed group held 46 people in total. Heart scans improved in both groups, with drops in right-to-left chamber ratio and lung artery pressure. Early care showed somewhat larger gains numerically. The comparison helps teams weigh speed against safety, bleeding, and intensive care stay.
pmc-13289341:
Lei Xu, Zezhong Zhang, and Ce Shang offer a 2026 demand study on cigarettes and e-cigarettes among United States adults who vape. How users shift spending when prices change guides tax design and harm reduction debates. The authors used a demand system model that estimates price and spending responses for both products at once.

The sample held 771 adults who use e-cigarettes, including dual users who also smoke and exclusive vapers. Monthly spending shares and unit prices fed the model, with state taxes used to handle price bias. Higher total tobacco spending lifted cigarette use far more than vaping in the estimates. Each product fell when its own price rose, while cross effects stayed small and unclear, suggesting taxes act mainly product by product.
pmc-13289541: Paolo Guidetti and coauthors are named on a brief 2026 correction notice fixing author name order for an earlier article on balanced scientific publishing and planetary health. Given and family names had been swapped in the byline panel. The notice lists the wrong and right orders in full and states the original article was updated. No new data or argument appears, so the record is thin by nature.
pmc-13289641:
Xueqin Lin and colleagues share a 2026 case report and review on tocilizumab for stubborn autoimmune brain inflammation called GFAP astrocytopathy. Most patients respond to first-line immune therapy, but some resist and fare poorly. A 17-year-old girl with fever, headache, coma, speech and mood changes, and weakness anchors the report with detailed brain imaging.

Antibody tests were positive in blood and spinal fluid, and scans showed swelling in deep brain areas and the hippocampus. Steroids, immune globulin, and rituximab gave little or fleeting help for her. After five infusions of tocilizumab, speech, movement, and mood improved a lot and remission held with no severe side effects. One prior similar case also improved after five cycles.
pmc-13289741:
Weili Liu and colleagues present a 2026 case report comparing predicted versus real outflow space after double valve-in-valve replacement in one session. Blocking the left ventricular outflow tract is a feared problem in catheter mitral work. A 74-year-old woman with worn-out surgical mitral and aortic valves had class IV heart failure, the most severe grade, at presentation.

Full-cycle gated scans predicted the tightest outflow area at a set heart phase, guiding the order: aortic valve first, then mitral, to avoid crushing the new mitral valve during aortic expansion. Post-procedure scans using the same workflow showed a slightly smaller area, lower by 20.3 mm2 as measured, with uneven protrusion. Flow stayed normal with no blockage.
pmc-13289841:
Lauren Ramsay and colleagues report a 2026 survey of what tuberculosis care costs patients in Toronto, Canada. Ontario sees more than six hundred TB cases a year, and care itself is publicly funded. Still, patients may pay in travel, lost work, and other ways that add up.

The team surveyed adults in treatment at two Toronto TB centers between April 2023 and April 2025. Forty-two people took part, using a survey adapted from the World Health Organization. A TB visit cost patients about forty-three Canadian dollars on average, though amounts varied widely. The survey also tracked missed work and strain on household budgets. The findings show that free care does not mean cost-free illness, a point that matters for support programs.
pmc-13290241:
Wrist fractures in children heal poorly more often than expected when certain risk factors stack up, a 2026 national database study by Katie Zehner and colleagues shows. The team examined scaphoid fractures, which are prone to nonunion, in patients under 18.

Drawing on the PearlDiver database for 2015 to 2023, they identified 26,364 pediatric scaphoid fractures, mostly in boys; the children averaged 13.54 years of age. Nonunion occurred in 1,102 patients, or 4.2% of cases, and was tied to older age, male sex, excess weight, displacement, and fractures nearer the proximal end. Most nonunions were spotted within three months, which the authors read as a sign that many children arrived late to care. About seven in ten nonunion patients went on to surgery.
pmc-13290341:
Abdullahi Isah and four colleagues published a 2026 study of phytase, an enzyme added to chicken feed, in broiler chickens. Phytase helps birds use phosphorus from plants and reduces the harmful effects of phytic acid in grain. The enzyme used here was produced locally by microbes.

The researchers varied the dose and measured effects across the whole bird. They checked the microbes living in the caecum, growth-related genes in the liver, carcass traits, and immune responses. Two liver signals mattered in particular: insulin-like growth factor 1 and the growth hormone receptor, both tied to growth. A full picture of dose effects helps farmers use the enzyme well and supports local production of feed additives.
pmc-13290441:
Going without reliable food raises the risk of depression in later life, and a small part of that link runs through faster biological aging, Junhua Zhu and colleagues reported in 2026. Their longitudinal study uses the US Health and Retirement Study.

Among 5,547 middle-aged and older adults, 1,320 developed depression over 7.9 years of follow-up. Compared with the food-secure, those with low food security faced clearly higher risk, and those with very low security higher still. The authors estimate about 9% of new cases were attributable to food insecurity. In a subsample with DNA methylation data, one epigenetic clock's age acceleration explained 5.3% of the association, a modest share. The results put food access on the list of upstream targets for preventing late-life depression.
pmc-13290841:
A laser fingerprint can flag tomato virus infection in the field, YongDe Xu and colleagues demonstrate in a proof-of-concept study from 2026. Tomato brown rugose fruit virus devastates crops, but the standard PCR test needs a lab, equipment, and trained staff, too slow for on-site screening.

Leaf extracts confirmed by PCR were placed on silver nanorod arrays and read by surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, whose spectra carry chemical traces of infection. Three machine learning classifiers were compared; a support vector machine won, scoring 91.67% accuracy with perfect sensitivity and an AUC of 0.993 in this dataset. The catch: plants were one cultivar, infected by hand, in a greenhouse. Xu and colleagues position the method as a fast, cheap first screen, never a PCR replacement, with field validation still to come.
pmc-13290941:
A pressure-relieving dressing on the sole slashes severe hand-foot skin reactions from cancer drugs, Asako Ryu and colleagues show in a phase 3 trial from 2026. The reaction is a dose-limiting toxicity of multikinase inhibitors, and this self-controlled study tested hydrocolloid dressing plus moisturizer against moisturizer alone in 50 patients on regorafenib or sorafenib.

Each patient's feet served as their own control. Grade 2 or worse reactions on the soles hit 20% with the dressing against 50% without, and time to that grade stretched significantly longer. Patient-reported moderate-or-worse symptoms also ran lower, 10% versus 32%. Ryu and colleagues conclude the cheap dressing prevents a side effect that otherwise forces dose cuts, and back it as standard prophylaxis for these drugs.
pmc-13291141:
Sleep trouble among Chinese oil workers in Iraq is studied by Ziming Liu and colleagues in a 2026 survey. These expatriate staff face long hours, harsh surroundings, and stress far from home. Yet little was known about how their sleep holds up in the Maysan oilfields.

The survey covered 917 staff, and 826 gave usable answers. Two tools measured sleep quality and sleep concern. Poor sleep grew more likely as mood symptoms rose. Job stress and burnout also tracked with worse sleep. More schooling linked to poorer sleep as well. Network analysis showed which factors sat closest to sleep trouble. The authors urge firms to watch mental health, not just work rosters.
pmc-13291541:
A checkpoint guards ribosome building inside the cell nucleus. Benjamin Lau leads a 2026 study of the small ribosome unit’s decoding center. That center reads genetic code with high accuracy. Its assembly starts in the nucleus and ends outside it.

A helper protein, Rrp12, coordinates the early steps. Fifteen mid-step forms were imaged with cryo-electron methods. Cutting Rrp12’s tail blocked partner release. It also shifted another helper out of place. One RNA helix settled too early as a result. Final RNA trimming failed under these defects. A quality kinase also woke too soon. Orderly checks thus protect accurate protein making.
pmc-13291641:
Paillart and colleagues tested in 2026 whether using living-brain electrical values improves radiofrequency safety modeling for MRI scans. Safety software predicts how much radio energy tissue absorbs, but it relies on conductivity values measured in dead tissue. Sixteen volunteers were scanned to map the transmit field in the head. The team compared those maps with simulations run at the standard dead-tissue value and at a higher living-tissue value drawn from recent studies.

Simulation matched measurement to about six percent error on field strength. Head shape drove strength errors, while conductivity drove phase errors, which fell by nearly half with the living-tissue value. Agreement on average absorbed energy in the brain also improved sharply, with the gap shrinking from about 62 percent to about 22 percent. The authors say in vivo conductivity values should replace database defaults in safety work.
pmc-13291741:
Xiaoge Ma and co-authors present a 2026 umbrella review of exercise treatments for sarcopenic obesity in middle-aged and older adults. That condition pairs excess body fat with low muscle mass and strength. The reviewers gathered systematic reviews built on pairwise or network meta-analysis, searching six databases through March 2026.

Eight reviews met their strict exercise-focused criteria, covering 33 unique primary studies with heavy overlap between reviews. Fat-related outcomes improved in every review, and grip strength and walking measures generally improved, while muscle-mass results were mixed. Method quality was low in most reviews, so the authors rate the overall certainty as low or very low. Resistance training gave the most consistent strength signal in their synthesis.
pmc-13291941:
Peng Wang and co-authors compare a 2026 biomechanics study of free-throw shooting between trained basketball players and beginners. Fifty right-handed adults aged 18 to 24, half athletes and half novices, each took 20 standardized free throws. Side-view video fed into Dartfish software yielded joint angles, trunk lean, hand speed, and ball release height, angle, and velocity.

Made shots in both groups shared a pattern: fuller elbow extension and a higher release point than missed shots. Those two measures also tied most strongly to success, with correlations at or above 0.63 in the data. Shoulder and wrist action helped moderately, while legs and trunk mainly supplied balance and energy. The authors advise coaches to drill release mechanics first, at every skill level.
pmc-13292441:
Yüksel Hakan Aydoğmuş and co-authors offer a 2026 viewpoint on how Türkiye pushed breastfeeding support out of hospitals and into whole provinces. Baby-Friendly hospital programs start breastfeeding well, but gains fade without community backing. Türkiye layered on family medicine and neonatal intensive care versions, then Baby-Friendly and Golden Baby-Friendly Province programs spanning pregnancy through infancy.

Activities sort into six themes, from one-to-one help for vulnerable mothers to sports-based outreach and public visual messaging. National and world breastfeeding weeks act as yearly campaign surges inside the year-round system. The authors describe provinces shifting from facility teaching toward community ownership and multisector teamwork. They present the model as transferable experience for other countries trying to sustain breastfeeding beyond discharge day.
pmc-13292541:
Franck Yvan Deugoue Djientcheu and co-authors record a 2026 comparison of heart rate variability in Cameroonian handball players, asking what training and gender each do to cardiac autonomic control. Sedentary men, male players, and female players each rested through ten-minute heart recordings. Standard variability measures such as SDNN, RMSSD, and pNN50 were computed alongside frequency-domain powers.

Male players unexpectedly showed higher resting heart rates than the women, 68.75 against 60.38 beats in the reported averages. Sedentary men scored far below male players on every time-domain measure, tying practice to richer variability. Between the sexes, very-low-frequency power ran higher in men, while low- and high-frequency components ran higher in women. Effect sizes for gender were small, and the authors decline a firm verdict on how gender steers the sympathetic-parasympathetic balance.
pmc-13292641:
Pavel Morozov and a large team shine a 2026 exotic light on lipofuscin, the pigment granules whose glow doctors use to judge retinal aging and macular degeneration risk. Standard glow readings have limited bite in the clinic, so the team built a lifetime imaging scope around a nanowire photon detector sensitive far beyond normal sensors. Pigment clumps from 100 human donor eyes, aged 50 to 75, were imaged before and after lab photo-oxidation.

The setup resolved decay components and spectra at each spot across 500 to 1,000 nanometers. Oxidation shifted the emission toward blue, mimicking disease-like change. Fitting a three-exponential model showed the mean fluorescence lifetime rose significantly after oxidation. The authors argue these lifetime signatures read out the pigment's oxidative state directly, opening a route to earlier, sharper diagnosis of retinal disease.
pmc-13292841:
Koki Kawada and colleagues examine pain after knee surgery in a 2026 study of torn meniscus roots. The operation studied pulls the torn medial meniscus root back into place, and the team asked which pre-surgery traits predict lasting pain.

Records covered 508 knees, mostly in women, with an average age the authors report near the mid-sixties. Pain scores were taken before surgery and at final follow-up, plus X-ray and scan measures. Greater outward shift of the meniscus before surgery linked to worse pain later, even after other factors were counted. No patient in follow-up needed bone realignment or joint replacement surgery.
pmc-13292941:
Linnea Ögren and colleagues present, in 2026, a light-based method to map where proteins sit on DNA inside living yeast cells. Finding those bound sites in untouched cells is hard, since most tools favor open DNA regions or need cell breakage.

Ultraviolet light marks bound spots by forming small DNA lesions, which later read as changes during sequencing, a method the team calls Deam-seq. Comparing treated cells with naked DNA gave sharp maps that matched known control sites and older footprint tests. Bound proteins mostly shielded DNA from light harm. The work offers a genome-wide way to study gene control in its natural setting.
pmc-13293441:
Yousif M. Elmosaad leads a 2026 survey in Al Ahsa, Saudi Arabia, on how stigma around mental illness affects whether people seek help. Most people with mental illness get no treatment, and shame is a major reason care is delayed or avoided.

A total of 1085 adults aged 18 and older answered a structured questionnaire on stigma and help-seeking. Stigma was present in 23.1% of respondents, a share the authors report, and 61.0% said stigma might stop them seeking help. People with stigma were clearly more likely to avoid help. Adults aged 30 to 41 were more willing to seek help than other age groups.
pmc-13293641:
Tomohiro Baba reports a 2026 surgical case of suspected Kounis syndrome, an allergic heart event, during lung surgery after a platelet transfusion. A 70-year-old man with low platelets from liver disease had keyhole surgery to remove his right lower lung lobe.

Three minutes after the platelet transfusion ended, his heart raced, blood pressure fell, and his face and arms flushed. Standard pressure drugs failed, so allergy drugs and adrenaline were given for suspected anaphylaxis. Heart tracings showed strain signs from the start of the collapse, yet heart damage markers stayed normal. He stabilized on adrenaline, surgery finished, and tracing changes cleared by the next day.
pmc-13293941:
Giulia Sapuppo and colleagues study survival by disease site in a 2026 retrospective series of radioiodine-refractory thyroid cancer. Such advanced cancers resist standard iodine treatment and often need kinase inhibitor drugs. The team reviewed 43 treated patients and split them by whether spread at drug start was mainly in neck structures or mainly distant.

Median age at diagnosis was 63.3 years, and just over half were women. Papillary tumors were most common. Counter to simple expectation, patients whose disease centered in the neck fared worse on disease-specific survival than those with distant spread. Site alone may therefore help forecast outcome and guide intensity of care.
pmc-13294141:
Songlin Sun and coauthors propose a 2026 scheme of spatial immune types for stomach and colon cancers. Checkpoint drugs change care mainly for the small MSI-H group. Most MSS tumors resist from the start. Cell counts miss the layout, so the authors sort tumors by how cell groups are placed.

Four types are named. One is a stromal wall that shuts immune cells out. One is a myeloid zone that calms attack by fuel use. One is an inflamed zone with mature lymph hubs. One is a thin watch zone at the tumor edge, lost as tumors evolve. Gut germs differ by organ and tilt the mix.
pmc-13294241: Pablo Lastra-Prados and coauthors issued a 2026 correction notice for their study of decay in teeth next to implant-supported prostheses. Only author details were wrong: one coauthor name had been printed with a doubled segment, and the university affiliation for four authors named the wrong institution. The notice gives the corrected name and affiliation and offers an apology. No data, methods, or findings change, and the authors state that the scientific conclusions stand. The original article has been updated to match.
pmc-13294341:
Alon Korngreen argues for reference-grade neuron models in a 2026 perspective. Detailed computer neurons now guide brain research, yet squeezing varied biology and measurement error into one parameter set hides which claims data truly support. Korngreen borrows habits from analytical chemistry: traceable standards, explicit uncertainty budgets, and ensemble forecasts instead of single answers.

Big reconstructions from projects like Blue Brain and Allen Institute efforts show both promise and risk, since scale alone can look like proof. Voltage recordings reduced to one best fit lose the spread that honest models should carry forward. A reference culture would label modeling choices plainly and keep circuit claims tied to evidence.
pmc-13294441:
Taner Dandinoğlu writes a 2026 letter about missed bone harm in a tough prolactinoma case report by Konindala and coauthors. The original case showed a large prolactin tumor resisting hormone drugs and repeated local plus body-wide treatments, ending with full pituitary failure on replacement therapy. Bone checks were never mentioned, and the letter argues that gap matters, above all in men.

High prolactin, low sex hormones, and long pituitary disruption all thin bone quietly. Older men start with weaker skeletons, so fractures of spine or hip can steal independence. Density scans and fracture history should join routine care for such patients, the letter urges.
pmc-13295041:
Mohammad Aadil and colleagues use dissolved salts to pull a stubborn green solvent out of freshly cast membranes, in a 2026 study. Membranes for water treatment are usually formed by plunging a polymer solution into water, a process called phase separation. A promising eco-friendly solvent, Polarclean, boils so high that it lingers inside the membrane and warps its pores. The team replaced heat with ions, adding chloride salts to the bath so the solvent leaves on its own.

Salt choice shifted the chemistry and timing of separation. Some salts pushed the mixture to split at lower water levels, but splitting too fast formed a dense skin that trapped solvent, a flaw fixed by adding water-loving polymers. The best recipe removed nearly all solvent and yielded a membrane passing water fast with a fine cutoff. The authors call it an energy-lean platform for greener membrane making.
pmc-13295141:
Vlad Alexandru Ionescu and colleagues untangle confusion in an older man in a 2026 case report. The 67-year-old, a long-term heavy drinker, arrived after a week of confused thinking. Many rival explanations were possible, from liver failure to stroke, kidney damage, or alcohol effects.

Blood tests showed severe excess calcium, kidney injury, mild anaemia, and raised protein, while ammonia stayed normal and brain scans found no stroke. Protein studies revealed a single abnormal antibody type pointing to multiple myeloma, a bone marrow cancer. Fluids plus steroid treatment cleared his thinking quickly, confirming high calcium as the driver and showing how a hidden cancer can first appear as confusion.
pmc-13295841:
Bilal Ahmad and colleagues build an electrochemical sensor that spots C-reactive protein, a blood mark of inflammation and infection, in a 2026 study. The sensor starts with a screen-printed carbon electrode dressed with gold nanoparticles and chitosan. Antibodies to the protein are fixed to the surface with a dual crosslinking step, so the target sticks where it can be read.

Binding of the protein raised the block to charge flow across the surface, and that rise gave the reading. Tuning set the best buffer and acidity for a clean signal. Spiked samples gave back nearly all the protein added, with tight spread, and the surface could be renewed for repeat use. The authors present the sensor as a keen, selective tool for early checks on inflammation.
pmc-13295941:
Francesco Ferrara and colleagues trace, in 2026, the rise and fall of antibody treatments for COVID-19. Early products given outside hospital cut admissions during earlier waves, while other antibodies calmed severe inflammation in admitted patients.

Once the Omicron variant spread, many spike-targeting antibodies lost their grip as the virus changed, and their use was curtailed. Newer versions aimed at steadier targets also struggled against continued drift, though host-directed antibodies kept working since they ignore the spike. The authors favour broadly acting antibodies, smarter delivery and live virus tracking for future outbreaks.
pmc-13296041:
Richard M Jacques and a large consortium analyse, in 2026, emergency care demand across 21 English hospitals using routine NHS data. Same-day ambulatory care can treat many urgent conditions without admission, but its share of the workload had not been mapped.

Over one year, such conditions made up nearly a third of emergency attendances and two-fifths of emergency admissions, with wide gaps between hospitals. Older patients were more likely to present with these conditions, while deprived areas showed lower rates. Half of these admissions lasted under two days. The authors say much demand could shift to same-day or community care.
pmc-13296141:
Kadriye Guney and colleagues compare hearing and well-being in long-term cochlear implant users with peers who hear typically, in a 2026 study. Thirty users and thirty peers took speech tests in quiet and in noise and filled scales for learned helplessness, depression, and anxiety, plus a rating of implant sound quality. The implant group had used their devices over the long term with rehabilitation.

Implant users scored plainly worse on speech perception, in quiet and in noise alike. Yet their helplessness, depression, and anxiety scores matched their peers. In the subgroup deaf from early life, age at implant tied to hearing thresholds and to speech scores. The authors read the pattern as real listening gains from long-term use, with mental health holding in the normal range despite daily listening strain.
pmc-13296241:
Qian Li and colleagues study, in 2026, whether blood mineral balance predicts dangerous clots after childbirth in a Chinese cohort of 25,792 women. They follow clot events in the six weeks after delivery and relate them to calcium, potassium and magnesium measured around birth.

A low calcium-to-potassium ratio stood out as an independent risk marker, with risk climbing below a clear threshold. Part of the link ran through lower haemoglobin and higher clot-breakdown markers. Magnesium showed a curved pattern, safest in the middle. The authors suggest watching mineral balance and anaemia could help cut clot burden after birth.
pmc-13296541:
Simone Carvalho dos Santos Cunha and co-authors review, in 2026, forty dogs treated with radiation for malignant nose tumours at a Brazilian clinic. Surgery is rarely possible for these cancers, which cause bleeding, discharge and facial swelling, so radiation is the main option.

Most dogs arrived with advanced disease. Tumours shrank or held steady in most cases and symptoms eased for most dogs, while side effects hit skin, mouth lining and eyes but stayed manageable. Dogs with later-stage tumours lived shorter lives. The authors say radiation brings real benefit and back earlier diagnosis.
pmc-13296941:
Sanjana C. Basak and Delphine Gomez review how methylation steers blood-vessel muscle cells between healthy and harmful states in a 2026 article. These cells can drop their contractile programme and start multiplying and migrating, a switch central to atherosclerosis. Methylation marks on DNA, histones, and RNA all help set which genes stay active.

The same chemical mark can switch genes on in one context and off in another, the review stresses. Inflammation, metabolism, and low oxygen reshape the enzymes that write and erase the marks. Several named enzymes also act through unusual routes beyond their classic targets. Understanding this layered control may expose drug targets for vessel disease.
pmc-13297241:
Joran Tanghe, Rüveyda Dok, and Sandra Nuyts review personalised treatment for head and neck cancers using functional imaging and artificial intelligence in a 2026 article. Tumours differ widely between patients, and standard chemoradiation is both toxic and often unsuccessful. Imaging that reveals tumour biology could sort patients before treatment begins.

Resistance grows from low oxygen, stem-like cells, altered metabolism, and strong DNA repair, the review explains. Artificial intelligence can mine scan patterns linked to those processes. Most tools, though, stall before reaching the clinic. The authors insist that models be built around tumour biology and judged on outcomes that matter to care, not on technical scores alone.
pmc-13297341:
Rosanna Squitti and co-authors study, in 2026, copper-zinc imbalance in bowel cancer, focusing on the loose, active fraction of copper rather than the total. Blood metals, sex hormones and tumour proteins were measured in 152 patients and 140 healthy controls, split by sex.

Patients carried more copper, less zinc and a sharply higher active-copper ratio. That ratio tracked with tumour size and stage, more with size in women and spread in men, and with tissue shifts marking cells loosening their epithelial character. The authors propose the ratio as an informative marker needing validation.
pmc-13297441:
Yi-Lin Chiu and colleagues pool animal studies on whether resveratrol, a plant compound in grapes, lowers a key inflammation signal, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. That signal, MCP-1, draws immune cells into tissue and drives inflammatory change. Twenty-seven studies with twenty-nine usable datasets met the rules.

Treated animals showed clearly lower MCP-1-linked readings than controls overall. The drop rested mainly on rat and mouse data, though, while a piglet dataset pointed the other way and rabbit data came from one study alone. Studies varied a great deal, and dose did not explain the spread. With only one database searched and known limits on how the body absorbs the compound, the authors bar direct clinical claims.
pmc-13297641:
Smail Bougouffa and Kamal Berrada model how a delicate quantum link among three photons fades and revives under noise with memory, in a 2026 theory study. The link, called steering, lets one photon's measurement sway the state of the others.
