Tongji Xie and co-authors built risk models that predict where lung adenocarcinoma will spread, using detailed maps of gene activity inside the primary tumor. Their 2026 study draws on 52 patients and combines spatial profiling, stained tissue images, and clinical records.

A random forest model read the tumor's spatial gene patterns and predicted spread to brain, liver, adrenal gland, and bone with high accuracy scores, all above 0.90. Distinct gene signatures marked each destination, some from tumor cells and others from immune cells nearby. Knowing the likely target organ in advance could guide scans and early treatment for a cancer whose spread is its main killer.
pmc-13396441:
János Rokai and co-authors put a portable brain-wave headset with semi-dry electrodes through three standard tests to judge whether it can serve brain-computer interface work. Their 2026 validation answers a practical worry: light, paste-free headsets are convenient, but their signals are often weaker than those of lab systems.

The MindRove headset was run beside a wet-electrode reference system while volunteers did tasks that produce a visual response, a P300 attention signal, and motor cortex patterns from movement. Signal-to-noise measures and task performance were compared across the two devices. The study tells labs which interface uses the portable headset can support, and where it falls short.
pmc-13396641:
TianTian Zhang and co-authors recount a 72-year-old woman whose low-blood-sugar episode looked exactly like a stroke, and review similar cases in a 2026 report. She had poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and had just started a stronger glucose-lowering regimen when she grew sleepy, tired, and slurred her speech.

Oddly, her blood sugar read 4.1 millimoles per liter, above the usual low threshold, and her symptoms lingered even after glucose was given. Because a real stroke could not be ruled out, doctors gave the clot-busting drug alteplase. She recovered about nine and a half hours after onset. The authors warn that sugar mimics can sit above textbook cutoffs.
pmc-13398141:
Jonas Aufdermauer and colleagues dissect how cancer-linked changes in the BCL-2 protein defeat the drug venetoclax. Their 2026 study compares frequent mutations inside and outside the drug's binding pocket. BCL-2 keeps cancer cells alive by shelving their self-destruct machinery, and venetoclax frees it, until resistant mutations appear during treatment.

Two known mutations, G101V and D103Y, do double duty: they block the drug and grip the cell's death proteins even harder. Four more mutations (V156D, A113G, R129L and R139H) are newly shown to confer resistance, through tricks such as weaker drug binding. Mapping each route matters because second-line drugs must answer the exact trick a tumour has learned.
pmc-13399341:
Emily J. Brown and co-authors ran two experiments during the 2024 United States presidential election on how drawing attention to Kamala Harris's race and gender changed voters' judgments of her, reporting in 2026. Harris, the Democratic nominee, became the first Black and South Asian woman to lead a major party ticket. Her campaign rarely foregrounded those identities, and the researchers tested whether media-style emphasis helped or hurt.

In the first study, a stratified national sample read a paragraph listing only Harris's qualifications, or the same text with her gender, her race, or both added. In the second study, the researchers separated her backgrounds. Highlighting her Black identity, not her South Asian identity nor the combination, drove the drop in evaluations across the political spectrum. The authors conclude that even subtle identity cues can shift how a candidate is judged.
pmc-13399841:
Liu and co-authors describe, in 2026, a modified single-bundle ACL reconstruction that uses only the semitendinosus tendon, sparing the gracilis that standard hamstring harvests sacrifice. The native anterior cruciate ligament is roughly 30 millimeters long and 10 millimeters wide, and its loss destabilizes the knee and invites osteoarthritis. Their quadrupled semitendinosus graft is fixed on the tibia with two knotless anchors and on the femur with suspensory fixation.

Folded four times, the single tendon reaches a graft diameter usually between 7 and 9 millimeters, adequate for reconstruction without taking the second tendon. Preserving the gracilis better maintains the muscle function it serves, including knee flexion support. The femoral tunnel entry is placed through the anteromedial approach, its midpoint 6 millimeters from the posterior edge of the lateral femoral condyle. The authors present the technique, documented on video, as functional reconstruction with minimal disturbance to the knee's original anatomy.
pmc-13400141:
Xiao-Min Lin and colleagues built a brain-and-spinal-cord imaging signature that predicts how much pain a person feels, in a 2026 study. The team trained a combined model, the Corticospinal Pain Intensity Pattern, on 330 simultaneous brain and spinal cord fMRI datasets. They then tested it on independent data.

The pattern out-predicted established brain signatures for pain intensity and generalized to a different pain type, electrical stimulation. It stayed insensitive to itch and to watching someone else in pain, evidence that it tracks felt pain rather than general unpleasantness. It also fell when nerve stimulation relieved pain in volunteers. In chronic pain patients, the same pattern computed from resting activity predicted their baseline pain, and its changes over treatment closely mirrored their relief. The authors present the model as a bridge between experimental and clinical pain measurement.
pmc-13400241:
Xianyang Wang and colleagues rebuilt an immune-stimulating antibody conjugate with engineering precision, tuning both its sugar coat and its payload attachment, in a 2026 study. The team's dual-enzyme strategy edits trastuzumab at two defined sites: one enzyme attaches the payload at a specific residue, while a second enzyme remodels the Fc glycan at another.

Comparison of the resulting defined variants showed that two design choices act as independent levers. An intact Fc glycan lacking fucose proved essential for strong tumor-cell killing. Linkers that can be cleaved inside the cell released the TLR7/8 agonist efficiently and boosted innate immune activation further. The authors present the platform as broad chemistry for next-generation antibody drugs, where architecture is specified rather than averaged.
pmc-13400741:
Shulang Lin and colleagues present, in 2026, a microscopy advance that sharpens chemical imaging of living cells without labels. Stimulated Raman scattering microscopy can map molecules by their vibrations, but fast three-dimensional imaging starves the signal and buries it in noise. Standard denoising lacks clean reference images for living samples.

Their framework, PHYSIQ, exploits the detection physics to record two perfectly aligned image channels at once, carrying the same signal but independent noise. That pairing trains a self-supervised restoration method with no ground truth needed. Signal quality rose by roughly twelve decibels while true chemical contrast held. The gain enables video-rate volumetric imaging and tracking of fat droplets moving inside live cells in three dimensions.
pmc-13401141:
Mao Yifan and co-authors test, in 2026, whether quercetin, a common plant flavonoid, can rescue placental cells struggling under low oxygen, a lab model of preeclampsia. This dangerous pregnancy condition ties to poor placental cell invasion. Quercetin helps in several diseases, but its mechanism here was unclear. Autophagy, the cells self-eating process, was the suspect.

Oxygen-starved trophoblast cells grew and invaded more slowly. They closed wounds more slowly too, died more and showed ramped-up autophagy, with a key growth pathway switched down. Quercetin reversed those changes. It restored growth and movement while calming the self-eating process through reactivating the pathway. Adding a pathway blocker erased quercetins benefits, supporting the proposed mechanism.
pmc-13401341:
Luiz Augusto Sousa Oliveira and co-authors wrote a 2026 review proposing a protocol to assess and replace protein and vitamins around plastic surgery operations. Wound breakdown, wounds splitting open, and surgical-site infection all track in part with a patient's nutritional state.

Enhanced recovery programmes have made nutrition a structural part of care. That is especially true in breast reconstruction with the patient's own tissue and in body contouring after weight-loss surgery. The review gathers evidence on supplementation roughly seven to fourteen days before and after surgery, leaning on American and European studies and on ERAS Society and nutrition society guidelines. Low albumin in the blood stands out as a fairly steady sign of risk for complications after surgery in large registry analyses, though the strength of that link varies.
pmc-13401441:
Avi Magid looks at how the World Health Organization's alcohol risk view should become public health policy. His 2026 viewpoint starts from the WHO's 2023 statement that no safe amount of alcohol for cancer and health can be set. Drinkers, it says, should be told in plain terms about cancer and other risks. Some countries now weigh that advice for rules, with some European nations urging total avoidance.

Magid proposes a common first step for all jurisdictions: formally noting that no safe threshold exists. He notes that risk varies by age and context, with near-zero intake cutting harm most for younger adults. Small amounts may track with lower overall risk for older adults in high heart-disease regions. The work argues for age- and context-specific guidance and an open debate across the policy spectrum, from informed choice to precautionary limits.
pmc-13401541:
Francis Zamora and colleagues published a 2026 cell study of how docosahexaenoic acid, an omega-3 fat known as DHA, protects Schwann cells from damage by palmitic acid, a saturated fat. Schwann cells insulate peripheral nerves, and fat overload in diabetes and obesity is tied to neuropathic pain.

In immortalized Schwann cells, palmitic acid exposure cut cell survival, jammed the cell's recycling system known as autophagy, raised endoplasmic reticulum stress, and left cells more vulnerable to a recycling blocker. The team tracked recycling flow using LC3-II and p62 markers, stress signalling, calcium balance, and the lipid-carrying protein FABP5. Adding DHA alongside the harmful fat modulated those pathways, and the study maps how lipid handling, stress responses, and autophagy connect in this nerve cell injury model.
pmc-13401641:
Jiatong Li and co-authors report a 2026 multicentre retrospective study of salvage radiotherapy. It covers extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer that has begun growing again in only a few places outside the skull after first-line therapy. This pattern, called extracranial oligoprogression, has no standard management.

Patients treated at three Chinese cancer centres between January 2020 and March 2025 were split into those who got radiotherapy after progression and those who did not. Propensity score matching balanced the groups on baseline features. The main results were survival measured from the second-line point, both overall and without progression, estimated with Kaplan-Meier curves. First-line systemic therapy is standard in this cancer. Failure is nearly universal, so whether aiming radiation at the few progressing sites extends life is a pressing question.
pmc-13402041:
Lizanne Berkenbosch and Saartje Straetemans describe a 12-year-old boy whose fast weight gain and stopped growth pointed to Cushing disease, yet standard hormone tests contradicted each other. The boy had been healthy before, and diet and exercise changes had not slowed the weight gain. After a watch-and-wait period, clinical doubt remained strong enough to try a different test.

Doctors measured cortisol in an 11 centimeter length of his hair, which stores hormone history over months. Values came back very high, backing the suspected diagnosis. A pituitary scan then showed a small tumor, confirmed after surgery as one making ACTH, the hormone that drives cortisol release. The full answer took 1.5 years from first presentation, likely because hormone output rose and fell in cycles.
pmc-13402441:
Shubhankar Adhikari, Jaya Mishra, and Siddharth Singh ask whether violence against mothers by partners tracks with poor growth in their young children in Madhya Pradesh, India. Working from the National Family Health Survey-5 of 2019 to 2021, they merged mother and child files into 1820 pairs and measured stunting, wasting, and underweight by World Health Organization scores. Partner violence was reported by 28.3 percent of women in the survey violence subsample.

Poor growth was common: 36.4 percent of children were stunted, 18.7 percent wasted, and 33.4 percent underweight. After adjustment for home wealth, schooling, residence, and mother age, violence alone showed no clear link to any of the three outcomes. Household wealth stood out instead as the strong protective factor across every measure. The authors argue policy should fuse violence prevention into mother and child health work while attacking poverty itself.
pmc-13402741:
Streubel and co-authors identify, in 2026, the kinase Nek1 as a second brake on centriole length, working alongside, but separately from, the known CP110-Cep97 cap. Centrioles, the barrel-shaped structures that organize centrosomes and cilia, must hold a characteristic length. Nek1 sits with CP110 and Cep97 at the centriole's distal end and interacts with Cep97 and Cep78 in their localization and binding experiments.

Removing Nek1 caused pronounced hyperelongation of the centriolar microtubules while the CP110-Cep97 cap stayed in place, proving Nek1 restrains growth by its own mechanism. The signal's disappearance in knockout cells confirmed the staining's specificity. Removing both Nek1 and CP110 together, but not Cep78, worsened the overgrowth beyond either single loss, demonstrating two parallel control branches. During cilia formation, Nek1 is stripped from the basal body in a Cep78-dependent manner. The authors present Nek1 as a safeguard of centriole structural integrity in cycling cells.
pmc-13402941:
Du Tang and co-authors review lymphatic endothelial cells, the lining of the lymph vessels, as varied and active regulators rather than passive plumbing. These cells drain tissue fluid, ferry fats, and move immune cells, and new lineage tracing, multiomics, and imaging work shows they adopt distinct states by tissue, vessel segment, and disease. A single framework tying origin, niche, and state changes together has been missing.

The review first maps where the states come from and how identity is maintained, then shows how specialized states run drainage, immune surveillance, and tolerance in health. Disease chapters follow the same cells reprogrammed in lymphatic disorders, inflammation and autoimmunity, cancer, cardiometabolic disease, and brain dysfunction. The authors close on translational openings, proposing precision lymphatic medicine aimed at these cell states.
pmc-13403041:
Mahin Nematollahi and Ahmad Ali Eslami build and validate a questionnaire that measures treatment adherence in dialysis patients through the lens of Social Cognitive Theory. Kidney patients on hemodialysis often drift from fluid, diet, and session rules, and generic adherence scales ignore the beliefs driving behavior. Starting from 57 candidate items shaped by literature and experts, they tested the tool in 181 patients in Isfahan, Iran.

The final instrument sorts 30 items into six domains. Self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and social support cover the belief side. Communication skills, disease acceptance, and self-regulation cover the action side. Content validity scores ran high, internal consistency reached a Cronbach alpha of 0.88, and factor analysis confirmed the six-part structure explaining 57.33 percent of variance, with acceptable fit in confirmatory testing. Self-regulation tied most strongly to actual adherence behavior. The authors offer the culturally adapted scale for planning behavior-change support.
pmc-13403641:
Jakeline Barbara Alves and Rosângela Aparecida Pimenta checked a digital teaching game in 2026 that trains health workers to spot sepsis in children. Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can kill fast without quick care. Expert nurses and doctors judged the game in two rounds.

Eleven judges reviewed the first version screen by screen, and every suggestion they made was taken in. Nine judges then scored the revised game. Their agreement hit 100 percent, with a validity index near 0.99 on the scale used. The cleared game can now serve as a teaching tool for a high-stakes topic.
pmc-13403741:
Peilin Wang and many co-authors reviewed in 2026 how tropical crops cope with harsh and shifting growing conditions. Sugarcane, banana, cassava, rubber, and oil palm feed much of the world, yet face heat, drought, poor soils, and pests that often strike together. The review pulls gene-level work across scales into one view.

Gene traits underlie each crop's complex makeup, and shuffled gene blocks drive key survival traits. Farming and breeding have reshaped those genomes for yield, sometimes at a cost to toughness. The authors urge wider use of wild relatives, gene editing, and mixed tree-crop farms to breed hardier tropical harvests.
pmc-13404441:
Pierrick Martinez and a broad team warned in 2026 that natural supplements in cancer care can help or harm, based on dose and setting. Shoppers tend to see such products as safe by default. The review covers ten common agents, from vitamin C and vitamin D to melatonin and selenium.

Each agent can swing between shielding cells and stressing them, much like a coin with two faces. What matters is dose, route, body uptake, and the tumor's own chemistry state. Four checks guide safer use in their frame. One check asks whether cancer-fighting action beats the shield effect. Framing supplements as context-bound tools, not sure goods, is the core shift.
pmc-13404841:
Ritah F Mutagonda and colleagues lay out a 2026 protocol following African children who live with both sickle cell disease and malaria risk. Malaria can trigger painful crises, severe anaemia and death in these children. How often infection strikes each month, country by country, is still poorly measured.

The one-year study will enrol 2,808 children aged 6 months to 17 years at consortium clinics in seven countries. Staff will test for malaria at monthly visits and at extra sick visits over 12 months. Records will cover family background, gene type, past illness and symptoms. Results should inform guidance on preventive malaria medicine for children with sickle cell disease.
pmc-13405641:
Fabiana Bononi do Carmo and colleagues describe a fungal infection that spread through a child's body to the eye socket, in a 2026 case report. Sporotrichosis usually stays in skin and nearby tissue after contact with the Sporothrix fungus. Spread to organs is rare and harder to recognise.

The adolescent was followed for twelve months with a back lesion and lymph channel involvement that later reached the left orbit bone. Culture of deep tissue grew Sporothrix, confirming disseminated disease. Oral itraconazole ran for twelve months as treatment. Skin and bone lesions had fully cleared by month five, and the patient left follow-up after a year in good shape.
pmc-13405741:
Felicia Kneifel and co-authors study patchy blood flow in donor livers kept on a perfusion machine, in a 2026 German series. Machine perfusion at body temperature helps use more donor organs, yet uneven flow can starve parts of the liver. How often this happens and what it costs patients was unclear.

Records cover transplants at Münster between 2019 and 2024 where a CT scan followed within thirty days. Of 91 patients, twenty-seven showed focal under-perfusion on imaging, a rate of 29.7 percent in the reported figures. Heavier grafts were the only independent predictor, and weight tracked with the size of the pale area. Survival was unaffected, but complications and intensive care stays rose.
pmc-13407041:
Vincenzo Crisci and colleagues review, in 2026, the kinds of drawing and copying mistakes made by people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Copying shapes taps spatial skill, planning, attention, and meaning, so the pattern of errors might help tell one condition from another.

Following standard review methods, the team searched three databases for work from 1990 to January 2026 and kept 25 studies using standard tasks with qualitative error scoring. Spatial mistakes and simplified drawings appeared most often across disorders, while repeated elements, rotations, and drawing squeezed against a model were rarer. Alzheimer's disease leaned toward spatial disorganisation, omissions, and conceptual faults. Shared scoring systems, the authors say, would make studies easier to compare.
pmc-13407941:
Aruni S. Areti and co-authors quantify, in 2026, the extra danger carried by patients who arrive for leg trauma surgery already colonised by MRSA, the drug-resistant staphylococcus. Colonisation is a known hazard in planned joint replacement but under-studied in trauma. The team therefore used a large research network covering twenty years. They matched 1,868 colonised patients one-to-one with non-colonised controls.

After matching, colonised patients faced significantly higher odds of wound splitting, pneumonia, sepsis, kidney failure, blood transfusion, deep vein clots, and lung clots, with sepsis odds nearly quadrupled. Surgical site infection rates, surprisingly, did not differ significantly after matching. The authors propose preoperative screening as a risk-stratification tool, with decolonisation or tailored prophylaxis where feasible to blunt the systemic complications.
pmc-13408441:
Anastasia Theodoropoulou, Anita Nasrallah, and a large team investigate in 2026 a Golgi protein whose job is keeping the cell's sorting station stocked with its own enzymes. The protein, GOLPH3, loads resident enzymes into return vesicles as Golgi compartments mature. What controls GOLPH3 itself, and what happens to a whole animal without it, were open questions.

Mice lacking the protein showed disturbed sugar tagging of proteins and fats, growth failure, and poor bone mineralisation, with some embryos not surviving. At the molecular level, two opposing fatty attachments flip how the protein sits on the membrane, and only one orientation exposes the surface that grips enzyme tails for the return trip. The work ties a lipid-based switch to vertebrate development itself.
pmc-13409041:
Samantha J. Goldenstein and co-authors check whether saliva can track the hormones estradiol and progesterone across the menstrual cycle as blood tests do. Saliva sampling is non-invasive and easy to repeat daily. Their 2026 study enrolled physically active women and followed one or two cycles each.

Participants gave saliva daily at home and blood five times across two cycles, with ovulation confirmed by home tests and blood progesterone. Salivary hormone patterns followed the expected cycle shape. Saliva and blood values correlated strongly for progesterone and for the estradiol-to-progesterone ratio, but not for estradiol alone. In cycles without confirmed ovulation, no associations appeared. Agreement in absolute values was poor, so the authors conclude saliva cannot replace blood measurements, though it may reflect the biologically active hormone fraction more closely and suits pattern tracking.
pmc-13410741:
Farah Chouchene and co-authors present in 2026 three Tunisian siblings whose shared inherited condition affected each child's teeth quite differently. Ectodermal dysplasia disturbs skin, hair, and teeth, and missing or odd-shaped teeth form its main dental burden. Same family, same condition, yet the picture varied a lot.

The children were missing between two and eight teeth, with peg-shaped teeth and deep-rooted molars in the mix. Jaw measures showed uneven growth of the tooth-bearing bones, and the teenager felt real social distress. Care ranged from resin reshaping to a removable partial denture for the youngest, with braces referral and two years of growth checks. Tailored, gentle care restored function and looks.
pmc-13411141:
Bakare and co-authors investigate, in 2026, why childhood vaccine card records disagree with what caregivers say actually happened in Kiyawa, a rural district of Jigawa State, Nigeria, where only 32.9 percent of toddlers were fully immunized in the 2024 national survey. Their mixed-methods study, run from September 2022 to July 2023, examined records for 4258 children under five from 3232 women, then interviewed health workers and held community focus groups.

Caregivers judged 441 cards inaccurate, 10.4 percent of those examined in the survey. The main causes were cards filled in for vaccines never given, sometimes because stock ran out after the card was completed, lost or misplaced cards, and card stock-outs when vaccine was given. Any maternal education, versus none, was among the factors associated with inaccuracy in adjusted models. The authors caution that incentive schemes rewarding paperwork over actual vaccination worsen the data, and propose vaccine bracelets and text-message reminders as immediate fixes.
pmc-13411741:
Jia Guo and colleagues ran a small 2026 trial of mixed-reality headsets for teaching ear anatomy from CT scans. Eight medical students learned eight key structures across 20 temporal bone cases in three phases, with one group using headsets and the other using textbooks and images.

The headset group reached steady performance sooner and scored better on labeling accuracy and speed, with the biggest edge on tricky structures like the tiny hearing bones and facial nerve. Half the headset users felt mild eye tiredness, so the paper backs mixed reality as a helpful add-on while calling for larger trials.
pmc-13414441:
Inês Amaro and co-authors review in 2026 the tangled link between obesity and tooth decay, two chronic conditions that stalk the same populations. Both share sugar-heavy diets, weak oral hygiene habits, and social disadvantage, which alone could manufacture an association. Their state-of-the-art synthesis also weighs saliva changes in obesity and the inflammatory and microbial threads that might bind the diseases biologically rather than merely socially.

Evidence supports shared roots, the authors conclude, not a direct causal arrow from body weight to cavities. Saliva in obesity does look more cavity-friendly, and inflammation markers plus mouth microbe shifts offer plausible bridges. Cross-sectional studies dominate the field, so they press for long-term work tracking both conditions together with standardized saliva measures across ages.
pmc-13414541:
Rhys-Jones and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how an ileal pouch adapts after surgery that removes the colon and builds a storage pouch from the small intestine's last stretch. The pouch must take over water absorption, storage, and controlled emptying in a new microbial setting, and early inflammation of its lining is common. The team searched the literature and weighed which adaptations help and which may feed pouchitis, the pouch's signature inflammation.

Useful changes include stronger water and salt recovery and the ability to stretch, while severe flattening of the absorptive fingers and altered bile acid handling may stir inflammation. Whether keeping small-intestine traits helps is unclear, and barrier leakiness and fuel use by lining cells remain poorly mapped. Knowledge of the ideal pouch microbe mix is thin, and current pouchitis treatments often disappoint. The authors call for studies joining structure, microbes, and diet to design targeted therapies.
pmc-13415741:
Alaa Bella and colleagues describe two Sudanese siblings with mucopolysaccharidosis, a rare inherited storage disorder, in a 2026 case series. An eighteen-year-old man and his thirteen-year-old half-sister showed progressive joint deformities plus problems across many body systems. Enzymes that should break down complex sugars called glycosaminoglycans are missing in this condition, so material builds up in tissues.

Coarse facial features, skeletal changes, and organ dysfunction form the classic pattern the authors used for clinical recognition. Enzyme and genetic testing are scarce in resource limited settings, which delays diagnosis there. Early suspicion still improves supportive care and genetic counseling for families, the authors argue.
pmc-13416441:
Benjamin R. Duewell and co-authors show how one lipid kinase throttles another to keep a key membrane lipid in balance, in 2026. The lipid PI(4,5)P2, though scarce, controls cell intake, movement, and channel activity, and its overproduction can feed cancer growth signals. pmc-13417641:
Jonquil Pinto and colleagues follow acupuncture patients over time to see how health behaviour change unfolds, in a 2026 study based on interviews and recorded visits. Nine patient and practitioner pairs took part. The patients were mostly women aged 23 to 55. Three women practitioners gave the care.

Patients at distinct stages of readiness needed distinct kinds of help. Those swamped by symptoms and stress first needed calm and control. Those more ready needed help to stay on track. Trust in the practitioner and clear reasons for advice built a cycle that made change feel doable. Feeling better after care also pushed patients to act.
pmc-13418241:
Iddon and colleagues describe a 2026 chemistry method for reading the unit order in lab-made chains called REMO. These chains pair with matching partners through hydrogen bonds, much like DNA strands, and can guide the copying of new chains. Until now there was no direct way to check a chain's exact sequence.

The method cuts the chain backbone in two steps. Methyl iodide first tags nitrogen atoms along the backbone while leaving side chains untouched. Methylamine then cuts at those tagged sites, and each cut yields three fragments that a mass-based tool can read. The team showed the cuts work on chains of varied length and side chains. They also used the method to test how faithfully a mixed-sequence template was copied, a key step toward molecules that copy themselves.
pmc-13418441:
Robert J Oldham and a large team show that blocking certain antibody receptors can strengthen checkpoint immunotherapy, in a 2026 study. Receptors called Fc gamma receptors can blunt antibody action by engaging the drug's tail region in unhelpful ways.

Two tailored blockers were matched to two checkpoint drugs. One boosted regulatory T cell removal and reprogrammed tumour immune cells, raising killer T cell activity. The other shielded drug coated T cells from being eaten by macrophages. Both routes overcame resistance in animal and human cell models. Human trials of the selective blocker are under way.
pmc-13418741:
Yichen Zhang and colleagues probe the spin pattern inside very thin films of ruthenium dioxide, a material at the center of debate over a new kind of magnetism. Bulk samples show no clear magnetic order, yet strain from a surface below might change the picture in films just 2 nanometers thick. The team grew such films under strong stretch from their base layer.

The maps showed two spin textures living side by side, one that flips under mirror reflection and one that stays the same. Careful symmetry checks ruled out plain nonmagnetic causes for the pattern. The result points to a strain-born spin order that relaxed or thick material does not show, opening fresh ground for oxide electronics research.
pmc-13418841:
Michael Fralick and colleagues report the vanguard phase in 2026 of a trial asking whether antibiotics help older adults whose delirium comes with bacteria in urine but no clear urinary infection. Thirty hospitalized patients aged 60 and older with delirium plus pyuria or bacteriuria were enrolled, excluding anyone with fever, urinary symptoms, or another antibiotic need.

Recruitment ran 0.05 to 1.8 patients monthly per recruiting site against a goal of four, adherence hit 100 percent, and withdrawals reached 6.7 percent against a goal under 5 percent. The paper gives trialists a frank feasibility readout before the full trial tests whether antibiotics actually clear delirium.
pmc-13418941:
Shreya Ramachandran and colleagues present a near-silent MRI method for filming body processes as they happen, such as contrast dye uptake. Standard dynamic scans are loud, which hurts success with newborns, young children, and other sound-sensitive patients. Their method sweeps the scan path in smooth arcs that rotate step by step, keeping coverage even while the picture updates fast.

Tests on phantoms and in living subjects held image quality steady across a range of speeds. The arc path raised noise slightly over the quietest standard, by 0.3 to 14.2 decibels across settings tested, yet stayed far below normal sequences. Those standard scans ran louder by 20 to 35 decibels in the same comparisons. Quieter dynamic scans could widen who can be imaged without sedation.
pmc-13419241:
Tian Tan and colleagues compare three close cousin constructions in Mandarin Chinese that pair a verb with a word for downward motion. The three forms look alike and share ground in grammar and meaning, which makes them hard to separate by feel alone. The team used a counting method that measures how strongly certain verbs are drawn to each form.

Counts of real usage showed which verb types cling to which construction and how far side meanings stretch from the core one. Each form carries its own center of meaning, with the others shading off in set directions. Maps of pull strength make those shades visible rather than guessed. Language teachers and grammar writers can use the maps to explain a contrast that textbooks often leave fuzzy.
pmc-13419341:
Ryan B Choi and Rohan Khera trace how artificial intelligence is changing the electrocardiogram from a simple diagnostic tracing into a digital biomarker. The heart tracing has anchored cardiac care for a century, read by eye for known patterns. Machine learning now mines the same lines for risks and traits no human reader can see.

The review covers deep learning methods, the use of tracing images, and small wearable devices that could spread the tools worldwide. Gains in reach come with open problems in openness of the models, in which traits they pick up, and in slow uptake at real clinics. The authors sort what is proven from what is promised. Clinicians get a map of where AI heart readings already help and where caution still rules.
pmc-13419441:
Aditi Ramakrishnan and colleagues argue that sexually transmitted infection care and antibiotic stewardship, long run as separate fields, should plan together. The trigger is doxy PEP, a dose of doxycycline taken after sex to prevent infection, which raises worries about breeding resistant germs. Gonorrhea resistant to that drug family already appears more often among users in trial data.

The authors lay out shared tools, from joint clinics to combined data systems, for guiding both the preventive drug and the tests around it. Resistance checks in related bacteria and in the gut are part of the plan. Working together could protect a useful prevention tool from losing power early. The piece gives program leaders concrete forms that the partnership could take.
pmc-13419641:
Dobihal and colleagues report a 2026 study of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium behind many drug-resistant hospital infections. One strain, ST258, dominates worldwide for unclear reasons. pmc-13420141:

pmc-13421741:

pmc-13423941:

pmc-13424141:

pmc-13424641:

pmc-13424741:

pmc-13425541:

pmc-13426941:
Abejirinde and colleagues built in 2026 a standard way to classify remote patient monitoring programs, so very different services can be compared fairly. pmc-13427341:

pmc-13427441:
Michihide Maeda and coauthors tested preoperative predictors of extra therapy after surgery for stage IB cervical cancer in a 2026 retrospective study of 191 patients. pmc-13427641:

The chance of finding it nearer formaldehyde fell from four fifths to three fifths of the time. pmc-13427741:

The authors compare the scheme to reporting rules already used for clinical trials and prediction models in medicine.
pmc-13427941:

By contrast, unruptured aneurysm cases sat near half a percent overall. Diabetes and kidneys already under strain added risk on their own. pmc-13428341:

pmc-13431641:

pmc-13431841:

pmc-13434041:

pmc-13434241:

pmc-13434741:

pmc-13436341:

pmc-13439641:

pmc-13439841:

pmc-13440441:

pmc-13440741:

pmc-13441341:

pmc-13442841:

pmc-13443541:

pmc-13444141:

pmc-13444741:

pmc-13446041:

pmc-13446641:

pmc-13447341:

pmc-13450241:
Ruiqin Peng and colleagues review in 2026 manganese oxide catalysts for lithium-oxygen batteries, a chemistry whose energy density could dwarf today's lithium-ion cells. The promise stalls on sluggish reactions, side products, and insulating lithium peroxide crusting the cathode until the battery chokes. Manganese oxides appeal as rescuers because they are abundant, cheap, and structurally varied, coming in tunnel, layered, and spinel forms with adjustable oxidation states that host oxygen reactions and lithium traffic.

The review organizes recent engineering moves: reshaping pores, tuning surface sites, punching in defects, doping with foreign atoms, and building composites. Each lever shifts the catalyst's electronic structure and steers whether lithium peroxide forms as films or particles and how cleanly it decomposes on recharge, which decides polarization losses and cycle life. The authors close with the field's remaining obstacles and design guidelines meant to carry these catalysts toward practical cells.
pmc-13450541:
Yi Luo and others built a cell-coated nano drug carrier for acute lung harm in 2026, to calm runaway swelling in the lungs. Acute lung harm starts when lung guard cells overreact and drive a flood of swelling signals, yet plain nano drugs fail to cross lung mucus and quiet that flood. The team hid a drug carrier in a guard-cell coat so it could reach sore lung tissue.

Cerium oxide bits were set on a porous dopamine base and wrapped in guard-cell skins, to form M-MPDA@CeO2. Dish tests scored its power to mop up free radicals and to shift guard-cell states, while a mouse lung-harm model tested its cure effect. The coated carrier joined homing with radical cleanup in one shot. The work gives a cell-like drug route for a lung state with few good drugs.
pmc-13452241:
Rengeerli Sa and co-authors feed in 2026 a creatine-building compound to Tibetan sheep and track meat quality through the gut-muscle path. The trial held 120 young male sheep in four groups for ninety days, with the compound at three doses over a base diet. Gut germ reads, muscle molecule scans, and meat tests were tied together.

The top dose shifted set gut germ groups and raised two useful gut acids. Muscle fat-path molecules moved, and meat in that group showed stronger antioxidant power, a redder tone, and a tenderer bite. Links among gut germs, muscle molecules, and meat traits backed the gut-muscle story. The authors back the compound as a feed plus for plateau sheep.
pmc-13453441:
Pascal Gottmann and nine co-authors ask why Göttingen minipigs resist fatty liver disease that plagues people and other pig breeds. Their 2026 study compares liver gene activity in these minipigs with that of humans, mice, and pig breeds prone to the disease. The disease, shortened to MASLD, builds fat in the liver and ties to diabetes and scarring.

The minipig liver switched 692 genes in a pattern no other group shared, touching fuel use and signal paths. Eleven gene switches, three liver made hormones, and six other secreted proteins stood out as the strongest candidates. A network analysis put two switches, HMBOX1 and PATZ1, at the hub, steering about 41 percent of the changed genes. The team offers these genes and proteins as leads for drugs that could copy the minipig's protection.
pmc-13454441:
Joonggon Kim and five colleagues present, in 2026, an image-based method to grade gray mold damage in stored kiwifruit without cutting the fruit open. The mold, Botrytis cinerea, shortens shelf life for the golden Haegeum variety. The team sorted infected fruit into four levels, from no marks to heavy fungal growth and tissue collapse.

Fruit softened as damage rose, and breathing rates climbed with each level. A ripening gas appeared at level three and spiked at level four. Their learning system focused on the lesion area rather than the whole photo. Three network designs each reached about 90 percent accuracy in sorting the levels. Heat maps confirmed the models looked at the mold itself, not the background. The authors offer the setup as a fair, explainable grader for packing sheds.
pmc-13455241:
Jingyi Liu and others tracked seasonal fly density and pathogen carriage in Shanghai urban villages in 2026, studying Pudong New Area from June to October 2024. Flies are mechanical vectors of zoonotic pathogens, posing diarrheal disease risks in urban villages with substandard sanitation. Taiping Village, a representative urban village, was monitored across six environments with standardized cage traps and sticky ribbons.

Sarcophagidae dominated the fly community at 60.75 percent, followed by A. illocata at 17.29 percent and L. sericata at 13.55 percent. Peak density occurred June to August at 1.48 flies per trap, with public toilet exteriors highest at 1.33 flies per trap. One hundred forty-nine pooled samples were screened by RT-PCR and microfluidic chip for thirty-one enteric pathogens including viruses, bacteria, and parasites. Public health teams gain seasonal and site-specific fly-pathogen data for urban village sanitation.
pmc-13457841:
Bogdán Asztalos and colleagues turn fencing and tennis results into evolving hierarchies in a 2026 network study. Rankings compress strength into one list, yet match-by-match wins and losses form a richer web that can reveal dominance, cycles and upset paths. The team built directed networks with players as nodes and winner-to-loser edges, comparing round-robin data with elimination tournaments and testing whether hierarchy position predicts future matches.

Elimination brackets produced strongly hierarchical networks by design, yet their dominance gaps proved weaker, with more circular win-loss loops than round-robin play. Hierarchy position plus other network measures predicted outcomes about as well as official ranking points or Elo ratings. Tournament designers and analysts gain a network lens that preserves pairwise history, useful for seeding, scheduling and modelling contests well beyond sport.
pmc-13458241:
Jacqueline A. Evans and colleagues review a decade of kidney disease in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy at their service. Modern treatment has reshaped which renal problems appear, mixing drug toxicity with classic HIV kidney disease. Their 2026 study covers 158 patients seen between 2011 and 2021, comparing 59 who had kidney biopsies with 99 who did not, and following outcomes to mid 2025.

Protein in the urine was the commonest presentation and ran higher in the biopsied group, especially with glomerulonephritis, yet its level said little about the microscopic damage scores. Filtration rate, by contrast, tracked both acute and chronic tissue injury closely. Stopping the drug tenofovir disoproxil fumarate eased proteinuria and stabilized filtration in patients with tubular injury. Proteinuria alone consistently predicted the combined bad outcome of kidney failure or death. The authors conclude biopsy remains essential for an exact diagnosis in this population, and proteinuria deserves priority as a danger signal.
pmc-13458741:
Yu Jiang, Juan Yang and Shanshan Yang published this 2026 study testing whether three blood markers together spot sepsis in newborns better than any one alone. Neonatal sepsis is a leading cause of newborn death, yet its early signs are vague. The markers, interleukin-6, procalcitonin and serum amyloid A, all rise with infection. The authors measured them at admission in babies in a neonatal intensive care unit, before antibiotics began.

The study enrolled 140 newborns: 60 with confirmed sepsis, 40 with suspected sepsis and 40 without infection. All three markers ran much higher in confirmed sepsis, and higher still in severe cases. Individually, the markers scored between 0.908 and 0.932 on the standard accuracy curve measure. Combined, the panel reached 0.985, catching 93.3 percent of cases while correctly clearing 92.5 percent of non-cases in this sample. The authors propose the trio as a fast support to blood culture for early diagnosis and severity grading.
pmc-13459341:
Dawei Wang and co-authors mapped the scale and drivers of urinary stone disease in eastern China using health records for nearly a million people. Their 2026 prospective cohort study drew on the Yinzhou electronic records system covering 966,481 participants followed between 2009 and 2022. The team estimated how incidence changed year by year and which lifestyle and metabolic factors raised risk, calculating how many cases might be prevented by removing each factor from the population.

Stone incidence climbed steadily, rising 5.3 to 6.8 percent per year from the mid-2010s to 2021, and roughly one in ten Chinese adults is affected overall. Smoking, drinking, high body mass index, diabetes, abnormal blood lipids, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease all raised risk, while regular exercise protected against stones. The prevention math was striking: weekly exercise carried the largest population benefit, needing only about twenty-one people active to avert one case in the reported measure.
pmc-13459841:
Qingting Bu, Jin Yang, Hua Cheng, Zhenyu Pan, and Tao Zhang measured in 2026 how unevenly the tuberculosis burden falls across countries. Drawing on Global Burden of Disease 2021 data for 204 countries and territories, they tracked disability-adjusted life years from 1990 to 2021. Two statistical lenses were used: a slope index capturing absolute inequality linked to social development, and a Gini index capturing relative spread.

Absolute inequality fell by more than half across the three decades, which sounds like progress. Relative inequality nevertheless crept upward, with the Gini index rising slightly over the same period. Regional gaps stayed wide, and both measures dipped then climbed with age. The authors urge research into the drivers behind these stubborn disparities.
pmc-13459941:
Priscila Machado and co-authors surveyed Australian adults on what they actually know about ultra processed foods, the industrial formulations now blamed for much diet related disease. Public debate uses the term constantly, but nobody had mapped lay understanding nationally. Their 2026 study questioned 1,086 adults aged twenty to sixty four in mid 2024 with free listing tasks. It also used image identification of products among twenty foods, knowledge scoring, and sorting tasks that reveal which attributes people attach to the ultra processed label.

Respondents described what came to mind for the term and attempted to classify real products, generating a functional knowledge score for each participant. Models then linked identification accuracy and knowledge scores to traits such as age and education. The sorting tasks exposed the attributes Australians associate with ultra processing, from packaging and additives to health halos. Mapping this folk understanding is prerequisite to food policy the public can use.
pmc-13460241:
Kim and co-authors explain how systems genetics can illuminate early-onset colorectal cancer in this 2026 paper. Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in the United States. Cases before age 50 have been rising for decades. The reasons mix genes and environment. Systems genetics treats genes as a network, combining gene activity patterns, protein interactions, and drug-gene links.

The paper does three things: it reviews recent systems genetics studies of this cancer, walks readers through a step-by-step protocol for running such analyses, and discusses current limits. Those limits include findings that may not generalize across populations and results that depend heavily on context. The authors hope the guide encourages cancer researchers to adopt network methods when hunting for diagnostic markers and candidate drugs.
pmc-13461841:
Jun Suzuki and colleagues lay out, in a 2026 guide, a standard two-port robotic method for removing one lung segment. Two chest openings keep the robot's strengths while limiting cuts between the ribs. Segment removal demands exact knowledge of small airways and vessels, plus a reliable segment border. Errors in naming an airway threaten safety, above all in complex cases.

Steps run from planning with a 3D model of the patient's anatomy, through port placement fitted to the treated side, to teamwork between console and bedside staff. A dye given into a vein lights up under special imaging to draw the border. Airway identity is double-checked when anatomy is tricky. Two videos show the sequence adapted to a right lower segment and a left upper segment. Results from hospital cases, covering operating time, blood loss, and tumor removal, frame the method as workable and safe.
pmc-13461941:
Zhi Wang and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a gene signature tied to a chemical tag process called lactylation. It predicts survival in lung adenocarcinoma, the common lung cancer type. Lactylation has been linked to tumor growth and immune control, yet its sorting value was unclear. The team combined single-cell and bulk data. One cohort served to build the model, and two outside cohorts checked it.

The signature held 15 genes and split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with different survival in all three cohorts. The model ranked patients accurately at home and moderately well outside. High-risk tumors showed sugar burning, low-oxygen responses, and growth signaling, plus an immune setting. Lab tests singled out one gene, TUBA1C, as a lead candidate. The authors present the signature as a checked tool for survival prediction, not yet a guide for drug choice.
pmc-13462041:
Juebin Gu, Yufei Dong, Mulin Liu, and Lin Lin test, in a 2026 hospital study, whether a fast gene-based blood test adds value for spotting bloodstream infection. Blood culture, the standard test, is slow, so early treatment choices are made blind. The gene test, droplet digital PCR, hunts pathogen DNA directly in blood. The team built a prediction model from routine signs in one patient group, then checked the added test in a second group.

The routine group held 814 patients. Age and one inflammation marker were the only signs tied to a positive culture, and the model sorted cases modestly. In the second group of 336 patients, adding the gene test lifted sorting accuracy, though not firmly by one strict test. Re-sorting measures improved clearly. The authors present the gene test as a helper for early risk sorting, not a stand-in for culture.
pmc-13462241:
Saartak Allena and colleagues benchmarked quantum machine learning methods for sorting breast cancer cases using clinical and gene data. Quantum models promise new pattern-finding power but must squeeze rich data onto very few simulated quantum bits.

The dataset held 2,509 patients, cut down from 63 features to at most 12 summary components for the quantum runs. The best quantum model, a quantum nearest-neighbour method, reached about 75 percent accuracy with an AUC of 0.8148 on held-out checks. Classical methods using all 63 features reached about 94 percent accuracy, well ahead of every quantum model. Shrinking the data hurt both families, Allena notes, so no quantum advantage appears at this scale yet.
pmc-13462441:
Xiang Bai and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that an enzyme gene called PRSS1 helps stomach cancer invade and spread. Public gene data flagged PRSS1 as a hub gene in stomach tumors. The team confirmed higher levels in tumor tissue, cancer cell lines, and patient blood. Those levels ran highest in advanced disease and tracked vessel invasion, stage, and lymph node spread.

Silencing PRSS1 in cancer cells slowed movement and invasion in dish tests and cut spread inside the belly in mice. Protein checks showed the silencing reversed a shape-shifting program that lets lining cells loosen and wander, called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Two cutting enzymes fell, while a sticking protein rose. A growth signaling route, MAPK/ERK, also quieted. The authors conclude PRSS1, easy to measure in blood, may serve as a marker of aggressive stomach cancer and a target worth testing.
pmc-13462841:
Selvi Helina and colleagues map, in a 2026 field study, a virus crippling chili pepper production in Lampung Province, Indonesia. The virus, pepper yellow leaf curl virus, is spread by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci and curls and yellows leaves. Surveys with lab confirmation covered the seven chili districts of the province. Symptoms ranged from curling and yellow mosaic to shrunken leaves and stunted plants, varying by farm setting.

Infection proved widespread. Disease incidence hit 91 percent in Tanggamus and 85 percent in West Lampung, with severity nearing four fifths in both. Gene tests confirmed the virus, and its sequences matched known Indonesian strains closely while forming one tight family group, apart from foreign viruses. That sameness fits rapid regional spread by the whitefly. The authors warn the virus threatens further spread to other growing centers. They urge combined control: suppressing the whitefly, planting resistant varieties, and developing mild-strain protection.
pmc-13463641:
François Ritter leads a team that projects a sharp fall in the carbon stored by European forests. These forests soak up carbon and help slow climate change, yet harvests, fires, storms, and beetle outbreaks now kill trees faster than regrowth replaces them. The group joined country reports with satellite maps of damage and tree mass.

Their model, run at eighteen-kilometer detail from 2010 to 2030, sees the EU-27 forest carbon sink drop by about thirty-nine percent. The 2030 sink would land about twenty-seven percent below the level tied to EU climate goals. Planting three billion trees alone cannot close the gap, the team finds. Pairing planting with a deep cut in harvests could still meet the target.
pmc-13463941:
Piotr Olejnik and three co-authors review how chronic kidney disease clouds thinking, stage by stage. More than a tenth of adults worldwide live with kidney disease, and memory and focus problems can appear at any stage. The review ties clinic records to the molecular paths behind the decline.

Small vessel damage, a leaky brain barrier, uremic toxins, and body-wide inflammation all feed the harm. Early stages lean on vessel and focus troubles, while late stages add toxin and dialysis swings to the mix. Transplant drugs bring their own risks after surgery. Sorting the pattern by stage, the authors argue, can sharpen both study design and day-to-day care.
pmc-13464241:
Nagao and colleagues reported in 2026 a drainage catheter that went in easily but refused to come out. After catheter ablation for a rhythm problem, a 66-year-old woman developed cardiac tamponade. Tamponade is dangerous fluid pressure around the heart. Doctors drained the fluid through a needle below the breastbone. A thin pigtail catheter was left in place and seemed correctly positioned.

Two days later, the catheter resisted removal with marked force. Scans revealed the problem. The tube had slipped through the transverse pericardial sinus, a natural passage behind the aorta. It had re-entered the heart sac from the other side. Draining the fluid collapsed the passage around its sharply bent course like a trap. The team refilled the sac with saline to reopen the passage. They eased the catheter out timed with the heart's relaxation phase. Smooth insertion, they warn, proves nothing about placement.
pmc-13464341:
Ruan and co-authors built in 2026 a scoring chart, called a nomogram, to estimate whether a small lung nodule is cancerous before surgery. The chart drew on 1,419 patients whose nodules of three centimeters or less were removed and examined between 2012 and 2025. Ordinary clinical details were combined with precise measurements from thin-slice CT scans. A held-out group of 425 patients checked the chart.

Four of every five removed nodules proved malignant. Seven factors fed the final score, and suspicious scan features dominated. They multiplied the odds of cancer roughly sixfold and more. Nodules wider than two centimeters roughly quadrupled the odds. Women faced higher odds than men. Patients found without symptoms had lower odds, a reminder that incidental nodules differ from symptomatic ones. The chart discriminated well, scoring about 81 percent on the accuracy curve in training and about 78 percent in validation. Predicted risks matched observed outcomes closely.
pmc-13465041:
Tianyu Liu and colleagues identified TRIM71 in 2026 as a brake on cervical cancer growth through a cell-adhesion target. TRIM71, an RNA-binding enzyme, was known in other cancers but untested in cervical tumours. The team measured it in cell lines and patient tissues, linked levels to features and survival, and tested its effects in dishes and mouse tumours.

Low TRIM71 marked aggressive tumours and shorter survival as an independent prognostic sign. Raising it slowed growth, movement, invasion, and vessel formation, while losing it sped them up. TRIM71 grips the Nectin4 message and destabilises it, quieting Wnt/beta-catenin signalling and cell shape-shifting, which makes the TRIM71-Nectin4 axis a candidate drug target.
pmc-13465141:
Rašeta and colleagues present a 2026 study validating pasteurization for wide chicken sausages, where standard temperature endpoints may overshoot and waste energy. In thick products, the center keeps cooking after heating stops, a cooling inertia that adds lethal effect on microbes. The team profiled temperatures across three commercial pasteurization runs of ninety-millimeter chicken sausages in plastic casings.

When active heating stopped at a lower core limit, the cooling phase more than tripled the accumulated lethality before the product cooled, reaching a high final value on the study's integrated scale. In other words, the process was safer than the thermometer at switch-off suggested. Counting cooling inertia honestly could let producers cut heating time and energy while keeping the same safety margin, and it separates later quality loss, from enzymes or oxidation, from microbial risk.
pmc-13465441:
Wysokinski and colleagues tracked sulphur through the life of pea plants in a two-year field study reported in 2026. Sulphur is a key nutrient for legumes. It supports the root nodules that capture nitrogen and the storage proteins in seeds. The team measured sulphur content, uptake, and several efficiency indices at six growth stages. Roots and shoots were analyzed separately, with seeds added at full ripeness.

The values moved in clear phases. Sulphur content and uptake rose early, between the four-leaf stage and stem elongation. Content then eased downward toward pod filling while uptake and the harvest index kept climbing. The nitrogen-to-sulphur ratio stayed in a healthy band throughout. By full maturity, none of the measures changed further. Both the study year and growth stage shaped the numbers, while the cultivar rarely did. The authors conclude the fertilizer dose kept plants adequately supplied all season.
pmc-13466241:
Melike Dönmez Tekin and co-authors review outcomes for patients whose head and neck cancer returned or spread and who received cetuximab-based treatment, in a 2026 single-center study. Fifty-seven patients treated at a Turkish university hospital between 2012 and 2025 form the group. Cetuximab regimens still matter here even as immune therapies spread.

Records supplied age, stage, lab values, and scan results for each patient. The team estimated time without disease worsening and overall survival, then tested which traits lined up with longer or shorter survival. Such prognostic sorting can help doctors judge who gains most from this older drug backbone and who should move to other options sooner.
pmc-13466641:
Lyu and a clinical team built a simple prediction model in 2026 for which mothers with sepsis will crash into septic shock. Existing warning scores perform poorly here. The study reviewed 139 women treated at one referral center over nearly a decade. Four factors measured at diagnosis fed the model. Records were split so the model faced patients it had not learned from.

The four predictors were surgery during pregnancy, a clotting time, a bacterial infection marker, and blood oxygen level. Together they sorted future shock cases well. The accuracy score reached 0.87 in both the learning and test groups, where 1.0 is perfect. Higher scores tracked with worse outcomes for mothers and babies. Lung infections were the commonest source, at about 45 percent of cases. Gram-negative bacteria caused most infections, and shock struck postpartum cases far more often, about 43 percent against 19 percent.
pmc-13466941:
Hongtao Sun and a large team engineer tiny spheres with a gradient of crosslinking from core to shell to block tumor blood vessels in liver cancer treatment, in a 2026 study. Blocking spheres face a trade-off: stiff ones resist crushing but cannot squeeze deep into vessels, while soft ones drift after placement. Their design grades the internal bonding to get strength and flexibility together.

Bench models of vessel networks showed the new spheres traveled distally and stayed put better than uniform or standard core-shell versions. Pig kidney tests confirmed the behavior in a living system. Human trials in liver cancer then verified that the spheres blocked vessels effectively and safely, tying mechanical design to clinical reach.
pmc-13467041:
Daniel Blaschke, a physicist, derives a far faster way to compute the limiting speeds of line defects gliding through crystals, in a 2026 methods paper. Dislocation theory predicts that elastic energy blows up at certain speeds that depend on crystal shape, splitting slow, middling, and faster-than-sound glide regimes. Those thresholds feed models of how materials hold up under extreme strain rates.

One awkward case, edge dislocations in crystals with mirror symmetry but certain stubborn elastic constants, had resisted every fast method. The new derivation handles exactly that case about a hundred times faster than the previous approach. Strength modelers who screen many crystal orientations gain the most from the shortcut.
pmc-13467541:
Andrés Baeza-Morales and co-authors test in 2026 a red pigment from a salt-loving microbe against several cancer cell models, including drug-resistant lung cancer. The pigment, bacterioruberin, comes from the archaeon Haloferax mediterranei and had barely been studied in solid tumors. The team exposed lung, breast, and melanoma cell lines to a pigment-rich extract and measured survival, growth, oxidative stress, and cell death.

The extract killed cancer cells and slowed their growth across the models. Treated cells showed more reactive oxygen species, a sign the pigment pushes cells toward oxidative damage, plus changes typical of apoptosis, the orderly form of cell death. Importantly, growth inhibition held up in lung cancer cells that resist standard drugs by pumping them out through the P-glycoprotein system. That reach into resistant cells is what makes the pigment worth further study.
pmc-13467641:
Hongyu Chen, Bowen Ke, and Ruotian Jiang review in 2026 whether classic psychedelics could help treat chronic pain. They frame chronic pain as a disorder of a maladapted central nervous system. In their account, pain signals traveling upward hold it in place, and so do the rigid expectations the brain brings to them. Standard painkillers rarely undo that rigidity, which is where psychedelics, known for loosening mental patterns, might fit.

The review gathers the research on what these drugs bind to in the brain, how they may change pain circuits, and what early clinical studies in pain patients show. It also confronts weak points in the field: psychedelic trials are hard to blind, and patient expectations can inflate results. The authors call for new validation strategies and argue that brain plasticity and subjective experience may each carry part of the benefit.
pmc-13467741:
Wei Li and five colleagues published this 2026 greenhouse study on whether silicon and nitrogen fertilisation can help rice defend itself against invasive apple snails, voracious grazers of paddy fields. Silicon can harden defences, while excess nitrogen from polluted water might soften them. The team grew rice seedlings under two silicon levels and three nitrogen levels, measured leaf chemistry and toughness, and let snails feed to gauge the protection.

Silicon made rice grow larger at low and high nitrogen, raised sulfur at every level, and lifted tannins and the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio at the middle level. For defence, silicon increased flavonoid content and the force needed to fracture leaves under all nitrogen regimes, and the snails grew less on silicon-fed plants. Nitrogen modified several effects but never erased the silicon benefit. The authors propose silicon amendment as a crop protection strategy amid eutrophication and invasion.
pmc-13467841:
Ma and co-authors teach machines to classify gout from routine clinical data. Their 2026 retrospective study draws 7,383 adults from a Jiangxi hospital's records between 2020 and 2026, labelling gout by the international classification framework and comparing against a mixed hospital population. Because a single uric acid value does not capture the disease, the models integrate inflammatory, metabolic, kidney, blood, demographic, and lifestyle variables.

After imputation of missing values and statistical feature selection, four algorithms were trained and tested on a hold-out split. Random forest performed best overall, reaching a discrimination score of about 0.90 in training while keeping sensitivity above 96 percent, and it stayed ahead in the test set. Calibration and decision-curve analyses accompanied the accuracy metrics. The authors present routine-variable models as a practical aid for flagging gout in ordinary clinical settings.
pmc-13468041:
Farhat Abbas and colleagues introduce a 2026 special issue on the three great families of plant pigments: anthocyanins, carotenoids, and betalains. These compounds paint flowers and fruits, help plants cope with stress, and shape ties with pollinators and enemies. They also carry nutritional, medicinal, and industrial value for people. The editors frame a collection of twelve original research and review articles gathered for the issue.

The collected works span the full arc from how pigment molecules are built and genetically regulated, through how plants use them to adapt, to applications in agriculture and industry. The editors note that the regulatory networks behind pigment production are intricate and fast-moving, leaving practical uses still open. Their introduction serves as a guide to the issue and an argument that pigment biology now connects molecular genetics to ecology and commerce in one continuous story.
pmc-13468341:
Mingming Chen and colleagues traced the evolution of ammonium transporter genes across green plants and mapped their activity in oilseed rape. These transporters pull ammonium, a key nitrogen feed, into plant cells, shaping how well crops use nitrogen.

The team catalogued 368 transporter genes from 35 species, split almost evenly between the AMT1 and AMT2 families. Small local duplications drove family growth across plant history, while whole-genome doubling dominated in the Brassica triangle group. Most rape transporters responded to hormones and low nitrogen, with tissue-specific patterns across the plant. Four genes stood out as breeding candidates, Chen reports, two of them linked to plant height and yield differences.
pmc-13468841:
Valdemar Farre and colleagues draft in 2026 a planning framework for beyond-5G and 6G networks that scatter antennas across a city instead of concentrating them in cell towers. Their four-layer scheme jointly places spread-out antenna arrays and passive reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, reflective panels that steer radio waves around corners. A digital twin loop inside an open radio access network runs multi-agent reinforcement learning and fractional math to tune active and passive beamforming in real time.

Monte Carlo simulations of a dense city setting reported a 45 percent increase in spectral efficiency. They also found a 30 percent cut in uplink interference, and 84 percent fewer coverage holes than legacy 5G layouts. Non-line-of-sight coverage grew by 40 percent without the capital cost of new towers. Operators facing 6G build-out bills get a blueprint claiming software and surfaces can stand in for concrete and steel.
pmc-13468941:
O’Keefe and colleagues wrote a methods communication in 2026 on reporting artificial intelligence use in horizon scanning. Horizon scanning means watching for emerging health technologies and trends to guide policy. The authors reviewed current guidelines, policies, and stakeholder statements on AI use in research and publishing.

From 139 collected data points, they consolidated a minimal set of 46 reporting items in six categories. The items aim to make AI use in scanning transparent, reliable, and responsible. They cover how AI tools are chosen, used, and checked across the research cycle. The authors present the set as an interim standard filling an immediate gap. They note the items still need validation with users before becoming a firm framework. They urge scanning teams to keep embedding AI openly while standards mature.
pmc-13469041:
Dingzhi Liu and co-authors reanalyze public single-cell data in 2026 to find the signaling conversations that help liver cancer suppress its immune attackers. Hepatocellular carcinoma is among the deadliest cancers, and its microenvironment is crowded with regulatory T cells that brake immunity and exhausted T cells that have given up. The team pulled single-cell RNA sequencing data from a public repository and processed it with standard clustering and cell annotation workflows.

Their reanalysis highlights a candidate axis between the signal MIF and the receptor PTGDR as an immunoregulatory program tied to those dysfunctional T-cell states. Mapping which cells send and receive such signals matters because immunotherapy for liver cancer works in only a minority of patients. A named sender-receiver axis gives drug developers a specific conversation to interrupt, and the study shows public data, carefully re-mined, can still yield fresh targets.
pmc-13469141:
Zhongyan Liu and colleagues traced in 2026 how a yak-derived probiotic shields the gut lining from pathogenic E. coli. Yaks on the high plateau suffer diarrhoea from gut bacteria, while vaccines are thin and antibiotic resistance grows. The team tested Lactobacillus yoelii Lac-2 on gut cell layers, manipulating zonulin and the MAPK signal path with activators and blockers.

Raising zonulin or switching on MAPK weakened the barrier, cut mucin and tight-junction proteins, and let more bacteria cross, while the probiotic did the opposite by damping zonulin through MAPK blockade. Barrier resistance rose and leakage plus cell death fell under probiotic protection. The strain may offer a high-altitude probiotic for yak diarrhoea, pending animal and field trials.
pmc-13469341:
Zhang and colleagues identify a new switch for bacterial virulence in this 2026 plant pathology study. The bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola causes bacterial leaf streak of rice and depends on a type III secretion system, a needle-like structure that injects proteins into plant cells. A control chain called HrpG-HrpX turns this system on, but what sits above it in this bacterium was unclear.

Deleting the gene for a regulator named GpaR made the bacteria far less damaging to rice and weakened their effect on a test plant. Levels of hrpG, hrpX, and related secretion genes dropped sharply without GpaR. Binding tests showed GpaR attaches directly to the start regions of both genes and switches them on, and restoring either gene largely brought back virulence.
pmc-13470341:
Harikrishna and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on computer stress modeling in dentistry. Finite element analysis splits a tooth or implant into tiny blocks for math testing. It predicts where biting forces pile up inside oral structures. The review traces the method from engineering roots into dental labs.

The authors survey uses across implants, braces, root work, and crowns. Modeling guides implant shapes and tool designs before patient testing begins. It also maps stress in enamel, dentin, jawbone, and gum ligaments. No bench test matches its three-dimensional detail, the authors argue. Weak material data and loose modeling habits still limit trust, they warn. The search reached back to 1969 across five major databases. Nine dental specialties fall within the review's wide survey scope.
pmc-13470941:
Zian Wang built a linear forecast model in 2026 for portal vein clot risk in liver scarring. Clots complicate liver scarring care, yet doctors lacked a simple tool to flag high-risk patients before events. pmc-13473541:

pmc-13473941:

pmc-13474841:
Veerle Van Oeckel and co-authors evaluate a co-design process in 2026 that tackled sitting time at school among teens in Flanders, Belgium. pmc-13475341:
Alireza Maboudi argues in 2026 that artificial intelligence in drug work misses the craft that turns a molecule into a medicine. pmc-13477141:
Laura Maitoza and coauthors report in 2026 on using whole blood for babies having heart surgery with a heart-lung machine. The study covers infants under two months old treated at one center between 2019 and 2023. Whole blood filled the bypass circuit and met early transfusion needs, instead of separate blood parts given one by one.

Babies given whole blood were exposed to fewer donors, a median of three compared with five, and needed fewer separate blood parts during surgery. Hospital stay, breathing support time, and later transfusion needs did not differ clearly, so the authors call for more research on whether the approach improves recovery.
pmc-13477641:
Marcus Hunter and Luis R. Martinez published a 2026 review on cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, a dangerous flare that can follow HIV treatment. Up to a quarter of survivors develop the syndrome after starting HIV drug treatment, when the returning immune system meets leftover fungus in the brain.

During recovery, surging T cells, uneven control, and guiding signals draw killer cells into the brain, where the response can turn harmful. The authors discuss new mouse models, compare a related fungal species, and survey immune-focused treatments and vaccines now being tested.
pmc-13478341:
Vijaykumar and colleagues developed a double-layer seed coating for oilseed crops in 2026, wrapping seeds in plant-based polymers that carry a fungicide, a helpful fungus, and crop-matched fertilizer bacteria. Layers keep the chemical and living inputs apart so each releases in turn. pmc-13478741:
Kathryn Bowles and eleven colleagues build human stem cell lines that carry a tau gene splice fault, in a twenty twenty-four study. pmc-13479241:
Francesc Franquesa-Garcia and the DIADEMA investigators published a 2026 multicenter study using artificial intelligence to measure fluid in diabetic macular edema, a swelling that threatens vision in diabetes. Eyes received a dexamethasone implant, a slow-release steroid placed inside the eye. Baseline eye scans were quantified by validated software that measures fluid pockets in nanoliters.

The real-world Spanish database held 101 previously untreated eyes. More fluid inside the retina at baseline predicted larger letter gains by month twelve yet worse final vision, a pattern suggesting severe disease that improves but cannot fully recover. Fluid under the retina predicted worse final vision more cleanly. Shrinking intraretinal fluid by 100 nanoliters at three months tracked with about one and a half extra letters gained. The authors propose objective fluid volumes as counseling tools.
pmc-13479441:
Hafize Gökben Ulutaş and coauthors published a 2026 study of how lingering corneal infiltrates after viral eye infection change the cornea's physical behavior. Subepithelial infiltrates, cloudy spots under the surface, can persist after adenoviral epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and blur vision. Patients kept for at least six months after the acute episode were compared with healthy controls.

The study covered 23 affected eyes from twelve patients and 32 control eyes. Affected eyes saw worse, showed steeper corneal curvature readings, more optical distortion, and higher corneal cloudiness values, mainly in front and central zones. An air-puff device that films corneal bending found one movement measure, the first applanation length, significantly shorter in affected eyes. The authors conclude the infiltrates leave measurable mechanical fingerprints, not just optical ones.
pmc-13479541:
Xue Han and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial on timing a single dose of dexmedetomidine to blunt the pain sensitivity caused by the anesthetic remifentanil. Only the skin-closure group showed less pain sensitivity around the wound at twenty-four hours. Resting pain scores, rescue medication use, recovery quality scores, circulation stability, and side effects were also tracked. pmc-13479641:
Linda van der Spek and colleagues published a 2025 review of what helps or hinders paying parents and expectant parents to quit smoking. The review aims to help new programs copy what worked rather than hitting the same walls again.
pmc-13479741:

pmc-13480741:

pmc-13481641:
Maria Carmela Saturno and co-authors report a 2026 case of two germs attacking the retina at once in a woman with a sound immune system. pmc-13481841:

pmc-13482341:

pmc-13482541:

pmc-13482641:

pmc-13483141:

pmc-13483541:

pmc-13483641:

pmc-13483741:

pmc-13483941:

pmc-13486041:

pmc-13486641:

pmc-13486941:

pmc-13487241:

pmc-13487341:

pmc-13487941:

pmc-13490441:

pmc-13491341:

pmc-13491641:

pmc-13491741:

pmc-13491841:

pmc-13492641:

pmc-13493741:

pmc-13494041:
