pmc-13495441:
Claudio Bertiola-Flores leads a team reviewing, in a 2026 article, peer tutoring inside clinical simulation for health sciences students. Both methods push active, safe, team learning, yet their joint gains had never been summed. The team searched three databases for trials and near-trials from 2020 to 2025.

Eleven studies with 860 students and 107 tutors qualified, mostly in low- to mid-complexity simulation rooms. Gains showed in hands-on skills and in softer ones: confidence, communication, drive, and reflection. Students reported high satisfaction and less anxiety, in rooms that felt safe to fail in. Tutors, close in age and stage to learners, gave feedback and set a trusting tone. The authors call the pairing cheap and sound, while flagging small samples and short follow-up, and they urge formal tutor training under faculty watch.
pmc-13498741:
Bhavna Singla and co-authors review in 2026 computer systems that use live, updating hospital data to predict sepsis early. Sepsis is a dangerous body-wide response to infection, and late recognition delays treatment. Artificial intelligence tools promise earlier warnings, yet their quality and readiness for ward use remain unclear, prompting a structured search of three major databases for studies from 2015 to mid-2025.

Eight studies met the rules, covering intensive care, emergency departments, and multi-hospital systems, with patient counts from several hundred to over half a million. Model types ranged from boosted decision methods to deep neural networks, and accuracy was generally moderate to high, with several tools warning hours before onset. Most studies carried moderate bias risk from backward-looking designs and varied sepsis definitions, so the authors call for forward testing in real workflows.
pmc-13499041:
Sunghyun Jun, Colleen Marie Arrasmith, and Volha Liaudanskaya draw together in 2026 what is known about chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a brain degeneration linked to repeated head impacts. Connecting years of knocks to later disease has lacked a single clear mechanism. Their synthesis spans population studies, brain tissue work, and clinical reports to build one chain from exposure to decline.

Initial injury sets off energy failure in brain cells, inflammation, and damage to nerve fibres across several cell types. Over time those processes promote misfolded proteins, including tau, which gathers in a distinctive pattern around small blood vessels deep in the brain's folds. Symptoms vary widely and current scans and fluid tests lack precision, while no single lab model captures the full course, leaving detection during life as a central research need.
pmc-13499341:
Shi and colleagues report a 2026 study of how tomato plants defend themselves against a fungus gnat, Bradysia impatiens, whose larvae chew roots, stems, and leaves and cut yields. The team combined two profiling methods, gene activity and small-molecule chemistry, on leaves one week after larvae were introduced to the soil.

Feeding triggered wide gene reprogramming: nearly three thousand genes changed activity. The changed genes clustered in defense pathways, including MAPK signaling, hormone signals, pathogen-interaction routes, and the building of phenylpropanoid compounds, a class of plant defense chemicals. Chemistry profiles shifted alongside the genes. Because larvae also damaged stems and roots, the leaf response mixes direct chewing defense with whole-plant alarm signals. The mapped response gives breeders candidate genes and chemicals for tomatoes that resist this pest with less insecticide.
pmc-13500441:
Arefayne Mesfen Dessye explores in 2026 what he calls the Ethiopian paradox, where a nation famous for distance-running dominance also loses many elite runners early to burnout and injury. His mixed-methods study compared 60 retired elite Ethiopian endurance runners in two equal groups. One group's careers lasted at least ten years and the other's ended within seven, blending training log analysis and psychological surveys with in-depth interviews.

Durable runners showed steadier training loads, stronger coping with adversity, and lower maladaptive perfectionism, each difference statistically significant in the reported comparisons. Interviews distilled three separating themes, covering coaching that granted guided autonomy, an athletic identity integrated with the rest of life, and community support acting as a buffer. Combining the strands produced a three-pillar durability profile offered to coaches as a framework for building long careers rather than burning bright and short.
pmc-13500841:
Longfei Dang leads a four-author team proposing a 2026 imaging algorithm for borehole radar, a tool lowered into drill holes to picture rock formations underground. Existing logging methods force a trade-off: they see a few metres in fine detail or reach far with blur. The new time-frequency joint algorithm uses the direct wave, the signal that travels straight from transmitter to receiver, as a stable reference for normalizing amplitude and synchronizing timing, which suppresses source jitter.

Wavelet and Fourier filtering clean out-of-band noise, and adaptive amplification that grows with time compensates for signal spreading and absorption in rock. In experiments the method stretched the detection range to about 8.5 to 10 metres, well beyond the under-3-metre reach of conventional high-resolution logging. Spatial resolution at the same time improved to the centimetre level, roughly 5 to 10 centimetres. The authors flag that wider geological testing is still needed.
pmc-13501841:
Jinrui Xing leads an eight-author team with a 2026 study of the gut-brain axis in adolescent mice made depressed by chronic unpredictable mild stress. Stressed mice lost interest in sugar water, gave up sooner in a swim test, and moved less in an open field, the standard behavioural signature. The team sequenced gut microbes from intestinal contents and measured brain-linked chemicals in the gut lining by mass spectrometry, then correlated microbes, chemicals, and behaviour.

Microbe variety fell in the stressed group, and community structure shifted modestly but clearly. In the colon lining, the whole serotonin pathway sagged: serotonin itself, its precursor, its breakdown product, and kynurenine all dropped, while phenylethylamine and norepinephrine rose. One bacterium, Lactobacillus acidophilus, tracked with both happier behaviour and healthier chemistry. The authors stress the work is correlational, a map for future causal tests.
pmc-13501941:
Madsen and colleagues compared intimacy and relationship life between partnered cancer survivors and people without a cancer history in Denmark's nationally representative Project SEXUS cohort. Their 2026 study covers 47,718 partnered adults, including more than three thousand survivors. Cancer is well known to damage sexual function, but whether it changes how much people value intimacy, why they have sex, and how their relationships feel was less clear.

Madsen found survivors rated the importance of various kinds of intimacy, their reasons for having sex, and their relationship characteristics the same as peers without cancer. This held after demographic weighting and adjustment. The similarity held for both sexes and for survivors within five years of diagnosis as well as longer-term ones. The authors argue that survivorship care should treat sexual health holistically, recognizing that intimacy and relational strengths often survive cancer intact and can buffer the functional difficulties that do occur.
pmc-13502141:
Linrong Li leads a five-author team with a 2026 review of antibody-encapsulated drugs, a proposed successor to antibody-drug conjugates in cancer therapy. Conjugates weld a poison to an antibody, but the welding is uneven: drug-to-antibody ratios vary, linkers can leak early, and production is complex. The new platform instead tucks a fixed number of drug molecules inside an antibody without a covalent bond, using a technique called single protein encapsulation. That promises exact dosing, less premature release, and simpler production.

The proof-of-concept pairs trastuzumab, a HER2-targeting antibody, with actinomycin D sealed inside it. Across cancer models with varying HER2 levels the construct killed tumours while showing a friendly toxicity profile in animals. Parallel trials of albumin-encapsulated medicines support the wider platform. The authors position the approach as a way past conjugate resistance and limits, widening which payloads and proteins can be used.
pmc-13502641:
Liang-Ting Wu leads a four-author team with a 2026 study of why fluorinating an ether solvent makes lithium-metal battery electrolytes resist oxidation. Fluorinated versions of an ether had shown excellent stability in tests, but solvent design remained guesswork. The team attacked the question at three scales. Density functional theory covered electronic structure, ab initio molecular dynamics covered short-time behaviour, and a machine-learning force field covered longer interfacial simulations at the cathode surface.

Three fluorine effects emerged. Beta-fluorination stabilizes the ethoxy carbon-hydrogen bonds through an inductive effect. Shifted electrons weaken the solvent's grip on the nickel-rich cathode surface, discouraging oxidation and carbon-carbon bond activation there. The fluorinated molecule's dipole moment makes it line up one way, shielding its methoxy group from the surface. Together the three explain the stability jump, and the authors offer the dissection as a template for electrolyte design.
pmc-13503141:
Li and a large team chart how tobacco's disease burden splits by sex across three decades in twenty twenty-six. Smoking, secondhand smoke, and chewing tobacco all hit men and women unevenly. The team used the Global Burden of Disease twenty twenty-three data set. Burden trends were split by place, time, and age, then projected to twenty fifty.

Men carried the heavier burden in every risk and year. Growth and aging of populations drove most of the absolute rise. Exposure shifts pushed the sexes along unlike paths. Some regions showed near parity for smoking, led by rich countries. Future gaps hinge on which exposure path unfolds.
pmc-13503841:
Hadil Faris Alotaibi leads a team that uses machine learning to predict how well drug cocrystals will dissolve, in a 2026 study. Cocrystals pair a drug with a partner compound to help poor drugs mix with water. Picking the right partner depends on how the two parts interact.

The team fed 181 samples, each with 86 traits from two descriptor methods, into three tree-based models. A search method modeled on dragonflies tuned each model. One model, Extra Trees, beat the rest on all three solubility outputs, with fit scores above 0.86. Traits from both descriptor sources mattered. The authors say the tool can speed the screening of partner compounds before lab work begins.
pmc-13504141:
Jintao Cui leads a team building a breast cancer outlook score from genes tied to a contact zone between two cell parts, in a 2026 study. The zone links the energy factories to the protein-folding workshop, and its faults can steer tumor growth and immune response. Its value for forecasting care was not yet clear.

From 83 such genes, the team distilled a four-gene score that split patients into high and low risk across several cohorts. Low-risk tumors held more immune cells and were tipped to answer better to immune therapy. High-risk tumors looked more open to chemo and targeted drugs. Single-cell maps showed where each gene acts in the tumor. Lab tests confirmed three of the four genes run high in breast cancer cells.
pmc-13505141:
Emad Shamsan and co-authors studied a severe parasitic liver disease caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, which grows into liver tissue and scars it over time. They focused on a signalling pair, the protein IL-33 and its receptor ST2, and asked whether blocking ST2 changes the course of infection. Work combined liver tissue from patients with a mouse model of the disease.

Patient tissue showed raised IL-33 and ST2 alongside markers of immune activity and scarring. In infected mice, blocking ST2 shrank parasite lesions and reduced liver invasion. Treated livers carried less scar tissue, fewer gathered immune cells, and lower levels of several inflammatory signals in the blood. Because parasite burden also fell, the authors note that further work must separate direct anti-scarring effects from effects that follow from controlling the parasite.
pmc-13505741:
Minji Jeong and co-authors improved how perovskite solar films are grown by vacuum deposition, a route valued for even coatings. The weak point is the start of growth: one ingredient lands first and clumps into islands, leaving pinholes and defects where the film meets the electron-transport layer. Their fix pre-lays an extremely thin lead iodide layer that acts as a seed bed.

That seed layer converts fully as the remaining ingredients arrive, so grains start evenly and grow sideways into a coherent film. Grains ended up larger, defect counts in the bulk and at the interface fell, and charge carriers lived nearly twice as long before recombining. Cells built this way reached a stabilised efficiency close to twenty percent. The authors offer the seeding trick as a general recipe for cleaner vacuum-grown films in future optoelectronic devices.
pmc-13507441:
Emilie Bechard, Jean-Yves Le Guennec, and Marie Demion study how a fatty acid switches on a potassium channel in a 2026 paper. The channel, found in many cells, normally lets more current flow one way than the other. The fatty acid, known as DHA, can flip it into an even, leak like mode. The team tested the normal channel and a mutated version in cultured human cells.

DHA increased current across all voltages by putting more channels into a conducting state. Breaking the channel's filter gate blunted the effect, suggesting DHA works by stabilizing that gate. Starting activity varied a lot between cells, explaining uneven responses. The findings show how fatty acids can tune cell excitability through this channel.
pmc-13508041:
De Manincor and colleagues ran an experimental warming study on plant and pollinator communities to see how climate warming breaks their partnership, in a 2026 ecology paper. The usual suspect is timing mismatch, flowers and bees shifting seasons at different rates, but direct experimental evidence was missing. The team warmed whole spring communities and tracked timing, traits, behavior, and the fitness of both partners.

De Manincor found warming shifted both flowering and bee activity yet kept the partners in step with each other, so timing mismatch was not the culprit. Instead warming cut flower numbers, lowered the nectar and pollen rewards, reduced bee visits, and depressed bee survival, weakening the mutualism through body condition and behavior rather than calendars. Both plant and bee fitness fell as a result. The authors argue conservation attention should move from phenology alone toward the physiological and behavioral pathways that quietly erode species interactions.
pmc-13508341:
Ju Chang and seven co-authors test whether spraying tiny silica particles on bamboo leaves improves seedling nutrition, in 2026 work. Bamboo locks away carbon and guards forests, yet how nano-silica shapes its nutrient balance was unclear. Seedlings of a large bamboo species received six spray strengths, from none up to the highest dose. The team measured leaf greenness, silica content, and the levels and ratios of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in the plants. Patterns were checked with correlation and grouping analyses.

A middle dose gave the best overall result. It raised leaf greenness and boosted silica, phosphorus, and potassium stores while keeping nitrogen high. The top dose backfired, cutting greenness and nutrient stores. Greenness tracked closely with silica, nitrogen, and phosphorus levels. The authors suggest a moderate spray can sharpen seedling quality for planting programs, while warning that more is not better with these particles.
pmc-13508441:
Meryem Bekmezci and Mehmet Semih Demirtas compare blood inflammation scores in pregnancies exposed to methamphetamine and in matched controls, in 2026 work. The drug is known to harm birth outcomes, and simple blood ratios may flag that risk. Records covered 52 exposed pregnancies and 93 controls at a university hospital. Inflammation indices were built from admission blood counts for mothers. For babies, counts existed for only 28 exposed newborns, drawn when doctors judged them needed. Paired tests compared mother and baby scores.

Mothers in the exposed group ran higher on every inflammation measure, including cell counts and combined indices. Their scores were far above controls by clear statistical margins. Mother and baby scores also differed from each other in paired checks. The authors suggest cheap blood indices could help flag exposed pregnancies needing closer watch, while noting the small newborn set limits how far the baby findings stretch.
pmc-13509141:
Dima and Cosgarea tell of SPAM, a new cut way to widen jaw bone with sinus bone. The way uses the host's own sinus plate for the build step. It runs with sinus lift and tooth post set in one meet. Eight hosts with thin back jaw bone took the care. Ages ran 52 to 71, with seven dames in the set. Two hosts in the set smoked in the tale facts.

Side build used the cut wall of the sinus port as graft. A stock graft part joined that wall in the build step. In sum, 24 posts went in with SPAM and lift at once. Heal ran smooth in all cases post the cut work. Bone width gain ran near 9.28 at first read post care. It held near 8.37 at the long track read in the set.
pmc-13509841:
Fernanda Carvalho and Joana P. Costa survey metal compounds built around camphor-based parts as possible cancer and germ fighters, in a 2026 mini-review. Camphor comes from a familiar plant source, and chemists can reshape its structure and attach different metal centers to tune how the resulting compounds act on cells. The review draws together lab findings on these compounds and their effects.

Choosing the right metal and shaping the camphor part can strengthen killing of cancer cells while also adding action against bacteria or fungi. That double action makes the compounds attractive for settings where infection and cancer risks meet. The authors point to a next step of loading such compounds into body-friendly materials, such as mineral coatings or gels, to make wound dressings and other composites that treat as they cover.
pmc-13510841:
Pampalakis and Pontiki profile an obscure family of nerve agents entirely by computer. Their 2026 paper studies the phosphonate esters of alkyl acetoacetates. These little-known members of the V-agent class, which includes VX, exist as two geometric forms. The E and Z isomers have largely unmeasured properties. The authors applied computational tools to predict absorption, chemical behaviour, and structure-related toxicity.

The models predict these agents penetrate skin, making them contact hazards, and also cross the gut wall and the blood-brain barrier. Certain liver enzymes were predicted to handle the two isomers differently, which may explain reports that the E forms are far more toxic than their Z counterparts. Stability analysis likewise supported the reported fragility of the Z forms. The authors present this first detailed in-silico description as groundwork for countermeasures, requiring targeted laboratory validation.
pmc-13511541:
Pan Tang and eight co-authors build a nanoparticle vaccine against a pig diarrhea virus that costs the swine industry heavily, in 2026 work. Current shots give weak immune responses, poor gut-level protection, and short cover. The team mounted the virus's S1 spike part onto ferritin protein shells using a snap-together tag system, then checked particle shape and size before testing in mice and piglets.

After two doses, piglets made strong antibody levels that topped those from a standard killed-virus vaccine, alongside higher virus-blocking titers and higher immune signal levels. When challenged with the live virus, vaccinated piglets were fully protected and showed far milder diarrhea and gut damage than unprotected animals. Mice also mounted strong body-wide and cell-based responses. The authors call the candidate promising while noting this is an early step before farm rollout.
pmc-13511741:
Marci K. Sontag and Susanna A. McColley introduce a special issue on newborn screening for cystic fibrosis, a testing practice now nearly fifty years old, in 2026 work. Screening methods, teaching approaches, and treatments have all advanced since the first programs. The issue spans lab testing, screening accuracy, hard diagnostic cases, and the effect of newer modulator drugs on the screening picture.

One anchor piece sets out United States consensus guidelines for the best screening setup, drawn up to catch as many affected infants as possible. A companion commentary weighs the load those aims place on public health programs. State programs also report their own fixes, including seasonal cut-off tuning in California and a full pathway review in Georgia. Wide variation between programs drives the push for shared standards that still fit local limits.
pmc-13512541:
Mingyuan Yuan and Fei Zhou propose a shared control frame for boosting artemisinin output in the plant Artemisia annua, in 2026 work. The compound, a frontline malaria drug ingredient, is made and stored in tiny hair-like glands on the plant. Yield is capped by a tug-of-war among gland number, chemical flow through the pathway, and total plant growth. The review centers on a family of switch proteins called bHLH factors that tie those threads together.

One family member merges two hormone signals to switch on core production genes. Another links gland birth to pathway flow and teams with partners to amplify key enzymes. A third stretches the control to the whole plant, matching gland formation with photosynthesis and carbon use. The authors argue that editing several hubs at once, guided by multi-layer data, could break the growth-versus-defense trade-off that breeding alone has not.
pmc-13513141:
Huang and colleagues compared a 2026 cohort of older patients given indobufen or aspirin after heart bypass surgery for unstable angina. Patients aged seventy and above face a fine balance between preventing clots and causing bleeding. Indobufen blocks the same enzyme as aspirin but is less studied after bypass operations.

The single centre study covered operations from 2017 to 2021 and kept seventy-nine patients after screening, forty-nine on aspirin pathways and thirty on indobufen. Huang weighted the groups statistically to balance sixteen baseline traits before comparing two year outcomes. No significant difference appeared in major heart and brain events, serious bleeding, or the combined outcome. Graft checks were available for most patients at one and two years, and the authors call for larger prospective trials.
pmc-13513941:
Ahmed and Cao published a 2026 study on steering a blood protein's shape on titanium implants. Fibrinogen, a clotting protein, is among the first to coat any implant. Its shape on the surface steers how tissues accept the device later. The team coated titanium with chalk-like calcite using electric deposition.

Longer coating times thickened the layer to near-full surface coverage overall. Calcium leaking from the coat reshaped fibrinogen into sponge-like clumps. A three-hour coat produced the strongest sponge effect in their tests. Surface scans confirmed the protein's new bonding pattern after reshaping. Guided protein shaping could help implants knit with tissue better. Calcium release rose with coating time in a steady climb. Coverage neared 99.8 percent after the longest coating run in tests.
pmc-13515541:
Marcelina Niemiec-Urbanczyk and co-authors track quality of life, as given by patients, after endoscopic surgery for sinonasal inverted papilloma. Their 2026 cohort study tracked patients over time. It comes from one clinic linked to a university.

Sixty-nine adults with tumours that were shown to be of that type were treated by endoscopic surgery. At each visit, they filled in a sino-nasal outcome questionnaire. A broad questionnaire on quality of life was added from 2022 on. Mean follow-up was about sixty-three months. The tumours came back in about thirty percent of patients. Hundreds of checks made after surgery were read with models for how scores move over time. The study deals with a gap. In the past, results given by patients over the long term were few, and were in many cases from one point in time.
pmc-13517041:
Zuzana Hudáková and four colleagues link long non-coding RNAs to drug resistance in glioblastoma in a 2026 cell study. The standard drug temozolomide fails often against this brain tumour. Three tumour cell lines with different drug sensitivity, plus normal star-shaped brain cells, were exposed to the drug for up to three days. The team tracked survival, cell-cycle behaviour, a repair protein called MGMT, and nine candidate RNA regulators.

The A172 line proved most sensitive and the T98G line most resistant. Sensitive cells jammed in the run-up to division, while resistant cells barely reacted and carried far more MGMT. RNA patterns split the lines clearly: MALAT1 fell across the board, while NCK1-AS1 surged, above all in the resistant line. Drug exposure itself shifted several regulators, hinting at active adaptation. Hudáková's team names four RNAs as candidate markers and targets for tackling resistance.
pmc-13518841:
Vladimir Nikora, Hongwei Fang, Guojian He, and Lei Huang argue in 2026 that flowing surface water helped life make the leap from single cells to multicellular forms. Bigger, many-celled organisms burn far more energy, so they need faster nutrient supply. Rising oxygen in the Neoproterozoic era gets most of the credit in standard accounts.

Nikora and colleagues propose that widespread water movement boosted nutrient delivery to microbes, acting as a necessary partner to oxygen. They define three testable flow regimes governing uptake for both attached and free-floating microbes. Streambeds, where water meets the bottom, may have been breeding grounds for early multicellularity. Their framework yields predictions linking organism size, flow, and habitat.
pmc-13519041:
Yamin Li and Zuoxiang He review thyroid cancers that stop responding to radioactive iodine treatment, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Such cancers cause most thyroid cancer deaths, and survival with spread disease is near ten percent at ten years. Experts still disagree on the exact definition of this state. The review traces how gene changes silence the cell part that pulls iodine in.

Care has shifted over the last decade toward targeted drugs that block vessel growth and faulty growth switches. Some drug pairs can wake iodine uptake again in chosen patients. Immune drugs help a rare subgroup. The authors sort options by gene driver and proof level, and note that patient burden gets less space in most reviews.
pmc-13519441:
Mokshada Badadare and colleagues examined how dental implant material relates to peri-implantitis, the inflammation and bone loss that can undo an implant. Published in 2026, the clinical study at a tertiary dental center recorded probing depth, bleeding, X-ray bone loss, plaque scores, and implant material for treated patients. Implant makeup and surface finish shape how microbes settle and how the immune system reacts.

Rougher surfaces and heavier plaque went with higher inflammation, showing the trade-off behind surfaces built to grip bone well. The authors urge careful material choice, smoother engineering where it fits, and strict upkeep to cut disease risk. Readers learn why the same roughness that helps an implant bond can also invite the biofilm that threatens it, and what maintenance habits keep that balance safe.
pmc-13520241:
Ming Wang leads a large team in 2026 building turmeric-derived nanovesicles to calm the runaway immune response that erodes bone in gum disease. Excess web-like traps cast out by neutrophils, called NETs, feed inflammation and bone-eating cell activity in a self-amplifying loop. Single-cell data from public sets flagged faulty trap formation as a treatment target.

The tiny plant vesicles, loaded with turmeric's own active compounds, were eagerly taken up by neutrophils. Treated cells cast far fewer traps, showing lower oxidative stress markers and less expelled DNA. Gene profiles confirmed quieter trap pathways alongside stronger antioxidant defenses. In mice with periodontitis, vesicles gathered at inflamed sites, slowed bone loss, and preserved bone structure.
pmc-13522441:
Kedziora and co-authors demonstrate in 2026 a way to steer the spin of light inside perovskite microwires, thin crystal channels that guide light like optical fibers. They worked with exciton-polaritons, hybrid particles that are part light and part matter excitation, which can condense into a coherent state. Controlling the polarization, or spin, of such signals is a step toward photonic circuits that encode information in spin.

Above the condensation threshold, the microwires emitted polarized light from their edges in a pattern matching the optical spin Hall effect, where opposite spins travel to opposite sides. The emitted light showed chirality exceeding eighty percent, meaning one spin direction strongly dominated, and the spin-polarized signal propagated over tens of micrometers along the wire. The crystals form a natural cavity without mirrors. The authors present these CsPbBr3 waveguides as a platform for spin-coded information transport on a chip.
pmc-13522541:
Guo and colleagues identified in 2026 a receptor for a bacterial signal molecule in Lactiplantibacillus plantarum, a gut-friendly bacterium. The signal, c-di-AMP, is a small ring-shaped messenger that shapes how bacteria interact with their host, but its role in this species was unclear. The team found a protein named RwpL, made of a single DNA-binding part, that senses the messenger and controls gene activity.

Guo showed RwpL can both switch genes off and on, depending on where it binds near each gene's start. It blocked one gene whose product helps the bacterium grip fibronectin, a surface protein of gut lining cells, and boosted a gene for an enzyme that breaks down matrix. When signal levels rose, RwpL loosened its grip on DNA and its partner protein, flipping both effects and raising adhesion to gut cells. The dual, reversible switch tunes host contact.
pmc-13523241:
Toshiyuki Suzuki and colleagues identify tissue features tied to pancreatic leakage after surgery in a 2026 study. A fistula, an abnormal leak of pancreatic fluid, is a serious complication after removal of the body and tail of the pancreas. One hundred eighty-six patients were studied, with thickness measured on preoperative scans and the cut surface examined under a microscope for small duct branches and scarring.

One third of patients developed a clinically relevant leak. Risk rose with a thicker pancreas at the cut site, a higher density of branched small ducts, and a lower share of fibrous scarring. Thick glands also tended to show denser branching and less scarring, suggesting the features travel together. The authors propose that gland anatomy and tissue makeup jointly shape leak risk and could guide surgical technique.
pmc-13523341:
Fanny Iafrate-Luterbacher and colleagues track a heart risk marker over time in young people with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically set blood fat particle usually measured once in a lifetime, yet its behavior in childhood was poorly known. Annual fasting measurements from two hundred eighty-six patients at a Geneva hospital between 2012 and 2023 were analyzed.

More than fourteen hundred measurements were available. At first testing, about one quarter of participants had elevated levels. Among those measured repeatedly, nearly one third fluctuated by more than half of their personal maximum, and about one in eight crossed the clinical risk threshold at some point. Levels peaked in late childhood and varied modestly by season. The authors challenge the single lifetime measurement approach for this group.
pmc-13523441:
Hilda Machika Kanjedza, Ditress Nyirongo, and Genesis Chorwe-Sungani report a 2026 validation study from postnatal clinics in Lilongwe, Malawi, for a Chichewa version of the City Birth Trauma Scale. The scale measures post-traumatic stress linked to childbirth and follows DSM-5 criteria. Malawi previously had no validated Chichewa tool and no prevalence data for this condition after birth.

Working at Bwaila Hospital and Area 25 Health Centre, the team translated and adapted the scale, then enrolled 384 postnatal mothers through systematic random sampling. A structured medical interview put prevalence near one in five mothers, while the scale itself gave a lower figure. Reliability and accuracy measures were acceptable, with an optimal cut-off above 23. The authors conclude that the translated scale can support screening in Malawian postnatal care.
pmc-13524941:
C. Kishor Kumar Reddy and others propose, in a 2026 study, a sonar system that copies echolocation principles and pairs them with machine learning for underwater detection and navigation. Standard sonar uses much energy, suffers noise, and weakens in changing water conditions. Their model adjusts the pulses it sends on the fly in response to the environment.

Its signal steps include special filtering, wavelet decomposition, and adaptive thresholding to clean echoes. A convolutional network and a memory network then sort the echoes. In simulation tests tuned to real ocean data, the system reached 92.7 percent classification accuracy against 85.4 percent for standard methods. Energy use fell by about a fifth, signal clarity rose, false alarms dropped, and depth readings grew sharper through a sound speed fix. Trials stayed in simulation rather than open water.
pmc-13526741:
Hui Yu and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a cell adhesion protein called ITGA7 restrains thyroid cancer by binding fibronectin and quieting a growth pathway. Thyroid cancer is the commonest endocrine malignancy and usually curable, yet some patients relapse. ITGA7 levels were compared between tumor and neighboring normal tissue.

Expression of ITGA7 was lower in cancers at both message and protein levels, including in cell lines. Removing ITGA7 made cancer cells grow, divide, migrate, and invade more, while resisting cell death. Binding tests confirmed a physical partnership with fibronectin, whose levels rose in tumors and moved opposite to ITGA7. Silencing fibronectin impeded tumor behavior, and pathway blots plus a mouse graft model supported the proposed chain through the PI3K and AKT signaling route.
pmc-13527141:
Diksha Arora, Jhilik Bhattacharya, and Chinmaya Panigrahy present, in a 2026 study, a deep learning method that reads rice leaf nutrient levels from drone multispectral images, instead of slow wet-lab chemistry. Knowing leaf nutrient levels guides fertilizer choices and yield. Their system searches for a good network design while using polynomial approximation functions and adaptive activations to cope with small training sets.

Field trials ran at Punjab Agricultural University across treatments and growth stages. The model read eleven macro and micro nutrients with low average errors in two review settings. Error ranges came with the predictions, and feature maps showed leaves with similar nutrient values grouping together. Ablation and cross checks by treatment and plot confirmed each part's role, and the method beat standard deep and machine learning baselines.
pmc-13528041:
Zina Bai and ten colleagues published this 2026 study on irisin, a hormone released from muscle during exercise, as a treatment for flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Earlier work hinted irisin protects lungs, but the mechanism was murky. The team measured irisin and its receptor, integrin αVβ5, in lung tissue, then modelled smoke and toxin lung injury in mice and cells to trace how irisin acts.

In patients, irisin levels were lowest in smokers with COPD, while the receptor and a stress marker ran high. In mice, irisin improved lung function and eased emphysema and inflammation. Blocking the receptor with the drug cilengitide abolished those benefits, and silencing the receptor in cells did too. Irisin bound the receptor, steadied the cell's protein-folding compartment through a PERK pathway, and activated the energy sensor AMPK. The authors propose the receptor pathway as a treatment direction for COPD.
pmc-13528141:
Masayuki Kaneda and three colleagues study which Japanese hospitals claim an advanced ward pharmacy fee in a 2026 paper. The fee signals pharmacists doing deep ward-based care. pmc-13528541:

pmc-13529841:

pmc-13530141:

pmc-13530241:
Taghi Shirzad and colleagues image underground fractures in 2026 at the Geysers geothermal field in California using tiny earthquakes as their light source. Slow zones fell into three kinds: fault damage with altered rock, boundaries near the steam cap, and patches tied to injection work. Combined with quake locations, the map tracks fluid movement and stress change.
pmc-13531741:

pmc-13532241:

pmc-13533041:
Gamze Babur Guler and colleagues reply in 2026 to comments on their single-centre study of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a thickened heart muscle condition. Follow-up had a median of 13 months, which they call short for a slow disease.

pmc-13533841:

pmc-13534441:
Nawaz and seven co-authors study small RNA regulators in muscle in type two diabetes, in work from twenty twenty-six. MicroRNAs tune gene activity and shift in diabetes, both inside cells and in blood. Whether those shifts come from the body milieu or are built into cells was unclear.

The team grew muscle cells from stem cells of diabetic and healthy donors, a disease in a dish model. Cell and secreted microRNAs were profiled. Diabetic cells kept distinct microRNA patterns even outside the body, proving a cell intrinsic effect. Matching gene and protein data showed the regulators hit protein levels far more than gene messages.
pmc-13534741:
Fuad S Al-Duais and colleagues propose in 2026 an uncertainty-aware framework that reads chest X-rays for pneumonia, lung scarring, and fluid build-up. Many image models give overconfident answers, which is risky in high-stakes diagnosis. Their system joins a vision transformer, a two-way sequence module, and a Bayesian fusion layer.

Training used two large public chest image collections after lung outlining and heavy augmentation. The model reached high accuracy with a top ranking score and very low calibration error. Calibrated confidence helps clinicians tell safe calls from risky ones that need human review.
pmc-13535741:
Juan Li and colleagues analyse in 2026 the spread and drivers of human brucellosis in Zhejiang Province, China, from 2018 to 2023. The animal-spread disease has risen even in developed regions with little livestock farming. Case data from 11 city areas fed Bayesian space-time models plus checks for clustering and risk factors.

Cases clustered clearly, with higher risk in four areas and lower risk in five coastal or urban areas. Live sheep imports and slaughter volume were the dominant drivers, each tied to higher incidence. Tighter control of sheep transport and slaughter in high-risk areas is recommended.
pmc-13536641:
Moga and coauthors adapt a tooth-age method for children in Romania. Tooth growth helps dentists and courts guess a child true age. Global charts may not fit each group of children well. The team tested a classic staging method on local X-rays.

They read 860 jaw X-rays of children aged 3 to 15. Each tooth got a stage score by the classic method. A math curve linked total score to true age. They compared the local curve with the global chart. Checks showed how close each guess came to true age. A local fit may serve clinics and courts more fairly.
pmc-13536841:
Qiuxian Ye and colleagues examine why nurses speak up with ideas to improve care in a 2026 three-wave survey in China. Nurses caring for vulnerable patients face heavy pressure, so the study tests whether a trauma-aware workplace climate encourages constructive suggestions. A total of 508 matched replies came from nurses in six hospitals and related sites in two provinces, spaced two weeks apart. Models traced links through felt empowerment and cultural humility.

A stronger trauma-aware climate tracked with more speaking up and stronger felt empowerment. That feeling in turn tracked with speaking up and carried part of the climate link. The indirect path grew stronger when cultural humility, meaning openness to other backgrounds, ran high. The authors stress that the patterns show association rather than proof of cause, and they highlight supportive conditions for nurse voice.
pmc-13538641:

When blood flow returns after a blocked brain artery, a second wave of damage follows, and metabolism may steer it through gene switches. The enzyme, which makes a key building block from citrate, rose after vessel blockage and reperfusion in mouse brains. Blocking or silencing it in animals and cultured neurons was tested.

The enzyme raised the building block supply, boosting gene switch tags on the promoter regions of power unit chain genes, which improved power unit function and curbed oxidative stress. The authors nominate the pathway as a fresh stroke treatment target.
pmc-13538741:
A Rumanes and colleagues examine foot ulcers as a warning marker in people with both diabetes and heart failure in a 2026 Dutch cohort study. Records covered 4,937 adults treated at one large center over two decades, split by whether a foot ulcer had occurred. Death and heart failure admissions were tracked over three years, with five-year death checks and bias-aware models.

When timing started at ulcer diagnosis, one-year death rates ran dramatically higher in the ulcer group. A time-aware model tied ulcer occurrence independently to nearly triple the death hazard. The authors cast ulcers as a marker of advanced disease meriting intensified team care.
pmc-13540341:

pmc-13540841:

States ran from healthy gums to early periodontitis. Bacterial diversity ran higher in women. It also rose in the group with both gastritis and early gum disease.
pmc-13541641:

Trials in children who have never met the virus show no sign of the vaccine-enhanced respiratory disease that haunted the field. The authors weigh newer platforms honestly: shots that protect newborns through their mothers fade within the first year.
pmc-13542441:

pmc-13543341:

pmc-13543641:

pmc-13547241:

pmc-13547941:

pmc-13548641:

pmc-13548941:

pmc-13550541:

pmc-13550641:

pmc-13551841:

pmc-13553241:

pmc-13554241:

pmc-13555641:

pmc-13555941:

pmc-13556041:

pmc-13556141:

pmc-13556241:

pmc-13558641:

pmc-13558741:

pmc-13559141:

pmc-13559541:

pmc-13560141:

pmc-13560241:

pmc-13560441:

pmc-13560541:

pmc-13561241:

Antibiotics and intensive support were given, but blood thinners were withheld because of the active bleeding. She improved steadily and left hospital in stable condition.
pmc-13561441:
Yuanyuan Yang and colleagues pilot a nudge-based phone app for blood pressure self-management. Their mixed methods study from twenty twenty-six targets younger patients. Young and middle-aged patients often manage hypertension poorly. Limited mental bandwidth is part of the problem, they argue.

Users rated the app favourably on a standard scale. Interviews added six themes explaining how nudges helped. Small prompts at the right moment beat heavy instruction. The pilot supports a larger trial of behavioural app design.
pmc-13561741:
Kwang Jin Ko and Jae Hoon Chung report early bladder function findings after single-port transvesical robot-assisted prostate removal, an approach credited with fast continence recovery. Their 2026 prospective case series studies eleven prostate cancer patients of one surgeon, all without spread on imaging. Full urodynamic testing and questionnaires were completed three months after surgery.

Continence climbed steeply, with zero-pad rates reaching 90.9 percent by three months in the small series. Cancer control lagged, though: positive margins hit 45.5 percent of specimens and PSA persisted in two patients in the reported outcomes. With no preoperative studies or control group, the authors refuse claims of superiority and urge careful patient selection.
pmc-13562541:
Vahid Parvaz and Jabbar Ganji build a tool that estimates how severe electricity losses from theft, faulty meters, and billing errors are, rather than flagging them. Utilities lose money on such non-technical losses, and inspectors need to know where the damage is biggest. A boosted-tree regression model, pruned by a feature-elimination routine, predicts that gap from smart-meter data.

Its uncertainty bands behaved well, catching about 94 percent of cases inside the nominal 95 percent range. Load-related features drove the deviations most. The authors frame the output as a ranked risk guide for inspections, never as proof that a given customer stole power.
pmc-13562641:
Gongyu Zhang and seven colleagues build a score that predicts which patients will still hold titanium clips in the stomach six months after an endoscopic procedure. Clips close the wound left when early stomach lesions are cut out through a scope. Most fall away as healing completes, yet lingering clips may cause trouble. The 2026 study reviewed 1,055 patients, split into training and two validation groups. Regression analysis searched their records for traits tied to clips staying put.

Overall, 132 patients, 12.5 percent, kept clips at six months. Three traits predicted it: a tumour in the upper third of the stomach, worth two points, plus diabetes and the use of eight or more clips, worth one point each. Scores sorted patients into risk bands whose rates climbed from a few percent to over half. The score held up on fresh data, and clinicians could use it to plan follow-up where need is likeliest.
pmc-13562741:
Oluwakemi O. Onabanjo and six colleagues turn discarded banana flowers into a sponge for a stubborn synthetic dye in wastewater. Methylene blue lingers in water and threatens people and aquatic life, while treatment plants need cheap capture materials. Uptake peaked under alkaline conditions. The acid-treated material held 48.6 milligrams of dye per gram, against 29.9 for the raw waste, a clear gain from a cheap step. Its surface measured 106.3 square metres per gram with pores near 6.1 nanometres wide. Heat calculations showed the capture runs spontaneously and absorbs warmth. The authors offer farm waste as a low-cost candidate for dye cleanup.
pmc-13563741:
Hongliang Gao and eight colleagues test whether stimulating two acupuncture points beats one alone at preventing sickness after womb-scope surgery. Nausea and vomiting trouble many patients after hysteroscopic procedures. Their 2026 trial enrolled 90 women and split them three ways: thumbtack needles at both the Neiguan wrist point and the Zusanli leg point, Neiguan alone, or a sham device as control. Nausea and vomiting were tracked across the first day after surgery, along with pain scores and gut restart time.

The combined group pulled ahead of everyone: its pain scores at six, twelve, and twenty-four hours were the lowest, and its bowels woke soonest. Single-point treatment helped, but the pairing did more. The authors recommend the two-point routine as a cheap layer of protection for these operations.
pmc-13563841:
Yuchen Pan and four colleagues pool published findings on a failure mode of hepatitis B prevention: babies protected at birth who still catch the virus. Their 2026 review, registered and run to reporting standards, searched five databases for people born to infected mothers, and forty studies qualified. Breakthrough was defined as turning positive for the surface antigen, or for a core antibody that marks infection, at age two or later.

The authors argue for optimised schedules and follow-up in this group, since exposure accumulates even when disease stays rare.
pmc-13564441:
Simpson, Dey, Lees, Da Silva, Bristowe, and Senn wrote in twenty twenty-six on linking electric and magnetic order. They aimed to build that link at near room temperature. Stuff that links the two orders is prized for future devices. Design rules are clear for simple perovskites but scarce for complex frames. Their model was a hexagonal form of a manganite crystal. One tilt fault in the crystal units breaks the balance of the form.

That tilt makes electric polarization and a magnetic moment arise together. Beam tests and magnetic checks confirmed both orders last to high heat. The form's order held to about four hundred fifty kelvin. The method rests on symmetry study plus first-principles math. The team offers it as a design frame for other such materials too. It should carry to other frame materials, not just this crystal.
pmc-13570941:
Ng and a large team of co-authors tracked spinal fusion technology in this study from twenty twenty-six. Surgeons can now use navigation screens or robots to guide screws during spine fusion. How widely these tools have spread across the United States was unclear. The team mined a national sample of hospital stays from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-two.

Over two million fusions were counted. Only about seven percent used navigation or robots, though the share rose from under three percent to over thirteen percent. Navigation grew steadily, while robotics grew faster from a smaller base. Raw complication rates looked higher in the technology groups. The authors warn that sicker, harder cases may explain that gap and call for better data.
pmc-13571241:
Isabelle Fleury leads a 2026 letter reporting real-world evidence on fixed-duration venetoclax treatment for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The question is what works after the disease progresses on a covalent BTK inhibitor, a common first targeted drug. Venetoclax, which blocks a survival protein in leukemia cells, can be given for a set period with an antibody partner.

Earlier trials and records showed durable responses after BTK inhibitor exposure, yet few patients in those analyses had truly progressed on the drug rather than stopping for side effects. The letter introduces an analysis from a large joint real-world study focused on exactly that progression group. Clinicians get evidence aimed at the hardest ordering question in this leukemia.
pmc-13571741:
Elloumi and a large team of colleagues build a web hub for gene work on a harsh lung cancer in this twenty twenty-six paper. This cancer lacks a spot in the big shared gene bank that most types enjoy. Its data sits split by ward, stage, and cure state in small sets.

Inside, the hub joins gene reads from two groups of sick folks on two shores. One group had slipped past first cures, while the next had had no cure yet. Tools in the hub sort types, map paths, grade risk, and flag drug marks. Two cell-top marks tied to new drugs get their own hunt tools in the hub. One add-on tool frames a test aid for one case at a time.
pmc-13572041:
Sun and six co-authors reviewed in twenty twenty-six tiny drug packs that carry more than one drug at once to fight tumors. Drugs that wake the body's defense can fail when a tumor hides or fights back. One drug alone is thus too weak for many cases.

Packing drugs with unlike acts into one tiny carrier keeps their mix fixed on the way to the tumor. The packs can boost the show of tumor marks, lift the block on defense, or kill cells in a way that draws defense in. The review weighs design, dose mix, and release pace. It also lists blocks to safe, large-scale use in clinics.
pmc-13572241:
Five researchers led by Zheng Zhang surveyed over two thousand teens in China on conflict between parents, their own anxiety, exercise habits, and gender. Marital conflict at home is known to track with teen anxiety, but the daily habits in between are less clear. The team tested whether exercise forms one such link.

More conflict at home went with more anxiety and less exercise, and less exercise went with more anxiety. Exercise carried only a small share of the link, about two percent. Gender changed how conflict related to exercise. The authors call activity a modest path worth note, not a fix, and suggest family support matters most.
pmc-13572441:
Anita Monteverdi and colleagues combined two modelling styles to map early dementia from brain scans. Mild cognitive impairment sits at the start of the dementia path, but its varied course makes a prognosis for one person hard. Their 2026 study used graph theory, which treats brain wiring as a network, plus virtual-brain models, on MRI data from people with mild impairment, healthy controls, and Alzheimer's patients.

Brain links were deeply reshaped, hitting default-mode, limbic, attention, and sensory networks hardest. Alzheimer marker status tracked with network structure, while a model value for repeat excitation tracked with lower overall thinking scores. Together, the two methods explained about 70 percent of variation in thinking-test scores. The authors suggest this per-person profile could one day guide personal prognosis and care in early dementia.
pmc-13574141:
Xingchi Chen, with 11 colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of a drug bath that makes immune cells better at killing leukaemia. The cells are gamma delta T cells, a type that can attack cancer without matching tissue types, which suits off-the-shelf use. A short bath in venetoclax, a drug that primes cell death pathways, had boosted a sister cell type before.

Pre-treated cells killed acute myeloid leukaemia cells harder and grew faster, with fewer signs of exhaustion. They held more cell powerhouses and burned fat for fuel, a profile tied to stamina. In mice, the treated cells held the disease down over time. The same bath also lifted engineered CAR versions of the cells. The authors propose adding the step to cell manufacturing for this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13574441:
Qin and colleagues study in twenty twenty-six how a body roundness score links to death risk in heart attack survivors. The score, built from height and waist size, gauges body shape better than weight alone. The team followed about two thousand survivors from a national United States health survey for a median of nine years.

The link took an L shape with a clear turning point. Below that point, higher roundness linked to markedly lower death risk. Above it, roundness showed no link to risk at all. The pattern held across subgroups. The authors suggest that very low roundness may flag frailty or poor nutrition in survivors. Keeping the score above the threshold may aid survival, they propose.
pmc-13574841:
Ji-Hyun Seo and Sang-Jin Shin report a 2026 study of keyhole repair for shoulders that are both loose and stiff. A dislocated shoulder can heal into frozen stiffness, a rare clash that stalls surgery plans. The team reviewed patients who had both faults and still went ahead with a scope repair of the torn rim.

Of 442 repair patients from 2019 to 2022, nineteen met the stiff-and-loose bar, and they were followed for near three years. Seventeen of the nineteen regained full motion. Forward reach, outward turn, and inward reach all rose sharply, while pain fell to near none. Two standard shoulder scores climbed into the top range. No patient needed a second operation or met a complication. The authors back scope repair for this mixed picture.
pmc-13575241:
Clara D C Claveau, Lauren Human, and Francesca Capozzi study eye contact during live conversation in a 2026 paper. Eye contact is widely believed to sharpen first impressions and shared attention, yet most past work used photos or videos on screens. Their study used real face-to-face meetings instead.

Participants met four people one at a time, rated each person's personality, then did a gaze-cueing task that measures joint attention. People mostly looked at their partners' eyes, more so when the eyes were easy to see. Eye contact barely predicted how accurate the personality ratings were. Early links did appear between gaze during the meetings and joint attention afterwards. The authors argue eyes carry real social weight in daily life, with effects that are subtle rather than sweeping.
pmc-13575441:
Lisa Merkel and four co-authors study RNA-based pest control in the pea aphid in two thousand twenty-six. Aphids damage crops by fast breeding, insecticide resistance, and spreading plant viruses. RNA interference could kill them in a species-specific way, but results in aphids are erratic.

Protective coatings, including chitosan and clay nanosheets, improved stability and switched on RNAi genes. Silencing of a target gene stayed inconsistent even so. The authors say better formulas and targets are needed before RNA sprays can be reliable.
pmc-13576141:
Chendi Qin leads a 2026 study building a quick sensor for a key tuberculosis drug, isoniazid. Knowing a patient's drug level helps set the dose and cut side effects, yet lab testing is slow. Their sensor uses a nanozyme, a nanomaterial that acts like an enzyme, whose colour reaction fades as drug levels rise.

The bench method measured levels from 1 to 30 micromolar units, the phone method from 3 to 30 in the same units. Spiked samples of tablets and rat serum recovered close to the true amounts. Among three learning models, a convolutional network read phone photos best and stayed accurate under room light. The authors pitch the platform for routine drug monitoring.
pmc-13578441:
Habib Amiri Savadroodbari and colleagues tune a cotton yarn process by running a trained neural network in reverse, in a 2026 study. Factories set twist levels by trial and error to hit a target yarn strength. Their network first learned how settings map to strength from plant data. Twist direction proved the biggest lever on strength, ahead of twist amounts. The best recipe used matching high twists in each single strand, a slightly lower combined twist, and a Z direction wrap. Strength rose by about a quarter over the starting yarn. A rival genetic search matched the cost score yet needed nearly four times the computing tries.
pmc-13578841:
Jennifer McNeely and a large trial team test a team based care plan for risky opioid use in primary care, in a 2026 trial across five United States sites. Patients who used opioids in risky ways, without severe addiction, often get no preventive help. Clinics were assigned by chance to the new plan or to boosted usual care, covering 202 patients in all.

Most patients carried heavy pain loads and below average health at the start. pmc-13579641:
Cheng-Ying Hsu and seven colleagues review ten years of records for patients who need regular blood transfusions for thalassemia, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Better care now lets these patients live near normal lifespans, yet hormone problems and weak bones stay common. The team studied forty-four adults to find what drives these issues and what helps bone density improve.

More than four in five patients had at least one hormone problem, and weak bones were the most common. Shorter gaps between transfusions linked to more diabetes and hormone loss in women. Over half the weak-bone patients gained bone strength with no bone drug at all. Not having diabetes was the clearest link to bone gains. Vitamin D and calcium helped in simple tests but faded in full models.
pmc-13579741:
David M Ndetei and colleagues survey anxiety symptoms among young people in the Nairobi region of Kenya, in a 2026 study. Close to two thousand participants aged fourteen to twenty five came from colleges and neighborhoods across city and fringe areas. Standard questionnaires covered anxiety, depression, trauma, and drug use, along with family wealth and background facts.

Worry and nervousness were the most common complaints. Women and city dwellers scored clearly higher than men and fringe residents, across every score type. Poorer youth scored higher as wealth fell. pmc-13581941:
Danilo Crispim Massuela and colleagues published a plant study in 2026. They grew medicinal cannabis indoors under controlled watering. Two high-CBD, low-THC types were compared. The question was whether mild drought saves water safely. Past work on drought and cannabinoids had disagreed. The team varied both drought strength and timing. pmc-13582641:
Katarzyna Smilowska and co-authors probe whether Parkinson's disease that starts young strains marriages more, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Four hundred seventy people from an online cohort with full records split by start age fifty. Divorce rates were compared across the split.

The young-start group showed a divorce share near eighteen percent, versus six in the late group. Only seven splits sat in the small young group, though. A fuller model found no firm predictors, with hints of lower odds for men and late starts. The authors label the find a lead, not a verdict. Bigger, longer cohorts must test it. Readers get a tender stat handled with care.
pmc-13582741:

Mentorship and early clinical exposure kept students going, while money troubles and thin social support held them back. pmc-13583341:

Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases differ upstream but all erode memory step by step. pmc-13584341:

Hepatitis B affects close to 300 million people, and liver cancer can arise even before the liver scars badly. Cancer rates rose with longer follow-up in both groups, so the gap matters more over time. The authors say the findings support widening treatment rules to reach non-cirrhotic patients sooner, while calling for studies on when to start.
pmc-13585941:

pmc-13586641:

Both shortages cut the greenness index and nudged a protective compound index up. The protective index rose far less under magnesium shortage than nitrogen shortage. Nitrogen shortage marked young upper leaves first in their time-lapse tracking. Magnesium shortage began at the tips of older, lower leaves instead. Leaf age, they stress, must guide any sensor-based feeding decision. Sugar buildup inside leaves differed sharply between the two shortages too.
pmc-13587741:

A deep eutectic solvent based on choline chloride and glycerol won the screening. With ultrasound help, the tuned recipe yielded about seventy-three percent more flavonoids than heated alcohol. Microscopy showed ultrasound tearing the plant matrix open, speeding release. The extract scored higher on three antioxidant tests and protected liver cells from peroxide injury in dishes. Fifteen flavonoids were identified, some new to this species.
pmc-13589941:

Turning STING on inside tumors can rouse immune attack, yet most such drugs spread through the body and miss the tumor. The particles stayed stable, released drug faster in acid, and entered cells well. In mice with skin cancer they reached tumors and woke STING there. Immune attack grew strong after shots into the tumor or into a vein. The team says a carrier free design also avoids harm from carrier stuff.
pmc-13590441:

pmc-13591641:

That framing guides the tests the team reports.
pmc-13594241:

The authors call for testing in lower-risk groups before wider use.
pmc-13594341:

Over sixty percent said they leaned on the tools, with a mean lean score of 21.91.

Hopes of good grades, school stress, and peer sway each went with more lean, while sharp thought went with less lean. The authors urge schools to cast chat AI as a mind prop, not a crutch: build sharp thought and set clear use rules so students learn with the tools, not through them.
pmc-13595141:

In metastases it varies more, shaped by the tumor's origin and the brain environment. That biology supports PSMA-targeted PET imaging with high lesion contrast. Clinical uses under study include grading gliomas and judging treatment response. Turning the same target into therapy faces delivery challenges. The review weighs imaging promise against therapeutic difficulty.
pmc-13595641:

Eight distinct ways of living the conflict emerged. Their names include Self-Sacrifice, Invisible Loneliness, and Threat to Self-Identity. Thirteen narrative scenarios sat alongside them. The scenarios link job strain, family demands, and illness to the decision to seek rehabilitation. Some patterns resembled depression or burnout symptoms, yet patients insisted they named something distinct: the daily experience of failing two roles at once. pmc-13598041:

Activation then matched the diagnosis: a chemical ionophore, the recombinant protein itself, or both together. Each single approach rescued fertilization about as well as the other. The dual treatment transformed results, though. Fertilization rose from about a quarter to nearly three quarters of eggs. Ongoing pregnancy rose from none to nearly two thirds of couples. pmc-13598141:

The change was not brief: brain patterns of those memories, measured days later under a normal hormone state, stayed altered. The authors read that lasting mark as proof that one recall under suppressed cortisol can rewrite how a memory is stored. They suggest the process deserves study as a possible route to easing painful memories in care.
pmc-13599741:

Nicotine both stimulates and relaxes the brain, and it can delay sleep, shorten it, and scramble its stages. Poor sleep in students is tied to worse grades and health. The team at a university in Tbilisi, Georgia, compared current smokers with peers who had not smoked for at least a year. The trackers recorded the sleep-wake cycle objectively over days, while surveys captured how students felt about their rest. The study design lets the authors set the machine record against self-report, a check on how well students judge their own smoking's cost to sleep.
pmc-13600941:

They resolved a large photosystem II supercomplex carrying four antenna trimers that cleaning usually strips away. Energy transfer figures from that shape closely matched readings in living tissue, backing its real-world fit. pmc-13601541:

Screening thresholds were crossed by 47 percent for autism and 20 percent for ADHD. Every measure correlated with the others. The authors read this as a possible mechanism: the arousal system may link variant connective tissue and neurodivergent traits.
pmc-13601641:

pmc-13602441:

pmc-13603541:

pmc-13608141:

pmc-13608641:

pmc-13609841:

pmc-13610041:

pmc-13612641:
Josefine Andreasson, Louise Bennet, Jonas Björk, and Dominik Dietler ask in a 2026 Swedish study whether catching SARS-CoV-2 can set off new type 2 diabetes in adults. pmc-13613141:

pmc-13613441:

pmc-13614141:

pmc-13614641:

pmc-13614941:

pmc-13616541:

pmc-13618041:

pmc-13618941:

pmc-13619041:

pmc-13619341:

pmc-13619441:

pmc-13620241:

pmc-13620441:

pmc-13620841:

pmc-13623141:

pmc-13623441:

pmc-13624141:

pmc-13624541:

pmc-13624841:

pmc-13625041:

pmc-13626641:

pmc-13627941:

pmc-13629241:

pmc-13630541:

pmc-13631141:

pmc-13632341:

pmc-13633441:

pmc-13635041:

pmc-13635241:

pmc-13638041:

pmc-13639641:

pmc-13642441:

pmc-13642941:

pmc-13645741:

pmc-13646141:

pmc-13648141:

pmc-13649741:
